0.title: The King Has Come
0.overview:
Matthew begins where the Old Testament ends — with promises. His opening genealogy is not a genealogy at all; it is a theology compressed into names. Abraham to David to the exile to Jesus: the whole arc of Israel’s story, told in three movements, arriving at the one name toward which every other name was pointing. Matthew’s first words are biblos geneseos — the book of origins, the book of genesis. A new creation has begun.

Matthew wrote for Jewish Christians, probably in Antioch, in the decades after the destruction of Jerusalem. His readers knew the Old Testament. They had grown up with the promises of a coming King from David’s line, a new Moses who would deliver God’s people, a suffering servant who would bear the sins of many, a son of man who would receive an everlasting dominion. Matthew’s argument, sustained across twenty-eight chapters, is that all of these promises find their yes in Jesus of Nazareth (2 Cor. 1:20). The fulfillment formula — to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet — appears again and again like a refrain, stitching the Old Testament to the New until you cannot see the seam.

The great theme of Matthew is the kingdom of heaven. Where Mark asks who this man is, and Luke traces the universal reach of grace, Matthew announces the arrival of a reign. Heaven’s rule has broken into earth’s disorder in the person of the King. He teaches with authority (not as the scribes). He heals with a word. He calms the sea. He feeds the multitude. He raises the dead. And then he goes to the cross not as a victim of circumstances but as the King who lays down his life to ransom many (20:28) — the supreme act of royal authority disguised as utter weakness.

Matthew’s Jesus is the new Moses, but greater. Moses gave the law from Sinai; Jesus gives the new law from the mountain (chapters 5–7). Moses delivered Israel through the Red Sea; Jesus passes through death and comes out the other side. Moses saw the promised land from a distance and died; Jesus enters it, conquers it, and invites all nations to follow him in. “I have not come to abolish the Law or the Prophets but to fulfil them” (5:17). In Jesus, the Old Testament does not end — it arrives.

The name given to him in chapter 1 is the key that unlocks the whole: Emmanuel — God with us. And the Gospel ends with the same promise, spoken now in resurrection glory: I am with you always, to the end of the age (28:20). Matthew is bracketed by the presence of God. What began in a manger in Bethlehem does not end at a tomb in Jerusalem. It ends with a commission that will reach every tongue and tribe and nation — because the one who sends is the one to whom all authority in heaven and on earth has been given.

Read Matthew as someone meeting the King for the first time. Let the authority of his teaching arrest you. Let the tenderness of his healing move you. Let the cross unmake your comfortable religion. And let the resurrection send you — into all the world, making disciples, baptising, teaching. The Gospel of Matthew is not a story that ends; it is a commission that begins.

1.title: Emmanuel — God With Us
1.text: <sup>1</sup>The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham. <sup>2</sup>Abraham was the father of Isaac, and Isaac the father of Jacob, and Jacob the father of Judah and his brothers, <sup>3</sup>and Judah the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar, and Perez the father of Hezron, and Hezron the father of Ram, <sup>4</sup>and Ram the father of Amminadab, and Amminadab the father of Nahshon, and Nahshon the father of Salmon, <sup>5</sup>and Salmon the father of Boaz by Rahab, and Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth, and Obed the father of Jesse, <sup>6</sup>and Jesse the father of David the king. And David was the father of Solomon by the wife of Uriah, <sup>7</sup>and Solomon the father of Rehoboam, and Rehoboam the father of Abijah, and Abijah the father of Asaph, <sup>8</sup>and Asaph the father of Jehoshaphat, and Jehoshaphat the father of Joram, and Joram the father of Uzziah, <sup>9</sup>and Uzziah the father of Jotham, and Jotham the father of Ahaz, and Ahaz the father of Hezekiah, <sup>10</sup>and Hezekiah the father of Manasseh, and Manasseh the father of Amos, and Amos the father of Josiah, <sup>11</sup>and Josiah the father of Jechoniah and his brothers, at the time of the deportation to Babylon. <sup>12</sup>And after the deportation to Babylon: Jechoniah was the father of Shealtiel, and Shealtiel the father of Zerubbabel, <sup>13</sup>and Zerubbabel the father of Abiud, and Abiud the father of Eliakim, and Eliakim the father of Azor, <sup>14</sup>and Azor the father of Zadok, and Zadok the father of Achim, and Achim the father of Eliud, <sup>15</sup>and Eliud the father of Eleazar, and Eleazar the father of Matthan, and Matthan the father of Jacob, <sup>16</sup>and Jacob the father of Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ. <sup>17</sup>So all the generations from Abraham to David were fourteen generations, and from David to the deportation to Babylon fourteen generations, and from the deportation to Babylon to the Christ fourteen generations. <sup>18</sup>Now the birth of Jesus Christ took place in this way. When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together she was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit. <sup>19</sup>And her husband Joseph, being a just man and unwilling to put her to shame, resolved to divorce her quietly. <sup>20</sup>But as he considered these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying, “Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary as your wife, for that which is conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. <sup>21</sup>She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.” <sup>22</sup>All this took place to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet: <sup>23</sup>“Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Immanuel” (which means, God with us). <sup>24</sup>When Joseph woke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord commanded him: he took his wife, <sup>25</sup>but knew her not until she had given birth to a son. And he called his name Jesus.
1.overview:
Matthew opens not with a manger scene but with a list of names — and the list is the point. Every name in the genealogy is a promise kept. From Abraham, through whom all nations would be blessed (Gen. 12:3), to David, whose throne would endure forever (2 Sam. 7:16), to the exile and back: the whole history of Israel’s faithfulness and failure, strung together like beads on a single cord that ends at the name Jesus. God’s covenant faithfulness spans every generation, including the dark ones. Especially the dark ones.

The genealogy contains surprises that Matthew intends. Four women appear — Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and “the wife of Uriah” — each associated with scandal, foreignness, or irregularity. Matthew is signalling from the first page that this King comes not for the respectable but for the broken, not only for Israel but for the nations. Grace does not run through clean lines; it runs through history as it actually happened, mess and all.

Then the birth narrative proper, and its two names. Jesus: he will save his people from their sins (v. 21). The name carries the whole gospel in four letters — Y’shua, the LORD saves. And Emmanuel: God with us (v. 23). The fulfilment of Isaiah’s sign (Isa. 7:14) is no longer a child born in the eighth century BC as a near-term reassurance to Ahaz; it is the Son of God entering human flesh, the Creator wearing the creature’s nature, the infinite becoming finite — without ceasing to be infinite. This is the doctrine of the incarnation, announced in a single breath in a single verse, and it changes everything.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — The Genealogy of Jesus Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Matthew opens not with a narrative but with a name-list, and in doing so announces that the gospel is rooted in real history. The genealogy traces Jesus' legal descent through Joseph from Abraham and David, grounding him in both the Abrahamic covenant (promise of blessing to all nations, Gen. 12:3) and the Davidic covenant (promise of an eternal throne, 2 Sam. 7:12–16). Three groups of fourteen generations form a theological argument, not an exhaustive record: Jesus is the divinely appointed culmination of redemptive history. Four women — Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, Bathsheba — appear unexpectedly, each associated with scandal or Gentile origin, signaling that this King's grace reaches beyond the expected. Three kings are missing at verse 8 — Ahaziah, Joash and Amaziah (1 Chron. 3:11-12) — which is not an error: the phrase rendered "father of" means ancestor of throughout Scripture, and a Jewish genealogy was a legal document establishing descent rather than a birth register. Matthew wants his three fourteens and prunes to get them; all three omitted kings descended from Athaliah, daughter of Ahab and Jezebel. Two names look wrong — "Asaph" for king Asa and "Amos" for king Amon — and these are simply the fuller Greek forms Matthew used, which modern translations keep rather than tidy. The third group has thirteen names, not fourteen; Jeconiah is probably counted twice, standing as the hinge of the exile. And Jeconiah carries a curse: God had sworn that none of his offspring would sit on David's throne (Jer. 22:30), yet the royal line runs straight through him — which the virgin birth resolves, since Jesus receives the legal throne-right through Joseph without receiving Jeconiah's blood. Luke's genealogy, tracing physical descent, comes down through David's other son Nathan and never touches him. The dark names are the point: Ahaz burned his own son as an offering (2 Kgs. 16:3) and is the very king to whom Isaiah 7:14 was spoken — the verse Matthew quotes at v. 23. Manasseh, the worst man in the list, repented in a Babylonian prison and was heard (2 Chr. 33:12-13). And the six names after Zerubbabel appear nowhere else in Scripture, spanning the five-hundred-year silence between the return from exile and the carpenter's shop. Finally, verse 16 breaks the pattern: thirty-nine times Matthew has written "A was the father of B" with an active verb, and at the fortieth link he goes passive and feminine — "of whom Jesus was born" — asserting the virgin birth in the grammar two verses before he explains it.
verseByVerse.theology: The genealogy establishes Jesus as Messiah (Christ = Anointed One), Son of David (royal heir), and Son of Abraham (heir of the covenant). The 14-14-14 structure — possibly reflecting the numerical value of David's name in Hebrew — underscores divine superintendence: God has been ordering history toward this moment across centuries of faithfulness, failure, exile, and return. Providence is not the absence of scandal; it is the sovereign use of all things toward the appointed end.
verseByVerse.examples: This genealogy reminds us that salvation is not a timeless philosophy but a historical event rooted in a long chain of real covenantal faithfulness. God's promises survived murder, adultery, exile, and foreign domination to arrive at their fulfillment. What he has promised, he performs — across generations, across continents, across every human failure. The God who kept his word to Abraham keeps his word to you.

verseByVerse.quote: The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham. Abraham was the father of Isaac, and Isaac the father of Jacob, and Jacob the father of Judah and his brothers,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Matthew opens by naming who Jesus is before he tells a single event: he is the Messiah, the heir of David’s throne, and the heir of the promise God made to Abraham. In him, every promise God made to Israel comes to its goal.

The setting. Matthew was one of the Twelve, a former tax collector (9:9). He writes chiefly for Jewish believers, probably in the AD 60s, to show that Jesus is the Messiah the Old Testament promised. He quotes or alludes to the Old Testament more than any other Gospel writer, often with the words “to fulfil what was spoken”. His Gospel stands first in the New Testament because it is the bridge from the Old.

The book of the genealogy. Literally “the book of the genesis”. The Greek Old Testament used the same phrase in Genesis 2:4 (the generations of the heavens and the earth) and Genesis 5:1 (the generations of Adam). A Jewish reader would hear the echo: something as great as creation is beginning again. It also introduces the genealogy that follows, and perhaps the whole story of Jesus.

Jesus Christ. “Jesus” is his personal name (see v. 21). “Christ” is not a surname but a title: the Greek form of “Messiah”, meaning “anointed one”. In Israel, kings, priests and sometimes prophets were anointed with oil to set them apart for their office (1 Samuel 16:13). The prophets promised a final Anointed One, the King God would send to save his people. Matthew’s first claim is that Jesus is that King.

The son of David. God promised David that one of his descendants would reign on his throne for ever (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Isaiah 9:6–7; 11:1). By the time of Jesus, “Son of David” was a title for the Messiah. Matthew uses it more than any other Gospel (9:27; 12:23; 21:9).

The son of Abraham. God promised Abraham that in his offspring all the nations of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3; 22:18). Jesus is the offspring through whom that blessing comes (Galatians 3:16).

The order. David comes first because Matthew’s main theme is Jesus as King. But Abraham is there to show that the King is for the nations too. Matthew’s Gospel begins with the son of Abraham and ends with the command to make disciples of all nations (28:19).

Abraham … Isaac … Jacob … Judah. The genealogy begins with Abraham, the father of Israel, not Adam as Luke’s does (Luke 3:38). Matthew is tracing Jesus’ place in Israel’s history. From Jacob’s twelve sons, Judah is named, because God promised that the sceptre would not depart from Judah (Genesis 49:10): the royal tribe.

Why a genealogy? Modern readers often skip it. But for Matthew’s first readers it was essential, for three reasons. First, it anchors Jesus in real history: these are real people whose records could be checked. The gospel is not a myth or a parable. Second, in Israel a genealogy was a legal document: it established a person’s right to land, to the priesthood, or to a throne. Matthew enters Jesus’ legal claim to David’s throne at once. Third, it shows that the story of Jesus did not begin in Bethlehem. It began two thousand years earlier, with God’s promise to Abraham, and every generation in between was carrying that promise forward.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus’ importance rests on his ancestry, as if he were great because his family was. The point is the reverse: his family matters because God promised that the Saviour would come through it. Nor does it mean that salvation is inherited by birth. John the Baptist will warn the Jews not to trust in having Abraham as their father (3:9).

In a sentence. Jesus is the Messiah, the promised King from David’s line and the promised blessing from Abraham’s line, the one in whom God keeps all his promises.

On a Tuesday. God kept a promise across two thousand years and forty-two generations. When his promises to you seem slow, remember that he does not forget what he has said.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of David” marks Jesus as the promised king; “son of Abraham” as the one through whom the nations would be blessed.

parallels.desc: Luke’s genealogy, traced back to Adam
the promise of a son of David on the throne forever
all the families of the earth blessed in Abraham

verseByVerse.quote: and Judah the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar, and Perez the father of Hezron, and Hezron the father of Ram, and Ram the father of Amminadab, and Amminadab the father of Nahshon, and Nahshon the father of Salmon,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The line runs through Judah to Perez, and Matthew does something unexpected: he names Tamar, the mother. With her name he reminds every reader of one of the most shameful stories in Genesis, and shows that God’s promise was carried through a family scarred by sin and injustice.

Women in a genealogy. Jewish genealogies normally listed fathers only. Matthew names five women: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, “the wife of Uriah”, and Mary. Each is unexpected. The first four were foreigners or connected with foreigners, and each had a story involving scandal or irregularity. Matthew includes them on purpose.

The story of Tamar (Genesis 38). Tamar married Judah’s eldest son Er, who was wicked, and the Lord put him to death. By the custom later written into the law (Deuteronomy 25:5–6), the next brother, Onan, was to give her a child to carry on his dead brother’s name. He refused, and he too died. Judah, afraid for his youngest son, Shelah, sent Tamar back to her father’s house, promising that she could marry Shelah when he grew up. He never kept the promise. She was left a childless widow, without standing or future.

What she did. Years later, Tamar disguised herself as a prostitute by the roadside. Judah, now a widower, hired her, leaving his seal, cord and staff as a pledge. She became pregnant. When Judah heard that his daughter-in-law was pregnant, he ordered her to be burned, until she produced his seal and staff. Judah confessed that she was more righteous than he, because he had not given her to his son Shelah (Genesis 38:26). She bore twins, Perez and Zerah.

Why Matthew names her. With one name, he reminds the reader of the whole story: a wronged woman, a hypocritical patriarch, a shameful act, and a line that continued anyway. Judah, the royal tribe’s father, behaved disgracefully; Tamar, probably a Canaanite, took a desperate and sinful way to what was hers by right. The Messiah’s family tree begins its royal line with this.

Perez and Zerah. Perez means “breach” or “breaking through”, because he burst out ahead of his twin at birth (Genesis 38:29). The royal line runs through him to David (Ruth 4:18–22).

Hezron … Nahshon … Salmon. The generations in Egypt and the wilderness. Nahshon was the leader of the tribe of Judah in the wilderness (Numbers 1:7; 7:12). Through the centuries of slavery in Egypt, when nothing seemed to happen, the promise was still being carried.

What it does not mean. Not that God approved of Judah’s or Tamar’s sin. Scripture records it honestly and does not excuse it. The point is that God’s grace works through sinful people without making their sin less sinful. Nor does it suggest that the line of the Messiah was pure in itself: it needed the Messiah as much as anyone.

In a sentence. God carried his promise through Judah and Tamar, a family marked by sin and injustice, showing from the first page that grace, not respectability, runs through the Messiah’s line.

On a Tuesday. If you think your family’s failures put you beyond God’s use, read Tamar’s name again. God did not tidy the Messiah’s family tree before he used it.
verseByVerse.note: Tamar is the first of four women Matthew includes before Mary, each with an irregular story.

parallels.desc: the line from Perez to Nahshon

verseByVerse.quote: and Salmon the father of Boaz by Rahab, and Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth, and Obed the father of Jesse, and Jesse the father of David the king. And David was the father of Solomon by the wife of Uriah,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Matthew names two more women, both foreigners, Rahab and Ruth, and then refers to David’s great sin by calling Bathsheba “the wife of Uriah”. The Messiah’s family needed grace, and God wrote outsiders and sinners into his story.

Salmon the father of Boaz by Rahab. Rahab was a Canaanite prostitute in Jericho, a city under God’s judgment. She hid the Israelite spies because she believed that the LORD was God in heaven above and on the earth beneath, and she and her family were spared when the city fell (Joshua 2; 6:22–25). She is honoured for her faith (Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25). The Old Testament does not record her marriage to Salmon; Matthew does. Some have questioned whether this is the same Rahab, since Salmon lived about two centuries before David, but genealogies often skip generations (see vv. 7–8), and Matthew clearly means the famous Rahab.

Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth. Ruth was a Moabite. The Moabites descended from Lot’s incest with his daughter (Genesis 19:36–37), and the law barred Moabites from the assembly of the LORD to the tenth generation (Deuteronomy 23:3). Yet Ruth, a widow, chose Israel’s God: your people shall be my people, and your God my God (Ruth 1:16). Boaz, a kinsman-redeemer, married her and redeemed her family’s land. Their son Obed was David’s grandfather.

Jesse the father of David the king. David is the only one in the genealogy called “king”. He is the hinge of the list (v. 17), the man to whom God promised an everlasting throne.

David was the father of Solomon by the wife of Uriah. Matthew does not write Bathsheba’s name. He names her husband instead: Uriah the Hittite, a foreigner and one of David’s most loyal soldiers. David committed adultery with Bathsheba while Uriah was at war, then arranged for Uriah to be killed in battle to hide the pregnancy (2 Samuel 11). By naming Uriah, Matthew makes it impossible to read the line without remembering the murder. Israel’s greatest king appears in one breath as king and as adulterer and murderer. Yet God gave David and Bathsheba Solomon, the heir, after David’s deep repentance (2 Samuel 12; Psalm 51).

The four women together. Not the honoured mothers of Israel, Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah, but Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and Bathsheba. All four were foreigners or married to a foreigner. All four had stories involving sexual scandal, real or suspected. Matthew’s reasons, held together: (1) to show that the Messiah came for Gentiles as well as Jews; (2) to show that God works through sinners and outsiders by grace; and (3) to prepare for Mary, whose pregnancy also looked scandalous, though she was innocent (vv. 18–19).

What it does not mean. Not that sin does not matter. Matthew’s refusal to name Bathsheba is there precisely so we remember a murdered man. Grace that pretends nothing happened is not grace. Nor is it a criticism of the women: Rahab and Ruth are models of faith, and Bathsheba was more sinned against than sinning. And it does not mean that a good family gives anyone standing before God, any more than a bad one removes it. What runs down this list is not merit, but God’s promise.

In a sentence. God brought the Messiah through foreigners and through a royal scandal, showing that his family, like ours, is made of people who need grace.

On a Tuesday. Is there a part of your family’s story nobody speaks about, the affair, the prison sentence, the parent who left? The Messiah’s family tree reads like that. God can write your story into his.
verseByVerse.note: Rahab was a Canaanite of Jericho and Ruth a Moabite — Gentiles in the royal line. “The wife of Uriah” is Bathsheba.

verseByVerse.quote: and Solomon the father of Rehoboam, and Rehoboam the father of Abijah, and Abijah the father of Asaph, and Asaph the father of Jehoshaphat, and Jehoshaphat the father of Joram, and Joram the father of Uzziah,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The line passes through the kings of Judah, good and bad alike, listed with no comment. God’s promise did not depend on the quality of the men who carried it, but on the faithfulness of the God who made it.

The kings of Judah. After Solomon the kingdom split in two (1 Kings 12). The northern kingdom, Israel, had no kings from David’s line. The southern kingdom, Judah, was ruled by David’s descendants for nearly four centuries. These verses list them.

Good and bad together. Some were faithful: Asa removed idols (1 Kings 15:11–14); Jehoshaphat sought the LORD (2 Chronicles 17:3–6). Some were wicked: Rehoboam’s foolishness split the kingdom; Joram murdered all his brothers (2 Chronicles 21:4) and married into the idolatrous house of Ahab. Uzziah was a strong king who grew proud and was struck with leprosy for burning incense in the temple, a task only priests could do (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). Matthew writes them all in the same rhythm, with no verdict. The chain does not thicken at the good names or wear thin at the bad ones.

Three kings missing. Matthew writes that Joram was the father of Uzziah, but 1 Chronicles 3:11–12 lists Ahaziah, Joash and Amaziah between them. “Father of” in Hebrew and Greek can mean “ancestor of”, just as Jesus is called “son of David” a thousand years later. Genealogies were not birth registers; they traced descent, and they were often shortened to make a pattern easier to remember. Matthew omits names to arrive at his three groups of fourteen (v. 17). No first-century reader would have counted this an error.

Why these three? Perhaps because they were descendants of Athaliah, daughter of Ahab and Jezebel, who brought Baal worship into David’s line and murdered the royal family (2 Kings 11:1). God had pronounced judgment on Ahab’s house (1 Kings 21:21–22). Matthew may be letting that judgment show. We cannot be sure, and he does not say. Omitting names from a list does not remove the men from history; the line itself was unbroken.

Textual note: Asaph. The ESV reads “Asaph”, following the oldest manuscripts; the king was Asa. Later manuscripts and many translations read “Asa”. Verdict: “Asaph” is probably original, either an alternative spelling of the king’s name or a deliberate echo of Asaph the psalmist. Either way, the king meant is Asa.

What it does not mean. Not that God does not care whether his servants are faithful. The books of Kings and Chronicles judge each king carefully, and faithfulness brought blessing while sin brought judgment. But God’s promise to David did not fail because of his sons’ sins (2 Samuel 7:14–16; Psalm 89:30–37).

In a sentence. God carried his promise through good kings and wicked ones, because it rested on his faithfulness, not theirs.

On a Tuesday. Do you think God’s purposes depend more on your faithfulness than on his? He keeps his promises even through weak and failing people. That should make you humble and grateful, not careless.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read Asa for Asaph. Matthew’s list skips several kings between Joram and Uzziah; “father of” can mean ancestor.

verseByVerse.quote: and Uzziah the father of Jotham, and Jotham the father of Ahaz, and Ahaz the father of Hezekiah, and Hezekiah the father of Manasseh, and Manasseh the father of Amos, and Amos the father of Josiah,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The list now includes both the best kings of Judah, Hezekiah and Josiah, and the very worst, Ahaz and Manasseh. All four are links in one chain. Even the worst of them was not beyond God’s mercy.

Ahaz. One of the worst kings in Judah’s history. He sacrificed his own son in the fire, following the practices of the pagan nations (2 Kings 16:3), copied a pagan altar for the temple, and finally shut the doors of the LORD’s house (2 Chronicles 28:24). Yet Ahaz is the king to whom Isaiah spoke the promise Matthew will quote at the end of this chapter: the virgin shall conceive and bear a son (Isaiah 7:14). Ahaz was terrified of an invasion, refused to ask God for a sign, and was given one anyway. The greatest promise of the Old Testament was spoken to one of its worst kings, who did not want it.

Hezekiah. A great reforming king who trusted the LORD, destroyed idols, and saw Jerusalem miraculously delivered from the Assyrian army (2 Kings 18–19).

Manasseh. Hezekiah’s son, and the worst of all. He reigned fifty-five years, the longest reign in Judah, and filled them with idolatry, sorcery, child sacrifice and so much innocent blood that God declared Jerusalem would be wiped as one wipes a dish (2 Kings 21:1–16). His sins were the reason God gave for the exile (2 Kings 24:3–4).

Manasseh’s repentance. But 2 Chronicles 33:10–17 adds what Kings does not record. The Assyrians took Manasseh captive with hooks and chains to Babylon. There, in distress, he humbled himself greatly before God and prayed, and God heard him and brought him back to Jerusalem. Manasseh then removed the idols he had set up. The worst man in the genealogy is the strongest proof in Scripture that no one is beyond God’s mercy.

Amos … Josiah. Manasseh’s son Amon (the ESV reads “Amos”, following the oldest manuscripts, as with Asaph in v. 7) was wicked and was murdered after two years. His son Josiah became king at eight and led the greatest reformation in Judah’s history, after the Book of the Law was rediscovered in the temple (2 Kings 22–23).

The lesson of the four. Ahaz the faithless, Hezekiah the faithful, Manasseh the monstrous and repentant, Josiah the reformer. The line of promise ran through all of them. A godly father did not guarantee a godly son, and a wicked father did not prevent one.

What it does not mean. Not that Manasseh’s sins had no consequences: the damage he did led to the exile, even after his repentance (2 Kings 23:26). God forgives, but sin often leaves wounds in history. Nor does it mean that repentance can be safely put off until the end of a wicked life. Manasseh wasted decades, and countless people suffered for his sins.

In a sentence. The promised line ran through the best and worst kings of Judah, and even the worst of them found mercy when he repented.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone you have privately given up on, for whom you have stopped praying? Remember Manasseh, and pray again.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read Amon for Amos. Hezekiah and Josiah were reforming kings; Manasseh was the worst.

verseByVerse.quote: and Josiah the father of Jechoniah and his brothers, at the time of the deportation to Babylon. And after the deportation to Babylon: Jechoniah was the father of Shealtiel, and Shealtiel the father of Zerubbabel,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The line of kings ends in disaster, the exile to Babylon, and passes through a king whom God had cursed. Yet the line continues through the exile and out the other side. God’s promise survived both the worst catastrophe and a divine curse.

Josiah the father of Jechoniah. Josiah was in fact Jechoniah’s grandfather; Jehoiakim, Josiah’s son, stands between them (1 Chronicles 3:15–16). As in verse 8, “father of” means “ancestor of”. Jechoniah (also called Jehoiachin or Coniah) reigned only three months before Nebuchadnezzar took him to Babylon in 597 BC (2 Kings 24:8–15).

And his brothers. Perhaps Jechoniah’s uncles and relatives, including Zedekiah, the last king, who saw Jerusalem destroyed in 586 BC.

The deportation to Babylon. The great catastrophe of Israel’s history. The temple was burned, Jerusalem destroyed, the king blinded and taken captive, and the people carried away (2 Kings 25). To those who lived through it, it seemed that God’s promises to David had failed: no throne, no temple, no land. Matthew builds his genealogy around it (v. 17). The exile is a turning point, not the end.

The curse on Jechoniah. God had said through Jeremiah that this man was to be written down as childless, and that none of his offspring would succeed in sitting on the throne of David (Jeremiah 22:24–30). Yet Matthew runs the royal line straight through him. How can the Messiah sit on David’s throne if he descends from Jechoniah?

The answer. Jesus is Joseph’s son legally, not biologically (v. 16). The legal right to David’s throne passed to him through Joseph, the heir of Solomon and Jechoniah. But Jesus was not physically descended from Jechoniah, because he was born of Mary by the Holy Spirit, not fathered by Joseph. Luke’s genealogy, which most likely traces Jesus’ physical descent, runs through David’s son Nathan, and never touches Jechoniah (Luke 3:31). So the curse stands, and the promise stands. The virgin birth is the way God kept both.

After the deportation … Shealtiel … Zerubbabel. In exile, the line continued. Jechoniah was released from prison in Babylon and treated kindly (2 Kings 25:27–30). His grandson Zerubbabel led the first group of exiles home in 538 BC and governed Judah while the temple was rebuilt (Ezra 3:8; Haggai 1:1). God called Zerubbabel his signet ring (Haggai 2:23), the very image he had used when he rejected Jechoniah (Jeremiah 22:24). The curse was not the last word.

What it does not mean. Not that God changed his mind or broke his word. The curse on Jechoniah’s physical descendants was kept: none of them sat on David’s throne. The promise to David was kept too, through a Son who received the legal right but not the curse.

In a sentence. God carried his promise through the exile and through a cursed king, and the virgin birth is how he kept both his curse and his promise.

On a Tuesday. Is there a loss you have treated as the end of God’s promises: a death, a divorce, a failure? The exile was not the end for Israel, and your loss is not the end of God’s purposes for you.
verseByVerse.note: The deportation to Babylon came in 597 and 586 BC. Zerubbabel later led the return and the rebuilding of the temple.

parallels.desc: Zerubbabel as the LORD’s signet ring

verseByVerse.quote: and Zerubbabel the father of Abiud, and Abiud the father of Eliakim, and Eliakim the father of Azor, and Azor the father of Zadok, and Zadok the father of Achim, and Achim the father of Eliud,
verseByVerse.commentary:
After Zerubbabel come names that appear nowhere else in Scripture. For five silent centuries, God carried his promise through ordinary, unknown people, and their unrecorded lives were essential to his plan.

Unknown names. Abiud, Eliakim, Azor, Zadok, Achim, Eliud: we know nothing about them. Matthew probably took the names from family or public records. No king, no prophet, no recorded word. They lived under Persian, Greek and Roman rule in a small, occupied country.

The silent centuries. Between Zerubbabel (about 520 BC) and Jesus, about five centuries passed. Persia gave way to Alexander the Great; Alexander’s generals divided his empire; the Greek king Antiochus IV desecrated the temple in 167 BC; the Maccabees led a revolt and briefly won independence; and Rome took control in 63 BC. During all this time, after Malachi, there was no prophet in Israel. Jews called it the time when prophecy had ceased.

Not empty. But the silence was not emptiness. The promise was moving through men whose names survive only because Matthew wrote them down. They worked, married, raised children, buried their parents and died, without any idea where the line they carried would end.

What it does not mean. Not that God was absent or inactive during these centuries. He was preparing the world for Christ: the spread of the Greek language, the Roman roads and peace, the scattering of Jews and synagogues through the empire, and the translation of the Scriptures into Greek. Paul calls the moment of Christ’s coming the fullness of time (Galatians 4:4).

In a sentence. Through five silent centuries, God quietly carried his promise in ordinary lives that no one remembered but him.

On a Tuesday. Are you measuring the worth of your faithfulness by whether anyone will remember it? Not one of these men did anything the Bible recorded, and every one was essential.
verseByVerse.note: These men after Zerubbabel are mentioned nowhere else in Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: and Eliud the father of Eleazar, and Eleazar the father of Matthan, and Matthan the father of Jacob, and Jacob the father of Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the last link, Matthew changes the pattern. He does not say that Joseph was the father of Jesus, but that Joseph was the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born. Jesus is Joseph’s legal son and heir, but not his natural son. He was born of Mary alone, and he is the Christ.

Eleazar … Matthan … Jacob … Joseph. Joseph’s father is Jacob. Luke calls Joseph the son of Heli (Luke 3:23); see verse 17 for how the two genealogies relate.

The broken pattern. Thirty-nine times Matthew has written “A was the father of B”, with an active verb, a man fathering a son, like a drumbeat. At the end, the beat breaks. Matthew writes not “Joseph the father of Jesus” but “Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born”. In Greek, “of whom” is feminine singular: it refers to Mary alone. And the verb is passive: Jesus “was born”, not “was fathered”. Matthew has not yet said the word “virgin”, but he has already said it in his grammar.

The husband of Mary. Joseph and Mary were betrothed, which counted legally as married (v. 18), and Joseph took her as his wife (v. 24). As Mary’s husband who named and received Jesus, Joseph became his legal father, and passed on to him the legal rights of David’s line.

Legal descent. In Israel, adoption gave full legal rights. A son by adoption was a true heir. So Jesus is truly the son of David through Joseph, though not by blood. (He may also be David’s descendant by blood through Mary, if Luke traces her line; see v. 17.)

Who is called Christ. “Christ” means the Messiah, the Anointed One (see v. 1). The whole genealogy has been travelling toward this title. Every promise to Abraham and David arrives at this one man.

What it does not mean. Not that Joseph was unimportant. God chose him to be Jesus’ legal father, to protect and raise him, and to give him his place in David’s line. Nor that Mary is the source of Jesus’ divinity: he was conceived by the Holy Spirit (v. 20), and she was the human mother through whom the eternal Son took our nature.

In a sentence. Jesus is Joseph’s legal son and David’s heir, yet born of Mary alone: the promised Christ.

On a Tuesday. Is Jesus to you simply a figure of history, or the Christ, the King God promised? The genealogy was written to bring you to that question.
verseByVerse.note: Matthew breaks the pattern at the end: Jesus was born of Mary, not fathered by Joseph. “Christ” means anointed one, the Messiah.

parallels.desc: “being the son (as was supposed) of Joseph”

verseByVerse.quote: So all the generations from Abraham to David were fourteen generations, and from David to the deportation to Babylon fourteen generations, and from the deportation to Babylon to the Christ fourteen generations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Matthew sums up the genealogy in three groups of fourteen generations: Abraham to David, David to the exile, the exile to the Christ. History is not random. God was steering it, through promise, through apparent ruin, and through long waiting, to Jesus.

Three groups of fourteen. Matthew shows the shape of his list. The first group rises from Abraham to David: the promise given and the kingdom established. The second falls from David to the exile: the kingdom’s decline and destruction. The third waits from the exile to Christ: the long, silent preparation. Promise, ruin, fulfilment.

Why fourteen? Probably because of David. In Hebrew, letters also served as numbers, and the consonants of David’s name (D-V-D) add up to fourteen (4 + 6 + 4). Three times fourteen says “David, David, David”: this is the Son of David. Others point out that three fourteens make six sevens, so Jesus begins the seventh seven, the number of completion. Either way, Matthew is showing design.

Counting the names. If you count the third group you find thirteen names, not fourteen. The likely explanation is that Jechoniah is counted twice, at the end of the second group and the start of the third, since the exile divides his life. Or Matthew is counting generations rather than names. Matthew’s numbers are a teaching structure, not a census, and his first readers would understand that.

Matthew and Luke. Luke’s genealogy (Luke 3:23–38) differs from Matthew’s. From David, Matthew traces the line through Solomon, Luke through Nathan; Matthew names Joseph’s father as Jacob, Luke as Heli. Christians have offered three main explanations:

1. Mary’s line. Luke gives Mary’s genealogy, with Joseph as Heli’s son-in-law; Matthew gives Joseph’s.

2. Levirate marriage. One of Joseph’s fathers was legal and the other natural, through a levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5–6), as the early church historian Julius Africanus suggested.

3. Royal and physical lines. Matthew traces the legal royal succession, the line of throne-heirs through Solomon; Luke traces Joseph’s physical descent through Nathan.

Verdict: we cannot be certain, but the third best fits Matthew’s purpose: he traces the legal, royal line by which David’s throne passed to Joseph’s son (see vv. 11–12). Each explanation is held by careful readers, and none requires an error in Scripture. Both genealogies agree on what matters: Jesus is the son of David and the son of Abraham.

What it does not mean. Not that we should look for secret codes in the numbers of Scripture. Matthew tells us his pattern openly; it is a memory aid and a theological statement, not a puzzle.

In a sentence. God guided history through promise, ruin and waiting, all the way to Christ.

On a Tuesday. Can you trust that God is steering the confusing chapters of your life toward his purpose? He steered forty-two generations to Bethlehem.
verseByVerse.note: Three sets of fourteen give the story its shape: rise to David, fall to exile, and the wait for the Christ. The counts are arranged, not exhaustive.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–25 — The Birth of Jesus Christ: God with Us
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Matthew tells the nativity through Joseph's eyes. He discovers Mary's pregnancy, intends to divorce her quietly (sparing her public disgrace), and is then visited by an angel who reveals the child's supernatural origin. Joseph's response is exemplary and immediate: he did as the angel commanded. Two names define the child — Jesus (he will save his people from their sins) and Immanuel (God with us). The birth fulfills Isaiah 7:14, establishing the pattern of scriptural fulfillment that runs through Matthew's entire Gospel. Two things more. Verse 22 introduces the formula that will ring out ten times in this Gospel — "all this took place to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet" — which is not proof-texting but the claim that these events complete Israel's whole story; and the verse-by-verse handles the controversy over Isaiah's word for "virgin" (Hebrew almah), including the fact that Jewish scholars translating their own Scriptures into Greek nearly two centuries before Christ rendered it parthenos, the ordinary Greek word for a virgin. The "virgin" reading was not a Christian invention. Verse 25's "knew her not until she had given birth" is Scripture's modest way of speaking about a husband and wife (as at Gen. 4:1), and the little word "until" fixes attention on the one thing at issue — that Jesus was conceived with no human father — rather than hinting at anything else. Note also that this is the first of four times God speaks to Joseph in a dream (1:20; 2:13; 2:19; 2:22), and that he obeys immediately every time; and that Joseph never speaks a single recorded word anywhere in the New Testament.
verseByVerse.theology: The virgin birth is not incidental decoration but theological necessity. If Jesus is to be the sinless substitute for sinners, he cannot enter the world through ordinary generation under fallen Adam. The Holy Spirit's agency in the conception ensures both his full humanity (born of woman, Gal. 4:4) and his freedom from the entail of the first Adam's sin. The two names capture the whole gospel: he is God who has come to be with us (Immanuel), and in being with us he saves us from our sins (Jesus). Doctrine and salvation are inseparable from the first moment.
verseByVerse.examples: Joseph's obedience is one of Scripture's quietly great acts of faith. He received no applause, no public vindication, no explanation beyond the angel's word. He obeyed at enormous personal cost — accepting social suspicion, raising a child not his own, surrendering his right to defend his reputation. In an age that demands visible proof and public validation before any commitment, Joseph's silent, costly fidelity is a rebuke and a model. God still calls his people to act on his word before the full picture is visible.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the birth of Jesus Christ took place in this way. When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together she was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit. And her husband Joseph, being a just man and unwilling to put her to shame, resolved to divorce her quietly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Matthew now tells how Jesus was born. Mary, legally pledged to Joseph, was found to be pregnant before they came together, by the Holy Spirit. Joseph, a righteous man who did not want to shame her, decided to end the betrothal quietly. His response shows that true righteousness joins justice with mercy.

The birth of Jesus Christ took place in this way. “Birth” is again genesis (see v. 1). Matthew tells the story from Joseph’s side; Luke tells it from Mary’s (Luke 1:26–38).

Betrothed. Betrothal was not like a modern engagement. It was a legally binding marriage contract, usually made when the girl was in her early teens. The couple were called husband and wife, but did not yet live together; that came about a year later, when the husband took the bride to his home. Only a formal divorce could end a betrothal, and unfaithfulness during it was treated as adultery, punishable under the law by death (Deuteronomy 22:23–24), though in Jesus’ time this was rarely carried out.

Before they came together. Before they lived together and had sexual relations.

She was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit. Matthew tells the reader immediately where the child came from, so that we are never in doubt. But Joseph did not yet know. What he saw was a pregnant bride, and he knew the child was not his.

Her husband Joseph, being a just man. “Just” (dikaios) means righteous: a man who kept God’s law. That righteousness pulled him two ways. The law required him not to treat an apparently adulterous marriage as if nothing had happened. But he also did not want to humiliate her.

Unwilling to put her to shame. He could have made a public accusation before the village court, exposing her to disgrace and possibly to punishment.

Resolved to divorce her quietly. Instead, he decided on a private divorce, before two or three witnesses, with as little shame for her as possible. He would take the ambiguity onto himself.

What Joseph shows. True righteousness is not harsh legalism. Joseph did not pretend that nothing had happened, but he chose the least harmful honest course. He asked not only “What am I entitled to do?” but “What does mercy allow me to do with what I am entitled to?” And God met him on the road he had already begun to walk (v. 20).

Mary’s position. Mary said nothing in these verses. She had obeyed God, and now her reputation was ruined, and she could not explain what had happened in a way anyone would believe. She shows what it is to do right and pay for it in the eyes of others.

What it does not mean. Not that mercy means ignoring sin, or that wrongs must never be named or acted on. Joseph still intended to divorce her. Nor does it mean that Mary was guilty: Matthew has already told us the truth. Joseph acted rightly on what he knew.

In a sentence. When Mary was found pregnant, Joseph, a righteous man, chose mercy over public shame, showing that true righteousness joins justice with kindness.

On a Tuesday. When you have been wronged, or think you have, are you looking for the remedy that heals, or the one that humiliates?
verseByVerse.note: Betrothal was a binding agreement, stronger than modern engagement; ending it required a divorce. The couple did not yet live together.

parallels.desc: the law on a betrothed woman

verseByVerse.quote: But as he considered these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying, "Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary as your wife, for that which is conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sent an angel to Joseph in a dream to explain: the child was conceived by the Holy Spirit. Joseph must take Mary as his wife and name the child Jesus, because he will save his people from their sins. Here, at the start, Matthew tells us who Jesus is and why he came.

As he considered these things. Joseph had made his decision, but he had not yet acted. God intervened while he was thinking it over.

An angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream. The first of several dreams in which God guides Joseph (2:13, 19, 22). Joseph’s namesake in Genesis, Joseph son of Jacob, was also a man of dreams, who protected his family by going to Egypt.

Joseph, son of David. The angel calls him by his royal ancestry. This reminds Joseph, and us, why his role matters: through him, the child will receive his legal place in David’s line (v. 16).

Do not fear to take Mary as your wife. Joseph’s fear was reasonable: of disgrace, of marrying an apparently unfaithful woman, of breaking God’s law. The angel does not argue with the fear; he answers it with the truth.

That which is conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. No human father was involved. This is the virgin conception: the Holy Spirit created the child’s human life in Mary’s womb. The Spirit who hovered over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2) is beginning a new creation. Luke records the angel’s words to Mary: the Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the child will be called holy (Luke 1:35).

Why the virgin conception matters. Every child of Adam inherits a sinful nature (Psalm 51:5; Romans 5:12). Jesus was truly human, Mary’s real son, but his conception was a fresh act of God, so that he was without sin. Only a sinless Saviour could save sinners: a Redeemer who was himself under Adam’s guilt would need redeeming. And the virgin conception shows that salvation comes from God’s side, not from human achievement.

She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. “Jesus” is the Greek form of the Hebrew Joshua (Yehoshua), meaning “the LORD saves”. It was a common name. Joshua led Israel into the promised land; this Jesus will lead his people into a greater inheritance. By naming the child, Joseph would adopt him legally as his son.

For he will save his people from their sins. The explanation of the name. Not “may save”, but “will save”: he will certainly accomplish it. And it says what he saves from. First-century Jews longed to be saved from Rome. The angel says the real enemy is sin. Psalm 130:8 had said that the LORD would redeem Israel from all his iniquities; now that work of the LORD is given to Jesus. At the Last Supper Jesus explains how: his blood of the covenant, poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins (26:28).

What “saved from their sins” includes. From sin’s penalty: no condemnation for those in Christ (Romans 8:1). From sin’s power: sin will not rule over them (Romans 6:14). And finally from sin’s presence: in the new creation, nothing unclean will enter (Revelation 21:27).

His people. Those who belong to him. At first this sounds like Israel, but by the end of Matthew it includes believers from all nations (28:19). Reformed theology sees here the definite purpose of Christ’s saving work: he came not merely to make salvation possible for everyone, but actually to save his people. This is called definite or particular atonement (John 10:11, 15; Ephesians 5:25). It does not limit the offer of the gospel, which goes to all (28:19), but it assures believers that Christ’s death actually achieved their salvation.

What it does not mean. Not that Mary was sinless or had no need of a Saviour. She called God her Saviour (Luke 1:47). Roman Catholic teaching holds that Mary was conceived without original sin (the Immaculate Conception, defined in 1854), but Scripture never says so, and it would only move the problem back a generation. Jesus’ sinlessness comes from the Spirit’s work in his conception, not from Mary.

Where Christians differ: the virgin birth. Since the nineteenth century, liberal theologians have denied the virgin birth as a legend added to make Jesus seem divine. But it is plainly taught by both Matthew and Luke, independently, and confessed in the earliest creeds (the Apostles’ Creed: conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the virgin Mary). Verdict: the virgin birth is historical fact and essential Christian doctrine.

In a sentence. Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit, without sin, and named Jesus because he came to save his people from their sins.

On a Tuesday. Have you come to Jesus to be saved from your sins, or only from your troubles? He came for the first, and that is the deeper need.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that Jesus is the Greek form of Joshua, meaning “the LORD saves.”

parallels.desc: the name given to Mary too
he will redeem Israel from all its iniquities

verseByVerse.quote: All this took place to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet: "Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Immanuel" (which means, God with us).
verseByVerse.commentary:
Matthew explains that all this fulfilled the prophecy of Isaiah: a virgin would conceive and bear a son called Immanuel, which means “God with us”. In Jesus, God himself has come to be with his people, truly God and truly man.

All this took place to fulfil. The first of Matthew’s ten or more “fulfilment” formulas (2:15, 17, 23; 4:14; 8:17; 12:17; 13:35; 21:4; 27:9). “Fulfil” means more than a prediction coming true. It means filling up, completing: the events of Jesus’ life bring Israel’s whole story and Scriptures to their intended goal.

What the Lord had spoken by the prophet. God is the speaker; Isaiah is his mouthpiece. Matthew holds a high view of Scripture: the words of the prophets are the words of God.

Isaiah’s original setting. Around 734 BC, Syria and the northern kingdom of Israel attacked Jerusalem. King Ahaz was terrified (Isaiah 7:2). Isaiah told him to trust God and offered him a sign. Ahaz refused, preferring to seek help from Assyria. So God gave a sign anyway: a young woman would conceive and bear a son, called Immanuel, and before the child knew right from wrong, the two kings Ahaz feared would be gone (Isaiah 7:14–16). In its own day the sign said: God has not abandoned his people.

Fulfilled in Jesus. But the prophecy reached beyond Ahaz. Isaiah goes on to speak of a child born, a son given, whose name is Wonderful Counsellor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace, who would sit on David’s throne for ever (Isaiah 9:6–7). The sign in Ahaz’s day pointed forward to its full meaning: the day when God would be with his people not by sending help, but by coming himself.

The virgin. Isaiah’s Hebrew word, almah, means a young woman of marriageable age, and in the Old Testament it never refers to a married woman. About two hundred years before Christ, Jewish scholars translating Isaiah into Greek (the Septuagint) rendered it parthenos, the ordinary Greek word for virgin. The reading “virgin” was not a Christian invention; it was already in the Jews’ own Greek Bible.

Immanuel. Hebrew for “God with us”. No one in the Gospels calls Jesus “Immanuel” as a name. He is named Jesus. The prophecy is fulfilled not in what people called him, but in who he is: God present with his people in a human life. Matthew frames his whole Gospel with this truth: it begins with “God with us” (1:23) and ends with Jesus’ promise, I am with you always, to the end of the age (28:20).

Truly God and truly man. The virgin conception means that Jesus is fully human, born of a woman, and fully God, the eternal Son come in the flesh (John 1:14). The Council of Chalcedon (AD 451) confessed this: one Person in two natures, without confusion, change, division or separation. He is not God disguised as a man, nor a man who became divine, but the eternal Son who took a true human nature. Both are necessary: only God can save us, and only a man can stand in our place.

What it does not mean. Not that the virgin birth is borrowed from pagan myths. Pagan stories told of gods having sexual relations with women. That is entirely different from a conception with no sexual union at all. And Matthew’s first readers were Jews, the people least likely to borrow pagan myths. Matthew grounds the virgin birth in Isaiah, not in pagan legend.

In a sentence. In Jesus, born of a virgin as Isaiah promised, God himself has come to be with his people.

On a Tuesday. Do you live as though God is truly with you today? In Christ, he is, in the office, the hospital ward, and the empty house.

For worship. Worship the God who did not stay distant but came to be with us.

verseByVerse.quote: When Joseph woke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord commanded him: he took his wife, but knew her not until she had given birth to a son. And he called his name Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph obeyed at once. He took Mary as his wife, had no sexual relations with her until Jesus was born, and named the child Jesus, receiving him as his own son into David’s line.

When Joseph woke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord commanded him. Immediate, complete obedience. No delay, no negotiation. Each of the four times God speaks to Joseph, he responds the same way, at once (2:14, 21–22). Joseph never speaks a recorded word in the Gospels; his faith speaks through his obedience.

He took his wife. He brought Mary into his home, completing the marriage. This meant accepting the village’s gossip about the timing of the birth for the rest of his life. It cost him his reputation.

But knew her not. “Knew” is the Bible’s modest word for sexual union (Genesis 4:1). Joseph and Mary had no sexual relations before Jesus’ birth. This guards the truth of the virgin birth: no one could claim that Joseph was the father.

Until she had given birth to a son. “Until” states only what did not happen before the birth. But the natural meaning is that afterwards they lived as a normal married couple.

And he called his name Jesus. By naming the child, Joseph formally acknowledged him as his son. This gave Jesus his legal standing as a son of Joseph, and so as a son of David (v. 16).

What it does not mean. Not that sexual union in marriage is unclean or unspiritual. Joseph abstained to protect a unique sign, not because marriage is less holy. Scripture celebrates sexual union within marriage (Genesis 2:24; 1 Corinthians 7:3–5).

Where Christians differ: did Mary have other children? Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches teach that Mary remained a virgin all her life (her perpetual virginity), and explain Jesus’ brothers and sisters as cousins or as Joseph’s children from an earlier marriage. Some Reformers, including Luther, also held this view. But the natural reading of Matthew’s “until”, together with his naming of Jesus’ brothers James, Joseph, Simon and Judas, and his sisters (13:55–56; 12:46), is that Mary and Joseph had other children after Jesus. Verdict: Mary was a faithful wife who bore other children after her firstborn. This takes nothing away from her honour.

In a sentence. Joseph obeyed immediately, protected the sign of the virgin birth, and gave Jesus his legal place in David’s line.

On a Tuesday. When God’s word is clear, how long do you take to obey it? Joseph’s quiet, costly obedience changed history, and no one recorded a single word he said.
verseByVerse.note: “Knew her not” means they had no sexual relations until the birth.

1.theology:
The Incarnation and the Hypostatic Union. Matthew 1:23 is the first New Testament statement of what the Council of Chalcedon (451 AD) would define as the hypostatic union: Jesus Christ is fully God and fully man, two natures in one person. Emmanuel — God with us. The one born of Mary is not a divine being wearing a human costume, nor a human being elevated to divine status. He is the eternal Son of God who took to himself a true and complete human nature, remaining what he was while becoming what he was not.

Reformed theology has insisted on both sides of this confession with equal force. Against those who diminish the humanity (docetism), the reformers affirm: he was born of a woman, grew in wisdom, wept, hungered, died. Against those who diminish the divinity, the reformers affirm: he is the Lord who saves, the one who forgives sins, who raises the dead, who will judge the living and the dead. The incarnation is not a compromise between deity and humanity; it is the union of both in one Person, the only foundation on which salvation is possible.
1.examples:
Then: The women in the genealogy — Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, Bathsheba — represent the scandalous grace of God that runs through broken and foreign vessels to accomplish his purposes. The rabbis of Matthew’s day would have found their inclusion in a royal genealogy offensive. Matthew includes them precisely because the gospel offends the self-righteous and welcomes the unlikely. The same grace that wrote Rahab the harlot into the ancestry of the Messiah writes sinners into the family of God through faith.

Now: We live in a world that determines worth by background, achievement, and social position. The genealogy of Matthew 1 demolishes every such calculation. The line of the King runs through exiles, foreigners, adulterers, and the forgotten. If your story has chapters you would rather not name in public, you are in good company in this genealogy. The God who included Rahab and Ruth and Tamar in the ancestry of his Son includes broken people in his family — not despite their stories but through them, weaving even the darkest threads into the tapestry of his redeeming purpose.

2.title: The King and the Nations
2.text: <sup>1</sup>Now after Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of Herod the king, behold, wise men from the east came to Jerusalem, <sup>2</sup>saying, “Where is he who has been born king of the Jews? For we saw his star when it rose and have come to worship him.” <sup>3</sup>When Herod the king heard this, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him; <sup>4</sup>and assembling all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he inquired of them where the Christ was to be born. <sup>5</sup>They told him, “In Bethlehem of Judea, for so it is written by the prophet: <sup>6</sup>‘And you, O Bethlehem, in the land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall come a ruler who will shepherd my people Israel.’” <sup>7</sup>Then Herod summoned the wise men secretly and ascertained from them what time the star had appeared. <sup>8</sup>And he sent them to Bethlehem, saying, “Go and search diligently for the child, and when you have found him, bring me word, that I too may come and worship him.” <sup>9</sup>After listening to the king, they went on their way. And behold, the star that they had seen when it rose went before them until it came to rest over the place where the child was. <sup>10</sup>When they saw the star, they rejoiced exceedingly with great joy. <sup>11</sup>And going into the house, they saw the child with Mary his mother, and they fell down and worshiped him. Then, opening their treasures, they offered him gifts, gold and frankincense and myrrh. <sup>12</sup>And being warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they departed to their own country by another way. <sup>13</sup>Now when they had departed, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream and said, “Rise, take the child and his mother, and flee to Egypt, and remain there until I tell you, for Herod is about to search for the child, to destroy him.” <sup>14</sup>And he rose and took the child and his mother by night and departed to Egypt <sup>15</sup>and remained there until the death of Herod. This was to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet, “Out of Egypt I called my son.” <sup>16</sup>Then Herod, when he saw that he had been tricked by the wise men, became furious, and he sent and killed all the male children in Bethlehem and in all that region who were two years old or under, according to the time that he had ascertained from the wise men. <sup>17</sup>Then was fulfilled what was spoken by the prophet Jeremiah: <sup>18</sup>“A voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and loud lamentation, Rachel weeping for her children; she refused to be comforted, because they are no more.” <sup>19</sup>But when Herod died, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt, <sup>20</sup>saying, “Rise, take the child and his mother and go to the land of Israel, for those who sought the child's life are dead.” <sup>21</sup>And he rose and took the child and his mother and went to the land of Israel. <sup>22</sup>But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning over Judea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there, and being warned in a dream he withdrew to the district of Galilee. <sup>23</sup>And he went and lived in a city called Nazareth, so that what was spoken by the prophets might be fulfilled, that he would be called a Nazarene.
2.overview:
Chapter 2 is a chapter of contrasts. From the east, pagan Magi travel hundreds of miles to worship a Jewish king they have never met, guided by a star and driven by a longing they cannot fully name. In Jerusalem, the chief priests and scribes know exactly where the Messiah is to be born — they can quote the prophecy from memory — and do not move a single step toward Bethlehem. Knowledge without seeking is useless; seeking without knowledge leads to Jerusalem first and then to the star. The Magi needed both, and they found the King.

The flight to Egypt is Matthew’s second great fulfilment: Out of Egypt I called my son (Hos. 11:1). What Hosea said of Israel, Matthew applies to Jesus — because Jesus is the true Israel, recapitulating the nation’s story in his own person. Israel went into Egypt to be preserved; Israel came out of Egypt to receive the law at Sinai. Jesus goes into Egypt as an infant; he comes out to receive baptism at the Jordan and give the new law on the mountain. He is not just a figure from Israel’s history; he is Israel’s history compressed and completed.

The massacre of the innocents is the chapter’s darkest moment, and Matthew does not diminish it. Rachel weeping for her children (Jer. 31:15) — the ancient lament of exile reactivated by Herod’s paranoid terror. Children died because the King had come. This is not a comfortable note, and it should not be. The incarnation provokes powers that kill to protect themselves. And yet those children are the first martyrs — the first to die because of the King who would die for all.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Visit of the Magi
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wise men from the East arrive in Jerusalem following a star, seeking the one born King of the Jews. Their arrival triggers the first of Matthew's great ironies: Gentiles travel from afar to worship the Jewish Messiah, while the Jewish king plots his murder and the religious establishment is unmoved. Herod's response — feigned interest concealing murderous intent — foreshadows the opposition that will culminate at Golgotha. The magi's worship, their gifts, and their Spirit-warned departure set the pattern: the nations come to the light while those who hold the Scriptures remain in darkness. Two things more. Verses 7-8: Herod's secrecy is his first tell — he does not want Jerusalem to know what he is planning — and the detail he extracts from the magi, the time the star appeared, is precisely the data that produces the age-range of the massacre at verse 16. His "that I too may come and worship him" is a lie welding devotion to murder, which is the enemy's own signature (Jn. 8:44). Verses 9-10: the star resumes only after the Scriptures have sent them to Bethlehem, and by verse 9 the light is behaving less like an object in the sky than like the pillar of fire that went before Israel (Exod. 13:21) — it goes ahead of them at walking pace and halts over one house. Matthew's Greek for their reaction piles up four words where one would do: they rejoiced with joy exceedingly great. And note what caused it — not the sight of the child, whom they had not yet reached, but a light they had followed for months finally standing still.
verseByVerse.theology: The magi's journey is the fulfillment of Isaiah's vision: the nations streaming to Zion's light (Isa. 60:1–6). Their gifts — gold for a king, incense for a priest, myrrh for one destined to die — have long been read as prophetic of Christ's three offices. Herod represents all who will acknowledge Christ's kingship only to oppose it: knowing who he is changes nothing if the heart is not transformed. The Scripture the chief priests quote from memory (Micah 5:2) but do not obey is a standing rebuke to knowledge without submission - and the loose form of their quotation, examined at vv. 5-6, only sharpens the point: they had the text near enough to recite and far enough to ignore.
verseByVerse.examples: The magi traveled perhaps a thousand miles, following light they only partially understood, to bring costly gifts to a child. Their worship was costly, inconvenient, and preceded by great uncertainty. Many who have never left their town have more theological knowledge than these men had — and far less devotion. The question the magi's story presses: what are you willing to travel, spend, and risk to find and worship Christ?

verseByVerse.quote: Now after Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of Herod the king, behold, wise men from the east came to Jerusalem, saying, "Where is he who has been born king of the Jews? For we saw his star when it rose and have come to worship him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Soon after Jesus was born, Gentile scholars from the east arrived in Jerusalem looking for the newborn King of the Jews, because they had seen his star and had come to worship him. The first people in Matthew to worship Jesus are foreigners.

The connection. Chapter 1 showed who Jesus is: the son of David and son of Abraham, Immanuel. Chapter 2 shows how the world responds to him. Gentiles come to worship; the king of Israel tries to kill him; the religious experts know where he is and do not go. The whole Gospel is foreshadowed here.

Bethlehem of Judea. A small town about six miles (ten kilometres) south of Jerusalem, the hometown of David (1 Samuel 16:1). “Of Judea” distinguishes it from another Bethlehem in Galilee. Matthew does not describe the birth itself; Luke does (Luke 2:1–20).

In the days of Herod the king. Herod the Great ruled Judea for Rome from 37 to 4 BC. He was not a Jew by birth but an Idumean (an Edomite), which made many Jews resent him as king. He was a brilliant builder, who rebuilt the Jerusalem temple on a magnificent scale, but also ruthlessly cruel and paranoid. He had his favourite wife, her mother, three of his own sons and many others executed because he suspected plots. Since Herod died in 4 BC, Jesus was born a little before that, probably around 6–5 BC. (Our calendar was calculated in the sixth century and is a few years out.)

Wise men from the east. Greek magoi, “magi”. Originally a priestly caste in Persia, they became known as experts in astrology, dream interpretation and ancient wisdom, serving at royal courts. They probably came from Persia or Babylon, where many Jews had lived since the exile and where Daniel had been head of the wise men (Daniel 2:48). They may have known Jewish hopes of a coming king. Matthew does not say how many there were; the tradition of three comes from the three gifts. Nor were they kings; that idea came later from Psalm 72:10–11 and Isaiah 60:3.

Where is he who has been born king of the Jews? Not “who will become king”, but “who has been born king”. He is king by birth. The title will appear again only at the end of the Gospel, on the lips of Pilate and the soldiers, and on the sign over the cross (27:11, 29, 37). The Gentiles call him King at his birth and at his death.

For we saw his star when it rose. “When it rose” can also be translated “in the east”. Many explanations have been offered: a conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn (which happened three times in 7 BC), a comet, or a nova. But the star in verse 9 moves ahead of them and stops over a particular house, which no natural star does. Verdict: most likely a supernatural light, a sign God gave, perhaps in a form these star-watchers would understand. Some connect it with Balaam’s prophecy: a star shall come out of Jacob, and a sceptre shall rise out of Israel (Numbers 24:17).

And have come to worship him. The Greek word (proskyneō) means to bow down, to fall prostrate in homage. It can be used of honouring a king, but in Matthew it regularly describes worship of Jesus (14:33; 28:9, 17). The magi came a long way, at great cost, to bow before a child.

What it does not mean. Not that astrology is a valid way to know God’s will. Scripture forbids divination and the worship of the stars (Deuteronomy 18:10–12; Isaiah 47:13–14). God met these men where they were, but he led them finally by his word (vv. 5–6) to the Christ. The star brought them to Jerusalem; Scripture brought them to Bethlehem.

In a sentence. Gentile scholars travelled far to worship the newborn King of the Jews, a first sign that Jesus came for the nations.

On a Tuesday. The magi came a long way to worship. How far are you willing to go, what inconvenience will you accept, to seek Christ?
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “wise men” renders the Greek magi — scholars of the stars, probably from Persia or Babylon. Herod the Great ruled Judea for Rome until 4 BC.

parallels.desc: a star shall come out of Jacob
nations bring gold and frankincense to the light

verseByVerse.quote: When Herod the king heard this, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him; and assembling all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he inquired of them where the Christ was to be born.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herod was alarmed by the news of a newborn king, and all Jerusalem with him. He called together the religious leaders and asked them where the Messiah was to be born.

When Herod the king heard this, he was troubled. Herod had a title, “king of the Jews”, given to him by the Roman Senate. Now foreigners were asking for someone born to that title. To a paranoid old king, this meant a rival. He had already killed members of his own family to protect his throne.

And all Jerusalem with him. Why would the city be troubled at the news of the Messiah? Because they knew Herod. When Herod was disturbed, people died. The city feared what he might do. And perhaps many were comfortable with things as they were and did not want disruption, even from God.

Assembling all the chief priests and scribes of the people. The chief priests were the high priest and the leading priestly families who ran the temple, mostly Sadducees. The scribes were experts in the law of Moses who taught and interpreted it, mostly Pharisees. Together they formed much of the Sanhedrin, the Jewish council. These were the people who knew the Scriptures best.

He inquired of them where the Christ was to be born. Herod connects “king of the Jews” with “the Christ”, the Messiah. He understands that this is about God’s promised King.

What it does not mean. Not that every person in Jerusalem was hostile. Luke tells of Simeon and Anna in the temple, longing for the Messiah (Luke 2:25–38). But as a whole, the capital was troubled rather than glad.

In a sentence. News of the true King filled Herod, and the city that feared him, with alarm.

On a Tuesday. Jesus disturbs every throne, including the one in your own heart. Does the thought of his rule trouble you, or gladden you?
verseByVerse.note: Herod was notoriously jealous of rivals; he had members of his own family killed. The chief priests and scribes were the experts in the Scriptures.

verseByVerse.quote: They told him, "In Bethlehem of Judea, for so it is written by the prophet: 'And you, O Bethlehem, in the land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall come a ruler who will shepherd my people Israel.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The experts answered at once: the Messiah would be born in Bethlehem, as the prophet Micah wrote, for from there would come a ruler who would shepherd God’s people Israel.

In Bethlehem of Judea. They did not hesitate. It was common knowledge among the scholars that the Messiah would come from David’s town (John 7:42).

For so it is written by the prophet. Micah 5:2, written about seven hundred years earlier, combined with 2 Samuel 5:2.

And you, O Bethlehem … are by no means least. Micah’s Hebrew says that Bethlehem is little among the clans of Judah. Matthew’s quotation says it is by no means least. The two are not in conflict: Bethlehem was small in size, but because the Messiah would come from it, it is by no means least in importance. Matthew draws out the meaning in the light of the fulfilment. God chooses small places, as he chooses small people (1 Corinthians 1:27–28).

For from you shall come a ruler. Micah goes on to say that this ruler’s coming forth is from of old, from ancient days (Micah 5:2): a hint that the ruler’s origin is older than Bethlehem.

Who will shepherd my people Israel. These words come from 2 Samuel 5:2, where God told David that he would shepherd Israel. In the ancient world kings were often called shepherds, and in Israel the image meant caring for, feeding, guiding and protecting the people (Ezekiel 34). The prophets condemned the false shepherds who fed themselves instead of the flock, and promised that God himself would shepherd his people through a new David (Ezekiel 34:11–24). Herod was a wolf-king; Jesus is the Shepherd-King (John 10:11).

The irony. The scholars knew exactly where the Messiah would be born, quoted the right verse, and did not walk six miles to see. The magi, who knew far less, made the journey. Knowing the Bible is not the same as following its Christ.

What it does not mean. Not that knowledge of Scripture is unimportant: it was Scripture that pointed the way to Bethlehem. But knowledge without response hardens. James says that even the demons believe, and shudder (James 2:19).

In a sentence. Scripture had foretold that the Shepherd-King would come from small Bethlehem, and the experts knew it but did not go.

On a Tuesday. Do you know your Bible better than you obey it? The scribes had the address and stayed at home.
verseByVerse.note: Bethlehem, David’s hometown, lies about six miles south of Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: “You shall be shepherd of my people Israel”

verseByVerse.quote: Then Herod summoned the wise men secretly and ascertained from them what time the star had appeared. And he sent them to Bethlehem, saying, "Go and search diligently for the child, and when you have found him, bring me word, that I too may come and worship him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herod met the magi secretly, found out exactly when the star had appeared, and sent them to Bethlehem with instructions to report back, pretending he wanted to worship the child too.

Then Herod summoned the wise men secretly. He did not want public attention, or his plan to be known.
