And the righteousness that "exceeds" the Pharisees comes in two layers — first the perfect righteousness of Christ credited to us through faith, the only righteousness that truly opens the kingdom, and then the real if imperfect righteousness the Spirit grows in a regenerate heart. So the very law that drives the unbeliever to Christ by exposing his sin becomes, for the believer, the shape of a Spirit-empowered life of love. Read this way, the towering standard of verse 48 humbles without crushing: it sends us to Christ for a righteousness we cannot produce, and then to the Spirit who produces it in us.
verseByVerse.examples: The demand for perfection (v. 48) has driven interpreters in two directions: some make it an impossible ideal that drives us to grace; others read it as a call to wholeness or completeness (the Greek teleios can mean "complete" or "mature"). Both are partially right: the standard is God's own character, which we cannot reach by effort, but which the Spirit progressively conforms us to (2 Cor. 3:18). The sermon is both a mirror that shows us our need and a map of the life the Spirit produces in those who have received the kingdom.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them. For truly, I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, not an iota, not a dot, will pass from the Law until all is accomplished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus did not come to abolish the Old Testament law and prophets, but to fulfil them: to bring them to their goal and complete them in himself. Every part of God’s word stands until all that it points to is accomplished.

Do not think that I have come to abolish. Jesus was already being accused of disregarding the law, since he ate with sinners and healed on the Sabbath. He answers the accusation before it is fully made. “Abolish” means to tear down, destroy, set aside.

The Law or the Prophets. The Old Testament Scriptures as a whole (7:12; 22:40). “The Law” is the five books of Moses; “the Prophets” includes the historical books and the prophetic books.

I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them. “Fulfil” (plēroō) means to fill up, to complete, to bring to its intended goal. Jesus fulfils the Old Testament in several ways at once. He fulfils its prophecies by bringing them to pass (1:22). He fulfils its commands by obeying them perfectly (3:15). He fulfils its ceremonies (sacrifices, priesthood, temple, purity rules) by being what they foreshadowed (Hebrews 10:1–14; Colossians 2:16–17). And he fulfils its meaning by revealing what the law truly required all along, as he does in verses 21–48. The Old Testament is not cancelled; it reaches its goal in him.

For truly, I say to you. “Truly” is amēn. Others said “amen” at the end of a statement, to agree with it. Jesus says it at the start, to affirm his own authority. Only Jesus speaks this way.

Until heaven and earth pass away. As long as the present world lasts.

Not an iota, not a dot. The iota is the smallest Greek letter (corresponding to the Hebrew yod, the smallest Hebrew letter, like an apostrophe). The “dot” (literally “horn”) is a tiny stroke that distinguishes one Hebrew letter from another. Not even the smallest detail of God’s word will be lost.

Will pass from the Law until all is accomplished. Until everything the law points to has happened. Christ accomplished much of it in his life, death and resurrection; the rest will be complete at his return.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians must keep every Old Testament law in the same way Israel did. Jesus himself declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19); the sacrifices ended with his once-for-all sacrifice (Hebrews 10:18); the temple was replaced by Christ and his people. The Reformed tradition distinguishes the moral law (summed up in the Ten Commandments, reflecting God’s character, still binding), the ceremonial law (fulfilled in Christ, no longer practised), and the civil law of Israel as a nation (expired with that nation, though its general principles of justice remain useful) (Westminster Confession 19.3–5). Every part of the law is still God’s word, and still teaches us, but we read it through Christ. Nor does it mean that we are saved by keeping the law. Christ kept it for us.

Where Christians differ: the law and the Christian. Antinomians hold that the Old Testament law has no role for Christians. Theonomists hold that Israel’s civil laws, including their penalties, should still be applied by nations today. Some in “New Covenant Theology” hold that the Mosaic law as a whole has been replaced by “the law of Christ”. Verdict: the threefold distinction of the Reformed confessions. The moral law remains the rule of life for believers, not to earn salvation, but as the shape of love (Romans 13:8–10).

In a sentence. Jesus came not to cancel God’s word but to fulfil it completely, and every part of it stands until all is accomplished.

On a Tuesday. Do you treat the Old Testament as out of date? Read it this week looking for how it points to Christ and how its moral teaching shapes your life.
verseByVerse.note: The iota is the smallest Greek letter; the “dot” is a tiny stroke of a letter. Nothing in the law is too small to matter.

parallels.desc: Christ is the end of the law

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore whoever relaxes one of the least of these commandments and teaches others to do the same will be called least in the kingdom of heaven, but whoever does them and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven. For I tell you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because God’s law stands, anyone who weakens even its smallest command and teaches others to do the same will be least in the kingdom. And unless the disciples’ righteousness goes deeper than that of the scribes and Pharisees, they will not enter the kingdom at all.

Therefore. Because the law stands (v. 18).

Whoever relaxes one of the least of these commandments. “Relaxes” means loosens, sets aside, treats as not binding. The rabbis distinguished “light” and “heavy” commandments. Jesus agrees that some matter more than others (23:23), but says no command is to be treated lightly.

And teaches others to do the same. Teachers carry a special responsibility (James 3:1).

Will be called least in the kingdom of heaven. Notice: still in the kingdom, but least. Jesus speaks of degrees of honour within the kingdom. Such a person is not necessarily excluded, but they are at the bottom.

But whoever does them and teaches them will be called great. Doing comes before teaching. A teacher’s life must match his words.

Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees. A shock to the first hearers. The scribes and Pharisees were the most righteous people they knew. They tithed even their garden herbs (23:23), fasted twice a week (Luke 18:12), and kept the Sabbath in minute detail. How could anyone exceed that?

Exceeds how? Not in quantity, more rules, but in kind. The Pharisees’ righteousness was largely external: actions, not the heart; the letter, not the spirit; and often done to be seen (6:1–18; 23:25–28). It also tended to lower the law to what could be managed, while adding human traditions (15:1–9). Jesus demands a righteousness of the heart: no anger, no lust, no deceit, no revenge, love for enemies. Verses 21–48 show what he means.

You will never enter the kingdom of heaven. Not “least” but excluded. A merely external religion does not belong to the kingdom.

How can anyone have this righteousness? In two ways, held together by the Reformers. First, Christ’s righteousness is credited to those who trust him: he fulfilled the law perfectly in their place (Romans 3:21–22; Philippians 3:9). This is the only righteousness that counts before God’s judgment. Second, God gives his people a new heart and writes his law on it (Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 36:26–27), so that a real, inward righteousness grows in them by the Spirit. This does not earn entry, but it marks those who have entered. Both are gifts.

What it does not mean. Not that we must out-do the Pharisees by our own efforts to earn heaven. That would make the sermon a crushing burden. The demand drives us first to Christ, whose righteousness is perfect. Nor does it mean that all the Pharisees were hypocrites: some, like Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea, came to faith.

In a sentence. God’s law must be kept and taught in full, and only a righteousness deeper than the Pharisees’, a righteousness of the heart, belongs to the kingdom.

On a Tuesday. Are you content with outward religion: attending, giving, avoiding obvious sins? Ask God to search your heart, and rest your standing on Christ’s righteousness, not yours.

parallels.desc: the righteousness from God that depends on faith

verseByVerse.quote: You have heard that it was said to those of old, "You shall not murder; and whoever murders will be liable to judgment." But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment; whoever insults his brother will be liable to the council; and whoever says, "You fool!" will be liable to the hell of fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first of six examples. The law said, do not murder. Jesus says that anger and contempt in the heart, and insulting words, are murder at the root, and are just as liable to God’s judgment.

The six antitheses. Verses 21–48 contain six examples, each beginning “You have heard that it was said … But I say to you”. They show what the deeper righteousness of verse 20 looks like. Jesus is not contradicting the law of Moses. He is correcting the way it had been taught and limited, and revealing its full meaning. The issues are anger, lust, divorce, oaths, revenge and love for enemies.

You have heard that it was said to those of old. “You have heard”: most people heard the law read and explained in the synagogue, rather than reading it themselves. “Those of old” are the generations of Moses and after. What they heard included the law itself plus later interpretations.

You shall not murder. The sixth commandment (Exodus 20:13). “Murder” means unlawful killing of a human being.

And whoever murders will be liable to judgment. A summary of the law’s penalty (Exodus 21:12; Numbers 35:16–21), referring to a human court. The popular teaching stopped there: as long as you have not killed anyone, you have kept the commandment.

But I say to you. Jesus speaks on his own authority, as the lawgiver himself. The prophets said, “Thus says the LORD.” Jesus says, “I say to you.”

Everyone who is angry with his brother. Anger is the root of murder. Cain was angry before he killed Abel (Genesis 4:5–8). God sees the heart. “Brother” means a fellow believer, or more widely a fellow human being. The sinful anger Jesus means is the anger of resentment, hatred and contempt. (On righteous anger, see Ephesians 4:26.)

Will be liable to judgment. The same phrase as for murder. Anger is as serious before God’s court as murder is before a human court.

Whoever insults his brother. Literally “says Raca”, an Aramaic insult meaning “empty-head”, “idiot”, a word of contempt.

Will be liable to the council. The Sanhedrin, the highest Jewish court.

Whoever says, “You fool!” Greek mōre, from which we get “moron”. In Scripture, the “fool” is a person who is morally and spiritually worthless, who says there is no God (Psalm 14:1). To call someone that is to write them off as beyond value.

Will be liable to the hell of fire. “Hell” is Gehenna, from the Valley of Hinnom, just south of Jerusalem. There, wicked kings of Judah had sacrificed their children to Molech (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31). Josiah defiled it, and in later tradition it became a picture of God’s final judgment, a place of fire and destruction (Isaiah 66:24). Jesus uses it for the final punishment of the wicked.

The progression. Anger, then contempt, then writing someone off: the judgment rises from a local court, to the supreme court, to hell itself. Jesus is not setting out a legal code with exact penalties; he is showing that the inner attitudes that lead to murder are themselves deadly before God.

What it does not mean. Not that all anger is sin. Jesus himself was angry at hard-hearted people (Mark 3:5), and God’s wrath is holy. The sin is the anger of personal resentment, contempt and hatred. Nor does it mean that every use of the word “fool” is forbidden: Jesus himself called the Pharisees blind fools (23:17). The issue is contempt, writing a person off, not truthful description of folly. And it does not mean that anger is as harmful to others as murder: murder is worse in its effects, and human courts rightly treat it more severely. But before God, the heart that hates is guilty (1 John 3:15).

In a sentence. God judges not only murder but the anger and contempt in the heart from which murder grows.

On a Tuesday. Whom do you secretly despise or write off? Contempt for a colleague, a politician or a family member is murder at the root. Confess it and ask God to replace it with love.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “insults” renders the Aramaic term of abuse Raca. “Hell” renders Gehenna, the Valley of Hinnom by Jerusalem, once a place of child sacrifice. “The council” is the Sanhedrin.

parallels.desc: child sacrifice in the Valley of Hinnom
everyone who hates his brother is a murderer

verseByVerse.quote: So if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because anger matters so much to God, reconciliation is urgent. If you are about to worship and remember that someone has a grievance against you, leave your offering and go to make peace first, then come back and offer it.

So. Because anger is so serious (vv. 21–22).

If you are offering your gift at the altar. A sacrifice brought to the temple in Jerusalem. For a Galilean, the journey to Jerusalem took about three days. Jesus imagines someone who has made the long journey, is standing in the temple court, about to hand his animal to the priest.

And there remember that your brother has something against you. Notice: not that you have something against him, but that he has something against you. You have wronged him, or he thinks you have. Your responsibility is to take the initiative.

Leave your gift there before the altar and go. Startling. Leave the sacrifice, travel home, and deal with the relationship. God values reconciliation more than ritual. The prophets taught the same: God desires mercy, not sacrifice (Hosea 6:6; 1 Samuel 15:22).

First be reconciled to your brother. “First” is the key word. Worship and broken relationships do not belong together. John says that whoever does not love his brother whom he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen (1 John 4:20).

And then come and offer your gift. Worship is not cancelled; it is postponed until it can be offered with integrity.

What it does not mean. Not that we cannot worship until every conflict is resolved, which in some cases is impossible because the other person refuses. Paul says, if possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all (Romans 12:18). Our part is to make the effort. Nor is the point about the temple: for Christians today, the same principle applies to prayer, the Lord’s Supper and public worship (1 Corinthians 11:27–29).

In a sentence. Reconciliation with those you have wronged comes before worship, because God cares more about relationships than ritual.

On a Tuesday. Before you next go to church or take the Lord’s Supper, ask: is there anyone who has something against me? Make the call, write the message, or go.
verseByVerse.note: The gift at the altar is a sacrifice brought to the temple.

parallels.desc: forgive, so that your Father may forgive you
so far as it depends on you

verseByVerse.quote: Come to terms quickly with your accuser while you are going with him to court, lest your accuser hand you over to the judge, and the judge to the guard, and you be put in prison. Truly, I say to you, you will never get out until you have paid the last penny.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Settle disputes quickly, before they reach court, while you still can. If you wait, the judge will decide against you and you will pay in full. Behind the picture is a warning about God’s judgment: be reconciled now, while there is time.

Come to terms quickly with your accuser. Make friends, settle, come to an agreement. The accuser is someone suing you, perhaps for a debt.

While you are going with him to court. In the ancient world, a creditor could drag a debtor to the judge. There was still time on the way.

Lest your accuser hand you over to the judge, and the judge to the guard. The process of law: once it starts, it cannot be stopped. The guard is the court officer who carries out the sentence.

And you be put in prison. Debtors’ prison was common in the Roman world: a debtor was imprisoned until the debt was paid, often by family.

You will never get out until you have paid the last penny. The “penny” (kodrantēs, Latin quadrans) was the smallest Roman coin, a tiny fraction of a day’s wage. Every last bit must be paid.

Two levels. First, practical wisdom: settle disputes quickly, even at a cost, rather than let them escalate. Second, a deeper warning. In Matthew, a judge, prison and full payment often picture God’s final judgment (18:34–35). The point is urgency: we are all on our way to God’s court. Be reconciled with others now, and above all be reconciled with God now, while there is time (2 Corinthians 5:20; 6:2).

What it does not mean. Not that Christians may never use courts or stand up for justice. Paul appealed to Caesar (Acts 25:11). But Christians should not be quick to sue, especially fellow believers (1 Corinthians 6:1–8). Nor does “until you have paid the last penny” teach purgatory, as some Roman Catholic interpreters have argued, a place where believers pay off their sins after death before entering heaven. Christ has paid the debt of believers in full (Colossians 2:13–14); there is no purgatory in Scripture.

In a sentence. Settle disputes quickly, because delay makes things worse, and we are all on our way to God’s court.

On a Tuesday. Is there a dispute you are letting drag on out of pride? Settle it, even if it costs you something.
verseByVerse.note: The “penny” (Latin quadrans) was a small Roman copper coin, worth about 1/64 of a denarius.

verseByVerse.quote: You have heard that it was said, "You shall not commit adultery." But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second example. The law said, do not commit adultery. Jesus says that looking at a woman with the purpose of desiring her sexually is adultery already committed in the heart.

You have heard that it was said, “You shall not commit adultery.” The seventh commandment (Exodus 20:14). Adultery is sexual intercourse between a married person and someone other than their spouse. The popular teaching limited the command to the act itself: as long as you have not slept with another man’s wife, you are innocent.

But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent. The Greek is literally “looks at a woman in order to desire her”. It is not a passing glance or an involuntary thought, but a deliberate look aimed at sexual desire, feeding the imagination. The tenth commandment already forbade coveting your neighbour’s wife (Exodus 20:17). Job made a covenant with his eyes not to gaze at a virgin (Job 31:1).

Has already committed adultery with her in his heart. God sees the heart. What is entertained in the imagination is sin before him, even if it never becomes an act. The heart is where adultery begins (15:19).

Why the man? In that culture, men had more freedom and power, and women were often blamed for men’s lust. Jesus puts the responsibility squarely on the one who looks. The principle applies equally to women.

What it does not mean. Not that noticing someone is attractive is sin, or that every sexual thought that comes into the mind is adultery. As with all temptation (see 4:1 and Ephesians 5:3), the first thought is not yet sin; it is entertaining it, dwelling on it, and feeding it that is sin. Luther said that you cannot stop the birds from flying over your head, but you can stop them nesting in your hair. Nor does it condemn sexual desire itself, which God created good, for its proper place in marriage (Song of Songs; 1 Corinthians 7:3–5). Nor does it mean that lust in the heart is as harmful to others as adultery committed, or that a person who has lusted might as well commit the act. The act adds betrayal, harm to others, and often children and broken families. But before God, both are sin, and both need forgiveness.

Today. In an age of pornography and sexualised advertising, this word cuts deep. Pornography is exactly what Jesus describes: looking at someone in order to desire them sexually. It is not harmless; it is adultery of the heart, and it exploits real people.

In a sentence. Deliberately looking at someone in order to desire them sexually is adultery in the heart before God.

On a Tuesday. What do your eyes linger on, on your phone, on the street, on screens? Turn away from the second look. And if you have fallen, there is forgiveness in Christ; confess it to God, and if it is a habit, to a trusted Christian friend.

parallels.desc: you shall not covet your neighbour’s wife

verseByVerse.quote: If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away. For it is better that you lose one of your members than that your whole body be thrown into hell. And if your right hand causes you to sin, cut it off and throw it away. For it is better that you lose one of your members than that your whole body go into hell.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Deal with sin radically. If your eye or hand leads you into sin, cut it off. It is better to lose something precious than for your whole self to be thrown into hell.

If your right eye causes you to sin. “Causes you to sin” (skandalizei) means trips you up, makes you stumble, like the bait-stick of a trap. The right eye and right hand were considered the most valuable. The eye connects with lustful looking (v. 28); the hand with what we do.

Tear it out and throw it away. Jesus is using deliberate exaggeration, a vivid way of speaking common in Jewish teaching. He does not mean literal self-mutilation. Even with one eye, a person can still lust; the problem is the heart (15:19). The early church condemned Origen, a third-century scholar, for literally castrating himself on the basis of a similar verse (19:12). Jesus means: take decisive, costly action to remove whatever leads you into sin.

For it is better that you lose one of your members than that your whole body be thrown into hell. The logic is simple: if surgery saves your life, you accept the loss. Losing something you value is better than losing everything. Sin is that serious, and hell is that real.

What “cutting off” means today. Removing the internet from your phone, installing filters and accountability, ending a relationship that leads you into sin, changing your route home to avoid a bar, cancelling a subscription, refusing to be alone with a certain person, changing jobs if necessary. Paul calls it putting to death what is earthly in you (Colossians 3:5) and making no provision for the flesh (Romans 13:14).

What it does not mean. Not literal self-harm. Nor that we can make ourselves holy by removing temptations alone; the heart must be changed by the Spirit (Romans 8:13). But the Spirit works through our decisive obedience. Nor does it mean that a believer who struggles will certainly be lost: the warning is that a life of unrepented, cherished sin leads to hell, and true believers take such warnings seriously and fight.

In a sentence. Take drastic action against whatever leads you into sin, because losing it is better than losing yourself.

On a Tuesday. What is the “eye” or “hand” in your life, the thing that repeatedly leads you into sin? What would it cost to cut it off? Do it today.
verseByVerse.note: The right eye and hand were thought the more valuable. Jesus is using deliberate exaggeration to demand radical action against sin, not self-mutilation.

parallels.desc: put to death what is earthly in you

verseByVerse.quote: It was also said, "Whoever divorces his wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce." But I say to you that everyone who divorces his wife, except on the ground of sexual immorality, makes her commit adultery, and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third example. People took the law about the certificate of divorce as permission to divorce easily. Jesus says that divorce, except for sexual immorality, makes a person complicit in adultery. Marriage is meant to be permanent.

It was also said, “Whoever divorces his wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce.” A summary of Deuteronomy 24:1–4. That law did not command or approve divorce; it regulated it. It required a husband who sent his wife away to give her a written certificate, which protected her by freeing her to remarry, and it forbade him to take her back after she had married another. Jesus later explains that Moses allowed divorce because of the hardness of people’s hearts, but from the beginning it was not so (19:8).

The debate in Jesus’ day. Deuteronomy 24:1 allows divorce when a husband finds “some indecency” in his wife. The rabbis argued about what this meant. The school of Shammai said it meant only serious sexual sin. The school of Hillel said it could mean anything that displeased the husband, even burning his food; the later teacher Akiba said it could mean finding someone prettier. In practice, divorce was easy for men, and women were left vulnerable.

But I say to you that everyone who divorces his wife. Jesus returns to God’s original design: one man and one woman, becoming one flesh, for life (Genesis 2:24; 19:4–6). What God has joined, let no one separate.

Except on the ground of sexual immorality. “Sexual immorality” (porneia) is a broad word for sexual sin, including adultery. Where one partner has broken the marriage covenant by sexual unfaithfulness, divorce is permitted, though not commanded. Forgiveness and restoration are better where possible (Hosea).

Makes her commit adultery. In that culture, a divorced woman would almost always need to remarry to survive. A husband who divorced his wife without just cause effectively pushed her into another marriage that, in God’s eyes, was adulterous, because the first marriage had not been rightly ended. The husband bears the guilt.

And whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery. That is, a woman divorced without just cause. Her marriage to her first husband is, before God, still binding.

What it does not mean. Not that divorced people are second-class Christians or beyond God’s forgiveness. Divorce, like every sin, can be forgiven, and many divorced people were the wronged party. Nor does it mean that a person must stay in a marriage where they or their children are in danger. Separation for safety is not the same as divorce, and the church must protect the vulnerable. Nor does Jesus’ word mean that the innocent party in a marriage broken by adultery sins by divorcing.

Where Christians differ: divorce and remarriage. Roman Catholic teaching holds that a valid sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved, so divorce and remarriage are not permitted (though annulments are granted). Some Protestants hold that divorce is permitted for adultery, but remarriage is not. Others allow divorce and remarriage widely. The Westminster Confession (24.5–6) holds that adultery, and wilful desertion by an unbelieving spouse that cannot be remedied (1 Corinthians 7:15), are the only grounds for divorce, and that the innocent party may remarry. Verdict: the Westminster position. Marriage is lifelong; divorce is permitted only for sexual unfaithfulness or desertion; and the innocent party is free to remarry. Each case needs careful, compassionate pastoral wisdom.

In a sentence. Marriage is meant to be for life, and divorce except for sexual unfaithfulness leads to adultery in God’s sight.

On a Tuesday. If you are married, invest in your marriage today: a kind word, an apology, time together. If you have been through divorce, bring your grief and guilt to Christ, who forgives and restores.
verseByVerse.note: A certificate of divorce freed a woman to remarry. Rabbis disputed the grounds for divorce, some allowing it for trivial reasons.

verseByVerse.quote: Again you have heard that it was said to those of old, "You shall not swear falsely, but shall perform to the Lord what you have sworn." But I say to you, Do not take an oath at all, either by heaven, for it is the throne of God, or by the earth, for it is his footstool, or by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King. And do not take an oath by your head, for you cannot make one hair white or black. Let what you say be simply "Yes" or "No"; anything more than this comes from evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fourth example. People taught that you must keep oaths sworn by God, but could be looser with oaths sworn by lesser things. Jesus says: do not use oaths to manipulate truth at all. Let your plain yes mean yes and your no mean no.

You shall not swear falsely, but shall perform to the Lord what you have sworn. A summary of several laws: do not swear falsely by God’s name (Leviticus 19:12); keep the vows you make to the LORD (Numbers 30:2; Deuteronomy 23:21–23). An oath is a solemn statement calling on God as witness that you are telling the truth or will keep a promise.

The problem. People had developed a system of evasion. An oath sworn by God’s name was binding. But an oath sworn by heaven, by earth, by Jerusalem, or by one’s own head, was considered less binding, or not binding at all. People used these lesser oaths to sound convincing while leaving themselves a way out. Jesus exposes the same trick in 23:16–22.

But I say to you, Do not take an oath at all. Jesus cuts through the whole system.

Either by heaven, for it is the throne of God. You cannot avoid God by swearing by heaven: heaven is his throne (Isaiah 66:1).

Or by the earth, for it is his footstool. Also from Isaiah 66:1.

Or by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King. From Psalm 48:2. Jerusalem belongs to God.

And do not take an oath by your head, for you cannot make one hair white or black. Even your own head is not yours to control; it belongs to God. Every oath, whatever it is sworn by, involves God, because everything belongs to him.

Let what you say be simply “Yes” or “No”. A person of integrity does not need oaths. Their plain word is enough. James repeats this teaching (James 5:12).

Anything more than this comes from evil. Or “from the evil one”. The need for oaths exists only because lying is common. A society full of oaths is a society full of liars. The habit of adding “I swear” or “honestly” suggests that our normal words cannot be trusted.

What it does not mean. Not that every oath is forbidden in every circumstance. God himself swears oaths (Genesis 22:16; Hebrews 6:13–18). Jesus answered under oath before the high priest (26:63–64). Paul called God as his witness (Romans 1:9; 2 Corinthians 1:23; Galatians 1:20). What Jesus forbids is the casual, manipulative use of oaths in everyday speech to create two levels of truthfulness.

Where Christians differ: oaths in court. Quakers, Mennonites and some other Anabaptist groups refuse to take any oath, including in court, and take this verse literally. Most Christians, including the Reformed tradition, hold that lawful oaths, such as in court or when taking office, are permitted when required by legitimate authority for a serious purpose (Westminster Confession 22.1–3). Verdict: lawful oaths are permitted; casual and evasive oaths are forbidden. In many countries, those with conscientious objections may make an affirmation instead, which is a reasonable accommodation.

In a sentence. Be so truthful that your plain yes and no are enough, without oaths to prop them up.

On a Tuesday. Notice how often you say “honestly” or “to be truthful”. Aim for a life in which your simple word can always be trusted.
verseByVerse.note: People swore by heaven or Jerusalem instead of by God, treating such oaths as less binding.

parallels.desc: do not swear by my name falsely
do all that proceeds out of his mouth
heaven my throne, the earth my footstool
the city of the great King

verseByVerse.quote: You have heard that it was said, "An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth." But I say to you, Do not resist the one who is evil. But if anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also. And if anyone would sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fifth example. The law’s rule of “an eye for an eye” limited punishment in court to what was fair. People used it to justify personal revenge. Jesus says: do not retaliate against someone who wrongs you. Absorb the insult, and give more than is demanded.

An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth. From Exodus 21:24, Leviticus 24:20 and Deuteronomy 19:21. This law, called the lex talionis (law of retaliation), was a principle for judges, not for individuals. Its purpose was to limit punishment, so that it was proportionate to the crime: no more than an eye for an eye, not a life for an eye. It was a merciful law, preventing escalating blood feuds. In practice, it was often applied through compensation rather than literal injury (Exodus 21:26–27). But people had turned a principle of justice in court into a licence for private revenge.

But I say to you, Do not resist the one who is evil. Do not retaliate against someone who harms you; do not take revenge. Paul echoes this: repay no one evil for evil; never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God (Romans 12:17–19).

But if anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also. Most people are right-handed. To strike someone on the right cheek, you would use the back of your right hand. In Jewish culture, a backhanded slap was a deliberate insult, a way of treating someone as an inferior, and the law specified double compensation for it. Jesus is talking about insult, not a life-threatening attack. Do not retaliate to defend your honour; accept the insult. Jesus himself was struck, and did not strike back (26:67; 1 Peter 2:23).

And if anyone would sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well. The tunic was the inner garment; the cloak was the outer garment, used also as a blanket at night. By law, a poor man’s cloak could not be kept overnight as a pledge (Exodus 22:26–27). Jesus says: if someone takes you to court for your tunic, give him even the cloak you have a legal right to keep. Do not insist on your rights.

What it does not mean. This is one of the most misunderstood passages of the sermon. Jesus is speaking about personal relationships and personal insults, not the duties of governments. It does not mean that the state should not punish criminals: Paul says that the government is God’s servant to punish wrongdoers (Romans 13:1–4). It does not mean that Christians must never defend the vulnerable: protecting your wife, children or neighbour from an attacker is an act of love, not revenge. It does not mean that victims of abuse must stay and accept it: Jesus himself withdrew from danger (Luke 4:30; John 10:39), and Paul escaped over a wall (Acts 9:25) and used his rights as a citizen (Acts 16:37; 22:25). And it does not mean that evil should go unpunished: it means that we leave vengeance to God and to lawful authority, not to ourselves.

Where Christians differ: pacifism. Some Christian traditions (Mennonites, Quakers and others) take this passage to forbid all use of force, including military service and police work. Most of the church, following Augustine and the Reformers, has held that the state may use force justly (the “just war” tradition), and that Christians may serve as soldiers and police (Luke 3:14; Acts 10). Verdict: Jesus forbids personal revenge and retaliation, not the lawful use of force by governments, nor the defence of the vulnerable. Christians who hold pacifist convictions should be respected.

In a sentence. Do not take personal revenge when you are insulted or wronged; absorb it, and leave justice to God.

On a Tuesday. When someone insults you today, by email, at work, in traffic, resist the instinct to hit back. Let the insult stop with you.
verseByVerse.note: “Eye for eye” was a rule for judges, to keep punishment in proportion, not a licence for private revenge. A slap on the right cheek — probably with the back of the hand — was an insult. The cloak was the outer garment, used as a blanket at night.

parallels.desc: a cloak taken in pledge returned by sunset

verseByVerse.quote: And if anyone forces you to go one mile, go with him two miles. Give to the one who begs from you, and do not refuse the one who would borrow from you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Go further than you are forced to go. If a soldier forces you to carry his load one mile, carry it two. Give to those who ask, and do not turn away those who want to borrow.

If anyone forces you to go one mile. Roman soldiers had the legal right to compel a civilian to carry their equipment for one Roman mile (about 1,500 metres, slightly shorter than an English mile). Simon of Cyrene was forced to carry Jesus’ cross in this way (27:32). For Jews, it was a hated symbol of foreign occupation.

Go with him two miles. Do the second mile voluntarily. The first mile was forced; the second is a free gift. It turns an act of oppression into an act of service. It disarms the oppressor and shows a different spirit. Jesus is not commending the occupation; he is showing how to respond to it without bitterness.

Give to the one who begs from you. Be generous. God is generous to all (v. 45). The law commanded generosity to the poor (Deuteronomy 15:7–11).

And do not refuse the one who would borrow from you. Lending to the poor was a duty in Israel, without charging interest to fellow Israelites (Exodus 22:25; Deuteronomy 15:7–8).

What it does not mean. Not that we must give everyone everything they ask for, in every situation. Paul says that if anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat (2 Thessalonians 3:10). Giving money to an addict for drugs, or enabling someone’s laziness or sin, is not love. Wise generosity sometimes gives something other than what is asked: food rather than cash, a job rather than a handout. And it does not mean we must neglect our own family to give to others (1 Timothy 5:8). The point is a generous heart that looks for ways to give, rather than a grasping heart that looks for reasons not to.

In a sentence. Respond to demands with willing generosity, going beyond what is required.

On a Tuesday. Where can you go the second mile today: the extra task at work, the extra help for a neighbour, the extra patience with a demanding person?
verseByVerse.note: Roman soldiers could compel a civilian to carry their gear for a mile, as Simon of Cyrene was compelled to carry the cross.

parallels.desc: Simon compelled to carry the cross
open your hand to the poor

verseByVerse.quote: You have heard that it was said, "You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy." But I say to you, Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven. For he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust. For if you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Do not even the tax collectors do the same? And if you greet only your brothers, what more are you doing than others? Do not even the Gentiles do the same? You therefore must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sixth and final example. People said: love your neighbour, and hate your enemy. Jesus says: love your enemies, and pray for those who persecute you. That is how God’s children reflect their Father, who sends sun and rain on good and evil alike. You must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.

You shall love your neighbor. From Leviticus 19:18. In its context, “neighbour” meant a fellow Israelite, though Leviticus 19:34 extends the command to foreigners living among them.

And hate your enemy. These words are not in the Old Testament. They were a popular inference: if I must love my neighbour, I may hate my enemy. The Dead Sea Scrolls community at Qumran taught its members to love the sons of light and hate the sons of darkness. Some psalms ask God to judge the wicked (Psalm 139:21–22), but those are prayers about God’s enemies, not permission for personal hatred.

But I say to you, Love your enemies. “Love” here is agapē: not warm feelings, but active goodwill, seeking another’s good whatever they deserve. You cannot always feel affection for an enemy, but you can act for their good. Luke adds: do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you (Luke 6:27–28). Even the Old Testament commanded helping an enemy’s ox or donkey (Exodus 23:4–5), and feeding a hungry enemy (Proverbs 25:21).

And pray for those who persecute you. Prayer is the hardest and deepest form of love. It is very difficult to hate someone you are sincerely praying for. Jesus prayed for those who crucified him (Luke 23:34); Stephen prayed for those who stoned him (Acts 7:60).

So that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven. Not to become God’s children by loving enemies, but to show that you are, by sharing his character (see v. 9).

For he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust. God shows kindness even to those who hate him. Every sunrise and every rainfall, which farmers depended on, is a gift to the wicked as well as the righteous. Theologians call this common grace: God’s goodness to all people, not only to believers (Acts 14:17). God loved his enemies supremely by sending his Son to die for them (Romans 5:8, 10).

For if you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Anyone can do that. It is not distinctive.

Do not even the tax collectors do the same? Tax collectors were Jews who collected taxes for the Romans or for Herod, often cheating and overcharging, and were despised as traitors and thieves. Even they love their friends.

And if you greet only your brothers. Greeting in that culture meant wishing someone peace and wellbeing. It was a sign of acceptance.

Do not even the Gentiles do the same? Pagans do it too.

You therefore must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect. “Perfect” (teleios) means complete, whole, mature, undivided. In context, it means being complete in love: loving not just friends but enemies, as God does. Luke’s parallel says, be merciful, even as your Father is merciful (Luke 6:36). The standard is God himself. It echoes Leviticus 19:2: you shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians must achieve sinless perfection in this life, or that they are lost if they fall short. No one keeps this command perfectly except Christ. It is the goal of the Christian life, the direction we grow, and it drives us to Christ for forgiveness and to the Spirit for strength. Nor does loving enemies mean pretending they are not enemies, trusting them naively, or failing to seek justice. Love can pray for an abuser while reporting him to the police.

Where Christians differ: perfectionism. Some Wesleyan and holiness traditions teach that Christians can reach “entire sanctification” in this life, a state of perfect love in which they no longer sin deliberately. The Reformed tradition holds that believers remain sinners until death, though truly and increasingly made holy (1 John 1:8; Romans 7:14–25; Westminster Confession 13.2). Verdict: perfection is the goal, never fully reached in this life; complete only when we see Christ (1 John 3:2).

In a sentence. Love your enemies and pray for them, as your Father does good even to the wicked, for his complete love is your standard.

On a Tuesday. Who is your enemy, the person who has hurt you or opposes you? Pray for them by name today, asking God to bless them.

For worship. Thank God that while you were his enemy, he loved you and gave his Son for you.
verseByVerse.note: “Hate your enemy” is not in the law; it was a popular inference from it. Tax collectors were despised as collaborators.

parallels.desc: you shall be holy, for I am holy

5.theology:
The Law and the Gospel: The Threefold Use of the Law. Reformed theology has distinguished three uses of the law: the civil use (restraining evil in society), the pedagogical use (revealing sin and driving us to Christ), and the normative use (guiding the life of the believer). Matthew 5 exercises the second use with particular intensity: Jesus presses the law so deeply inward that no one can claim compliance, and in doing so drives every hearer to the mercy of the one who fulfilled what we cannot.

But Matthew 5 also exercises the third use: the Beatitudes, the salt and light images, and the love of enemies are not legal demands for the unregenerate but the description of the life the Spirit produces in those who are already citizens of the kingdom. The Sermon on the Mount is simultaneously gospel (this is what the kingdom looks like) and law (this is what you cannot achieve without the Spirit). Held together, they produce the only life worth living: dependent, transformed, and directed toward the glory of the Father.
5.examples:
Then: The Beatitudes describe the whole history of faithful Israel: Abel the righteous who was persecuted, Abraham the meek who sojourned in a land not his own, Hannah who mourned and was comforted, David the poor in spirit who wrote “a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise” (Ps. 51:17). The Beatitudes are not new values; they are the values of the faithful covenant people, now fully embodied in the King who pronounces them and perfectly exemplified in his own life.

Now: The world’s beatitudes are the inverse of Jesus’: blessed are the confident, the successful, the powerful, the popular, the comfortable. The Sermon on the Mount is a collision with that value system at every point. The Christian who takes these beatitudes seriously will find themselves increasingly out of step with the surrounding culture — and increasingly at home in the kingdom. The persecution promised in verses 10–12 is not a possible outcome but a promised one: the world does not celebrate the values of the kingdom because the world is not the kingdom. But the kingdom is coming — and the persecuted will inherit it.

6.title: The Hidden Life of the Kingdom
6.text: <sup>1</sup>“Beware of practicing your righteousness before other people in order to be seen by them, for then you will have no reward from your Father who is in heaven. <sup>2</sup>“Thus, when you give to the needy, sound no trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may be praised by others. Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward. <sup>3</sup>But when you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing, <sup>4</sup>so that your giving may be in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you. <sup>5</sup>“And when you pray, you must not be like the hypocrites. For they love to stand and pray in the synagogues and at the street corners, that they may be seen by others. Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward. <sup>6</sup>But when you pray, go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you. <sup>7</sup>“And when you pray, do not heap up empty phrases as the Gentiles do, for they think that they will be heard for their many words. <sup>8</sup>Do not be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask him. <sup>9</sup>Pray then like this: “Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name. <sup>10</sup>Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. <sup>11</sup>Give us this day our daily bread, <sup>12</sup>and forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors. <sup>13</sup>And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. <sup>14</sup>For if you forgive others their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you, <sup>15</sup>but if you do not forgive others their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses. <sup>16</sup>“And when you fast, do not look gloomy like the hypocrites, for they disfigure their faces that their fasting may be seen by others. Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward. <sup>17</sup>But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, <sup>18</sup>that your fasting may not be seen by others but by your Father who is in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you. <sup>19</sup>“Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal, <sup>20</sup>but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in and steal. <sup>21</sup>For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. <sup>22</sup>“The eye is the lamp of the body. So, if your eye is healthy, your whole body will be full of light, <sup>23</sup>but if your eye is bad, your whole body will be full of darkness. If then the light in you is darkness, how great is the darkness! <sup>24</sup>“No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money. <sup>25</sup>“Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat or what you will drink, nor about your body, what you will put on. Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothing? <sup>26</sup>Look at the birds of the air: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they? <sup>27</sup>And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life? <sup>28</sup>And why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin, <sup>29</sup>yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. <sup>30</sup>But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which today is alive and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, will he not much more clothe you, O you of little faith? <sup>31</sup>Therefore do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘What shall we wear?’ <sup>32</sup>For the Gentiles seek after all these things, and your heavenly Father knows that you need them all. <sup>33</sup>But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you. <sup>34</sup>“Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Sufficient for the day is its own trouble.
6.overview:
Chapter 6 is a sustained meditation on hiddenness. Give in secret. Pray in secret. Fast without showing it. The recurring phrase is “your Father who sees in secret will reward you” — and it upends the entire economy of religious performance. If God sees in secret, then the audience that matters most cannot be seen. The religious life that performs for human approval has traded the eternal reward for the temporary one, and the exchange is catastrophic.

At the centre of the chapter stands the Lord’s Prayer — six petitions that together describe the whole of what the kingdom life looks like in communion with the Father. First, God’s glory: hallowed be your name. Then God’s reign: your kingdom come. Then dependence: daily bread. Then forgiveness: both received and given. Then protection: from temptation, from evil. The prayer moves from adoration to petition, from God’s agenda to human need, from the cosmic to the daily. It is the complete grammar of prayer in a few short lines.

The chapter ends with an antidote to anxiety that is also a diagnosis of its cause. Anxiety is the fruit of serving the wrong master (v. 24). When God and money compete for ultimate allegiance, anxiety is the symptom of the conflict. The cure is not financial security but reorientation of treasure: seek first the kingdom, and the Father who clothes the lilies and feeds the birds will add what you need. This is not a prosperity promise; it is a priority promise. When the kingdom is first, everything else finds its proper place.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — Piety Before the Father: Giving, Prayer, and Fasting
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus addresses three practices central to Jewish piety — almsgiving, prayer, and fasting — and in each case distinguishes the performance of these acts for human recognition from the genuine practice of them before God. The hypocrites have their reward: human applause, now and fully paid. Those who give, pray, and fast before the Father alone receive what the Father alone can give. The section includes the Lord's Prayer as the model of kingdom-oriented prayer: God-centered in its priorities, dependent in its petitions, and honest about the human need for forgiveness. Some details the summary passes over, all treated in the verse-by-verse. The prayer's shape: six petitions in two halves of three — the first three each say your (name, kingdom, will), the second three each say us (give us, forgive us, lead us not). Nothing about our needs appears until God has been addressed three times, and the first three are not requests for God to acquire anything — his name is already holy and his will already done in heaven; they ask that these become true here. Every pronoun in the prayer is plural. There is not one singular pronoun in it: a man praying alone at three in the morning still cannot say "me", and is asking for bread for people he has never met. Daily (v. 11) is epiousios, a word that appears nowhere in Greek literature before this — Origen, a native speaker, thought the evangelists had coined it. The two likely readings ("necessary for existence" and "for the coming day") arrive at the same place: one day's supply, asked one day at a time, which is the manna arrangement of Exodus 16 put into every Christian's mouth. Debts (v. 12) is Matthew's word, the commercial term for what is owed; Luke has "sins"; the familiar "trespasses" came in through Tyndale and the Prayer Book. A trespass is a line crossed and is over when it is over; a debt is a sum outstanding, which is the truer picture. And the tense of "as we also have forgiven" is past — already done, before the asking — matching 5:23-24, where the gift is left at the altar until the matter downstairs is settled.
verseByVerse.theology: The three acts — giving, prayer, fasting — are not optional extras but the basic disciplines of covenant life: relationship with the neighbor (giving), relationship with God (prayer), and relationship with the self (fasting). Jesus does not question whether his disciples will do these things; he assumes they will ("when you give," "when you pray," "when you fast"). The question is motive and audience. Hypocrisy is not performing religious acts — it is performing them for the wrong audience. The hypocrite plays to the crowd; the disciple plays to the Father. The Father's reward — his presence, his approval, his delight — is infinitely superior to human applause.
verseByVerse.examples: The Lord's Prayer contains the whole theology of the kingdom in miniature. It begins with the Father's character and glory (hallowed be your name, your kingdom come, your will be done) before turning to human need (daily bread, forgiveness, protection). The order is the order of Christian living: God first, then us. The disciple who prays this prayer daily is being trained in a way of seeing the world: God's kingdom is the primary reality; my needs are real but secondary; forgiveness received must be forgiveness extended.

verseByVerse.quote: Beware of practicing your righteousness before other people in order to be seen by them, for then you will have no reward from your Father who is in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus now turns from what we do to why we do it. Be careful not to perform your religious duties in order to be admired by people. If that is your aim, the admiration is all the reward you will get; your Father in heaven will give you none.

The connection. Chapter 5 showed a righteousness deeper than the Pharisees’ in what we do (5:20). Chapter 6 shows it in why we do it. The Pharisees’ religion was often performed for an audience. Jesus takes three central acts of Jewish devotion, giving to the poor, prayer and fasting, and shows how each can be ruined by the desire to be seen (vv. 2–18).

Beware. Pay close attention. The danger is real and subtle, and it is a danger for religious people especially.

Practicing your righteousness. Doing religious duties: acts that are right in themselves. Jesus assumes his disciples will give, pray and fast (“when you give”, “when you pray”, “when you fast”, vv. 2, 5, 16). The issue is not whether but how.

Before other people in order to be seen by them. The words “in order to be seen” are the key. The Greek word for “seen” (theathēnai) gives us “theatre”. Religion becomes a performance, and other people the audience.

For then you will have no reward from your Father who is in heaven. God rewards what is done for him. If we do it for human praise, we have chosen our reward, and that is the one we receive. The sense is: you cannot have both.

The reward. Jesus speaks freely about reward (5:12; 6:4, 6, 18; 10:42). The reward is not wages earned, as if God were in our debt, but God’s generous and fatherly recognition of what his children do for him. Above all, the reward is God himself: his approval, his presence, and the joy of the kingdom. C. S. Lewis observed that the proper rewards are not simply tacked on to the activity, but are the activity itself in its completion, as marriage is the proper reward of real love.

What it does not mean. Not that good works must always be hidden. Jesus has just said, let your light shine so that people see your good works (5:16). The difference is the aim: in 5:16 the goal is that people glorify God; here the goal is that people admire me. Public prayer, giving and worship are not wrong. Nor is it wrong to want God’s reward: Jesus himself appeals to it as a motive. What is wrong is seeking human applause for acts meant for God.

In a sentence. Do not perform religious duties to be admired by people, or human admiration will be your only reward.

On a Tuesday. Before you post about your church activity, your Bible reading or your charity, ask yourself honestly: for whose eyes am I doing this?

parallels.desc: they do all their deeds to be seen

verseByVerse.quote: Thus, when you give to the needy, sound no trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may be praised by others. Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward. But when you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing, so that your giving may be in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When you give to the poor, do not make a show of it as the hypocrites do to win praise. They have their reward already. Give so secretly that even your own left hand does not know what your right hand is doing, and your Father, who sees in secret, will reward you.

When you give to the needy. Literally “when you do mercy”, almsgiving. Giving to the poor was a central duty in Judaism (Deuteronomy 15:7–11), counted along with prayer and fasting as one of the three pillars of devotion.

Sound no trumpet before you. Probably a figure of speech for publicising one’s generosity, like “blowing your own trumpet”. Some suggest it refers to trumpet-shaped collection boxes in the temple, which rang loudly when coins were thrown in, or to trumpets blown at public fasts when gifts were made. Either way: do not advertise your giving.

As the hypocrites do. “Hypocrite” (hypokritēs) was the Greek word for a stage actor, who wore a mask and played a part. A religious hypocrite plays the part of a godly person for an audience. Jesus uses the word more in Matthew than anywhere else, especially of the Pharisees (chapter 23).

In the synagogues and in the streets. The public places where people would notice.

That they may be praised by others. Their real aim.

Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward. “Received” (apechousin) was a commercial term written on receipts: “paid in full”. They wanted praise; they got it; the account is closed. There is nothing more to come.

But when you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing. A vivid exaggeration. Give so quietly that it is almost hidden from yourself. Do not even congratulate yourself or keep a mental record of your generosity. Self-admiration is as dangerous as the admiration of others.

So that your giving may be in secret. Away from the audience.

And your Father who sees in secret will reward you. God sees everything, including what no one else does. Nothing done for him is overlooked. Notice “your Father”: the relationship changes everything. A child does not perform for a father; he loves him.

What it does not mean. Not that every gift must be anonymous, or that it is wrong for a church to know what members give, or for public gifts to be recorded for accountability. Barnabas’ gift was known (Acts 4:36–37). The issue is the motive. Nor does “reward” mean that giving is an investment that God will repay with money, as the prosperity gospel teaches. God’s reward is his approval and eternal treasure (v. 20), not necessarily earthly wealth.

In a sentence. Give to the needy quietly, for God and not for applause, and your Father who sees in secret will reward you.

On a Tuesday. Give something this week that no one will ever know about, and do not mention it to anyone.
verseByVerse.note: “Sound no trumpet” is probably a figure of speech for making a show of giving.

verseByVerse.quote: And when you pray, you must not be like the hypocrites. For they love to stand and pray in the synagogues and at the street corners, that they may be seen by others. Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward. But when you pray, go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When you pray, do not be like the hypocrites who love to pray where people can see and admire them. Go into a private room, shut the door, and pray to your Father, who is there in secret. He sees, and he will reward you.

When you pray. Jesus assumes his disciples pray. Devout Jews prayed at set times each day, often three times: morning, afternoon (the hour of the temple sacrifice) and evening (Daniel 6:10; Acts 3:1).

You must not be like the hypocrites. Actors in religion (see v. 2).

For they love to stand and pray in the synagogues and at the street corners. Standing was the normal posture for prayer. If the hour of prayer came while one was out, one stopped and prayed where one was. The hypocrites made sure they were in the most public places when the hour arrived: the street corner, where crowds passed, or a prominent position in the synagogue.

That they may be seen by others. Their prayer was addressed to God, but aimed at people.

They have received their reward. Paid in full (see v. 2).

But when you pray, go into your room. The word (tameion) means an inner storeroom. Most homes in Galilee had one room for living, and perhaps a small storeroom, which was the only place with a door that could be shut. It was the most private place in the house.

And shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret. God is not seen, but he is present. Prayer is a meeting with a person, not a performance before an audience. Shutting the door shuts out distraction and the desire to be seen.

And your Father who sees in secret will reward you. God hears and answers. Prayer is not wasted, even when no one else knows.

What it does not mean. Not that public prayer is wrong. Jesus prayed publicly (11:25; John 11:41–42), and the early church prayed together (Acts 1:14; 4:24). Jesus teaches a prayer that begins “Our Father” and is meant to be prayed together (v. 9). The point is that private prayer is the test of true prayer. A person who prays eloquently in public but never in private is praying to people.

In a sentence. Pray in private to your Father, not in public to be admired, and he who sees in secret will answer.

On a Tuesday. Find your “room” today: a place and a time, even ten minutes, where you can shut the door on distractions and speak with your Father.
verseByVerse.note: Jews commonly prayed standing, at set hours; the “room” was an inner storeroom, the one private space in a small house.

parallels.desc: the Pharisee and the tax collector

verseByVerse.quote: And when you pray, do not heap up empty phrases as the Gentiles do, for they think that they will be heard for their many words. Do not be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When you pray, do not pile up meaningless words, as pagans do, thinking that God will listen if they say enough. Do not be like them, because your Father already knows what you need before you ask.

Do not heap up empty phrases. The word (battalogēsēte) may imitate the sound of babbling: “blah-blah”. It means repeating words mechanically, without thought or heart.

As the Gentiles do. Pagan religions often used long lists of divine names and titles, magic formulas and endless repetitions to get the gods’ attention or force their hand. The prophets of Baal cried “O Baal, answer us!” from morning to noon (1 Kings 18:26). The crowd in Ephesus shouted “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” for two hours (Acts 19:34).

For they think that they will be heard for their many words. The pagan idea of prayer was a technique: the right words, enough times, would obtain the result. Prayer became a way of manipulating God.

Do not be like them. The first wrong motive in prayer was to impress people (v. 5); the second is to manipulate God.

For your Father knows what you need before you ask him. God is not ignorant, distant or reluctant. He is a Father who knows and cares. We do not pray to inform him or persuade him to be kind; we pray because he is our Father, who wants his children to come to him, depend on him, and receive from his hand.

If God knows, why pray? Because prayer is not about giving God information. It is about relationship: children talking with their Father. It expresses our dependence and trust. And God has chosen to work through the prayers of his people; he gives some things because we ask (James 4:2). Calvin said that we pray not to inform God, but to stir ourselves to seek him, to learn to bring every desire to him, and to receive his gifts with thanks.

What it does not mean. Not that long prayers or repeated requests are wrong. Jesus prayed all night (Luke 6:12), repeated the same prayer three times in Gethsemane (26:44), and taught persistence in prayer (Luke 18:1–8). The problem is not length or repetition but empty words and a magical view of prayer. Nor does it forbid written or set prayers: Jesus gives one in the next verse. The danger is reciting any prayer, written or spontaneous, without meaning it.

In a sentence. Do not try to manipulate God with many words; pray as a child to a Father who already knows what you need.

On a Tuesday. When you next say the Lord’s Prayer or grace before a meal, slow down and mean every word.

parallels.desc: the prophets of Baal cry from morning to noon

verseByVerse.quote: Pray then like this: "Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus gives a model prayer, the Lord’s Prayer. It begins with God: addressing him as our Father in heaven, and asking that his name be honoured, his kingdom come, and his will be done on earth as perfectly as it is in heaven.

Pray then like this. Not “pray only these words”, but “pray like this”, in this way, with this pattern. Luke’s version is slightly different and shorter (Luke 11:2–4), showing that Jesus gave it as a model, not a fixed formula. But it can also rightly be prayed word for word, as the church has always done.

The shape. The prayer has two parts. The first three requests concern God: his name, his kingdom, his will. The second three concern our needs: bread, forgiveness, protection. God’s glory comes first, then our needs. The order teaches us what matters most.

Our Father. “Father” in Aramaic is Abba, the word Jesus used in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36), and the Spirit teaches believers to say it (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6). Jews sometimes called God “Father” in prayer, but the intimacy with which Jesus addressed God, and taught his disciples to do so, was new. We may call God “Father” only because we are adopted into his family through Christ (Ephesians 1:5; John 1:12). “Our”: the prayer is plural. Even when prayed alone, it is prayed as one of a family.

In heaven. Our Father is near, but he is also above us, sovereign, holy and all-powerful. “Our Father” gives intimacy; “in heaven” gives reverence. He is a Father who is able to do what we ask.

Hallowed be your name. “Hallow” means to make holy, treat as holy, honour as holy. God’s “name” means not just his title, but himself as he has revealed himself: his character, reputation and glory (Exodus 34:5–7). We cannot make God holier than he is. We ask that he would be recognised, honoured and worshipped as holy: in our lives, in the church and throughout the world. It is the prayer that God would be treated as God. The third commandment forbids taking his name in vain (Exodus 20:7); this prayer asks for the opposite.

Your kingdom come. God’s kingdom is his reign (see 3:2). It came with Jesus, and it grows as the gospel spreads and people submit to him. It will come in full when Christ returns. We pray for both: the spread of the gospel now, and the coming of Christ at the end. The early church prayed Maranatha, “Our Lord, come!” (1 Corinthians 16:22; Revelation 22:20).

Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. In heaven, God’s will is done perfectly, gladly and immediately by the angels (Psalm 103:20–21). We pray that it would be done that way on earth: in the world, in the church, and in our own lives. To pray this sincerely means surrendering our own wills. Jesus prayed it in Gethsemane: not my will, but yours, be done (26:39, 42). “On earth as it is in heaven” probably belongs to all three requests.

What it does not mean. Not that “your will be done” is a passive resignation, a shrug that whatever happens is God’s will. It is an active prayer for God’s commands to be obeyed and his purposes to triumph. Nor does “your kingdom come” mean that we bring the kingdom by our own efforts, social or political. It is God’s kingdom; we pray for it, proclaim it, and live under it, but he brings it.

In a sentence. Pray first that God, our Father in heaven, would be honoured as holy, that his reign would come, and that his will would be done on earth as in heaven.

On a Tuesday. Before you bring your requests to God today, spend a few minutes praying for his name, his kingdom and his will. Let your concerns take second place to his.

For worship. Pray these words slowly now, meaning each one.
verseByVerse.note: “Hallowed” means treated as holy.

parallels.desc: I will vindicate the holiness of my great name

verseByVerse.quote: Give us this day our daily bread,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prayer turns to our needs. First: give us today the bread we need for today. We depend on our Father for everything, even our daily food.

Give us. We ask as dependents. Everything we have comes from God (James 1:17). Even those who earn their own food receive it from God, who gives the health to work, the rain and the harvest (Deuteronomy 8:17–18).

This day. One day at a time. Like the manna in the wilderness, which was given daily and could not be stored (Exodus 16:4, 19–21), God teaches his people to depend on him day by day.

Our daily bread. “Bread” stands for all the necessities of life: food, clothing, shelter, health. Luther’s Small Catechism explains daily bread as everything that belongs to the support and needs of the body: food, drink, clothing, home, family, work, good government, peace, health and friends. “Daily” (epiousios) is a rare word, found almost nowhere else in Greek. It may mean “for today”, “necessary”, or “for tomorrow” (asked for each morning). Proverbs 30:8–9 is a good parallel: give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the food that is needed for me.

What it does not mean. Not a prayer for luxuries, but for needs. Nor is it a reason not to work: God usually provides daily bread through work (2 Thessalonians 3:10–12). Nor does it mean that physical needs are unspiritual. Jesus puts them in the prayer. God cares about our bodies. Some early Christian writers spiritualised “bread” to mean the Lord’s Supper or Christ himself; Christ is the bread of life (John 6:35), but the first meaning here is ordinary food.

In a sentence. Ask your Father each day for the things you need for that day, and trust him for tomorrow.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for your next meal before you eat it, and remember those who will pray this prayer today with empty cupboards. How might you be God’s answer to their prayer?

parallels.desc: feed me with the food that is needful for me

verseByVerse.quote: and forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Next: forgive us our sins, which are like debts we owe God, just as we have forgiven those who have sinned against us. Those who are forgiven must forgive.

And forgive us. We need forgiveness as much as we need bread. Every believer must pray this daily. Even forgiven Christians still sin and need to come back to their Father for cleansing (1 John 1:8–9).

Our debts. Sin pictured as a debt. We owe God perfect love and obedience; every sin is a failure to pay what we owe, adding to an unpayable debt (18:24). Luke’s version says “sins” (Luke 11:4). The traditional English form “trespasses” comes from verses 14–15. To forgive a debt is to cancel it: the creditor bears the loss. God can cancel our debt because Christ paid it (Colossians 2:13–14).

As we also have forgiven our debtors. Not that our forgiving earns God’s forgiveness. Rather, a person who has received God’s forgiveness will forgive others. The tense in Greek suggests we have already forgiven before we ask. We cannot honestly ask God to forgive our vast debt while we hold others to their small debts against us (18:21–35). This is the only request in the prayer that Jesus explains further (vv. 14–15). It is that important.

What it does not mean. Not that forgiveness depends on our performance, as if God forgives us in exact proportion to our forgiving others. That would be salvation by works. God forgives freely, for Christ’s sake. But the unwillingness to forgive shows a heart that has not truly grasped grace. Nor does forgiving someone mean pretending they did nothing wrong, trusting them again immediately, or removing all consequences (see Ephesians 4:32).

In a sentence. Ask God to forgive your sins, as those who have already forgiven others.

On a Tuesday. When you pray this today, name the person you find hard to forgive. Ask God for grace to cancel the debt.
verseByVerse.note: Sin is pictured as a debt owed to God.

verseByVerse.quote: And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Finally: do not bring us into the place of testing where we would fall, but rescue us from evil and the evil one. Believers know they are weak, and ask their Father to protect them.

And lead us not into temptation. The word (peirasmos) means both testing and temptation (see 4:1). God does not tempt anyone to sin (James 1:13). But he does lead his people into testing: he led Jesus into the wilderness (4:1), and he tested Abraham (Genesis 22:1). The request means: do not let us be brought into trials that overwhelm us; keep us from situations where we would fall. It is the prayer of someone who knows their weakness and does not trust themselves. Jesus told the disciples in Gethsemane to watch and pray that they might not enter into temptation (26:41). Peter, who boasted he would never fall, fell that same night.

But deliver us from evil. “Deliver” means rescue, snatch away from danger. “Evil” can be translated “the evil one”, the devil (the ESV footnote). Both are possible. The devil is the tempter (4:3); evil is his work. Either way, we need rescuing, and only God can rescue us.

The doxology. Many later manuscripts add “For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory, forever. Amen.” This ending is not in the earliest manuscripts, and it was probably added in early church worship, following David’s prayer in 1 Chronicles 29:11. It is a fitting, biblical ending, and the church rightly uses it in worship, but it was probably not part of what Matthew wrote.

What it does not mean. Not that God might lure us into sin if we do not ask him not to. He never does that. Nor does the prayer promise that believers will never face temptation or trials: James says to count it all joy when you meet trials (James 1:2), because they strengthen faith. God promises that with every temptation he will provide the way of escape (1 Corinthians 10:13). The prayer asks him to keep us, in and through testing.

In a sentence. Ask your Father to keep you from testing that would overwhelm you, and to rescue you from evil and the evil one.

On a Tuesday. Where do you know you are weak? Pray this request about that specific area before you enter the day, and avoid walking into the temptation you are praying against.

For worship. Yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory, for ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes the alternative “the evil one,” and that some manuscripts add “For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory, forever. Amen.”

parallels.desc: God will not let you be tempted beyond your ability
keep them from the evil one

verseByVerse.quote: For if you forgive others their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you, but if you do not forgive others their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus explains the request about forgiveness. If you forgive others, your Father will forgive you. But if you refuse to forgive others, your Father will not forgive you.

For if you forgive others their trespasses. “Trespasses” (paraptōmata) means false steps, wrongs (see Ephesians 2:1). Jesus returns to the one request that needs comment.
