Your heavenly Father will also forgive you. Those who forgive show that they belong to the forgiven family.

But if you do not forgive others their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses. A solemn warning. Someone who refuses to forgive cannot have truly received God’s forgiveness, because grace received makes a person gracious. The parable of the unforgiving servant (18:23–35) shows the logic: the servant who was forgiven ten thousand talents and then choked a fellow servant over a hundred denarii proved he had never understood the forgiveness he had received.

The order. God’s forgiveness comes first; ours flows from it. Paul says, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you (Ephesians 4:32). Our forgiveness of others is not the cause of God’s forgiveness, but its fruit and evidence.

What it does not mean. Not that a Christian who struggles to forgive, or who has to forgive the same hurt many times, is unforgiven. Forgiveness of deep wounds is often a long process, and Jesus’ words are aimed at a settled refusal to forgive, not at the struggle. Nor does it mean that forgiving others earns salvation. God forgives freely, for Christ’s sake, those who come to him in repentance; and repentance includes letting go of our grudges against others. And forgiveness does not require us to deny the wrong, to trust the other person again immediately, or to stop seeking justice through proper authority.

In a sentence. Those who have truly received God’s forgiveness will forgive others; a settled refusal to forgive shows that grace has not been received.

On a Tuesday. Is there a grudge you are nursing? Bring it to God today, remembering how much he has forgiven you.

parallels.desc: forgive your brother from your heart

verseByVerse.quote: And when you fast, do not look gloomy like the hypocrites, for they disfigure their faces that their fasting may be seen by others. Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward. But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, that your fasting may not be seen by others but by your Father who is in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When you fast, do not look miserable so that people notice how devout you are. Groom yourself as usual, so that only your Father, who sees in secret, knows you are fasting. He will reward you.

When you fast. Fasting is going without food (sometimes also drink) for a period, for a spiritual purpose. Jesus assumes his disciples will fast (9:15). In the Old Testament, the only required fast was on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29–31). But people fasted in times of mourning, repentance, danger, or seeking God (Judges 20:26; 2 Samuel 12:16; Esther 4:16; Daniel 9:3; Joel 2:12). Some Pharisees fasted twice a week, on Mondays and Thursdays (Luke 18:12).

Do not look gloomy like the hypocrites. Some made a show of their fasting, looking sad and pale.

For they disfigure their faces. Perhaps by not washing, leaving their hair unkempt, or putting ashes on their heads. The word means to make unrecognisable, and is a wordplay with “appear” in Greek: they make their faces disappear so that they may appear to be fasting.

That their fasting may be seen by others. The motive again (v. 1).

But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face. Anointing the head with olive oil was part of normal grooming, like combing your hair. Look normal.

That your fasting may not be seen by others but by your Father who is in secret. Fasting is between you and God.

Why fast? Fasting expresses humility and dependence on God; it sharpens prayer; it expresses sorrow for sin; and it trains us to say no to the body’s appetites, which helps us say no to sin. It is not a way of forcing God to act or earning his favour, but a way of seeking him with our whole self. Isaiah 58 condemns fasting that is combined with injustice, and calls for a fast that shares bread with the hungry.

What it does not mean. Not that fasting is commanded at fixed times for Christians, or that it earns merit. The Reformers rejected compulsory fasts on set days, while encouraging voluntary fasting. Nor does it mean that a church may not call a corporate fast publicly (Acts 13:2–3; 14:23). The issue is showing off. And fasting is not a way of losing weight or a health practice in this context; it is a spiritual discipline. Those with medical conditions or eating disorders should seek wise counsel; there are other ways to deny oneself.

In a sentence. Fast quietly, for God alone, without letting people see, and your Father will reward you.

On a Tuesday. Consider fasting from one meal this week, using the time to pray for something specific. Tell no one.
verseByVerse.note: Anointing the head with oil was part of ordinary grooming. Some Pharisees fasted twice a week (Luke 18:12). A wordplay: they disfigure (aphanizousin, literally “make invisible”) their faces so that they may appear (phanōsin) to others.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–34 — Treasure, Vision, and Trust: Seeking the Kingdom First
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second half of chapter 6 addresses anxiety about material provision through three related teachings. Disciples are commanded not to store up earthly treasure (perishable, vulnerable) but heavenly treasure (imperishable, secure). The eye as the lamp of the body: a healthy eye (generous spirit) fills the whole person with light; a diseased eye (stinginess) fills it with darkness. You cannot serve both God and money. Then the great anxiety passage: do not be anxious about food or clothing, because the Father who feeds the birds and clothes the lilies knows your needs. Seek first the kingdom and his righteousness, and everything else will be added. The three enemies of treasure are not decorative: wealth took three forms and Jesus names the destroyer of each — fine cloth eaten by moth, grain and metal by the second word (which means "eating away" and covers rust, corrosion and vermin), and coin, which neither can touch, taken by the thief, whose verb means "to dig through" (mud-brick walls were tunnelled, not forced). Every exit is closed before the point is made. The eye is a Hebrew idiom, not an optical metaphor: "a good eye" meant a generous person and "an evil eye" a stingy one (Prov. 22:9; 28:22), which is why these verses sit between the treasure and the money rather than interrupting them. And mammon is an Aramaic word Jesus leaves untranslated, whose root appears to be the one behind Hebrew "faith" and our "amen" — most likely meaning that in which one puts one's trust, which makes the sentence almost self-evident. On the anxiety passage, note that the command comes three times (vv. 25, 31, 34), that the birds are not idle (they do not sow, reap or store — that is, they do not hoard against a future they cannot see), that the "lilies" are probably the wild anemones that carpet Galilee for a few weeks and are then swept up as oven fuel, and that "O you of little faith" is a word almost unique to Matthew which he uses four times, every time to disciples and never to unbelievers. The guard on anxiety is the most important thing in the section and is given in full below: this passage has been used to tell people with anxiety disorders that their illness is sin, and that is a cruelty the text does not authorise.
verseByVerse.theology: The teaching on anxiety is not a command to be carefree but to be properly ordered: anxiety is the symptom of inverted priorities — seeking the lesser things first and trusting God to manage them, rather than seeking God first and trusting him to manage everything else. The birds and lilies do not "seek" anything in the human sense; they simply exist in dependence on the Creator who provides. The disciple is not to live without thought for the future but without anxious preoccupation with it — trusting the Father's knowledge and provision while attending to the kingdom. Anxiety is fundamentally a theological problem: it reflects a practical unbelief in the Father's care.
verseByVerse.examples: "Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness" is the organizing principle of the entire Sermon on the Mount. Everything else — the beatitudes, the antitheses, the disciplines of chapter 6 — flows from this reorientation of desire. The person who is genuinely seeking God's kingdom first finds that anxiety about secondary things diminishes, not because circumstances change, but because the center of gravity of the heart has shifted. Worry is the heart occupied with what it fears it won't have; trust is the heart occupied with the One who has everything and gives freely.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal, but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in and steal. For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. The eye is the lamp of the body. So, if your eye is healthy, your whole body will be full of light, but if your eye is bad, your whole body will be full of darkness. If then the light in you is darkness, how great is the darkness! No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not pile up wealth on earth, where it decays or is stolen, but store up treasure in heaven, where it is safe for ever. What you treasure will capture your heart. Your eye, the way you see and desire, determines whether your whole life is in light or darkness. And you cannot serve both God and money.

Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth. “Lay up” means to store, accumulate, hoard. “For yourselves”: for selfish security and enjoyment.

Where moth and rust destroy. In the ancient world, wealth was often stored as fine clothing, which moths ate, or as metal and grain, which rust or vermin destroyed. The word “rust” (brōsis) literally means “eating”: anything that consumes.

And where thieves break in and steal. Houses in Palestine were often made of mud brick. Thieves could literally “dig through” the walls (the Greek word). Earthly treasure is never secure. Today it may be inflation, market crashes, fraud, or simply death, which takes us away from everything we own (Luke 12:20).

But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven. Treasure in heaven is everything done for God and his kingdom: generosity to the poor (19:21; Luke 12:33), faithful service, people won to Christ, a life spent for God. It cannot be destroyed. And above all, treasure in heaven is God himself (Psalm 73:25–26).

For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. The key principle. The heart follows the money. Whatever you value most will capture your thoughts, desires and loyalty. If your wealth is on earth, your heart is chained to earth. You can tell what you treasure by what you think about when your mind is free, what you worry about, and where you spend your money.

The eye is the lamp of the body. In the ancient world, the eye was thought to be like a lamp, letting light into the body. A healthy eye lets you see clearly.

So, if your eye is healthy. “Healthy” (haplous) means single, sound, and also generous. A “healthy eye” is a generous, undivided focus on God.

But if your eye is bad. “Bad” (ponēros) also means evil. In Jewish idiom, an “evil eye” meant a stingy, envious, grasping attitude (20:15; Deuteronomy 15:9; Proverbs 28:22). So the picture is about money too: a generous heart fills your life with light; a greedy one darkens everything.

If then the light in you is darkness, how great is the darkness! If the very thing that should give you light is corrupted, you are in deep darkness without knowing it. Greed blinds.

No one can serve two masters. “Serve” means to be a slave. A slave could not belong to two owners with full loyalty.

For either he will hate the one and love the other. Hebrew idiom for preferring one over the other (Genesis 29:31; Luke 14:26).

You cannot serve God and money. “Money” translates mamōnas, an Aramaic word, “mammon”, meaning wealth, property, possessions. Jesus personifies it as a rival master, almost a god. Money is not neutral: it demands loyalty, promises security, and competes with God for our trust and love. You can have money; the question is whether it has you.

What it does not mean. Not that owning property, saving, or planning for the future is wrong. Scripture commends the ant that stores up food (Proverbs 6:6–8) and the wise person who leaves an inheritance to his grandchildren (Proverbs 13:22). Paul says a man who does not provide for his family is worse than an unbeliever (1 Timothy 5:8). Stewardship is not covetousness. The difference: stewardship holds money as God’s, uses it for him, saves wisely, gives generously, and trusts God, not the bank balance. Covetousness hoards for its own sake, wants more for self, and trusts wealth instead of God (Luke 12:15–21; 1 Timothy 6:17–19). The question is not how much you have, but what you trust, what you love, and what you do with it.

In a sentence. Invest in what lasts for ever, because your heart follows your treasure, and you cannot serve both God and money.

On a Tuesday. Look at your bank statement this month. What does it say your treasure is? Make one decision this week that moves treasure from earth to heaven.
verseByVerse.note: Wealth was often stored as fine clothing (eaten by moths). A “bad” eye was an idiom for stinginess. The ESV notes that “money” renders mammon, a Semitic word for money or possessions.

parallels.desc: your eye look grudgingly on your poor brother

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat or what you will drink, nor about your body, what you will put on. Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothing? Look at the birds of the air: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they? And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life? And why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin, yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which today is alive and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, will he not much more clothe you, O you of little faith? Therefore do not be anxious, saying, "What shall we eat?" or "What shall we drink?" or "What shall we wear?" For the Gentiles seek after all these things, and your heavenly Father knows that you need them all. But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you. Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Sufficient for the day is its own trouble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore do not be anxious about the basic needs of life: food, drink, clothing. Your Father feeds the birds and clothes the flowers; you are worth far more. Anxiety cannot add an hour to your life. Instead, seek first God’s kingdom and his righteousness, and he will provide what you need. Do not worry about tomorrow; today has enough trouble of its own.

Therefore. Because you serve God, not money (v. 24). The person who trusts money is anxious when money is short; the person who trusts God need not be.

Do not be anxious about your life. “Anxious” (merimnaō) means to be pulled apart, distracted, troubled by care. The word appears six times in this passage. Jesus speaks to people for whom food and clothing were real daily worries: many in Galilee lived at subsistence level, one bad harvest from hunger.

Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothing? God gave you life and a body, the greater gifts. Will he not give the lesser things needed to sustain them?

Look at the birds of the air. Birds do not plant, harvest, or store food in barns. Yet God feeds them. (Jesus does not say birds do not work: they hunt and gather. He says they do not worry or hoard.)

Are you not of more value than they? An argument from lesser to greater: if God cares for birds, he cares far more for his children, made in his image.

And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life? Or “a single cubit to his height” (ESV footnote). Either way: worry achieves nothing. It cannot lengthen your life; if anything, it shortens it.

Consider the lilies of the field. Wildflowers, perhaps the red anemones that covered Galilean hillsides in spring.

They neither toil nor spin. They do not work to make clothes (spinning thread was women’s daily work).

Even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. Solomon was famous for his wealth and splendour (1 Kings 10). A single wildflower, clothed by God, is more beautiful.

The grass of the field, which today is alive and tomorrow is thrown into the oven. Dried grass and weeds were used as fuel for clay ovens. Wildflowers are worth almost nothing, yet God clothes them beautifully.

O you of little faith. A gentle rebuke Jesus gives his disciples several times (8:26; 14:31; 16:8). Anxiety is at root a failure to trust our Father.

For the Gentiles seek after all these things. Pagans, who do not know God as Father, make food and clothing the focus of life. They have nothing else to trust.

And your heavenly Father knows that you need them all. The heart of the passage. You are not an orphan in a hostile universe; you have a Father who knows exactly what you need.

But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness. Make God’s reign and his righteous will your first priority: before food, before clothing, before career, before comfort. “His righteousness” means living as he wills (5:6, 20). “First” does not mean only, but foremost.

And all these things will be added to you. God will provide what you truly need. Not necessarily luxury, but provision. This is a promise to those who seek the kingdom first. David said that he had never seen the righteous forsaken or his children begging for bread (Psalm 37:25).

Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Do not borrow tomorrow’s troubles. God gives grace for each day as it comes.

Sufficient for the day is its own trouble. Each day has enough difficulty. Deal with today’s, and trust God for tomorrow’s.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should not work, plan or save. Birds work; Paul worked; Proverbs commends planning (Proverbs 21:5; 24:27). The difference is between planning and worrying. Planning thinks ahead and takes reasonable steps, then trusts God; worry runs the same fears round and round without trusting him. Nor does it mean that faithful Christians will never go hungry. Paul knew hunger and need (2 Corinthians 11:27; Philippians 4:12), and believers in persecution and famine have died. The promise is that God will provide what we need to do his will and that nothing can separate us from his love (Romans 8:35–39). Nor is anxiety always simple sin. Clinical anxiety is an illness that may need medical care as well as spiritual help, and Christians who struggle with it should not be shamed. Jesus calls us to trust, and he is gentle with the weak.

In a sentence. Do not be eaten up by worry about life’s needs; your Father knows them and will provide, so seek his kingdom first and live one day at a time.

On a Tuesday. Write down what you are anxious about today. Then pray over each item, telling your Father, and leave it with him (Philippians 4:6–7; 1 Peter 5:7). Then do the one thing you can do today.

For worship. Thank your Father for one specific way he has provided for you this week.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “a single hour to his span of life” can also be read “a single cubit to his stature.” Dry grass was used as fuel for clay ovens.

parallels.desc: do not be anxious about anything
cast all your anxieties on him

6.theology:
Prayer and the Fatherhood of God. The Lord’s Prayer is the fullest Trinitarian statement about prayer in the New Testament. We pray to the Father, in the name of the Son (the one who taught us to pray this way and who intercedes for us, Rom. 8:34), in the power of the Spirit (who helps us in our weakness and intercedes with groaning too deep for words, Rom. 8:26). Reformed theology has always understood prayer as Trinitarian from beginning to end: the Father hears, the Son mediates, the Spirit enables.

The address “Our Father” is the fruit of adoption — the doctrine that those who trust in Christ are received into the family of God with all the rights and privileges of sons (Gal. 4:5–6). We do not pray as strangers petitioning a distant deity; we pray as children talking to a Father who knows us, loves us, and has already given us his Son. The confidence of Christian prayer rests entirely on the prior act of God in adoption, not on the fervency or frequency of the one praying.
6.examples:
Then: The contrast between secret devotion and public performance runs through the Old Testament. Hannah prayed so quietly that Eli thought she was drunk (1 Sam. 1:13) — and God heard. Daniel opened his window toward Jerusalem and prayed three times a day without announcement, in full view of a hostile empire (Dan. 6:10). The great saints of Israel prayed to an audience of One — and their prayers are the ones that shaped history. The hypocrites who prayed on street corners are forgotten; their reward was fully paid and fully spent.

Now: The anxiety Jesus addresses in verses 25–34 is the defining emotional experience of our age. Financial anxiety, career anxiety, health anxiety, relationship anxiety — the modern world has more to worry about (in terms of information access about possible threats) than any previous generation. Jesus’ answer is not information management but kingdom orientation: seek first the kingdom, and the Father who holds all things will hold yours. This is not naive — it is the most realistic posture available to a creature who is not God. You are not in control of tomorrow; the Father is. Trust the Father.

7.title: The Narrow Gate
7.text: <sup>1</sup>“Judge not, that you be not judged. <sup>2</sup>For with the judgment you pronounce you will be judged, and with the measure you use it will be measured to you. <sup>3</sup>Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but do not notice the log that is in your own eye? <sup>4</sup>Or how can you say to your brother, ‘Let me take the speck out of your eye,’ when there is the log in your own eye? <sup>5</sup>You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother’s eye. <sup>6</sup>“Do not give dogs what is holy, and do not throw your pearls before pigs, lest they trample them underfoot and turn to attack you. <sup>7</sup>“Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. <sup>8</sup>For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened. <sup>9</sup>Or which one of you, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? <sup>10</sup>Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a serpent? <sup>11</sup>If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him! <sup>12</sup>“So whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them, for this is the Law and the Prophets. <sup>13</sup>“Enter by the narrow gate. For the gate is wide and the way is easy that leads to destruction, and those who enter by it are many. <sup>14</sup>For the gate is narrow and the way is hard that leads to life, and those who find it are few. <sup>15</sup>“Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves. <sup>16</sup>You will recognize them by their fruits. Are grapes gathered from thornbushes, or figs from thistles? <sup>17</sup>So, every healthy tree bears good fruit, but the diseased tree bears bad fruit. <sup>18</sup>A healthy tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor can a diseased tree bear good fruit. <sup>19</sup>Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. <sup>20</sup>Thus you will recognize them by their fruits. <sup>21</sup>“Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven. <sup>22</sup>On that day many will say to me, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works in your name?’ <sup>23</sup>And then will I declare to them, ‘I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of lawlessness.’ <sup>24</sup>“Everyone then who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house on the rock. <sup>25</sup>And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house, but it did not fall, because it had been founded on the rock. <sup>26</sup>And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house on the sand. <sup>27</sup>And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat against that house, and it fell, and great was the fall of it.” <sup>28</sup>And when Jesus finished these sayings, the crowds were astonished at his teaching, <sup>29</sup>for he was teaching them as one who had authority, and not as their scribes.
7.overview:
Chapter 7 concludes the Sermon on the Mount with a series of choices, each framed as a binary: the wide gate or the narrow, the false prophet or the true, the one who hears and does or the one who hears and does not. The Sermon that began with Beatitudes ends with warnings. The kingdom is real and its entrance is narrow; the alternatives are easy and lead to destruction. This is not the comfortable conclusion of a TED talk; it is the solemn close of the greatest sermon ever preached.

The famous “Judge not” (v. 1) is the most misquoted verse in the Bible. Jesus is not prohibiting all moral discernment — he commands it in verse 6 (discern who receives what is holy) and verses 15–16 (recognise false prophets by their fruit). He is prohibiting hypocritical judgment: condemning in others what you excuse in yourself. The log-and-speck image is both humorous and devastating — the person with a beam in their eye offering to perform eye surgery. Self-examination must precede fraternal correction.

The parable of the two builders is the Sermon’s climax and its challenge. Both builders hear the words of Jesus; both face the same storm. The difference is foundation: rock or sand. And the foundation is not intellectual agreement with Jesus’ teaching but doing it — the obedience that grows from genuine faith. The crowds are astonished at the end because Jesus teaches with authority, not as the scribes. He does not say “thus says the LORD”; he says “I say to you.” He is the rock on which the house is built.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–29 — Judgment, Prayer, and the Two Ways: Concluding the Sermon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Sermon on the Mount concludes with four warnings and a call. The warning against judging hypocritically (vv. 1–6), the invitation to persistent prayer (vv. 7–12), and the double warning about the narrow gate and false prophets (vv. 13–23) all converge on the final parable of the two builders (vv. 24–27). The Sermon does not end gently: it ends with a stark choice between two gates, two trees, two confessions, two foundations — and the crowds are astonished not by the gentleness of what they heard but by the authority of the one who said it. The verse-by-verse fills in what a 29-verse summary cannot. On "judge not": the proof that it cannot mean what the world takes it to mean is inside this same chapter — v. 6 requires the hearer to identify "dogs" and "pigs", vv. 15-20 require him to identify false prophets by their fruit, and vv. 21-23 have Jesus distinguishing those who did the Father's will from those who did not. All within twenty-two verses of the command. Elsewhere he settles it in one sentence: "Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment" (Jn. 7:24); and Paul asks, "Is it not those inside the church whom you are to judge?" (1 Cor. 5:12). "With the measure you use" is a rabbinic formula (measure for measure) and is an offer of a choice — a man sets the standard he will be tried by. The speck and the log are a tradesman's joke: karphos is a wood chip, dokos is a roof beam, both from the same building yard, told by a carpenter to people who had watched carpenters work. And v. 6 is a crossover (an X): it is the pigs that trample and the dogs that turn and attack. On prayer (vv. 7-11): "how much more" is the standard rabbinic argument from lesser to greater — and the premise slipped in without pause is that the audience are evil, stated as an agreed fact on the way to proving how kind God is. Bread/stone and fish/serpent are things that look alike (Galilean limestone weathers into loaf-shaped lumps; the lake held a whiskered catfish a Jew could not eat) — so the fear being answered is not malice but substitution. The golden rule (v. 12) is treated at length below. On false prophets: "sheep's clothing" may be the prophetic uniform itself (Zech. 13:4 has false prophets putting on a hairy cloak to deceive), and "ravenous" is harpax, from the verb to snatch — what defines him is that he is taking something. The fruit test cannot be run quickly, and that is not a defect: much damage has been done by men whose fruit would have been obvious in five years and who were given authority in five weeks. "I never knew you" (vv. 21-23) is likewise absent above and is given the fullest treatment in the chapter below. On the two houses: Luke supplies the detail that bites — the wise man dug deep (Lk. 6:48). In that country a dry wadi bed is the most inviting summer site there is, flat and easy to dig; digging down is slow, costly, and invisible when the house is finished. Both houses look identical. And "these words of mine" puts his own sayings where Israel's wisdom tradition put the Torah (Ps. 1:2). Note finally that this closing section is four pairs narrowing — two gates, two trees, two confessions, two foundations — and in every one the wrong option is the comfortable one and the two are hard to tell apart from outside. On the closing formula (v. 28): "when Jesus finished these sayings" occurs five times in Matthew and only five (7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1), each sealing a discourse — five books of teaching from a man who came out of Egypt, through the water, and through forty days in the wilderness. Moses gave five books from a mountain. And "astonished" is ekplesso, to be struck out of position, in the imperfect: they went on being knocked sideways.
verseByVerse.theology: The command not to judge (v. 1) is the most misquoted verse in the Sermon and one of the most misunderstood in the Bible. Jesus does not prohibit discernment (he commands it in v. 6 and vv. 15–20); he prohibits the hypocritical judgment that ignores one's own sin while scrutinizing another's. The warning about false prophets extends the theme: discernment is required, but it must begin with self-examination. The Sermon ends where it must — with the question of foundation. Hearing Jesus's words and not doing them is not neutrality; it is the choice of sand. The storm will decide what you built on.
verseByVerse.examples: The final verse — "he was teaching them as one who had authority, and not as their scribes" — is Matthew's first and defining portrait of Jesus as teacher. The scribes taught by citing authorities: "Rabbi X says..." Jesus taught by assertion: "I say to you." This is either the most arrogant teaching in human history or the teaching of the one to whom all authority belongs. Matthew does not leave the reader in the middle. The crowd was astonished. The question is what they did with the astonishment.

verseByVerse.quote: Judge not, that you be not judged. For with the judgment you pronounce you will be judged, and with the measure you use it will be measured to you. Why do you see the speck that is in your brother's eye, but do not notice the log that is in your own eye? Or how can you say to your brother, "Let me take the speck out of your eye," when there is the log in your own eye? You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother's eye. Do not give dogs what is holy, and do not throw your pearls before pigs, lest they trample them underfoot and turn to attack you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be harsh, fault-finding judges of others, because God will judge you by the same standard you use. Deal first with the great fault in yourself before trying to correct a small fault in someone else. Yet use discernment too: do not keep pressing holy things on those who treat them with contempt.

Judge not. “Judge” (krinō) has a wide range: to evaluate, to decide, to condemn. Here it means the critical, condemning, fault-finding spirit that sets itself up as judge over others, looking for their faults and passing sentence on them. The Pharisees often judged in this way (Luke 18:9–11).

That you be not judged. By God. The passive is often a reverent way of saying “God will do this”.

For with the judgment you pronounce you will be judged. The standard you apply to others will be applied to you. If you condemn harshly, without mercy, you will be judged without mercy (James 2:13). Paul says that in passing judgment on another you condemn yourself, because you practise the very same things (Romans 2:1).

And with the measure you use it will be measured to you. A picture from the market: a merchant measuring grain. If you use a mean measure on others, God will use it on you.

Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye. A speck (karphos) is a tiny splinter, a bit of straw or sawdust.

But do not notice the log that is in your own eye? A log (dokos) is a beam, a roof timber. Jesus, a carpenter’s son, uses a deliberately comic picture: a man with a plank sticking out of his eye trying to remove a speck of sawdust from someone else’s. We see others’ faults sharply and our own hardly at all. Often the faults that irritate us most in others are our own.

You hypocrite. An actor (see 6:2). The judgmental person plays the part of a righteous judge while hiding his own sin.

First take the log out of your own eye. Begin with self-examination and repentance.

And then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother’s eye. Notice: Jesus does not say leave the speck. He says deal with yourself first, and then you will be able to help your brother. Removing a speck from an eye is delicate work. It requires clear sight, a gentle hand, and humility. Paul says, if anyone is caught in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness, keeping watch on yourself (Galatians 6:1).

Do not give dogs what is holy, and do not throw your pearls before pigs. Dogs here are not pets but wild scavengers; pigs were unclean animals to Jews. Both picture people who treat holy things with contempt. “What is holy” may refer to meat from sacrifices, which must never be thrown to dogs. Pearls were very precious. Pigs would not value them; they would trample them and turn on the giver. The holy things and pearls are the gospel and the truths of God’s kingdom.

Lest they trample them underfoot and turn to attack you. Some people respond to God’s truth with mockery and violence. Do not keep pressing it on them. Jesus told his disciples to shake the dust off their feet when a town rejected them (10:14), and Paul turned from those who rejected the gospel to others (Acts 13:46; 18:6).

The balance. Verses 1–5 warn against being too critical; verse 6 warns against being undiscerning. Disciples must not be judgmental, but they must not be naive. They must judge between holy and unholy, true and false (v. 15). The same chapter that says “judge not” also says “beware of false prophets” and “you will recognise them by their fruits” (vv. 15–20).

What it does not mean. “Judge not” is often quoted to mean that no one may ever say anything is wrong. That is not what Jesus means. He himself called the Pharisees hypocrites. Paul commands the church to judge those inside it who persist in sin (1 Corinthians 5:12–13). Jesus says to judge with right judgment (John 7:24). Courts, parents, church elders and employers must make judgments. What Jesus forbids is a self-righteous, fault-finding, condemning spirit that judges others without examining oneself, that assumes the worst, and that pronounces final verdicts that belong only to God. Nor does verse 6 permit us to write off people as “pigs” easily. The same Jesus who said this ate with sinners. It applies to those who have clearly and repeatedly treated the gospel with contempt.

In a sentence. Do not be harsh critics of others; examine yourself first, then help others humbly, while using discernment about those who scorn holy things.

On a Tuesday. Think of the fault that annoys you most in someone else. Ask honestly: is there a log of the same wood in my eye?
verseByVerse.note: Dogs and pigs were unclean animals, images of those who scorn what is holy.

parallels.desc: in passing judgment you condemn yourself

verseByVerse.quote: Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened. Or which one of you, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a serpent? If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keep asking, seeking and knocking in prayer, because everyone who does so receives. If human fathers, sinful as they are, give their children good things and not harmful ones, how much more will your Father in heaven give good things to those who ask him?

The connection. After the demands of the sermon, which we cannot meet in our own strength, Jesus points us to prayer. We need God’s help to live this way, and he gives it to those who ask.

Ask … seek … knock. Three pictures, each stronger than the last. Asking is like a child asking a parent. Seeking is like searching for something lost. Knocking is like standing at a closed door and calling to be let in. In Greek, all three are present imperatives, meaning keep on asking, keep on seeking, keep on knocking. Jesus is teaching persistence in prayer (Luke 11:5–10; 18:1–8).

And it will be given to you … you will find … it will be opened to you. Each command has a promise. The passive “will be given” and “will be opened” point to God as the giver.

For everyone who asks receives. Not some, but everyone. This is a promise to God’s children.

Or which one of you, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? The round, flat loaves of Galilee looked like the smooth stones of the region (see 4:3). What father would trick his hungry child?

Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a serpent? Some fish of the Sea of Galilee, like eels or catfish, looked like snakes. No father would give a dangerous snake instead of food.

If you then, who are evil. A remarkable phrase. Jesus assumes that all human beings, even good fathers, are evil: sinful by nature (see Ephesians 2:3). Yet even sinful parents love their children.

Know how to give good gifts to your children. Ordinary parental love.

How much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him! An argument from lesser to greater. God is not a reluctant giver. He is a good Father who delights to give. Luke’s version says, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him (Luke 11:13): the Spirit is the greatest of the good things.

What it does not mean. Not that God will give us anything we ask for, if only we persist. A good father does not give his child everything he asks for: not a knife to a toddler, not sweets for every meal. God gives “good things”, and he decides what is good. Sometimes the answer is “no” or “wait”, because he has something better. John says that we receive what we ask when we ask according to his will (1 John 5:14–15). Nor is persistence a way of wearing God down or forcing his hand (6:7–8). It is the persistence of trust, which keeps coming to the Father because it believes he is good.

In a sentence. Keep praying, because your Father in heaven is far more generous than the best earthly father and delights to give good things to his children.

On a Tuesday. What have you stopped praying for because you gave up? Start asking again, trusting your Father’s goodness and his timing.
verseByVerse.note: Flat loaves could look like stones, and some fish like snakes.

parallels.desc: every good gift is from above
if we ask according to his will

verseByVerse.quote: So whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them, for this is the Law and the Prophets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Treat others the way you would want them to treat you. This sums up everything the Law and the Prophets teach about how to live with others.

So whatever you wish that others would do to you. Think about how you would like to be treated: with kindness, honesty, patience, respect, generosity, forgiveness.

Do also to them. Then treat them that way, first, without waiting for them to do it. This is called the Golden Rule.

The positive form. Other ancient teachers stated the rule negatively. The Jewish teacher Hillel, a generation before Jesus, said: what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour; that is the whole law. Confucius and others taught similar negative forms. The negative form says: do not harm. Jesus’ positive form says: actively do good. It is far more demanding. You could keep the negative form by doing nothing; you can keep the positive form only by love in action.

For this is the Law and the Prophets. It summarises the Old Testament’s teaching on how to treat others. Jesus later says that the whole Law and the Prophets hang on two commandments: love God, and love your neighbour as yourself (22:37–40). The Golden Rule is a practical way of applying the second. It also forms a bracket with 5:17, where Jesus mentioned the Law and the Prophets: everything in between explains what fulfilling them means.

What it does not mean. Not that we should give people whatever they want. We should treat them as we would rightly wish to be treated, by someone who truly loves us, which sometimes means telling hard truths or refusing harmful requests. Nor is the Golden Rule the whole of Christianity, or the way of salvation, as if we could earn heaven by being nice. No one keeps it perfectly. It shows us our sin, drives us to Christ, and then becomes the shape of the new life he gives.

In a sentence. Actively treat others the way you would want to be treated, for that is the heart of God’s law about our neighbours.

On a Tuesday. Before your next difficult conversation, ask: how would I want to be spoken to if I were in their place?
verseByVerse.note: Other ancient teachers put this rule negatively (“do not do what you would hate”); Jesus puts it positively.

parallels.desc: the whole law in one word

verseByVerse.quote: Enter by the narrow gate. For the gate is wide and the way is easy that leads to destruction, and those who enter by it are many. For the gate is narrow and the way is hard that leads to life, and those who find it are few.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There are only two ways. Enter by the narrow gate. The gate is wide and the road easy that lead to destruction, and many take it. But the gate is narrow and the road hard that lead to life, and few find it.

The conclusion of the sermon. Verses 13–27 call for a decision through a series of contrasts: two gates, two roads, two kinds of trees, two kinds of fruit, two kinds of builder, two foundations. There is no third option, no neutral ground.

Enter by the narrow gate. A command. It is not enough to admire the sermon; one must enter.

For the gate is wide and the way is easy that leads to destruction. “Easy” literally means broad, spacious. The wide gate admits anyone, with any baggage, any belief, any way of life. The broad road has room for everything: no self-denial, no repentance, no discipline. It is the way of the crowd. It feels comfortable, but it leads to destruction, eternal ruin.

And those who enter by it are many. Popularity is no proof of truth.

For the gate is narrow and the way is hard that leads to life. “Hard” (tethlimmenē) means pressed, constricted, and is related to the word for affliction and persecution. The narrow gate is Christ himself, the only way to God (John 10:9; 14:6). It is narrow because it admits only those who come through him, by repentance and faith, leaving behind their self-righteousness and their sin. The way is hard because following Christ involves self-denial, opposition and suffering (16:24; Acts 14:22). But it leads to life, eternal life with God.

And those who find it are few. “Find” suggests that it must be sought. Jesus does not give numbers; he gives a warning. When asked whether those being saved are few, he answered: strive to enter through the narrow door (Luke 13:23–24). The point is not to calculate others’ fate, but to make sure of your own.

What it does not mean. Not that salvation is earned by a hard, difficult life, or that Christians must make life as hard as possible for themselves. The gate is entered by grace through faith; the hardness of the road is the cost of following Christ in a hostile world. Jesus also says his yoke is easy and his burden is light (11:30): the road is hard from the world’s side, but sweet in his company. Nor does “few” mean that heaven will be thinly populated: Revelation sees a great multitude that no one can number from every nation (Revelation 7:9). In any generation, compared with the crowd, true disciples are few; across history, they are a vast multitude.

Where Christians differ: exclusivism. Pluralists hold that all religions are equally valid paths to God. Inclusivists hold that people may be saved through Christ without knowing him explicitly. Verdict: exclusivism. There is one gate, Christ, and salvation is found in no one else (Acts 4:12). This is why the gospel must be preached to all nations.

In a sentence. There are only two roads: the easy, popular one to destruction, and the narrow one through Christ to life.

On a Tuesday. Are you on the narrow road, or only near it, admiring it? And are you willing to be different from the crowd for Christ’s sake?

parallels.desc: life and death set before you
the way of the wicked will perish

verseByVerse.quote: Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep's clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves. You will recognize them by their fruits. Are grapes gathered from thornbushes, or figs from thistles? So, every healthy tree bears good fruit, but the diseased tree bears bad fruit. A healthy tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor can a diseased tree bear good fruit. Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. Thus you will recognize them by their fruits.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Watch out for false prophets. They look like sheep, harmless members of the flock, but inside they are ravenous wolves. You will recognise them by their fruit: what their teaching and lives produce. Every bad tree will be cut down and burned.

Beware of false prophets. On the narrow road there will be people pointing the wrong way. A prophet claims to speak for God. A false prophet claims to, but does not. The Old Testament warned of them repeatedly (Deuteronomy 13:1–5; 18:20–22; Jeremiah 23:16–22). Jesus warns that they will multiply (24:11, 24).

Who come to you in sheep’s clothing. They look like believers. They use Christian words, attend church, may even be leaders. Prophets sometimes wore a rough cloak of animal skin (Zechariah 13:4; 3:4), so the picture may also suggest the costume of a prophet.

But inwardly are ravenous wolves. Their real aim is to devour: to exploit, deceive and destroy the flock for their own gain, whether money, power, sex or fame. Paul warned the Ephesian elders that fierce wolves would come in among them, not sparing the flock (Acts 20:29–30).

You will recognize them by their fruits. “Fruit” is what a tree produces. For a false prophet, the fruit includes their character and conduct (greed, sexual immorality, pride, love of power: 2 Peter 2:1–3, 14), their teaching (does it agree with Scripture and exalt Christ? 1 John 4:1–3; Galatians 1:8–9), and the effect on their followers (do they become more like Christ, or more proud, divided, and worldly?).

Are grapes gathered from thornbushes, or figs from thistles? Obviously not. A plant produces according to its nature. Some thornbushes had small black berries that might look like grapes from a distance; some thistles had heads that might look like figs. But up close, the difference was clear.

So, every healthy tree bears good fruit, but the diseased tree bears bad fruit. Character produces conduct. The heart shows itself in time.

Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. The same words John the Baptist used (3:10). False prophets face God’s judgment.

Thus you will recognize them by their fruits. Jesus repeats it for emphasis. The test takes time. Fruit is not visible in the first season.

What it does not mean. Not that we should be suspicious of every Christian leader, or treat every mistake or weakness as proof of false prophecy. All teachers sin and make mistakes (James 3:1–2). The test is the pattern of life and the substance of teaching over time. Nor are impressive results proof of a true prophet: large crowds, miracles and charisma can accompany false teaching (24:24; 2 Thessalonians 2:9). The next verses make this clear.

In a sentence. Beware of teachers who look like believers but are wolves; you will recognise them by the fruit of their lives and teaching.

On a Tuesday. Whose teaching are you following: online preachers, popular authors, podcasters? Test them by Scripture, and by the fruit of their lives over time, not by their popularity.

parallels.desc: the axe laid to the root

verseByVerse.quote: Not everyone who says to me, "Lord, Lord," will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven. On that day many will say to me, "Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works in your name?" And then will I declare to them, "I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of lawlessness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not everyone who calls Jesus “Lord” will enter the kingdom, but only those who do his Father’s will. On the last day, many will point to their prophesying, exorcisms and miracles done in his name. He will say: I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of lawlessness.

Not everyone who says to me, “Lord, Lord”. The double “Lord, Lord” expresses fervour or familiarity. These people use the right words, the right confession. But words are not enough.

Will enter the kingdom of heaven. Jesus speaks of the final judgment.

But the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven. Doing God’s will is the mark of a true disciple (12:50). Not perfect obedience, but a life of genuine submission to God, shown in repentance and in obedience to Christ’s words (v. 24).

On that day. A standard phrase for the day of judgment (Isaiah 2:11; Malachi 3:17; 2 Timothy 1:12).

Many will say to me. Jesus is the Judge. Only God judges the world (Genesis 18:25). Jesus quietly claims to be the one before whom everyone will stand (25:31–46; John 5:22).

Did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works in your name? Impressive religious activity, done in Jesus’ name, with apparent power. Yet it is not enough. Judas was among the Twelve who were sent to heal and cast out demons (10:1–8). Spiritual gifts and results are not proof of saving faith.

I never knew you. In the Bible, “to know” often means a personal, covenant relationship (Amos 3:2; John 10:14, 27; 2 Timothy 2:19). Jesus does not say “I used to know you” or “you lost your salvation”, but “I never knew you”. They were never his. Their religion was a performance, without a relationship.

Depart from me. From Psalm 6:8. The most terrible words in the Bible: banishment from Christ’s presence (25:41; 2 Thessalonians 1:9).

You workers of lawlessness. “Lawlessness” (anomia) means living without regard to God’s law. Their impressive works covered lives that did not submit to God’s will.

What it does not mean. Not that we are saved by doing God’s will, as if our obedience earns heaven. Jesus has opened the sermon with grace (5:3). Doing God’s will is the fruit and evidence of true faith, not its root (Ephesians 2:8–10; James 2:17–18). Nor does it mean that true believers must live in constant fear of being rejected. The warning is for those who are religious but not truly converted. Those who trust Christ and love his will can be assured that he knows them (John 10:27–29; 1 John 3:18–24). And it does not mean that a believer can lose their salvation: “I never knew you” shows these people were never saved.

In a sentence. Calling Jesus “Lord” and doing impressive works in his name are not enough; only those who truly belong to him and do his Father’s will enter the kingdom.

On a Tuesday. Do you know Christ, or only about him? Is your religion a relationship that shows itself in obedience, or a performance?

parallels.desc: depart from me, all you workers of evil

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone then who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house on the rock. And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house, but it did not fall, because it had been founded on the rock. And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house on the sand. And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat against that house, and it fell, and great was the fall of it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus ends the sermon with a parable of two builders. The one who hears his words and does them builds on rock, and his house stands through the storm. The one who hears and does not do them builds on sand, and his house falls with a great crash.

Everyone then who hears these words of mine and does them. “These words of mine”: the whole Sermon on the Mount. Jesus claims that our eternal destiny depends on how we respond to his words. Only God’s word carries that weight (Isaiah 40:8). Both builders hear; the difference is doing.

Will be like a wise man who built his house on the rock. In Galilee, the wise builder dug down through the soil to the bedrock and built his foundations there (Luke 6:48). It took more time and effort, and the work was hidden underground.

And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house. In the dry season, the beds of wadis (seasonal streams) looked like flat, sandy, convenient building sites. But in the rainy season, sudden torrential storms turned them into raging torrents in minutes. The storm pictures all the trials of life, and above all the final judgment of God (Isaiah 28:16–17; Ezekiel 13:10–14).

But it did not fall, because it had been founded on the rock. The foundation made the difference. The rock is Christ and his words, received and obeyed (1 Corinthians 3:11).

And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house on the sand. Easier, quicker, and from the outside the house looked the same. The foolish builder’s problem was not ignorance; he heard. It was not hostility; he was building a house too, perhaps a religious one. His problem was that he heard and did not do.

And it fell, and great was the fall of it. The sermon ends not with comfort but with a crash. Jesus leaves his hearers with the urgency of a decision.

What it does not mean. Not that we build our own salvation by obeying Jesus’ teaching perfectly. The rock is Christ himself; we build on him by trusting him and following him. Obedience is the evidence that we have dug down to the rock. James says that whoever hears the word and does not do it deceives himself (James 1:22–25). Nor does it mean that wise builders escape storms. Both houses face the same storm. Faith in Christ does not exempt us from trouble; it keeps us standing through it.

In a sentence. Those who hear Jesus’ words and do them build on rock and stand through every storm; those who hear and do not do them build on sand and fall.

On a Tuesday. Which part of the Sermon on the Mount have you heard but not done: forgiving, giving in secret, refusing to worry, loving an enemy? Act on it this week.
verseByVerse.note: Wadis (dry stream beds) flood suddenly in the rainy season; a house on sand could be swept away overnight.

parallels.desc: a wall smeared with whitewash falls

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus finished these sayings, the crowds were astonished at his teaching, for he was teaching them as one who had authority, and not as their scribes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus finished, the crowds were amazed at his teaching, because he taught with his own authority, not like their scribes.

And when Jesus finished these sayings. A formula Matthew uses to end each of the five great teaching sections (11:1; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1).

The crowds were astonished at his teaching. “Astonished” means struck, overwhelmed, amazed. The crowds who had gathered around the disciples (5:1) had been listening throughout.

For he was teaching them as one who had authority. His own authority: “But I say to you” (5:22, 28, 32, 34, 39, 44). He did not quote earlier rabbis; he did not say “Thus says the LORD” like a prophet. He spoke as the one whose word is final: who fulfils the law (5:17), who will judge the world (7:22–23), and whose words are the rock on which life stands (7:24).

And not as their scribes. The scribes taught by quoting traditions and earlier authorities: “Rabbi so-and-so said, and Rabbi so-and-so replied.” Their authority was borrowed. Jesus’ authority was his own.

What it does not mean. Not that astonishment is the same as faith. The crowds were amazed, but amazement does not save. Many who were astonished later turned away. The right response to Jesus’ authority is not admiration, but obedience (v. 24).

In a sentence. The crowds were amazed that Jesus taught with his own divine authority, not borrowed authority like the scribes.

On a Tuesday. Do you treat Jesus’ words as interesting advice, or as the final authority over your life?

For worship. Bow before the one whose word is final, and whose word is the rock you stand on.
verseByVerse.note: Scribes taught by citing earlier authorities; Jesus spoke on his own authority (“But I say to you”).

7.theology:
Hearing and Doing: Faith and Works in Reformed Theology. Matthew 7:24–27 has sometimes been read as teaching salvation by works: do the words of Jesus and be saved. Reformed theology reads it more carefully. The doing is not the foundation; the rock is. The foundation is Christ himself, received by faith. The doing is the evidence and expression of genuine faith — what James calls the faith that works (Jas. 2:17).

Calvin wrote that we are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone. The wise builder who hears and does is the person who has been genuinely changed by the words of Jesus — not merely intellectually persuaded but existentially transformed. The doing of the Sermon on the Mount is not the cause of salvation but its fruit; not the foundation but the superstructure. And the foundation, as Paul will make clear (1 Cor. 3:11), is Jesus Christ himself — the one whose words these are.
7.examples:
Then: The two builders have their Old Testament counterparts in the wise and foolish in Proverbs: the one who builds their house on wisdom (Prov. 9:1) and the one who builds on folly (Prov. 9:13–18). Israel’s history is the extended parable of a nation that heard God’s word at Sinai and alternately built on it (David, Hezekiah, Josiah) and ignored it (the cycle of judges, the divided monarchy, the exile). The storm that came on the sandbuilders in Israel’s history was Babylon — and Jeremiah watched the great fall of it (Jer. 7:1–15, which echoes this passage).

Now: The Sermon on the Mount ends with the most personal challenge of the entire Gospel so far: what are you building on? The storm is coming — the storms of suffering, of loss, of death — and the question that will matter then is being answered now by what you build with your ordinary days. The person who reads the Sermon and is intellectually impressed but does nothing with it is the sand builder. The person who allows its demands to drive them to the Christ who fulfils them, and who in the Spirit begins to do what the Sermon commands — that person is building on rock. The flood will reveal the foundation. Build now while the weather is good.

8.title: The King’s Authority Over All
8.text: <sup>1</sup>When he came down from the mountain, great crowds followed him. <sup>2</sup>And behold, a leper came to him and knelt before him, saying, “Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.” <sup>3</sup>And Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, “I will; be clean.” And immediately his leprosy was cleansed. <sup>4</sup>And Jesus said to him, “See that you say nothing to anyone, but go, show yourself to the priest and offer the gift that Moses commanded, for a proof to them.” <sup>5</sup>When he had entered Capernaum, a centurion came forward to him, appealing to him, <sup>6</sup>“Lord, my servant is lying paralyzed at home, suffering terribly.” <sup>7</sup>And he said to him, “I will come and heal him.” <sup>8</sup>But the centurion replied, “Lord, I am not worthy to have you come under my roof, but only say the word, and my servant will be healed. <sup>9</sup>For I too am a man under authority, with soldiers under me. And I say to one, ‘Go,’ and he goes, and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes, and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.” <sup>10</sup>When Jesus heard this, he marveled and said to those who followed him, “Truly, I tell you, with no one in Israel have I found such faith. <sup>11</sup>I tell you, many will come from east and west and recline at table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven, <sup>12</sup>while the sons of the kingdom will be thrown into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” <sup>13</sup>And to the centurion Jesus said, “Go; let it be done for you as you have believed.” And the servant was healed at that very moment. <sup>14</sup>And when Jesus entered Peter’s house, he saw his mother-in-law lying sick with a fever. <sup>15</sup>He touched her hand, and the fever left her, and she rose and began to serve him. <sup>16</sup>That evening they brought to him many who were oppressed by demons, and he cast out the spirits with a word and healed all who were sick. <sup>17</sup>This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah: “He took our illnesses and bore our diseases.” <sup>18</sup>Now when Jesus saw a crowd around him, he gave orders to go over to the other side. <sup>19</sup>And a scribe came up and said to him, “Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go.” <sup>20</sup>And Jesus said to him, “Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.” <sup>21</sup>Another of the disciples said to him, “Lord, let me first go and bury my father.” <sup>22</sup>And Jesus said to him, “Follow me, and leave the dead to bury their own dead.” <sup>23</sup>And when he got into the boat, his disciples followed him. <sup>24</sup>And behold, there arose a great storm on the sea, so that the boat was being swamped by the waves; but he was asleep. <sup>25</sup>And they went and woke him, saying, “Save us, Lord; we are perishing.” <sup>26</sup>And he said to them, “Why are you afraid, O you of little faith?” Then he rose and rebuked the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm. <sup>27</sup>And the men marveled, saying, “What sort of man is this, that even winds and sea obey him?” <sup>28</sup>And when he came to the other side, to the country of the Gadarenes, two demon-possessed men met him, coming out of the tombs, so fierce that no one could pass that way. <sup>29</sup>And behold, they cried out, “What have you to do with us, O Son of God? Have you come here to torment us before the time?” <sup>30</sup>Now a herd of many pigs was feeding at some distance from them. <sup>31</sup>And the demons begged him, saying, “If you cast us out, send us away into the herd of pigs.” <sup>32</sup>And he said to them, “Go.” So they came out and went into the pigs, and behold, the whole herd rushed down the steep bank into the sea and drowned in the waters. <sup>33</sup>The herdsmen fled, and going into the city they told everything, especially what had happened to the demon-possessed men. <sup>34</sup>And behold, all the city came out to meet Jesus, and when they saw him, they begged him to leave their region.
8.overview:
Matthew 8 is a gallery of authority. Coming down from the mountain where he gave the law of the kingdom, the King now demonstrates the power of the kingdom. In rapid succession Jesus heals a leper with a touch, a Gentile servant with a word, a feverish woman with a hand, and a raging sea with a rebuke. The crowds ask the right question: “What sort of man is this?” Matthew intends the reader to answer: the Son of God, in whom all authority in heaven and on earth is vested.

The chapter also sounds the notes of grace toward outsiders. A leper — ritually unclean, excluded from community — is touched rather than avoided. A Roman centurion — a Gentile, an occupier — displays faith that shames Israel. Jesus announces that many from east and west will recline at the messianic banquet while presumptuous insiders face exclusion. The kingdom breaks every boundary of ethnic privilege. The centurion’s faith is the model: he grasps that Jesus’ authority is absolute, that his word accomplishes what he speaks. This is saving faith — resting wholly on the word of the King.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — The Messiah Heals: Authority over Leprosy, Paralysis, and Fever
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Matthew groups ten miracles in chapters 8-9, presenting Jesus as the one Isaiah promised: "He took our illnesses and bore our diseases" (v. 17, citing Isa. 53:4). The leper, the centurion's servant, and Peter's mother-in-law are the first three — representing the ritually unclean, the Gentile, and the woman. Jesus heals all with equal authority and without discrimination. The verse-by-verse fills in what these three lines cannot. On the leper: Leviticus prescribes torn clothes, loose hair, a covered lip and a shouted "Unclean, unclean", and dwelling alone outside the camp (Lev. 13:45-46) — so this man had not been touched by anyone for as long as the disease had lasted. Note that he broke the law to approach, and that his prayer is the reverse of ours: he is certain of the power and unsure of the willingness. And Jesus did not need to touch him — the very next healing in this chapter is done at a distance, by a spoken word — so the contact was gained for its own sake. He touched him first and said "be clean" second. The command to show himself to the priest handed the priesthood a ceremony (Lev. 14: two birds, cedar, scarlet, hyssop, running water) that they had learned and almost certainly never performed — in the whole Old Testament only Miriam and Naaman were cleansed of this. On the centurion: Matthew has him speak to Jesus directly while Luke has him send Jewish elders and then friends (Lk. 7:3-8); this is the ordinary convention by which a man does what he does through agents, and Luke supplies the reason the elders would carry his message — he had built their synagogue. His "I am not worthy" is not self-disparagement but consideration: a Jew entering a Gentile house contracted defilement, and he is protecting Jesus from a cost he judges unnecessary. His sentence has stood in the liturgy for centuries. And Jesus marvels exactly twice in the Gospels — here at faith, and at Nazareth's unbelief (Mk. 6:6) — so faith in its presence and its absence is the only thing recorded as astonishing him.
verseByVerse.theology: Each healing is an enacted parable of salvation: Jesus touches what is untouchable (the leper), heals at a distance by his word alone (the centurion's servant), and raises up those laid low by sickness. The healing of disease and the forgiveness of sins are not unrelated — both are expressions of the same redemptive authority. Isaiah 53:4 locates these healings within the atonement: Jesus bore our diseases not merely by healing them but ultimately by carrying them on the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: The centurion's faith astonishes Jesus and becomes the template for Gentile inclusion: "not even in Israel have I found such faith." Faith is not a Jewish property or a product of religious background; it is the trust that recognizes authority and rests in it. The centurion understood command-and-response because he lived under authority. His insight: if Jesus commands, it is done.

verseByVerse.quote: When he came down from the mountain, great crowds followed him. And behold, a leper came to him and knelt before him, saying, "Lord, if you will, you can make me clean."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Jesus came down from the mountain, a man with leprosy, an outcast who was forbidden to approach people, came and knelt before him: Lord, if you are willing, you can make me clean. He had no doubt of Jesus’ power; his only question was whether Jesus would want to.

The connection. Chapters 5–7 showed Jesus’ authority in word. Chapters 8–9 show his authority in deed: ten miracles, in three groups, over disease, nature, demons and death. Matthew sums up both in 4:23 and 9:35: teaching, preaching and healing. The King who taught with authority (7:29) now acts with authority.

When he came down from the mountain. Like Moses coming down from Sinai (Exodus 34:29).

A leper. “Leprosy” in the Bible (Hebrew tsara’at, Greek lepra) covers a range of skin diseases, not only what is now called Hansen’s disease. Leviticus 13–14 gave detailed laws. A person with such a disease was ritually unclean: he had to live outside the camp or town, wear torn clothes, leave his hair loose, cover his upper lip, and cry “Unclean, unclean!” to warn others away (Leviticus 13:45–46). Anyone who touched him became unclean too. He was cut off from worship at the temple, from family, from work and from all human touch. Rabbis regarded curing leprosy as being as difficult as raising the dead (2 Kings 5:7). In the Bible, leprosy also became a vivid picture of sin: a defilement that separates us from God and others, which we cannot cleanse ourselves.

Came to him. He should not have. The law required him to keep his distance. Desperation drove him past the rules.

And knelt before him. The word (prosekynei) is the same as “worship” (2:11). He bowed low in reverence.

Lord, if you will, you can make me clean. “Lord” may simply mean “sir”, but in Matthew it carries more. His faith is clear: “you can”. He does not doubt Jesus’ power. His question is Jesus’ will: does Jesus want to touch someone like me? He asks to be made “clean”, not just “healed”: he wants restoration to God’s people and to worship.

What it does not mean. Not that “if you will” shows weak faith. It is humble faith, which leaves the outcome to Christ. Jesus does not rebuke him for it. Nor is it a model for doubting God’s willingness to forgive. When we come to him for cleansing from sin, he is always willing (John 6:37; 1 John 1:9). We may pray “if you will” about healing or circumstances, because God has not promised them; we need not pray it about forgiveness, because he has.

In a sentence. An outcast leper came to Jesus in humble faith, certain he could heal him, and asking only whether he would.

On a Tuesday. Is there something you feel makes you untouchable to God: a sin, a shame, an illness? Come to Jesus as the leper did, and kneel.
verseByVerse.note: “Leprosy” in the Bible covers a range of skin diseases. A leper had to live apart and was ritually unclean.

parallels.desc: the leper must live alone, crying “Unclean”

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, "I will; be clean." And immediately his leprosy was cleansed. And Jesus said to him, "See that you say nothing to anyone, but go, show yourself to the priest and offer the gift that Moses commanded, for a proof to them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus reached out and touched the leper: I am willing; be clean. At once he was healed. Jesus told him to tell no one, but to show himself to the priest and offer the sacrifice Moses commanded, as evidence to them.

And Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him. This is astonishing. Jesus could have healed with a word (as he does in v. 13). Instead he touched the untouchable. This man may not have been touched by anyone for years. By the law, touching a leper made a person unclean (Leviticus 5:3). But when Jesus touches the leper, Jesus does not become unclean; the leper becomes clean. Holiness flows outward from Jesus, instead of uncleanness flowing in. He is greater than the law’s categories.

Saying, “I will; be clean.” The direct answer to the man’s question. Jesus is willing. And his word has power: he speaks, and it happens, as God spoke at creation (Psalm 33:9).

And immediately his leprosy was cleansed. Instantly and completely.

See that you say nothing to anyone. Jesus often told people not to spread news of his miracles (9:30; 12:16). This is sometimes called the “messianic secret”. Reasons: to avoid crowds who wanted only miracles, which hindered his teaching (Mark 1:45); to avoid the political misunderstanding that he was a military Messiah who would overthrow Rome; and so that his identity would be revealed in God’s time, through the cross.

But go, show yourself to the priest. The law required a cleansed leper to be examined by a priest, who would declare him clean (Leviticus 14:1–32). Only then could he return to society and worship. Jesus respects the law of Moses (5:17). He wants the man fully restored, not just healed.

And offer the gift that Moses commanded. The offering of two birds, lambs, flour and oil, set out in Leviticus 14. It was a sacrifice of thanksgiving and cleansing.

For a proof to them. A testimony to the priests: evidence that something extraordinary had happened, and that the one who cleanses lepers had come. When John the Baptist later asks whether Jesus is the Messiah, Jesus points to this: lepers are cleansed (11:5).

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus disregarded the law: he sends the man to keep it. Nor that his touch was necessary for the healing: it was an act of compassion. And the command to silence does not mean we should keep quiet about Jesus today. After the resurrection, the command is to tell everyone (28:19–20).

In a sentence. Jesus willingly touched and cleansed the leper, and sent him to be restored to God’s people according to the law.

On a Tuesday. Who are the “untouchables” in your community: the lonely, the stigmatised, the outcast? Jesus touched them. Will you?

For worship. Thank Jesus that he is willing to make you clean, and that his holiness overcomes your uncleanness.

verseByVerse.quote: When he had entered Capernaum, a centurion came forward to him, appealing to him, "Lord, my servant is lying paralyzed at home, suffering terribly."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Capernaum, a Roman centurion, a Gentile soldier, came to Jesus and appealed for his servant, who lay paralysed at home in terrible pain.

When he had entered Capernaum. Jesus’ home base (4:13).

A centurion. A Roman army officer commanding about a hundred soldiers (a “century”). Centurions were the backbone of the Roman army: experienced, disciplined, responsible men. This one was probably serving Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, whose troops were organised on the Roman pattern. He was a Gentile. Luke adds that he loved the Jewish nation and had built their synagogue, and that Jewish elders came to Jesus on his behalf (Luke 7:3–5). Matthew shortens the story and presents the request as the centurion’s own, as a message sent through others is the sender’s message. In the New Testament, centurions are often presented positively (27:54; Acts 10).

Came forward to him, appealing to him. A Roman officer, a man of power, coming to a Jewish teacher with a request. A reversal of normal social order.

Lord, my servant. The word (pais) can mean “boy”, “child” or “servant”; Luke uses the word for slave (Luke 7:2). The centurion cared deeply for a slave, someone his society regarded as property. That itself was unusual.

Is lying paralyzed at home, suffering terribly. In great pain, perhaps near death (Luke 7:2).

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus’ mission at this stage was to Gentiles in general: he came first to Israel (15:24). But this encounter is a preview of the Gentiles coming to Christ (v. 11).

In a sentence. A Gentile officer came humbly to Jesus to ask help for his suffering servant.

On a Tuesday. The centurion used his position to help someone below him. If you have authority, at work or at home, use it to care for those under you.
verseByVerse.note: A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers. This one was a Gentile, probably serving Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, "I will come and heal him." But the centurion replied, "Lord, I am not worthy to have you come under my roof, but only say the word, and my servant will be healed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus offered to come and heal the servant. But the centurion said he was not worthy to have Jesus enter his house. Jesus did not need to come: he only needed to say the word, and the servant would be healed.

I will come and heal him. Jesus is willing to go, even to a Gentile’s house. (Some translate it as a question: “Shall I come and heal him?”, as if Jesus were testing the man, since Jews did not enter Gentile homes. Either way, Jesus responds to the request.)

Lord, I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. A devout Jew who entered a Gentile’s house became ritually unclean (Acts 10:28; 11:12). The centurion knows this, and does not want to put Jesus in that position. But his words go deeper than ritual. “Not worthy” expresses real humility. The Jewish elders said he was worthy (Luke 7:4); he says he is not. True greatness knows its unworthiness before Christ.

But only say the word, and my servant will be healed. He believes that Jesus’ word alone has power, even at a distance. Jesus does not need to be present, touch, or perform a ritual. His word is enough.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus’ presence is unimportant, or that touch and physical means do not matter.
