Jesus touched the leper (v. 3), and God works through physical means such as baptism, the Lord’s Supper, and the laying on of hands. But the centurion grasped that the power is in Jesus himself and in his word. The Roman Catholic Mass uses a version of his words before Communion: Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only say the word and my soul shall be healed. The words express true humility.

In a sentence. The Gentile centurion confessed his unworthiness and trusted that Jesus’ word alone could heal at a distance.

On a Tuesday. Do you believe that Jesus’ word is enough, even when you cannot see him act? Rest on his promises today.
verseByVerse.note: A devout Jew would not normally enter a Gentile house; the centurion spares Jesus the problem.

parallels.desc: unlawful for a Jew to visit a foreigner
he sent out his word and healed them

verseByVerse.quote: For I too am a man under authority, with soldiers under me. And I say to one, "Go," and he goes, and to another, "Come," and he comes, and to my servant, "Do this," and he does it." When Jesus heard this, he marveled and said to those who followed him, "Truly, I tell you, with no one in Israel have I found such faith."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The centurion explained his faith from his own experience: he knew how authority works. He obeyed his superiors, and his soldiers obeyed him. Jesus has that kind of authority over sickness. Jesus was amazed and said he had not found such faith in all Israel.

For I too am a man under authority. He is part of a chain of command: he obeys his superiors (a tribune, the governor, ultimately the emperor), and his authority comes from them.

With soldiers under me. He also has authority over others.

And I say to one, “Go,” and he goes. He does not have to do things himself; he speaks, and his orders are carried out.

The logic. The centurion reasons: just as I can give orders and they are obeyed, because I carry the authority of Rome, so Jesus carries the authority of God. Sickness and disease are under his command. He speaks, and they obey. The centurion has understood something many in Israel had not: Jesus’ authority is divine.

When Jesus heard this, he marveled. “Marvelled” means amazed, astonished. Only twice in the Gospels is Jesus said to marvel: here, at faith, and in Nazareth, at unbelief (Mark 6:6). Jesus was truly human: he could be surprised and moved.

And said to those who followed him, “Truly, I tell you, with no one in Israel have I found such faith.” Israel had the Scriptures, the covenants and the promises (Romans 9:4–5). Yet a Gentile soldier, with none of these advantages, showed greater faith than anyone in Israel. Faith here means trusting Jesus’ authority and power, and relying on his word alone.

What it does not mean. Not that no one in Israel had faith: the disciples had followed him. But none had yet grasped his authority so clearly. Nor is faith a force or a technique that makes miracles happen. Its power lies in its object. The centurion’s faith was great because he saw how great Jesus is.

In a sentence. The centurion understood that Jesus commands sickness as he commanded his soldiers, and Jesus marvelled at faith greater than he had found in Israel.

On a Tuesday. Faith grows by seeing how great Jesus is. Read a Gospel passage today that shows his authority, and let it enlarge your trust.

verseByVerse.quote: I tell you, many will come from east and west and recline at table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven, while the sons of the kingdom will be thrown into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. And to the centurion Jesus said, "Go; let it be done for you as you have believed." And the servant was healed at that very moment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus declared that many Gentiles from east and west would sit at the great feast of the kingdom with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, while many of Israel, who seemed to be heirs, would be thrown out into the darkness. Then he told the centurion to go: it would be done as he believed. The servant was healed at that moment.

Many will come from east and west. From the ends of the earth: the Gentile nations (Isaiah 49:12; 59:19; Malachi 1:11). The centurion is the first of a great multitude.

And recline at table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven. At formal banquets, guests reclined on couches around a low table. The prophets pictured the age to come as a great feast that God would prepare for all peoples, with rich food and fine wine (Isaiah 25:6–9). The patriarchs Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the founders of Israel, will be there. And Gentiles will sit beside them, as members of the family, not as servants. Abraham’s blessing reaches the nations (Genesis 12:3).

While the sons of the kingdom will be thrown into the outer darkness. “Sons of the kingdom” means those who seemed to be its natural heirs: Jews who relied on their descent from Abraham (3:9). Many will be excluded. The banquet hall is pictured as brightly lit at night, and “outer darkness” is the darkness outside, away from the light, warmth and joy.

In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. A phrase Matthew uses six times for final judgment (13:42, 50; 22:13; 24:51; 25:30). Weeping is grief and regret; gnashing of teeth is anguish, and perhaps anger. It is a picture of hell: exclusion from God’s presence and joy.

And to the centurion Jesus said, “Go; let it be done for you as you have believed.” He received what he trusted Jesus for.

And the servant was healed at that very moment. At a distance, by a word. The centurion’s faith was proved right.

What it does not mean. Not that God has rejected the Jewish people as a whole, or that all Jews will be excluded. The apostles, and the earliest church, were Jews; Paul expects many Jews to come to faith (Romans 11:25–26). Jesus is warning against relying on privilege, and declaring that faith, not ancestry, determines who sits at the feast. Nor does “as you have believed” mean that we get whatever we believe hard enough for. The centurion trusted Christ’s authority, and Christ honoured it. Faith receives; it does not command.

In a sentence. Gentiles who trust Christ will feast with the patriarchs in the kingdom, while those who rely on privilege without faith will be shut out.

On a Tuesday. Are you relying on your Christian background or church membership, or on Christ? Faith, not privilege, brings us to the table.
verseByVerse.note: Guests reclined at a banquet. “Weeping and gnashing of teeth” is Matthew’s recurring picture of final judgment.

parallels.desc: from the north and from the west

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus entered Peter's house, he saw his mother-in-law lying sick with a fever. He touched her hand, and the fever left her, and she rose and began to serve him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Peter’s house, Jesus found Peter’s mother-in-law in bed with a fever. He touched her hand, the fever left her, and she got up and began to serve him.

When Jesus entered Peter’s house. In Capernaum. Archaeologists have found a house there that was venerated by Christians from the first century as Peter’s, later built over by a church.

His mother-in-law. Peter was married. Paul mentions that Peter took his wife with him on his travels (1 Corinthians 9:5).

Lying sick with a fever. In the ancient world, a fever could be serious and even fatal, with no effective medicine.

He touched her hand. Another touch (v. 3). A rabbi would not normally touch a woman who was not his relative. Jesus is not bound by such customs when compassion calls.

And the fever left her. Completely and at once.

And she rose and began to serve him. Normally, after a fever, a person needs days to recover strength. She got up immediately, fully restored. “Serve” (diakoneō) means to wait on, to provide a meal. Her response to being healed was service. This is the pattern of the Christian life: those whom Christ restores serve him (20:28).

The three healings. The first group of miracles (vv. 1–15) shows Jesus healing three kinds of people who were on the margins of Jewish religious life: a leper (ritually unclean), a Gentile’s servant (an outsider), and a woman (who had a lesser place in religious life). Jesus’ kingdom welcomes those whom others keep at a distance.

What it does not mean. Not that women’s calling is only domestic service. “Serve” is the same word used of the angels serving Jesus (4:11) and of Jesus’ own mission (20:28). Service is the highest calling of every disciple.

In a sentence. Jesus healed Peter’s mother-in-law with a touch, and she rose at once to serve him.

On a Tuesday. How can you serve Christ today out of gratitude for what he has done for you?

parallels.desc: Peter was married, and his wife travelled with him

verseByVerse.quote: That evening they brought to him many who were oppressed by demons, and he cast out the spirits with a word and healed all who were sick, This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah: "He took our illnesses and bore our diseases."
verseByVerse.commentary:
That evening, crowds brought to Jesus many who were demon-possessed and sick. He drove out the spirits with a word and healed everyone, fulfilling Isaiah: he took our weaknesses and carried our diseases.

That evening. Mark tells us it was the Sabbath (Mark 1:21, 32). When the Sabbath ended at sunset, people could carry the sick without breaking the Sabbath rules.

They brought to him many who were oppressed by demons. Demon-possession is a condition in which an evil spirit controls or severely afflicts a person. The Gospels distinguish it from illness, though they sometimes overlap. Jesus’ casting out of demons shows that he has come to defeat Satan’s kingdom (12:28–29).

And he cast out the spirits with a word. No rituals, incantations or long prayers, as exorcists of the time used. Just a command. His word has authority over the spiritual world.

And healed all who were sick. All, not some.

This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah. Isaiah 53:4.

He took our illnesses and bore our diseases. Isaiah 53 describes the Servant of the LORD who suffers for his people. The verse in Hebrew speaks of him bearing our griefs and carrying our sorrows; the next verse says he was pierced for our transgressions. Matthew applies the first part to Jesus’ healing ministry. Jesus does not catch our diseases; he takes them away. But Matthew’s choice of Isaiah 53 points ahead: the healings are possible because of the cross, where the Servant bore the root of all disease, which is sin (1 Peter 2:24). Every healing in Jesus’ ministry was a down payment on the full healing that his death and resurrection would secure: a new body, in a new creation, without sickness or death (Revelation 21:4).

What it does not mean. Not that physical healing is guaranteed to every believer now, as part of the atonement, so that sickness shows a lack of faith. This is taught by some in the “health and wealth” movement. The atonement does secure our complete healing, but at the resurrection, not necessarily now. Believers in the New Testament were sick and not healed (2 Corinthians 12:7–9; 1 Timothy 5:23; 2 Timothy 4:20). Jesus’ healings were signs of the kingdom’s arrival, not a promise that every Christian will be healed before death.

In a sentence. Jesus drove out demons and healed every sickness, fulfilling Isaiah’s picture of the Servant who carries our weaknesses, as a preview of the full healing his cross secures.

On a Tuesday. If you are living with illness, bring it to Christ in prayer. He may heal; and if not now, he will at the resurrection, and he carries you through it.

parallels.desc: by his wounds you have been healed

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–34 — The Cost of Following and the Lord of Storm and Demons
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second half of chapter 8 moves from healing to the cost of discipleship and the authority of Jesus over creation and the demonic. Two would-be followers learn that Jesus offers no earthly security (no place to lay his head, no leave for burial rites). Then Jesus stills a storm with a rebuke and casts demons into pigs, and the Gadarenes ask him to leave. The sequence shows that following Jesus is neither comfortable nor universally welcomed. Four things more, all treated below. The scribe says "Teacher" and the next man says "Lord" (vv. 19, 21) — and that distinction runs through Matthew, where disciples say Lord while opponents, enquirers and the rich young man say Teacher, and Judas alone at the supper says Rabbi. The scribe files his own assessment in his first word. Note too that across the Gospels the people who volunteer are tested and the people who are called simply go. Matthew's word for the storm is not the word for a storm: he writes seismos megas, a great shaking — the standard Greek for an earthquake — where Mark has the ordinary term for a squall. And he uses it twice more, at the crucifixion (27:51-54) and at the tomb (28:2), each time as the setting for a declaration of who Jesus is. The sleeping is the only time the Gospels record it, and the scene is Jonah replayed and inverted: a man asleep below decks in a storm, woken by terrified sailors with almost these words (Jon. 1:5-6) — but Jonah slept fleeing God and was the cause of the storm and had to be thrown into the sea, while this sleeper is the end of it, and will himself be swallowed for three days (12:39-41). On the place name, the manuscripts genuinely divide between Gadarenes, Gerasenes and Gergesenes; Gerasa is thirty miles inland, Gadara six, and Gergesa (Kursi) is on the shore with the steep bank the story requires. And the pigs raise a question the passage does not answer — two thousand animals, somebody's business, destroyed — which is faced squarely below rather than tidied away.
verseByVerse.theology: The stilling of the storm is the Christological center of the chapter: "What sort of man is this, that even winds and sea obey him?" The disciples' question is Matthew's question to the reader. Only the Creator can command his creation. The storm-still and the Gadarene exorcism together display authority over the two great threats of the ancient world — chaos (the sea) and the demonic (the Legion). Both submit instantly. The appropriate response is not comfort but worship — and the disciples begin to learn it.
verseByVerse.examples: The Gadarenes' request that Jesus leave their region is one of the saddest verses in the Gospels. They preferred their pigs to their Deliverer. The economy of the region mattered more than the liberation of two men in chains. This is not ancient history; every age chooses its pigs. The question Jesus poses to every community: what do you value more than the healing he brings?

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus saw a crowd around him, he gave orders to go over to the other side. And a scribe came up and said to him, "Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus saw the crowd, he gave orders to cross the lake. A scribe came and promised to follow him wherever he went.

The second section. Verses 18–34 move from healing to discipleship and authority. Before the next miracles, Jesus faces two would-be followers. What does following him cost?

He gave orders to go over to the other side. To the eastern shore of the Sea of Galilee, Gentile territory. Jesus withdraws from the crowds, who were drawn by miracles.

And a scribe came up. An expert in the law (see 2:4). Most scribes opposed Jesus, but not all (13:52).

Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go. An enthusiastic, impressive promise. He calls Jesus “Teacher”, the title used by outsiders in Matthew; disciples call him “Lord”. He sees Jesus as a great rabbi to join.

What it does not mean. Not that enthusiasm is wrong. But enthusiasm without counting the cost does not last (13:20–21).

In a sentence. A scribe made an enthusiastic promise to follow Jesus anywhere.

On a Tuesday. Promises to follow Christ are easy to make on a good day. What will it take to keep them on a hard one?

parallels.desc: “Let us go across to the other side”

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to him, "Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head." Another of the disciples said to him, "Lord, let me first go and bury my father." And Jesus said to him, "Follow me, and leave the dead to bury their own dead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered that foxes have holes and birds have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head. Following him means giving up security. When another disciple asked first to bury his father, Jesus said: follow me, and let the dead bury their own dead. Following him comes before everything.

Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests. Even wild animals have a place to rest and shelter.

But the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head. Jesus had no permanent home during his ministry. He depended on others’ hospitality (Luke 8:3). Following him means sharing his homelessness, his insecurity and his rejection. The scribe had not counted that cost.

The Son of Man. The first time in Matthew that Jesus uses this title, his favourite way of referring to himself (about thirty times in Matthew). It can simply mean a human being, as in Psalm 8:4 and Ezekiel 2:1. But it comes especially from Daniel 7:13–14, where “one like a son of man” comes with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of Days and is given everlasting dominion over all peoples. Jesus uses the title both for his humility and suffering (here, and 17:22; 20:28) and for his glory and coming as judge (24:30; 26:64). It hid and revealed his identity at once: people could not easily turn it into a political slogan.

Another of the disciples said to him, “Lord, let me first go and bury my father.” Burying one’s father was one of the most sacred duties in Jewish life, taking priority over almost everything, including some religious duties. Burial happened on the day of death. If the father had just died, the son would not be standing with Jesus but at home. So the man probably meant: let me wait until my father has died (perhaps years later), fulfil my family duties, and receive my inheritance; then I will follow. “First” is the key word: he wanted something else first.

And Jesus said to him, “Follow me, and leave the dead to bury their own dead.” A shocking statement. “The dead” who bury are probably the spiritually dead, those who do not follow Christ (see Ephesians 2:1). Let them take care of such duties. Jesus’ call is urgent and comes before every other loyalty, even sacred family duty (10:37; Luke 9:59–62).

Two kinds of would-be disciple. The first was too quick: enthusiastic but unaware of the cost. The second was too slow: willing, but not yet. Both needed to understand that following Jesus is total and immediate.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should neglect their parents, or not attend family funerals. Jesus condemned those who used religion as an excuse to neglect parents (15:3–6), and on the cross he provided for his mother (John 19:26–27). The point is priority: when following Christ and family duty conflict, Christ comes first. Nor must every Christian literally be homeless. But every Christian must hold home and security loosely, and be willing to give them up for Christ.

In a sentence. Following Jesus means giving up security and putting him before every other loyalty, even sacred family duty, without delay.

On a Tuesday. What is the “first let me” in your life, the thing you are waiting to do before you fully follow Christ? He says, follow me now.
verseByVerse.note: Burying a father was a sacred duty; the man may have meant waiting until his father died. Jesus’ call outranks even that.

parallels.desc: no one who looks back is fit for the kingdom

verseByVerse.quote: And when he got into the boat, his disciples followed him. And behold, there arose a great storm on the sea, so that the boat was being swamped by the waves; but he was asleep. And they went and woke him, saying, "Save us, Lord; we are perishing."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus got into the boat and his disciples followed him. A violent storm arose and the waves swamped the boat, but Jesus was asleep. The disciples woke him in terror: Lord, save us, we are dying!

And when he got into the boat, his disciples followed him. Matthew uses the word “followed” deliberately after verses 18–22. This is what following Jesus looks like: getting into the boat with him, and into the storm.

And behold, there arose a great storm on the sea. The word for storm (seismos) usually means earthquake, a great shaking. The Sea of Galilee lies about seven hundred feet (210 metres) below sea level, surrounded by hills. Cold air from the hills can rush down onto the warm water and create sudden, violent storms. Several of the disciples were experienced fishermen, and they were terrified, so this was no ordinary storm.

So that the boat was being swamped by the waves. Literally “covered” by the waves. The boat was filling with water.

But he was asleep. Jesus was truly human, and truly exhausted after a long day of ministry. His sleep also shows complete trust in his Father. The psalmist says: in peace I will both lie down and sleep, for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety (Psalm 4:8). Jonah also slept in a storm (Jonah 1:5), but Jonah was fleeing from God; Jesus was resting in him.

And they went and woke him, saying, “Save us, Lord; we are perishing.” A cry of panic, but also of faith: they turned to Jesus. “Save us” is the prayer of every believer in trouble. “Lord” and “save” are words with deep meaning in Matthew: Jesus’ very name means “the LORD saves” (1:21).

What it does not mean. Not that following Jesus means calm seas. The disciples were in the storm precisely because they followed him. Christians are not promised freedom from trouble; they are promised his presence in it (Isaiah 43:2). Nor does Jesus’ sleep mean he does not care. Mark records that the disciples asked whether he cared that they were perishing (Mark 4:38). He did; he was with them.

In a sentence. Following Jesus into the boat led the disciples into a terrifying storm, and they cried out to him to save them.

On a Tuesday. If you are in a storm because you followed Christ, you are not out of his will. Cry out to him; he is in the boat.
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Galilee lies low and ringed by hills; sudden violent storms are common.

parallels.desc: the sleeping prophet in the storm

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Why are you afraid, O you of little faith?" Then he rose and rebuked the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm. And the men marveled, saying, "What sort of man is this, that even winds and sea obey him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus asked why they were afraid, with such little faith. Then he got up, rebuked the wind and the sea, and there was a great calm. The disciples were amazed: what kind of man is this, that even winds and sea obey him?

Why are you afraid, O you of little faith? Jesus speaks to the disciples first, before the storm. “Little faith” (oligopistoi) is not no faith: they did call on him. But their faith was small and mixed with panic. Jesus gently rebukes their fear. In Matthew, Jesus uses this word only of his disciples (6:30; 14:31; 16:8; 17:20). He is patient with weak faith, but he wants it to grow.

Then he rose and rebuked the winds and the sea. He spoke to the storm as one rebukes a disobedient servant, or as he rebuked demons (17:18). In the Old Testament, the raging sea often pictured chaos and evil powers opposed to God, and only God could rule it (Psalm 65:7; 89:9; 107:23–30; Job 38:8–11). God rebuked the Red Sea, and it dried up (Psalm 106:9).

And there was a great calm. A great storm (v. 24), and a great calm. Normally, after a storm, the waves continue for a long time. Here, the sea became calm at once.

And the men marveled. “The men”: perhaps Matthew stresses their humanity, in contrast to him.

What sort of man is this, that even winds and sea obey him? The key question of the passage. Psalm 107:23–30 describes sailors in a storm who cried to the LORD, and he made the storm still and hushed the waves. The disciples have just seen Jesus do what only God does. The answer to their question is that he is not merely a man. He is Immanuel, God with us (1:23). They will confess it fully later: truly you are the Son of God (14:33).

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus always calms the storms of our lives immediately when we ask. Sometimes he calms the storm; sometimes he calms the disciple. The story is first about who Jesus is: Lord of creation. It assures believers that no storm is outside his control.

In a sentence. Jesus rebuked the disciples’ fear and then the storm, showing that he has the authority over creation that belongs to God alone.

On a Tuesday. What storm are you afraid of? Bring it to the one whom winds and sea obey, and let the question “What sort of man is this?” strengthen your faith.

For worship. Worship Jesus as Lord of wind and sea.

parallels.desc: you rule the raging of the sea
he made the storm be still

verseByVerse.quote: And when he came to the other side, to the country of the Gadarenes, two demon-possessed men met him, coming out of the tombs, so fierce that no one could pass that way. And behold, they cried out, "What have you to do with us, O Son of God? Have you come here to torment us before the time?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the other side of the lake, in Gentile territory, two violently demon-possessed men came out of the tombs to meet Jesus. They were so dangerous that no one could use that road. The demons cried out: what do you want with us, Son of God? Have you come to torment us before the appointed time?

The country of the Gadarenes. The region around Gadara, a Gentile city of the Decapolis, about six miles (ten kilometres) southeast of the lake. Mark and Luke call it “the country of the Gerasenes” (Mark 5:1; Luke 8:26), after Gerasa, a larger city further away; manuscripts also vary. The place names refer to regions, not just cities; the event probably happened near a village on the eastern shore, perhaps Gergesa, now Kursi, where there are steep slopes near the water.

Two demon-possessed men. Mark and Luke mention only one, probably because he was the more prominent and later became a witness (Mark 5:18–20). Mentioning one does not deny that there were two. Matthew often mentions two where others mention one (9:27; 20:30), perhaps because two witnesses were needed for testimony under the law (Deuteronomy 19:15).

Coming out of the tombs. Tombs were caves cut into the hillside. They were unclean places, associated with death and, people believed, with evil spirits. The men lived there, cut off from society.

So fierce that no one could pass that way. Mark describes the man breaking chains and cutting himself with stones (Mark 5:3–5). Demonic possession destroys the person: their mind, their body, their relationships.

What have you to do with us, O Son of God? A Hebrew idiom meaning: what is there between us? Why are you interfering with us? The demons recognise Jesus immediately as the Son of God, before the disciples confess it (14:33; 16:16). James says even the demons believe, and shudder (James 2:19). Recognising who Jesus is does not save; demons have the knowledge without the trust or love.

Have you come here to torment us before the time? The demons know that a time of judgment is coming, when they will be punished (25:41; Revelation 20:10). They are afraid that Jesus has come to bring it early. In a sense he has: his coming means the beginning of their defeat (12:28–29).

What it does not mean. Not that every mental illness is demonic. The Gospels distinguish demon-possession from other illnesses (4:24). Those who suffer from mental illness need care, medical help and love, not exorcism. Nor should Christians fear demons: they fear Jesus.

In a sentence. In Gentile territory, two violently possessed men met Jesus, and the demons in them recognised and feared him as the Son of God and their coming Judge.

On a Tuesday. The powers of evil know who Jesus is and tremble. Do you trust him as much as they fear him?
verseByVerse.note: Gadara was a Gentile city of the Decapolis, south-east of the lake; Mark and Luke say “Gerasenes” and mention only one man. Tombs were unclean places.

parallels.desc: even the demons believe — and shudder

verseByVerse.quote: Now a herd of many pigs was feeding at some distance from them. And the demons begged him, saying, "If you cast us out, send us away into the herd of pigs."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nearby a large herd of pigs was feeding. The demons begged Jesus: if you drive us out, send us into the pigs.

A herd of many pigs. Mark says about two thousand (Mark 5:13). Pigs were unclean animals for Jews (Leviticus 11:7). A large herd shows that this was Gentile territory. It was probably a valuable source of income for the owners.

And the demons begged him. They pleaded. They have no power to resist Jesus; they can only beg. They know they must leave.

If you cast us out, send us away into the herd of pigs. Why? Perhaps because demons seek to inhabit and destroy something. Luke adds that they begged not to be sent into the abyss (Luke 8:31), the place of their final confinement. They wanted to stay in the region, even in pigs.

What it does not mean. Not that demons have any authority to negotiate with Jesus. He permits their request for his own purposes. Nor does it mean that we should seek to converse with demons or learn their secrets. Jesus did not hold a discussion; he gave a command.

In a sentence. The demons, powerless before Jesus, begged to be sent into a herd of unclean pigs.

On a Tuesday. Evil has no power to bargain with Christ. Whatever has a grip on you, it must obey him.
verseByVerse.note: Pigs were unclean animals under the law; a large herd shows this was Gentile country.

parallels.desc: the pig is unclean to you

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Go." So they came out and went into the pigs, and behold, the whole herd rushed down the steep bank into the sea and drowned in the waters. The herdsmen fled, and going into the city they told everything, especially what had happened to the demon-possessed men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said one word: Go. The demons left the men and entered the pigs, and the whole herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake and drowned. The herdsmen ran to the town and reported everything.

And he said to them, “Go.” One word, and the demons must obey. This is the same authority by which he calmed the storm (v. 26).

So they came out and went into the pigs. The men were freed. Mark says the man was found sitting, clothed and in his right mind (Mark 5:15).

And behold, the whole herd rushed down the steep bank into the sea and drowned in the waters. The destruction of the pigs shows several things. First, the reality of the deliverance: everyone could see that the demons had left. Second, the destructive nature of demons: wherever they go, they destroy (John 10:10). What they did to the pigs they had been doing to the men. Third, the value Jesus places on people: two human beings were worth more than two thousand pigs (12:12).

The herdsmen fled, and going into the city they told everything. They were frightened by what they had seen.

Especially what had happened to the demon-possessed men. The news spread quickly.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus disregarded the owners’ property carelessly. He is Lord of all creation, and he judged that freeing two people was worth more. Some ask whether it was unjust. But the pigs were destroyed by the demons, not by Jesus directly, and their loss was the price of the men’s freedom. The deeper question is the one the townspeople faced: what do you value more, your livelihood or the presence of the one who sets captives free?

In a sentence. At Jesus’ single word the demons left the men, entered the pigs and destroyed them, showing both Christ’s authority and the destructive nature of evil.

On a Tuesday. Jesus valued two broken men more than two thousand pigs. Do you value people above money and possessions?

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, all the city came out to meet Jesus, and when they saw him, they begged him to leave their region.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole town came out to Jesus, and when they saw him, they begged him to leave their district.

And behold, all the city came out to meet Jesus. A large crowd. Normally this phrase describes a welcome for a king.

And when they saw him, they begged him to leave their region. A tragic reversal. The demons begged Jesus not to send them away (v. 31); the townspeople begged Jesus to go away. They had seen a great deliverance, two of their neighbours restored to sanity, but they were frightened by Jesus’ power and angry at the loss of the pigs. They preferred their pigs and their comfort to the presence of the Son of God. Luke says they were seized with great fear (Luke 8:37).

And Jesus left. Jesus does not force himself on those who do not want him. But Mark tells us he left the freed man behind as a witness, to tell what the Lord had done for him (Mark 5:19–20), and later, when Jesus returned to the Decapolis, crowds came to him (Mark 7:31–37). The man’s testimony bore fruit.

The pattern of chapter 8. Matthew has shown Jesus’ authority over disease (vv. 1–17), nature (vv. 23–27) and demons (vv. 28–34). In each scene there is a response: faith from a Gentile soldier, little faith from the disciples, and rejection from a Gentile town. The question is not whether Jesus has authority, but how we will respond to it.

What it does not mean. Not that the town’s fear was a right fear. There is a fear of God that leads people to worship him (Luke 5:8–10), and a fear that drives people away. The Gadarenes had the wrong kind.

In a sentence. Faced with Christ’s power to free people, the town valued its pigs more and asked him to leave.

On a Tuesday. Is there any part of your life where you would rather Jesus left you alone, because his presence would cost you something you value? Invite him in instead.

8.theology: The authority of Christ. Chapter 8 is a sustained meditation on the authority of the Son of God. He has authority over disease (leper, fever), over distance (servant healed at a word), over demons (v. 16), and over creation (storm). Reformed theology insists that this authority is not delegated but inherent: Jesus is not a prophet with God’s power on loan but the eternal Son in whom all the fullness of deity dwells bodily (Col 2:9). His healing word and his saving word are the same — both accomplish what they declare. The centurion’s faith grasps this: faith is resting on the word of One who has absolute authority to perform what he promises.
8.examples:
Then: A Roman officer, trained in chains of command, recognized the absolute authority of Jesus. His faith put to shame those who had grown up with the Scriptures but had domesticated their expectations of the Messiah.

Now: We live in a therapeutic culture that regards faith as a psychological coping mechanism. The centurion’s faith is the opposite: it is epistemically grounded in the nature of the One trusted. We trust Christ not because belief makes us feel better but because he is the Lord of heaven and earth whose word does not return void. When we pray, we address the One who stilled the Sea of Galilee.

9.title: The King’s Authority to Forgive
9.text: <sup>1</sup>And getting into a boat he crossed over and came to his own city. <sup>2</sup>And behold, some people brought to him a paralytic, lying on a bed. And when Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, “Take heart, my son; your sins are forgiven.” <sup>3</sup>And behold, some of the scribes said to themselves, “This man is blaspheming.” <sup>4</sup>But Jesus, knowing their thoughts, said, “Why do you think evil in your hearts? <sup>5</sup>For which is easier, to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’? <sup>6</sup>But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—he then said to the paralytic—“Rise, pick up your bed and go home.” <sup>7</sup>And he rose and went home. <sup>8</sup>When the crowds saw it, they were afraid, and they glorified God, who had given such authority to men. <sup>9</sup>As Jesus passed on from there, he saw a man called Matthew sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, “Follow me.” And he rose and followed him. <sup>10</sup>And as Jesus reclined at table in the house, behold, many tax collectors and sinners came and were reclining with Jesus and his disciples. <sup>11</sup>And when the Pharisees saw this, they said to his disciples, “Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?” <sup>12</sup>But when he heard it, he said, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. <sup>13</sup>Go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.’ For I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.” <sup>14</sup>Then the disciples of John came to him, saying, “Why do we and the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast?” <sup>15</sup>And Jesus said to them, “Can the wedding guests mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast. <sup>16</sup>No one puts a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment, for the patch tears away from the garment, and a worse tear is made. <sup>17</sup>Neither is new wine put into old wineskins. If it is, the skins burst and the wine is spilled and the skins are destroyed. But new wine is put into fresh wineskins, and so both are preserved.” <sup>18</sup>While he was saying these things to them, behold, a ruler came in and knelt before him, saying, “My daughter has just died, but come and lay your hand on her, and she will live.” <sup>19</sup>And Jesus rose and followed him, with his disciples. <sup>20</sup>And behold, a woman who had suffered from a discharge of blood for twelve years came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment, <sup>21</sup>for she said to herself, “If I only touch his garment, I will be made well.” <sup>22</sup>Jesus turned, and seeing her he said, “Take heart, daughter; your faith has made you well.” And instantly the woman was made well. <sup>23</sup>And when Jesus came to the ruler’s house and saw the flute players and the crowd making a commotion, <sup>24</sup>he said, “Go away, for the girl is not dead but sleeping.” And they laughed at him. <sup>25</sup>But when the crowd had been put outside, he went in and took her by the hand, and the girl arose. <sup>26</sup>And the report of this went through all that district. <sup>27</sup>And as Jesus passed on from there, two blind men followed him, crying aloud, “Have mercy on us, Son of David.” <sup>28</sup>When he entered the house, the blind men came to him, and Jesus said to them, “Do you believe that I am able to do this?” They said to him, “Yes, Lord.” <sup>29</sup>Then he touched their eyes, saying, “According to your faith let it be done to you.” <sup>30</sup>And their eyes were opened. And Jesus sternly warned them, “See that no one knows about it.” <sup>31</sup>But they went away and spread his fame through all that district. <sup>32</sup>As they were going away, behold, a demon-oppressed man who was mute was brought to him. <sup>33</sup>And when the demon had been cast out, the mute man spoke. And the crowds marveled, saying, “Never was anything like this seen in Israel.” <sup>34</sup>But the Pharisees said, “He casts out demons by the prince of demons.” <sup>35</sup>And Jesus went throughout all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues and proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom and healing every disease and every affliction. <sup>36</sup>When he saw the crowds, he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd. <sup>37</sup>Then he said to his disciples, “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; <sup>38</sup>therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.”
9.overview:
Chapter 9 begins with the most audacious claim in Jesus’ ministry: “Your sins are forgiven.” The scribes immediately see the implication — only God can forgive sins — and charge blasphemy. Jesus responds by healing the paralytic as evidence that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins. The miracle is the sign; forgiveness is the substance. This is Matthew’s thesis: Jesus has come not primarily to heal bodies but to heal souls, not primarily to liberate from Roman occupation but to liberate from the bondage of sin and guilt.

The call of Matthew himself is a microcosm of the gospel. A tax collector — a collaborator with Rome, a social and religious outcast — is called with a two-word summons. He rises and follows. The banquet that follows is a picture of the kingdom: Jesus eating with the unworthy, the Pharisees scandalized, Jesus quoting Hosea 6:6 (“I desire mercy, not sacrifice”). The chapter closes with Jesus surveying the harassed crowds with compassion and calling for labourers. The mission of the King now extends through his people.

Read straight through, the chapter reveals a second pattern woven beneath the miracles: in story after story faith stands beside unbelief, and the two are sifted apart. The paralytic comes carried by friends whose faith Jesus sees (v. 2) — while the scribes silently cry blasphemy. Matthew rises at a word — while the Pharisees mutter at the table. The ruler kneels and the unclean woman reaches, both in bold faith — while the hired mourners laugh him to scorn. The blind men confess “Yes, Lord” — while the watching Pharisees, at the chapter’s climax, sneer that he casts out demons “by the prince of demons” (v. 34). The same Jesus, the same works — and they divide every heart that meets them: some come empty-handed and receive everything, while others, certain they need nothing, receive nothing and only harden. This is the dividing line the whole Gospel will trace, and it is why the chapter closes not in triumph but in compassion for the harassed and helpless crowds (vv. 36–38) — the harvest is plentiful, and this faith must be carried to them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — Forgiveness, Fellowship, and Fasting: Who Has Authority?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus returns to Capernaum and heals a paralyzed man by first forgiving his sins — triggering the first direct conflict with the scribes. He then calls Matthew the tax collector and eats with sinners, outraging the Pharisees. When John's disciples ask why Jesus's disciples don't fast, Jesus answers with three images: the bridegroom, the unshrunk cloth, and the new wine. The old forms cannot contain the new reality that has arrived. The scribes never spoke — Matthew says they said it "to themselves" (v. 3), and Jesus answers the unspoken charge, which is itself a claim as large as the one being disputed (Jer. 17:10; 1 Kgs. 8:39). And their theology is correct: only the offended party can waive an offence, and no priest in Israel ever forgave anybody — he declared a forgiveness God had granted. So the alternatives really are God or blasphemer, and they could see it. Jesus does not call their conclusion mistaken but evil (poneros) — the indictment is of a heart that settled the question before weighing it. On the title: Son of Man does two contradictory things at once, which is why he chose it. In Hebrew idiom it means simply "a human being" (God calls Ezekiel that ninety times), and in Daniel 7:13-14 it is the highest title in the Old Testament — dominion, glory, an everlasting kingdom. Innocuous enough to say in public, loaded enough that anyone who had read Daniel knew. And the two decisive words in v. 6 are on earth: everyone believed sins were forgiven in heaven; the disputed point is that the transaction can be completed here, by a voice, without temple, priest or sacrifice. Note also that the crowd's "authority to men" is plural (v. 8) — Matthew alone has it, and this is the Gospel that will record the keys given to Peter (16:19) and binding and loosing given to the church (18:18). On Matthew's booth: it was a customs post on the Via Maris at the frontier between Antipas's and Philip's territory, and the point most often missed is that Peter could go back to fishing and Matthew could not — a tax franchise was a purchased concession with men queuing for it. He burned the bridge in the act of crossing it. And Hosea 6:6 is Matthew's own verse: he quotes it twice (9:13; 12:7) and no other New Testament writer quotes it at all, both times against men who are technically correct and pastorally monstrous.
verseByVerse.theology: The paralytic episode is the theological pivot: Jesus claims authority to forgive sins, which belongs to God alone. The scribes are theologically right that only God forgives sins; they are catastrophically wrong in their conclusion that Jesus is therefore blaspheming. The miracle of healing is offered as proof of the greater miracle of forgiveness — the visible confirms the invisible. Matthew's call and the meal with sinners then demonstrate what forgiveness looks like in practice: the Physician comes for the sick, not the healthy.
verseByVerse.examples: The three images of newness — bridegroom, cloth, wineskins — announce that Jesus is not a reform of Judaism but its fulfillment and transformation. The joy of the bridegroom's presence cannot be contained in old mourning forms. The new covenant is not a patch on the old but its completion. The Pharisees' question about fasting reveals that they are still thinking in terms of the old forms; Jesus is announcing that the age of the bridegroom has begun.

verseByVerse.quote: And getting into a boat he crossed over and came to his own city. And behold, some people brought to him a paralytic, lying on a bed. And when Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, "Take heart, my son; your sins are forgiven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Back in Capernaum, people brought Jesus a paralysed man on a mat. When Jesus saw their faith, he said first not “be healed” but: take heart, son, your sins are forgiven.

And getting into a boat he crossed over and came to his own city. Rejected by the Gadarenes (8:34), Jesus returns to Capernaum (4:13).

Some people brought to him a paralytic, lying on a bed. A man who could not walk, carried on a mat or stretcher by his friends. Mark and Luke tell how they dug through the roof to lower him down (Mark 2:1–12; Luke 5:17–26). Matthew tells the story briefly, focusing on Jesus’ words.

When Jesus saw their faith. Faith can be seen: in this case, by the effort the friends made to bring the man to Jesus. “Their” faith includes the friends’ and probably the man’s. Faith that brings others to Jesus is noticed by him.

He said to the paralytic, “Take heart, my son.” “Take heart” means be encouraged, have courage. “My son” (literally “child”) is warm and affectionate.

Your sins are forgiven. Unexpected. The man’s obvious need was physical. But Jesus addresses his deepest need first. Paralysis would end at death; unforgiven sin would last for eternity. Jesus saw that this man needed forgiveness more than he needed to walk. The present tense means the forgiveness is happening now, on Jesus’ word.

Sin and sickness. Was the man’s paralysis caused by a specific sin? Sometimes sickness can be connected with sin (John 5:14; 1 Corinthians 11:30). But Jesus also denied that sickness is always the result of the sufferer’s own sin (John 9:1–3). All sickness belongs to a world fallen through sin, but individual illness is not usually a punishment for individual sin. Here, Jesus simply shows that forgiveness is the deeper need of every person.

What it does not mean. Not that the friends’ faith saved the man without his own trust in Christ. Each person must believe for themselves. But the faith of friends, in bringing someone to Jesus and praying for them, is precious, and Jesus responds to it. Nor does it mean that physical needs are unimportant: Jesus also healed him (v. 7).

In a sentence. Seeing the faith of the paralysed man and his friends, Jesus first met his deepest need: the forgiveness of his sins.

On a Tuesday. Whom could you carry to Jesus in prayer, or bring to hear about him? And remember that your own deepest need is not your circumstances, but forgiveness, which Christ gives.
verseByVerse.note: “His own city” is Capernaum, his base in Galilee.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, some of the scribes said to themselves, "This man is blaspheming." But Jesus, knowing their thoughts, said, "Why do you think evil in your hearts?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some scribes said to themselves that Jesus was blaspheming, claiming to forgive sins. Jesus knew what they were thinking and asked why they harboured such evil in their hearts.

Some of the scribes said to themselves. Silently, in their hearts.

This man is blaspheming. Blasphemy means speaking against God, insulting him, or claiming for oneself what belongs to God alone. The scribes reasoned correctly that only God can forgive sins (Mark 2:7; Isaiah 43:25). A person can forgive wrongs done to himself, but sin is ultimately against God (Psalm 51:4). For a man to declare someone’s sins forgiven was to claim to be God. If Jesus was not God, they were right: it would be blasphemy. Under the law, blasphemy was punishable by death (Leviticus 24:16). This is the first mention of the charge for which Jesus will finally be condemned (26:65).

But Jesus, knowing their thoughts. Jesus knew what they were thinking without being told. Only God knows the heart (1 Samuel 16:7; Jeremiah 17:10). In answering their unspoken accusation that he claims to be God, he does something only God can do.

Why do you think evil in your hearts? Their evil was not in their logic, which was right, but in their refusal to consider that Jesus might be who his words implied. They assumed the worst.

What it does not mean. Not that the scribes were wrong to be concerned about blasphemy. Concern for God’s honour is good. Their error was in refusing to see the evidence of who Jesus was.

In a sentence. The scribes rightly saw that forgiving sins was God’s prerogative and accused Jesus of blasphemy, but Jesus read their hearts as only God can.

On a Tuesday. Jesus knows your thoughts. That is a warning against secret sin and a comfort in secret sorrow.
verseByVerse.note: Blasphemy is speaking against God or claiming what belongs to him alone.

verseByVerse.quote: "For which is easier, to say, 'Your sins are forgiven,' or to say, 'Rise and walk'? But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins" — he then said to the paralytic — "Rise, pick up your bed and go home."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus asked which is easier to say: your sins are forgiven, or get up and walk? To prove that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins, he told the paralysed man to get up, take his bed and go home.

For which is easier. A clever question. To say “your sins are forgiven” is easier, because no one can see whether it has happened. To say “rise and walk” is harder, because everyone will immediately see whether it works. But actually to do either is equally impossible for a mere man; both require the power of God.

But that you may know. Jesus will do the visible thing to prove the invisible thing. The healing is evidence of the forgiveness.

That the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins. “Son of Man” (see 8:20). In Daniel 7:13–14, the Son of Man receives authority from God. “Authority” (exousia) means the right and the power to act. Here is astonishing news: God’s authority to forgive is now exercised on earth, by a man, in person. People do not have to wait for the Day of Atonement or the final judgment to know if they are forgiven; they can hear it from Jesus’ lips.

He then said to the paralytic, “Rise, pick up your bed and go home.” Three commands, each impossible for a paralysed man. Carrying his own bed would show the healing was complete.

What it does not mean. Not that priests or ministers today have the authority to forgive sins in themselves. Jesus has authority as God. The church announces his forgiveness to those who repent and believe (John 20:23; 2 Corinthians 5:18–20), but it does not create it. The Roman Catholic practice of priestly absolution in the confessional claims more than this. Reformed churches declare the gospel’s assurance of pardon to the penitent, as messengers of Christ, not as judges in his place.

In a sentence. Jesus healed the paralysed man to prove that, as the Son of Man, he has God’s authority on earth to forgive sins.

On a Tuesday. If you trust Christ, his forgiveness is as certain as that man’s walking. Hear his word: your sins are forgiven.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of Man” is Jesus’ favourite title for himself.

parallels.desc: one like a son of man receives everlasting dominion

verseByVerse.quote: And he rose and went home. When the crowds saw it, they were afraid, and they glorified God, who had given such authority to men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man got up and went home. When the crowds saw it, they were filled with awe and praised God, who had given such authority to human beings.

And he rose and went home. Immediately, in full view of everyone. The healing proved the forgiveness.

When the crowds saw it, they were afraid. “Afraid” here means filled with awe, reverent fear at seeing God at work.

And they glorified God. The right response. Unlike the scribes (v. 3), the crowds praised God.

Who had given such authority to men. The crowds see that a man has been given God’s authority. They do not yet grasp fully that this man is God himself. But they rightly see God’s hand. “Men” (plural) may also look ahead: the authority to declare forgiveness in Christ’s name would be given to his church (16:19; 18:18).

What it does not mean. Not that the crowds had faith in Jesus as Son of God: their response was praise, but not yet full understanding.

In a sentence. The man walked home, and the crowds praised God for giving such authority to a man.

For worship. Praise God that he has given his Son authority to forgive sins, including yours.

verseByVerse.quote: As Jesus passed on from there, he saw a man called Matthew sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, "Follow me." And he rose and followed him. And as Jesus reclined at table in the house, behold, many tax collectors and sinners came and were reclining with Jesus and his disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Jesus walked on, he saw a tax collector named Matthew sitting at his tax booth and said, follow me. Matthew got up and followed him. Then Jesus ate in Matthew’s house with many tax collectors and sinners, and with his disciples.

He saw a man called Matthew sitting at the tax booth. The author of this Gospel. Mark and Luke call him Levi (Mark 2:14; Luke 5:27); many Jews had two names. In his own Gospel, he calls himself Matthew and adds “the tax collector” to his name in the list of apostles (10:3), never forgetting where he came from. His tax booth was probably on the main road near Capernaum, collecting customs duties on goods passing between the territories of Herod Antipas and Philip.

Tax collectors. They were hated by fellow Jews for three reasons. They collaborated with the occupying powers (Rome, or Herod who served Rome). They were often dishonest, collecting more than required and keeping the profit (Luke 3:12–13; 19:8). And their frequent contact with Gentiles made them ritually unclean. They were classed with prostitutes and sinners (21:31), and were barred from serving as witnesses in Jewish courts. For a rabbi to call one as his disciple was scandalous.

And he said to him, “Follow me.” The same call as to the fishermen (4:19).

And he rose and followed him. Immediately. Fishermen could go back to fishing (John 21:3); a tax collector who left his post could not easily get it back. Matthew gave up a lucrative career. The one who had grown rich by taking now followed the one who gave.

As Jesus reclined at table in the house. Matthew’s house (Luke 5:29). He held a great feast for Jesus and invited his friends, other tax collectors and “sinners”. His first instinct as a disciple was to introduce his friends to Jesus.

Many tax collectors and sinners came and were reclining with Jesus. “Sinners” here means people known for immoral lives, or who did not keep the law as the Pharisees did, and so were treated as outcasts. Eating together in that culture expressed friendship and acceptance. Jesus ate with them.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus approved of their sin. He calls them to repentance (Luke 5:32). But he went to them, accepted them as people, and called them, rather than waiting for them to clean up first.

In a sentence. Jesus called Matthew, a despised tax collector, who left everything to follow him and threw a feast for his fellow outcasts to meet Jesus.

On a Tuesday. When Matthew met Jesus, he invited his friends to meet him too. Who among your friends could you invite to a meal with other believers?
verseByVerse.note: Mark and Luke call this tax collector Levi. Tax collectors were despised as collaborators and cheats.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the Pharisees saw this, they said to his disciples, "Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?" But when he heard it, he said, "Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick." Go and learn what this means: "I desire mercy, and not sacrifice." For I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees complained to the disciples that their teacher ate with tax collectors and sinners. Jesus answered: healthy people do not need a doctor; the sick do. Go and learn what God meant when he said, I desire mercy, not sacrifice. I came to call sinners, not the righteous.

Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners? To the Pharisees, eating with such people made one unclean and showed approval of their way of life. Rabbis kept away from them. The Pharisees saw holiness as separation from sinners.

Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. A proverb. A doctor goes to the sick; that is his job. Jesus came as a doctor for sin-sick souls. He does not become sick by being among the sick; he heals them. This reverses the Pharisees’ view of holiness: Jesus’ holiness is not contaminated by sinners; it transforms them (see 8:3).

Go and learn what this means. A rabbinic phrase used to send students back to study a text. Jesus tells the Bible experts to go back and study their Bibles.

I desire mercy, and not sacrifice. From Hosea 6:6. God had rebuked Israel for offering sacrifices while lacking steadfast love and faithfulness. God does not reject sacrifice altogether (he commanded it); the Hebrew idiom means “mercy more than sacrifice”. God values compassion more than ritual. The Pharisees kept rituals carefully but lacked mercy toward sinners. Jesus quotes the same verse again in 12:7.

For I came not to call the righteous, but sinners. “The righteous” are those who think they are righteous, like the Pharisees, who see no need of a doctor. In reality, no one is righteous (Romans 3:10). Jesus calls those who know they are sinners. The only qualification for being called by Jesus is to need him.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus overlooked sin, or that Christians should make their closest friends among those who lead them into sin (1 Corinthians 15:33). Jesus went among sinners as a doctor, to heal and call them to repentance, not as one who joins in their sin. Nor does it mean that the Pharisees were truly righteous and did not need Jesus. Jesus is speaking with irony: those who think they are healthy cannot be healed.

In a sentence. Jesus ate with sinners because he came as a doctor for the sick, showing that God values mercy above religious ritual.

On a Tuesday. Are you more like the Pharisees, keeping your distance from people you disapprove of, or like Jesus, going to them with mercy? And do you know yourself to be one of the sick he came to heal?

parallels.desc: I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice
to seek and to save the lost

verseByVerse.quote: And then the disciples of John came to him, saying, "Why do we and the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast?" And Jesus said to them, "Can the wedding guests mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast. No one puts a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment, for the patch tears away from the garment, and a worse tear is made." Neither is new wine put into old wineskins. If it is, the skins burst and the wine is spilled and the skins are destroyed. But new wine is put into fresh wineskins, and so both are preserved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John the Baptist’s disciples asked why Jesus’ disciples did not fast like them and the Pharisees. Jesus answered that wedding guests cannot mourn while the bridegroom is with them; they will fast when he is taken away. And new wine needs new wineskins: the new life he brings cannot be poured into the old forms.

The disciples of John came to him. John was in prison (4:12). His disciples continued to follow his austere way of life.

Why do we and the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast? Pious Jews fasted regularly, and Pharisees twice a week (Luke 18:12). Jesus’ disciples were feasting with sinners (vv. 10–11). It looked unspiritual.

Can the wedding guests mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? Fasting was associated with mourning and sorrow. A Jewish wedding was a week-long celebration. The wedding guests (literally “sons of the bridal chamber”, the bridegroom’s close friends) were excused from religious duties such as fasting during the festivities. Jesus is the bridegroom. In the Old Testament, God is the bridegroom of his people (Isaiah 54:5–6; 62:5; Hosea 2:19–20). Jesus takes that role. His coming is a wedding feast, the time of joy that the prophets promised. John himself had called Jesus the bridegroom (John 3:29).

The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast. “Taken away” suggests violent removal: Jesus’ first hint in Matthew of his death. After his death and ascension, his disciples would fast (Acts 13:2–3; 14:23).

No one puts a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment. A new patch, not yet shrunk, sewn onto an old garment would shrink when washed and tear the old cloth, making the hole worse.

Neither is new wine put into old wineskins. Wineskins were made from goatskins. New wine continues to ferment and expand. A new skin is soft and stretches; an old skin has become hard and brittle, and would burst under the pressure.

But new wine is put into fresh wineskins, and so both are preserved. The new life of the kingdom that Jesus brings cannot simply be added to the old system of Pharisaic tradition. The joy and freedom of the gospel will burst the old forms. The kingdom needs new forms: a new covenant, a new people.

What it does not mean. Not that the Old Testament is worthless or that everything old must go. Jesus came to fulfil the law and prophets (5:17). Luke adds that people who have drunk old wine say “the old is good” (Luke 5:39): people often prefer the familiar. The “old wineskins” are the human traditions and religious system of Judaism as practised by the Pharisees, not the Scriptures themselves. Nor does it mean that Christians should not fast. Jesus says they will (v. 15; 6:16–18).

In a sentence. Jesus’ presence is a wedding feast, not a time for mourning, and the new life he brings needs new forms, not the old religious system.

On a Tuesday. Is your Christian life marked by joy in Christ’s presence? And are there human traditions you are clinging to that hinder the new life of the gospel?
verseByVerse.note: Wineskins were goatskins. New wine still ferments and expands; an old skin has lost its stretch and splits.

parallels.desc: as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–38 — The Harvest Is Plentiful: Four More Healings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Matthew compresses four more miracles into a rapid sequence: a ruler's dead daughter raised, a hemorrhaging woman healed on the way, two blind men given sight, a mute demoniac freed. The chapter ends with a summary of Jesus's teaching and healing throughout all the cities and villages, and the saying about the plentiful harvest and the few laborers. The pace is breathless — Matthew is showing the sheer scope of Jesus's ministry, the range of human need he addresses, and the consistency of his compassion. Three things more. This is the tenth miracle of a set Matthew has gathered into two chapters, arranged by design rather than chronology — leper, centurion's servant, Peter's mother-in-law, storm, demoniacs, paralytic, ruler's daughter, the woman with the flow of blood, two blind men, mute man. In a Gospel that has already drawn Jesus as the new Moses (a slaughter of infants, called out of Egypt, water, forty days, a mountain, a law), ten mighty works after a mountain of teaching is the shape of the Exodus — with the difference that Moses' ten were plagues that destroyed, and these ten fall on disease, death, storm and the demonic. Verse 34 is the first Beelzebul charge, and it is worth seeing why they had to reach for it: nobody in the New Testament ever denies the miracles, so having ruled out God there was one explanation left. Its position is what chills — the same day and the same evidence produce "never was anything like this seen in Israel" from one group and "he casts out demons by the prince of demons" from the other. (A few early manuscripts omit the verse; the evidence for keeping it is good.) and the closing summary has three words stronger than any English can afford: "harassed and helpless" is eskylmenoi (flayed, mangled — the verb for skinning) and errimmenoi (thrown down, left lying where it fell); "compassion" is splagchnizomai, the churning of the inward organs, the strongest word for pity the language had; and "send out labourers" is ekballo, the very verb Matthew has used all chapter for casting out demons — beg the owner of the field to thrust workers into it. Note too that harvest in the prophets is nearly always judgement (Joel 3:13); Jesus takes the sickle out of it.
verseByVerse.theology: The two miracles of verses 18-26 are intertwined: the ruler's daughter dies while Jesus is on the way to heal her, and the hemorrhaging woman receives healing by touching his garment. Both cases involve women (a girl and a woman), both involve twelve years (the woman's illness, the girl's age in Mark's account), and both require faith that presses past social convention. Jesus stops for the bleeding woman even while the child lies dying — he does not hurry past need in order to reach crisis. Both receive exactly what they need.
verseByVerse.examples: The harvest saying (vv. 37-38) is the theological conclusion of the two miracle chapters: the need is vast, the laborers few, and the solution is prayer — not human strategy, not program development, but asking the Lord of the harvest to send workers. The church has often responded to the harvest by increasing activity; Jesus commands increasing prayer. The two are not incompatible, but prayer is the first and foundational response.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was saying these things to them, behold, a ruler came in and knelt before him, saying, "My daughter has just died, but come and lay your hand on her, and she will live." And Jesus rose and followed him, with his disciples. And behold, a woman who had suffered from a discharge of blood for twelve years came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment, for she said to herself, "If I only touch his garment, I will be made well." Jesus turned, and seeing her he said, "Take heart, daughter; your faith has made you well." And instantly the woman was made well. And when Jesus came to the ruler's house and saw the flute players and the crowd making a commotion, he said, "Go away, for the girl is not dead but sleeping." And they laughed at him. But when the crowd had been put outside, he went in and took her by the hand, and the girl arose. And the report of this went through all that district.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While Jesus was speaking, a synagogue ruler knelt before him: my daughter has just died, but come and lay your hand on her, and she will live. On the way, a woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years touched the fringe of his cloak, and Jesus healed her. At the ruler’s house, he put out the mourners, took the girl by the hand, and she rose.

A ruler came in and knelt before him. Mark and Luke tell us he was Jairus, a ruler of the synagogue (Mark 5:22; Luke 8:41), responsible for organising services. A respected leader humbled himself before Jesus.

My daughter has just died. Mark and Luke say she was dying when he came, and news of her death arrived on the way. Matthew shortens the story and gives the outcome from the start.

But come and lay your hand on her, and she will live. Remarkable faith: he believed Jesus could raise the dead.

And behold, a woman who had suffered from a discharge of blood for twelve years. Probably a chronic menstrual or uterine bleeding. Under the law, such a woman was ritually unclean, and anyone she touched became unclean (Leviticus 15:25–27). For twelve years she had been excluded from worship and from normal contact, probably unable to marry or remain married. Mark adds that she had spent all she had on doctors and had only grown worse (Mark 5:26).

Came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment. She came from behind, secretly, because she was ashamed and knew she should not touch anyone. The “fringe” (kraspedon) was one of the tassels that Jewish men wore on the corners of their outer garment, as God commanded, to remind them of his commandments (Numbers 15:37–41).

For she said to herself, “If I only touch his garment, I will be made well.” Her faith was real, perhaps mixed with superstition. She believed Jesus’ power was so great that even his clothes could heal.

Jesus turned, and seeing her he said, “Take heart, daughter; your faith has made you well.” Jesus would not let her slip away unseen. He called her “daughter”, the only time he uses that word in the Gospels, welcoming her into God’s family. “Your faith has made you well” (literally “has saved you”): not the touch or the cloth, but her trust in Jesus. The word “saved” (sesōken) includes both physical healing and the wider salvation of the whole person. Her uncleanness did not pass to him; his power passed to her.

And instantly the woman was made well. Twelve years of suffering ended in a moment.

And when Jesus came to the ruler’s house and saw the flute players and the crowd making a commotion. Mourning in that culture was loud and public. Even poor families hired at least two flute players and a professional mourning woman. Wailing and lament filled the house.

Go away, for the girl is not dead but sleeping. Jesus does not deny that she has died physically; the mourners know she has. But for him, death is like sleep, because he is about to wake her. In the New Testament, “sleep” becomes a Christian way of speaking of the death of believers (John 11:11–14; 1 Thessalonians 4:13–14), because they will be raised.

And they laughed at him. The mourners’ grief turned instantly to mockery. Unbelief laughs at Christ’s promises.

He went in and took her by the hand, and the girl arose. Again Jesus touches the unclean: a dead body made a person unclean (Numbers 19:11). Again, life flows from him. Mark records his words in Aramaic: Talitha cumi, “Little girl, I say to you, arise” (Mark 5:41).

And the report of this went through all that district. News of a resurrection could not be hidden.

Twelve years. Mark notes that the girl was twelve (Mark 5:42). The woman had been suffering for as long as the girl had been alive. One was a respected man’s daughter, one an outcast woman; Jesus made both whole.

What it does not mean. Not that touching objects associated with Jesus, or with saints, carries healing power. The power was in Jesus, and he made clear it was her faith in him that mattered. Nor does it mean that faith always brings physical healing. But it shows that no condition is too hopeless for Jesus, not even death.

In a sentence. Jesus healed a woman unclean for twelve years and raised a dead girl, showing that his power overcomes both uncleanness and death.

On a Tuesday. Is there a long, hidden suffering you have carried in shame? Come to Jesus. He will not push you away; he will call you son or daughter.

For worship. Praise Jesus, who calls death sleep because he will wake his people.
verseByVerse.note: Mark and Luke name the ruler Jairus, a synagogue leader. A woman with a flow of blood was ritually unclean and made others unclean by touch. Hired flute players and mourners were customary at a death. The “fringe” was the tassel the law required on garments.

parallels.desc: a woman with a discharge of blood

verseByVerse.quote: And as Jesus passed on from there, two blind men followed him, crying aloud, "Have mercy on us, Son of David." When he entered the house, the blind men came to him, and Jesus said to them, "Do you believe that I am able to do this?" They said to him, "Yes, Lord." Then he touched their eyes, saying, "According to your faith let it be done to you." And their eyes were opened. And Jesus sternly warned them, "See that no one knows about it." But they went away and spread his fame through all that district.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two blind men followed Jesus, crying, have mercy on us, Son of David! In the house Jesus asked whether they believed he could do this. They said yes, and he touched their eyes: according to your faith be it done to you. Their sight was restored. Though he warned them to tell no one, they spread the news everywhere.

Two blind men followed him. Blindness was common in the ancient world, caused by disease, injury and poor hygiene. Blind people usually lived by begging. Isaiah promised that in the age of salvation the eyes of the blind would be opened (Isaiah 35:5; 42:7).

Crying aloud, “Have mercy on us, Son of David.” “Have mercy” (eleēson) is the cry of those who have no claim and can only appeal to kindness. The church has prayed it for centuries: Kyrie eleison, “Lord, have mercy”. “Son of David” is a messianic title (see 1:1). Remarkably, the blind see who Jesus is when many sighted people do not.

When he entered the house, the blind men came to him. Jesus did not respond on the road. He waited until they had followed him into the house, perhaps testing their persistence, and avoiding a public messianic demonstration.

Do you believe that I am able to do this? Jesus asks about their faith in him personally: not whether they believe in healing, but whether they trust him.

They said to him, “Yes, Lord.” A simple, clear confession.

Then he touched their eyes, saying, “According to your faith be it done to you.” Their faith in him received what he gave. “According to” does not mean “in proportion to”, as though a little faith gets a little sight. It means “in response to”: faith is the hand that receives.

And their eyes were opened. A sign that the Messiah had come (11:5).

And Jesus sternly warned them, “See that no one knows about it.” “Sternly” means strongly, with deep feeling. Jesus did not want to be known chiefly as a miracle-worker, or as a political “Son of David” who would lead a revolt (see 8:4).

But they went away and spread his fame through all that district. They disobeyed. Understandable, but disobedience nonetheless. Gratitude does not excuse ignoring Jesus’ word.

What it does not mean. Not that faith is a power that produces results by itself. The two men had faith in Jesus’ ability, and Jesus healed them. Nor does it mean that people who are not healed lack faith (2 Corinthians 12:7–10).

In a sentence. Two blind men recognised Jesus as the Son of David, trusted his power, and received their sight.

On a Tuesday. Pray “Lord, have mercy” today, for yourself and for someone you love. It is a prayer Jesus always hears.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of David” is a title for the Messiah, the king of David’s line.

parallels.desc: the eyes of the blind opened

verseByVerse.quote: As they were going away, behold, a demon-oppressed man who was mute was brought to him. And when the demon had been cast out, the mute man spoke. And the crowds marveled, saying, "Never was anything like this seen in Israel." But the Pharisees said, "He casts out demons by the prince of demons."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then a man who could not speak because of a demon was brought to Jesus. When the demon was driven out, the man spoke. The crowds were amazed: nothing like this had ever been seen in Israel. But the Pharisees said that he drove out demons by the prince of demons.

A demon-oppressed man who was mute. Here the inability to speak was caused by a demon. Not every disability is demonic (see 4:24), but in this case it was.

And when the demon had been cast out, the mute man spoke. Isaiah promised that the tongue of the mute would sing for joy (Isaiah 35:6).

And the crowds marveled, saying, “Never was anything like this seen in Israel.” The crowds sum up chapters 8–9: ten miracles, unmatched in Israel’s history. Moses, Elijah and Elisha did great works, but nothing like this.

But the Pharisees said, “He casts out demons by the prince of demons.” The Pharisees cannot deny the miracles, so they explain them away: Jesus is in league with Satan. This is the beginning of their charge that Jesus is demonic. Jesus will answer it fully in 12:22–32: a kingdom divided against itself cannot stand, and to call the Spirit’s work Satan’s is a terrible sin.

Two responses. The same miracle produced amazement in the crowds and hostility in the leaders. Evidence alone does not produce faith. The heart that does not want to submit to Jesus will find a way to explain him away.

What it does not mean. Not that amazement is the same as faith. The crowds marvelled, but many later turned away. Wonder needs to become trust and obedience.

In a sentence. Jesus freed a mute man from a demon, and while the crowds marvelled, the Pharisees accused him of working by Satan’s power.

On a Tuesday. When you hear evidence for Christ, do you look for reasons to believe or for reasons to dismiss it? The heart decides how we read the evidence.

parallels.desc: the tongue of the mute sing for joy

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus went throughout all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues and proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom and healing every disease and every affliction. When he saw the crowds, he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd. Then he said to his disciples, "The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few;" therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus went through all the towns and villages, teaching, preaching the good news of the kingdom and healing every disease.
