When he saw the crowds, he was moved with compassion, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd. He told his disciples: the harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few. Pray to the Lord of the harvest to send out workers.

And Jesus went throughout all the cities and villages. Almost word for word the summary of 4:23. Matthew brackets chapters 5–9 with these summaries: Jesus’ words (5–7) and works (8–9) together show the kingdom has come.

Teaching in their synagogues and proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom and healing every disease and every affliction. Teaching, preaching, healing: the three parts of Jesus’ ministry (see 4:23).

When he saw the crowds, he had compassion for them. “Compassion” (splanchnizomai) is a strong word, literally a movement of the inward parts: deep, gut-level pity that moves a person to act. In the Gospels it is used almost only of Jesus (14:14; 15:32; 20:34) and of characters in his parables who picture God (18:27; Luke 15:20). Jesus did not look at crowds as statistics or as an audience, but as people in need.

Because they were harassed and helpless. “Harassed” means troubled, worn out, torn, as if mauled by wild animals. “Helpless” means thrown down, lying prostrate, unable to get up. The people were exhausted by life, oppressed by Rome and burdened by the religious leaders’ demands (23:4), and without anyone to care for them.

Like sheep without a shepherd. An Old Testament image (Numbers 27:17; 1 Kings 22:17). In Ezekiel 34, God condemns Israel’s shepherds, the leaders who fed themselves instead of the flock, so that the sheep were scattered; and he promises that he himself will shepherd his people, through his servant David. Jesus is that Shepherd (2:6; John 10:11).

Then he said to his disciples, “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few.” Jesus changes the picture from sheep to a harvest field. The harvest is people ready to be gathered into God’s kingdom. In the prophets, harvest often pictured the final judgment (Joel 3:13), but here it pictures the gathering of people by the gospel (John 4:35–38). There are many to be reached, and few to reach them.

Therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest. God is the Lord of the harvest: he owns it and directs it. The first response to the need is not to organise but to pray. “Pray earnestly” (deēthēte) means to beg, to plead.

To send out laborers into his harvest. “Send out” (ekbalē) is a strong word, the same used for casting out demons: thrust out, drive out. Workers are needed, and God must send them. The prayer often turns back on the one who prays: in the next verses, Jesus sends out the very disciples he told to pray (10:1–5).

What it does not mean. Not that only full-time missionaries and pastors are “labourers”. Every disciple has a part in the harvest (5:14–16; 28:19). Nor does “plentiful” mean that everyone will believe. The harvest is ready; but workers are needed to gather it.

In a sentence. Moved by compassion for weary, shepherdless crowds, Jesus told his disciples to pray for God to send workers into his plentiful harvest.

On a Tuesday. Pray today for God to send workers into the harvest: missionaries, pastors, and ordinary believers in your workplace and street. And be ready to be the answer to your own prayer.

For worship. Thank Jesus for his compassion toward you when you were harassed and helpless.

parallels.desc: not as sheep that have no shepherd
scattered, because there was no shepherd

9.theology: Justification and the forgiveness of sins. The healing of the paralytic is Matthew’s clearest window into the doctrine of justification. Jesus pronounces forgiveness as a judicial declaration — he does not say “God will forgive you if…” but “your sins are forgiven,” accomplished fact. This is the forensic heart of the gospel: the guilty are declared righteous by the word of the Judge himself, on the basis of the Son’s merit, through faith. The Reformers called this the article by which the church stands or falls. Matthew 9 shows it enacted in history by the King who has authority on earth to forgive sins — the same authority he will exercise from the cross, bearing the penalty that makes the declaration just.
9.examples:
Then: Matthew the tax collector was the last person anyone expected in the kingdom. His conversion was a public scandal and a public testimony. The banquet he threw was evangelism by hospitality: bring the ones who need the physician to the physician.

Now: Every church that welcomes the broken, the addicted, the socially marginal, and the morally compromised is continuing Matthew’s banquet. The temptation of respectable Christianity is the Pharisees’ error: to protect the purity of the community by excluding the sick. Jesus reverses the logic. The church is not a museum of saints but a hospital for sinners — a place where the Great Physician practices.

10.title: Sent as Sheep Among Wolves
10.text: <sup>1</sup>And he called to him his twelve disciples and gave them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to heal every disease and every affliction. <sup>2</sup>The names of the twelve apostles are these: first, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother; James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother; <sup>3</sup>Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas and Matthew the tax collector; James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus; <sup>4</sup>Simon the Zealot, and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him. <sup>5</sup>These twelve Jesus sent out, instructing them, “Go nowhere among the Gentiles and enter no town of the Samaritans, <sup>6</sup>but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. <sup>7</sup>And proclaim as you go, saying, ‘The kingdom of heaven is at hand.’ <sup>8</sup>Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons. You received without paying; give without pay. <sup>9</sup>Acquire no gold or silver or copper for your belts, <sup>10</sup>no bag for your journey, or two tunics or sandals or a staff, for the laborer deserves his food. <sup>11</sup>And whatever town or village you enter, find out who is worthy in it and stay there until you depart. <sup>12</sup>As you enter the house, greet it. <sup>13</sup>And if the house is worthy, let your peace come upon it, but if it is not worthy, let your peace return to you. <sup>14</sup>And if anyone will not receive you or listen to your words, shake off the dust from your feet when you leave that house or town. <sup>15</sup>Truly, I say to you, it will be more bearable on the day of judgment for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah than for that town. <sup>16</sup>“Behold, I am sending you out as sheep in the midst of wolves, so be wise as serpents and innocent as doves. <sup>17</sup>Beware of men, for they will deliver you over to courts and flog you in their synagogues, <sup>18</sup>and you will be dragged before governors and kings for my sake, to bear witness before them and the Gentiles. <sup>19</sup>When they deliver you over, do not be anxious how you are to speak or what you are to say, for what you are to say will be given to you in that hour. <sup>20</sup>For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you. <sup>21</sup>Brother will deliver brother over to death, and the father his child, and children will rise against parents and have them put to death, <sup>22</sup>and you will be hated by all for my name’s sake. But the one who endures to the end will be saved. <sup>23</sup>When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next, for truly, I say to you, you will not have gone through all the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes. <sup>24</sup>“A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his master. <sup>25</sup>It is enough for the disciple to be like his teacher, and the servant like his master. If they have called the master of the house Beelzebul, how much more will they malign those of his household. <sup>26</sup>“So have no fear of them, for nothing is covered that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known. <sup>27</sup>What I tell you in the dark, say in the light, and what you hear whispered, proclaim on the housetops. <sup>28</sup>And do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell. <sup>29</sup>Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father. <sup>30</sup>But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. <sup>31</sup>Fear not, therefore; you are of more value than many sparrows. <sup>32</sup>So everyone who acknowledges me before men, I also will acknowledge before my Father who is in heaven, <sup>33</sup>but whoever denies me before men, I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven. <sup>34</sup>“Do not think that I have come to bring peace to the earth. I have not come to bring peace, but a sword. <sup>35</sup>For I have come to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law. <sup>36</sup>And a person’s enemies will be those of his own household. <sup>37</sup>Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me, and whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me. <sup>38</sup>And whoever does not take his cross and follow me is not worthy of me. <sup>39</sup>Whoever finds his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for my sake will find it. <sup>40</sup>“Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. <sup>41</sup>The one who receives a prophet because he is a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward, and the one who receives a righteous person because he is a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward. <sup>42</sup>And whoever gives one of these little ones even a cup of cold water because he is a disciple, truly, I say to you, he will by no means lose his reward.”
10.overview:
Chapter 10 is the mission discourse — the second of Matthew’s five great discourses. Jesus commissions the Twelve, gives them his authority, and sends them first to Israel. But the instructions quickly expand beyond a local mission trip to describe the entire missionary existence of the church until the end of the age. Persecution is not an accident but the normal condition of mission: “I am sending you out as sheep in the midst of wolves.” The sheep do not become wolves; they remain sheep — dependent, vulnerable, and under the care of the Shepherd.

The antidote to the fear of persecution is the fear of God. Three times Jesus says “fear not” (vv. 26, 28, 31), anchoring each command in the sovereign knowledge and care of the Father. Not a sparrow falls without him; the hairs of the head are numbered. If the Father governs such small things, he governs the sufferings of his missionaries. The cross appears explicitly in verse 38: discipleship is cruciform. The disciple takes up the cross before the resurrection — only those who lose their lives for Christ’s sake will find them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — The Twelve Sent Out: Authority, Message, and Provision
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus calls the Twelve, names them, and sends them out with authority over unclean spirits and disease. Their mission is confined to Israel: go to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, not to the Gentiles or Samaritans. They are to preach the kingdom, heal the sick, raise the dead, and cast out demons — exactly what Jesus himself has been doing. Their provision is radical dependence: no gold, no bag, no extra tunic. Worthy households will host them; unworthy towns will receive judgment. This is the only time Matthew uses the word "apostles" — once in twenty-eight chapters, at the exact moment they stop learning and start being sent. The Twelve is a claim, not a headcount: ten tribes had been gone for seven hundred years, and Jesus says himself that these men will judge the twelve tribes (19:28), so appointing exactly twelve is the reconstituting of Israel. Note the limits of the delegation — authority over unclean spirits and disease, but not to forgive sins, which is nowhere handed over. The list is in pairs because he sent them out two by two (Mk. 6:7): Peter and Andrew, James and John, Philip and Bartholomew, Thomas and Matthew, James and Thaddaeus, Simon the Zealot and Judas. Which sharpens the incompatibility until it draws blood: the Zealot movement existed to expel Rome by violence, and the Jews they killed first were collaborators — men like Matthew, a few names away in the same list. Nothing suggests Jesus arranged a reconciliation or that either changed his politics. On the charge: "raise the dead" is in it, and Matthew alone records that. "You received without paying, give without pay" is dorean twice — and the guard is supplied two verses later, since "the labourer deserves his food" (v. 10) is quoted by Paul to argue that preachers should be supported (1 Cor. 9:14; 1 Tim. 5:18). A worker may be supported; a gift may not be sold. "worthy" (axios) occurs four times in vv. 10-13 and the definition is purely practical — a worthy house is one that opens its door. And staying in one house forecloses the patron-shopping that itinerant teachers were notorious for; a Christian handbook of the next century, the Didache, has to legislate against exactly that. The dust-shaking was the gesture a Jew made leaving pagan soil — performed now on a Jewish town, it is a verdict delivered in mime.
verseByVerse.theology: The mission of the Twelve is an extension of Jesus's own mission: he gives them his authority (10:1) and his message (10:7). Disciples are not innovators but ambassadors — they carry the word and power of the one who sent them, not their own. The restriction to Israel (v. 5-6) is not permanent exclusion of Gentiles but the priority of the gospel going first to the lost sheep of Israel, as Paul will later articulate (Rom. 1:16). The Great Commission (28:18-20) will remove the restriction after the resurrection.
verseByVerse.examples: Radical dependence — no gold, no bag, no sandals beyond what they are wearing — is not poverty for its own sake but trust in the Lord of the harvest to provide through the households that receive them. The kingdom worker is not self-sufficient; they are wholly dependent on God's provision through his people. This dependence is not weakness but testimony: the worker who needs nothing from you has nothing to demonstrate about the kingdom's power to provide.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called to him his twelve disciples and gave them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to heal every disease and every affliction. The names of the twelve apostles are these: first, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus called his twelve disciples and gave them his own authority to drive out evil spirits and heal every disease. These twelve are named as apostles: men sent out with his authority.

The connection. At the end of chapter 9, Jesus told his disciples to pray for workers for the harvest (9:38). Now he sends the very disciples who prayed. Chapter 10 is the second of Jesus’ five great teaching sections in Matthew: the mission discourse. It covers their first mission (vv. 5–15) and then looks far beyond it, to the mission of the church in a hostile world (vv. 16–42).

And he called to him his twelve disciples. Jesus had many disciples, but chose twelve to be with him and to be sent out (Mark 3:14). Twelve matches the twelve tribes of Israel. Jesus is forming a new Israel, the restored people of God, around himself. The Twelve will sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes (19:28), and their names are on the foundations of the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:14).

And gave them authority. His own authority (see 7:29; 9:6). They do not have power of their own; it is delegated, as an ambassador carries the authority of his king.

Over unclean spirits, to cast them out. “Unclean spirits” is another name for demons: they are morally impure and defile those they possess.

And to heal every disease and every affliction. The same words used of Jesus’ ministry (4:23; 9:35). The disciples extend his work.

The names of the twelve apostles are these. The only time Matthew uses the word “apostles”. An apostle (apostolos) is one sent, a messenger or envoy with the authority of the sender. In Jewish law, a person’s authorised agent was regarded as the person himself (see v. 40).

First, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother. “First” does not only mean first in the list; Peter is the leader and spokesman of the Twelve throughout the Gospels (16:16–19). He always appears first in the lists of apostles (Mark 3:16–19; Luke 6:14–16; Acts 1:13), and Judas always last. The list is in pairs, perhaps because Jesus sent them out two by two (Mark 6:7).

James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother. With Peter, the inner circle (see 4:21).

What it does not mean. Not that Peter was given authority over the other apostles as a pope over the church. He was first among equals, a leader and spokesman. (See 16:18.) Nor does it mean that every Christian has the same authority the Twelve had. The apostles had a unique, foundational role (Ephesians 2:20). But every Christian shares in the mission they began (28:19–20).

In a sentence. Jesus gave his twelve chosen apostles his own authority over demons and disease and sent them out as the foundation of a new Israel.

On a Tuesday. The disciples who prayed for workers became the workers. Be ready for God to send you as the answer to your own prayers.
verseByVerse.note: “Apostle” means one who is sent. Twelve matches the twelve tribes of Israel.

parallels.desc: the twelve apostles on the city’s foundations

verseByVerse.quote: James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother; Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas and Matthew the tax collector; James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus; Simon the Zealot, and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The list of the twelve continues: James and John, Philip, Bartholomew, Thomas, Matthew the tax collector, James son of Alphaeus, Thaddaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him.

Philip and Bartholomew. Philip came from Bethsaida, the same town as Peter and Andrew (John 1:44). Bartholomew means “son of Tolmai”; he is often identified with Nathanael, whom Philip brought to Jesus (John 1:45–49), because in John’s Gospel Philip and Nathanael are paired, and Bartholomew appears next to Philip in the lists.

Thomas. Known for doubting the resurrection until he saw Jesus, and then for one of the greatest confessions in the Gospels: my Lord and my God (John 20:24–29). His name means “twin”.

And Matthew the tax collector. The author of this Gospel. Only Matthew adds “the tax collector” to his own name. He never forgot the grace that called him (9:9).

James the son of Alphaeus. Probably also called “James the less” or “the younger” (Mark 15:40).

And Thaddaeus. Probably the same person Luke calls “Judas the son of James” (Luke 6:16; Acts 1:13). Some manuscripts call him Lebbaeus. Many people had more than one name.

Simon the Zealot. Literally “the Cananaean”, from an Aramaic word meaning “zealous”. Luke calls him “the Zealot” (Luke 6:15). He may have belonged to the Zealots, a nationalist movement willing to use violence to overthrow Rome; or the name may simply describe his zeal for the law. Either way, it is striking that Jesus chose both Matthew, who had collaborated with Rome, and Simon, who had probably wanted to fight Rome. In Jesus’ new community, political enemies became brothers.

And Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him. “Iscariot” probably means “man of Kerioth”, a town in southern Judea; he may have been the only one of the Twelve not from Galilee. He always comes last, labelled by his betrayal (26:14–16, 47–50). Jesus chose him knowingly (John 6:70–71). His presence among the Twelve is a solemn warning: it is possible to be close to Jesus, to share in his ministry, even to do miracles in his name (7:22), and yet not belong to him.

The kind of people. Fishermen, a tax collector, a zealot: ordinary, unremarkable, very different men. None were religious leaders, scholars or priests. Jesus chooses the weak and lowly to shame the strong (1 Corinthians 1:26–29).

What it does not mean. Not that Judas was forced to betray Jesus against his will. God’s plan included the betrayal (Acts 2:23), and Scripture had foretold it (Psalm 41:9), but Judas acted freely and was fully responsible (26:24). God’s sovereignty and human responsibility are both true.

In a sentence. Jesus chose twelve ordinary and very different men, including a tax collector, a zealot, and the one who would betray him.

On a Tuesday. Jesus puts very different people together in his church. Who is the “Simon the Zealot” to your “Matthew”? Love them as a brother or sister in Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Bartholomew is often identified with Nathanael of John’s Gospel. Thaddaeus is probably the “Judas the son of James” of Luke’s lists.

verseByVerse.quote: These twelve Jesus sent out, instructing them, "Go nowhere among the Gentiles and enter no town of the Samaritans, but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus sent the Twelve out with instructions: do not go to the Gentiles or to Samaritan towns, but go to the lost sheep of Israel.

These twelve Jesus sent out. The verb is related to “apostle”: he sent them as his envoys.

Go nowhere among the Gentiles and enter no town of the Samaritans. A surprising restriction. The Samaritans lived in the region between Judea and Galilee. They were descendants of Israelites from the northern kingdom who intermarried with foreigners after the Assyrian conquest of 722 BC (2 Kings 17:24–41). They accepted only the five books of Moses and worshipped on Mount Gerizim instead of in Jerusalem (John 4:20). Jews and Samaritans despised each other.

But go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. “Lost sheep” echoes 9:36: the people of Israel were like sheep without a shepherd. God had made his covenant promises to Israel, and the Messiah came first to them. Jesus said the same of his own mission (15:24). Paul’s principle was to the Jew first, and also to the Greek (Romans 1:16; Acts 13:46).

Why the restriction? Not because Jesus did not care about Gentiles. He has already healed a Gentile’s servant and praised his faith (8:5–13), and he will command his disciples to go to all nations (28:19). The order reflects God’s plan in history: first Israel, then the nations. The prophets pictured Israel restored first, and then the nations streaming to Zion (Isaiah 2:2–3; 49:6). After the resurrection, the mission goes to Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria and the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8).

What it does not mean. Not that this restriction applies to the church today. It was for this first mission. The Great Commission sends the church to all nations (28:19–20). Nor does “lost” here mean that every Israelite was unsaved; it describes the nation as scattered and neglected by its leaders, needing its Shepherd.

In a sentence. On their first mission, the Twelve were sent only to Israel’s lost sheep, because God’s plan was to come to Israel first and then to the nations.

On a Tuesday. God works in order and in his time. Trust his plan when you do not yet see why one door is open and another closed.
verseByVerse.note: Samaritans lived between Judea and Galilee, a people of mixed descent who worshipped on Mount Gerizim rather than in Jerusalem. The mission to the nations would come after the resurrection.

parallels.desc: the lost sheep of the house of Israel

verseByVerse.quote: And proclaim as you go, saying, "The kingdom of heaven is at hand." Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons. You received without paying; give without pay.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The message and the work: proclaim that the kingdom of heaven has come near; heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons. You received freely; give freely.

And proclaim as you go. The disciples were heralds (see 3:1).

The kingdom of heaven is at hand. The same message as John (3:2) and Jesus (4:17). God’s reign has arrived in Jesus.

Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons. Exactly what Jesus did in chapters 8–9. The disciples’ works were signs that confirmed their message: the kingdom is here, and its power is driving back sickness, death and evil.

You received without paying; give without pay. They had received authority and the message freely from Jesus. They must not charge for it. In the ancient world, wandering philosophers and miracle-workers often made money from their teaching and healing. Jesus’ messengers must not. Simon the magician later tried to buy the power of the Spirit, and Peter rebuked him severely (Acts 8:18–24). Grace freely received must be freely given.

What it does not mean. Not that those who preach the gospel may not be supported by others. Jesus immediately says the worker deserves his food (v. 10), and Paul defends the right of ministers to be paid (1 Corinthians 9:14; 1 Timothy 5:17–18). The point is that the gospel is never sold, and ministry is not done for money. Nor does the command to heal and raise the dead mean that every Christian today has these powers. These were special signs given to the apostles to confirm the message (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4).

In a sentence. The apostles were to announce the kingdom and show its power in works of healing, freely giving what they had freely received.

On a Tuesday. What have you freely received from God: forgiveness, grace, gifts, time? Give freely to others today, without expecting anything back.

parallels.desc: what I have I give you

verseByVerse.quote: Acquire no gold or silver or copper for your belts, no bag for your journey, or two tunics or sandals or a staff, for the laborer deserves his food.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not take money, a travel bag, spare clothing, sandals or a staff. Travel light, and depend on God to provide through the people you serve: a worker deserves his food.

Acquire no gold or silver or copper for your belts. Coins were often carried in the folds of a cloth belt. Gold, silver and copper: no money at all.

No bag for your journey. A traveller’s bag for food and supplies, or possibly a beggar’s bag for collecting gifts. They were not to beg.

Or two tunics or sandals or a staff. No spare clothes, no extra sandals, no walking stick. (Mark says they could take a staff and sandals, Mark 6:8–9. The difference may be that Matthew means do not acquire additional ones, and Mark means take the ones you have.)

For the laborer deserves his food. Those who receive the gospel should support those who bring it. The disciples were to trust God to provide through hospitality. Paul quotes the same principle (1 Timothy 5:18).

The point. The mission was urgent, and the disciples needed to learn to depend on God. Travelling light also distinguished them from the travelling teachers who made money from their audiences.

What it does not mean. Not a permanent rule for all missionaries. At the Last Supper, Jesus told the disciples that from then on they should take a moneybag and a knapsack (Luke 22:35–36). Conditions changed. But the principles remain: simplicity, urgency, dependence on God, and the duty of God’s people to support those who serve them with the gospel.

In a sentence. The apostles were to travel light and depend on God’s provision through those who received them, since a worker deserves his food.

On a Tuesday. Do you support those who teach you God’s word (Galatians 6:6)? And what could you let go of to travel lighter in following Christ?
verseByVerse.note: Coins were carried in the belt. The “bag” was a traveller’s pack for supplies.

parallels.desc: those who proclaim the gospel get their living by it

verseByVerse.quote: And whatever town or village you enter, find out who is worthy in it and stay there until you depart. As you enter the house, greet it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In each town, find someone worthy and stay with them until you leave. When you enter a house, greet it.

Find out who is worthy in it. “Worthy” here means a person open to the message, ready to welcome God’s messengers: someone like the “son of peace” in Luke 10:6. Not morally perfect, but receptive.

And stay there until you depart. Do not move from house to house looking for better hospitality. Be content and avoid giving offence.

As you enter the house, greet it. The normal greeting was Shalom, “peace” (Luke 10:5). From Jesus’ messengers, it was more than a polite word: it was a blessing, offering the peace of the kingdom.

What it does not mean. Not that only respectable or good people are “worthy” of the gospel. Jesus ate with sinners (9:10). Worthiness here is openness, not merit.

In a sentence. The apostles were to stay with those who welcomed them and bring the blessing of peace to each household.

On a Tuesday. Hospitality to Christian workers is a ministry. Could you open your home to a missionary, a visiting preacher or a new believer?

verseByVerse.quote: And if the house is worthy, let your peace come upon it, but if it is not worthy, let your peace return to you. And if anyone will not receive you or listen to your words, shake off the dust from your feet when you leave that house or town.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If a house welcomes you, let your peace rest on it; if not, let your peace return to you. If a town or house rejects you and your message, shake its dust off your feet as you leave.

If the house is worthy, let your peace come upon it. The blessing of peace comes on those who receive it. Peace here is the shalom of the kingdom: God’s blessing and salvation.

But if it is not worthy, let your peace return to you. If they reject it, the blessing does not take effect on them. It is not wasted, but it is withdrawn.

And if anyone will not receive you or listen to your words. Rejection of the messengers and of their message.

Shake off the dust from your feet when you leave that house or town. Strict Jews returning from Gentile lands would shake off the dust from their feet, so as not to bring unclean soil into the holy land. For the disciples to do this to a Jewish town was a startling symbolic act: it declared that the town, by rejecting the Messiah, had made itself like a pagan land, and that the messengers were no longer responsible for it. Paul and Barnabas did exactly this at Pisidian Antioch (Acts 13:51).

What it does not mean. Not an act of personal anger or contempt. It was a solemn warning, done with sorrow, leaving the town to God. Nor does it mean that Christians should give up quickly on people. The disciples’ mission was urgent and their time short; in ordinary life, Christians often keep loving and praying for those who reject the gospel for many years.

In a sentence. Those who receive the messengers receive peace; those who reject them are solemnly left to God.

On a Tuesday. When someone rejects the gospel, you are not responsible for their response, only for your faithfulness. Leave the results to God.
verseByVerse.note: Shaking off the dust was a sign that a town was being left to God’s judgment.

parallels.desc: Paul and Barnabas shake off the dust

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, I say to you, it will be more bearable on the day of judgment for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah than for that town.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus warned that on the day of judgment it will be more bearable for Sodom and Gomorrah than for a town that rejects his messengers.

Truly, I say to you. A solemn statement of Jesus’ authority (see 5:18).

It will be more bearable on the day of judgment. There are degrees of judgment. All who reject God face judgment, but not all equally (11:22–24; Luke 12:47–48).

For the land of Sodom and Gomorrah. Cities destroyed by fire from heaven for their great wickedness, including violence, pride, sexual immorality and neglect of the poor (Genesis 18–19; Ezekiel 16:49–50; Jude 7). They became a byword for God’s judgment.

Than for that town. A shocking comparison for Jewish hearers. Sodom was the worst example of a wicked city. Yet a town in Israel that rejects the Messiah’s messengers will face worse judgment. Why? Because greater light brings greater responsibility. Sodom never heard the gospel or saw the Messiah’s works. To reject him with full knowledge is a greater sin.

What it does not mean. Not that Sodom will escape judgment. Nor that sexual sin does not matter. The point is that rejecting Christ, with knowledge, is the most serious sin of all (John 3:18–19; Hebrews 10:26–29).

In a sentence. Those who reject Christ’s messengers, having heard the gospel, will face a heavier judgment than even Sodom.

On a Tuesday. You have heard the gospel more clearly than most people in history. Greater privilege brings greater responsibility. Do not treat it lightly.

parallels.desc: the fall of Sodom and Gomorrah

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–42 — Persecution, Confession, and the Cross: The Cost of the Mission
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second half of the mission discourse turns from method to cost. Jesus warns the disciples of coming persecution — before synagogues, governors, and kings — and promises the Spirit's help in that moment. He sets family divisions as the expected consequence of his mission and demands that disciples value him above father, mother, son, and daughter. The section culminates in the cross-bearing saying and the principle that whoever loses their life for Jesus will find it. Four things more. The backbone of vv. 26-31 is three "do not fear" commands, each with a different ground: because everything hidden will come out (v. 26), because there is a worse thing than dying (v. 28), because you are valued (v. 31) — the fear of being misrepresented, of being killed, and of being insignificant, each answered with a fact rather than an exhortation. On v. 28, the one to be feared is God, not Satan (who has no such authority, and cf. Lk. 12:5) — and the strangeness of hearing that beside "your Father" attends to sparrows is the point, not a problem. gehenna is a place name: the Valley of Hinnom, where children were burned to Molech until Josiah defiled the site (2 Kgs. 23:10; Jer. 7:31). The sparrow arithmetic is exact — two for a penny here, but five for two pennies in Luke 12:6, so the fifth was the makeweight thrown in free; and Luke's promise is that not one of them is forgotten. And vv. 29-31 need a guard, because they read like a promise of safety and cannot be: the sparrow falls, and by early tradition many of the men hearing this died violent deaths. The promise is not that the worst will not happen but that it will not happen unnoticed. Note too that v. 38 is the first mention of a cross in Matthew — and it comes six chapters before Jesus says anything about his own death (16:21), so the twelve heard it with no idea their master would die on one. Varus had crucified two thousand Jews within living memory; the image is the walk, carrying the beam past everyone you know. And "not peace but a sword" is glossed by Luke as division (Lk. 12:51) — while the Micah 7:6 Jesus quotes was a standard description of the birth-pangs of the messianic age, and its very next verse is "but as for me, I will look to the LORD".
verseByVerse.theology: The persecution discourse is not pessimism but realism: "a disciple is not above his teacher." Jesus himself will be persecuted; his followers will share his fate. The Spirit's provision in persecution is specific — not general spiritual support but particular words at the moment of trial. This is the promise that has sustained Christian martyrs across every century: the one who sends into danger is the one who speaks in danger. The fearlessness Jesus commands is grounded not in courage but in theology: God knows, God values, God reigns.
verseByVerse.examples: The cross-bearing saying (v. 38) appears here before the crucifixion — Jesus uses the cross as a metaphor before it is a fact. Every disciple must take up their own cross, not his. This is the death of the self-directed life: a public alignment with a man under sentence, at the cost of respectability and safety alike. The paradox of verses 39 is the deepest saying in the chapter: the one who clutches their life loses it; the one who surrenders it for Jesus finds it.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I am sending you out as sheep in the midst of wolves, so be wise as serpents and innocent as doves. Beware of men, for they will deliver you over to courts and flog you in their synagogues,
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am sending you out like sheep among wolves. So be shrewd as snakes and innocent as doves. Be on your guard: people will hand you over to councils and flog you in their synagogues.

The wider horizon. From verse 16 onward, Jesus looks beyond the first short mission to the whole future mission of the church: governors, kings, Gentiles, and persecution until he returns (vv. 18, 22–23). Much of this did not happen on the first mission, but it happened in Acts and has happened ever since.

Behold, I am sending you out as sheep in the midst of wolves. Sheep are defenceless; wolves are predators. The disciples will be vulnerable in a hostile world. But note: “I am sending you”. Jesus knows exactly where he is sending them, and he is the Shepherd (9:36).

So be wise as serpents. Snakes were proverbially shrewd and cautious (Genesis 3:1). Disciples must be wise, prudent and alert: not naive, not taking unnecessary risks, not provoking needless trouble.

And innocent as doves. “Innocent” (akeraioi) means pure, unmixed, without guile. Doves were proverbially gentle and harmless. Wisdom without innocence becomes cunning; innocence without wisdom becomes foolishness. Disciples need both.

Beware of men. Do not trust people naively. Opposition will come from people, including religious people.

For they will deliver you over to courts. “Courts” is synedria, local Jewish councils (the word is related to Sanhedrin).

And flog you in their synagogues. Synagogues had authority to discipline Jews by flogging. The law allowed forty lashes (Deuteronomy 25:3), and the practice was thirty-nine, to avoid exceeding the limit. Paul received this five times (2 Corinthians 11:24).

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should be suspicious of everyone, or that all opposition is persecution for righteousness. “Wise as serpents” includes not bringing trouble on ourselves by foolishness or rudeness. Nor does it permit deceit: the dove’s innocence rules out lies and trickery.

In a sentence. Jesus sends his disciples like defenceless sheep among wolves, so they must be wise and pure, and ready for opposition even from religious authorities.

On a Tuesday. Where do you need more wisdom in your witness, and where do you need more innocence? Ask God for both.
verseByVerse.note: Synagogues had the authority to flog; the law allowed up to forty lashes, kept to thirty-nine in practice.

parallels.desc: five times the forty lashes less one

verseByVerse.quote: and you will be dragged before governors and kings for my sake, to bear witness before them and the Gentiles. When they deliver you over, do not be anxious how you are to speak or what you are to say, for what you are to say will be given to you in that hour.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You will be dragged before governors and kings because of me, to bear witness to them and to the nations. When you are arrested, do not worry about what to say, because you will be given the words at that moment.

And you will be dragged before governors and kings for my sake. Governors were Roman officials, like Pilate, Felix and Festus; kings were client rulers, like Herod Agrippa. Paul stood before all of these (Acts 23–26). Peter and John stood before the Sanhedrin (Acts 4–5). James was executed by Herod (Acts 12:2).

To bear witness before them and the Gentiles. Persecution becomes an opportunity for witness. The trial room becomes a pulpit. Paul preached to governors and kings because he was arrested (Acts 26:1–29). Here the Gentiles are mentioned: the mission will reach beyond Israel.

When they deliver you over, do not be anxious how you are to speak or what you are to say. “Anxious” is the same word as in 6:25–34. Jesus forbids worry about a trial, as he forbade worry about food.

For what you are to say will be given to you in that hour. God will provide the words when they are needed, as he provided for Moses (Exodus 4:12). Stephen spoke with such wisdom that his opponents could not resist it (Acts 6:10).

What it does not mean. Not that preachers do not need to prepare sermons. This is a promise for those suddenly put on trial for their faith, not an excuse for laziness in teaching. Paul urged Timothy to study and work hard at teaching (2 Timothy 2:15). Nor is it a promise of acquittal: Stephen spoke well and was killed (Acts 7).

In a sentence. Persecution will bring disciples before rulers as witnesses, and they need not worry about what to say, because God will give them the words.

On a Tuesday. If you are anxious about speaking of Christ in a hostile situation, pray, and trust him to help you in that moment.

verseByVerse.quote: For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you. Brother will deliver brother over to death, and the father his child, and children will rise against parents and have them put to death,
verseByVerse.commentary:
It will not be you speaking but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you. Persecution will divide families: brother will betray brother to death, a father his child, and children their parents.

For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you. The Holy Spirit will speak through them. This is the first mention of the Spirit in Matthew since 4:1. “The Spirit of your Father”: the same Father who cares for sparrows (v. 29) gives his Spirit to his persecuted children.

Brother will deliver brother over to death, and the father his child. The gospel will divide families. In the early church, converts from Judaism or paganism were sometimes disowned, reported to authorities, or killed by their own families. This still happens today in many parts of the world. Micah 7:6 had described a time of such social breakdown (quoted in vv. 35–36).

And children will rise against parents and have them put to death. The deepest bonds of human life will be broken by hatred of Christ.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should expect or provoke family division. The gospel brings peace to many families. But when family members reject Christ, loyalty to him may bring painful division.

In a sentence. The Spirit will speak through persecuted disciples, even when their own families turn against them.

On a Tuesday. Pray for believers today who have been rejected or endangered by their families because of Christ, especially converts from other religions.

parallels.desc: a man’s enemies are the men of his own house

verseByVerse.quote: and you will be hated by all for my name's sake. But the one who endures to the end will be saved. When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next, for truly, I say to you, you will not have gone through all the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You will be hated by everyone because of my name. But the one who endures to the end will be saved. When you are persecuted in one town, flee to the next. You will not finish going through the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes.

And you will be hated by all for my name’s sake. “All” means people of every kind, not literally every individual. “For my name’s sake”: because you belong to Jesus. The world hated him first (John 15:18–20).

But the one who endures to the end will be saved. “Endure” means to remain, to persevere, to hold on under pressure. “To the end” may mean to the end of one’s life, or to the end of the age. True faith perseveres. Those who fall away under persecution show that their faith was not genuine (13:20–21; 1 John 2:19).

When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next. Fleeing persecution is not cowardice. The disciples are not to seek martyrdom, but to keep spreading the message. Persecution in Jerusalem scattered the church and spread the gospel (Acts 8:1–4).

For truly, I say to you, you will not have gone through all the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes. A difficult verse. What “coming” does Jesus mean? Several views:

1. The resurrection and ascension. The Son of Man “comes” in vindication when he is raised and receives all authority (28:18; Daniel 7:13–14).

2. The destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70. A coming in judgment on the nation that rejected him (24:30, 34).

3. The second coming. The mission to Israel will continue until Christ returns at the end of the age; it will never be finished.

Verdict: most likely the coming in judgment in AD 70 (view 2), within the generation of the disciples, as Jesus says in 16:28 and 24:34, though this event itself foreshadows the final coming. On any view, the point is: the mission to Israel is urgent, and it will not be complete before the Son of Man acts.

What it does not mean. Not that salvation is earned by endurance. Endurance is the evidence and fruit of true faith, and God himself gives it. Those whom God has saved, he will keep to the end (John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6). This is the doctrine called the perseverance of the saints (Westminster Confession 17). The warning and the promise belong together: God keeps his people precisely by moving them to persevere. Nor does Jesus’ word mean that he was mistaken about the timing of his return. It refers to a coming in his own generation.

In a sentence. Disciples will be hated for Christ’s name, but those who persevere to the end will be saved; they should flee persecution and keep spreading the message.

On a Tuesday. Endurance is built day by day. What is one small act of faithfulness you can do today to keep going?

parallels.desc: the one who endures to the end

verseByVerse.quote: A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his master. It is enough for the disciple to be like his teacher, and the servant like his master. If they have called the master of the house Beelzebul, how much more will they malign those of his household.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his master. It is enough for a disciple to be treated like his teacher. If they called the head of the house Beelzebul, they will say even worse about the members of his household.

A disciple is not above his teacher. A proverb. Students do not expect better treatment than their teacher.

It is enough for the disciple to be like his teacher. If Jesus was rejected and persecuted, his disciples should expect the same. Being like him is honour enough (John 15:20).

If they have called the master of the house Beelzebul. The Pharisees had accused Jesus of casting out demons by the prince of demons (9:34; 12:24). “Beelzebul” was a name for Satan, perhaps meaning “lord of the dwelling” (which fits “master of the house”), or a form of Baal-zebub, meaning lord of the flies, the god of the Philistine city of Ekron (2 Kings 1:2). They called Jesus the devil.

How much more will they malign those of his household. If they insulted the head of the house, they will insult his family.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should expect only rejection. Some will receive them (vv. 11, 40–42). But they must not be surprised when they are treated as their Lord was (1 Peter 4:12–14).

In a sentence. If the world called Jesus the devil, his disciples must expect similar treatment, and count it an honour to share his lot.

On a Tuesday. When you are misrepresented for your faith, remember what they said about your Master. You are in good company.
verseByVerse.note: Beelzebul is a name for Satan.

parallels.desc: a servant is not greater than his master

verseByVerse.quote: So have no fear of them, for nothing is covered that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known. What I tell you in the dark, say in the light, and what you hear whispered, proclaim on the housetops.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So do not be afraid of them. Everything hidden will be revealed. What I tell you privately, speak in the light; what you hear whispered, proclaim from the rooftops.

So have no fear of them. The first of three “do not fear” commands (vv. 26, 28, 31). Fear of people is the great enemy of witness (Proverbs 29:25).

For nothing is covered that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known. The truth will come out. God will vindicate his people and expose their persecutors at the judgment. And the gospel, which now seems hidden and small, will be known by all.

What I tell you in the dark, say in the light. Jesus taught his disciples privately, often explaining things he did not explain to the crowds (13:10–11). After his resurrection, they must proclaim it all openly.

And what you hear whispered, proclaim on the housetops. Houses had flat roofs, used as public spaces. Announcements were made from rooftops, where they could be heard across the village. The gospel is not secret wisdom for a few, but public news for all.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians must be loud or aggressive. But they must not be silent from fear.

In a sentence. Do not fear opponents, because the truth will be revealed; proclaim openly what Jesus taught privately.

On a Tuesday. What has Christ taught you in private, in your Bible reading and prayer, that you need to share with someone today?
verseByVerse.note: Flat roofs were public places; announcements were made from them.

verseByVerse.quote: And do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell. Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not fear those who can kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Fear God, who can destroy both soul and body in hell. Yet that same God cares for sparrows, the cheapest of birds: not one falls to the ground apart from your Father.

And do not fear those who kill the body. The worst persecutors can do is kill the body.

But cannot kill the soul. The soul, the inner self, survives the death of the body. Persecutors cannot touch the believer’s relationship with God or eternal life. Here the Bible distinguishes body and soul, and teaches that the soul continues after death (Luke 23:43; 2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23).

Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell. God. “Hell” is Gehenna (see 5:22). Fear of God is not cringing terror, but reverent awe of the one who holds final judgment. Fear of God drives out fear of people. Those who fear God fear nothing else (Isaiah 8:12–13).

Destroy both soul and body. Some (annihilationists) take “destroy” to mean that the wicked cease to exist. But the same word is used of the lost sheep (v. 6), who are not annihilated but ruined. Elsewhere Jesus speaks of eternal punishment (25:46) and unquenchable fire (3:12). Verdict: “destroy” means ruin, the loss of all that makes life life, not cessation of existence. The traditional view of hell as conscious, eternal punishment is the biblical one.

Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? Sparrows were the cheapest birds sold for food. A “penny” (assarion) was a small copper coin, about a sixteenth of a day’s wage. Luke says five sparrows for two pennies (Luke 12:6): buy four, and one was thrown in free.

And not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father. God is in control of the smallest events: the death of a sparrow. “Apart from your Father” means without his knowledge and will. This is the doctrine of providence: God governs all things, great and small (Westminster Confession 5.1). If he governs the death of a sparrow, he governs the death of his children.

The balance. Fear God as the Judge; trust God as your Father. The same God who can destroy soul and body in hell is the Father who watches every sparrow. For those who belong to him, the fear of God becomes the foundation of confidence.

What it does not mean. Not that sparrows, or believers, never fall. They do. But they never fall outside the Father’s will. Persecution and death come, but not by accident.

In a sentence. Fear God, not people, and trust him as your Father, who governs even the death of a sparrow.

On a Tuesday. Whose opinion do you fear most? Bring that fear to God, and let fear of him, and trust in his care, replace it.
verseByVerse.note: “Hell” renders Gehenna. Sparrows were the cheapest birds sold for food; the “penny” was a small copper coin.

verseByVerse.quote: But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not, therefore; you are of more value than many sparrows.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God knows even the number of hairs on your head. So do not be afraid: you are worth more than many sparrows.

But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Most people have over 100,000 hairs. God knows exactly how many. Nothing about you is too small for his attention. This is personal, detailed care.

Fear not, therefore. The third “do not fear” (vv. 26, 28, 31).

You are of more value than many sparrows. A gentle, almost humorous comparison: if God cares for sparrows, how much more for you, his children, made in his image and redeemed by his Son.

What it does not mean. Not that God’s care guarantees freedom from suffering or death. The context is persecution, even martyrdom. But it guarantees that nothing happens by chance, and that God’s children are precious to him through all of it. Paul says nothing can separate us from God’s love, not even death (Romans 8:35–39).

In a sentence. God knows you in every detail and values you greatly, so you need not fear.

For worship. Thank God that he knows you completely, down to the hairs of your head, and values you.

parallels.desc: not one hair of his head shall fall

verseByVerse.quote: So everyone who acknowledges me before men, I also will acknowledge before my Father who is in heaven, but whoever denies me before men, I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who openly acknowledges Jesus before people, he will acknowledge before his Father in heaven. But whoever denies him before people, he will deny before his Father.

So everyone who acknowledges me before men. “Acknowledge” (homologeō) means to confess, to declare publicly, to say the same thing. To acknowledge Jesus is to say openly that you belong to him and that he is Lord (Romans 10:9–10). Under persecution, this could cost one’s life.

I also will acknowledge before my Father who is in heaven. At the final judgment, Jesus will say: this one is mine. Jesus presents himself as the one whose word decides our eternal destiny before God.

But whoever denies me before men, I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven. To deny Jesus is to disown him, to say “I do not know him”. Jesus will say the same of them: I never knew you (7:23).

Peter’s denial. Peter denied Jesus three times (26:69–75). Was he lost? No. He wept bitterly and was restored (John 21:15–19). The warning is about a settled, final rejection of Christ, not a moment of weakness followed by repentance. Peter’s denial and restoration show that Jesus is gracious to those who fall and return.

What it does not mean. Not that every moment of cowardice or silence damns a person. All believers fail. But a life that refuses to acknowledge Christ when it counts shows that he is not truly treasured. Nor does acknowledging Jesus mean only words: our lives also confess or deny him (Titus 1:16).

In a sentence. Those who openly confess Christ will be confessed by him before the Father; those who finally disown him will be disowned.

On a Tuesday. Where are you tempted to hide that you are a Christian: at work, among friends, online? Acknowledge him today, gently and clearly.

parallels.desc: if we deny him, he also will deny us

verseByVerse.quote: Do not think that I have come to bring peace to the earth. I have not come to bring peace, but a sword. For I have come to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not think that Jesus came to bring a peace that leaves everything undisturbed. He came to bring a sword: his call divides even families, setting a son against his father, a daughter against her mother.

Do not think that I have come to bring peace to the earth. Surprising words from the Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6). Jesus does bring peace: peace with God (Romans 5:1), and peace among those reconciled to God (Ephesians 2:14). But the immediate effect of his coming is division, because people respond to him in opposite ways.

I have not come to bring peace, but a sword. The sword is a picture of division, not of violence by his followers. Jesus rebuked Peter for using a real sword (26:52). The sword cuts between those who follow him and those who reject him (Luke 12:51 says “division”). Hebrews 4:12 says that the word of God is sharper than any two-edged sword. Simeon said that Jesus was set for the fall and rising of many and as a sign that is opposed (Luke 2:34–35).

For I have come to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law. Jesus quotes Micah 7:6, which describes a time of social and family breakdown in Israel’s sinfulness. Jesus uses it to describe the effect of his coming. When one member of a family follows Christ and others do not, their deepest loyalties now differ.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should cause division in their families or treat unbelieving relatives with hostility. Peter tells believing wives to win unbelieving husbands by their conduct (1 Peter 3:1–2). The division comes from the different responses to Christ, not from Christian aggression. Nor does it mean that Jesus wants families to break up. He wants them all to follow him.

In a sentence. Jesus’ call divides people, even families, because some follow him and others do not.

On a Tuesday. If following Christ has created tension in your family, keep loving and praying for them, and do not give up your loyalty to him.

parallels.desc: son against father, daughter against mother

verseByVerse.quote: and a person's enemies will be those of his own household. Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me, and whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A person’s enemies may be members of his own household. Whoever loves father or mother, son or daughter, more than Jesus is not worthy of him.

And a person’s enemies will be those of his own household. The end of the quotation from Micah 7:6. The worst opposition sometimes comes from those closest to us.

Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me. An astonishing claim. In Jewish law, honouring father and mother was one of the highest duties (Exodus 20:12). Jesus claims a loyalty above even that. Only God could claim such loyalty: the first commandment says, you shall have no other gods before me (Exodus 20:3). Jesus is implicitly claiming to be God. Luke’s version uses stronger language: if anyone does not “hate” his father and mother he cannot be my disciple (Luke 14:26), a Hebrew idiom meaning “love less” (see 6:24).

And whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me. Even our love for our children must come second to Christ.

Not worthy of me. Not fit to be his disciple. Not that anyone earns worthiness, but that a person who puts anything above Christ has not truly received him as Lord.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should love their families less, or neglect them. Christ commands love and care for family (15:4–6; 1 Timothy 5:8; Ephesians 5:25; 6:4). Loving Christ first actually makes us love our families better, with a love that is unselfish and rightly ordered. The point is priority: when loyalty to family and loyalty to Christ conflict, Christ must win. And this is not only for martyrs: it applies in decisions about career, marriage, where to live, and how to raise children.

In a sentence. Jesus must be loved more than our dearest family members, and whoever puts family above him is not fit to be his disciple.

On a Tuesday. Is there a family expectation or love that is competing with your obedience to Christ? Love your family by loving Christ first.

parallels.desc: a man’s enemies are the men of his own house

verseByVerse.quote: And whoever does not take his cross and follow me is not worthy of me. Whoever finds his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for my sake will find it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever does not take up his cross and follow Jesus is not worthy of him. Whoever holds on to his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for Jesus’ sake will find it.

And whoever does not take his cross and follow me. The first mention of the cross in Matthew. In the Roman world, crucifixion was the cruellest and most shameful form of execution, used for slaves, rebels and criminals. A condemned man carried his own crossbeam through the streets to the place of execution, in front of jeering crowds (27:32; John 19:17). The Romans had crucified thousands of Jews in Galilee after revolts. Everyone listening knew exactly what carrying a cross meant: a man walking to his death, publicly shamed, with no way back.

What “taking up the cross” means. Not putting up with ordinary hardships (“my bad back is my cross to bear”). It means dying to self: renouncing the right to run your own life, accepting rejection and shame for Christ, and being willing to die if necessary. It is a decisive, total surrender. Jesus will repeat it after he first predicts his own death (16:24), and Luke adds “daily” (Luke 9:23).

Is not worthy of me. See verse 37.

Whoever finds his life will lose it. “Life” (psychē) means the self, the soul, one’s whole life. Whoever tries to save their life by avoiding the cost of following Christ, protecting their comfort, reputation and safety, will in the end lose everything, including their soul (16:26).

And whoever loses his life for my sake will find it. Whoever gives up their life for Christ, in martyrdom or in daily self-giving, will find true life: life with God now and for ever. The paradox of the gospel: the way to life is through death. Jesus himself walked it first (John 12:24–25).

For my sake. Not any self-sacrifice, but sacrifice for Christ. Losing your life for a cause, a career or an ideology is not the same.

What it does not mean. Not that we earn salvation by suffering. Christ carried his cross to save us; we carry ours because we have been saved and now follow him. Nor does it mean that Christians should seek suffering for its own sake, or despise ordinary joys. The cross is the willingness to give up anything for Christ, not the rejection of God’s good gifts (1 Timothy 4:4).

In a sentence. Following Jesus means dying to self like a condemned man carrying his cross, and those who lose their lives for him find true life.

On a Tuesday. What do you need to die to today, a right, a reputation, a comfort, in order to follow Jesus?
verseByVerse.note: Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. The one who receives a prophet because he is a prophet will receive a prophet's reward, and the one who receives a righteous person because he is a righteous person will receive a righteous person's reward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever welcomes Jesus’ messengers welcomes Jesus, and whoever welcomes Jesus welcomes the Father who sent him. Whoever welcomes a prophet or a righteous person because of who they are will share their reward.

Whoever receives you receives me. The apostles are Jesus’ representatives (see v. 2). In Jewish thought, a man’s agent was as the man himself. To welcome them is to welcome Jesus. To reject them is to reject him (Luke 10:16).

And whoever receives me receives him who sent me. Jesus is the Father’s agent. To welcome him is to welcome God (John 13:20).

The one who receives a prophet because he is a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward. “Because he is a prophet” means for the sake of his message, recognising him as God’s messenger. Someone who supports God’s messenger shares in the messenger’s work and reward. The widow of Zarephath, who fed Elijah, shared in God’s provision (1 Kings 17:8–16); the Shunammite woman who welcomed Elisha received a son (2 Kings 4:8–17).

And the one who receives a righteous person because he is a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward. “Righteous person” probably means an ordinary faithful disciple. Those who support and welcome believers because they belong to Christ share in their reward.

What it does not mean. Not that welcoming Christian workers earns salvation. The reward is God’s gracious recognition of faith shown in action. Nor does it mean that every person claiming to be a prophet should be welcomed (7:15). The welcome is for true messengers of Christ.

In a sentence. Welcoming Christ’s messengers is welcoming Christ and the Father, and those who support them share in their reward.

On a Tuesday. You may not be a missionary or preacher, but you can share their reward by welcoming, supporting and praying for them. Whom could you support this month?

parallels.desc: the widow of Zarephath receives Elijah

verseByVerse.quote: And whoever gives one of these little ones even a cup of cold water because he is a disciple, truly, I say to you, he will by no means lose his reward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the smallest act of kindness, a cup of cold water given to one of Jesus’ humble followers because he is a disciple, will never go unrewarded.

And whoever gives one of these little ones. “Little ones” means humble, ordinary disciples, those who seem least important (18:6, 10, 14). The apostles were “little ones” too: unimpressive fishermen.

Even a cup of cold water. The simplest, cheapest act of kindness. In a hot climate, cold water from a deep well was a real refreshment, but it cost almost nothing.

Because he is a disciple. Literally “in the name of a disciple”: because the person belongs to Jesus. The motive matters: kindness to a believer for Christ’s sake.

Truly, I say to you, he will by no means lose his reward. God notices the smallest act of kindness done for his people. Nothing is wasted (25:40; Hebrews 6:10).

The end of the chapter. The mission discourse began with authority to cast out demons and raise the dead (v. 8), and ends with a cup of cold water. Both matter to Jesus. Not everyone is called to great public ministry, but everyone can give a cup of water.

What it does not mean. Not that kindness to non-Christians does not matter. Jesus commands love to all, even enemies (5:44). Here he speaks specifically of supporting his messengers. Nor does reward mean that we earn heaven; it is grace recognising the fruit of faith (see 6:1).

In a sentence. Even the smallest kindness to one of Christ’s humblest followers, done for his sake, will be rewarded by God.

On a Tuesday. What is a “cup of cold water” you could give to a fellow believer today: a meal, a text, a lift, a word of encouragement?

For worship. Thank God that he notices every small act of love done for his people.

parallels.desc: as you did it to one of the least of these

10.theology: Providence and mission. Matthew 10 grounds the missionary enterprise in the doctrine of divine providence. The disciples go out into hostility, vulnerability, and probable suffering — not because God has abandoned them but because God governs every detail of their mission. The Reformed tradition has always insisted that providence is not merely the general oversight of large events but the meticulous governance of all things, including the suffering of God’s people. This is not fatalism — it does not make the missionary passive — but it is the foundation of missionary courage. The one who governs the sparrow governs the jail cell, the court, and the execution ground.
10.examples:
Then: The Twelve went out with no bag, no extra tunic, no staff, wholly dependent on the hospitality of those who received the gospel. Their very poverty was a sign: the kingdom of heaven advances not by human resources but by divine power through human weakness.

Now: The church in every generation is sent as sheep among wolves. In contexts of comfort and freedom, the temptation is to reverse the commission: to make the church a refuge from the world rather than a mission into it. In contexts of persecution — which most of the global church knows — Matthew 10 is a survival manual. Fear not the one who can kill the body; fear the One who holds the soul.

11.title: Are You the One Who Is to Come?
11.text: <sup>1</sup>When Jesus had finished instructing his twelve disciples, he went on from there to teach and preach in their cities. <sup>2</sup>Now when John heard in prison about the deeds of the Christ, he sent word by his disciples <sup>3</sup>and said to him, “Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?” <sup>4</sup>And Jesus answered them, “Go and tell John what you hear and see: <sup>5</sup>the blind receive their sight and the lame walk, lepers are cleansed and the deaf hear, and the dead are raised up, and the poor have good news preached to them. <sup>6</sup>And blessed is the one who is not offended by me.” <sup>7</sup>As they went away, Jesus began to speak to the crowds concerning John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? <sup>8</sup>What then did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in kings’ houses. <sup>9</sup>What then did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. <sup>10</sup>This is he of whom it is written, “‘Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you.’ <sup>11</sup>Truly, I say to you, among those born of women there has arisen no one greater than John the Baptist. Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he. <sup>12</sup>From the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven has suffered violence, and the violent take it by force. <sup>13</sup>For all the Prophets and the Law prophesied until John, <sup>14</sup>and if you are willing to accept it, he is Elijah who is to come. <sup>15</sup>He who has ears to hear, let him hear. <sup>16</sup>“But to what shall I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplaces and calling to their playmates, <sup>17</sup>“‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not mourn.’ <sup>18</sup>For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, ‘He has a demon.’ <sup>19</sup>The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, ‘Look at him! A glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ Yet wisdom is justified by her deeds.” <sup>20</sup>Then he began to denounce the cities where most of his mighty works had been done, because they did not repent. <sup>21</sup>“Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes. <sup>22</sup>But I tell you, it will be more bearable on the day of judgment for Tyre and Sidon than for you. <sup>23</sup>And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You will be brought down to Hades. For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Sodom, it would have remained until this day. <sup>24</sup>But I tell you that it will be more tolerable on the day of judgment for the land of Sodom than for you.” <sup>25</sup>At that time Jesus declared, “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children; <sup>26</sup>yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. <sup>27</sup>All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him. <sup>28</sup>Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. <sup>29</sup>Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. <sup>30</sup>For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”
11.overview:
Chapter 11 is built around a single question: “Are you the one who is to come?” John the Baptist, the greatest of the prophets, sits in Herod’s prison and sends his disciples to ask Jesus the question. Doubt is not always the opposite of faith; sometimes it is faith in extremity, crying out for reassurance. Jesus answers with Isaiah’s sign: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, the poor have good news (Isa 35:5–6; 61:1). The messianic age has arrived. John is the last and greatest of the prophets, the Elijah who prepared the way, standing at the threshold of the new era.

The chapter turns on the city of unbelief. Chorazin, Bethsaida, Capernaum — cities that witnessed the greatest miracles in history — did not repent. They will face a worse judgment than Sodom. Privilege entails responsibility; greater revelation means greater accountability. The chapter closes with the most tender invitation in the Gospels: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” The King who demands a cross is also the Lord who bears the burden of all who come to him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–30 — John's Question, Jesus's Invitation: The Kingdom in Paradox
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John the Baptist, imprisoned, sends disciples to ask whether Jesus is the one who is to come. Jesus answers by pointing to his deeds and pronounces John the greatest of all born of women — yet the least in the kingdom is greater. He condemns the generation that rejected both John and himself, pronounces woes on unrepentant cities, and closes with the great invitation: "Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden." The chapter moves from doubt to judgment to grace. The most important thing in the chapter is something Jesus leaves out. His reply to John is stitched from Isaiah 35:5-6, 26:19 and 61:1 — and Isaiah 61:1 continues "to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to those who are bound". That is the one clause in the whole quarry that speaks to a man in a cell, and it is the one clause omitted. He takes the poor and drops the prisoners, in a message sent to a prisoner who had asked. Which is why the last line is what it is: "blessed is the one who is not offended by me" — the kingdom has come, I am the one, and I am not getting you out. The reed (v. 7) was Herod Antipas's emblem, stamped on the coins of his new capital at Tiberias — and Herod is the man holding John; while "soft clothing in kings' houses" points at a palace with a prophet in camel hair underneath it. The Malachi quotation (v. 10) is altered in one pronoun: Malachi 3:1 has God say the messenger prepares the way "before me", and Jesus quotes it as "before your face... prepare your way". The way prepared for the coming of God is the way prepared for him, and the claim is made by changing a pronoun and saying nothing. "the least is greater" is not moral but chronological: John died before the crucifixion and never heard that the tomb was empty. Verse 12 is genuinely disputed — biazetai can be middle or passive, giving either "the kingdom suffers violence and violent men plunder it" (which fits a prophet in a dungeon) or "the kingdom is forcefully advancing and forceful men lay hold of it" (which fits Luke 16:16); both are held by serious men, and Luke's parallel tips the balance toward the second. On Elijah, John's flat "I am not" (Jn. 1:21) denies the popular expectation of the historical Elijah returning; Jesus affirms the office, as Gabriel had before John was born (Lk. 1:17). "a glutton and a drunkard" (v. 19) is a legal formula — the exact charge in the rebellious-son law of Deuteronomy 21:20, for which the penalty is stoning. Capernaum's doom (v. 23) quotes the taunt against the king of Babylon (Isa. 14:13-15), applied to a fishing village of fifteen hundred people — and all three towns named are now ruins, with Bethsaida's site still disputed. "the wise and understanding" (v. 25) is lifted from Isaiah 29:14, a judgement oracle against the religious establishment, and "little children" is nepioi, infants. And verse 27 is the "Johannine thunderbolt" — a sentence that reads like the fourth Gospel, found in Matthew and Luke and not in John, which disposes of the claim that a high Christology is late.
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter's center is the paradox of the kingdom: John is the greatest prophet and yet less than the least kingdom citizen, because the kingdom has arrived in a greater reality than any prophet foresaw. The "violent" who take the kingdom by force are not the arrogant but the eager — those who press urgently into what God has opened. The cities of Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum had seen the greatest miracles in history and remained unmoved; their judgment will exceed Sodom's because their privilege exceeded Sodom's.
verseByVerse.examples: The great invitation of verses 28-30 is the gospel in miniature. "All who labor and are heavy laden" — the exhausted self-righteous crushed by law-keeping, the sinners crushed by guilt, the anxious crushed by the weight of life. "Come to me" — not to a program, a religion, or a therapy, but to a person. The yoke of Jesus is easy not because it demands less but because it is borne with him, by one who is gentle and lowly in heart. Learning from him is not hard labor but rest — the deep rest of a soul that has found what it was made for.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus had finished instructing his twelve disciples, he went on from there to teach and preach in their cities.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus had finished instructing the Twelve, he went on teaching and preaching in the towns of Galilee.

When Jesus had finished instructing his twelve disciples. The formula that closes each of Jesus’ five great discourses in Matthew (see 7:28). The mission discourse (chapter 10) is over.

He went on from there to teach and preach in their cities. While the Twelve went out, Jesus continued his own ministry. “Their cities” means the towns of Galilee.

The new section. Chapters 11–12 show growing responses to Jesus: doubt (John’s question, 11:2–6), indifference (this generation, 11:16–19), unrepentance (the cities, 11:20–24), and open hostility (the Pharisees, chapter 12). In the middle stands Jesus’ invitation to the weary (11:28–30).

In a sentence. After sending out the Twelve, Jesus continued his own teaching and preaching.

On a Tuesday. Jesus did not delegate everything; he kept working. Those who lead others in ministry should keep serving themselves.
