verseByVerse.quote: Now when John heard in prison about the deeds of the Christ, he sent word by his disciples and said to him, "Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?" And Jesus answered them, "Go and tell John what you hear and see:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
John the Baptist, in prison, heard about what Jesus was doing and sent his disciples to ask: are you the one who is to come, or should we expect someone else?

Now when John heard in prison. Herod Antipas had imprisoned John for condemning his marriage to Herodias, his brother’s wife (14:3–4). The historian Josephus says John was held at Machaerus, a fortress-palace east of the Dead Sea. He had been there for months, perhaps a year.

About the deeds of the Christ. The works of chapters 8–9: healings, exorcisms, the raising of the dead. Matthew calls them “the deeds of the Christ”: he wants the reader to know they are the Messiah’s works.

He sent word by his disciples. John still had followers who visited him.

Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another? “The one who is to come” was a title for the Messiah (3:11; Psalm 118:26; Malachi 3:1). Why would John, who had baptised Jesus and seen the Spirit descend (3:13–17), now ask this? Probably because Jesus was not doing what John expected. John had announced a Messiah with a winnowing fork and fire, who would cut down fruitless trees (3:10–12). Instead, Jesus was healing, eating with sinners, and showing mercy, while John himself sat in prison, and Herod went unpunished. Where was the judgment? Where was the freedom for the captives (Isaiah 61:1)?

What it does not mean. Not that John had lost his faith. He sent his question to Jesus himself, which is what faith does with doubt. Honest questions brought to Christ are not unbelief. The psalmists did the same (Psalm 13; 22). Nor does it mean John was wrong about the judgment. He was right that the Messiah would judge; he did not yet see that judgment would come later, at Christ’s return, and that first he would come in mercy.

In a sentence. John, in prison and puzzled that Jesus was not bringing judgment, brought his doubt to Jesus himself.

On a Tuesday. When God does not act as you expected, and you are confused, bring your questions to Jesus, as John did. Doubt taken to him becomes the way to deeper faith.
verseByVerse.note: John was imprisoned by Herod Antipas, according to Josephus in the fortress of Machaerus east of the Dead Sea.

verseByVerse.quote: the blind receive their sight and the lame walk, lepers are cleansed and the deaf hear, and the dead are raised up, and the poor have good news preached to them. And blessed is the one who is not offended by me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered by pointing to what was happening: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the poor hear good news. These are the signs Isaiah promised. Blessed is anyone who does not stumble over me.

Go and tell John what you hear and see. Jesus does not answer “yes” directly. He points to the evidence and lets John draw the conclusion from Scripture.

The blind receive their sight and the lame walk. Isaiah 35:5–6: then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, the ears of the deaf unstopped, the lame shall leap like a deer. Isaiah 35 describes God coming to save his people.

Lepers are cleansed and the deaf hear, and the dead are raised up. Isaiah 26:19 promises that the dead will live. Cleansing lepers is not in Isaiah’s lists, but Elisha did it (2 Kings 5), and Jesus did it (8:2–3).

And the poor have good news preached to them. Isaiah 61:1: the Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me to bring good news to the poor. This was the passage Jesus read in the synagogue at Nazareth, saying it was fulfilled (Luke 4:18–21). The climax of the list is not a miracle but preaching: the gospel to the poor.

The answer to John. Jesus is the Messiah of Isaiah’s promises. But notice what he leaves out: Isaiah 61:1–2 also speaks of liberty to the captives and the day of vengeance of our God. Jesus does not mention these. Release from prison would not come for John; the day of vengeance would come later. Jesus gently tells John: I am fulfilling the promises, but in God’s order: mercy now, judgment later.

And blessed is the one who is not offended by me. “Offended” (skandalisthē) means caused to stumble, tripped up. Blessed are those who do not reject Jesus because he does not fit their expectations. Many stumbled over a humble, merciful, suffering Messiah (1 Corinthians 1:23).

What it does not mean. Not that miracles alone prove Jesus is the Messiah. False messiahs could appear to do signs (24:24). It is the combination of the works with Scripture’s promises, and above all the preaching of good news to the poor, that identifies him. Nor does the omission of judgment mean that Jesus would never judge. He will (25:31–46).

In a sentence. Jesus pointed John to his works as the fulfilment of Isaiah’s promises, and blessed those who do not stumble over the way he fulfils them.

On a Tuesday. Is there something about Jesus or his ways that troubles you? Do not let it trip you up. Look at what he has done, and trust his timing.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus answers with the language of Isaiah’s promises.

parallels.desc: the blind see, the lame leap

verseByVerse.quote: As they went away, Jesus began to speak to the crowds concerning John: "What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? What then did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in kings' houses."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As John’s disciples left, Jesus spoke to the crowds about John. What did you go out to the desert to see? A reed blown about by the wind? A man dressed in soft, fine clothes? No: those are found in kings’ palaces.

As they went away, Jesus began to speak to the crowds concerning John. Jesus defends John immediately, so that no one would think less of him because of his question.

What did you go out into the wilderness to see? Crowds had gone out in great numbers to hear John (3:5).

A reed shaken by the wind? Reeds grew in abundance along the Jordan, bending with every breeze. Was John a weak, vacillating man who changed with public opinion? No. He stood firm against kings. Some suggest a further point: Herod Antipas put a reed on his coins, so “a reed shaken by the wind” may hint at Herod himself, who swayed with every pressure.

A man dressed in soft clothing? Fine, luxurious clothes of the wealthy. John wore camel hair (3:4).

Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in kings’ houses. John was in a king’s house too, but in the dungeon, not the court. The comfortable courtiers of Herod were the opposite of John. He would not flatter the powerful, and he paid for it.

What it does not mean. Not that fine clothing or wealth is sinful in itself. The point is the contrast between John’s fearless integrity and the comfortable compromise of those who serve the powerful.

In a sentence. Jesus reminded the crowds that John was no weak reed or pampered courtier, but a man of unbending conviction.

On a Tuesday. Are you more like a reed shaken by the wind, changing your convictions with the pressure of the crowd, or like John?

verseByVerse.quote: What then did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. This is he of whom it is written, "Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Did you go out to see a prophet? Yes, and more than a prophet. John is the messenger of whom Malachi wrote: God’s messenger sent ahead to prepare the way.

A prophet? The people regarded John as a prophet (21:26), the first in Israel in about four hundred years.

Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. John was not only a prophet; he was the subject of prophecy. Other prophets spoke about the Messiah from a distance; John pointed to him in person.

This is he of whom it is written. Malachi 3:1, combined with Exodus 23:20.

Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you. In Malachi, God says: I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple. In Exodus 23:20, God sends an angel before Israel in the wilderness. Jesus changes “before me” to “before your face”. The one for whom John prepares the way is the Lord God himself, coming in Jesus. Once again, Jesus is identified with the LORD (see 3:3).

What it does not mean. Not that John was greater than Jesus. John was the forerunner; Jesus is the Lord whose way he prepared.

In a sentence. John was more than a prophet: he was the messenger Malachi foretold, preparing the way for the Lord himself, who is Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Like John, your calling is to prepare the way for Christ in the lives of others. Whose way can you prepare today?

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, I say to you, among those born of women there has arisen no one greater than John the Baptist. Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he. From the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven has suffered violence, and the violent take it by force.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one born of a woman is greater than John. Yet the least person in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he. From the time of John until now, the kingdom has been advancing forcefully, and forceful people have been attacking it.

Among those born of women there has arisen no one greater than John the Baptist. “Born of women” means human beings. Of all the great people of the old covenant, Abraham, Moses, David, Elijah, Isaiah, none was greater than John. Why? Because of his unique role: he was the one who stood at the hinge of history and pointed directly to the Messiah.

Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he. A remarkable statement. It does not mean that every Christian is a better person than John. It means that the least believer in the new age of the kingdom has a greater privilege. John stood at the threshold, announcing what was coming; believers after the cross and resurrection see it fulfilled, receive the Spirit poured out at Pentecost, and know the full gospel. Prophets and kings longed to see what they see (13:16–17; 1 Peter 1:10–12). Greatness here is privilege of position, not personal merit.

From the days of John the Baptist until now. From the start of John’s ministry to the present: a short period, but the turning point of history.

The kingdom of heaven has suffered violence, and the violent take it by force. One of the most difficult sayings in the Gospels. The Greek verb (biazetai) can be passive (“suffers violence”) or middle (“forcefully advances”). Two main views:

1. The kingdom is attacked. The kingdom has suffered violence from violent people who try to seize or destroy it. John was imprisoned; Jesus would be killed; the disciples would be persecuted (10:16–25). The ESV text follows this reading.

2. The kingdom advances. The kingdom has been forcefully advancing (the ESV footnote), and forceful people, those who press in with urgency, are laying hold of it. Luke has a similar saying: everyone forces his way into it (Luke 16:16).

Verdict: the first fits best in Matthew’s context, between John’s imprisonment and the opposition of chapters 11–12. Since John came, the kingdom has broken in with power, and it has met violent opposition. Both truths are taught in the Gospels.

What it does not mean. Not that we must seize the kingdom by violence or human force. The kingdom is God’s gift (5:3). Nor does “least in the kingdom” mean that John is not in the kingdom. He will sit at the feast with Abraham (8:11). He belongs to the age of promise, standing at its very end.

In a sentence. John was the greatest of the old era, yet the least in the kingdom has a greater privilege, and the kingdom, breaking in since John, has met violent opposition.

On a Tuesday. You have a greater privilege than John the Baptist: you know the cross, the resurrection and the Spirit. Live like it.
verseByVerse.note: Verse 12 is a notoriously difficult saying; it may describe the kingdom’s forceful advance or the violent opposition to it.

verseByVerse.quote: For all the Prophets and the Law prophesied until John, and if you are willing to accept it, he is Elijah who is to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All the Prophets and the Law prophesied until John. And if you are willing to accept it, John is the Elijah who was to come.

For all the Prophets and the Law prophesied until John. The whole Old Testament looked forward. It pointed to the coming of the Messiah and his kingdom. John was the last voice of that age of anticipation. Unusually, Jesus says the Law “prophesied” too: the law pointed forward to Christ (5:17).

And if you are willing to accept it. Jesus knows this will be hard for some to accept, because John did not look like what they imagined Elijah would be.

He is Elijah who is to come. Malachi 4:5–6, the last words of the Old Testament, promised that God would send Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day of the LORD, to turn hearts. Many Jews expected Elijah himself to return (Elijah did not die, 2 Kings 2:11). Jesus says John fulfilled this promise. John came in the spirit and power of Elijah (Luke 1:17), dressed like him (3:4), and preached repentance as he did.

But John denied being Elijah. In John 1:21, when asked “Are you Elijah?”, John answered, “I am not.” Is this a contradiction? No. John denied being Elijah literally, returned from heaven, as the people meant. Jesus affirms that he was the Elijah of prophecy, fulfilling his role. Both are true.

What it does not mean. Not reincarnation, as some have claimed. John was a new person, born to Zechariah and Elizabeth, who fulfilled Elijah’s prophetic role. Nor do we wait for another Elijah before Christ returns. Jesus says the promise has been fulfilled (17:10–13).

In a sentence. John ended the age of prophecy and fulfilled Malachi’s promise of the coming Elijah.

On a Tuesday. The whole Old Testament points to Christ. When you read it, ask where it is pointing.

parallels.desc: I will send you Elijah the prophet
in the spirit and power of Elijah

verseByVerse.quote: He who has ears to hear, let him hear. But to what shall I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplaces and calling to their playmates,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever has ears, let them hear. Then Jesus asked what this generation was like: like children sitting in the market square, calling to their playmates.

He who has ears to hear, let him hear. A phrase Jesus uses after important or puzzling teaching (13:9, 43). Everyone has ears; not everyone listens. It is a call to pay close attention, to understand and to respond.

But to what shall I compare this generation? “This generation” means the people of Jesus’ time, especially those who rejected both John and Jesus. In Matthew it is often a negative phrase: an evil and adulterous generation (12:39, 45; 16:4; 23:36).

It is like children sitting in the marketplaces. The marketplace (agora) was the town square, where children played while adults did business.

And calling to their playmates. The picture is explained in verse 17.

In a sentence. Jesus calls for careful listening and compares his generation to children in the market square.

On a Tuesday. Are you listening to Jesus with ears that hear, ready to respond?

verseByVerse.quote: "We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not mourn." For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, "He has a demon."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The children complain: we played wedding music, and you would not dance; we played funeral songs, and you would not mourn. So it was with John, who fasted and lived austerely, and people said he had a demon.

We played the flute for you, and you did not dance. Children played at weddings, with flutes and dancing.

We sang a dirge, and you did not mourn. They also played at funerals, with wailing and beating the chest. One group of children calls to another to join in the game, but the others refuse whatever game is offered. Happy or sad, they will not play. The picture is of sulky, childish people who cannot be pleased.

For John came neither eating nor drinking. John lived an austere life: fasting, eating locusts and wild honey, drinking no wine (3:4; Luke 1:15). His message was the funeral song: mourn for your sins.

And they say, “He has a demon.” His strictness was dismissed as madness or demon-possession.

In a sentence. Like sulky children who refuse every game, the people rejected John’s call to mourn, calling him demon-possessed.

On a Tuesday. Do you find excuses to dismiss God’s messengers whatever they are like: too strict, too relaxed, too serious, too joyful? The problem may be in you.
verseByVerse.note: Children played at weddings and funerals; some refused whichever game was offered.

verseByVerse.quote: The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, "Look at him! A glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!" Yet wisdom is justified by her deeds. Then he began to denounce the cities where most of his mighty works had been done, because they did not repent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Jesus came, eating and drinking, and people said he was a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners. Yet wisdom is proved right by what it does. Then Jesus began to rebuke the towns where most of his miracles had been done, because they had not repented.

The Son of Man came eating and drinking. Jesus’ ministry was the wedding song: joy, feasting, the bridegroom present (9:15). He ate with all kinds of people (9:10).

And they say, “Look at him! A glutton and a drunkard.” An insult with a serious edge: Deuteronomy 21:20 describes a stubborn and rebellious son, a glutton and a drunkard, who was to be brought before the elders. They were accusing him of being a rebel against God.

A friend of tax collectors and sinners! Meant as an insult, but it is gloriously true (9:10–13). Jesus is the friend of sinners. The name has become one of his most beloved titles.

The point. John fasted, and they rejected him; Jesus feasted, and they rejected him. The problem was not the messengers’ style but the people’s hearts. They did not want God’s message, whatever form it came in.

Yet wisdom is justified by her deeds. “Wisdom” is God’s wisdom, at work in both John and Jesus. In Proverbs 8, wisdom is personified as present with God at creation. “Justified” means proved right, vindicated. God’s wisdom will be vindicated by its results: by the changed lives of the sinners who repented, and by the works of the Christ (v. 2, where Matthew used the same word, “deeds”). Some see Jesus here as Wisdom itself in person (1 Corinthians 1:24, 30).

Then he began to denounce the cities where most of his mighty works had been done, because they did not repent. The next verses. “Mighty works” (dynameis) means miracles, deeds of power. The purpose of the miracles was to lead people to repentance, and they had not.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus approved of gluttony or drunkenness. He ate and drank in moderation and holiness; the accusation was a slander. Nor does being a friend of sinners mean that he joined in their sins. He befriended them to call them to repentance (Luke 5:32).

In a sentence. The people rejected Jesus’ joy as they had rejected John’s austerity, but God’s wisdom is proved right by its results.

On a Tuesday. Jesus is the friend of sinners, including you. Whom could you befriend for his sake, among people others avoid?

For worship. Thank Jesus that he is the friend of sinners.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes. But I tell you, it will be more bearable on the day of judgment for Tyre and Sidon than for you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you, Chorazin and Bethsaida! If the miracles done in you had been done in the pagan cities of Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes. On judgment day, it will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon than for you.

Woe to you. “Woe” is a cry of grief and warning, the opposite of “blessed” (5:3–12). It announces coming disaster, but with sorrow, not glee. The prophets used it (Isaiah 5:8–23).

Chorazin. A town about two miles (three kilometres) north of Capernaum, in the hills. Its ruins, including a synagogue, can still be seen. The Gospels record no miracle there, yet Jesus says many were done. The Gospels record only a fraction of what Jesus did (John 21:25).

Bethsaida. A fishing village on the northern shore of the lake, the hometown of Peter, Andrew and Philip (John 1:44). Jesus fed the five thousand nearby (Luke 9:10) and healed a blind man there (Mark 8:22–26).

For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon. Tyre and Sidon were wealthy Gentile ports on the Mediterranean coast, north of Galilee, condemned by the prophets for their pride, wealth and wickedness (Isaiah 23; Ezekiel 26–28). To Jews, they were symbols of pagan arrogance.

They would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes. Sackcloth was rough cloth made of goat’s hair, worn in mourning. Ashes were sprinkled on the head or sat in. Both were signs of deep grief and repentance (Jonah 3:5–8; Daniel 9:3). Pagan cities would have repented; the Jewish towns that saw Jesus did not.

But I tell you, it will be more bearable on the day of judgment for Tyre and Sidon than for you. Greater privilege brings greater responsibility (see 10:15). Those who have seen more light will face a heavier judgment.

A question about knowledge. This verse shows that God knows not only what will happen, but what would have happened under other circumstances. Some theologians call this “middle knowledge”, and use it to explain election. The Reformed tradition affirms that God knows all possibilities, but holds that his decree, not his foreknowledge of what people would do, is the basis of election (Ephesians 1:4–5; Westminster Confession 3.2).

What it does not mean. Not that God was unfair to Tyre and Sidon. They were judged for their own sins, according to the light they had (Romans 1:18–21; 2:12). But those who had greater light, and rejected it, are more guilty. Nor does it mean that miracles inevitably produce repentance. Chorazin saw them and did not repent. Repentance is the work of God in the heart.

In a sentence. The towns that saw Jesus’ miracles and refused to repent will face a heavier judgment than pagan cities that never saw them.

On a Tuesday. How much light have you received: a Christian upbringing, Bibles, preaching? Respond to it. Privilege that is ignored becomes judgment.
verseByVerse.note: Chorazin and Bethsaida were towns near Capernaum at the north end of the lake. Tyre and Sidon were Gentile port cities. Sackcloth was coarse goat-hair cloth worn in mourning.

verseByVerse.quote: And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You will be brought down to Hades. For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Sodom, it would have remained until this day. But I tell you that it will be more tolerable on the day of judgment for the land of Sodom than for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Capernaum, Jesus’ own base, which thought itself raised high: it will be brought down to Hades. If Sodom had seen such miracles, it would still be standing. On judgment day it will be more bearable for Sodom than for Capernaum.

And you, Capernaum. Jesus’ own city (4:13; 9:1), where he did more miracles than anywhere else: the centurion’s servant, Peter’s mother-in-law, the paralysed man, Jairus’ daughter, and many others.

Will you be exalted to heaven? Capernaum was proud: perhaps of its prosperity, perhaps of Jesus’ presence there. Jesus’ words echo Isaiah 14:13–15, the taunt against the king of Babylon, who said in his heart that he would ascend to heaven, but was brought down to Sheol. Capernaum’s pride is like Babylon’s.

You will be brought down to Hades. “Hades” is the Greek name for the realm of the dead (Hebrew Sheol), the lowest place. Here it means deep humiliation and judgment. Capernaum was later abandoned and fell into ruin.

For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Sodom, it would have remained until this day. Sodom, the most notorious city of judgment (10:15), would have repented if it had seen what Capernaum saw.

But I tell you that it will be more tolerable on the day of judgment for the land of Sodom than for you. Even Sodom’s judgment will be lighter than Capernaum’s.

What it does not mean. Not that everyone in Capernaum rejected Jesus. Peter, Andrew, Matthew and others came to faith there. The city as a whole did not repent. Nor does it mean that physical nearness to Jesus saves. Capernaum had Jesus living in it, and still did not repent.

In a sentence. Capernaum, which saw more of Jesus than any other town and still did not repent, will be judged more severely than Sodom.

On a Tuesday. Being near Jesus, at church, in a Christian family, among believers, is not the same as turning to him. Have you repented?
verseByVerse.note: Hades is the realm of the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Jesus declared, "I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children; yes, Father, for such was your gracious will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At that very time, Jesus prayed: I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and learned and revealed them to little children. Yes, Father, for this was your gracious will.

At that time Jesus declared. “Declared” (apokritheis) literally means “answered”: Jesus responds to the unbelief of the cities by turning to his Father in prayer. Rejection does not shake him; he rests in the Father’s plan.

I thank you, Father. Jesus calls God “Father” with intimacy. He gives thanks even in the face of rejection.

Lord of heaven and earth. God is sovereign over all things. What he does, he has the right to do.

That you have hidden these things. “These things” are the truths of the kingdom: who Jesus is, and what his works mean.

From the wise and understanding. Not truly wise, but those wise in their own eyes: the scribes, Pharisees and religious experts, proud of their learning, who rejected Jesus. God hides the truth from the proud, in judgment on their pride (1 Corinthians 1:18–29). Isaiah 29:14 says that the wisdom of their wise men shall perish.

And revealed them to little children. “Little children” (nēpioi) means infants, the simple, those who are not learned or important: the disciples, fishermen, tax collectors and sinners. God reveals the truth to those who receive it humbly, as children receive from a parent (18:3–4). Revelation is God’s gift: no one can work it out for themselves (16:17).

Yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. Literally “for thus it was good pleasure before you”. The same idea as Ephesians 1:5, 9. God chooses to reveal himself to the humble, and it pleases him. Jesus does not merely accept this; he rejoices in it (Luke 10:21).

What it does not mean. Not that education or intelligence are bad, or that God only saves the uneducated. Paul was highly educated. The issue is pride: God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble (James 4:6). Nor does God’s hiding make people who reject Christ innocent victims. They were responsible for refusing the light (vv. 20–24). God’s sovereignty and human responsibility stand side by side in this passage: the cities are condemned for not repenting (v. 20), and the Father hides and reveals according to his will (v. 25). And the very next verse invites everyone who is weary to come (v. 28). God’s sovereign choice does not limit the free offer of the gospel; it guarantees that some will come.

Where Christians differ: God’s choice. Arminians hold that God reveals the truth to those he foresees will be humble and believe. Reformed theology holds that God’s revealing is his sovereign, gracious choice, which creates the humility and faith (v. 27; Ephesians 1:4–5; 2:8). Verdict: God’s revealing is according to his good pleasure (v. 26), not caused by anything in us. That is why it is grace, and why there is no room for boasting.

In a sentence. Jesus thanked the Father for hiding the truth from the proud and revealing it to the humble, according to his gracious will.

On a Tuesday. If you understand the gospel, it is because God revealed it to you. Thank him, and come to his word as a child, not as a critic.

For worship. Thank the Father for revealing his Son to you, by his gracious choice.

parallels.desc: God chose what is foolish in the world

verseByVerse.quote: All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him. Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus declares that the Father has handed over all things to him. Only the Father truly knows the Son, and only the Son truly knows the Father, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him. Then he invites everyone who is weary and burdened to come to him for rest.

All things have been handed over to me by my Father. All authority, all knowledge, all revelation. Before the resurrection, Jesus already claims what he will declare after it: all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me (28:18). “Handed over” is the language of passing on a tradition or an inheritance.

And no one knows the Son except the Father. The Son’s identity is a mystery known fully only to God. The crowds and the cities did not understand who Jesus was; only the Father knows him completely.

And no one knows the Father except the Son. An astonishing claim. Jesus has a unique, exclusive, perfect knowledge of God, as a son knows his father. This is a claim to equality with God. It sounds like the Gospel of John (John 1:18; 10:15; 14:6–9), showing that the same high view of Jesus is found in all the Gospels.

And anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him. “Chooses” (boulētai) means wills, decides. Knowledge of God comes only through Christ, as he chooses to reveal it. The Son does what the Father does: he reveals according to his will (vv. 25–26).

Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden. Then immediately, the widest invitation in the Gospels. The one who chooses whom to reveal the Father to now invites all. “Labour” means to toil to the point of exhaustion. “Heavy laden” means carrying a heavy load, like a pack animal. Who are they? Especially those burdened by the religious leaders’ demands: the scribes and Pharisees tied up heavy burdens, hard to bear, and laid them on people’s shoulders (23:4). They are also everyone weary of sin, guilt, the effort to earn God’s favour, and the troubles of life.

And I will give you rest. Not more rules, but rest. “Rest” (anapausis) means refreshment, relief, ceasing from labour. Jesus offers what only God can give: rest for the soul (Jeremiah 6:16; Exodus 33:14). He gives it himself (“I will give”), personally.

What it does not mean. Not that sovereign revealing contradicts the open invitation. Both are true together. The invitation goes to all; those who come are those to whom the Son reveals the Father. No one who comes will be turned away (John 6:37). Nor is the rest Jesus gives a life without effort or duty. It is rest from the burden of earning God’s favour, and from the weight of sin, so that we can serve him freely (v. 29).

In a sentence. Jesus, who alone knows the Father and has all authority, invites everyone who is exhausted and burdened to come to him for rest.

On a Tuesday. What is weighing you down today: guilt, anxiety, religious performance, life’s troubles? Come to Jesus with it, in prayer, now.

parallels.desc: the Father has given all things into his hand
whoever has seen me has seen the Father

verseByVerse.quote: Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take my yoke on you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. My yoke is easy and my burden is light.

Take my yoke upon you. A yoke was a wooden frame placed over the necks of two oxen so they could pull a plough or cart together. In Jewish teaching, the yoke was a picture of submission: rabbis spoke of “the yoke of the law” and “the yoke of the kingdom of heaven”, meaning to accept God’s rule and commandments. Jesus invites people to take his yoke: to submit to him, to become his disciples. Rest does not come by throwing off every yoke, but by taking the right one.

And learn from me. Become my disciples, my students. Learn his teaching, and learn him (see Ephesians 4:20).

For I am gentle and lowly in heart. The only place in the Gospels where Jesus describes his own heart. “Gentle” (praus) is the same word as “meek” (5:5). “Lowly” (tapeinos) means humble. Unlike the harsh, proud religious teachers who loaded burdens on others, Jesus is gentle with the weak and humble toward the lowly. He does not crush bruised reeds (12:20). His heart toward weary sinners is not impatience but tenderness.

And you will find rest for your souls. From Jeremiah 6:16, where God tells Israel to ask for the ancient paths, where the good way is, and walk in it, and find rest for their souls. They refused. Jesus offers the same rest, and he is the good way.

For my yoke is easy. “Easy” (chrēstos) means kind, well-fitting, good. A carpenter like Jesus would make yokes carefully shaped to fit the ox’s neck so they did not chafe. His yoke fits.

And my burden is light. Not that following Jesus involves no demands (16:24), but that his commands are not burdensome (1 John 5:3), because he gives the strength to keep them and carries the weight with us. The burden of earning salvation is replaced by the light burden of serving a gracious Master who has already saved us. Augustine said that the burden of Christ is like wings to a bird: they seem to add weight, but they lift it up.

What it does not mean. Not that the Christian life is effortless or free of suffering. Jesus has just spoken of persecution and the cross (10:16–39). The yoke is easy in comparison with the crushing burden of sin and works-religion, and because we bear it with him. Nor does “rest” mean laziness. Oxen in a yoke work, but they work with a strong partner.

In a sentence. Submit to Jesus and learn from him, because he is gentle and humble, and his yoke is well-fitting and light, giving rest to the soul.

On a Tuesday. Are you carrying a yoke of your own making: perfectionism, people-pleasing, trying to earn God’s love? Exchange it today for Jesus’ yoke.

For worship. Thank Jesus that his heart toward you is gentle and lowly.
verseByVerse.note: A yoke joined animals to pull together; teachers spoke of the “yoke” of the law.

parallels.desc: you will find rest for your souls
a yoke our fathers could not bear

11.theology: The gentleness of Christ. “I am gentle and lowly in heart” (v. 29) is the only place in the Gospels where Jesus describes his own inner character. The word “gentle” (praus) is the same word used of Moses in Numbers 12:3 and of the meek in the Beatitudes. Christ’s gentleness is not weakness but strength under restraint: the one who has all authority in heaven and earth bends to receive the weary. Thomas Goodwin wrote that Christ’s heart is more moved by our miseries than by all his own glory. The invitation “Come to me” is the theological centre of grace: not “make yourself worthy,” not “prepare yourself,” not “clean yourself up first,” but “come.”
11.examples:
Then: John the Baptist in prison represents every believer whose faith has been tested by circumstances that did not match expectation. The answer Jesus gives is always the same: look at what the Scriptures say I would do, and look at what I am doing. Faith is anchored in the word.

Now: The invitation of 11:28–30 is the greatest recruitment speech in history. Every generation of tired, guilt-laden, performance-exhausted people is addressed. The church that does not centre its preaching on this invitation has lost the gospel. The yoke of Christ is easy not because it makes no demands but because the one who makes the demands has already borne their weight.

12.title: Lord of the Sabbath
12.text: <sup>1</sup>At that time Jesus went through the grainfields on the Sabbath. His disciples were hungry, and they began to pluck heads of grain and to eat. <sup>2</sup>But when the Pharisees saw it, they said to him, “Look, your disciples are doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath.” <sup>3</sup>He said to them, “Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, and those who were with him: <sup>4</sup>how he entered the house of God and ate the bread of the Presence, which it was not lawful for him to eat nor for those who were with him, but only for the priests? <sup>5</sup>Or have you not read in the Law how on the Sabbath the priests in the temple profane the Sabbath and are guiltless? <sup>6</sup>I tell you, something greater than the temple is here. <sup>7</sup>And if you had known what this means, ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice,’ you would not have condemned the guiltless. <sup>8</sup>For the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.” <sup>9</sup>He went on from there and entered their synagogue. <sup>10</sup>And a man was there with a withered hand. And they asked him, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?”— so that they might accuse him. <sup>11</sup>He said to them, “Which one of you who has a sheep, if it falls into a pit on the Sabbath, will not take hold of it and lift it out? <sup>12</sup>Of how much more value is a man than a sheep! So it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath.” <sup>13</sup>Then he said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” And the man stretched it out, and it was restored, healthy like the other. <sup>14</sup>But the Pharisees went out and conspired against him, how to destroy him. <sup>15</sup>Jesus, aware of this, withdrew from there. And many followed him, and he healed them all <sup>16</sup>and ordered them not to make him known. <sup>17</sup>This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah: <sup>18</sup>“Behold, my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved with whom my soul is well pleased. I will put my Spirit upon him, and he will proclaim justice to the Gentiles. <sup>19</sup>He will not quarrel or cry aloud, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets; <sup>20</sup>a bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not quench, until he brings justice to victory; <sup>21</sup>and in his name the Gentiles will hope.” <sup>22</sup>Then a demon-oppressed man who was blind and mute was brought to him, and he healed him, so that the man spoke and saw. <sup>23</sup>And all the people were amazed, and said, “Can this be the Son of David?” <sup>24</sup>But when the Pharisees heard it, they said, “It is only by Beelzebul, the prince of demons, that this man casts out demons.” <sup>25</sup>Knowing their thoughts, he said to them, “Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and no city or house divided against itself will stand. <sup>26</sup>And if Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself. How then will his kingdom stand? <sup>27</sup>And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges. <sup>28</sup>But if it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you. <sup>29</sup>Or how can someone enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man? Then indeed he may plunder his house. <sup>30</sup>Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters. <sup>31</sup>Therefore I tell you, every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven people, but the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven. <sup>32</sup>And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come. <sup>33</sup>“Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad, for the tree is known by its fruit. <sup>34</sup>You brood of vipers! How can you speak good, when you are evil? For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. <sup>35</sup>The good person out of his good treasure brings forth good, and the evil person out of his evil treasure brings forth evil. <sup>36</sup>I tell you, on the day of judgment people will give account for every careless word they speak, <sup>37</sup>for by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.” <sup>38</sup>Then some of the scribes and Pharisees answered him, saying, “Teacher, we wish to see a sign from you.” <sup>39</sup>But he answered them, “An evil and adulterous generation seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. <sup>40</sup>For just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. <sup>41</sup>The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here. <sup>42</sup>The queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here. <sup>43</sup>“When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, but finds none. <sup>44</sup>Then it says, ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ And when it comes, it finds the house empty, swept, and put in order. <sup>45</sup>Then it goes and brings with it seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they enter and dwell there, and the last state of that person is worse than the first. So also will it be with this evil generation.” <sup>46</sup>While he was still speaking to the people, behold, his mother and his brothers stood outside, asking to speak to him. <sup>48</sup>But he replied to the man who told him, “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” <sup>49</sup>And stretching out his hand toward his disciples, he said, “Here are my mother and my brothers! <sup>50</sup>For whoever does the will of my Father in heaven is my brother and sister and mother.”
12.overview:
Chapter 12 marks a decisive turning point in Matthew. The Pharisees, having sought ways to trap Jesus, now plot his destruction (v. 14). The conflict comes to a head over the Sabbath, the temple, and the identity of Jesus. Jesus makes two enormous claims: “something greater than the temple is here” (v. 6) and “the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath” (v. 8). The temple was the dwelling place of God; the Sabbath was the sign of the covenant. To claim authority over both is to claim divine identity.

The chapter also introduces the sin against the Holy Spirit — attributing the works of the Spirit to Beelzebul. This is not a sudden slip but the settled, hardened rejection of the evidence of God’s kingdom. The Pharisees have seen the blind healed, the deaf hearing, the demon-possessed set free; they call it the work of Satan. This deliberate, informed, hardened reversal of moral and spiritual categories is the sin that cannot be forgiven — not because the blood of Christ is insufficient but because the one who commits it has placed himself permanently beyond repentance.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — Lord of the Sabbath and Servant of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 12 opens the extended conflict section of Matthew. The Pharisees attack Jesus twice on Sabbath observance: first for his disciples plucking grain, then for healing a man with a withered hand. Jesus defends both from Scripture and declares himself Lord of the Sabbath. The Pharisees then plot his destruction, and Matthew quotes Isaiah's first Servant Song at length, identifying Jesus as the gentle, bruised-reed-not-breaking Servant of the LORD. Note the link across the chapter break: "at that time" follows immediately on the offer of rest (11:28-29), so the man who has just promised rest is challenged about the day of rest. And Matthew alone adds that the disciples were hungry, because that is the hinge of the argument — David was hungry too. The charge was not theft (Deut. 23:25 permits plucking by hand) but Sabbath-breaking: rabbinic tradition listed thirty-nine forbidden classes of work, and reaping, threshing and winnowing are among them. The David precedent is stranger than it looks — David lied to Ahimelech, and the episode ends with Doeg reporting it and Saul slaughtering eighty-five priests (1 Sam. 22:18-19). Jesus reaches for an incident with a body count, and the parallel is exact: the anointed king not yet in his kingdom, hungry, with his men, pursued. The priestly argument: the Sabbath doubled the temple workload (two extra lambs, Num. 28:9-10), so the Sabbath has always yielded to something. And "something greater than the temple" is neuter — as are "greater than Jonah" (v. 41) and "greater than Solomon" (v. 42). Three times in one chapter, and the three are the pillars of Israel's life: the temple where God met his people, the prophet through whom he spoke, the king through whom he ruled. The trap at v. 10 is precise: rabbinic law allowed Sabbath healing only where life was in danger, and a withered hand is not — so the honest answer on their terms was "wait until sundown", and Jesus heals anyway. Note which day the murder plot is formed on: restoring a hand is a Sabbath violation; convening to arrange a killing is not. Mark records the only named anger of Jesus in the Gospels at exactly this point (Mk. 3:5). And the Servant Song is the longest OT quotation in Matthew — used, remarkably, to explain not a miracle but the absence of spectacle.
verseByVerse.theology: The Sabbath controversies reveal the Pharisees' fundamental error: they have turned a gift (the Sabbath rest) into a burden, and a sign (rest pointing to God's shalom) into a system of control. Jesus does not abolish the Sabbath; he fulfills it. He is the one in whom the true Sabbath rest is found (11:29) — the rest that the weekly day always pointed toward. The Servant Song quotation (Isa. 42:1-4) interprets his retreat from conflict not as weakness but as fulfillment: the Servant does not "quarrel or cry aloud" but pursues justice to victory through gentleness.
verseByVerse.examples: The healing of the withered hand poses the sharpest question of the controversy: "Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?" Jesus answers with an argument from worth: if you would rescue a sheep that fell in a pit on the Sabbath, how much more a person? The comparative worth of persons over animals is the premise; the compassionate action follows from it. Every Sabbath restriction that would prevent healing a human being has missed the Sabbath's point — the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27).

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Jesus went through the grainfields on the Sabbath. His disciples were hungry, and they began to pluck heads of grain and to eat. But when the Pharisees saw it, they said to him, "Look, your disciples are doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath."
verseByVerse.commentary:
One Sabbath, Jesus’ hungry disciples picked heads of grain as they walked through a field and ate them. The Pharisees protested that they were breaking the Sabbath.

At that time. Matthew links this directly to Jesus’ offer of rest (11:28–30). The Sabbath was the day of rest. Who gives true rest: the Pharisees’ rules, or Jesus?

The Sabbath. The seventh day, Saturday, from sunset on Friday to sunset on Saturday. God commanded Israel to rest from work on it, remembering both his rest after creation (Exodus 20:8–11) and his rescue of Israel from slavery (Deuteronomy 5:12–15). It was a sign of the covenant between God and Israel (Exodus 31:13–17). By Jesus’ time, Jewish teachers had built a detailed system of rules about what counted as work. The Mishnah, a later collection of rabbinic teaching, lists thirty-nine categories of forbidden work, including reaping and threshing.

His disciples were hungry, and they began to pluck heads of grain and to eat. The law allowed travellers to pick grain by hand from a neighbour’s field, though not to use a sickle (Deuteronomy 23:25). That was not the issue. The issue was the day.

But when the Pharisees saw it, they said to him, “Look, your disciples are doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath.” In the Pharisees’ rules, plucking grain was “reaping” and rubbing it in the hands (Luke 6:1) was “threshing”: two forbidden kinds of work. They held Jesus responsible for his disciples’ actions, as a teacher was for his students.

What it does not mean. Not that the Sabbath command itself was bad or unimportant. It was God’s gift. The problem was the Pharisees’ traditions, which turned the day of rest into a burden, and their harsh spirit.

In a sentence. The Pharisees accused Jesus’ hungry disciples of breaking the Sabbath by picking grain, according to their rules.

On a Tuesday. Do you add your own rules to God’s and then judge others by them?
verseByVerse.note: Picking grain by hand from a neighbour’s field was allowed; the objection was that plucking counted as harvesting, which was work on the Sabbath.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, and those who were with him: how he entered the house of God and ate the bread of the Presence, which it was not lawful for him to eat nor for those who were with him, but only for the priests?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered from Scripture: have you not read what David did when he and his men were hungry? He went into the house of God and ate the holy bread that only priests were allowed to eat.

Have you not read. A sharp question to the Bible experts (also vv. 5; 19:4; 21:16, 42; 22:31). Of course they had read it; they had not understood it.

What David did when he was hungry, and those who were with him. 1 Samuel 21:1–6. David was fleeing from King Saul. He came to the tabernacle at Nob and asked the priest Ahimelech for food. There was none except the holy bread.

How he entered the house of God and ate the bread of the Presence. Twelve loaves, one for each tribe, were placed on a golden table in the holy place each Sabbath, before the LORD (Leviticus 24:5–9). When replaced, the old loaves were eaten by the priests only, in a holy place.

Which it was not lawful for him to eat nor for those who were with him, but only for the priests. David broke a ceremonial law, and was not condemned. The priest gave him the bread, and Scripture does not criticise it.

The argument. Two points. First, human need (hunger) can take priority over ceremonial rules. God’s ceremonial laws were never meant to keep people starving. Second, David was God’s anointed king, and he and his men were allowed this exception. Jesus is the greater Son of David. If David could do this, how much more the Messiah and his followers.

What it does not mean. Not that God’s laws can be ignored whenever it is convenient. Jesus is distinguishing between God’s moral law and ceremonial regulations, and showing that the ceremonial laws were meant to serve people, not to harm them. Nor does it mean that the end justifies any means.

In a sentence. Jesus pointed to David eating the holy bread to show that ceremonial rules give way to human need, especially for God’s anointed.

On a Tuesday. God’s laws are for our good. When religious rules hurt people in real need, ask whether we have misunderstood God’s purpose.
verseByVerse.note: The bread of the Presence was twelve loaves set before the LORD each Sabbath and eaten by the priests.

verseByVerse.quote: Or have you not read in the Law how on the Sabbath the priests in the temple profane the Sabbath and are guiltless? I tell you, something greater than the temple is here.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus gave a second argument: the priests in the temple work on the Sabbath, offering sacrifices, and are not guilty. And something greater than the temple is here.

Or have you not read in the Law how on the Sabbath the priests in the temple profane the Sabbath and are guiltless? On the Sabbath, the priests worked harder than on other days. They had to change the holy bread (Leviticus 24:8) and offer extra sacrifices, double the normal number (Numbers 28:9–10). Technically, this was work. Yet the law commanded it. Temple service took priority over Sabbath rest.

I tell you, something greater than the temple is here. An astonishing claim. The temple was the most sacred place on earth, where God dwelt among his people. Jesus says something greater is here: himself. If the temple service could override the Sabbath, how much more the service of the one who is greater than the temple. Jesus is God present among his people (1:23; John 2:19–21). (The Greek “something greater” is neuter: it may refer to Jesus himself, or to the kingdom he brings; the point is the same.)

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus despised the temple. He called it his Father’s house (21:13). But he is its fulfilment. The temple pointed to God dwelling with his people; in Jesus, God is with us in person.

In a sentence. If priests may work on the Sabbath for the temple, how much more may Jesus’ disciples serve him, since he is greater than the temple.

For worship. Worship Jesus, who is greater than the temple: God present with his people.
verseByVerse.note: The priests worked hardest on the Sabbath, offering extra sacrifices.

verseByVerse.quote: And if you had known what this means, "I desire mercy, and not sacrifice," you would not have condemned the guiltless. For the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you had understood what God meant by “I desire mercy, not sacrifice”, you would not have condemned the innocent. For the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.

And if you had known what this means, “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.” Hosea 6:6, which Jesus quoted before (9:13). God values compassion above ritual. The Pharisees were strict about Sabbath rules but showed no mercy to hungry men.

You would not have condemned the guiltless. The disciples were innocent. They had broken the Pharisees’ traditions, not God’s law.

For the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath. The climax. The Sabbath was God’s day: the Sabbath of the LORD your God (Exodus 20:10). Jesus claims authority over it. He has the right to say what the Sabbath means and how it should be kept. Only God could make this claim. Mark adds that the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27).

The Sabbath and Christ. The Sabbath pointed forward to a greater rest. Hebrews says that a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God, entered by faith in Christ (Hebrews 4:1–11). Jesus has just offered rest to the weary (11:28). He is the true rest the Sabbath pictured. After his resurrection on the first day of the week, Christians gathered on that day, the Lord’s Day (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2; Revelation 1:10).

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus abolished the principle of rest and worship. He kept the Sabbath himself, worshipping in the synagogue (Luke 4:16). But as Lord of the Sabbath, he fulfils it.

Where Christians differ: the Sabbath today. Some (Seventh-day Adventists, Seventh Day Baptists) hold that Christians must keep Saturday as the Sabbath. Many Reformed and Presbyterian Christians (following the Westminster Confession 21.7–8) hold that the Sabbath command continues, transferred to Sunday as the Christian Sabbath, to be kept holy with rest from ordinary work and devotion to worship. Others hold that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, so that no day is binding as the Sabbath (Colossians 2:16–17; Romans 14:5), while Sunday is the Lord’s Day for the church’s gathering. Verdict: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our true rest. The Lord’s Day is not a burden of rules but a privilege: a gift for gathering with God’s people for worship and for rest. Christians who keep a stricter Sabbath should be respected, and none should be judged by others in this (Colossians 2:16).

In a sentence. Jesus, the Lord of the Sabbath, shows that God values mercy above ritual and that he himself is the true rest the Sabbath pointed to.

On a Tuesday. How do you use the Lord’s Day? As a burden of rules, a day like any other, or a gift: for worship, rest and doing good?

parallels.desc: I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice

verseByVerse.quote: He went on from there and entered their synagogue. And a man was there with a withered hand. And they asked him, "Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?" — so that they might accuse him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the synagogue that Sabbath was a man with a withered hand. The Pharisees asked Jesus whether it was lawful to heal on the Sabbath, looking for a reason to accuse him.

He went on from there and entered their synagogue. “Their” synagogue: the Pharisees’. The tension is rising.

And a man was there with a withered hand. A hand that was shrunken or paralysed. Luke says it was his right hand (Luke 6:6), which meant he probably could not work. His condition was not life-threatening.

And they asked him, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?” The rabbis taught that healing was work, and allowed it on the Sabbath only if life was in danger. Since a withered hand could wait until the next day, healing it would be breaking the Sabbath in their view.

So that they might accuse him. Their question was a trap, not an honest inquiry. They wanted to bring a charge against him before the local council. They used a suffering man as bait.

What it does not mean. Not that asking questions about God’s law is wrong. The problem was their motive.

In a sentence. The Pharisees used a disabled man as bait, asking whether healing on the Sabbath was lawful in order to accuse Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Do you ever use religious questions to trap or score points against others, rather than to seek the truth?
verseByVerse.note: A “withered” hand is shrunken or paralysed. In the rabbis’ rulings, healing a condition that was not life-threatening had to wait until the Sabbath was over.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "Which one of you who has a sheep, if it falls into a pit on the Sabbath, will not take hold of it and lift it out? Of how much more value is a man than a sheep! So it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered: if one of your sheep falls into a pit on the Sabbath, will you not pull it out? A person is worth far more than a sheep. So it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath.

Which one of you who has a sheep, if it falls into a pit on the Sabbath, will not take hold of it and lift it out? Most rabbis permitted rescuing an animal on the Sabbath, or at least providing food for it until the next day. (The Dead Sea Scrolls community was stricter and forbade it.) Jesus appeals to their own practice.

Of how much more value is a man than a sheep! An argument from lesser to greater. If you would help an animal, how much more should you help a human being, made in God’s image (Genesis 1:27; 9:6; 10:31).

So it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath. The Sabbath was made for doing good, not for preventing it. Mark adds Jesus’ question: is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to kill? (Mark 3:4). The irony: Jesus was doing good on the Sabbath, while the Pharisees were plotting to kill him (v. 14).

What it does not mean. Not that the Lord’s Day is like any other day, to be spent on ordinary work. It means that works of mercy and necessity are fitting on the day of rest. The Westminster Confession speaks of the day spent in public and private worship, and in the duties of necessity and mercy (21.8).

In a sentence. If people rescue sheep on the Sabbath, how much more may Jesus heal a person, for it is right to do good on the Sabbath.

On a Tuesday. How could you use the Lord’s Day to do good: visiting someone lonely, sharing a meal, helping a neighbour?

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to the man, "Stretch out your hand." And the man stretched it out, and it was restored, healthy like the other. But the Pharisees went out and conspired against him, how to destroy him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus told the man to stretch out his hand. He did, and it was restored, as healthy as the other. But the Pharisees went out and began plotting how to destroy Jesus.

Then he said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” A command he could not obey in his own strength. Jesus’ command carried the power to obey it.

And the man stretched it out, and it was restored, healthy like the other. Jesus did no “work” in the Pharisees’ sense: he did not touch him or use any treatment. He spoke, and the man stretched out his hand. There was nothing for the Pharisees to charge him with, except the healing itself.

But the Pharisees went out and conspired against him, how to destroy him. The first mention in Matthew of a plot to kill Jesus. A terrible irony: they treated healing on the Sabbath as a sin, while plotting murder on the same day. Mark adds that they plotted with the Herodians, supporters of Herod (Mark 3:6), unlikely allies against Jesus.

What it does not mean. Not that all Pharisees were murderous. Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea came to faith. But this group’s religious zeal had become hatred of the very God they claimed to serve.

In a sentence. Jesus healed the man’s hand with a word, and the Pharisees, enraged, began plotting to kill him.

On a Tuesday. Religious zeal without love can become cruel. Ask God to keep your devotion to rules from hardening your heart toward people.

parallels.desc: seeking to kill him over the Sabbath

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus, aware of this, withdrew from there. And many followed him, and he healed them all and ordered them not to make him known.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowing about the plot, Jesus withdrew. Large crowds followed him, and he healed them all, but ordered them not to make him known.

Jesus, aware of this, withdrew from there. Not out of fear, but because his time had not yet come (26:18). He would not provoke a premature confrontation. Matthew often says Jesus “withdrew” in the face of opposition (2:22; 4:12; 14:13; 15:21), and each time his ministry continues.

And many followed him, and he healed them all. Opposition did not stop his compassion.

And ordered them not to make him known. Jesus did not want to be known chiefly as a miracle-worker, or to stir up political messianic hopes (see 8:4). Matthew immediately explains this from Isaiah: the Messiah is a quiet, gentle Servant, not a loud self-promoter.

In a sentence. Jesus withdrew from his enemies but kept healing the crowds, without seeking publicity.

On a Tuesday. Jesus did good without seeking attention. Can you serve today without needing anyone to know?

verseByVerse.quote: This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah: "Behold, my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved with whom my soul is well pleased. I will put my Spirit upon him, and he will proclaim justice to the Gentiles."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This fulfilled Isaiah’s prophecy of the Servant: God’s chosen and beloved one, in whom he delights. God puts his Spirit on him, and he will announce justice to the nations.

This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah. Isaiah 42:1–4, the longest Old Testament quotation in Matthew. It is the first of four “Servant Songs” in Isaiah (42:1–9; 49:1–13; 50:4–11; 52:13–53:12), which describe the Servant of the LORD, who brings justice and salvation and suffers for the sins of the people.

Behold, my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved with whom my soul is well pleased. The Father’s words at Jesus’ baptism echoed this (3:17): beloved, well pleased. Jesus is the Servant. His greatness is the greatness of a servant (20:28).

I will put my Spirit upon him. Fulfilled when the Spirit came on Jesus at his baptism (3:16). Jesus casts out demons by this Spirit (v. 28).

And he will proclaim justice to the Gentiles. “Justice” (krisis) means God’s right order, his righteous rule and judgment, set right in the world. The Servant brings it not only to Israel but to the nations. Matthew stresses this: the Messiah is for the Gentiles too (v. 21; 28:19).

What it does not mean. Not that “justice” is only political or social. It includes God’s whole saving order: forgiveness, righteousness, and the setting right of all wrongs.

In a sentence. Jesus is Isaiah’s chosen and beloved Servant, filled with God’s Spirit, bringing God’s justice to the nations.

For worship. Worship Jesus, the Father’s beloved Servant, in whom he delights.

parallels.desc: my chosen servant, with my Spirit upon him
the Father’s voice at the baptism

verseByVerse.quote: He will not quarrel or cry aloud, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets; a bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not quench, until he brings justice to victory;
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Servant will not quarrel or shout or make a noise in the streets. He will not break a bruised reed or snuff out a smouldering wick, until he brings justice to victory.

He will not quarrel or cry aloud, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets. The Servant is not a noisy self-promoter, a political agitator or a street-corner demagogue. He does not force his way. This explains why Jesus withdrew and told people not to publicise him (vv. 15–16).

A bruised reed he will not break. A reed was a weak, hollow plant growing by water. A bruised, bent reed was useless; most people would snap it off and throw it away. The Servant does not.

And a smoldering wick he will not quench. A lamp-wick that is only smouldering, smoking and almost out, would normally be snuffed out and replaced. The Servant gently fans it back to flame.

Who are they? The weak, the failing, the crushed, those with almost no faith left, those whom others have given up on: the sick he healed, the sinners he ate with, the weary he called (11:28). The Puritan Richard Sibbes wrote a famous book on this verse, The Bruised Reed (1630), to comfort struggling Christians: Christ is gentle with weak faith.

Until he brings justice to victory. His gentleness is not weakness. He will persevere until justice triumphs completely. The gentle Servant is also the conquering King.

What it does not mean. Not that Christ is soft on sin or never confronts evil. He rebuked the Pharisees fiercely (chapter 23). His gentleness is for the broken and repentant; his severity is for the proud and hard-hearted.

In a sentence. The Servant is gentle with the weak and failing, never crushing them, and he will persevere until justice triumphs.

On a Tuesday. If your faith feels like a smouldering wick, Christ will not snuff it out. Bring it to him. And be gentle with the bruised reeds around you.

For worship. Thank Christ that he does not break bruised reeds.
verseByVerse.note: A bruised reed and a smouldering lamp-wick are pictures of the weak and failing, easily finished off.

parallels.desc: he will not cry aloud, nor break a bruised reed

verseByVerse.quote: and in his name the Gentiles will hope.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And in his name the nations will put their hope.

And in his name the Gentiles will hope. The end of the quotation from Isaiah 42:4 (following the Greek Old Testament). “His name” means his person, character and authority. The nations, who were without hope (Ephesians 2:12), will find hope in the Servant. The Pharisees rejected him; the nations will trust him.

In a sentence. The nations will put their hope in the Servant, Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Pray for the nations today, that people in every land will find their hope in Christ.

parallels.desc: the coastlands wait for his law
in him will the Gentiles hope

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–50 — The Unforgivable Sin, the Sign of Jonah, and True Family
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter's second half escalates the conflict. Jesus heals a blind and mute demoniac; the Pharisees attribute it to Beelzebul. Jesus dismantles the accusation with three arguments, then pronounces the solemn warning about blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. The scribes and Pharisees demand a sign; Jesus offers only the sign of Jonah. The chapter ends with a redefinition of family: those who do the will of the Father are Jesus's true mother and brothers. Four things more. The crowd's question in v. 23 expects the answer no — closer to "this can't be the Son of David, can it?" They are edging toward a confession and flinching. And the title fits this miracle exactly: Solomon, David's son, had a reputation as master of spirits, and Josephus describes a Jewish exorcist working "according to the methods of Solomon" — with a ring and a root. Jesus says "go". Luke records v. 28 with one word different — "by the finger of God" (Lk. 11:20), which is a quotation: it is what Pharaoh's magicians said when they could no longer reproduce the plagues (Exod. 8:19). The exorcisms are a new exodus, and the Pharisees are standing where the magicians stood. "come upon you" is ephthasen — arrived, overtaken; not an offer drawing near but a thing that has landed. "every careless word" is argos, literally not-working: the unemployed remark that achieved nothing and was forgotten within the hour — and the guard that "by your words you will be justified" is forensic, evidence rather than payment. Both witnesses at the judgement are Gentiles: Nineveh, capital of the empire that destroyed the northern kingdom, which had one reluctant preacher; and the queen of Sheba, who had a rumour and a long journey. Neither had Scripture, temple, covenant or promise. The returning Spirit finds the house "empty, swept, and put in order" — three approving words, and the first is fatal. It is not a passage about losing salvation; there is no indwelling in the story, which is the whole problem. And v. 50 names brother, sister and mother — but not father, because the Father is already in the sentence (cf. 23:9). Mark tells us why the family came: they thought he was out of his mind (Mk. 3:21); John notes his brothers did not believe (Jn. 7:5); and Mary is in the upper room in Acts 1:14. She did not stay outside.
verseByVerse.theology: The blasphemy against the Holy Spirit — attributing the Spirit's work to Satan — is the one sin Jesus calls unforgivable. It is not unforgivable because it exceeds God's mercy but because it closes the door through which mercy enters: it calls the Spirit of conviction a demon, and the person who has hardened to that degree has no remaining capacity to receive the grace they are calling evil. The Pharisees are approaching this condition, if they have not already reached it. The warning is pastoral, not vindictive: it is the warning of a doctor who sees a patient choosing death.
verseByVerse.examples: The sign of Jonah — three days and three nights in the earth — is the only sign Jesus offers to an evil and adulterous generation. The resurrection is the final and definitive sign, the one that vindicates all his claims. No amount of healing, no accumulation of miracles, will convince those whose hearts are already set against him; only the empty tomb is sufficient — and even that will not convince those determined not to believe (28:13-15).

verseByVerse.quote: Then a demon-oppressed man who was blind and mute was brought to him, and he healed him, so that the man spoke and saw. And all the people were amazed, and said, "Can this be the Son of David?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A demon-possessed man who was blind and mute was brought to Jesus, and he healed him, so that he could speak and see. The crowds were amazed and asked: could this be the Son of David?

A demon-oppressed man who was blind and mute. A doubly tragic condition, caused by a demon. He was cut off from seeing and speaking.

And he healed him, so that the man spoke and saw. Complete healing, and freedom from the demon.

And all the people were amazed, and said, “Can this be the Son of David?” The Greek expects a hesitant answer: “This can’t be the Son of David, can it?” The crowds are beginning to wonder whether Jesus is the Messiah (see 1:1; 9:27). They are close to faith.

In a sentence. Jesus freed and healed a blind, mute, demon-possessed man, and the crowds began to wonder if he was the Messiah.

On a Tuesday. The crowds wondered; wonder must become faith. Is Jesus to you a question, or a confession?
verseByVerse.note: “Son of David” is a title for the Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the Pharisees heard it, they said, "It is only by Beelzebul, the prince of demons, that this man casts out demons." Knowing their thoughts, he said to them, "Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and no city or house divided against itself will stand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees answered that Jesus cast out demons only by the power of Beelzebul, the prince of demons. Jesus, knowing their thoughts, replied: every kingdom divided against itself is ruined, and every city or household divided against itself will not stand.

But when the Pharisees heard it. They saw the crowds moving toward faith and acted to stop it.

It is only by Beelzebul, the prince of demons, that this man casts out demons. They could not deny the miracle, so they attributed it to Satan (see 9:34; 10:25). “Beelzebul” was a name for Satan. This is the most serious accusation they could make: Jesus is in league with the devil.

Knowing their thoughts. As in 9:4. Jesus knows the heart.

Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste. Civil war destroys nations. History was full of examples, including Israel’s own civil wars.

And no city or house divided against itself will stand. Division destroys families and communities.

In a sentence. The Pharisees claimed Jesus worked by Satan’s power, and Jesus began to show the absurdity of the charge: a divided kingdom cannot stand.

On a Tuesday. Division destroys. Guard the unity of your family and church (Ephesians 4:3).
verseByVerse.note: Beelzebul is a name for Satan, probably related to Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron.

verseByVerse.quote: And if Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself. How then will his kingdom stand? And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If Satan drives out Satan, he is fighting himself; how could his kingdom stand? And if Jesus drives out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do the Pharisees’ own followers drive them out? They will judge you.

And if Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself. The first argument: it is absurd. Satan would be destroying his own work. Why would he free people he had enslaved?

How then will his kingdom stand? Satan has a kingdom, an organised realm of evil (Colossians 1:13; Ephesians 2:2; 6:12). He is not foolish enough to destroy it.

And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? The second argument: inconsistency. “Your sons” means the Pharisees’ followers or other Jewish exorcists of the time (Acts 19:13–16). The Pharisees approved of their exorcisms; why condemn Jesus’ as satanic? Unlike them, Jesus used no incantations, but cast out demons by a word, with complete success.

Therefore they will be your judges. Their own followers expose their inconsistency.

In a sentence. The Pharisees’ charge was absurd, since Satan would not fight himself, and inconsistent, since they approved of their own exorcists.

On a Tuesday. Watch for double standards in how you judge others, especially those you dislike.
verseByVerse.note: Other Jewish exorcists were active at the time; “your sons” probably means Jewish exorcists of their own circle.

verseByVerse.quote: But if it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you. Or how can someone enter a strong man's house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man? Then indeed he may plunder his house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if Jesus drives out demons by the Spirit of God, then God’s kingdom has arrived. No one can enter a strong man’s house and steal his goods without first tying him up. Jesus has bound the strong man, Satan, and is plundering his house.

But if it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons. The true explanation: God’s Spirit, who came on Jesus at his baptism (3:16; 12:18). Luke says “by the finger of God” (Luke 11:20), echoing the Egyptian magicians’ words when they saw Moses’ miracles: this is the finger of God (Exodus 8:19).

Then the kingdom of God has come upon you. Here Matthew uses “kingdom of God”, not his usual “kingdom of heaven”. “Has come upon you” means it has already arrived, here and now. The exorcisms are proof that God’s reign has broken into the world in Jesus. This is the “already” of the kingdom.

Or how can someone enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man? A parable. The strong man is Satan. His house is the world, or the people he holds captive. His goods are the people he enslaves. To rob a strong man, you must first overpower and tie him up. Isaiah 49:24–25 asks whether prey can be taken from the mighty, and answers that God will do it.

Then indeed he may plunder his house. Jesus is the stronger one (3:11; Luke 11:22). He has bound Satan, beginning with his victory in the wilderness (4:1–11), and completing it at the cross (Colossians 2:15; Hebrews 2:14–15; John 12:31). Every exorcism, and every person set free from sin, is Jesus plundering Satan’s house.

What it does not mean. Not that Satan is now powerless or inactive. He still prowls like a roaring lion (1 Peter 5:8). But he is bound in the sense that he cannot stop the advance of the gospel or hold on to those whom Christ frees. Revelation 20:1–3 pictures Satan bound so that he can no longer deceive the nations. Reformed amillennialists see this binding as beginning with Christ’s first coming, which is the present gospel age, not a future millennium. Verdict: Satan is bound now, in the sense this verse describes, and the gospel is plundering his house among the nations.

In a sentence. Jesus drives out demons by God’s Spirit, proving that God’s kingdom has come and that he has bound Satan and is setting his captives free.

On a Tuesday. Whatever has held you captive, Christ is stronger. He has bound the strong man; ask him to set you free.

For worship. Praise Christ, the stronger one, who has bound Satan and set you free.

parallels.desc: the prey taken from the mighty
he disarmed the rulers and authorities

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters. Therefore I tell you, every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven people, but the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
