There is no neutral ground: whoever is not with Jesus is against him, and whoever does not gather with him scatters. Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven, but blasphemy against the Spirit will not.

Whoever is not with me is against me. In the war between Jesus and Satan, there is no neutrality. Not to side with Jesus is to side with his enemy. The Pharisees thought they were serving God; by opposing Jesus, they were serving Satan.

And whoever does not gather with me scatters. A picture from shepherding, or harvest. Jesus is gathering his flock or harvest (9:36–38); those who do not help him gather are scattering it.

Therefore I tell you, every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven people. A great promise. No sin is too great to be forgiven, including blasphemy, if it is repented of. Paul had been a blasphemer and was forgiven (1 Timothy 1:13).

But the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven. The one exception, which verse 32 explains.

What it does not mean. Not that a person can be neutral about Jesus and safe. Elsewhere Jesus says, whoever is not against us is for us (Mark 9:40). Both are true: about Jesus himself, there is no neutrality; about those doing good in his name, we should not be suspicious.

In a sentence. No one can be neutral about Jesus, and while every sin can be forgiven, blasphemy against the Spirit cannot.

On a Tuesday. Are you with Jesus, or only watching from the side? There is no safe middle.

verseByVerse.quote: And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come. Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad, for the tree is known by its fruit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anyone who speaks against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but anyone who speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or the age to come. A tree is known by its fruit: make the tree good, and the fruit will be good.

Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven. People who misunderstood Jesus, or spoke against him in ignorance, could be forgiven. Jesus’ identity was partly veiled during his earthly life. Peter denied him and was forgiven; Paul persecuted him and was forgiven.

But whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come. What is this “unforgivable sin”? In context, the Pharisees had seen the Spirit’s work clearly, the casting out of demons, and deliberately called it the work of Satan (vv. 24, 28). They were not ignorant; they were calling light darkness and good evil, against the evidence, because they hated Jesus. Mark adds the explanation: because they were saying, “He has an unclean spirit” (Mark 3:30).

Why is it unforgivable? Not because God’s grace is too small, but because this sin rejects the only source of forgiveness. The Holy Spirit is the one who convicts people of sin and draws them to Christ (John 16:8–11). To reject his testimony deliberately and finally, calling it satanic, is to shut the only door to forgiveness. Such a person does not want forgiveness and will not repent. It is a settled, wilful hardening of the heart against God’s clear revelation of Christ.

Either the tree is good and its fruit good, or the tree is bad and its fruit bad. A tree is known by its fruit (7:16–20). The fruit of Jesus’ ministry, people freed, healed and restored, is good; so the tree, Jesus, is good, not satanic. And the Pharisees’ fruit, slander and plotting murder, reveals what they are.

What it does not mean. Many anxious Christians fear they have committed this sin. Those who are worried that they have committed it have not. The person who has committed it does not care; they are hardened. A believer’s anxiety about having offended God is itself a sign of the Spirit’s work in them. Nor is it a single careless word, a doubt, or a sin committed in weakness, even a serious one. It is a settled, deliberate rejection of Christ in the face of the Spirit’s clear witness. And “in this age or the age to come” does not imply that other sins may be forgiven after death, as in purgatory. It is a Jewish way of saying “never”.

In a sentence. Those who deliberately call the Spirit’s clear work in Christ the work of Satan reject the only source of forgiveness, and so cannot be forgiven.

On a Tuesday. If you fear you have committed this sin, your fear shows that you have not. Come to Christ: he will not turn you away (John 6:37).

verseByVerse.quote: You brood of vipers! How can you speak good, when you are evil? For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. The good person out of his good treasure brings forth good, and the evil person out of his evil treasure brings forth evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus called the Pharisees a brood of snakes: how can evil people say good things? What fills the heart comes out of the mouth. A good person brings good things out of the good stored in them; an evil person brings evil out of the evil stored in them.

You brood of vipers! The same words John the Baptist used (3:7). Their poisonous slander showed their nature.

How can you speak good, when you are evil? Words reveal character.

For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. “Abundance” means overflow. Like water overflowing from a full container, words come from what fills the heart. The Pharisees’ slander against Jesus was not a slip; it revealed hatred in their hearts.

The good person out of his good treasure brings forth good. “Treasure” here means a storehouse. What we store in our hearts, our thoughts, loves and beliefs, eventually comes out in our words (6:21).

And the evil person out of his evil treasure brings forth evil. Evil stored in the heart produces evil words.

What it does not mean. Not that every harsh word reveals a wholly evil heart. Christians still sin with their tongues (James 3:2). But our words are a window into our hearts. The solution is not just to control our speech, but to change our hearts, which only God can do.

In a sentence. Our words overflow from what fills our hearts, revealing whether they are good or evil.

On a Tuesday. Listen to your own words today: what do they reveal about what is in your heart?

parallels.desc: what comes out of the mouth

verseByVerse.quote: I tell you, on the day of judgment people will give account for every careless word they speak, for by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On judgment day, people will give an account for every careless word they have spoken. By your words you will be acquitted, and by your words you will be condemned.

I tell you, on the day of judgment people will give account for every careless word they speak. “Careless” (argon) means idle, useless, thoughtless: words spoken without thinking, the casual remark, the joke at someone’s expense, the gossip. If even careless words matter to God, how much more deliberate ones like the Pharisees’ slander.

For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned. “Justified” here means declared righteous at the final judgment. Words are evidence of what is in the heart (v. 34). At the judgment, our words will show whether our hearts belonged to God.

What it does not mean. Not that we are saved by our words, as if careful speech earns heaven. We are justified by faith in Christ (Romans 3:28). But words, like works, are evidence of genuine faith or its absence (James 2:18; 3:2–12). A person whose heart has been changed will have changed speech. Nor does it mean every careless word will condemn a believer. Christ’s blood covers all their sins, including sins of the tongue (1 John 1:7). But no one should treat words lightly.

In a sentence. God will judge every careless word, because our words reveal our hearts.

On a Tuesday. If you had to give an account for every word you said yesterday, what would it reveal? Ask God to forgive your careless words and to guard your mouth today (Psalm 141:3).

parallels.desc: death and life are in the power of the tongue

verseByVerse.quote: Then some of the scribes and Pharisees answered him, saying, "Teacher, we wish to see a sign from you." But he answered them, "An evil and adulterous generation seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some scribes and Pharisees asked Jesus for a sign. He replied that an evil and adulterous generation demands a sign, but no sign will be given except the sign of the prophet Jonah.

Teacher, we wish to see a sign from you. A “sign” means a miraculous proof of his authority, something spectacular, on their terms. They had just seen a demon cast out (v. 22) and called it Satan’s work. Their request was not honest seeking but unbelief demanding more.

An evil and adulterous generation seeks for a sign. “Adulterous” is the prophets’ word for Israel’s unfaithfulness to God, like a wife unfaithful to her husband (Hosea 1–3; Jeremiah 3). This generation claimed to belong to God but did not love him.

But no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. Jesus will not perform on demand. The only sign they will get is the sign of Jonah, which he explains next.

What it does not mean. Not that asking God for help or confirmation is always wrong. Gideon asked for a sign, and God graciously gave it (Judges 6:36–40). The problem is demanding proof from a heart that has already decided not to believe.

In a sentence. Jesus refused to perform signs for an unfaithful generation, except for the sign of Jonah.

On a Tuesday. Are you demanding that God prove himself on your terms, while ignoring the evidence he has already given?
verseByVerse.note: “Adulterous” is the prophets’ word for Israel’s unfaithfulness to God.

verseByVerse.quote: For just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Jonah was three days and nights in the belly of the great fish, so the Son of Man will be three days and nights in the heart of the earth. The people of Nineveh will rise at the judgment and condemn this generation, because they repented at Jonah’s preaching, and something greater than Jonah is here.

For just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish. Jonah 1:17. Jonah was swallowed by a great fish and then came out alive. It was like a death and resurrection.

So will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. Jesus predicts his death, burial and resurrection. The sign of Jonah is the resurrection: the greatest sign of all. “Three days and three nights” was a Jewish way of counting any part of a day as a whole day. Jesus was in the tomb from Friday afternoon to Sunday morning, which counts as three days (16:21; 27:63–64).

The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it. Nineveh was the capital of Assyria, Israel’s most brutal enemy, a pagan city of great wickedness. When Jonah preached, the whole city repented, from the king down (Jonah 3:5–10). At the final judgment, their example will condemn this generation, which did not repent.

For they repented at the preaching of Jonah. Jonah was a reluctant, angry prophet who performed no miracles and preached a short message of judgment. Yet Nineveh repented.

And behold, something greater than Jonah is here. Jesus is greater than Jonah: a willing Saviour, not a reluctant prophet; the Son of God, not a mere messenger; doing miracles, not only preaching. If Nineveh repented at Jonah, how much more should Israel repent at Jesus.

What it does not mean. Not that the story of Jonah is merely a myth. Jesus treats Jonah and the repentance of Nineveh as real history, alongside his own resurrection. Nor does “three days and three nights” require seventy-two hours exactly.

In a sentence. Jesus’ death and resurrection will be the sign of Jonah, and repentant Nineveh will condemn a generation that would not repent at one greater than Jonah.

On a Tuesday. The resurrection is the sign God has given. Have you repented at the preaching of one greater than Jonah?
verseByVerse.note: “Three days and three nights” was a way of counting any part of a day as a day. Nineveh was the capital of Assyria.

parallels.desc: three days and three nights in the fish

verseByVerse.quote: The queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here. When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, but finds none.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The queen of the South will also rise at the judgment and condemn this generation, because she travelled from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom, and something greater than Solomon is here.

The queen of the South. The queen of Sheba, from southwest Arabia (modern Yemen), about 1,200 miles (2,000 kilometres) from Jerusalem. She came to test Solomon with hard questions, was overwhelmed by his wisdom, and praised his God (1 Kings 10:1–13). She was a Gentile.

Will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it. She made a long, costly journey to hear wisdom; this generation would not walk a few steps to listen to Jesus.

For she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon. Solomon was the wisest king in Israel’s history, the son of David.

And behold, something greater than Solomon is here. Jesus is greater than Solomon: the true Son of David, Wisdom itself (11:19; 1 Corinthians 1:24, 30; Colossians 2:3). In this chapter Jesus has claimed to be greater than the temple (v. 6), than Jonah the prophet (v. 41), and than Solomon the king (v. 42): greater than priest, prophet and king.

In a sentence. A Gentile queen who travelled far for Solomon’s wisdom will condemn those who ignored one far greater than Solomon.

On a Tuesday. What effort do you make to hear the wisdom of Christ? The queen travelled 1,200 miles for a lesser king.
verseByVerse.note: The queen of the South is the queen of Sheba, in south-west Arabia.

parallels.desc: the queen of Sheba visits Solomon

verseByVerse.quote: Then it says, "I will return to my house from which I came." And when it comes, it finds the house empty, swept, and put in order. Then it goes and brings with it seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they enter and dwell there, and the last state of that person is worse than the first. So also will it be with this evil generation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When an unclean spirit leaves a person, it wanders looking for rest and finds none. Then it says: I will go back to my house. It finds the house empty, swept and tidy, and brings back seven other spirits worse than itself. The person ends up worse than before. So it will be with this evil generation.

When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest. Deserts were thought to be the home of demons (Isaiah 13:21; 34:14). The spirit is restless without a person to inhabit.

Then it says, “I will return to my house from which I came.” The person is still its “house”, because no one else has moved in.

And when it comes, it finds the house empty, swept, and put in order. The house has been cleaned up, but left empty. The person has been reformed, but not filled with God’s presence.

Then it goes and brings with it seven other spirits more evil than itself. Seven: a complete number. A full occupation.

And the last state of that person is worse than the first. Reformation without regeneration leaves a person more vulnerable than before.

So also will it be with this evil generation. The application. Israel had experienced reform and renewal: through John’s preaching, and through Jesus’ exorcisms and healings. But if they did not receive Jesus, the Spirit would not fill the house. Their condition would become worse. This happened in the following decades, ending in the disaster of AD 70.

What it does not mean. Not that a true believer, indwelt by the Holy Spirit, can be repossessed by demons. A house filled by the Spirit is not empty (1 John 4:4). The warning is about moral reform without new birth: cleaning up one’s life without receiving Christ. Getting rid of bad habits is not enough; the heart must be filled with Christ.

In a sentence. Moral cleaning without being filled by God leaves a person, or a nation, worse off than before.

On a Tuesday. Is your faith only a tidying-up of your life, or have you received Christ himself to fill it?

parallels.desc: the last state worse than the first

verseByVerse.quote: While he was still speaking to the people, behold, his mother and his brothers stood outside, asking to speak to him. Someone told him, "Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking to speak to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
While Jesus was still speaking, his mother and brothers stood outside, wanting to speak to him. Someone told him they were waiting.

His mother and his brothers. Mary and Jesus’ brothers, James, Joseph, Simon and Judas (13:55). Mark tells us that his family had come to take him home, because they thought he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21, 31). His brothers did not believe in him at this time (John 7:5). After the resurrection, they became believers; James became a leader of the Jerusalem church and wrote the letter of James, and Judas (Jude) wrote the letter of Jude (Acts 1:14; 15:13; Galatians 1:19).

Stood outside, asking to speak to him. Outside the house or the crowd. Physically, and perhaps spiritually, they were outside.

Textual note. Some important early manuscripts omit verse 47 (“Someone told him, ‘Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, asking to speak to you’”). It may have been accidentally skipped because verses 46 and 47 end with the same words. Verdict: probably original; it is needed for verse 48 to make sense.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus’ brothers were cousins or Joseph’s sons by an earlier marriage. The natural reading is that they were Mary’s later children (see 1:25).

In a sentence. Jesus’ mother and brothers, who did not yet understand him, came wanting to speak to him.

On a Tuesday. Even Jesus’ family misunderstood him for a time. If your family misunderstands your faith, you are in good company, and there is hope: his brothers came to believe.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts insert verse 47: “Someone told him, ‘Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, asking to speak to you.’”

verseByVerse.quote: But he replied to the man who told him, "Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?" And stretching out his hand toward his disciples, he said, "Here are my mother and my brothers!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus asked: who is my mother, and who are my brothers? Pointing to his disciples, he said: here are my mother and my brothers.

Who is my mother, and who are my brothers? A shocking question in a culture where family was everything. Jesus is not rejecting his family, but redefining what family means in God’s kingdom.

And stretching out his hand toward his disciples. A gesture of welcome and claim.

Here are my mother and my brothers! His disciples are his true family. The bond of faith is deeper than the bond of blood. The church is a family: brothers and sisters, with God as Father (23:8–9).

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus despised his mother. On the cross he provided for her care (John 19:26–27). Nor does it mean that natural family does not matter (15:4–6). But family loyalty is not the highest loyalty (10:37). And this passage gives no support for devotion to Mary as a mediator. Jesus pointed away from his family to his disciples.

In a sentence. Jesus declared that his disciples are his true family.

On a Tuesday. Your church is your family. Who in it needs a brother, sister, mother or father this week?

verseByVerse.quote: For whoever does the will of my Father in heaven is my brother and sister and mother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever does the will of my Father in heaven is my brother and sister and mother.

For whoever does the will of my Father in heaven. Membership in Jesus’ family is not by birth, but by doing God’s will: repenting, believing in Jesus, and obeying him (7:21; John 6:29). Anyone may join.

Is my brother and sister and mother. Notice “sister”: Jesus includes women explicitly. In the church, there are spiritual mothers, sisters and brothers. Jesus is not ashamed to call them brothers (Hebrews 2:11).

What it does not mean. Not that we earn a place in Jesus’ family by our works. Doing the Father’s will begins with believing in the Son he sent (John 6:29). Those adopted into God’s family by grace (Ephesians 1:5) show it by doing his will.

In a sentence. Everyone who does the Father’s will belongs to Jesus’ family.

On a Tuesday. If you trust and obey Christ, he calls you his brother or sister. Live today as a member of his family.

For worship. Thank Jesus that he is not ashamed to call you his brother or sister.

parallels.desc: you are my friends if you do what I command

12.theology: Christ as the fulfilment of the Sabbath. The Sabbath controversy of chapter 12 points to one of the great themes of biblical theology: Jesus as the antitype of every Old Testament type. The Sabbath rest of creation (Gen 2) and covenant (Exod 20) pointed forward to the final rest that God’s people would enjoy in the new creation. Hebrews 4 draws this line explicitly: the rest that Joshua could not give, the rest that the weekly Sabbath symbolised, is found in Christ. When Jesus says “the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath,” he is claiming to be both the giver and the substance of that rest. The Lord’s Day, the day of resurrection, is a weekly proclamation that the rest has arrived in Christ and will be consummated at his return.
12.examples:
Then: The Pharisees’ religion had become a burden rather than a delight. Rules multiplied around the Sabbath until the day of rest was a day of anxiety. Jesus exposed the inversion: when religious observance crushes the people it was meant to bless, something has gone terribly wrong.

Now: The temptation of every religious tradition is to mistake the form for the substance, the sign for the thing signified. The Sabbath becomes a test case: are we worshipping the living God who gives rest, or performing compliance with a schedule? The Lord’s Day is meant to be a foretaste of heaven, a weekly resurrection celebration, not a legal obligation. Christ is Lord of it — and he gives it as a gift.

13.title: The Kingdom in Parables
13.text: <sup>1</sup>That same day Jesus went out of the house and sat beside the sea. <sup>2</sup>And great crowds gathered about him, so that he got into a boat and sat down. And the whole crowd stood on the beach. <sup>3</sup>And he told them many things in parables, saying: “A sower went out to sow. <sup>4</sup>And as he sowed, some seeds fell along the path, and the birds came and devoured them. <sup>5</sup>Other seeds fell on rocky ground, where they did not have much soil, and immediately they sprang up, since they had no depth of soil, <sup>6</sup>but when the sun rose they were scorched. And since they had no root, they withered away. <sup>7</sup>Other seeds fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked them. <sup>8</sup>Other seeds fell on good soil and produced grain, some a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty. <sup>9</sup>He who has ears, let him hear.” <sup>10</sup>Then the disciples came and said to him, “Why do you speak to them in parables?” <sup>11</sup>And he answered them, “To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given. <sup>12</sup>For to the one who has, more will be given, and he will have an abundance, but from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away. <sup>13</sup>This is why I speak to them in parables, because seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear, nor do they understand. <sup>14</sup>Indeed, in their case the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled that says: ”’“You will indeed hear but never understand, and you will indeed see but never perceive.” <sup>15</sup>For this people’s heart has grown dull, and with their ears they can barely hear, and their eyes they have closed, lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them.’ <sup>16</sup>But blessed are your eyes, for they see, and your ears, for they hear. <sup>17</sup>For truly, I say to you, many prophets and righteous people longed to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it. <sup>18</sup>“Hear then the parable of the sower: <sup>19</sup>When anyone hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it, the evil one comes and snatches away what has been sown in his heart. This is what was sown along the path. <sup>20</sup>As for what was sown on rocky ground, this is the one who hears the word and immediately receives it with joy, <sup>21</sup>yet he has no root in himself, but endures for a while, and when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word, immediately he falls away. <sup>22</sup>As for what was sown among thorns, this is the one who hears the word, but the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and it proves unfruitful. <sup>23</sup>As for what was sown on good soil, this is the one who hears the word and understands it. He indeed bears fruit and yields, in one case a hundredfold, in another sixty, and in another thirty.” <sup>24</sup>He put another parable before them, saying, “The kingdom of heaven may be compared to a man who sowed good seed in his field, <sup>25</sup>but while his men were sleeping, his enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat and went away. <sup>26</sup>So when the plants came up and bore grain, then the weeds appeared also. <sup>27</sup>And the servants of the master of the house came and said to him, ‘Master, did you not sow good seed in your field? How then does it have weeds?’ <sup>28</sup>He said to them, ‘An enemy has done this.’ So the servants said to him, ‘Then do you want us to go and gather them?’ <sup>29</sup>But he said, ‘No, lest in gathering the weeds you root up the wheat along with them. <sup>30</sup>Let both grow together until the harvest, and at harvest time I will tell the reapers, “Gather the weeds first and bind them in bundles to be burned, but gather the wheat into my barn.”’” <sup>31</sup>He put another parable before them, saying, “The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his field. <sup>32</sup>It is the smallest of all seeds, but when it has grown it is larger than all the garden plants and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and make nests in its branches.” <sup>33</sup>He told them another parable. “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, till it was all leavened.” <sup>34</sup>All these things Jesus said to the crowds in parables; indeed, he said nothing to them without a parable. <sup>35</sup>This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet: “I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter what has been hidden since the foundation of the world.” <sup>36</sup>Then he left the crowds and went into the house. And his disciples came to him, saying, “Explain to us the parable of the weeds of the field.” <sup>37</sup>He answered, “The one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man. <sup>38</sup>The field is the world, and the good seed is the sons of the kingdom. The weeds are the sons of the evil one, <sup>39</sup>and the enemy who sowed them is the devil. The harvest is the end of the age, and the reapers are angels. <sup>40</sup>Just as the weeds are gathered and burned with fire, so will it be at the end of the age. <sup>41</sup>The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all causes of sin and all law-breakers, <sup>42</sup>and throw them into the fiery furnace. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. <sup>43</sup>Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. He who has ears, let him hear. <sup>44</sup>“The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field, which a man found and covered up. Then in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field. <sup>45</sup>“Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant in search of fine pearls, <sup>46</sup>who, on finding one pearl of great value, went and sold all that he had and bought it. <sup>47</sup>“Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net that was thrown into the sea and gathered fish of every kind. <sup>48</sup>When it was full, men drew it ashore and sat down and sorted the good into containers but threw away the bad. <sup>49</sup>So it will be at the end of the age. The angels will come out and separate the evil from the righteous <sup>50</sup>and throw them into the fiery furnace. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. <sup>51</sup>“Have you understood all these things?” They said to him, “Yes.” <sup>52</sup>And he said to them, “Therefore every scribe who has been trained for the kingdom of heaven is like a master of a house, who brings out of his treasure what is new and what is old.” <sup>53</sup>And when Jesus had finished these parables, he went away from there, <sup>54</sup>and coming to his hometown he taught them in their synagogue, so that they were astonished, and said, “Where did this man get this wisdom and these mighty works? <sup>55</sup>Is not this the carpenter’s son? Is not his mother called Mary? And are not his brothers James and Joseph and Simon and Judas? <sup>56</sup>And are not all his sisters with us? Where then did this man get all these things?” <sup>57</sup>And they took offense at him. But Jesus said to them, “A prophet is not without honor except in his hometown and in his own household.” <sup>58</sup>And he did not do many mighty works there, because of their unbelief.
13.overview:
Chapter 13 is the third great discourse of Matthew — a collection of seven parables about the kingdom of heaven. Jesus shifts to parables at a moment of escalating opposition (chapters 11–12), and explains to his disciples that parables reveal to the insiders and conceal from the hardened outsiders. This is not capricious; it is the judicial hardening of those who have repeatedly refused the light (v. 15, quoting Isa 6:9–10).

The parables themselves paint a picture of a kingdom that is present but not yet consummate, growing but not yet glorious, mixed but not yet purified. The mustard seed and leaven speak of unexpected, hidden growth from small beginnings. The wheat and tares speak of a kingdom growing alongside counterfeit until the final harvest. The treasure and pearl speak of the surpassing value of the kingdom that makes all sacrifice worthwhile. Together they answer the perennial question: why is the kingdom not more obvious? Because this is the age of seed-sowing, not harvest. The harvest is coming.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–23 — The Parable of the Sower and the Mystery of the Kingdom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus goes to the seashore and teaches in parables for the first time in Matthew. The parable of the sower describes four kinds of reception of the kingdom's word — the path, the rocky ground, the thorns, and the good soil. When the disciples ask why he teaches in parables, Jesus answers that parables reveal the kingdom to those with ears to hear and conceal it from those whose hearts are hardened. He then interprets the parable of the sower in detail. What the summary cannot hold. First-century sowing came before ploughing, not after: a man broadcast seed across the whole field as it stood and then turned the soil to cover it. So the sower is not careless — the path, the rock shelf and the thorn roots are all ground he is about to plough, and the parable is about ground rather than about a fool with a bag. "rocky ground" is not soil with stones in it but a shelf of limestone a few inches down, extremely common in Galilee — and thin soil over rock warms faster, which is exactly why that seed comes up first. The fastest green in the field is growing over the shallowest ground. The yields are the point and are usually skimmed: a normal harvest returned seven to tenfold, so thirty is triple a good year and a hundredfold is what Genesis records of Isaac as a Mark of extraordinary blessing (Gen. 26:12). One patch of good ground repays the whole sowing many times over — the parable is not pessimistic arithmetic. On the hardening, Matthew and Mark genuinely differ: Matthew has "because (hoti) seeing they do not see"; Mark has "so that (hina)... lest they should turn and be forgiven" (Mk. 4:12). Consequence and purpose. Both are in the Isaiah passage both writers quote — "their eyes they have closed" is active and theirs, and "lest they should turn, and I would heal them" is purpose and God's. Anybody who resolves that has dropped one half. Isaiah 6:9-10 is quoted in all four Gospels and in Acts; it is the settled apostolic explanation for Israel's unbelief. And "grown dull" is epachynthe, thickened — the language of a callus, which is formed by repetition rather than by one injury.
verseByVerse.theology: The parable of the sower is really a parable of soils — the sower and the seed are constant; the variable is the heart that receives the word. The four soils are not four types of people as if fixed in their category, but four ways the same heart can receive or resist the word. The parable is both diagnostic (what kind of soil am I?) and eschatological (the harvest will reveal what was real). The interpretation makes explicit that the word of the kingdom is the seed and the devil, persecution, worldly care, and the deceitfulness of riches are the enemies of fruitfulness.
verseByVerse.examples: The mystery of the kingdom — given to the disciples, hidden from others — is not arbitrary divine caprice but the consistent pattern of revelation-and-response: those who have ears to hear receive more; those who have closed their ears lose even what they have. The disciple's responsibility is to cultivate the good soil of an open, honest, persevering heart — "hear the word and understand it" (v. 23) — so that the seed which is sown can bear its appointed fruit.

verseByVerse.quote: That same day Jesus went out of the house and sat beside the sea. And great crowds gathered about him, so that he got into a boat and sat down. And the whole crowd stood on the beach.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same day, Jesus sat by the Sea of Galilee. So many people gathered that he got into a boat and taught from it, while the crowd stood on the shore.

The connection. Chapter 13 is the third of Jesus’ five great teaching sections: the parables of the kingdom. It follows directly from the growing rejection of chapters 11–12. Why do some receive Jesus and others reject him, if the kingdom has really come? The parables answer: the kingdom comes quietly, like seed; it meets different kinds of soil; it grows hidden; and good and evil will exist side by side until the final harvest.

That same day. The day of the Beelzebul controversy and the sign of Jonah (chapter 12).

Jesus went out of the house and sat beside the sea. Teachers sat to teach (5:1).

So that he got into a boat and sat down. The boat, pushed a little out from the shore, became a pulpit. The water carried his voice to the crowd. A cove near Capernaum forms a natural amphitheatre where a voice carries well to thousands.

And the whole crowd stood on the beach. Crowds in large numbers, as throughout Galilee.

In a sentence. Jesus taught the great crowds from a boat beside the lake.

On a Tuesday. Jesus used whatever was at hand, a boat, the shore, to teach. Look for ordinary opportunities to share God’s word.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers sat to teach; the boat let the crowd on the shore hear him.

verseByVerse.quote: And he told them many things in parables, saying: "A sower went out to sow. And as he sowed, some seeds fell along the path, and the birds came and devoured them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus taught in parables. The first: a farmer went out to sow seed. As he scattered it, some fell on the path, and birds came and ate it.

Parables. A parable (parabolē, “something thrown alongside”) is a story or picture from everyday life placed alongside a spiritual truth to illustrate it. The Hebrew equivalent (mashal) includes proverbs, riddles and illustrations. Jesus’ parables use farming, fishing, cooking, buying and selling. They usually make one main point, sometimes a few; they are not detailed allegories where every detail has a hidden meaning, though Jesus does interpret some details (vv. 18–23, 36–43).

A sower went out to sow. In Galilee, seed was usually sown by hand, scattered broadly from a bag, often before ploughing. Seed would fall everywhere.

And as he sowed, some seeds fell along the path. The path was the hard-trodden footpath between or through fields. The soil was packed hard by feet, and the seed could not sink in.

And the birds came and devoured them. Seed lying on the surface was eaten at once.

The four soils. The parable is often called the parable of the sower, but its focus is on the four kinds of soil: the path, the rocky ground, the thorns, and the good soil. The seed is the same; the soils differ. Jesus explains it in verses 18–23.

In a sentence. In the first parable, a farmer scatters seed, and some falls on a hard path where birds eat it at once.

On a Tuesday. The parable will ask you: what kind of soil is your heart?
verseByVerse.note: Seed was scattered by hand, and some fell on the hard footpaths between fields.

verseByVerse.quote: Other seeds fell on rocky ground, where they did not have much soil, and immediately they sprang up, since they had no depth of soil, but when the sun rose they were scorched. And since they had no root, they withered away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Other seed fell on rocky ground, with little soil. It sprang up quickly because the soil was shallow, but when the sun rose it was scorched and withered, because it had no root.

Other seeds fell on rocky ground. Not soil full of stones, but a thin layer of soil over limestone bedrock, common in Galilee.

Where they did not have much soil. Shallow.

And immediately they sprang up, since they had no depth of soil. The shallow soil warmed quickly in the sun, so the seed sprouted fast. It looked promising.

But when the sun rose they were scorched. The roots could not go deep to find water. The same sun that made them sprout quickly also killed them.

And since they had no root, they withered away. No root, no endurance.

In a sentence. Seed on shallow, rocky ground sprouted quickly but withered in the heat, because it had no root.

On a Tuesday. Quick enthusiasm is not the same as deep roots. How deep do your roots in Christ go?
verseByVerse.note: Much of Galilee has limestone bedrock just under a thin layer of soil.

verseByVerse.quote: Other seeds fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked them. Other seeds fell on good soil and produced grain, some a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty. He who has ears, let him hear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Other seed fell among thorns, which grew up and choked it. But other seed fell on good soil and produced a crop: a hundred, sixty or thirty times what was sown. Whoever has ears, let them hear.

Other seeds fell among thorns. Ground where thorn roots remained. The thorns had not yet appeared when the seed was sown.

And the thorns grew up and choked them. The thorns grew faster and stronger, taking the light, water and nutrients. The plants survived, but produced nothing.

Other seeds fell on good soil and produced grain. Deep, soft, clean soil.

Some a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty. A normal harvest in Palestine was perhaps seven to tenfold. Thirtyfold was excellent; a hundredfold was astonishing. Isaac reaped a hundredfold in the year God blessed him (Genesis 26:12). The point is that, despite losses, the good soil produces an extraordinary harvest. God’s kingdom will succeed abundantly. Different amounts: not every believer bears the same quantity of fruit, but every true believer bears fruit.

He who has ears, let him hear. A call to listen carefully, and respond (see 11:15). The parable is itself a test of the hearer.

In a sentence. Seed among thorns was choked, but seed in good soil produced an extraordinary harvest.

On a Tuesday. Are there thorns growing alongside God’s word in your heart, crowding it out?
verseByVerse.note: A hundredfold would be an extraordinary harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the disciples came and said to him, "Why do you speak to them in parables?" And he answered them, "To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given. For to the one who has, more will be given, and he will have an abundance, but from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples asked why Jesus spoke to the crowds in parables. He answered: the secrets of the kingdom have been given to you to understand, but not to them. Whoever has will be given more; whoever does not have will lose even what he has.

Why do you speak to them in parables? Jesus had taught plainly before (chapters 5–7). Now he uses parables to the crowds. Why?

To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of heaven. “Secrets” (mystēria, “mysteries”) means truths once hidden, now revealed by God (see Ephesians 3:3). The mystery here is that the kingdom has come in Jesus, but not in the way people expected: not with crushing force, but like seed, hidden and growing, received by some and rejected by others, until the harvest. “It has been given”: the passive points to God as the giver. Understanding the kingdom is a gift (11:25–27; 16:17).

But to them it has not been given. To the unbelieving crowds and leaders, who have rejected Jesus (chapters 11–12).

For to the one who has, more will be given, and he will have an abundance. A principle of spiritual life. Those who receive and respond to the truth receive more understanding. Faith grows by use.

But from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away. Those who reject the light they have will lose even that. Truth ignored is lost.

What it does not mean. Not that God is unfair, hiding the truth from people who wanted it. Those who did not receive it had already hardened their hearts (v. 15; 12:24). Nor does it mean the disciples were cleverer. Their understanding was a gift.

In a sentence. Jesus gives understanding of the kingdom’s secrets to his disciples as a gift, while those who reject the light lose even what they had.

On a Tuesday. Use the understanding God has given you; respond to the truth you know, and he will give you more.
verseByVerse.note: A “secret” (mystery) in the New Testament is something once hidden and now revealed by God.

parallels.desc: to everyone who has will more be given

verseByVerse.quote: This is why I speak to them in parables, because seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear, nor do they understand. Indeed, in their case the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled that says: "You will indeed hear but never understand, and you will indeed see but never perceive."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus speaks in parables because, though people see, they do not truly see; though they hear, they do not truly hear or understand. This fulfils Isaiah’s prophecy.

This is why I speak to them in parables. Parables both reveal and conceal. To those open to the truth, they illuminate. To those who have hardened their hearts, they remain riddles, and that is itself a judgment.

Because seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear, nor do they understand. They saw the miracles and heard the teaching, but did not grasp what they meant. Physical sight without spiritual sight.

Indeed, in their case the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled. Isaiah 6:9–10, from Isaiah’s call. God sent Isaiah to preach to a people who would not listen. His preaching would harden them further. This passage is quoted again in the New Testament to explain Israel’s rejection of Christ (John 12:39–41; Acts 28:25–28; Romans 11:8).

You will indeed hear but never understand, and you will indeed see but never perceive. The emphatic Hebrew form: “hearing, you will hear”: plenty of hearing, but no understanding.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus was trying to prevent people from being saved who wanted to be. The hardening is a judgment on those who have already rejected the truth. God gives them over to what they have chosen (Romans 1:24). Nor does it mean that parables are meant only to confuse. They also teach; the disciples received the explanations, and many who heard the parables later understood.

In a sentence. Parables conceal truth from those who have hardened their hearts, fulfilling Isaiah’s prophecy that they would hear but not understand.

On a Tuesday. You can sit through sermons for years and not truly hear. Ask God for ears that hear and a heart that understands.

verseByVerse.quote: "For this people's heart has grown dull, and with their ears they can barely hear, and their eyes they have closed, lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them." But blessed are your eyes, for they see, and your ears, for they hear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaiah’s prophecy continues: the people’s heart has grown dull, their ears hard of hearing, and they have closed their eyes, so that they will not turn and be healed. But blessed are your eyes, because they see, and your ears, because they hear.

For this people’s heart has grown dull. “Dull” literally means “fat”, thick, insensitive. The heart has become hardened, unresponsive to God.

And with their ears they can barely hear. Hard of hearing.

And their eyes they have closed. Notice: they closed their own eyes. The blindness is their own choice. God’s judgment confirms it.

Lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them. “Turn” is repentance. The tragedy: if they turned, God would heal them. He is willing to heal; they are not willing to turn.

But blessed are your eyes, for they see, and your ears, for they hear. The disciples are blessed, not because they are better, but because God has opened their eyes and ears. The same Beatitude form as 5:3–12.

The balance. The hardening is both God’s judgment and the people’s own choice. They closed their eyes; God confirmed it. Pharaoh hardened his heart, and God hardened Pharaoh’s heart (Exodus 8:15; 9:12). The disciples see because God gave them sight. In both cases God is sovereign, and people are responsible.

What it does not mean. Not that God refuses those who come to him. Whoever comes will be received (John 6:37). The hardening falls on those who have refused to come.

In a sentence. The people closed their own eyes and hardened their hearts so they would not turn and be healed, but the disciples are blessed because God has opened their eyes.

For worship. If you see and hear the truth of Christ, thank God for opening your eyes and ears.

parallels.desc: make the heart of this people dull

verseByVerse.quote: For truly, I say to you, many prophets and righteous people longed to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it. Hear then the parable of the sower:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many prophets and righteous people longed to see what the disciples see, and to hear what they hear, but did not. Jesus then explains the parable of the sower.

For truly, I say to you, many prophets and righteous people longed to see what you see, and did not see it. Abraham, Moses, David, Isaiah and the faithful of Israel looked forward to the Messiah, but died without seeing him (Hebrews 11:13, 39–40; 1 Peter 1:10–12). The disciples are seeing the fulfilment of all their hopes, in person.

And to hear what you hear, and did not hear it. The teaching of the Messiah himself.

Hear then the parable of the sower. Jesus explains it to those who have been given understanding. The sower is Jesus himself, and those who preach his word after him (v. 37).

In a sentence. The disciples see and hear what the prophets longed for, and Jesus explains the parable to them.

On a Tuesday. You know more of Christ than Abraham, Moses and Isaiah did. Do you value the privilege?

verseByVerse.quote: When anyone hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it, the evil one comes and snatches away what has been sown in his heart. This is what was sown along the path. As for what was sown on rocky ground, this is the one who hears the word and immediately receives it with joy,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seed on the path is the person who hears the message of the kingdom and does not understand it: the evil one comes and snatches it away. The seed on rocky ground is the person who hears the word and receives it at once with joy.

When anyone hears the word of the kingdom. The seed is the word: the message of the kingdom, the gospel (Luke 8:11 says “the word of God”).

And does not understand it. Not merely intellectual failure, but refusal to take it in. The heart is hard, like a trodden path. The word lies on the surface. Many hear sermons this way: the words enter the ears but never reach the heart.

The evil one comes and snatches away what has been sown in his heart. The birds are Satan. He takes the word before it can take root, through distraction, doubt, mockery or forgetfulness. Paul says the god of this world has blinded the minds of unbelievers (2 Corinthians 4:4).

This is what was sown along the path. The first soil: hard, unresponsive.

As for what was sown on rocky ground, this is the one who hears the word and immediately receives it with joy. The second soil. An enthusiastic, emotional response. Quick, joyful, impressive. It looks like conversion.

What it does not mean. Not that joy in receiving the gospel is suspicious. Good soil also receives the word with joy (1 Thessalonians 1:6). The problem with the rocky soil is not joy, but lack of root (v. 21).

In a sentence. Some hearers do not take the word in, and Satan snatches it away; others receive it quickly and joyfully, but without depth.

On a Tuesday. After you hear a sermon today or this Sunday, take a moment to reflect and pray over it, so that the birds do not take it away.

verseByVerse.quote: yet he has no root in himself, but endures for a while, and when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word, immediately he falls away. As for what was sown among thorns, this is the one who hears the word, but the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and it proves unfruitful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rocky-ground hearer has no root and lasts only a while. When trouble or persecution comes because of the word, he quickly falls away. The thorny ground is the one who hears the word, but the worries of this life and the deceitfulness of wealth choke it, and it produces nothing.

Yet he has no root in himself. The response is shallow. It has not gone down into the heart and will.

But endures for a while. For a time, it looks real.

And when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word. The scorching sun (v. 6). Trouble comes because of the word: opposition, mockery, loss. Christianity costs something.

Immediately he falls away. “Falls away” (skandalizetai) means stumbles, is offended. As quickly as he came, he goes. The faith that sprang up overnight withers overnight.

As for what was sown among thorns, this is the one who hears the word. The third soil. This person goes further. The word takes root and grows.

But the cares of the world. “Cares” is the same word as anxiety in 6:25–34. Worries about life: money, health, family, work, the future. Not open sin, but ordinary preoccupations that crowd out God.

And the deceitfulness of riches. Wealth deceives: it promises security, satisfaction and happiness, and does not deliver (6:19–24; 1 Timothy 6:9–10). It makes people feel they do not need God. Mark adds “the desires for other things” (Mark 4:19).

Choke the word, and it proves unfruitful. The plant survives but bears no fruit. This person may stay in church for years, but their life shows no real fruit, because worry and wealth have crowded out the word.

What it does not mean. Not that true believers can lose their salvation. The rocky and thorny soils describe people who appeared to receive the word but never truly did. Their faith was never rooted (1 John 2:19). Jesus’ point is that a real response is shown by perseverance and fruit. Nor does it mean that every Christian who worries or has money is thorny ground. The danger is when these things choke the word, so that it bears no fruit.

In a sentence. Shallow hearers fall away when trouble comes, and preoccupied hearers let worry and wealth choke the word until it bears no fruit.

On a Tuesday. What thorns are growing in your life: anxieties, the pursuit of money, distractions? Root them out, so the word can bear fruit.

verseByVerse.quote: As for what was sown on good soil, this is the one who hears the word and understands it. He indeed bears fruit and yields, in one case a hundredfold, in another sixty, and in another thirty."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The good soil is the one who hears the word and understands it. That person bears fruit: a hundred, sixty or thirty times what was sown.

As for what was sown on good soil, this is the one who hears the word and understands it. Understanding here means grasping the word with the heart, receiving it deeply. Luke says: holding it fast in an honest and good heart, and bearing fruit with patience (Luke 8:15). The good soil hears, understands, holds fast, and endures.

He indeed bears fruit and yields, in one case a hundredfold, in another sixty, and in another thirty. Fruit is the mark of the good soil: a changed life, the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23), good works (Ephesians 2:10), and other people brought to Christ. The amounts differ, but all good soil bears fruit.

Where does good soil come from? Not from our own efforts. Every heart by nature is hard like the path (Ephesians 2:1–3). God must make the soil good: he gives a new heart (Ezekiel 36:26), opens hearts to listen (Acts 16:14), and gives the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6–7). But we are called to receive the word humbly (James 1:21) and to guard our hearts.

The lessons of the parable. For hearers: test what kind of soil you are, and pray for a receptive heart. For preachers and witnesses: do not be discouraged when many do not respond. The sower sows widely, knowing that much seed will be lost, but trusting that some will fall on good soil and produce a great harvest. The problem is never the seed.

What it does not mean. Not that the parable divides people into four fixed types for ever. By God’s grace, hard ground can be broken, and rocky soil can be deepened. Nor does it mean that fruitful Christians are better than others. All fruit is God’s work (John 15:5).

In a sentence. The good soil hears and understands the word, holds it fast, and bears an abundant harvest of fruit.

On a Tuesday. Pray today: Lord, make my heart good soil for your word. And keep sowing the word, whatever response you see.

For worship. Thank God for making your heart receptive to his word.

parallels.desc: whoever abides in me bears much fruit

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–58 — Six More Parables: The Kingdom's Hidden Growth and Coming Judgment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Six parables follow the sower: the wheat and weeds (growing together until harvest), the mustard seed (tiny beginning, great growth), the leaven (invisible transformation of the whole), the hidden treasure and pearl of great price (discovering and selling everything for the kingdom), and the dragnet (mixed catch sorted at the end). Jesus then returns to Nazareth, where his neighbors take offense at him. More to notice. The weed has a name: zizania is bearded darnel, and three facts make the parable bite. It is indistinguishable from wheat until the ear forms — Jewish tradition treated it as degenerate wheat. It is poisonous, regularly fungus-infected, and the Latin temulentum means drunken because that is how a person looks who has eaten the bread. And sowing it in an enemy's field was a crime under Roman law, which means it happened often enough to legislate for. The master's refusal to weed is agriculturally exact — darnel roots interlace with wheat roots. This was the text at the centre of the donatist controversy, and Augustine answered the rigorists from it; but note the guard runs both ways, since "let both grow together" is not a ban on church discipline (18:15-17). Discipline addresses conduct and is reversible; what is forbidden is sorting by identity, which requires seeing the ear before it has formed. On the mustard seed objection — orchid seed is smaller — three answers: it was a proverb for the very small, the comparison is among seeds a farmer actually sowed ("in his field"), and this is ordinary descriptive speech, as when we say the sun rises. And the image of a great tree with birds nesting is imperial — Nebuchadnezzar's dream tree (Dan. 4:12), Ezekiel's Assyria and his cedar (Ezek. 17:23; 31:6). Jesus attaches empire-language to a garden herb. The chapter is bracketed by a door: he goes out of the house to the crowds (v. 1) and back into the house for the explanations (v. 36). "the field is the world" — not the church, and Jesus defines it explicitly. The two kinds are described by parentage, not performance, which is why sorting by inspection cannot work. The reapers are angels, and the harvest is the end of the age — the sorting is removed from human hands and from the growing season in one sentence. Note also that the weeds are gathered out of his kingdom (v. 41), so the kingdom in its present form contains what will have to be removed; and "causes of sin" is skandala, the trap-word running through 11:6, 13:21 and 13:57. The dragnet is a sagene, not a cast-net — it sweeps everything, and Levitical law (Lev. 11:9-12) meant a Jewish crew sorted catch into permitted and forbidden every working day. And v. 52's scribe trained for the kingdom is very probably Matthew's self-portrait: the evangelist who quotes the Old Testament some sixty times, structures his book in five discourses, and alone records this saying.
verseByVerse.theology: The parables of growth — mustard seed and leaven — correct the disciples' expectation that the kingdom would arrive with obvious power and immediate separation of righteous from wicked. The kingdom begins invisibly, grows slowly, works from within, and will only be sorted at the harvest. The "already-not-yet" structure of the kingdom is the key: it is genuinely present now (the treasure is in the field; the leaven is in the dough) but not yet fully revealed (the harvest is coming). Patience and trust in the hidden growth are the kingdom virtues these parables require.
verseByVerse.examples: The two treasure parables (hidden treasure, pearl) express the supreme value of the kingdom: it is worth selling everything to obtain. The joy of the man who finds the treasure is the joy of someone who has found what makes every other thing trivially small by comparison. This is the experience of genuine conversion — not reluctant sacrifice but joyful exchange, because the thing found is worth infinitely more than everything surrendered. The kingdom is not burdensome; it is the treasure that makes all other burdens light.

verseByVerse.quote: He put another parable before them, saying, "The kingdom of heaven may be compared to a man who sowed good seed in his field, but while his men were sleeping, his enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat and went away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus told another parable. The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field. But while everyone was asleep, his enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat, and went away.

He put another parable before them. The second of seven parables in this chapter.

The kingdom of heaven may be compared to a man who sowed good seed in his field. “May be compared” means: this is what the kingdom is like, in this respect. The man is the Son of Man (v. 37).

But while his men were sleeping. At night, when no one could see.

His enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat and went away. The weeds are probably darnel (zizania), a poisonous ryegrass that looks almost identical to wheat in its early stages. Only when the heads form can they be told apart. Darnel often carries a fungus that is toxic to humans. Roman law had penalties for sowing darnel in someone else’s field as an act of revenge: this was a real crime.

What it does not mean. Not that God is careless or that evil happened without his permission. The sleeping servants simply mean it happened secretly. Jesus explains the meaning in verses 36–43.

In a sentence. In a second parable, an enemy secretly sowed poisonous weeds among a man’s good wheat.

On a Tuesday. Evil is real, and it often works secretly. Stay alert.
verseByVerse.note: The weeds are probably darnel, a poisonous grass that looks like wheat until the heads form.

verseByVerse.quote: So when the plants came up and bore grain, then the weeds appeared also. And the servants of the master of the house came and said to him, "Master, did you not sow good seed in your field? How then does it have weeds?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the wheat grew and formed heads, the weeds appeared too. The servants asked their master: didn’t you sow good seed? Where did the weeds come from?

So when the plants came up and bore grain, then the weeds appeared also. At first, darnel and wheat look the same. The difference becomes visible only when they bear grain.

Sir, did you not sow good seed in your field? The servants know their master sowed only good seed.

How then does it have weeds? The ancient question: if God is good and his work is good, where does evil come from?

In a sentence. As the crop matured, the weeds became visible, and the servants asked where they had come from.

On a Tuesday. When you see evil in the world, or even in the church, you are not the first to ask “where did this come from?”.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "An enemy has done this." So the servants said to him, "Then do you want us to go and gather them?" But he said, "No, lest in gathering the weeds you root up the wheat along with them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The master said: an enemy has done this. The servants asked whether they should go and pull up the weeds. He said no: in pulling up the weeds you might uproot the wheat with them.

An enemy has done this. Evil is not God’s work. It is the work of an enemy, the devil (v. 39).

Then do you want us to go and gather them? The servants want to remove the weeds immediately.

No, lest in gathering the weeds you root up the wheat along with them. The roots of wheat and darnel would be intertwined. Pulling up the weeds would damage the wheat. And at this stage, the servants might mistake wheat for weeds.

What it does not mean. Not that the church should never exercise discipline over its members. Jesus himself commands church discipline (18:15–20), and Paul tells the Corinthians to remove a man living in open sin (1 Corinthians 5). In Jesus’ explanation, the field is the world (v. 38), not the church. The point is that God’s people must not try to remove all evil from the world by force before the judgment. That task belongs to God at the end.

In a sentence. The master forbids pulling up the weeds now, because the wheat would be damaged with them.

On a Tuesday. Be patient with a world where good and evil grow together. God will sort it out in his time, without any mistakes.

parallels.desc: do not pronounce judgment before the time

verseByVerse.quote: Let both grow together until the harvest, and at harvest time I will tell the reapers, "Gather the weeds first and bind them in bundles to be burned, but gather the wheat into my barn." He put another parable before them, saying, "The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his field."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let both grow together until the harvest. Then I will tell the reapers to gather the weeds first and bind them in bundles to be burned, and gather the wheat into my barn. Then Jesus told another parable: the kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed planted in a field.

Let both grow together until the harvest. Good and evil will exist side by side in the world until the end of the age (v. 39).

And at harvest time I will tell the reapers. The reapers are the angels (v. 39).

Gather the weeds first and bind them in bundles to be burned. Dried darnel was used as fuel. The weeds’ end is fire: judgment.

But gather the wheat into my barn. The wheat, God’s people, are gathered safely into his kingdom (3:12).

He put another parable before them, saying, “The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his field.” The third parable begins. The mustard seed is explained in the next entry.

What it does not mean. Not that the wicked and the righteous are indistinguishable for ever, or that God is indifferent to evil. The delay is mercy, giving time for repentance (2 Peter 3:9), and it ends in a sure judgment.

In a sentence. Good and evil will grow together until the harvest, when the weeds will be burned and the wheat gathered into God’s barn.

On a Tuesday. The delay of judgment is a time of mercy. Use it to pray for and witness to those who do not yet know Christ.

parallels.desc: the wheat gathered, the chaff burned

verseByVerse.quote: "It is the smallest of all seeds, but when it has grown it is larger than all the garden plants and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and make nests in its branches." He told them another parable. "The kingdom of heaven is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, till it was all leavened."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mustard seed is the smallest of seeds, but it grows into the largest of garden plants, a tree in which birds come and nest. The kingdom is also like yeast that a woman mixed into a large amount of flour until all of it was leavened.

It is the smallest of all seeds. The black mustard seed was proverbially tiny, about a millimetre across. Jews spoke of something “as small as a mustard seed” (17:20). It was the smallest seed farmers in Galilee commonly sowed, though not the smallest seed in the world. Jesus speaks as people spoke.

But when it has grown it is larger than all the garden plants and becomes a tree. The mustard plant grew in one season up to three metres high (ten feet), large enough to look like a tree.

So that the birds of the air come and make nests in its branches. In the Old Testament, a great tree with birds in its branches pictures a great kingdom that shelters the nations (Daniel 4:10–12, 20–22; Ezekiel 17:23; 31:6). The kingdom of God, though it starts small, will become great and shelter people from all nations.

The meaning. The kingdom began in an obscure way: a carpenter from Nazareth, twelve ordinary disciples, rejected by the leaders. It looked insignificant. Yet it would grow into a worldwide kingdom. Today the church is found in nearly every nation.

He told them another parable. “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven.” Leaven was a lump of old, fermented dough kept from the previous batch and mixed into new flour to make it rise, like yeast.

That a woman took and hid in three measures of flour. Three measures (sata) was about forty litres of flour, enough to make bread for about a hundred people. Sarah used the same amount when baking for the Lord’s visit (Genesis 18:6). “Hid” is the word used: the leaven disappears into the dough.

Till it was all leavened. The leaven works quietly, invisibly, from within, until it has permeated everything.

The two parables together. The mustard seed shows the kingdom’s outward growth: from small beginnings to great size. The leaven shows its inward growth: quiet, hidden, pervasive transformation from within.

What it does not mean. Leaven in Scripture often pictures evil (16:6; 1 Corinthians 5:6–8), so some interpret this parable as evil corrupting the church. But here Jesus says the kingdom of heaven is like leaven; the point is its spreading power, not its moral quality. Nor does the parable promise that the whole world will become Christian before Christ returns. Postmillennialists read it that way: the gospel will gradually Christianise the world, leading to a golden age before Christ’s return. Amillennialists see the parables as describing the kingdom’s sure growth through the whole gospel age, alongside continuing evil (the weeds), until the harvest at Christ’s return. Verdict: amillennial. The kingdom will grow powerfully among all nations, but good and evil grow together until the end.

In a sentence. The kingdom starts small but grows into a great tree that shelters the nations, and works quietly from within like yeast until it permeates everything.

On a Tuesday. Do not despise small beginnings: a small Bible study, a single conversation, a little act of faithfulness. God’s kingdom grows from mustard seeds.
verseByVerse.note: Mustard seed was proverbially tiny; the plant can grow taller than a man. Three measures of flour is a very large batch — about what Sarah baked for her three guests.

parallels.desc: birds nest in the cedar’s branches

verseByVerse.quote: All these things Jesus said to the crowds in parables; indeed, he said nothing to them without a parable. This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet: "I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter what has been hidden since the foundation of the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus taught the crowds in parables, and said nothing to them without a parable. This fulfilled the words of the psalm: I will open my mouth in parables; I will declare what has been hidden since the foundation of the world.

All these things Jesus said to the crowds in parables; indeed, he said nothing to them without a parable. At this stage, Jesus taught the crowds only in parables, explaining them privately to his disciples (Mark 4:33–34).

This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet. Psalm 78:2. The psalm was written by Asaph, who is called a seer (2 Chronicles 29:30), which is why Matthew calls him a prophet.

I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter what has been hidden since the foundation of the world. In Psalm 78, Asaph retells Israel’s history as a lesson, revealing its meaning: God’s faithfulness and Israel’s unfaithfulness. Jesus is the greater teacher who reveals God’s purposes, hidden from the beginning and now made known in the kingdom.

What it does not mean. Not that the psalm was a direct prediction about Jesus. Matthew sees a pattern: as Asaph used parables to reveal hidden truth, so Jesus fulfils and surpasses him.

In a sentence. Jesus taught the crowds in parables, fulfilling the psalm’s picture of one who reveals what has been hidden from the beginning.

On a Tuesday. God’s purposes are not random. What has been hidden from the foundation of the world is now revealed in Christ. Seek to understand it.
verseByVerse.note: The psalm’s author, Asaph, is called a seer in Chronicles; Matthew calls him “the prophet.”

parallels.desc: I will open my mouth in a parable

verseByVerse.quote: Then he left the crowds and went into the house. And his disciples came to him, saying, "Explain to us the parable of the weeds of the field." He answered, "The one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus left the crowds and went into the house. His disciples asked him to explain the parable of the weeds. He said: the one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man.

Then he left the crowds and went into the house. Away from the crowds, to teach his disciples privately.

Explain to us the parable of the weeds of the field. The disciples asked, and Jesus answered. Those who seek understanding receive it (v. 12).

The one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man. Jesus himself (see 8:20). He is the sower of the kingdom.

In a sentence. The disciples asked Jesus to explain the parable of the weeds, and he began by identifying the sower as himself.

On a Tuesday. When you do not understand something in Scripture, ask the Lord, and keep seeking.

verseByVerse.quote: the field is the world, and the good seed is the sons of the kingdom. The weeds are the sons of the evil one, and the enemy who sowed them is the devil. The harvest is the end of the age, and the reapers are angels.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The field is the world. The good seed is the people of the kingdom. The weeds are the people of the evil one. The enemy who sowed them is the devil. The harvest is the end of the age, and the reapers are angels.

The field is the world. Not the church, but the whole world. This is important for interpretation (see v. 29).

And the good seed is the sons of the kingdom. True believers, God’s people. In 8:12, “sons of the kingdom” referred to those who seemed to be heirs but were excluded; here it refers to the true heirs.

The weeds are the sons of the evil one. Those who belong to Satan, sharing his character (John 8:44; 1 John 3:10).

And the enemy who sowed them is the devil. Satan works in the world to oppose God’s kingdom, planting his own people among God’s.

The harvest is the end of the age. The end of the present world, at Christ’s return (24:3; 28:20).

And the reapers are angels. Angels will gather people for judgment (24:31; 25:31).

What it does not mean. Not that people are born as wheat or weeds and cannot change. Paul was a persecutor and became an apostle. The parable describes the state of the world at the harvest, not a fixed destiny regardless of response. Nor does it teach that the devil creates people. He sows them in the sense of influencing them and placing them to oppose God’s work.

In a sentence. In the world, the Son of Man’s people and the devil’s people grow together until the angels gather them at the end of the age.

On a Tuesday. The world is a mixed field. Do not be surprised by evil around you, and do not lose heart: the harvest is coming.

parallels.desc: put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe

verseByVerse.quote: Just as the weeds are gathered and burned with fire, so will it be at the end of the age. The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all causes of sin and all law-breakers,
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the weeds are gathered and burned, so it will be at the end of the age. The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom everything that causes sin and all who do evil.

Just as the weeds are gathered and burned with fire, so will it be at the end of the age. The certainty of judgment.

The Son of Man will send his angels. Jesus is the Judge, and the angels are his (16:27; 24:31). He who now sows will then reap.

And they will gather out of his kingdom. Christ’s kingdom now extends over the whole world (28:18), though not all acknowledge it. At the end, everything that opposes him will be removed from his realm.

All causes of sin. Literally “all stumbling blocks” (skandala): everything that leads people into sin.

And all law-breakers. Those who live in lawlessness (see 7:23).

In a sentence. At the end of the age, Christ’s angels will remove from his kingdom everything that causes sin and everyone who does evil.

On a Tuesday. One day, every cause of sin will be removed. Long for that day, and begin now to remove the stumbling blocks in your own life.

parallels.desc: I will sweep away the stumbling blocks
he will send out his angels

verseByVerse.quote: and throw them into the fiery furnace. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. He who has ears, let him hear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The evildoers will be thrown into the fiery furnace, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Then the righteous will shine like the sun in their Father’s kingdom. Whoever has ears, let them hear.

And throw them into the fiery furnace. A picture of hell (Daniel 3:6; Revelation 20:15). Fire is a picture of God’s holy judgment.

In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Grief and anguish (see 8:12).

Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. From Daniel 12:3: those who are wise shall shine like the brightness of the sky. The righteous, freed from all sin, will be glorified, reflecting God’s glory (Philippians 3:21; 1 John 3:2). Jesus shone like the sun at the transfiguration (17:2); his people will share his glory.

He who has ears, let him hear. A call to take this seriously (see v. 9).

What it does not mean. Not that “the righteous” are those who earned righteousness by their works. They are those made righteous by God’s grace in Christ (5:6; Romans 3:22–24). Nor is hell a mere metaphor without reality. The pictures (fire, darkness, weeping) describe a real, terrible condition of separation from God (see 3:12; 25:46).

In a sentence. The wicked will be thrown into the fire of judgment, and the righteous will shine like the sun in their Father’s kingdom.

For worship. Thank God for the glory he has promised his people, to shine like the sun in his kingdom.

parallels.desc: the wise shall shine like the brightness of the sky

verseByVerse.quote: The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field, which a man found and covered up. Then in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field. Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant in search of fine pearls,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field. A man found it, hid it again, and in his joy sold everything he had and bought that field. It is also like a merchant searching for fine pearls.

The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field. In a world without banks, people often buried valuables in the ground for safekeeping, especially in times of war. Sometimes the owner died, and the treasure was forgotten.

Which a man found and covered up. Perhaps a labourer ploughing someone else’s field stumbled on it by accident.

Then in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field. The key word is joy. He does not sell everything grudgingly, as a painful sacrifice, but gladly, because the treasure is worth far more than everything he owns. Selling everything feels like nothing compared to what he gains.
