Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant in search of fine pearls. Pearls were among the most valuable things in the ancient world, more valuable than gold. A merchant dealing in pearls would search far and wide for the best ones.

The two parables. The treasure is found by accident; the pearl is found after searching. Some people stumble on the kingdom unexpectedly; others search for it for years. Either way, when they find it, they give up everything for it with joy.

What it does not mean. Not that we can buy the kingdom by giving up our possessions. The kingdom is God’s gift (5:3). The parables show the worth of the kingdom and the response it calls for: giving up everything to have it. Nor is Jesus commenting on the ethics of hiding the treasure from the field’s owner. Under Jewish law, treasure found in a field might belong to the finder. The parable is about the value of the kingdom, not about property law.

In a sentence. The kingdom is worth more than everything we have, and those who find it give up everything for it with joy.

On a Tuesday. Does following Christ feel like a sacrifice, or like a treasure? Ask God to show you the worth of what you have in him.
verseByVerse.note: With no banks, people commonly buried valuables in the ground. Pearls were among the most prized luxuries of the ancient world.

parallels.desc: counting everything as loss for Christ

verseByVerse.quote: who, on finding one pearl of great value, went and sold all that he had and bought it. Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net that was thrown into the sea and gathered fish of every kind,
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the merchant found one pearl of great value, he went and sold everything he had and bought it. The kingdom is also like a net thrown into the sea, which caught fish of every kind.

Who, on finding one pearl of great value. One pearl, worth more than all his others.

Went and sold all that he had and bought it. As with the treasure. The kingdom is worth everything.

Christ the pearl. Many have seen Christ himself as the pearl of great value, worth giving up all for (Philippians 3:7–8). Paul counted everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus. To have the kingdom is to have the King.

Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net that was thrown into the sea. A dragnet (sagēnē): a long net with floats on top and weights at the bottom, drawn between two boats or pulled to shore, catching everything in its path.

And gathered fish of every kind. Good and bad, clean and unclean.

In a sentence. The merchant gave up everything for one priceless pearl, and the kingdom is also like a net that gathers every kind of fish.

On a Tuesday. Is Christ your pearl of great value? What would you be unwilling to give up for him?
verseByVerse.note: A dragnet was drawn between boats or to shore, catching everything in its path.

verseByVerse.quote: When it was full, men drew it ashore and sat down and sorted the good into containers but threw away the bad. So it will be at the end of the age. The angels will come out and separate the evil from the righteous
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the net was full, the fishermen pulled it ashore, sat down, and sorted the good fish into baskets and threw away the bad. So it will be at the end of the age: the angels will come and separate the evil from the righteous.

When it was full, men drew it ashore. The net gathers until it is full.

And sat down and sorted the good into containers but threw away the bad. Under the law, fish without fins and scales were unclean and could not be eaten or sold (Leviticus 11:9–12). Other fish were simply worthless. Sorting was a careful, final process.

So it will be at the end of the age. The same lesson as the weeds: the final separation (vv. 40–43).

The angels will come out and separate the evil from the righteous. The angels, not human beings, will do the sorting. Only God can judge the heart perfectly.

What it does not mean. Not that we should be careless about who is in the church. But the net gathers all kinds through the preaching of the gospel; final separation belongs to God.

In a sentence. Like fishermen sorting their catch, the angels will separate the evil from the righteous at the end of the age.

On a Tuesday. The gospel net catches all kinds of people. Cast it widely, and leave the final sorting to God.
verseByVerse.note: Fish without fins and scales were unclean under the law and could not be sold as food.

verseByVerse.quote: and throw them into the fiery furnace. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Have you understood all these things?" They said to him, "Yes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The evil will be thrown into the fiery furnace, with weeping and gnashing of teeth. Jesus asked his disciples: have you understood all these things? They said yes.

And throw them into the fiery furnace. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. The same words as verse 42. Jesus repeats the warning: the judgment is real and terrible.

Have you understood all these things? Understanding is the mark of good soil (v. 23). Jesus checks that they have grasped his teaching.

They said to him, “Yes.” Their understanding was real, though still limited. They would later misunderstand much (16:9–11). But they had grasped the main lessons of the kingdom.

In a sentence. After repeating the warning of judgment, Jesus asked whether the disciples had understood, and they said yes.

On a Tuesday. If Jesus asked you whether you have understood his teaching, what would you say? Keep studying until you can say yes.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Therefore every scribe who has been trained for the kingdom of heaven is like a master of a house who brings out of his treasure what is new and what is old." And when Jesus had finished these parables, he went away from there,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every teacher of the law who has become a disciple of the kingdom of heaven is like the owner of a house who brings out of his storeroom new treasures as well as old. When Jesus had finished these parables, he moved on.

Therefore every scribe who has been trained for the kingdom of heaven. A “scribe” was a teacher of the law (see 2:4). A scribe “trained for the kingdom” (literally “discipled”) is one who has become Jesus’ disciple. Matthew himself may have been such a scribe, as his Gospel combines the Old Testament with Jesus’ teaching.

Is like a master of a house, who brings out of his treasure what is new and what is old. “Treasure” means storeroom. The old treasures are the Old Testament: the law, the prophets and the promises. The new treasures are the teaching of Jesus and the gospel of the kingdom. A good teacher uses both, showing how the new fulfils the old (5:17). Augustine summed it up: the New Testament is concealed in the Old, and the Old is revealed in the New.

And when Jesus had finished these parables, he went away from there. The formula ending the third great discourse (see 7:28).

What it does not mean. Not that the new replaces the old entirely, nor that the old is enough without the new. Both are needed, understood together.

In a sentence. A disciple trained in the kingdom brings out both the old treasures of the Old Testament and the new treasures of Jesus’ teaching.

On a Tuesday. Read both Testaments. When you read the Old, look for Christ; when you read the New, look for the Old Testament roots.

parallels.desc: not to abolish but to fulfil

verseByVerse.quote: and coming to his hometown he taught them in their synagogue, so that they were astonished, and said, "Where did this man get this wisdom and these mighty works? Is not this the carpenter's son? Is not his mother called Mary? And are not his brothers James and Joseph and Simon and Judas?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus came to his hometown, Nazareth, and taught in their synagogue. The people were astonished: where did this man get this wisdom and these miracles? Isn’t he the carpenter’s son? Isn’t his mother Mary, and his brothers James, Joseph, Simon and Judas?

And coming to his hometown. Nazareth, where he grew up (2:23).

He taught them in their synagogue. On the Sabbath. Luke records a similar visit, perhaps the same one (Luke 4:16–30).

So that they were astonished. At his wisdom and power.

Where did this man get this wisdom and these mighty works? A fair question, with an answer they would not accept: from God.

Is not this the carpenter’s son? “Carpenter” (tektōn) means a builder or craftsman in wood or stone. Mark calls Jesus himself “the carpenter” (Mark 6:3). They knew him as a manual worker, who had built their houses and fixed their ploughs. How could an ordinary tradesman have such wisdom? They had no category for the incarnation: God in an ordinary man.

Is not his mother called Mary? They knew his family well.

And are not his brothers James and Joseph and Simon and Judas? Jesus’ brothers, most naturally Mary’s later children (see 1:25). James later led the Jerusalem church and wrote the letter of James; Judas (Jude) wrote the letter of Jude.

What it does not mean. Not that there was anything shameful about Jesus’ ordinary background. The Son of God worked with his hands for years, dignifying all honest labour. The problem was that familiarity bred contempt.

In a sentence. The people of Nazareth were astonished at Jesus’ wisdom and miracles, but could not accept that the carpenter they knew could be more than he seemed.

On a Tuesday. Familiarity can blind us to Jesus. Have you grown so used to the stories that they no longer astonish you?
verseByVerse.note: “Carpenter” is a general word for a builder or craftsman in wood or stone.

parallels.desc: “Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph?”

verseByVerse.quote: And are not all his sisters with us? Where then did this man get all these things?" And they took offense at him. But Jesus said to them, "A prophet is not without honor except in his hometown and in his own household."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Aren’t all his sisters here with us? Where did he get all this? They took offence at him. Jesus said: a prophet is not without honour except in his hometown and in his own household.

And are not all his sisters with us? Jesus had sisters too, unnamed. “All” suggests at least two, perhaps more. Jesus grew up in a large family.

Where then did this man get all these things? They cannot explain him, and will not accept the explanation.

And they took offense at him. “Took offence” (eskandalizonto) means stumbled over him (see 11:6). He did not fit their expectations. They knew his family, his job and his ordinary life; they could not believe he was the Messiah.

But Jesus said to them, “A prophet is not without honor except in his hometown and in his own household.” A proverb. People find it hardest to accept greatness in someone they grew up with. Even Jesus’ own brothers did not yet believe (John 7:5).

In a sentence. His hometown took offence at Jesus because they knew him and his family too well to believe.

On a Tuesday. If your family or old friends find it hard to take your faith seriously, Jesus understands. Keep living faithfully among them.

parallels.desc: his own people did not receive him

verseByVerse.quote: And he did not do many mighty works there, because of their unbelief.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus did not do many miracles there, because of their unbelief.

And he did not do many mighty works there. Mark says he could do no mighty work there, except heal a few sick people (Mark 6:5).

Because of their unbelief. Not because Jesus’ power was limited by their unbelief, as if he were helpless. Rather, miracles were signs meant to call people to faith; where people refused to believe, signs had no purpose. Jesus would not perform for sceptics (12:39). And unbelief closes the door to what God offers. Mark adds that Jesus marvelled at their unbelief (Mark 6:6).

The end of the chapter. The chapter of parables ends with a living example of the hard soil: the people who knew Jesus best did not receive him.

What it does not mean. Not that faith is a power that makes God act, or that a lack of miracles always shows a lack of faith. God is sovereign in what he does (Romans 9:15–18). But faith receives what God gives, and unbelief refuses it.

In a sentence. Because of their unbelief, Jesus did few miracles in his hometown.

On a Tuesday. Unbelief shuts out blessing. Ask God to replace your doubts with trust.

13.theology: The hiddenness and growth of the kingdom. The parables of Matthew 13 develop a theology of the kingdom that runs against both triumphalism and despair. Against triumphalism: the kingdom grows secretly, like leaven, not by worldly power or coercion. Against despair: the smallest seed becomes the largest tree; the handful of leavened dough leavens the whole batch. The kingdom’s smallness is not its failure but its method. Reformed theology has always insisted that the church advances through the ordinary means of grace — word, sacrament, prayer — not through political power or cultural dominance. The harvest will be glorious; the sowing is patient.
13.examples:
Then: The disciples were living through the mustard-seed phase of the kingdom. From their vantage point, a small band of Galileans following a rabbi who was being plotted against by the religious establishment, the kingdom’s glory was not obvious. Jesus tells them: do not judge the end by the beginning.

Now: Every era of church history has felt like the mustard-seed phase. Persecution, secularisation, nominalism — all seem to contradict the kingdom’s advance. The parables of Matthew 13 are the antidote to both despair and triumphalism. The Sower keeps sowing. The leaven keeps working. The net keeps gathering. The harvest belongs to the Lord.

14.title: Bread in the Wilderness
14.text: <sup>1</sup>At that time Herod the tetrarch heard about the fame of Jesus, <sup>2</sup>and he said to his servants, “This is John the Baptist. He has been raised from the dead; that is why these miraculous powers are at work in him.” <sup>3</sup>For Herod had seized John and bound him and put him in prison for the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife, <sup>4</sup>because John had been saying to him, “It is not lawful for you to have her.” <sup>5</sup>And though he wanted to put him to death, he feared the people, because they held him to be a prophet. <sup>6</sup>But when Herod’s birthday came, the daughter of Herodias danced before the company and pleased Herod, <sup>7</sup>so that he promised with an oath to give her whatever she might ask. <sup>8</sup>Prompted by her mother, she said, “Give me the head of John the Baptist here on a platter.” <sup>9</sup>And the king was sorry, but because of his oaths and his guests he commanded it to be given. <sup>10</sup>He sent and had John beheaded in the prison, <sup>11</sup>and his head was brought on a platter and given to the girl, and she brought it to her mother. <sup>12</sup>And his disciples came and took the body and buried it, and they went and told Jesus. <sup>13</sup>Now when Jesus heard this, he withdrew from there in a boat to a desolate place by himself. But when the crowds heard it, they followed him on foot from the towns. <sup>14</sup>When he went ashore he saw a great crowd, and he had compassion on them and healed their sick. <sup>15</sup>Now when it was evening, the disciples came to him and said, “This is a desolate place, and the day is now over; send the crowds away to go into the villages and buy food for themselves.” <sup>16</sup>But Jesus said, “They need not go away; you give them something to eat.” <sup>17</sup>They said to him, “We have only five loaves here and two fish.” <sup>18</sup>And he said, “Bring them here to me.” <sup>19</sup>Then he ordered the crowds to sit down on the grass, and taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing. Then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds. <sup>20</sup>And they all ate and were satisfied. And they took up twelve baskets full of the broken pieces left over. <sup>21</sup>And those who ate were about five thousand men, besides women and children. <sup>22</sup>Immediately he made the disciples get into the boat and go before him to the other side, while he dismissed the crowds. <sup>23</sup>And after he had dismissed the crowds, he went up on the mountain by himself to pray. When evening came, he was there alone, <sup>24</sup>but the boat by this time was a long way from the land, beaten by the waves, for the wind was against them. <sup>25</sup>And in the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea. <sup>26</sup>But when the disciples saw him walking on the sea, they were terrified, and said, “It is a ghost!” and they cried out in fear. <sup>27</sup>But immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying, “Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid.” <sup>28</sup>And Peter answered him, “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the water.” <sup>29</sup>He said, “Come.” So Peter got out of the boat and walked on the water and came to Jesus. <sup>30</sup>But when he saw the wind, he was afraid, and beginning to sink he cried out, “Lord, save me.” <sup>31</sup>Jesus immediately reached out his hand and took hold of him, saying to him, “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” <sup>32</sup>And when they got into the boat, the wind ceased. <sup>33</sup>And those in the boat worshiped him, saying, “Truly you are the Son of God.” <sup>34</sup>And when they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret. <sup>35</sup>And when the men of that place recognized him, they sent around to all that region and brought to him all who were sick <sup>36</sup>and implored him that they might only touch the fringe of his garment. And as many as touched it were made well.
14.overview:
Chapter 14 moves from Herod’s banquet of death (John’s head on a platter) to Jesus’ banquet of life (five thousand fed in the wilderness). The contrast is deliberate. Herod’s table is supplied by cruelty, vanity, and the murder of a prophet. Jesus’ table is supplied by compassion, prayer, and the creative power of the Creator multiplying what is surrendered to him. John’s death is the herald’s fate; Jesus will face his own; but the meals he gives point beyond death to the resurrection feast.

The feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle recorded in all four Gospels (besides the resurrection). Matthew frames it with Exodus typology: a desolate place (wilderness), manna-like provision, the Shepherd feeding his people. Jesus looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks, and gives — the same fourfold action he will perform at the Last Supper. Every Lord’s Supper echoes this meal. The chapter closes with Peter walking on water — and sinking. The disciples worship: “Truly you are the Son of God.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — The Death of John and the Feeding of the Five Thousand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Herod Antipas hears of Jesus and fears John has risen from the dead. Matthew then narrates the death of John the Baptist — arrested for condemning Herod's marriage to his brother's wife, beheaded to fulfill a rash oath at a banquet. Jesus withdraws on hearing the news, but the crowds follow him. He heals them and then feeds five thousand men from five loaves and two fish. The feeding is the great Eucharistic sign, anticipating the Last Supper and the heavenly banquet. What the summary cannot hold. Herod is a tetrarch, not a king — Herod the Great's realm was quartered at his death and this son got Galilee and Perea. He wanted the higher title, went to Rome to ask for it, and was exiled for his trouble. He came to power soon after the nativity and was still in power at the crucifixion, and Luke has Pilate send Jesus to him during the trial (Lk. 23:12). His explanation is theologically bizarre: nobody in Judaism expected an individual to be raised in the middle of history, so "this is John, he has been raised" is not a belief he is reaching for — he has invented it on the spot, and said it to his servants, the people who had watched the platter come in. On the geography, Josephus names the prison: Machaerus, a fortress-palace east of the Dead Sea with luxurious apartments above and cells below — so the banquet and the dungeon were in the same building. He also names the girl: Salome. And Matthew calls her a korasion, the diminutive, the same word used of Jairus's twelve-year-old (9:24-25) — a child, put up to it, who goes out to ask her mother what to say. The oath is a quotation: Mark gives it in full, "up to half my kingdom" (6:23), which is what Ahasuerus says to Esther three times, at her banquets (Est. 5:3, 6; 7:2). A drunken king, a rash promise, a woman with a prepared request, a man's life in the balance — and every element inverts. Esther's request saved a people from a murderer; this one murders a prophet. Note too that Herod and the chief priests are restrained by the same calculation, in almost identical words: both fear the crowd "because they held him to be a prophet" (14:5; 21:46). And verse 12 is the quietest sentence in the chapter — John's disciples walked into a royal fortress to ask for the body, buried what there was, and then went to the one man who had told them who John was. Matthew records no reply. The next thing Jesus does is withdraw; the next thing after that is to feed five thousand men, besides women and children. On the day he heard.
verseByVerse.theology: John's death is the dark center of the chapter: the fate of the forerunner anticipates the fate of the one he announced. Herod's fear that Jesus is John raised from the dead is simultaneously wrong (Jesus is not John) and prophetically ironic (the resurrection John could not achieve, Jesus will). The feeding of the five thousand is the messianic act par excellence: the shepherd-king who provides bread for his people in the wilderness, echoing the manna of the Exodus. Jesus takes, blesses, breaks, and gives — the fourfold action of the Last Supper.
verseByVerse.examples: The disciples' protest — "we have only five loaves here and two fish" — is the protest of faith that has not yet learned what it is living with. They are calculating from what they have; Jesus acts from who he is. "Bring them here to me" is the word for every situation where human resources fall desperately short of human need. The miracle occurs not in the disciples' hands but in his: he takes, blesses, breaks, gives — and twelve baskets remain. Twelve: one for each tribe of Israel, one for each disciple. The abundance of the kingdom always exceeds the need.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Herod the tetrarch heard about the fame of Jesus, and he said to his servants, "This is John the Baptist. He has been raised from the dead; that is why these miraculous powers are at work in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herod the ruler of Galilee heard about Jesus and said to his servants: this is John the Baptist, raised from the dead. That is why these powers are at work in him.

At that time Herod the tetrarch. Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great (2:1). When his father died in 4 BC, Rome divided the kingdom, and Antipas received Galilee and Perea (east of the Jordan). He ruled until AD 39. “Tetrarch” originally meant “ruler of a fourth part”, and came to mean a minor ruler, below a king. Jesus later called him “that fox” (Luke 13:32).

Heard about the fame of Jesus. News of Jesus’ miracles, and perhaps of the Twelve’s mission (10:1–8), had reached the palace.

This is John the Baptist. He has been raised from the dead. A guilty conscience. Herod had executed John (vv. 3–12), and now he feared that John had come back. Some people thought Jesus was Elijah or one of the prophets (16:14); Herod thought he was John. The irony: Herod’s superstitious fear came close to a truth he did not grasp. One greater than John had come, and would rise from the dead.

That is why these miraculous powers are at work in him. John did no miracles in his lifetime (John 10:41). Herod imagined a resurrected John would have new powers.

What it does not mean. Not that Herod believed in Jesus. His fear was superstition and guilt, not faith. Later he hoped to see Jesus perform a miracle, as a curiosity, and treated him with contempt (Luke 23:8–11).

In a sentence. Haunted by guilt, Herod thought Jesus was John the Baptist, whom he had executed, raised from the dead.

On a Tuesday. A guilty conscience cannot be silenced by killing the messenger. If your conscience troubles you, bring it to Christ, who forgives.
verseByVerse.note: Herod the tetrarch is Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, who ruled Galilee and Perea. A tetrarch was a ruler of part of a divided kingdom.

verseByVerse.quote: For Herod had seized John and bound him and put him in prison for the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip's wife, because John had been saying to him, "It is not lawful for you to have her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herod had arrested John, put him in chains and imprisoned him because of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife. John had told him: it is not lawful for you to have her.

For Herod had seized John and bound him and put him in prison. Matthew now goes back to explain how John died. John had been in prison since 4:12. According to Josephus, he was held at Machaerus, a fortress east of the Dead Sea.

For the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife. Herodias was the granddaughter of Herod the Great, and so the niece of both her husbands. She had married Herod’s half-brother (called Philip in the Gospels; Josephus calls him Herod). On a visit to Rome, Antipas fell in love with her; both divorced their spouses and married each other. Antipas’s first wife, the daughter of the Nabatean king Aretas, fled to her father, who later went to war with Antipas and defeated him.

Because John had been saying to him, “It is not lawful for you to have her.” “Had been saying”: repeatedly. The law forbade a man to marry his brother’s wife while the brother was alive (Leviticus 18:16; 20:21). John confronted the ruler publicly with God’s law. Like Elijah confronting Ahab and Jezebel (1 Kings 21), John stood up to a king and his wife. Josephus says Herod also feared John’s influence over the people.

What it does not mean. Not that preachers should comment on every personal sin of every politician. But John shows that God’s law applies to rulers as much as anyone, and that faithful prophets must sometimes speak hard truths to power, at personal cost.

In a sentence. John was imprisoned for telling Herod plainly that his marriage to his brother’s wife broke God’s law.

On a Tuesday. Are you willing to speak truth that may cost you, when love for God and for others requires it?
verseByVerse.note: Herodias had been married to Antipas’s half-brother; the law forbade marrying a brother’s wife while he lived.

parallels.desc: the nakedness of your brother’s wife

verseByVerse.quote: And though he wanted to put him to death, he feared the people, because they held him to be a prophet. But when Herod's birthday came, the daughter of Herodias danced before the company and pleased Herod,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herod wanted to kill John, but he feared the people, who regarded John as a prophet. But on Herod’s birthday, Herodias’ daughter danced before the guests and pleased Herod.

And though he wanted to put him to death. Mark adds that Herodias held a grudge against John and wanted him killed, while Herod feared John, knowing he was a righteous and holy man, and kept him safe; he was greatly perplexed by John, yet liked to listen to him (Mark 6:19–20). Herod’s heart was divided: he was drawn to John’s message, and resented it.

He feared the people, because they held him to be a prophet. Fear of public opinion restrained him, not conscience.

But when Herod’s birthday came. A lavish banquet for his officials, military commanders and the leading men of Galilee (Mark 6:21).

The daughter of Herodias danced before the company. Josephus names her Salome, Herodias’ daughter by her first marriage. She was probably a teenager. For a princess to dance before drunken men at a banquet was shameful; it suggests a sensual performance.

And pleased Herod. He was delighted, probably drunk, and inflamed.

In a sentence. Herod wanted John dead but feared the people, until his stepdaughter’s dance at his birthday banquet pleased him.

On a Tuesday. Herod liked to hear John but would not obey him. Listening to God’s word without obeying it leaves the heart open to disaster.
verseByVerse.note: The historian Josephus names Herodias’s daughter Salome.

verseByVerse.quote: so that he promised with an oath to give her whatever she might ask. Prompted by her mother, she said, "Give me the head of John the Baptist here on a platter."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Herod swore an oath to give her whatever she asked. Prompted by her mother, she said: give me the head of John the Baptist here on a platter.

So that he promised with an oath to give her whatever she might ask. A rash, extravagant oath, made in drunken excitement before guests. Mark adds “up to half of my kingdom” (Mark 6:23), an echo of the Persian king’s words to Esther (Esther 5:3), though Herod had no kingdom to give, only what Rome allowed. Jesus warned against casual oaths (5:33–37).

Prompted by her mother. Mark tells us she went out and asked her mother what to request (Mark 6:24). Herodias saw her chance.

She said, “Give me the head of John the Baptist here on a platter.” A horrifying request, spoken at a feast. A platter was a serving dish. John’s head would be served like a course at the banquet.

In a sentence. Herod rashly swore to give the girl anything, and at her mother’s prompting she asked for John’s head on a platter.

On a Tuesday. Rash promises made in the heat of the moment can trap us. Be slow to promise, and never let a promise bind you to sin.

parallels.desc: up to half of my kingdom

verseByVerse.quote: And the king was sorry, but because of his oaths and his guests he commanded it to be given. He sent and had John beheaded in the prison,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king was distressed, but because of his oaths and his dinner guests, he ordered it to be done. He sent and had John beheaded in prison.

And the king was sorry. Herod regretted his oath, but not enough to break it.

But because of his oaths and his guests. Two motives: his oath, and the fear of losing face before his guests. He valued his reputation more than an innocent man’s life. An oath to do evil should be broken, not kept. As the Westminster Confession says, no one may bind himself by oath to do anything sinful (22.7).

He commanded it to be given. Herod was called king by the people, but was actually a tetrarch. When he later asked Rome for the title of king, encouraged by Herodias, he was exiled instead (AD 39).

He sent and had John beheaded in the prison. John, the greatest of the prophets (11:11), the forerunner of the Messiah, was killed at a drunken party, to satisfy a vengeful woman and a weak man’s pride. He died alone in a dungeon. His death foreshadows Jesus’ own: another innocent man, killed by a ruler who knew he was innocent but feared the crowd (27:24).

What it does not mean. Not that God had abandoned John. John had finished the work God gave him: to prepare the way for Christ (3:3). From the world’s point of view his death was a tragedy; from God’s, it was the end of a faithful race. Jesus honoured him as the greatest of the old order (11:11).

In a sentence. To save face, Herod had John beheaded, though he knew it was wrong.

On a Tuesday. Fear of losing face leads people to terrible choices. Be willing to admit a wrong promise or decision publicly rather than compound it.
verseByVerse.note: Antipas was only a tetrarch, but was popularly called king.

verseByVerse.quote: and his head was brought on a platter and given to the girl, and she brought it to her mother. And his disciples came and took the body and buried it, and they went and told Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John’s head was brought on a platter and given to the girl, who brought it to her mother. John’s disciples came, took his body and buried it. Then they went and told Jesus.

And his head was brought on a platter and given to the girl, and she brought it to her mother. The horror is told plainly, without comment. Evil in power can be grotesque.

And his disciples came and took the body and buried it. A final act of love and loyalty. Proper burial was very important in Jewish culture.

And they went and told Jesus. They brought their grief to Jesus. Some of John’s disciples had already followed Jesus (John 1:35–37); now the rest came to him.

What it does not mean. Not that God was absent. His purposes went on. The worst the world could do did not stop the kingdom.

In a sentence. John’s disciples buried his body and brought the news to Jesus.

On a Tuesday. When you are grieving or shocked by evil, do what John’s disciples did: tell Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus heard this, he withdrew from there in a boat to a desolate place by himself. But when the crowds heard it, they followed him on foot from the towns. When he went ashore he saw a great crowd, and he had compassion on them and healed their sick.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus heard the news, he withdrew by boat to a remote place to be alone. But the crowds heard and followed him on foot from the towns. When Jesus landed and saw the great crowd, he had compassion on them and healed their sick.

Now when Jesus heard this. The death of John: his relative, his forerunner, the man who baptised him.

He withdrew from there in a boat to a desolate place by himself. To grieve, to pray, and perhaps to avoid Herod’s attention (Mark 6:31 also mentions the need for rest after the Twelve’s mission). Jesus was truly human. He needed solitude and grief. Luke places the feeding near Bethsaida (Luke 9:10), on the northeast shore of the lake.

But when the crowds heard it, they followed him on foot from the towns. They walked around the shore and arrived before him (Mark 6:33).

When he went ashore he saw a great crowd. His time alone was interrupted.

And he had compassion on them. Deep, gut-level compassion (see 9:36). In his own grief, Jesus did not turn the crowds away in irritation. He saw their need, and his heart went out to them.

And healed their sick. Compassion in action.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus never rested or that we must never protect our time. Jesus often withdrew to pray (14:23; Mark 1:35). Rest is necessary. But when he was interrupted by real need, he responded with compassion, not resentment.

In a sentence. Grieving John’s death, Jesus sought solitude, but when the crowds found him, he had compassion and healed them.

On a Tuesday. How do you respond to interruptions, especially when you are tired or sad? Ask God for Jesus’ compassion.
verseByVerse.note: Luke places the feeding near Bethsaida, at the north end of the lake.

parallels.desc: not as sheep without a shepherd

verseByVerse.quote: Now when it was evening, the disciples came to him and said, "This is a desolate place, and the day is now over; send the crowds away to go into the villages and buy food for themselves." But Jesus said, "They need not go away; you give them something to eat."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the evening, the disciples came to Jesus: this is a remote place, and it is getting late. Send the crowds away so they can go to the villages and buy food. Jesus answered: they do not need to go away. You give them something to eat.

Now when it was evening. Late afternoon, as the light was fading.

This is a desolate place. “Desolate” (erēmos) means wilderness, the same word used of the wilderness where Israel wandered (see 3:1). The setting recalls Israel in the desert, where God fed them with manna (Exodus 16).

And the day is now over; send the crowds away to go into the villages and buy food for themselves. A sensible, practical suggestion. The disciples saw the problem, but not the solution. They thought the crowd was not their responsibility.

But Jesus said, “They need not go away; you give them something to eat.” “You” is emphatic. Jesus puts the responsibility on the disciples. They had nothing, but Jesus was teaching them to bring what they had to him and depend on him. John says Jesus asked Philip where they could buy bread, to test him (John 6:5–6).

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus expected them to solve the problem by their own resources. He wanted them to see their inadequacy and his sufficiency.

In a sentence. When the disciples wanted to send the hungry crowd away, Jesus told them to feed it themselves.

On a Tuesday. When you see overwhelming need, do you say “send them away”, or do you bring what little you have to Jesus?

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "We have only five loaves here and two fish." And he said, "Bring them here to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples said: we have only five loaves and two fish. Jesus said: bring them here to me.

We have only five loaves here and two fish. John tells us they came from a boy, and were barley loaves, the bread of the poor (John 6:9). The fish were probably small, dried or salted, used as a relish with bread. Enough for one person’s meal.

And he said, “Bring them here to me.” The key moment. The little they had, brought to Jesus, was enough. God often works through small, ordinary means placed in his hands. The question is not how much we have, but whether we give it to him.

In a sentence. The disciples had almost nothing, and Jesus told them to bring it to him.

On a Tuesday. What small thing do you have, a skill, some time, a little money, that you could bring to Jesus for him to use?
verseByVerse.note: John adds that the loaves were barley loaves, the bread of the poor.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he ordered the crowds to sit down on the grass, and taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing. Then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds. And they all ate and were satisfied. And they took up twelve baskets full of the broken pieces left over.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus told the crowds to sit on the grass. He took the five loaves and two fish, looked up to heaven, gave thanks, broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples, who gave them to the crowds. Everyone ate and was satisfied, and the disciples picked up twelve baskets full of leftover pieces.

Then he ordered the crowds to sit down on the grass. Mark adds that it was green grass, in groups of hundreds and fifties (Mark 6:39–40). Spring, near Passover (John 6:4). The scene recalls Psalm 23: he makes me lie down in green pastures. The Good Shepherd is feeding his flock (9:36).

And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing. As the head of a Jewish household did at a meal, Jesus thanked God for the food. The Jewish blessing over bread was: Blessed are you, O Lord our God, King of the universe, who brings forth bread from the earth.

Then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds. The same four verbs appear at the Last Supper: took, blessed, broke, gave (26:26). The feeding looks forward to the Lord’s Supper and to the messianic banquet (8:11). Jesus works through his disciples: they distribute what he provides.

And they all ate and were satisfied. Not just a taste, but a full meal. “Satisfied” is the word used in 5:6: those who hunger will be satisfied.

And they took up twelve baskets full of the broken pieces left over. Twelve baskets: perhaps one for each of the disciples, or a sign of provision for the twelve tribes of Israel. The baskets (kophinoi) were the wicker baskets Jews carried for food. God’s provision is abundant: more left over than they started with.

The background. God fed Israel with manna in the wilderness (Exodus 16). Elisha fed a hundred men with twenty loaves, and there was some left (2 Kings 4:42–44). Jesus feeds thousands with five. Moses prayed for food; Jesus provides it himself. He is the greater Moses and the greater Elisha. John records that Jesus explained the sign: I am the bread of life (John 6:35).

What it does not mean. Not that the people simply shared their hidden lunches, as some liberal interpreters have suggested. The Gospel writers clearly describe a miracle of creation. All four Gospels record it, the only miracle besides the resurrection in all four.

In a sentence. Jesus, like the Shepherd of Psalm 23 and greater than Moses, fed the crowd abundantly from five loaves and two fish, through his disciples.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for your food today, as Jesus did. And remember that he provides through ordinary people, including you.

For worship. Praise Jesus, the bread of life, who satisfies.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus says the blessing as the head of a Jewish household did at a meal.

parallels.desc: Elisha feeds a hundred men with some left over
he took bread, blessed and broke it

verseByVerse.quote: And those who ate were about five thousand men, besides women and children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
About five thousand men ate, not counting women and children.

And those who ate were about five thousand men. “Men” (andres) means adult males. Counting only men was a common practice in that culture.

Besides women and children. Matthew alone adds this. The total may have been fifteen to twenty thousand people, more than the population of Capernaum and its surrounding villages. A staggering miracle.

In a sentence. Five thousand men, and many more women and children, were fed.

On a Tuesday. God’s provision is never small. Trust him with the needs that seem too big.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–36 — Walking on Water and Healings at Gennesaret
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Immediately after the feeding, Jesus sends the disciples ahead by boat and goes up the mountain alone to pray. In the early morning hours the disciples are struggling against the wind; Jesus walks to them on the sea. Peter walks on the water toward Jesus, sinks when he doubts, is rescued, and worship breaks out in the boat. They land at Gennesaret, and Jesus heals all who touch the fringe of his garment. Four things more. "he made the disciples get into the boat" is anankazo, to compel — the word for forcing someone to do what they do not want. They did not want to go, and John supplies the reason: the crowd was about to seize him and make him king (Jn. 6:15). Thousands of people on a Galilean hillside who have just watched dinner appear out of nothing is a political event, and the country had seen risings before. He got the twelve off the beach before it could form. The boat is "beaten" by the waves — basanizomenon, a word for torture, used of the demons begging not to be tormented (8:29). And "the fourth watch" is Roman reckoning, three to six in the morning: they had been rowing since evening, roughly nine hours, and had covered three or four miles of a lake they could normally cross in two (Jn. 6:19). Note that they were exactly where he had sent them — this was not a wrong turning, and Mark says he saw them from the mountain (6:48). Mark preserves one clause Matthew omits and it is the strangest in the account: "he meant to pass by them" (6:48). Read flatly that is baffling; but passing by is technical Old Testament language for a theophany — what God does for Moses in the cleft of the rock (Exod. 33:19-22) and for Elijah at Horeb (1 Kgs. 19:11). The intention was to be seen. He does not ask for ability; he asks to be commanded, having just watched a word do this to five loaves. The record stands that one man got out of a boat in a gale in the dark and walked on a lake, and Matthew reports it in a single sentence. Finally, "the fringe of his garment" is the kraspedon, the tzitzit commanded in Numbers 15:38-39 — and the Hebrew for the corner of a garment, kanaph, also means wing. Malachi's last page promises that "the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings" (Mal. 4:2). They were reaching for the corners of the robe of the one Malachi described, and finding that it was there.
verseByVerse.theology: Jesus walking on the water is another creation-sovereignty miracle: the same one who stilled the storm (8:26) now walks on it. In the Old Testament, God alone treads on the waves of the sea (Job 9:8; Ps. 77:19). Jesus is doing what God does. Peter's walking on the water is the only time anyone but his Master is recorded doing this, and it happens not by Peter's power but by Jesus's command: "Come." The sinking and rescue express the pattern of every disciple's faith: bold initial response, fear when looking at the circumstances, cry for help, rescue by the one who is always within reach.
verseByVerse.examples: The disciples' worship in the boat — "Truly you are the Son of God" — is the first time in Matthew that the disciples make this full confession. The storm-stilling produced "What sort of man is this?" (8:27); the water-walking produces "Truly you are the Son of God." The miracles are cumulative revelation. Each display of his authority over creation moves the disciples closer to the full confession that Peter will make at Caesarea Philippi (16:16). Faith grows through the accumulation of evidence seen with open eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: Immediately he made the disciples get into the boat and go before him to the other side, while he dismissed the crowds. And after he had dismissed the crowds, he went up on the mountain by himself to pray. When evening came, he was there alone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Immediately Jesus made his disciples get into the boat and go ahead of him to the other side, while he dismissed the crowds. Then he went up the mountain alone to pray. When evening came, he was there alone.

Immediately he made the disciples get into the boat. “Made” (ēnankasen) means compelled, insisted. Why the urgency? John tells us the crowd wanted to take Jesus by force to make him king (John 6:15). After the feeding, they saw him as a political Messiah who could lead a revolt against Rome. Jesus sent the disciples away quickly, perhaps to keep them from being swept up in this enthusiasm.

While he dismissed the crowds. He refused the crown they offered. His kingdom would come by the cross, not by a political uprising (4:8–10).

He went up on the mountain by himself to pray. Jesus prayed at moments of crisis and decision (26:36–46; Luke 6:12). He had been grieving John’s death, ministering all day, and refusing the crowd’s temptation. He needed to be alone with his Father.

When evening came, he was there alone. Solitude with God.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus did not care about the crowds. He had fed and healed them. But he would not let them define his mission.

In a sentence. Jesus sent his disciples away, refused the crowd’s political hopes, and went up the mountain alone to pray.

On a Tuesday. If Jesus needed to be alone with the Father, so do you. Find time today, even a few minutes, alone with God.
verseByVerse.note: John says the crowd wanted to make him king by force.

verseByVerse.quote: but the boat by this time was a long way from the land, beaten by the waves, for the wind was against them. And in the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By then the boat was far from land, battered by the waves, because the wind was against them. In the early hours of the morning, Jesus came to them, walking on the sea.

But the boat by this time was a long way from the land. John says they had rowed three or four miles (John 6:19), about halfway across the lake.

Beaten by the waves, for the wind was against them. “Beaten” (basanizomenon) means tormented, tortured. They were struggling against a strong headwind for hours. Unlike the storm in 8:24, Jesus is not in the boat.

And in the fourth watch of the night. The Romans divided the night into four watches. The fourth watch ran from about 3 to 6 a.m. The disciples had been struggling for perhaps nine hours.

He came to them, walking on the sea. In the Old Testament, only God walks on the sea: he alone trampled the waves of the sea (Job 9:8); his way was through the sea, his path through the great waters (Psalm 77:19). The sea pictured chaos and danger; God rules over it. Jesus walks on the waves as Lord of creation.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus was unaware of their struggle during those hours. Mark says he saw them straining at the oars (Mark 6:48). His timing was deliberate.

In a sentence. After the disciples had struggled all night against the wind, Jesus came to them walking on the sea, as only God can.

On a Tuesday. If you have been straining at the oars for a long time, Jesus sees you. He will come at the right time.
verseByVerse.note: The fourth watch of the night ran from about 3 to 6 a.m.

parallels.desc: who alone trampled the waves of the sea
your way was through the sea

verseByVerse.quote: But when the disciples saw him walking on the sea, they were terrified, and said, "It is a ghost!" and they cried out in fear. But immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying, "Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the disciples saw him walking on the sea, they were terrified and cried out in fear: it is a ghost! But Jesus spoke to them at once: take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid.

They were terrified, and said, “It is a ghost!” In the dark, before dawn, they saw a figure walking on the water. They thought it was a ghost (phantasma), perhaps an evil spirit of the sea. Sailors feared such things.

And they cried out in fear. Experienced fishermen, screaming in terror.

But immediately Jesus spoke to them. He did not leave them in their fear.

Take heart. Be of good courage (see 9:2, 22).

It is I. In Greek, egō eimi, literally “I am”. It can simply mean “It’s me”, but it is also the name of God revealed to Moses: I AM WHO I AM (Exodus 3:14), and God’s words in Isaiah: I am he; I, I am he who comforts you (Isaiah 43:10–13, 25; 51:12). Walking on the sea and saying “I am”, Jesus reveals himself as the LORD.

Do not be afraid. The words God often speaks when he reveals himself (Genesis 15:1; Isaiah 41:10).

In a sentence. When the disciples thought Jesus was a ghost, he comforted them with words that reveal his divine identity: take heart; I am; do not be afraid.

On a Tuesday. In your darkest fear, listen for Jesus’ voice: take heart; it is I; do not be afraid.
verseByVerse.note: “It is I” can also be heard as the divine name, “I am.”

parallels.desc: when you pass through the waters

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter answered him, "Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the water." He said, "Come." So Peter got out of the boat and walked on the water and came to Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter answered: Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the water. Jesus said, come. So Peter got out of the boat and walked on the water toward Jesus.

And Peter answered him. Only Matthew tells this part of the story. Peter, impulsive and bold, as always.

Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the water. Not presumption, but faith. Peter does not jump on his own; he asks for Jesus’ command. He wants to be where Jesus is, doing what Jesus does. “If it is you” is not doubt; it means “since it is you”.

He said, “Come.” One word, with all authority.

So Peter got out of the boat and walked on the water and came to Jesus. Astonishing. As long as Peter trusted Jesus’ word, he did what is humanly impossible. The other disciples stayed in the boat.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should demand miracles or take reckless risks to prove their faith. Peter acted on Jesus’ explicit command. Faith obeys Christ’s word; it does not invent its own tests (4:5–7).

In a sentence. At Jesus’ command, Peter stepped out of the boat and walked on the water toward him.

On a Tuesday. Is there a step of obedience that Christ has clearly called you to, but you have stayed in the boat? Step out on his word.
verseByVerse.note: Only Matthew records Peter walking on the water.

verseByVerse.quote: But when he saw the wind, he was afraid, and beginning to sink he cried out, "Lord, save me." Jesus immediately reached out his hand and took hold of him, saying to him, "O you of little faith, why did you doubt?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when Peter saw the wind, he was afraid. He began to sink and cried out: Lord, save me! Jesus immediately reached out his hand, caught him, and said: you of little faith, why did you doubt?

But when he saw the wind, he was afraid. Peter took his eyes off Jesus and looked at the storm. The wind had not changed; Peter’s focus had. Faith looks at Christ; fear looks at circumstances.

And beginning to sink he cried out, “Lord, save me.” The shortest prayer in the Bible, and one of the best. No eloquence, no formula, just desperate trust. Peter knew where to turn even as he sank.

Jesus immediately reached out his hand and took hold of him. Immediately: no delay, no lecture first. The Psalms speak of God reaching down from on high to draw his people out of many waters (Psalm 18:16; 144:7).

O you of little faith, why did you doubt? “Little faith” (see 8:26). “Doubt” (distazō) means to waver, to be in two minds, pulled in two directions. Peter had real faith, enough to step out of the boat, but it wavered. Jesus’ rebuke is gentle, spoken while holding him up.

What it does not mean. Not that Peter’s faith was worthless. He walked on water, which no one else did. But it was mixed with doubt. Nor does sinking mean that Jesus abandoned him. Even when our faith fails, Christ holds us (2 Timothy 2:13). Our safety rests on his grip, not ours.

In a sentence. When Peter looked at the wind instead of Jesus, he began to sink, cried for help, and Jesus caught him at once.

On a Tuesday. What “wind” are you staring at today? Turn your eyes back to Jesus. And if you are sinking, pray Peter’s prayer: Lord, save me.

parallels.desc: save me, O God, for the waters have come up to my neck
he drew me out of many waters

verseByVerse.quote: And when they got into the boat, the wind ceased. And those in the boat worshiped him, saying, "Truly, you are the Son of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they climbed into the boat, the wind stopped. The disciples in the boat worshipped Jesus, saying: truly you are the Son of God.

And when they got into the boat, the wind ceased. Jesus’ presence brought calm. John adds that immediately the boat was at the land where they were going (John 6:21).

And those in the boat worshiped him. “Worshipped” (prosekynēsan) means bowed down before him. After the first storm they asked, “What sort of man is this?” (8:27). Now they have the answer.

Saying, “Truly you are the Son of God.” The first time the disciples as a group confess Jesus as the Son of God in Matthew. They have seen him feed thousands, walk on water, say “I am”, and calm the wind. This confession anticipates Peter’s great confession in 16:16 and the centurion’s at the cross (27:54).

What it does not mean. Not that their understanding was complete. They still did not understand that the Son of God must suffer (16:21–23). But they had seen enough to worship.

In a sentence. When Jesus stilled the wind, the disciples worshipped him and confessed him as the Son of God.

For worship. Join the disciples: truly you are the Son of God.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret. And when the men of that place recognized him, they sent around to all that region and brought to him all who were sick
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had crossed over, they landed at Gennesaret. The people recognised Jesus and sent word throughout the region, and brought all their sick to him.

They came to land at Gennesaret. A fertile, well-watered plain about three miles long on the northwest shore of the lake, between Capernaum and Magdala. Josephus described it as extraordinarily fertile. The lake was sometimes called the Lake of Gennesaret (Luke 5:1).

And when the men of that place recognized him. His fame had spread.

They sent around to all that region and brought to him all who were sick. They did not keep him to themselves; they sent for everyone in need.

In a sentence. At Gennesaret, people recognised Jesus and brought all their sick to him.

On a Tuesday. When you know where Jesus can be found, tell others and bring them to him.
verseByVerse.note: Gennesaret was a fertile plain on the north-west shore of the lake.

verseByVerse.quote: and implored him that they might only touch the fringe of his garment. And as many as touched it were made well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They begged him to let the sick just touch the fringe of his cloak, and all who touched it were healed.

And implored him that they might only touch the fringe of his garment. Like the woman with the bleeding (9:20–22), news of whose healing may have spread. The fringe was the tassel on the corner of a Jewish man’s outer garment (Numbers 15:38–40; see 9:20). Malachi 4:2 speaks of the sun of righteousness rising with healing in its wings; the word “wings” could also mean the corners of a garment, and some Jews may have connected this with the Messiah.

And as many as touched it were made well. “Made well” (diesōthēsan) means completely saved, thoroughly healed. Not one was turned away.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus’ clothes had magical power, or that relics carry healing power. The power was Jesus’ own, received through faith (9:22).

In a sentence. Everyone who touched even the fringe of Jesus’ garment in faith was completely healed.

On a Tuesday. You cannot touch Jesus’ cloak, but you can come to him in faith through prayer. No one who comes to him is turned away.
verseByVerse.note: The fringe was the tassel the law required on the corners of a garment.

parallels.desc: the woman who touched the fringe

14.theology: Christ as the true bread from heaven. John 6 makes explicit what Matthew implies: the feeding of the five thousand points to Christ as the bread of life. He is the antitype of the manna — not merely a physical provision for the body but the living bread who gives eternal life to all who feed on him by faith. The Lord’s Supper is the sacramental extension of this meal: in it, we receive not merely bread and wine but Christ himself, the bread of heaven, by faith. The wilderness feeding thus stands at the intersection of Exodus typology, Eucharistic anticipation, and kingdom eschatology: we are fed by Christ in the wilderness of this age until the great feast of the new creation.
14.examples:
Then: Five loaves and two fish were laughably inadequate for five thousand people. The disciples knew it. Jesus knew it. He asked for them anyway. What he asks for is never the measure of what he can do with it.

Now: Every pastor, teacher, parent, and missionary knows the feeling of inadequate resources — not enough time, energy, money, or skill. Matthew 14 is not a promise that resources will always multiply visibly, but it is a call to bring what we have to Jesus and trust him with the rest. The twelve baskets of leftovers are the testimony: what is given to Christ is never wasted, and rarely runs out.

15.title: What Defiles a Person
15.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Pharisees and scribes came to Jesus from Jerusalem and said, <sup>2</sup>“Why do your disciples break the tradition of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat.” <sup>3</sup>He answered them, “And why do you break the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition? <sup>4</sup>For God commanded, ‘Honor your father and your mother,’ and, ‘Whoever reviles father or mother must surely die.’ <sup>5</sup>But you say, ‘If anyone tells his father or his mother, “What you would have gained from me is given to God,” <sup>6</sup>he need not honor his father.’ So for the sake of your tradition you have made void the word of God. <sup>7</sup>You hypocrites! Well did Isaiah prophesy of you, when he said: <sup>8</sup>“‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; <sup>9</sup>in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men.’” <sup>10</sup>And he called the people to him and said to them, “Hear and understand: <sup>11</sup>it is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth; this defiles a person.” <sup>12</sup>Then the disciples came and said to him, “Do you know that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this saying?” <sup>13</sup>He answered, “Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be rooted up. <sup>14</sup>Let them alone; they are blind guides. And if the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit.” <sup>15</sup>But Peter said to him, “Explain the parable to us.” <sup>16</sup>And he said, “Are you also still without understanding? <sup>17</sup>Do you not see that whatever goes into the mouth passes into the stomach and is expelled? <sup>18</sup>But what comes out of the mouth proceeds from the heart, and this defiles a person. <sup>19</sup>For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false witness, slander. <sup>20</sup>These are what defile a person. But to eat with unwashed hands does not defile anyone.” <sup>21</sup>And Jesus went away from there and withdrew to the district of Tyre and Sidon. <sup>22</sup>And behold, a Canaanite woman from that region came out and was crying, “Have mercy on me, O Lord, Son of David; my daughter is severely oppressed by a demon.” <sup>23</sup>But he did not answer her a word. And his disciples came and begged him, saying, “Send her away, for she is crying out after us.” <sup>24</sup>He answered, “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” <sup>25</sup>But she came and knelt before him, saying, “Lord, help me.” <sup>26</sup>And he answered, “It is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.” <sup>27</sup>She said, “Yes, Lord, yet even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table.” <sup>28</sup>Then Jesus answered her, “O woman, great is your faith! Let it be done for you as you desire.” And her daughter was healed instantly. <sup>29</sup>Jesus went on from there and walked beside the Sea of Galilee. And he went up on the mountain and sat down there. <sup>30</sup>And great crowds came to him, bringing with them the lame, the blind, the crippled, the mute, and many others, and they put them at his feet, and he healed them, <sup>31</sup>so that the crowd wondered, when they saw the mute speaking, the crippled healthy, the lame walking, and the blind seeing. And they glorified the God of Israel. <sup>32</sup>Then Jesus called his disciples to him and said, “I have compassion on the crowd because they have been with me now three days and have nothing to eat. And I am unwilling to send them away hungry, lest they faint on the way.” <sup>33</sup>And the disciples said to him, “Where are we to get enough bread in such a desolate place to feed so great a crowd?” <sup>34</sup>And Jesus said to them, “How many loaves do you have?” They said, “Seven, and a few small fish.” <sup>35</sup>And directing the crowd to sit down on the ground, <sup>36</sup>he took the seven loaves and the fish, and having given thanks he broke them and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds. <sup>37</sup>And they all ate and were satisfied. And they took up seven baskets full of the broken pieces left over. <sup>38</sup>Those who ate were four thousand men, besides women and children. <sup>39</sup>And after sending away the crowds, he got into the boat and went to the region of Magadan.
15.overview:
Chapter 15 confronts the deepest corruption in religion: the substitution of human tradition for the word of God. The Pharisees have constructed an elaborate system of ritual purity — washings, dietary rules, oral traditions — that they treat as divinely binding. Jesus cuts through it all with a single theological move: defilement is not external but internal. The heart is the problem. No ceremony can cleanse it; only the blood of the covenant can reach it.

Then, in a jarring turn, Jesus goes to Gentile territory and encounters a Canaanite woman whose persistence in faith stands in shaming contrast to the Pharisees' hypocrisy. She is the wrong ethnicity, the wrong gender, the wrong religion — and Jesus commends her as having “great faith.” She is the second Gentile in Matthew to receive this commendation (after the centurion in chapter 8). The kingdom breaks every ethnic and ritual boundary. The chapter closes with a second feeding miracle — four thousand this time, in Gentile territory — extending the bread of the messianic banquet to the nations.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — What Defiles a Person: Tradition and the Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pharisees from Jerusalem confront Jesus about his disciples eating without washing hands. Jesus counters by exposing how their tradition nullifies the command to honor parents, then teaches the crowd that defilement comes from within, not without. He explains privately to the disciples: it is what comes out of the heart that defiles a person — evil thoughts, murder, adultery, all the rest. What the summary cannot hold. The handwashing was not about dirt. It is netilat yadayim, a ritual pouring in prescribed quantity and order to remove ceremonial uncleanness — a man with filthy hands who performed it was clean, and a man who had scrubbed and not performed it was not. And the Torah requires it of priests, before the altar, on pain of death (Exod. 30:19-21); the tradition had extended priestly purity to everybody at every meal. The impulse is not contemptible — if Israel is a kingdom of priests, why not treat the table like the altar? — but it had become the thing a delegation walked ninety miles from Jerusalem to complain about. Watch the structure of the reply: they ask why his disciples break the tradition; he asks why they break the commandment for the sake of their tradition. Same verb, nouns exchanged, and it puts them on trial in one sentence. Note also that he says "your tradition" twice, where they had said "the tradition of the elders" — a phrase that gives it distance and belongs to nobody. And the two texts he cites are the fifth commandment and its capital sanction (Exod. 21:17), so nobody can claim a small matter is being inflated. "hypocrite" is the Greek theatre word for the masked actor — and the mask was not a disguise but a device for projecting a character to people too far off to see a face. Matthew uses it thirteen times, more than the rest of the New Testament together. On the quotation, Matthew follows the Greek of Isaiah 29:13, which sharpens the Hebrew rather than altering it. "in vain" is maten — not wrongly, not insincerely: useless, which is a colder verdict than hypocrisy about men who fasted twice a week and tithed their herb garden. And note what he does at v. 10: he stops answering the delegation, calls the crowd, and gives the answer to them directly.
verseByVerse.theology: The controversy exposes the Pharisees' deepest error: they have allowed their oral tradition to override the written word of God. The corban rule (declaring assets dedicated to God, thereby relieving oneself of the duty to support parents) is the example Jesus uses — a legal fiction that honored the letter of piety while violating the command to honor father and mother. Isaiah's word stands: "This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me." External religion without heart-transformation is hypocrisy by definition.
verseByVerse.examples: The list of defiling things in verses 19-20 is a heart-audit: from the inside come evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false witness, slander. These are not random vices; they map onto the second table of the Decalogue. Jesus is saying: the law you claim to keep is being broken from the inside out. Clean hands matter less than clean hearts — and clean hearts are precisely what the Pharisees have not addressed.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharisees and scribes came to Jesus from Jerusalem and said, "Why do your disciples break the tradition of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharisees and scribes came from Jerusalem and asked Jesus why his disciples broke the tradition of the elders: they did not wash their hands before eating.

Then Pharisees and scribes came to Jesus from Jerusalem. An official delegation from the religious capital, perhaps sent to investigate him. Opposition is growing (12:14).

Why do your disciples break the tradition of the elders? “The tradition of the elders” was the large body of oral rules that earlier rabbis had built around the law of Moses, to apply it to every situation and to “build a fence” around it so that no one would break it by accident. The Pharisees believed that this oral law had been given to Moses at Sinai alongside the written law, and passed down by word of mouth. It was later written down in the Mishnah (about AD 200).

For they do not wash their hands when they eat. Not hygiene but ritual purity. The law required priests to wash before serving in the tabernacle (Exodus 30:17–21). The Pharisees extended this to every Jew at every meal: water was poured over the hands in a special way to remove ceremonial uncleanness picked up from contact with Gentiles, unclean objects, or the marketplace (Mark 7:3–4). It was not commanded in Scripture.

What it does not mean. Not that tradition is always bad. The church has good traditions: creeds, confessions, forms of worship, which faithfully express Scripture (2 Thessalonians 2:15). The problem comes when human tradition is put on the same level as God’s word, or above it (v. 3).

In a sentence. Religious leaders from Jerusalem challenged Jesus because his disciples did not follow the elders’ rule about ritual handwashing.

On a Tuesday. Are there religious habits you treat as if they were God’s commands, and judge others for not keeping?
verseByVerse.note: The “tradition of the elders” was the body of oral rules built around the law. The washing was a ritual of purity, not hygiene.

parallels.desc: the Pharisee astonished that Jesus did not wash

verseByVerse.quote: He answered them, "And why do you break the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition? For God commanded, 'Honor your father and your mother,' and, 'Whoever reviles father or mother must surely die.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered with a question: why do you break God’s commandment for the sake of your tradition? God commanded: honour your father and mother, and whoever curses father or mother must be put to death.

And why do you break the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition? Jesus turns the accusation around. They accused the disciples of breaking human tradition; Jesus accuses them of breaking God’s law. Notice the contrast: “the commandment of God” and “your tradition”. Not “the tradition of the elders”, but “your” tradition: human, not divine.

For God commanded. Jesus treats the words of Moses as God’s own command. Scripture is God’s word.

Honor your father and your mother. The fifth commandment (Exodus 20:12). Honour includes respect, obedience when young, and practical care in old age, including financial support (see Ephesians 6:2).

Whoever reviles father or mother must surely die. Exodus 21:17. “Revile” means to curse, to speak evil of, to treat with contempt. God took this so seriously that it was a capital crime in Israel.

In a sentence. Jesus accused the Pharisees of breaking God’s commandment to honour parents for the sake of their own tradition.

On a Tuesday. How are you honouring your parents? Their care in old age is a command of God, not an optional kindness.

verseByVerse.quote: But you say, "If anyone tells his father or his mother, 'What you would have gained from me is given to God,' he need not honor his father." So for the sake of your tradition you have made void the word of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you teach that if someone tells his parents, “What you would have received from me is given to God”, he no longer needs to honour his father. So for the sake of your tradition you have made God’s word void.

But you say. In contrast to what God said (v. 4).

If anyone tells his father or his mother, “What you would have gained from me is given to God.” Mark gives the Aramaic word: Corban, meaning an offering dedicated to God (Mark 7:11). A son could declare his property “Corban”, dedicated to the temple. Once declared, it could not be used to support his parents, but he could often keep using it himself during his lifetime. It became a legal loophole: a way to escape the duty of caring for ageing parents while appearing pious.

He need not honor his father. By their tradition, such a vow had to be kept, even if it meant breaking the fifth commandment.

So for the sake of your tradition you have made void the word of God. “Made void” means cancelled, nullified, made of no effect. Their human rule had overruled God’s clear command. Mark adds: and many such things you do (Mark 7:13).

The principle. Whenever human tradition contradicts Scripture, Scripture must win. This is the Reformation principle of sola Scriptura: Scripture alone is the final authority over the church’s traditions (Westminster Confession 1.6, 1.10). The Reformers used this passage against medieval traditions that they believed had overruled the word of God.

What it does not mean. Not that giving to God is wrong, or that we should not give generously to the church. But no religious giving can replace the God-given duty to care for one’s family (1 Timothy 5:8).

In a sentence. The Pharisees used a religious vow to escape caring for their parents, cancelling God’s word by their tradition.

On a Tuesday. Is there a religious-sounding excuse you use to avoid a clear duty, at home, at work, or to your family?
verseByVerse.note: Mark gives the formula its Aramaic name, Corban — “given to God.” Property declared dedicated could no longer be used to support one’s parents.

verseByVerse.quote: You hypocrites! Well did Isaiah prophesy of you, when he said: "This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
You hypocrites! Isaiah prophesied rightly about you: this people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me.

You hypocrites! Actors playing a part (see 6:2). They looked devout, but their hearts were not given to God.

Well did Isaiah prophesy of you. Isaiah 29:13. Isaiah spoke to his own generation, but his words describe every generation with the same problem.

This people honors me with their lips. They said the right words: prayers, praise, religious language.

But their heart is far from me. Their inner life was not devoted to God. They went through the motions without love. This is the heart of the matter. God looks at the heart (1 Samuel 16:7).

In a sentence. Jesus called the Pharisees hypocrites, fulfilling Isaiah’s description of people who honour God with their lips while their hearts are far from him.

On a Tuesday. When you sing or pray on Sunday, is your heart near to God, or only your lips?

parallels.desc: this people draw near with their mouth

verseByVerse.quote: "in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men." And he called the people to him and said to them, "Hear and understand:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their worship is empty, because they teach human rules as if they were God’s commands. Then Jesus called the crowd and said: listen and understand.

In vain do they worship me. “In vain” means uselessly, emptily. Worship offered without the heart, according to human rules, achieves nothing before God.

Teaching as doctrines the commandments of men. They taught human rules as if they were divine law. This is the heart of the problem: adding to God’s word, and binding people’s consciences with rules God never gave. Paul warns against the same thing (Colossians 2:20–23).

The regulative principle. The Reformed tradition draws from verses like this that God is to be worshipped only in the ways he has commanded in Scripture, not by human invention (Westminster Confession 21.1). Others hold that whatever Scripture does not forbid is permitted in worship. Both agree that no human rule may be imposed on the conscience as if it were God’s command.

And he called the people to him and said to them, “Hear and understand.” Jesus now speaks to the crowd. The issue matters for everyone.

In a sentence. Worship according to human rules taught as divine commands is empty, so Jesus called the crowd to listen carefully.

On a Tuesday. Test what you believe and practise by Scripture: is this God’s command, or a human tradition?

verseByVerse.quote: it is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth; this defiles a person." Then the disciples came and said to him, "Do you know that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this saying?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of it. Then the disciples told Jesus that the Pharisees were offended by what he said.

It is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a person. “Defiles” (koinoi) means makes common, unclean, unfit for God’s presence. The Pharisees taught that eating with unwashed hands, or eating unclean food, made a person unclean before God. Jesus says that food cannot make a person morally unclean.

But what comes out of the mouth; this defiles a person. Words, and the heart from which they come (vv. 18–19; 12:34). Real uncleanness is moral and spiritual, not ritual.

Then the disciples came and said to him, “Do you know that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this saying?” “Offended” (eskandalisthēsan) means scandalised, made to stumble. Jesus had swept away a central part of their system of purity.

What it does not mean. Not that the Old Testament food laws were wrong. They were God’s commands for Israel, teaching the difference between clean and unclean and setting Israel apart from the nations (Leviticus 11:44–47). But they were symbols pointing to inner purity, and they are fulfilled in Christ. Mark says Jesus here declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19), and God confirmed it to Peter in a vision (Acts 10:9–16). Christians are free to eat any food with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:4–5), while being careful not to cause a weaker believer to stumble (Romans 14).

In a sentence. Food cannot make a person unclean before God; what comes out of the heart through the mouth does.

On a Tuesday. What comes out of your mouth reveals your heart. What have your words revealed this week?

verseByVerse.quote: He answered, "Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be rooted up. Let them alone; they are blind guides. And if the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted. Leave them alone: they are blind guides. And if a blind man leads a blind man, both will fall into a pit.

Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be rooted up. Israel was pictured as God’s planting (Isaiah 60:21; 61:3). The Pharisees and their teaching were not planted by God, and will be removed in judgment. Compare the weeds among the wheat (13:24–30).
