Let them alone. Do not worry about offending them. Do not follow them. Do not try to win their approval.

They are blind guides. The Pharisees saw themselves as guides to the blind (Romans 2:19). Jesus says they are blind themselves. They cannot see the truth about God, so they cannot lead others to it (23:16, 24).

And if the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit. A proverb. Following a blind guide leads to disaster for both. Pits were common hazards: cisterns, wells and ditches.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should ignore false teachers. Elsewhere we are told to warn against them (7:15; Titus 1:9–11). But we must not seek their approval, or follow them.

In a sentence. Teachers whom God has not planted will be removed; they are blind guides, and those who follow them will fall with them.

On a Tuesday. Whom are you following spiritually? Make sure they can see, by testing them against Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said to him, "Explain the parable to us." And he said, "Are you also still without understanding?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter asked Jesus to explain the saying. Jesus said: are you still without understanding?

But Peter said to him, “Explain the parable to us.” “Parable” here means the puzzling saying of verse 11. Peter, as spokesman, asks for the meaning. Asking is good (13:36).

And he said, “Are you also still without understanding?” A gentle rebuke. After all his teaching, the disciples were still influenced by the Pharisees’ way of thinking about purity. Old habits of thought die hard. But Jesus explains, patiently.

In a sentence. Peter asked for an explanation, and Jesus gently rebuked the disciples for still not understanding.

On a Tuesday. Jesus is patient with slow learners. Keep asking him to help you understand.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not see that whatever goes into the mouth passes into the stomach and is expelled? But what comes out of the mouth proceeds from the heart, and this defiles a person.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you not see that whatever goes into the mouth passes into the stomach and out of the body? But what comes out of the mouth comes from the heart, and this defiles a person.

Whatever goes into the mouth passes into the stomach and is expelled. Food goes into the body, not into the heart. It is digested and expelled. It cannot affect a person’s relationship with God. Mark adds the comment: thus he declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19).

But what comes out of the mouth proceeds from the heart. Words come from the heart, the centre of the person (12:34).

And this defiles a person. The source of real uncleanness is inside us, not outside us.

The significance. This was revolutionary. The Pharisees’ whole system located defilement outside the person: in food, objects, contact with unclean people. They tried to stay pure by avoiding contact with the unclean. Jesus says that the problem is within. You cannot stay pure by avoiding the world, because you carry the source of impurity in your own heart. Only a new heart can make a person clean (Ezekiel 36:25–26; Psalm 51:10).

In a sentence. Food passes through the body and cannot defile; what defiles comes from the heart.

On a Tuesday. You cannot keep yourself clean simply by avoiding bad places and people. The danger is within. Ask God for a clean heart.
verseByVerse.note: Mark adds, “Thus he declared all foods clean.”

parallels.desc: out of the abundance of the heart

verseByVerse.quote: For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false witness, slander. These are what defile a person. But to eat with unwashed hands does not defile anyone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Out of the heart come evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false witness and slander. These are what defile a person. Eating with unwashed hands does not.

For out of the heart come evil thoughts. First, and the source of the rest: evil thoughts, the inner plans and intentions of the heart. Sin begins in the mind before it becomes action (James 1:14–15). Jeremiah says that the heart is deceitful above all things (Jeremiah 17:9).

Murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false witness, slander. The list follows the order of the second half of the Ten Commandments: the sixth (murder), the seventh (adultery and sexual immorality), the eighth (theft) and the ninth (false witness and slander). These are what make a person unclean before God.

Sexual immorality. Porneia: every kind of sexual sin outside marriage between a man and a woman (see 5:32).

Slander. Blasphēmiai: speech that damages others, or insults God.

These are what defile a person. Not food, but sin.

But to eat with unwashed hands does not defile anyone. Jesus returns to the original question (v. 2). The Pharisees’ handwashing rule had nothing to do with real purity.

What it does not mean. Not that every person commits every one of these sins in action. But the seeds of all of them are in every human heart, and only God’s grace keeps them from growing (5:21–28). Nor does it mean that outward actions do not matter. They matter because they reveal and express the heart.

In a sentence. Evil thoughts and the sins they produce come from the heart and defile a person, not unwashed hands.

On a Tuesday. Which of these sins finds a home in your heart, even if it never becomes action? Confess it, and ask God to cleanse you.

parallels.desc: the heart is deceitful above all things

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–39 — The Canaanite Woman and the Feeding of the Four Thousand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus withdraws to the region of Tyre and Sidon, where a Canaanite woman cries out for her demon-oppressed daughter. After testing her faith through apparent reluctance, he heals the daughter and commends her great faith. Jesus then returns to Galilee, heals many on a mountain, and feeds four thousand people from seven loaves and a few fish. More to notice. This is the one time in his ministry that Jesus goes into Phoenicia — he had already crossed to the Gentile east bank at 8:28 and will go north to pagan Caesarea Philippi at 16:13, but Tyre and Sidon are foreign soil. Tyre and Sidon are Phoenician cities outside Israel, outside Herod's jurisdiction — and in the Old Testament they are bywords, with Ezekiel devoting three chapters to Tyre's fall and Jezebel a Sidonian princess. That is the address he withdraws to after Jerusalem sends a deputation about hand washing. And Matthew's word for her is deliberately archaic: Mark calls her a Syrophoenician, the ordinary current term; Matthew calls her a Canaanite — the Old Testament name for the nations Israel was to drive out, rarely heard in his day. He has reached back for maximum freight, and then has her say "Son of David". On the dogs, Greek has two words: kyon is the street scavenger and the word used when "dogs" is an insult (7:6; Phil. 3:2), and Jesus does not use it. He uses kynarion, the diminutive — the animal that lives in the house, belongs there, and is fed there. The saying is about order, not worth. But the shock should not be dissolved: he ignored her, the disciples asked him to send her away, and he answered her kneeling with a proverb about dogs. What resolves it is the outcome rather than the vocabulary. Her reply begins "yes, LORD" — she agrees, disputes nothing, and adds only "for even", staying inside his picture and finding that it contains her. And Jesus commends faith of this order in only two people: this woman (great is your faith) and the centurion (with no one in Israel have I found such faith, 8:10) — both Gentiles, both asking for somebody else, and neither present when the healing happens. The crowd at vv. 29-31 is Gentile, and Matthew signals it by how they worship: they glorified "the God of Israel", which is what an outsider says. Which explains the second feeding — and the two are not one story twice. The basket words differ consistently: kophinos at the five thousand (a small stiff wicker basket a Jew carried his own food in) and spyris at the four thousand (a hamper big enough to hold a man — the one Paul was lowered down the Damascus wall in, Acts 9:25). Jesus himself distinguishes the two events at 16:9-10.
verseByVerse.theology: The Canaanite woman episode is one of the most theologically dense in Matthew. Jesus's apparent reluctance — "I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel" and the difficult "dogs" saying — is best understood as testing her faith rather than expressing genuine exclusion. Her response — "Yes, Lord, yet even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters' table" — is the model of faith that does not demand, does not argue, does not claim rights, but presses through apparent rejection on the strength of the Savior's character. Jesus pronounces her faith "great" — the only time this word is used of any individual's faith in the Synoptics.
verseByVerse.examples: The second feeding (four thousand) parallels the first (five thousand) but occurs in Gentile territory — the region of the Decapolis. Where the first feeding fed a Jewish crowd (twelve baskets, echoing the twelve tribes), the second feeds a largely Gentile crowd (seven baskets, echoing the seven Gentile nations of Canaan). The Messiah who first came to the lost sheep of Israel is already extending his table to the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus went away from there and withdrew to the district of Tyre and Sidon. And behold, a Canaanite woman from that region came out and was crying, "Have mercy on me, O Lord, Son of David; my daughter is severely oppressed by a demon."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus withdrew to the region of Tyre and Sidon. A Canaanite woman from that area came out crying: have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David! My daughter is severely oppressed by a demon.

And Jesus went away from there and withdrew to the district of Tyre and Sidon. Gentile territory on the Mediterranean coast, north of Galilee, in modern Lebanon (see 11:21). Jesus left Jewish territory, perhaps to rest and to escape the hostility of the Pharisees. Having just declared that food laws do not make people unclean, he now goes among Gentiles, who were considered unclean.

And behold, a Canaanite woman from that region came out. Mark calls her a Syrophoenician by birth, a Greek (Mark 7:26). Matthew uses the ancient name “Canaanite”: the people who lived in the land before Israel, Israel’s old enemies, whom God had commanded Israel to drive out. To a Jewish reader, it was the most alien, pagan label possible. Yet Rahab, another Canaanite woman, is in Jesus’ genealogy (1:5).

And was crying, “Have mercy on me, O Lord, Son of David.” Remarkable. A pagan woman uses a Jewish messianic title: Son of David. She recognises who Jesus is, as the blind men did (9:27). “Have mercy”: she knows she has no claim on him.

My daughter is severely oppressed by a demon. She pleads for her daughter, not herself. A mother’s desperate love.

In a sentence. In Gentile territory, a Canaanite woman cried to Jesus as the Son of David, begging mercy for her demon-oppressed daughter.

On a Tuesday. Whom do you plead for before Jesus: a child, a friend, someone in deep trouble? Bring them to him as this mother did.
verseByVerse.note: Tyre and Sidon were Gentile cities on the coast north of Galilee. Mark calls her a Syrophoenician; Matthew uses the old name Canaanite, Israel’s ancient enemies.

parallels.desc: Elijah and the widow of Zarephath, near Sidon

verseByVerse.quote: But he did not answer her a word. And his disciples came and begged him, saying, "Send her away, for she is crying out after us." He answered, "I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus did not answer her a word. His disciples urged him to send her away, because she kept crying after them. He answered: I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.

But he did not answer her a word. A startling silence. Jesus, who always had compassion, said nothing. His silence was a test of her faith, which would make it shine all the more. Sometimes God is silent before he answers.

And his disciples came and begged him, saying, “Send her away, for she is crying out after us.” They found her annoying and embarrassing. “Send her away” may mean “Give her what she wants and get rid of her”, or simply “Get rid of her”. Either way, they had no compassion for her (compare 14:15).

He answered, “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” The same principle as 10:6. Jesus’ mission during his earthly ministry was first to Israel, the people of the covenant. This was God’s order: the Jew first, then the nations (Romans 1:16). The woman was outside that mission.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus was prejudiced against Gentiles, or that he did not care about her. He had already healed a Gentile’s servant (8:5–13). He was stating God’s plan for his earthly ministry, and testing her, as the outcome shows.

In a sentence. Jesus at first was silent, and then explained that his mission was to Israel, while the disciples wanted her sent away.

On a Tuesday. If God seems silent to your prayers, keep praying. His silence is not his last word.

parallels.desc: the lost sheep of the house of Israel
a servant to the circumcised, that the Gentiles might glorify God

verseByVerse.quote: But she came and knelt before him, saying, "Lord, help me." And he answered, "It is not right to take the children's bread and throw it to the dogs."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But she came, knelt before him, and said: Lord, help me. He answered: it is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.

But she came and knelt before him. She would not be put off. She came closer and bowed down before him (prosekynei, worshipped).

Saying, “Lord, help me.” The simplest prayer. She drops the title “Son of David”, which belonged to Israel, and appeals simply to him as Lord.

And he answered, “It is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.” A hard saying. The “children” are Israel; the “bread” is the blessings of the Messiah’s ministry; the “dogs” are Gentiles. Jews often called Gentiles “dogs” as an insult. But Jesus uses a diminutive word (kynaria), meaning “little dogs”, household pets, not wild street dogs. The picture is of a family meal, where the children are fed first, and the pets wait under the table. Mark adds the word “first”: let the children be fed first (Mark 7:27), implying that the Gentiles’ turn would come.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus was cruel or contemptuous. His words were a test, drawing out her faith, and they used a picture that left room for her answer. Nor does it mean that Gentiles are inferior. The priority of Israel was a matter of God’s order in history, not of human worth. Within months, the gospel would go to all nations (28:19).

In a sentence. She knelt and pleaded, and Jesus tested her with a picture of children’s bread not being given to the household dogs.

On a Tuesday. When God’s answer seems hard, keep coming. Persistent, humble prayer is not rejected.
verseByVerse.note: “Dogs” was a common Jewish insult for Gentiles; here the picture is of household dogs under the table.

verseByVerse.quote: She said, "Yes, Lord, yet even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters' table." Then Jesus answered her, "O woman, great is your faith! Let it be done for you as you desire." And her daughter was healed instantly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She said: yes, Lord, yet even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table. Jesus answered: woman, great is your faith! Let it be done for you as you desire. And her daughter was healed at that moment.

Yes, Lord. She accepts his words. She does not argue that she deserves the bread, or that she is as good as the children. She takes the place he has given her.

Yet even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table. A brilliant, humble answer. She takes Jesus’ own picture and finds hope in it. Even the household dogs get the crumbs. She does not ask for the children’s place, only for a crumb. And she understands that Jesus’ power is so great that even a crumb of it is enough to heal her daughter. The children can keep their bread; there is more than enough for her too.

Then Jesus answered her, “O woman, great is your faith!” The disciples were often called “of little faith” (8:26; 14:31; 16:8). This Gentile woman, like the Gentile centurion (8:10), is praised for great faith. Her faith was great because it was humble (she claimed nothing), persistent (she would not give up), and confident in Jesus’ power and mercy.

Be it done for you as you desire. Jesus gives her what she asked.

And her daughter was healed instantly. At a distance, like the centurion’s servant.

The lesson. The Pharisees had all the privileges of the children and rejected the bread; a Canaanite woman had no privileges, and received it by faith. It is a picture of the gospel going to the nations, and of the faith that God honours: humble, persistent, and trusting in his grace.

In a sentence. The woman humbly asked only for a crumb of Jesus’ mercy, and he praised her great faith and healed her daughter.

On a Tuesday. Great faith is humble faith. Come to God claiming nothing, but trusting everything to his mercy.

For worship. Thank God that there is more than enough of his mercy for outsiders like us.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus went on from there and walked beside the Sea of Galilee. And he went up on the mountain and sat down there. And great crowds came to him, bringing with them the lame, the blind, the crippled, the mute, and many others, and they put them at his feet, and he healed them,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus went on along the Sea of Galilee, went up on a mountain and sat down. Great crowds came to him, bringing the lame, the blind, the crippled, the mute and many others, and laid them at his feet, and he healed them.

Jesus went on from there and walked beside the Sea of Galilee. Mark places this in the Decapolis, the Gentile region east of the lake (Mark 7:31). The crowd was probably largely Gentile.

And he went up on the mountain and sat down there. As at the Sermon on the Mount (5:1).

And great crowds came to him, bringing with them the lame, the blind, the crippled, the mute, and many others. Isaiah’s list of the signs of salvation (Isaiah 35:5–6).

And they put them at his feet, and he healed them. The crowd laid their sick at his feet: a picture of dependence.

In a sentence. Great crowds, probably largely Gentile, brought their sick to Jesus on a mountain, and he healed them.

On a Tuesday. Lay your needs at Jesus’ feet today in prayer.
verseByVerse.note: Mark places this in the Decapolis, the Gentile region east of the lake.

parallels.desc: the lame leap and the mute sing

verseByVerse.quote: so that the crowd wondered, when they saw the mute speaking, the crippled healthy, the lame walking, and the blind seeing. And they glorified the God of Israel. Then Jesus called his disciples to him and said, "I have compassion on the crowd because they have been with me now three days and have nothing to eat. And I am unwilling to send them away hungry, lest they faint on the way."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd was amazed when they saw the mute speaking, the crippled made well, the lame walking and the blind seeing, and they glorified the God of Israel. Then Jesus called his disciples and said: I have compassion on the crowd, because they have been with me three days and have nothing to eat.

So that the crowd wondered. Amazement at God’s power.

And they glorified the God of Israel. The phrase suggests that the crowd was mainly Gentile: they praised Israel’s God, a God not their own. The prophets promised that the nations would come to worship Israel’s God (Isaiah 2:2–3).

Then Jesus called his disciples to him and said, “I have compassion on the crowd.” Deep compassion (see 9:36; 14:14).

Because they have been with me now three days and have nothing to eat. They had stayed so long that their food had run out. The longer meeting suggests great hunger for his teaching.

And I am unwilling to send them away hungry, lest they faint on the way. Jesus cares about their bodies. Some had come a long way (Mark 8:3).

In a sentence. The largely Gentile crowd praised Israel’s God for the healings, and Jesus had compassion on them after three days without food.

On a Tuesday. Jesus cares about practical needs as well as spiritual ones. Notice the hungry around you.
verseByVerse.note: “The God of Israel” may suggest a largely Gentile crowd.

verseByVerse.quote: And the disciples said to him, "Where are we to get enough bread in such a desolate place to feed so great a crowd?" And Jesus said to them, "How many loaves do you have?" They said, "Seven, and a few small fish."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples said: where can we get enough bread in this remote place to feed such a crowd? Jesus asked how many loaves they had. They said: seven, and a few small fish.

Where are we to get enough bread in such a desolate place to feed so great a crowd? Astonishingly, the disciples seem to have forgotten the feeding of the five thousand (14:13–21). Their question shows how slow they were to learn (16:9–10). We are often the same: God provides, and we forget at the next crisis.

How many loaves do you have? As before, Jesus starts with what they have.

They said, “Seven, and a few small fish.” More than last time, and a bigger crowd: but still nothing like enough.

In a sentence. The disciples, forgetting the earlier miracle, asked where bread could be found, and had only seven loaves and a few fish.

On a Tuesday. Remember God’s past provision when you face new needs. Write down how he has helped you before.

parallels.desc: Moses asks how so many can be fed

verseByVerse.quote: And directing the crowd to sit down on the ground, he took the seven loaves and the fish, and having given thanks he broke them and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus told the crowd to sit on the ground. He took the seven loaves and the fish, gave thanks, broke them and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds.

And directing the crowd to sit down on the ground. As before (14:19).

He took the seven loaves and the fish, and having given thanks he broke them and gave them to the disciples. The same pattern as the first feeding and the Last Supper: took, gave thanks, broke, gave (14:19; 26:26). “Given thanks” (eucharistēsas) is the word from which “Eucharist” comes.

And the disciples gave them to the crowds. Again Jesus works through his disciples.

In a sentence. Jesus gave thanks, broke the loaves, and gave them through his disciples to the crowd.

On a Tuesday. You are one of the disciples who distribute what Christ provides. Whom could you serve today?

verseByVerse.quote: And they all ate and were satisfied. And they took up seven baskets full of the broken pieces left over. Those who ate were four thousand men, besides women and children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They all ate and were satisfied, and the disciples gathered seven baskets full of leftover pieces. Those who ate were four thousand men, besides women and children.

And they all ate and were satisfied. Full provision, as before.

And they took up seven baskets full of the broken pieces left over. The word for “basket” here (spyris) is different from the one used at the feeding of the five thousand (14:20). These were large baskets, big enough to hold a man (Paul was let down from the wall of Damascus in one, Acts 9:25). Seven may suggest completeness.

Those who ate were four thousand men, besides women and children. A different event from the feeding of the five thousand. Jesus himself refers to both separately (16:9–10). The first feeding was mainly for a Jewish crowd, the second probably for a Gentile one. Some see a picture: Jesus is the bread of life for Jews and Gentiles alike.

What it does not mean. Not that this is a duplicate account of the same miracle. The numbers, place, baskets and audience differ, and Jesus distinguishes them.

In a sentence. Four thousand men, plus women and children, ate and were satisfied, and seven large baskets were left over.

For worship. Thank Jesus that he provides abundantly for all who come to him.
verseByVerse.note: The word for these baskets is different from the one used at the feeding of the five thousand, and could mean a large hamper.

parallels.desc: Paul let down in such a basket

verseByVerse.quote: And after sending away the crowds, he got into the boat and went to the region of Magadan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After sending the crowds away, Jesus got into the boat and went to the region of Magadan.

And after sending away the crowds. Jesus dismissed them with their needs met.

He got into the boat and went to the region of Magadan. The location is uncertain. Mark calls it Dalmanutha (Mark 8:10), also unknown. It was probably on the western shore of the lake, perhaps near Magdala, the home of Mary Magdalene. There the Pharisees and Sadducees will meet him (16:1).

In a sentence. Jesus dismissed the crowds and crossed to the region of Magadan.

On a Tuesday. Jesus moved from place to place, meeting needs wherever he went. Where might he be sending you this week?
verseByVerse.note: The location of Magadan is uncertain; Mark names it Dalmanutha.

15.theology: Total depravity and the need for regeneration. Matthew 15:18–19 is one of the clearest statements of the doctrine of the heart’s corruption in the Gospels. The evil that defiles comes not from outside but from within — from the heart that Jeremiah described as “deceitful above all things” (Jer 17:9). Reformed theology insists that this corruption is total in extent (reaching every faculty) though not infinite in degree (common grace restrains it). The implication is that the solution must be equally radical: not education, not ceremony, not moral effort, but the new heart promised in Ezekiel 36:26 — “I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh.” That is the work of regeneration by the Spirit, purchased by the cross of Christ.
15.examples:
Then: The Pharisees’ tradition had become a way of performing piety while avoiding its cost. The Corban ruling let a man appear devout while dishonoring his parents. Religion had become a loophole system. Jesus shut it down.

Now: Every generation finds ways to honour God with the lips while protecting the heart from real submission. Theological correctness without personal holiness, church attendance without costly love, tithing without generosity of spirit — all are versions of the Pharisaic trap. The Canaanite woman is the antidote: no credentials, no performance, just desperate faith in the mercy of Christ. That is always enough.

16.title: Who Do You Say I Am?
16.text: <sup>1</sup>And the Pharisees and Sadducees came, and to test him they asked him to show them a sign from heaven. <sup>2</sup>He answered them, “When it is evening, you say, ‘It will be fair weather, for the sky is red.’ <sup>3</sup>And in the morning, ‘It will be stormy today, for the sky is red and threatening.’ You know how to interpret the appearance of the sky, but you cannot interpret the signs of the times. <sup>4</sup>An evil and adulterous generation seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah.” So he left them and departed. <sup>5</sup>When the disciples reached the other side, they had forgotten to bring any bread. <sup>6</sup>Jesus said to them, “Watch and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” <sup>7</sup>And they began discussing it among themselves, saying, “We brought no bread.” <sup>8</sup>But Jesus, aware of this, said, “O you of little faith, why are you discussing among yourselves the fact that you have no bread? <sup>9</sup>Do you not yet perceive? Do you not remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many baskets you gathered? <sup>10</sup>Or the seven loaves for the four thousand, and how many baskets you gathered? <sup>11</sup>How is it that you fail to understand that I did not speak about bread? Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” <sup>12</sup>Then they understood that he did not tell them to beware of the leaven of bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees. <sup>13</sup>Now when Jesus came into the district of Caesarea Philippi, he asked his disciples, “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” <sup>14</sup>And they said, “Some say John the Baptist, others say Elijah, and others Jeremiah or one of the prophets.” <sup>15</sup>He said to them, “But who do you say that I am?” <sup>16</sup>Simon Peter replied, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” <sup>17</sup>And Jesus answered him, “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah! For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. <sup>18</sup>And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. <sup>19</sup>I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.” <sup>20</sup>Then he strictly charged the disciples to tell no one that he was the Christ. <sup>21</sup>From that time Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised. <sup>22</sup>And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him, saying, “Far be it from you, Lord! This shall never happen to you.” <sup>23</sup>But he turned and said to Peter, “Get behind me, Satan! You are a hindrance to me. For you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of man.” <sup>24</sup>Then Jesus told his disciples, “If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me. <sup>25</sup>For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will find it. <sup>26</sup>For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul? Or what shall a man give in return for his soul? <sup>27</sup>For the Son of Man is going to come with his angels in the glory of his Father, and then he will repay each person according to what he has done. <sup>28</sup>Truly, I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom.”
16.overview:
Chapter 16 is the turning point of Matthew’s Gospel. Peter’s confession — “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” — is the summit of the disciples’ journey of recognition. Jesus affirms it as divinely revealed, not humanly deduced, and builds the future of his church on this confession. But he immediately turns to the cross: the Christ, the Son of the living God, must go to Jerusalem and die. Peter, who has just made the highest confession of faith in the Gospel, immediately becomes “Satan” — a stumbling block — by refusing the necessity of the cross.

The pairing is deliberate and profound. You cannot confess Jesus as Christ without receiving the cross. Caesarea Philippi was a pagan city at the foot of Mount Hermon, a centre of Roman imperial cult and pagan worship. Here, at the edge of empire and paganism, Jesus declares that he will build his church — and the gates of hell will not prevail. The church is built on the confession, and on Peter only as the first man to make it; and it advances not by cultural power but by the cruciform mission of a cruciform King.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — The Sign of Jonah, Peter's Confession, and the Keys of the Kingdom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Pharisees and Sadducees demand a sign from heaven. Jesus refuses, offering only the sign of Jonah, and warns the disciples about the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees. At Caesarea Philippi he asks the disciples who they say he is, and Peter confesses: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." Jesus pronounces a blessing on Peter, declares he will build his church on this rock, and gives him the keys of the kingdom. Then, having accepted the confession, he forbids them to repeat it (v. 20): the title is true, but it is sealed until the cross can say what kind of Christ he is.
verseByVerse.theology: Peter's confession is the christological climax of the first half of Matthew's Gospel. The question Jesus asks — "But who do you say that I am?" — is addressed to the disciples after they have lived with him through chapters 4-15. Peter's answer is the only possible answer for those who have truly seen: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." Jesus responds with the foundational promise of the church's existence: "I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it." The church does not build itself; it is built by Christ on the confession of who he is. The first half of the section is a study in reading. Men who can forecast weather cannot read the moment they are standing in (vv. 1-4), and the only sign they will get is a grave and an empty tomb. The leaven warning that follows (vv. 5-12) names the two ways a faith is brought under human management: the Pharisees added to God's word until their tradition outranked it, the Sadducees subtracted from it until nothing supernatural was left, and verse 12 calls the two of them one teaching. And the section closes on a deliberate silence (v. 20). The confession is true and the definition in the hearers' heads is false, so the title goes under guard until Jerusalem explains it — and the ban is lifted only when the risen Christ commands the nations to be told (28:19).
verseByVerse.examples: "Who do you say that I am?" is the question every person must answer. The crowds reach for the biggest names they have — John the Baptist, Elijah, Jeremiah — and every one of them belongs to the past and is a forerunner, a signpost rather than a destination. Peter offers the only category that fits the evidence: Messiah, Son of the living God. The confession is the door through which everything else follows — the keys of the kingdom, the binding and loosing, the promise that the church will stand against the gates of hell. The church is not a human institution that may or may not endure; it is Christ's building, constructed on the indestructible foundation of the confession that he is Lord. Two practical edges run through the same section. The leaven warning is spoken to the Twelve about themselves, with no opponent present — it is not a licence to hunt heresy in other people but a question about which way your own faith drifts when nobody is checking: toward a list of things you are careful about, or toward a quiet removal of everything in the Bible that would be awkward to say out loud at work. And the silence of verse 20 is a warning to anyone impatient for results: it is entirely possible to get a man to say the right sentence about Jesus by leaving out what it costs. Our Lord had that option, with a crowd ready to take it, and chose silence instead.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Pharisees and Sadducees came, and to test him they asked him to show them a sign from heaven. He answered them, "When it is evening, you say, 'It will be fair weather, for the sky is red.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees and Sadducees came to test Jesus, demanding a sign from heaven. He answered: in the evening you say, it will be fair weather, for the sky is red.

And the Pharisees and Sadducees came. Normally rivals (see 3:7), they now join forces against Jesus. The Pharisees were strict about the law and traditions; the Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy who denied the resurrection. Shared opposition to Jesus united them.

And to test him. “Test” (peirazontes) is the word used of the devil tempting Jesus (4:1). Their request was not honest seeking, but a trap.

They asked him to show them a sign from heaven. Not another healing, which they explained away (12:24), but a spectacular sign in the sky, proving beyond doubt that God was with him: like Elijah calling down fire (1 Kings 18:38), or manna from heaven. They had already asked for a sign and been refused (12:38–39).

He answered them, “When it is evening, you say, ‘It will be fair weather, for the sky is red.’” A red sky in the evening meant good weather the next day. Farmers and fishermen read the sky expertly.

Textual note. Verses 2b–3 (“When it is evening … the signs of the times”) are missing in some important early manuscripts. They may have been added from a similar saying in Luke 12:54–56. Verdict: the evidence is divided; the saying is certainly authentic as Jesus’ teaching (Luke has a parallel), whether or not Matthew wrote it here. The ESV includes it.

In a sentence. Jesus’ united opponents demanded a sign from heaven to test him, and he began by pointing out how well they read the weather.

On a Tuesday. Demanding proof on our terms is not seeking God. Look at the evidence he has already given.

parallels.desc: reading the sky but not the times

verseByVerse.quote: "And in the morning, 'It will be stormy today, for the sky is red and threatening.' You know how to interpret the appearance of the sky, but you cannot interpret the signs of the times. An evil and adulterous generation seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah." So he left them and departed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the morning you say, it will be stormy today, because the sky is red and threatening. You know how to read the sky, but you cannot read the signs of the times. An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, but none will be given except the sign of Jonah. And he left them.

And in the morning, “It will be stormy today, for the sky is red and threatening.” A red sky in the morning warned of storms. (The English proverb: red sky at night, shepherd’s delight; red sky in the morning, shepherd’s warning.)

You know how to interpret the appearance of the sky, but you cannot interpret the signs of the times. They could read the weather, but not God’s work in history. The “signs of the times” were all around them: Jesus’ miracles, his teaching, the fulfilment of prophecy, John the Baptist. The kingdom had arrived, and they could not see it, because they did not want to (13:13–15).

An evil and adulterous generation seeks for a sign. The same words as 12:39 (see there).

But no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah. Jesus’ death and resurrection (12:40). The greatest sign was coming; they would not believe even that (28:11–15).

So he left them and departed. A solemn moment. Jesus walks away from those who refuse to see. There is a point when God leaves people to their unbelief.

In a sentence. The religious leaders could read the weather but not the signs of God’s kingdom, and Jesus refused them any sign but his resurrection, and left them.

On a Tuesday. Are you skilled at reading the markets, the news or the culture, but blind to what God is doing? Pray for eyes to see.

verseByVerse.quote: When the disciples reached the other side, they had forgotten to bring any bread. Jesus said to them, "Watch and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the disciples crossed the lake, they had forgotten to bring bread. Jesus said to them: watch out, and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.

When the disciples reached the other side, they had forgotten to bring any bread. Mark says they had only one loaf (Mark 8:14).

Jesus said to them, “Watch and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” “Leaven” (yeast) works invisibly through dough until it permeates the whole lump (see 13:33). In Scripture it often pictures a corrupting influence that spreads quietly (1 Corinthians 5:6–8; Galatians 5:9). At Passover, Israel had to remove all leaven from their homes (Exodus 12:15). Jesus warns his disciples that the teaching and attitudes of the religious leaders could spread into their own hearts.

In a sentence. Jesus warned his disciples against the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.

On a Tuesday. Wrong ideas spread quietly. What influences are working their way into your thinking without your noticing?
verseByVerse.note: Leaven (yeast) works invisibly through the whole lump; it often pictures a corrupting influence.

parallels.desc: a little leaven leavens the whole lump

verseByVerse.quote: And they began discussing it among themselves, saying, "We brought no bread." But Jesus, aware of this, said, "O you of little faith, why are you discussing among yourselves the fact that you have no bread?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples discussed it among themselves: it is because we brought no bread. Jesus, knowing this, said: you of little faith, why are you discussing among yourselves that you have no bread?

And they began discussing it among themselves, saying, “We brought no bread.” They took Jesus literally: they thought he was rebuking them for forgetting bread, or warning them not to buy bread from Pharisees. They were thinking on the level of food, while he was speaking of the spirit.

But Jesus, aware of this. Again he knows their thoughts (9:4; 12:25).

O you of little faith. See 6:30; 8:26; 14:31. Their worry about bread showed they had not trusted him.

Why are you discussing among yourselves the fact that you have no bread? After two miraculous feedings, why worry about bread?

In a sentence. The disciples misunderstood Jesus and worried about forgetting bread, and he rebuked their little faith.

On a Tuesday. What practical worry are you discussing endlessly, when you could simply trust Jesus with it?

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not yet perceive? Do you not remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many baskets you gathered? Or the seven loaves for the four thousand, and how many baskets you gathered?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you still not understand? Don’t you remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many baskets you gathered? Or the seven loaves for the four thousand, and how many baskets you gathered?

Do you not yet perceive? After all they have seen, they still do not understand.

Do you not remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many baskets you gathered? Twelve baskets (14:20).

Or the seven loaves for the four thousand, and how many baskets you gathered? Seven baskets (15:37). Jesus reminds them of both feedings, separately. Their memory of God’s past provision should have removed their anxiety. Forgetting what God has done is at the root of much unbelief (Psalm 78:11, 42; 103:2).

In a sentence. Jesus reminded the disciples of both miraculous feedings, to show that they had no reason to worry about bread.

On a Tuesday. Remember how God has provided for you in the past. Recall a specific time today, and let it strengthen your trust.

verseByVerse.quote: How is it that you fail to understand that I did not speak about bread? Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees." Then they understood that he did not tell them to beware of the leaven of bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees.
verseByVerse.commentary:
How can you fail to understand that I was not talking about bread? Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees. Then they understood that he meant their teaching, not the yeast in bread.

How is it that you fail to understand that I did not speak about bread? Jesus speaks in pictures; they must learn to think spiritually.

Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees. He repeats the warning.

Then they understood that he did not tell them to beware of the leaven of bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees. Their teaching: the Pharisees’ legalism and hypocrisy (Luke 12:1 calls their leaven hypocrisy), their human traditions overruling God’s word (15:1–9), and their demand for signs while rejecting the evidence; and the Sadducees’ worldly scepticism, denial of the resurrection, and compromise with power (22:23). Different errors, but both corrupting, and both opposed to Jesus. Mark adds the leaven of Herod (Mark 8:15): political worldliness.

What it does not mean. Not that every Pharisee or Sadducee taught nothing true. Jesus says elsewhere to do what the scribes teach from Moses, but not what they do (23:2–3). The danger was their characteristic errors, which could spread unnoticed.

In a sentence. The disciples finally understood that Jesus was warning them against the corrupting teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees.

On a Tuesday. The two main dangers are still with us: legalism (adding rules and pride) and scepticism (doubting the supernatural and compromising with the world). Which one are you more tempted by?

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus came into the district of Caesarea Philippi, he asked his disciples, "Who do people say that the Son of Man is?" And they said, "Some say John the Baptist, others say Elijah, and others Jeremiah or one of the prophets."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the region of Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asked his disciples: who do people say the Son of Man is? They answered: some say John the Baptist, others Elijah, others Jeremiah or one of the prophets.

Now when Jesus came into the district of Caesarea Philippi. A Gentile city about twenty-five miles (forty kilometres) north of the Sea of Galilee, at the foot of Mount Hermon, at one of the sources of the Jordan. It had been a centre for the worship of the Greek god Pan; there was a great cave and spring, with shrines carved into the rock face. Herod the Great built a white marble temple there to Caesar Augustus. His son Philip rebuilt the town and named it Caesarea in honour of Caesar, and “Philippi” after himself, to distinguish it from Caesarea on the coast. Against this backdrop of pagan gods, emperor worship and a great rock, Jesus asks who he is.

Who do people say that the Son of Man is? The turning point of Matthew’s Gospel. Jesus has taught and worked for months. Now he asks what people have concluded.

Some say John the Baptist. Like Herod (14:2).

Others say Elijah. The prophet whose coming was promised before the day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5).

And others Jeremiah. Only Matthew mentions Jeremiah. Jeremiah was the weeping prophet, who suffered and was rejected by his people. Some Jewish traditions expected Jeremiah to return before the Messiah.

Or one of the prophets. All were complimentary opinions. People held Jesus in high regard as a great prophet. But none was high enough.

What it does not mean. Not that these opinions were wicked. They were honourable, but inadequate. Many today hold similar views: Jesus was a great teacher, a prophet, a good man. But that is not enough.

In a sentence. At Caesarea Philippi, amid pagan shrines, Jesus asked who people thought he was, and the answers, though honourable, all fell short.

On a Tuesday. What do people around you say about Jesus? Listen, and be ready to say who he truly is.
verseByVerse.note: Caesarea Philippi was a Gentile city at the foot of Mount Hermon, north of the Sea of Galilee, with a shrine to the god Pan.

parallels.desc: Herod thinks he is John raised

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "But who do you say that I am?" Simon Peter replied, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Jesus asked: but who do you say that I am? Simon Peter answered: you are the Christ, the Son of the living God.

But who do you say that I am? “You” is plural and emphatic: you, my disciples. It is not enough to know what others think. Everyone must answer this question personally. It is the most important question anyone will ever answer.

Simon Peter replied. As spokesman for the Twelve.

You are the Christ. The Messiah, the Anointed One, the promised King of David’s line (see 1:1). Not merely a prophet who points to the Messiah, but the Messiah himself.

The Son of the living God. Not only a title of the Davidic king (Psalm 2:7), but more. The disciples had confessed him as the Son of God after he walked on the water (14:33). “The living God” is an Old Testament title contrasting the true God with dead idols (Joshua 3:10; Psalm 42:2; Jeremiah 10:10), especially fitting here, surrounded by the shrines of Pan and Caesar. Peter confesses that Jesus belongs to the one true, living God as his unique Son.

What it does not mean. Not that Peter fully understood what he said. He immediately showed that he did not understand that the Messiah must suffer (v. 22). But his confession was true, and it was revealed by God.

In a sentence. Peter confessed that Jesus is the Messiah and the Son of the living God.

On a Tuesday. Who do you say Jesus is? Not who your parents, church or culture say, but you.

For worship. Confess it with Peter: you are the Christ, the Son of the living God.

parallels.desc: “you are the Holy One of God”

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered him, "Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah! For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said: blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, because no human being revealed this to you, but my Father in heaven. And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.

Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah! “Bar-Jonah” is Aramaic for “son of Jonah” (John calls his father John, John 1:42; 21:15, perhaps a variant of the same name). Jesus calls him blessed: favoured by God (see 5:3).

For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you. “Flesh and blood” means human beings, human reasoning. Peter did not reach this conclusion by his own cleverness, or because others told him.

But my Father who is in heaven. God revealed it to him. Saving knowledge of Christ is always a gift of God’s grace (11:25–27; 1 Corinthians 12:3).

And I tell you, you are Peter. “Peter” (Petros) means rock or stone. Jesus had given Simon this name earlier (John 1:42); now he explains it.

And on this rock I will build my church. A wordplay: Petros (Peter) and petra (rock). In Aramaic, which Jesus probably spoke, both would be Kepha (Cephas). What is “this rock”? The main views:

1. Peter himself. Peter, as the first to confess Christ and the leader of the apostles, is the foundation stone on which Christ builds his church. This fits the wordplay best. It does not exclude the other apostles: the church is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:20; Revelation 21:14), with Peter first among them. Peter did lead the early church: he preached at Pentecost (Acts 2) and opened the door to the Gentiles (Acts 10).

2. Peter’s confession. The truth Peter confessed, that Jesus is the Christ, is the rock. Many Reformers held this.

3. Christ himself. Christ is the rock and the foundation (1 Corinthians 3:11; 1 Peter 2:4–8).

Verdict: the most natural reading is Peter himself, as the confessing apostle, the first stone of the foundation. But this gives no support to the papacy. Nothing in the text speaks of successors, of Rome, or of a supreme authority over the other apostles. Peter’s foundational role, like that of all the apostles, was unique and unrepeatable: a foundation is laid only once. The rock is Peter as the confessor of Christ: Peter and his confession cannot be separated.

I will build my church. “Church” (ekklēsia) means assembly, the gathered people of God. The Greek Old Testament used it for the assembly of Israel. Only here and in 18:17 does the word appear in the Gospels. “My” church: it belongs to Christ. “I will build”: Christ himself builds it. The church is his work, not ours.

And the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. “Hell” here is Hades, the realm of the dead (ESV footnote). “Gates” stand for the power of a city. The gates of Hades are the power of death. Death will not overcome Christ’s church. Christ, who will rise from the dead, holds the keys of death and Hades (Revelation 1:18). His people will be raised; the church cannot be destroyed.

Where Christians differ: Peter and the papacy. Roman Catholic teaching holds that Christ made Peter the head of the whole church, that Peter was the first bishop of Rome, and that his authority passes to each pope as his successor. Orthodox and Protestant churches reject this. Peter was a leader among the apostles, but Paul rebuked him publicly (Galatians 2:11–14); James led the council at Jerusalem (Acts 15:13–21); and Peter called himself a fellow elder (1 Peter 5:1). The New Testament says nothing about successors to Peter’s role or about Rome. Verdict: Peter had a unique foundational role, which no successor inherits. The church’s authority now rests on the apostolic teaching preserved in Scripture.

In a sentence. Jesus blessed Peter for a confession revealed by the Father, and promised to build his church on Peter, the confessing apostle, a church that death itself cannot overcome.

On a Tuesday. Christ is building his church, and nothing can destroy it. When you are discouraged about the church, remember whose church it is.
verseByVerse.note: Bar-Jonah means “son of Jonah.” Peter means “rock.” The ESV notes that “hell” here renders Hades, the realm of the dead; its gates stand for the power of death. A play on words: “Peter” (Petros) and “rock” (petra) are closely related Greek words.

parallels.desc: built on the foundation of the apostles

verseByVerse.quote: I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven." Then he strictly charged the disciples to tell no one that he was the Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you bind on earth will have been bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will have been loosed in heaven. Then he strictly told the disciples to tell no one that he was the Christ.

I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Keys represent authority: to open and shut, to admit and exclude. Isaiah 22:22 speaks of the key of the house of David given to a steward, who opens and no one shuts, and shuts and no one opens. Jesus gives Peter authority to open the kingdom to people. Peter used the keys when he preached at Pentecost and three thousand entered (Acts 2:14–41), when he preached to the Samaritans (Acts 8:14–17), and when he opened the door to the Gentiles in Cornelius’ house (Acts 10). The keys are the preaching of the gospel, which opens the kingdom to those who believe and shuts it to those who refuse. The scribes, by contrast, shut the kingdom in people’s faces (23:13).

And whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven. “Bind” and “loose” were rabbinic terms meaning to forbid and permit, and also to condemn and acquit. The Greek tense is a future perfect: “shall have been bound in heaven”. The apostles do not decide things that heaven then must follow; they declare on earth what God has already decided in heaven. Their authority is to declare God’s will, not to create it.

And whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven. To declare what is permitted, and to pronounce forgiveness to those who repent (John 20:23).

The same authority given to all. In 18:18, Jesus gives the same authority to bind and loose to all the disciples, and to the church in its discipline. The keys belong to the church as a whole, exercised through the preaching of the gospel and the discipline of the church (Westminster Confession 30.2).

Then he strictly charged the disciples to tell no one that he was the Christ. Why? Because the people had political expectations of the Messiah (see 8:4; 14:22). The disciples themselves did not yet understand that the Messiah must suffer and die (v. 21). Only after the cross and resurrection could the title be proclaimed without misunderstanding.

What it does not mean. Not that a church or minister can forgive or condemn arbitrarily. The keys work only in line with God’s word. Nor does it support the Roman Catholic doctrine of papal authority or priestly absolution as an independent power.

In a sentence. Jesus gave Peter the keys of the kingdom: authority to open it by the gospel and to declare on earth what God has decided in heaven.

On a Tuesday. Every time you share the gospel, you are using the keys: opening the kingdom to those who will believe.
verseByVerse.note: Keys give authority to open and shut. “Bind” and “loose” were used of forbidding and permitting.

parallels.desc: the key of the house of David
the same authority given to all the disciples

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–28 — The First Passion Prediction and the Call to Cross-Bearing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: From the moment of Peter's confession, Jesus begins to teach that he must go to Jerusalem, suffer, be killed, and rise on the third day. Peter rebukes him; Jesus rebukes Peter with the sharpest words in the Gospel: "Get behind me, Satan!" He then calls the crowd and disciples to cross-bearing: whoever loses his life for his sake will find it. The section ends with a warning about the coming of the Son of Man in his Father's glory. Between the two he asks what a man could possibly hand over in exchange for his soul (v. 26), and he closes by promising that some standing there will not taste death before they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom (v. 28) — a promise kept six days later on the mountain, as one of the men who heard it says himself (2 Pet 1:16-18).
verseByVerse.theology: The first passion prediction marks the watershed of Matthew's Gospel: the confession at Caesarea Philippi is the turning point from which Jesus now sets his face toward Jerusalem. The cross is not an unexpected tragedy but the appointed path. Peter's rebuttal — "Far be it from you, Lord! This shall never happen to you" — is the most natural human response and the most spiritually dangerous: it substitutes human preferences for divine purpose. "You are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of men" is the diagnosis of every theology that wants a cross-free Christianity. The section then puts a price on the choice. Verse 26 is a market question — what sum would buy back a soul? — and it is left unanswered until 20:28, where the Son of Man gives his own life as the ransom no man could pay. Verse 27 supplies the frame: he will repay each person according to what he has done. That is not a scoreboard, for Matthew twice rules one out — the impressive workers of 7:21-23 are turned away because they were never known, and the sheep of 25:31-46 cannot remember their own good deeds. Works are the evidence of a righteousness received, never the ground of it.
verseByVerse.examples: The cross-bearing saying moves from Jesus's cross to the disciple's: "If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me." The disciple's cross is not their personal hardships and inconveniences; it is the public cost of standing with a man under sentence, and the losing of a life organised around self-interest in order to find one organised around Christ. The paradox of verse 25 — finding life through losing it — is the gospel in miniature: the life surrendered to Jesus is the life truly found. Verse 26 makes the same point as a transaction. Ask a man what he would take for his car and he names a figure; ask what he would take for his son and he refuses the category outright. There is one thing in his possession that no market will quote, and it is himself. And verse 28 shows how this Master treats frightened followers: the cross-bearing call is issued on a Monday, so to speak, and by the following week three of them have been taken up a mountain and shown what the road ends in. The order of those two events is the mercy in them, and it is set out at vv. 23-24.

verseByVerse.quote: From that time Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised. And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him, saying, "Far be it from you, Lord! This shall never happen to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
From then on, Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem, suffer many things from the elders, chief priests and scribes, be killed, and on the third day be raised. Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him: far be it from you, Lord! This shall never happen to you.

From that time Jesus began. The second great turning point in Matthew (see 4:17). From now on, Jesus’ face is set toward Jerusalem and the cross.

To show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem. “Must” (dei): it is necessary, by God’s plan. Not an accident or a tragedy, but the purpose for which he came (20:28). The Scriptures required it (26:54; Luke 24:26).

And suffer many things from the elders and chief priests and scribes. The three groups who made up the Sanhedrin, the Jewish high council. The leaders of God’s people would reject God’s Messiah.

And be killed. A shocking statement. The Messiah was expected to conquer, not to die.

And on the third day be raised. The resurrection is part of the plan from the start. Jesus predicted his death and resurrection three times (16:21; 17:22–23; 20:18–19). The disciples heard the death, but apparently not the resurrection.

And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him. Peter, who had just confessed Jesus as the Christ, now presumes to correct him. “Rebuke” is a strong word: he scolded him.

Far be it from you, Lord! Literally “Mercy to you”, meaning “God forbid!”

This shall never happen to you. Peter loved Jesus and could not bear the thought of his death. And his idea of the Messiah had no room for suffering. A Messiah who dies is a defeated Messiah.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus was a victim of circumstances. He went to the cross willingly, by the Father’s plan (John 10:17–18; Acts 2:23).

In a sentence. Jesus began to teach that he must suffer, die and rise, and Peter, who could not accept it, rebuked him.

On a Tuesday. Do you want a Christ without a cross, a Christianity without suffering? Peter did. Accept God’s way, even when it is not yours.

verseByVerse.quote: But he turned and said to Peter, "Get behind me, Satan! You are a hindrance to me. For you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of man." Then Jesus told his disciples, "If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus turned and said to Peter: get behind me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to me, because you are thinking not as God thinks, but as people think. Then he told his disciples: anyone who wants to follow me must deny himself, take up his cross and follow me.

But he turned and said to Peter, “Get behind me, Satan!” Astonishing words, minutes after Jesus called Peter blessed. Peter was speaking Satan’s words: the same temptation Satan offered in the wilderness, the crown without the cross (4:8–10). Jesus used almost the same words then: “Be gone, Satan!” Satan can use even a loving friend to tempt us. “Get behind me” may also mean: get back in your place as a follower, behind me, not in front.

You are a hindrance to me. “Hindrance” is skandalon, a stumbling block, a trap. A wordplay: Peter, the “rock” on which the church would be built, has become a stone to trip over.

For you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of man. Peter was thinking by human standards: success, safety, power. God’s way was the way of the cross.

Then Jesus told his disciples, “If anyone would come after me.” Not only for the Twelve, but for anyone. Discipleship is defined.

Let him deny himself. Not deny himself things (like chocolate in Lent), but deny his self: say no to self as the master of his life. Peter would later deny Jesus (26:69–75); disciples must deny themselves instead.

And take up his cross. Like a condemned man carrying his crossbeam to execution (see 10:38). A willingness to die, to self and if necessary physically, for Jesus.

And follow me. Walk behind him, on the road he walks, which leads to the cross and through it to resurrection.

What it does not mean. Not that self-denial earns salvation, or that Christians should hate themselves. Self-denial is the response of those who have been loved and saved. Nor does it mean that Peter was demon-possessed or not a true disciple. He was a true disciple who, in that moment, spoke Satan’s thoughts.

In a sentence. Jesus rebuked Peter for speaking Satan’s temptation to avoid the cross, and called every disciple to deny himself, take up his cross and follow.

On a Tuesday. Where do you need to say no to yourself today in order to follow Jesus?

verseByVerse.quote: For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will find it. For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul? Or what shall a man give in return for his soul?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever wants to save his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for Jesus’ sake will find it. What will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and loses his soul? What can he give in exchange for his soul?

For whoever would save his life will lose it. “Life” (psychē) means the self, the soul, life itself. Those who try to protect their life, comfort and success by avoiding the cross will lose what matters most (see 10:39).

But whoever loses his life for my sake will find it. Those who give up their lives for Christ will find true and eternal life.

For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul? A business question: what is the profit? Imagine gaining everything the world offers: wealth, power, fame, pleasure. If you lose your soul, you have made the worst trade in history. The devil offered Jesus the whole world (4:8–9); Jesus refused.

Or what shall a man give in return for his soul? Nothing can buy back a lost soul. Psalm 49:7–9 says that no one can ransom another, for the ransom of their life is costly. Only Christ can pay that price (20:28).

In a sentence. Those who cling to their lives lose them, and those who give them up for Christ find them, because nothing in the world is worth one’s soul.

On a Tuesday. What are you trading your soul for: a career, a relationship, comfort? Count the cost honestly.

parallels.desc: the ransom of a life is costly

verseByVerse.quote: For the Son of Man is going to come with his angels in the glory of his Father, and then he will repay each person according to what he has done. Truly, I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Son of Man is going to come with his angels in his Father’s glory, and he will repay each person according to what he has done. Truly, some standing here will not taste death before they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom.

For the Son of Man is going to come with his angels in the glory of his Father. The one who must suffer (v. 21) will come in glory. The suffering Servant is also the glorious Judge of Daniel 7:13–14 (see 8:20).

And then he will repay each person according to what he has done. From Psalm 62:12 and Proverbs 24:12: God judges each person according to their works. At the final judgment, Christ will judge (25:31–46). Our works will show whether we truly followed him (7:21–23).

Truly, I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom. A puzzling verse. “Taste death” means die. What “coming” did Jesus mean? Several views:

1. The transfiguration. Six days later, three of the disciples saw Jesus in his glory (17:1–8). All three Synoptic Gospels place this saying immediately before the transfiguration, suggesting a link. Peter later described the transfiguration as seeing the power and coming of the Lord Jesus Christ (2 Peter 1:16–18).

2. The resurrection and ascension. Jesus received all authority and came into his kingly reign (28:18).

3. Pentecost and the spread of the church. The kingdom came with power (Mark 9:1).

4. The destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70. A coming in judgment within that generation (24:34).

Verdict: the transfiguration is the first fulfilment: a preview of his glory seen by some of those standing there. His resurrection and enthronement are the full reality the transfiguration previewed. On any view, Jesus was not mistaken about his return: he was speaking of events within his disciples’ lifetimes.

What it does not mean. Not that we are saved by our works. Christ will judge according to works, as the evidence of faith or unbelief (see 7:21). Those who are in Christ are judged as forgiven, and their works, imperfect as they are, will be graciously rewarded.

In a sentence. The suffering Son of Man will come in glory to judge everyone, and some of the disciples would see a preview of his kingly glory before they died.

On a Tuesday. Live today as one who will stand before Christ the Judge, and as one who belongs to him.

For worship. Worship the Christ who suffered for you and will come in glory.

parallels.desc: you will render to a man according to his work

16.theology: The church and the confession. Matthew is the only Gospel that records Jesus using the word “church” (ekklesia — the called-out assembly), and it appears on his lips in only two passages: here, and again in the discipline of 18:17. His promise is breathtaking in its confidence: he will build it, not we; and it will endure against all opposition. The church’s indestructibility rests not on its institutional strength or cultural influence but on the identity of its Lord and the truth of its confession. When the church loses the confession — that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God — it loses the rock on which it stands. The Reformation was at its heart a recovery of this confession: Christ alone, known through Scripture alone, received through faith alone, to the glory of God alone.
16.examples:
Then: Caesarea Philippi was the last place you would expect the church to be founded — a pagan city, politically dangerous territory, far from Jerusalem’s religious centre. Jesus chose it deliberately. The church is born at the margins, in hostile territory, by a divine confession that overturns every human calculation.

Now: The question “Who do you say that I am?” is not a theological quiz but an existential confrontation. Every person who hears the gospel must answer it. Correct doctrine about Jesus (acknowledging him as a great teacher, a moral exemplar, a historical figure) falls short of Peter’s confession. Jesus demands a verdict — not about what others say, but about what you say. The church is built on those who answer as Peter answered, by the same Spirit who revealed it to him.

17.title: The Transfiguration
17.text: <sup>1</sup>And after six days Jesus took with him Peter and James, and John his brother, and led them up a high mountain by themselves. <sup>2</sup>And he was transfigured before them, and his face shone like the sun, and his clothes became white as light. <sup>3</sup>And behold, there appeared to them Moses and Elijah, talking with him. <sup>4</sup>And Peter said to Jesus, “Lord, it is good that we are here. If you wish, I will make three tents here, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah.” <sup>5</sup>He was still speaking when, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them, and a voice from the cloud said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased; listen to him.” <sup>6</sup>When the disciples heard this, they fell on their faces and were terrified. <sup>7</sup>But Jesus came and touched them, saying, “Rise, and have no fear.” <sup>8</sup>And when they lifted up their eyes, they saw no one but Jesus only. <sup>9</sup>And as they were coming down the mountain, Jesus commanded them, “Tell no one the vision, until the Son of Man is raised from the dead.” <sup>10</sup>And the disciples asked him, “Then why do the scribes say that first Elijah must come?” <sup>11</sup>He answered, “Elijah does come, and he will restore all things. <sup>12</sup>But I tell you that Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him, but did to him whatever they pleased. So also the Son of Man will certainly suffer at their hands.” <sup>13</sup>Then the disciples understood that he was speaking to them of John the Baptist. <sup>14</sup>And when they came to the crowd, a man came up to him and, kneeling before him, <sup>15</sup>said, “Lord, have mercy on my son, for he has seizures and he suffers terribly. For often he falls into the fire, and often into the water. <sup>16</sup>And I brought him to your disciples, and they could not heal him.” <sup>17</sup>And Jesus answered, “O faithless and twisted generation, how long am I to be with you? How long am I to bear with you? Bring him here to me.” <sup>18</sup>And Jesus rebuked the demon, and it came out of him, and the boy was healed instantly. <sup>19</sup>Then the disciples came to Jesus privately and said, “Why could we not cast it out?” <sup>20</sup>He said to them, “Because of your little faith. For truly, I say to you, if you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move, and nothing will be impossible for you.” <sup>22</sup>As they were gathering in Galilee, Jesus said to them, “The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men, <sup>23</sup>and they will kill him, and he will be raised on the third day.” And they were greatly distressed. <sup>24</sup>When they came to Capernaum, the collectors of the two-drachma tax went up to Peter and said, “Does your teacher not pay the tax?” <sup>25</sup>He said, “Yes.” And when he came into the house, Jesus spoke to him first, saying, “What do you think, Simon? From whom do kings of the earth take toll or tax? From their sons or from others?” <sup>26</sup>And when he said, “From others,” Jesus said to him, “Then the sons are free. <sup>27</sup>However, not to give offense to them, go to the sea and cast a hook and take the first fish that comes up, and when you open its mouth you will find a shekel. Take that and give it to them for me and for yourself.”
17.overview:
The Transfiguration is a window into eternity opened for three disciples on a mountain. For a moment the veil of Jesus’ humanity is drawn back and the uncreated glory of the Son shines through: his face blazes like the sun, his garments become white as light. Moses and Elijah appear — the Law and the Prophets — converging on the one they pointed to, discussing the “exodus” he was about to accomplish in Jerusalem (Luke 9:31). The Father speaks from the cloud — the shekinah glory — as he did at the baptism: “This is my beloved Son; listen to him.”

The Transfiguration is the answer to Peter’s confusion in chapter 16. Peter could not accept a suffering Messiah. The mountain shows him why the cross is not a defeat: the one who will be crucified is the radiant Son of God, whose glory is momentarily unveiled. The cross does not contradict his glory; it is the appointed path through which his glory reaches the world. The disciples descend the mountain and immediately confront a demon-possessed boy they could not heal — from glory to weakness, from the height to the valley of need, which is always where the church must work.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Six days after Peter's confession, Jesus takes Peter, James, and John up a high mountain. He is transfigured before them — his face shining like the sun, his clothes white as light. Moses and Elijah appear and speak with him. A cloud overshadows them and the Father's voice speaks: "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased; listen to him." The disciples fall on their faces; Jesus touches them and they see no one but Jesus alone. Coming down, he forbids them to speak of the vision until he is raised from the dead, and answers their question about Elijah: Elijah has already come, in John the Baptist, and was not recognised but treated however his enemies pleased — and so also, he says, the Son of Man will suffer at their hands.
verseByVerse.theology: The Transfiguration is the mountain-top confirmation of Peter's confession: the Son of God whose glory was hidden in flesh is momentarily unveiled. Moses (the law) and Elijah (the prophets) appear alongside Jesus — the whole of the Old Testament represented — and then disappear. Jesus alone remains. The command "listen to him" supersedes Sinai and Carmel: not the law through Moses, not the prophetic word through Elijah, but the Son himself who is their fulfillment. The disciples' prostration and their rising at Jesus's touch enact the pattern of every encounter with the holy: undone by the presence, restored by the touch of grace. There is a quiet fitness in which two men were chosen to stand there. Moses and Elijah are the two men in the Old Testament who met God on Horeb, and each was given something less than an unveiled sight of his glory: Moses was hidden in a cleft of the rock and shown only the back of the glory as it passed (Exod 33:18-23), and Elijah wrapped his face in his cloak at the mouth of the cave and would not look (1 Kings 19:9-13). Now the two of them stand on a mountain with the glory in front of them, unveiled and in the open, holding a conversation with it. What neither prophet was permitted to see, both of them at last see in the face of a Galilean carpenter. And the descent (vv. 9-13) attaches the vision to the cross: the silence is to hold until the resurrection, and the Elijah question is answered by pointing at a man already dead. John came in Elijah's spirit and power and was killed on a whim; the pattern of the forerunner is the pattern of the King.
verseByVerse.examples: The descent from the mountain with the charge to silence (until the resurrection) and the discussion about Elijah frames the Transfiguration within the larger passion narrative. The glory on the mountain will be followed immediately by the failure to heal the epileptic boy in the valley — the constant movement between mountain-top and valley-floor, between the unveiled glory and the demanding need. The disciples are not left on the mountain; they descend with Jesus to where the need is. Two practical edges run through the descent itself. The first is the order to say nothing (v. 9): three men walk down to nine colleagues who were not invited and are about to have the worst day of their ministry, and they are to keep the greatest experience of their lives to themselves. Not everything God gives is given for circulation; some of it is given to be carried. The second is the plain warning of vv. 12-13. God's own forerunner, the greatest man born of women, was beheaded because a king did not want to look foolish in front of his dinner guests, and God did not prevent it. Faithfulness does not purchase a comfortable outcome. What it secures is a place in a pattern that runs through the Son himself and out the far side on the third day.

verseByVerse.quote: And after six days Jesus took with him Peter and James, and John his brother, and led them up a high mountain by themselves. And he was transfigured before them, and his face shone like the sun, and his clothes became white as light.
