On a Tuesday. Name, before God, the person you find hardest to forgive. Ask him for grace to forgive them from the heart, remembering your own great debt.

For worship. Thank God for forgiving you a debt you could never pay.

parallels.desc: if you do not forgive others

18.theology: Forgiveness and the gospel. Matthew 18:21–35 is among the most searching passages in the Gospels on the nature of Christian forgiveness. The parable does not ground forgiveness in the worthiness of the offender or the severity of the offence but in the prior, overwhelming forgiveness of God. This is the gospel logic of ethics: we forgive because we have been forgiven a debt we could never pay. The Reformers called this the indicative grounding the imperative — what God has done for us in Christ is the foundation and motive for what we are to do for one another. Forgiveness is not optional for the Christian; it is the evidence that the gospel has actually taken root in the heart.
18.examples:
Then: The disciples’ argument about greatness was entirely natural — they had left everything and wanted to know what the return on their investment would be. Jesus placed a child in their midst and dismantled their entire framework. The kingdom does not run on the world’s economy of status and reward.

Now: Church conflict is the great test of whether the gospel has penetrated the heart. It is easy to believe in forgiveness in the abstract; it is hard to forgive the specific person who sinned against you specifically. The unforgiving servant stands as a warning: the one who has truly received grace cannot hoard it. The debt we have been forgiven is always larger than the debt we are asked to forgive.

19.title: Marriage, Children, and the Rich Young Man
19.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when Jesus had finished these sayings, he went away from Galilee and entered the region of Judea beyond the Jordan. <sup>2</sup>And large crowds followed him, and he healed them there. <sup>3</sup>And Pharisees came up to him and tested him by asking, “Is it lawful to divorce one’s wife for any cause?” <sup>4</sup>He answered, “Have you not read that he who created them from the beginning made them male and female, <sup>5</sup>and said, ‘Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh’? <sup>6</sup>So they are no longer two but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.” <sup>7</sup>They said to him, “Why then did Moses command one to give a certificate of divorce and to send her away?” <sup>8</sup>He said to them, “Because of your hardness of heart Moses allowed you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it was not so. <sup>9</sup>And I say to you: whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another, commits adultery.” <sup>10</sup>The disciples said to him, “If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is better not to marry.” <sup>11</sup>But he said to them, “Not everyone can receive this saying, but only those to whom it is given. <sup>12</sup>For there are eunuchs who have been so from birth, and there are eunuchs who have been made eunuchs by men, and there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Let the one who is able to receive this receive it.” <sup>13</sup>Then children were brought to him that he might lay his hands on them and pray. The disciples rebuked the people, <sup>14</sup>but Jesus said, “Let the little children come to me and do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of heaven.” <sup>15</sup>And he laid his hands on them and went away. <sup>16</sup>And behold, a man came up to him, saying, “Teacher, what good deed must I do to have eternal life?” <sup>17</sup>And he said to him, “Why do you ask me about what is good? There is only one who is good. If you would enter life, keep the commandments.” <sup>18</sup>He said to him, “Which ones?” And Jesus said, “You shall not murder, You shall not commit adultery, You shall not steal, You shall not bear false witness, <sup>19</sup>Honor your father and mother, and, You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” <sup>20</sup>The young man said to him, “All these I have kept. What do I still lack?” <sup>21</sup>Jesus said to him, “If you would be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” <sup>22</sup>When the young man heard this he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions. <sup>23</sup>And Jesus said to his disciples, “Truly, I say to you, only with difficulty will a rich person enter the kingdom of heaven. <sup>24</sup>Again I tell you, it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.” <sup>25</sup>When the disciples heard this, they were greatly astonished, saying, “Who then can be saved?” <sup>26</sup>But Jesus looked at them and said, “With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.” <sup>27</sup>Then Peter said in reply, “See, we have left everything and followed you. What then will we have?” <sup>28</sup>Jesus said to them, “Truly, I say to you, in the new world, when the Son of Man will sit on his glorious throne, you who have followed me will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. <sup>29</sup>And everyone who has left houses or brothers or sisters or father or mother or children or lands, for my name’s sake, will receive a hundredfold and will inherit eternal life. <sup>30</sup>But many who are first will be last, and the last first.
19.overview:
Chapter 19 moves through three encounters that together form a sustained meditation on what it means to enter the kingdom. Marriage (vv. 1–12) is grounded in creation: the one-flesh union is God’s design, not a human arrangement, and cannot be dissolved at will. Children (vv. 13–15) are welcomed against the disciples’ protests: the kingdom belongs to those who come with empty hands. The rich young man (vv. 16–30) turns away sorrowful: he has great possessions, and they have him.

The three encounters build to the chapter’s most important theological statement: “With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.” Salvation is not a human achievement; it is a divine act. The disciples’ astonished question — “Who then can be saved?” — is the right question, and Jesus’ answer is the heart of the gospel: not the most religiously qualified, not the wealthiest, not even the morally most impressive, but those in whom God himself works the miracle of new birth.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus leaves Galilee for Judea, healing crowds. The Pharisees test him with the divorce question: is it lawful to divorce for any cause? Jesus answers by returning to creation — one man, one woman, one flesh — and distinguishes Moses' concession from God's original design. The disciples are troubled; Jesus adds teaching on celibacy. Children are brought to Jesus; the disciples rebuke those who bring them; Jesus rebukes the disciples and pronounces the kingdom belongs to such as these. At the centre of the exchange stands the one exception he names — sexual immorality (v. 9) — and the section closes with him laying his hands on the children and going away (v. 15), the last thing he does in that place.
verseByVerse.theology: The divorce question was a live controversy in first-century Judaism between the school of Shammai (divorce only for sexual immorality) and the school of Hillel (divorce for any cause, including burning the food). Jesus does not take sides in the rabbinic debate; he goes behind Moses to creation. The "hardness of heart" that occasioned the Mosaic permission (Deut. 24:1) was always a concession to human sin, not God's design. Jesus restores the original standard: what God has joined, let not man separate. Verse 9 adds the one exception Jesus names, and it is not the whole of Scripture's teaching: Paul supplies a second ground, when an unbelieving spouse deserts (1 Cor 7:15), and the Reformed churches have long held these two and no others. But the exception is a fence, not a loophole — its purpose is to guard the one-flesh covenant against the hardness of heart that treats it lightly. That must be said in both directions. Nothing here requires anyone to remain in a house where they are being harmed: separation for safety is nowhere forbidden (1 Cor 7:11), a spouse who makes a home unsurvivable has deserted it in substance whoever physically leaves, and the previous chapter has already said what Christ thinks of the man who damages one of these little ones (18:6). See the verse-by-verse on vv. 9-10.
verseByVerse.examples: The episode with the children immediately follows the marriage and divorce discussion — the connection is not incidental. The children whom the disciples dismiss as unimportant are the very ones who most perfectly embody the kingdom: they have no legal standing, no social status, no achievement to present. "Of such is the kingdom of heaven" — the kingdom belongs to those who receive it as a child receives a gift, with open hands and no pretense of deserving. Verse 15 is easily read past and should not be. Straight after the disciples had turned these families away, the last recorded act of Jesus in that district is that he laid hands on their children while the parents who had been told off stood watching. The people who received the blessing are the ones who declined to be embarrassed out of the queue. But the verse is not a guarantee that every child of a believing home will come to faith, and a parent grieving over a grown son who wants none of it must not read it as a verdict on their parenting.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus had finished these sayings, he went away from Galilee and entered the region of Judea beyond the Jordan. And large crowds followed him, and he healed them there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus finished these teachings, he left Galilee and went into the region of Judea beyond the Jordan. Great crowds followed him, and he healed them there.

Now when Jesus had finished these sayings. The formula ending the fourth great discourse (see 7:28).

He went away from Galilee. A turning point. Jesus leaves Galilee for the last time before his death. From here he travels toward Jerusalem and the cross (16:21; 20:17–19).

And entered the region of Judea beyond the Jordan. Probably Perea, the region east of the Jordan, ruled by Herod Antipas, the same ruler who had executed John the Baptist for speaking against his marriage (14:3–4). The question about divorce that follows was politically dangerous here.

And large crowds followed him, and he healed them there. His compassion continues on the road to the cross.

In a sentence. Jesus left Galilee for the last time and travelled south toward Jerusalem, healing the crowds on the way.

On a Tuesday. Jesus kept serving others as he walked toward his own suffering. Can you serve others even in your own hard season?
verseByVerse.note: “Judea beyond the Jordan” is Perea, the land east of the river, ruled by Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: And Pharisees came up to him and tested him by asking, "Is it lawful to divorce one's wife for any cause?" He answered, "Have you not read that he who created them from the beginning made them male and female,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some Pharisees came to test Jesus: is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any reason at all? He answered: have you not read that he who created them from the beginning made them male and female?

And Pharisees came up to him and tested him. A trap. Whatever he said would offend someone: one of the rabbinic schools, or Herod, who had divorced his wife to marry Herodias.

Is it lawful to divorce one’s wife for any cause? The debate between the two great rabbinic schools of the day (see 5:31–32). The school of Shammai held that Deuteronomy 24:1 allowed divorce only for serious sexual sin. The school of Hillel held that a man could divorce his wife for “any cause”: if she burned his food, or if he found someone prettier. Hillel’s view was the popular one. The Pharisees wanted Jesus to take sides.

He answered, “Have you not read.” Instead of entering the rabbinic debate, Jesus goes back to Scripture, and to the beginning (see 12:3).

That he who created them from the beginning made them male and female. Genesis 1:27. God created humanity in two sexes, male and female, both in his image. Marriage is grounded in creation, not in culture. Jesus moves the question from “what is permitted?” to “what did God intend?”.

In a sentence. When the Pharisees tested him about grounds for divorce, Jesus went back to creation: God made them male and female.

On a Tuesday. When facing a hard ethical question, start where Jesus started: what was God’s original design?
verseByVerse.note: Rabbis debated the grounds for divorce: some allowed it for almost any cause, others only for sexual immorality.

parallels.desc: male and female he created them

verseByVerse.quote: "and said, 'Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh'? So they are no longer two but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh. So they are no longer two but one flesh. What God has joined together, let no one separate.

And said, “Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife.” Genesis 2:24. Jesus says God said it: the words of Scripture are God’s words.

Leave. Marriage creates a new household. The primary loyalty shifts from parents to spouse. Not abandoning parents, who must still be honoured (15:4), but forming a new family unit.

Hold fast. “Hold fast” (kollēthēsetai) means to be glued, joined, bound. It describes a permanent, faithful commitment.

And the two shall become one flesh. A union of the whole person: physical (sexual union), but also emotional, spiritual and social: sharing one life. Paul calls it a profound mystery that pictures Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31–32).

So they are no longer two but one flesh. Jesus draws the conclusion: marriage makes a new unity.

What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate. The key sentence. God himself joins a husband and wife. Marriage is not merely a human contract that can be dissolved whenever people choose; it is a covenant made before God, which he has sealed (Malachi 2:14–16). No human authority, neither husband nor court, has the right to undo what God has done.

What it does not mean. Not that divorce is never permitted in any circumstances (v. 9; 1 Corinthians 7:15). But it means that divorce is always a tearing of what God has joined, a tragedy, never merely a lifestyle choice. And the passage shows God’s design for marriage as one man and one woman, for life. The historic Christian view of marriage and sexuality is grounded here, in Jesus’ own words about creation. It should be held with conviction and with compassion for those who struggle.

In a sentence. In marriage God joins a man and a woman into one flesh, and no one has the right to separate what God has joined.

On a Tuesday. If you are married, your marriage is God’s joining. Treat it as sacred today: with a word of love, a kindness, or an apology.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "Why then did Moses command one to give a certificate of divorce and to send her away?" He said to them, "Because of your hardness of heart Moses allowed you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it was not so."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees asked: then why did Moses command a man to give a certificate of divorce and send her away? Jesus said: because of your hardness of heart Moses allowed you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it was not so.

Why then did Moses command one to give a certificate of divorce and to send her away? They refer to Deuteronomy 24:1–4. They call it a command.

Because of your hardness of heart Moses allowed you to divorce your wives. Jesus corrects them: Moses did not command divorce; he permitted it. The law of Deuteronomy 24 regulated divorce, which was already happening, to protect women from even worse treatment: the certificate gave the woman legal proof that she was free to remarry. It was a concession to human sin, not God’s ideal. “Hardness of heart” means stubbornness, a heart closed to God and to love.

But from the beginning it was not so. God’s original design, before sin, was lifelong marriage. Laws that regulate sin do not change God’s ideal.

What it does not mean. Not that Moses’ law was wrong, or that God approved of easy divorce. The law reflected God’s mercy in a sinful world, limiting harm. Nor does “hardness of heart” mean that every divorced person is hard-hearted; often the hard heart is in the spouse who caused the breakdown.

In a sentence. Moses permitted divorce as a concession to human hardness of heart, but God’s design from the beginning was lifelong marriage.

On a Tuesday. Is there hardness in your heart toward your spouse, family member or friend? Ask God to soften it.

verseByVerse.quote: And I say to you: whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another, commits adultery." The disciples said to him, "If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is better not to marry."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I say to you: whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another commits adultery. The disciples said: if that is how things are between a man and his wife, it is better not to marry.

And I say to you. With his own authority (see 5:22).

Whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another, commits adultery. Divorce for “any cause” does not dissolve the marriage in God’s eyes. A second marriage after such a divorce is adultery, because the first marriage still stands. The exception is “sexual immorality” (porneia), sexual unfaithfulness, which breaks the marriage covenant. In that case, the innocent party may divorce and remarry (see 5:32). Jesus is stricter than both rabbinic schools: stricter than Hillel, and closer to Shammai, but grounded in creation, not in debate about Deuteronomy.

The disciples said to him, “If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is better not to marry.” The disciples are shocked. They had assumed the easy divorce of their culture. If marriage is for life, with no easy way out, is it wise to marry at all? Their reaction shows how radical Jesus’ teaching was.

What it does not mean. Not that divorced and remarried people can never be forgiven, or must divorce again. Divorce and remarriage outside these grounds is sin, but sin can be forgiven, and second marriages are real marriages to be honoured from then on. Nor does the exception mean that divorce is required after adultery: reconciliation is better where possible. The Westminster Confession adds desertion by an unbelieving spouse (1 Corinthians 7:15) as a second ground (24.6) (see 5:31–32).

In a sentence. Divorce and remarriage except for sexual unfaithfulness is adultery, a teaching so strict that the disciples thought it better not to marry.

On a Tuesday. Marriage is a serious commitment. If you are considering marriage, count the cost. If you are married, keep your vows.

verseByVerse.quote: But he said to them, "Not everyone can receive this saying, but only those to whom it is given. For there are eunuchs who have been so from birth, and there are eunuchs who have been made eunuchs by men, and there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Let the one who is able to receive this, receive it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said: not everyone can accept this saying, but only those to whom it is given. Some are eunuchs from birth, some were made eunuchs by others, and some have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Let anyone who can accept this accept it.

Not everyone can receive this saying, but only those to whom it is given. “This saying” is probably the disciples’ remark that it is better not to marry (v. 10). Not everyone can live a single life. It is a gift (1 Corinthians 7:7).

For there are eunuchs who have been so from birth. A eunuch was a man unable to marry or father children. Some were born unable, because of physical conditions.

And there are eunuchs who have been made eunuchs by men. Men castrated as servants for royal courts, a common practice in the ancient world (Acts 8:27). Under the law of Moses, eunuchs were excluded from the assembly of the LORD (Deuteronomy 23:1), but God promised them an everlasting name in his house (Isaiah 56:3–5).

And there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Not literal self-mutilation, but people who choose to remain unmarried and celibate in order to serve God’s kingdom more fully. Jesus himself was unmarried. Paul was single and commended singleness for those who have the gift, because it allows undivided devotion to the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:7, 32–35).

Let the one who is able to receive this receive it. It is a calling for some, not a command for all.

What it does not mean. Not that marriage is less holy than singleness, or that single people are second-class Christians. Both are callings from God (1 Corinthians 7:7). The Reformers rejected the medieval idea that celibacy is a higher spiritual state, and that clergy must be celibate (1 Timothy 4:1–3). And it does not mean literal castration: the early church condemned Origen for doing that. Some today read “eunuchs from birth” as a reference to people with same-sex attraction, but that is not what the word means; it refers to physical inability to father children. What the verse does show is that Jesus honours those who are single, whatever the reason, and that a single life can be lived fully for God. Christians who remain single and celibate out of faithfulness to Christ, including those who experience same-sex attraction, are following a path Jesus honours here.

In a sentence. Some people cannot marry, and some choose singleness to serve God’s kingdom; it is a gift given to some, not a command for all.

On a Tuesday. How does your church treat single people? Honour them as Jesus does, and include them as family.
verseByVerse.note: A eunuch was a man unable to marry or father children. Some, like Paul, remained single to serve the kingdom.

parallels.desc: a name better than sons and daughters

verseByVerse.quote: Then children were brought to him that he might lay his hands on them and pray. The disciples rebuked the people, but Jesus said, "Let the little children come to me and do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then children were brought to Jesus so that he could lay his hands on them and pray. The disciples rebuked the people. But Jesus said: let the little children come to me and do not hinder them, for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these.

Then children were brought to him. Luke says they were infants (Luke 18:15). Parents brought them, probably mothers.

That he might lay his hands on them and pray. Jewish parents brought children to rabbis and elders to be blessed. Laying hands on someone was a sign of blessing (Genesis 48:14).

The disciples rebuked the people. They thought Jesus was too busy and important for children, and that they were protecting him. They had forgotten the lesson of 18:1–5.

But Jesus said, “Let the little children come to me and do not hinder them.” Mark says Jesus was indignant (Mark 10:14). Jesus welcomes children. No one is too small or unimportant for him.

For to such belongs the kingdom of heaven. The kingdom belongs to those who are like children: humble, dependent, receiving it as a gift (18:3–4).

What it does not mean. Not that children are automatically saved by being children, or that they do not need Christ. They are sinners by nature too (Psalm 51:5; Ephesians 2:3). But Jesus welcomes them and blesses them.

Where Christians differ: infant baptism. Paedobaptists often cite this passage in support of baptising infants: if the kingdom belongs to children, they should receive the sign of the covenant. Credobaptists respond that this passage says nothing about baptism; Jesus blessed the children and prayed for them, he did not baptise them; and baptism signifies faith and union with Christ, which a person must profess. Verdict: credobaptist, held charitably. The passage teaches that children are welcome to Christ and should be brought to him in prayer and teaching, but it does not mandate infant baptism. Both sides agree that Christian parents must bring their children to Jesus.

In a sentence. When the disciples tried to keep children away, Jesus welcomed them, for the kingdom belongs to such as these.

On a Tuesday. How can you bring children to Jesus: your own, or those in your church? Pray for them by name, and teach them about him.

verseByVerse.quote: And he laid his hands on them and went away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus laid his hands on them and went on his way.

And he laid his hands on them. He blessed them, as the parents had asked. Mark says he took them in his arms (Mark 10:16). Jesus had time for children, even on the road to the cross.

And went away. He continued his journey to Jerusalem.

In a sentence. Jesus blessed the children with his hands and continued his journey.

For worship. Thank Jesus that he welcomes the small and unimportant, including you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–30 — The Rich Young Man and the Great Reversal
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A young man asks what good deed will earn eternal life. Jesus directs him to the commandments; he claims to have kept them all. Jesus says: sell your possessions, give to the poor, and follow me. The man goes away sorrowful, for he has great wealth. Jesus says it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom. The disciples are astonished. Jesus promises rewards for those who have left everything to follow him, and closes with the great reversal: the first shall be last and the last first. Two exchanges inside the section carry more weight than their length. Jesus meets the opening question with one of his own — why do you ask me about what is good, when there is only one who is good (v. 17)? And after the camel and the needle, Peter asks what the Twelve, who did leave everything, will have for it (v. 27); the promise of thrones and a hundredfold is his answer, and verse 30 is the warning attached to it.
verseByVerse.theology: The rich young man's failure reveals the nature of the commandment he thought he kept: "love your neighbor as yourself" (v. 19) was the final commandment in Jesus's list, and the sell-everything command is the test of whether it is actually operative. One cannot love one's neighbor as oneself while sitting on wealth that could address their need. The commandment was kept in its visible form (no theft, no fraud) but not in its spirit (genuine love that costs something). Jesus's diagnosis is precise: the man's wealth is not neutral; it is the specific obstacle between him and eternal life. Verse 17 is regularly produced as proof that Jesus denied being God — he pointed away from himself, so he cannot have thought himself divine. But he does not say I am not good. He asks a question, and the question is a door: you have called goodness a deed you can perform and me a teacher who knows the trick, and there is only One who is good, so think again about what you are asking and whom you are asking. The rest of the Gospel will not let the denial stand — this is the man who forgives sins as only God can (9:2-6), who says the Lord of the Sabbath is standing here (12:8), and who claims all authority in heaven and on earth (28:18).
verseByVerse.examples: The disciples' astonishment at the camel-and-needle saying reflects their assumption that wealth is a sign of divine blessing — the standard view. Jesus upends the assumption: wealth is a spiritual obstacle, not an advantage. The camel through the needle's eye is not a metaphor for difficulty but for impossibility — making the way of salvation clear. "With God all things are possible" is the only resolution: the rich man cannot save himself; only God can accomplish the transformation that makes a rich man enter the kingdom. Guard that promise, since it has been lifted off the page and attached to whatever a reader happens to want. The word this has an antecedent, and the antecedent is the salvation of a rich man; it is not a general assurance that anything is obtainable with enough belief. And Matthew has left the proof at the far end of his book. When the crucifixion is over, a man comes to Pilate for the body — and Matthew alone tells us he was rich, plousios, the same word used here of the man who cannot get in (27:57). The needle did not widen and the camel did not shrink. God did the thing he said only God could do.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, a man came up to him, saying, "Teacher, what good deed must I do to have eternal life?" And he said to him, "Why do you ask me about what is good? There is only one who is good. If you would enter life, keep the commandments."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man came to Jesus and asked: Teacher, what good thing must I do to have eternal life? Jesus said: why do you ask me about what is good? There is only one who is good. If you want to enter life, keep the commandments.

And behold, a man came up to him. Matthew later calls him young (v. 20); Luke calls him a ruler (Luke 18:18), probably a leader in a synagogue. He was wealthy (v. 22). He had everything his culture valued: youth, wealth, position, morality and religious seriousness.

Teacher, what good deed must I do to have eternal life? “Eternal life” means the life of the age to come, life in God’s kingdom (v. 23). His question assumes that eternal life is earned by doing something good: one more deed, one more achievement.

Why do you ask me about what is good? There is only one who is good. Mark and Luke record his question as “Good Teacher” and Jesus’ answer as “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone” (Mark 10:17–18). Jesus is not denying that he is good or that he is God. He is making the man think. Only God is truly good. If the man calls Jesus good, does he realise what he is saying? And goodness is not found in doing one good deed, but in God himself.

If you would enter life, keep the commandments. Jesus points him to God’s law. Not because the law can save, but because the law reveals God’s goodness and shows us our sin (Romans 3:20; 7:7). Jesus will show the man that he has not kept the law as he thinks.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus teaches salvation by keeping the law. He is using the law to expose the man’s heart. Nor does it mean that Jesus denied his own deity. The way he speaks of “one who is good” invites the man, and us, to recognise who Jesus is.

In a sentence. A man asked what good deed would earn eternal life, and Jesus pointed him to the one good God and his commandments.

On a Tuesday. Do you think of eternal life as something you earn by doing enough good? It is a gift from the only one who is good.
verseByVerse.note: Mark and Luke record the question as “Good Teacher.” Luke calls him a ruler.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to him, "Which ones?" And Jesus said, "You shall not murder, You shall not commit adultery, You shall not steal, You shall not bear false witness, Honor your father and mother, and, You shall love your neighbor as yourself."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man asked: which commandments? Jesus said: you shall not murder, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness, honour your father and mother, and you shall love your neighbour as yourself.

He said to him, “Which ones?” Perhaps he wanted to know which ones mattered most, or to check that he had kept them.

You shall not murder, You shall not commit adultery, You shall not steal, You shall not bear false witness, Honor your father and mother. The sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth and fifth commandments: the second half of the Ten Commandments, about how we treat others (Exodus 20:12–16).

And, You shall love your neighbor as yourself. Leviticus 19:18, which sums up the second half of the law (22:39; Romans 13:9).

What is missing. Jesus does not mention the tenth commandment: you shall not covet (Exodus 20:17). Nor the first: you shall have no other gods. These are the commandments the young man will be shown to have broken: his wealth was his god, and he coveted it.

In a sentence. Jesus listed the commandments about loving one’s neighbour, leaving out the ones about coveting and other gods.

On a Tuesday. Go through the Ten Commandments slowly today, especially the first and the tenth. Which ones expose your heart?
verseByVerse.note: Jesus lists the commandments about one’s neighbour and adds Leviticus 19:18.

parallels.desc: the second table of the Ten Commandments

verseByVerse.quote: The young man said to him, "All these I have kept. What do I still lack?" Jesus said to him, "If you would be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The young man said: I have kept all these. What do I still lack? Jesus said: if you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.

All these I have kept. He was sincere. Outwardly, he had kept these commands from his youth (Mark 10:20). He was not a hypocrite in the usual sense. But he had not understood the depth of the law (5:21–48): love for one’s neighbour includes the poor, and loving God means having no other god.

What do I still lack? He knew something was missing. Despite his morality, he had no assurance of eternal life.

If you would be perfect. “Perfect” (teleios) means complete, whole (see 5:48). What he lacked was wholehearted devotion to God.

Go, sell what you possess and give to the poor. Jesus puts his finger on the one thing that held his heart: his wealth. It was his god. To keep the first commandment, he must let it go. And to love his neighbour as himself, he must give to the poor.

And you will have treasure in heaven. See 6:19–21. He would exchange earthly treasure for heavenly.

And come, follow me. The real issue. Not only giving away money, but following Jesus. Eternal life is found not in doing a good deed, but in following the one who is good.

What it does not mean. Not that every Christian must sell everything they own. Jesus did not command this of everyone: Zacchaeus gave away half (Luke 19:8), and Joseph of Arimathea remained rich (27:57). He commanded it of this man, because wealth was his idol. The principle for all is that nothing may come before Christ, and everything we have belongs to him. Nor does it mean that giving away possessions earns eternal life. The man needed to give up his false god to follow the true one. Stewardship is not covetousness: Christians may own property and save wisely, but must hold it as God’s, use it generously, and be willing to give it up if Christ asks.

Where Christians differ: counsels of perfection. Medieval Catholic teaching distinguished between commands for all Christians and “counsels of perfection” (poverty, celibacy, obedience) for those seeking a higher spiritual state, especially monks and nuns. The Reformers rejected this two-level Christianity: every Christian is called to total devotion, in whatever calling God gives. Verdict: there is one standard of discipleship for all; Jesus addressed this man’s particular idol.

In a sentence. When the young man asked what he still lacked, Jesus told him to give up the wealth that ruled his heart and follow him.

On a Tuesday. What would Jesus put his finger on in your life, the one thing that holds your heart? Are you willing to let it go?

verseByVerse.quote: When the young man heard this he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions. And Jesus said to his disciples, "Truly, I say to you, only with difficulty will a rich person enter the kingdom of heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the young man heard this, he went away sorrowful, because he had great wealth. Jesus said to his disciples: truly, it is hard for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven.

When the young man heard this he went away sorrowful. The only person in the Gospels who walked away from Jesus’ personal call sad. He wanted eternal life, but not at that price. He was sorrowful because he knew what he was choosing.

For he had great possessions. Or rather, his possessions had him. He thought he owned his wealth; it owned him.

Truly, I say to you, only with difficulty will a rich person enter the kingdom of heaven. Wealth makes it hard to enter the kingdom. Why? Because wealth gives a false sense of security and independence. It makes people feel they do not need God. It competes for the heart’s loyalty (6:24). It chokes the word (13:22). It is very hard for someone with much to come to God as a child with nothing (18:3; 5:3).

What it does not mean. Not that rich people cannot be saved, or that poverty earns salvation. Abraham and Job were rich and righteous. Jesus will immediately say that with God all things are possible (v. 26). But wealth is a real spiritual danger. And by world standards, most people in Western countries are rich.

In a sentence. The young man went away sad because he would not give up his wealth, and Jesus warned that riches make it hard to enter the kingdom.

On a Tuesday. By global standards, you are probably rich. How does your wealth affect your trust in God and your generosity?

verseByVerse.quote: Again I tell you, it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God." When the disciples heard this, they were greatly astonished, saying, "Who then can be saved?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God. When the disciples heard this, they were astonished: who then can be saved?

It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle. The camel was the largest animal in Palestine; the eye of a needle the smallest opening. A deliberately absurd, impossible picture, like the rabbinic saying about an elephant going through a needle’s eye. Some have suggested a small gate in Jerusalem called “the Needle’s Eye”, through which a camel could squeeze by kneeling, but there is no evidence such a gate existed, and it weakens Jesus’ point. Others suggest a misreading of kamēlos (camel) as kamilos (rope), but that too is unnecessary. Jesus means it is humanly impossible.

Than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God. Matthew here uses “kingdom of God”, which he usually calls “kingdom of heaven” (v. 23). The two mean the same thing.

When the disciples heard this, they were greatly astonished. In their culture, wealth was often seen as a sign of God’s blessing (Deuteronomy 28:1–14). If the rich, whom God has blessed, cannot be saved, who can?

Saying, “Who then can be saved?” Exactly the right question. If salvation depends on human ability, no one can be saved.

What it does not mean. Not that wealth is a sign of God’s favour, as the prosperity gospel teaches. Jesus overturns that idea. Wealth is not a proof of blessing, and it can be a great obstacle.

In a sentence. Jesus said it is harder for a rich person to enter the kingdom than for a camel to go through a needle’s eye, and the astonished disciples asked who then can be saved.

On a Tuesday. Never think of your wealth as proof that God approves of you. It is a responsibility, and a danger.
verseByVerse.note: The camel was the largest animal in the land; the picture is deliberate exaggeration. The idea of a gate called “the Eye of the Needle” is a much later invention.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus looked at them and said, "With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible." Then Peter said in reply, "See, we have left everything and followed you. What then will we have?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus looked at them and said: with man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible. Peter said: we have left everything and followed you. What then will we have?

But Jesus looked at them and said, “With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.” The heart of the passage. Salvation is impossible by human effort, for rich and poor alike. No one can save himself. But God can do the impossible: he can save anyone, even the rich, by changing the heart (Genesis 18:14; Jeremiah 32:17). Salvation is God’s work from start to finish (Ephesians 2:8–9). Zacchaeus, a rich tax collector, was saved (Luke 19:1–10).

Then Peter said in reply, “See, we have left everything and followed you.” Peter compares the disciples with the rich young man. They did what he would not: they left their boats, nets and families (4:20, 22; 9:9).

What then will we have? An honest question, perhaps with a trace of self-interest. What is the reward for leaving everything?

In a sentence. Jesus declared that salvation, impossible for humans, is possible with God, and Peter asked what reward the disciples would receive for leaving everything.

On a Tuesday. Who do you know who seems impossible to save? With God, all things are possible. Pray for them.

For worship. Thank God that he did for you what was impossible for you to do.

parallels.desc: is anything too hard for the LORD?

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "Truly, I say to you, in the new world, when the Son of Man will sit on his glorious throne, you who have followed me will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. And everyone who has left houses or brothers or sisters or father or mother or children or lands, for my name's sake, will receive a hundredfold and will inherit eternal life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said: truly, in the new world, when the Son of Man sits on his glorious throne, you who have followed me will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. And everyone who has left houses, family or lands for my name’s sake will receive a hundredfold and will inherit eternal life.

Truly, I say to you, in the new world. “The new world” (palingenesia, “regeneration”, “rebirth”) means the renewal of all things at Christ’s return: the new heavens and new earth (Acts 3:21; Romans 8:19–23; Revelation 21:1–5). Creation itself will be born again.

When the Son of Man will sit on his glorious throne. From Daniel 7:9–14. The Son of Man will reign and judge (25:31).

You who have followed me will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. The apostles will share Christ’s rule over the renewed people of God. “Judging” may mean ruling, as Israel’s judges ruled. The twelve tribes picture the whole people of God (see 10:1). Paul says all the saints will judge the world (1 Corinthians 6:2).

And everyone who has left houses or brothers or sisters or father or mother or children or lands, for my name’s sake. Not only the Twelve, but every disciple who gives up things for Jesus.

Will receive a hundredfold. In this life, in the family of God: brothers, sisters, mothers and homes in the church (Mark 10:30 adds “with persecutions”). Every believer who loses family for Christ gains a much larger family.

And will inherit eternal life. The very thing the rich young man wanted (v. 16) and walked away from. It is given as an inheritance, a gift, not a wage.

What it does not mean. Not that we follow Jesus to get material rewards, as the prosperity gospel teaches. The hundredfold is chiefly the family of the church, and eternal life. Nor does it mean that the church replaces Israel in a way that excludes Jewish people. The twelve tribes picture the whole restored people of God, Jew and Gentile together in Christ.

In a sentence. In the renewed creation, the apostles will share Christ’s rule, and everyone who has given up anything for him will receive far more and inherit eternal life.

On a Tuesday. What have you given up for Christ? He has not forgotten it. Look around at your church family: they are part of the hundredfold.
verseByVerse.note: “The new world” is the renewal of all things at Christ’s return.

parallels.desc: I am making all things new

verseByVerse.quote: But many who are first will be last, and the last first.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But many who are first will be last, and the last first.

But many who are first will be last. The rich young man was first in the eyes of the world: rich, young, moral, important. He ended last, walking away from the kingdom.

And the last first. The disciples, poor fishermen and a tax collector, were last in the world’s eyes. They will be first, sitting on thrones. The kingdom reverses the world’s rankings.

A warning too. “But” suggests a warning to Peter and the disciples, after his question about reward (v. 27). Do not assume you will be first. Those who think they deserve a reward may find themselves last. Jesus immediately tells a parable about this (20:1–16), which ends with the same words (20:16).

What it does not mean. Not that every poor person will be first and every rich person last. The reversal is about God’s grace and human pride: those who rely on their own merit, status or sacrifice will be last; those who come with empty hands will be first.

In a sentence. God’s kingdom reverses the world’s rankings, and those who think themselves first may find themselves last.

On a Tuesday. Do you secretly think you deserve more from God than others because of what you have given up? Let grace keep you humble.

parallels.desc: the same saying ends the next parable

19.theology: Monergism and the impossibility of self-salvation. Matthew 19:26 is the clearest statement in this Gospel of the Reformed doctrine of monergism: God alone works the miracle of salvation; unaided human will cannot accomplish it. The rich young man is not an extreme case; he represents every human being before the grace of God. His idolatry is more visible than most, but every person has a god that competes with Christ. The new birth — God’s sovereign act of grace that overcomes the resistance of the sinful will — is what makes it possible for anyone to sell all, follow Christ, and inherit eternal life. This is the good news hidden inside the severe word: with God, even this is possible.
19.examples:
Then: The rich young man came running (Mark 10:17) — he was eager, sincere, morally serious. He went away sorrowful. Sincerity and moral seriousness are not sufficient for salvation. Only the miracle of grace is sufficient.

Now: Every generation has its version of the young man’s idol — wealth, reputation, career, family, comfort, security. Jesus’ question to every person is the same: what is the one thing you are not willing to surrender? That is the idol that must go. The command is not an obstacle to grace; it is the exposure of where grace needs to go.

20.title: First and Last
20.text: <sup>1</sup>“For the kingdom of heaven is like a master of a house who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard. <sup>2</sup>After agreeing with the laborers for a denarius a day, he sent them into his vineyard. <sup>3</sup>And going out about the third hour he saw others standing idle in the marketplace, <sup>4</sup>and to them he said, ‘You go into the vineyard too, and whatever is right I will give you.’ <sup>5</sup>So they went. Going out again about the sixth hour and the ninth hour, he did the same. <sup>6</sup>And about the eleventh hour he went out and found others standing. And he said to them, ‘Why do you stand here idle all day?’ <sup>7</sup>They said to him, ‘Because no one has hired us.’ He said to them, ‘You go into the vineyard too.’ <sup>8</sup>And when evening came, the owner of the vineyard said to his foreman, ‘Call the laborers and pay them their wages, beginning with the last, up to the first.’ <sup>9</sup>And when those hired about the eleventh hour came, each of them received a denarius. <sup>10</sup>Now when those hired first came, they thought they would receive more, but each of them also received a denarius. <sup>11</sup>And on receiving it they grumbled at the master of the house, <sup>12</sup>saying, ‘These last worked only one hour, and you have made them equal to us who have borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat.’ <sup>13</sup>But he replied to one of them, ‘Friend, I am doing you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for a denarius? <sup>14</sup>Take what belongs to you and go. I choose to give to this last worker as I give to you. <sup>15</sup>Am I not allowed to do what I choose with what belongs to me? Or do you begrudge my generosity?’ <sup>16</sup>So the last will be first, and the first last.” <sup>17</sup>And as Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, he took the twelve disciples aside, and on the way he said to them, <sup>18</sup>“See, we are going up to Jerusalem. And the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn him to death <sup>19</sup>and deliver him over to the Gentiles to be mocked and flogged and crucified, and he will be raised on the third day.” <sup>20</sup>Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee came up to him with her sons, and kneeling before him she asked him for something. <sup>21</sup>And he said to her, “What do you want?” She said to him, “Say that these two sons of mine are to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your kingdom.” <sup>22</sup>Jesus answered, “You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I am to drink?” They said to him, “We are able.” <sup>23</sup>He said to them, “You will drink my cup, but to sit at my right hand and at my left is not mine to grant, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father.” <sup>24</sup>And when the ten heard it, they were indignant at the two brothers. <sup>25</sup>But Jesus called them to him and said, “You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. <sup>26</sup>It shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant, <sup>27</sup>and whoever would be first among you must be your slave, <sup>28</sup>even as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” <sup>29</sup>And as they went out of Jericho, a great crowd followed him. <sup>30</sup>And behold, there were two blind men sitting by the roadside, and when they heard that Jesus was passing by, they cried out, “Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David!” <sup>31</sup>The crowd rebuked them, telling them to be silent, but they cried out all the more, “Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David!” <sup>32</sup>And stopping, Jesus called them and said, “What do you want me to do for you?” <sup>33</sup>They said to him, “Lord, let our eyes be opened.” <sup>34</sup>And Jesus in pity touched their eyes, and immediately they recovered their sight and followed him.
20.overview:
Chapter 20 is structured around the inversion of worldly values. The parable of the workers in the vineyard opens with the same reversal that closed chapter 19: “the last will be first, and the first last.” Those hired at the eleventh hour receive the same wage as those who worked all day. The vineyard owner’s generosity is not unfair to the all-day workers (he pays exactly what was agreed) but it offends their sense of merit-based distribution. The parable is not about labour economics but about grace: God owes nothing to anyone; every denarius of salvation is sheer mercy.

The third passion prediction follows (vv. 17–19), and immediately James and John’s mother requests the seats of honour. Jesus responds with the kingdom’s law of greatness: the leader is the servant, the first is the slave. He grounds it in his own mission: “the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” This is the only place in Matthew where Jesus explicitly calls his death a ransom. The chapter closes with two blind men healed on the Jericho road — men who call him “Son of David” and, having received their sight, follow him on the road to Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — The Parable of the Laborers in the Vineyard
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The parable of the workers hired at different hours — dawn, nine, noon, three, and five — all receiving the same denarius wage at day's end. Those hired first complain; the owner insists he has done them no wrong and is free to be generous with his own resources. "So the last will be first, and the first last." The parable illustrates the preceding reversal saying and the nature of God's grace: it is not a reward calculated by duration of service but a gift determined by sovereign generosity. Two mechanics inside the story carry it. Only the dawn workers negotiate a figure; everyone hired later goes into the vineyard on the owner's character alone, with no number (vv. 3-4, 7). And the owner instructs that the last be paid first (v. 8) — he could have paid in the obvious order and bought the dawn men's contentment for nothing, and instead he arranges for them to watch.
verseByVerse.theology: The parable's offense is intentional: the all-day workers' complaint is understandable by any standard of fairness. They worked more; they should receive more. The owner's response demolishes the complaint: he paid exactly what was agreed; his generosity to others does not diminish what they received. The problem is not injustice but envy — "is your eye evil because I am good?" The evil eye (stinginess, grudging spirit) cannot tolerate grace extended to others. The parable indicts the spirit of religious entitlement that calculates reward rather than receiving grace. Two further things the parable does deliberately. It sets the wage by need rather than by output: a denarius was a day's keep for a household, and an hour's honest pay would have sent the last man home with enough for nobody. There is only one wage in the story because there is only one thing God has to give, and eternal life does not come in grades. And the men who grumble are the only men on the estate with a figure in their heads — a man holding a contract can be disappointed, while a man trusting a person cannot, since the promise was kept. Note too that the eleventh-hour men are not blamed for their idleness: because no one has hired us (v. 7) stands without qualification.
verseByVerse.examples: The owner of the vineyard represents God, whose generosity is not constrained by human calculations of desert. Those hired last — with no track record, no extended service, no obvious claim — receive the same gift as those who bore the burden and heat of the day. This is the gospel: the deathbed convert and the lifelong believer receive the same eternal life, because eternal life is not a wage proportional to service but a gift given by the one who owns the vineyard. The men left standing have a name in every congregation: the long-term unemployed, the believer converted at sixty who does the arithmetic and concludes he has nothing to bring, the chronically ill Christian who cannot do the things his church visibly counts. And notice the direction of travel in every scene — not one labourer in the parable finds his own way to the vineyard. Each is there because the owner came down to the market and found him standing.

verseByVerse.quote: "For the kingdom of heaven is like a master of a house who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard. After agreeing with the laborers for a denarius a day, he sent them into his vineyard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The kingdom of heaven is like a landowner who went out early in the morning to hire workers for his vineyard. He agreed to pay them a denarius for the day and sent them into his vineyard.

The connection. “For” links this parable to 19:30: many who are first will be last, and the last first. Peter had just asked what the disciples would receive for leaving everything (19:27). The parable answers: rewards in God’s kingdom are a matter of grace, not of calculation. It ends with the same saying (v. 16).

For the kingdom of heaven is like a master of a house who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard. The landowner pictures God. The vineyard was a common picture of Israel or of God’s kingdom (Isaiah 5:1–7). At harvest time, especially the grape harvest in September, extra workers were needed urgently before the rains came. Day labourers gathered in the marketplace at dawn, hoping to be hired.

After agreeing with the laborers for a denarius a day. A denarius was the standard day’s wage for a labourer, enough to feed a family for a day. The law required workers to be paid at the end of each day (Deuteronomy 24:14–15), because the poor lived from day to day.

He sent them into his vineyard. The working day ran from sunrise to sunset, about twelve hours.

In a sentence. A landowner hired workers at dawn for an agreed fair wage of a denarius for the day.

On a Tuesday. Do you think of your relationship with God as a contract: so much work for so much reward? The parable will challenge that.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage for a labourer. The working day ran from sunrise to sunset.

parallels.desc: do not hold back a hired worker’s wages overnight

verseByVerse.quote: And going out about the third hour he saw others standing idle in the marketplace, and to them he said, "You go into the vineyard too, and whatever is right I will give you." So they went.
verseByVerse.commentary:
About nine in the morning he went out and saw others standing idle in the marketplace. He told them: you go into the vineyard too, and I will give you whatever is right. So they went.

And going out about the third hour. Hours were counted from sunrise. The third hour was about 9 a.m.

He saw others standing idle in the marketplace. Unemployed workers, waiting to be hired. “Idle” does not mean lazy; no one had hired them.

You go into the vineyard too, and whatever is right I will give you. No fixed wage this time. They must trust him to be fair.

So they went. They trusted his word.

In a sentence. At nine in the morning, the landowner hired more workers, promising to pay whatever was right.

On a Tuesday. Trust God to do what is right for you, even without a contract.
verseByVerse.note: The third hour was about 9 a.m.

verseByVerse.quote: Going out again about the sixth hour and the ninth hour, he did the same. And about the eleventh hour he went out and found others standing. And he said to them, "Why do you stand here idle all day?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He went out again at noon and at three in the afternoon and did the same. And about five in the afternoon he went out and found others standing there. He asked them: why have you been standing here idle all day?

Going out again about the sixth hour and the ninth hour, he did the same. Noon and 3 p.m. He keeps going out to bring more people in.

And about the eleventh hour. About 5 p.m., one hour before sunset, when the work would end. These workers would hardly be worth hiring for one hour. No normal employer would do this.

He went out and found others standing. The last of the unemployed: perhaps the weakest, oldest or least wanted, whom no one had chosen.

Why do you stand here idle all day? A question, not necessarily a rebuke.

In a sentence. The landowner kept hiring throughout the day, even finding workers at five o’clock, an hour before the end.

On a Tuesday. God keeps calling people into his kingdom, even late in life. It is never too late to come.
verseByVerse.note: The sixth hour was about noon, the ninth about 3 p.m., the eleventh about 5 p.m. — an hour before the day ended.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "Because no one has hired us." He said to them, "You go into the vineyard too." And when evening came, the owner of the vineyard said to his foreman, "Call the laborers and pay them their wages, beginning with the last, up to the first."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They said: because no one has hired us. He told them: you go into the vineyard too. When evening came, the owner told his foreman: call the workers and pay them their wages, beginning with the last and ending with the first.

Because no one has hired us. No one had wanted them. Now the landowner does.

You go into the vineyard too. He takes them, with no mention of pay. They are simply welcomed.

And when evening came. Sunset, the time to pay wages (Deuteronomy 24:15). Evening pictures the end of the age, the day of judgment.

The owner of the vineyard said to his foreman. The manager who handled the payroll.

Call the laborers and pay them their wages, beginning with the last, up to the first. The order is deliberate. The first workers would see what the last workers received. The story is set up for the surprise.

In a sentence. The landowner hired even the last, unwanted workers, and at evening ordered that the last be paid first.

On a Tuesday. In God’s kingdom, the order of the world is reversed. Those who seem last may be first.

parallels.desc: give him his wages on the same day

verseByVerse.quote: And when those hired about the eleventh hour came, each of them received a denarius. Now when those hired first came, they thought they would receive more. But each of them also received a denarius.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those hired at five o’clock came, and each received a full denarius. When those hired first came, they expected to receive more, but each of them also received a denarius.

And when those hired about the eleventh hour came, each of them received a denarius. A full day’s wage for one hour’s work. Astonishing generosity. They would be able to feed their families that night.

Now when those hired first came, they thought they would receive more. Reasonably, by human standards. If the one-hour workers got a denarius, surely the twelve-hour workers would get twelve.

But each of them also received a denarius. Exactly what they had agreed (v. 2).

In a sentence. The last workers received a full day’s wage, and the first workers, expecting more, received the same.

On a Tuesday. Would you be glad or resentful if someone who came to faith on their deathbed received the same eternal life as you?

verseByVerse.quote: And on receiving it they grumbled at the master of the house, saying, "These last worked only one hour, and you have made them equal to us who have borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they received it, they grumbled against the landowner: these last worked only one hour, and you have made them equal to us, who have borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat.

And on receiving it they grumbled at the master of the house. “Grumbled” is the word used of Israel grumbling in the wilderness (Exodus 16:7–8; 1 Corinthians 10:10).

These last worked only one hour, and you have made them equal to us. Their complaint was not that they had been cheated, but that others had been treated equally. Their problem was comparison. Equality offended them.

Who have borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat. The sirocco, the hot east wind, made afternoon work exhausting. They had worked hard, and they thought they deserved more than the latecomers.

Who are they? They are like the Pharisees, who grumbled that Jesus welcomed tax collectors and sinners (9:11; Luke 15:2), and like the elder brother in the parable of the prodigal son (Luke 15:28–30). And they are like Peter, who asked what he would get for leaving everything (19:27). Anyone who serves God for a long time can fall into this attitude.

In a sentence. The first workers grumbled that latecomers had been made equal to them, after they had worked all day in the heat.

On a Tuesday. Do you resent grace shown to others? That resentment shows you think you have earned God’s favour.

verseByVerse.quote: But he replied to one of them, "Friend, I am doing you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for a denarius? Take what belongs to you and go. I choose to give to this last worker as I give to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The landowner answered one of them: friend, I am doing you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for a denarius? Take what belongs to you and go. I choose to give this last man the same as I give you.

But he replied to one of them, “Friend.” “Friend” (hetaire) was a polite but cool address, used when someone is in the wrong. Jesus uses it to Judas in Gethsemane (26:50).

I am doing you no wrong. Justice was done. They received exactly what they agreed to.

Did you not agree with me for a denarius? They had a fair contract, and it was honoured.

Take what belongs to you and go. Accept what is yours.

I choose to give to this last worker as I give to you. “I choose” (thelō, “I will”): the generosity is the owner’s free decision. He is sovereign over his gifts.

In a sentence. The landowner said he had been perfectly fair to the first workers, and was free to be generous to the last.

On a Tuesday. God never treats anyone unfairly. But he is free to give more than anyone deserves, and he does.

verseByVerse.quote: "Am I not allowed to do what I choose with what belongs to me? Or do you begrudge my generosity?" So the last will be first, and the first last.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Am I not allowed to do what I choose with what belongs to me? Or are you envious because I am generous? So the last will be first, and the first last.

Am I not allowed to do what I choose with what belongs to me? God is sovereign. Salvation and its rewards are his to give as he wills (Romans 9:15–16). He owes no one more than justice, and he is free to give grace.

Or do you begrudge my generosity? Literally “Is your eye evil because I am good?” An “evil eye” was the Jewish idiom for envy and stinginess (see 6:23). The problem was not the owner’s injustice, but the workers’ envy of his goodness.

So the last will be first, and the first last. The same saying as 19:30, framing the parable. Those who came last, and received grace, are first. Those who think they deserve more, and grumble at grace, are last.

The meaning. The parable is about grace. Eternal life is not a wage earned in proportion to work, but a gift given equally to all who are called into the kingdom, whether early or late. The thief on the cross, saved in his last hour, receives the same eternal life as the apostles (Luke 23:43). Grace is offensive to those who think in terms of merit. It is wonderful to those who know they have none.

What it does not mean. Not that there are no different rewards in God’s kingdom. Elsewhere Jesus teaches that faithfulness will be rewarded according to what each has done (16:27; 25:14–30; 1 Corinthians 3:12–15). The parable’s point is that salvation itself, entry into the kingdom and eternal life, is all of grace, and no one can complain about God’s generosity to others. Nor does it encourage people to put off coming to God until the last moment. The latecomers came as soon as they were called. And it is not a parable about employment law, or a model for paying workers.

In a sentence. God is free to be generous, and those who resent his grace to others show that they think they have earned it.

On a Tuesday. Rejoice when someone who seems undeserving comes to faith. You were undeserving too.

For worship. Thank God that he gives by grace, not by wages.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “do you begrudge” is literally “is your eye bad” — an idiom for envy.

parallels.desc: I will have mercy on whom I have mercy

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–34 — The Third Passion Prediction, the Mother's Request, and Two Blind Men
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the road to Jerusalem, Jesus gives the fullest passion prediction yet: delivered to the Gentiles, mocked, flogged, crucified, raised. Immediately the mother of James and John asks for her sons to sit at Jesus's right and left in his kingdom. Jesus corrects the request: greatness is service, and the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many. Two blind men at Jericho cry out "Son of David, have mercy on us" and receive their sight. Between the request and the healing the other ten turn on the two brothers (v. 24) — not from principle but because they wanted the same thing and were beaten to it — and Jesus answers all twelve rather than the two who asked.
verseByVerse.theology: The timing of the mother's request — immediately after the passion prediction — reveals the distance between the disciples' understanding and Jesus's reality. He has just announced crucifixion; she asks for thrones. The response of Jesus is not irritated dismissal but patient teaching: "You do not know what you are asking." The cup he must drink and the baptism he must undergo are not metaphors for achievement but for suffering. The right and left are not his to give; they are the Father's appointment. The contrast between the Gentile rulers who "lord it over" others and the Son of Man who gives his life is the most concentrated leadership theology in the Gospels. Two things guard it from becoming a slogan. Jesus does not abolish ambition: the sentence is whoever would be great among you, and only the object of the wanting is changed. And the standard is not an attitude but a cross — he does not say be like a servant, he says the Son of Man came to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many. The many of v. 28 is Isaiah's word for a multitude nobody could number (Isa 53:11-12), not a word that fences people out.
verseByVerse.examples: The two blind men at Jericho echo the two blind men of 9:27-31. The title "Son of David, have mercy on us" is the messianic title of chapter 9, and it elicits the same response: Jesus stops, asks, heals. Their sight is the last healing miracle before the triumphal entry — a fitting preparation for Jerusalem. Those who cry "Son of David" will soon hear the crowds cry "Hosanna to the Son of David." The blind who gain sight anticipate the seeing of what Jerusalem refuses to see. Matthew also asks the same question twice in this chapter, and the two answers are the spine of it: What do you want? to the mother of James and John (v. 21), and What do you want me to do for you? to the beggars (v. 32). One asks for the two best seats in the kingdom; the other asks for eyes. And in both Jericho scenes the obstacle between a needy person and Christ is the crowd already following him — as it was with the children in the previous chapter (19:13).

verseByVerse.quote: And as Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, he took the twelve disciples aside, and on the way he said to them, "See, we are going up to Jerusalem. And the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn him to death"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, he took the twelve disciples aside privately and told them: we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn him to death.

And as Jesus was going up to Jerusalem. Jerusalem is about 2,500 feet (750 metres) above sea level, high in the Judean hills. Travellers always went “up” to Jerusalem. The road from Jericho climbed steeply through desert. Pilgrims were travelling to the Passover.

He took the twelve disciples aside. Privately, away from the crowds of pilgrims.

See, we are going up to Jerusalem. Jesus walks toward the cross deliberately. Mark says he walked ahead of them, and they were amazed and afraid (Mark 10:32).

And the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and scribes. “Delivered over” (see 17:22). The Jewish leaders.

And they will condemn him to death. The Sanhedrin would sentence him (26:66).

In a sentence. On the way up to Jerusalem, Jesus told the Twelve privately that he would be handed over to the Jewish leaders and condemned to death.

On a Tuesday. Jesus walked toward suffering on purpose, for you. Let that strengthen you to walk faithfully through hard things for him.
verseByVerse.note: Jerusalem stands high in the hills; one always went “up” to it.

verseByVerse.quote: "and deliver him over to the Gentiles to be mocked and flogged and crucified, and he will be raised on the third day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They will hand him over to the Gentiles to be mocked, flogged and crucified, and he will be raised on the third day.

And deliver him over to the Gentiles. The Romans. Only the Roman governor had the authority to carry out the death penalty (John 18:31).

To be mocked and flogged and crucified. The third prediction of his death (see 16:21; 17:22–23) is the most detailed, and the first to name crucifixion. Everything happened exactly as he said: mocked by the soldiers (27:27–31), flogged (27:26), and crucified (27:35). Flogging with the Roman whip, a scourge with pieces of bone and metal tied into its leather thongs, often tore the skin to shreds; some victims died from it. Crucifixion was the most cruel and shameful death the Romans used.

And he will be raised on the third day. As always, the resurrection follows. Jesus knew the end of the story.

In a sentence. Jesus foretold that the Romans would mock, flog and crucify him, and that he would rise on the third day.

On a Tuesday. Jesus knew every detail of what he would suffer, and went anyway. That is the measure of his love.

For worship. Worship the Saviour who walked open-eyed into suffering for you, and rose.
verseByVerse.note: This third prediction is the first to name crucifixion.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee came up to him with her sons, and kneeling before him she asked him for something. And he said to her, "What do you want?" She said to him, "Say that these two sons of mine are to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your kingdom."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the mother of James and John came to Jesus with her sons, knelt before him and asked for a favour. He asked what she wanted. She said: grant that my two sons may sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your kingdom.

Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee came up to him with her sons. Right after Jesus spoke of his death. She was probably Salome, who was present at the crucifixion (27:56; Mark 15:40), and possibly the sister of Jesus’ mother Mary (John 19:25), which would make James and John Jesus’ cousins. In Mark, the brothers make the request themselves (Mark 10:35); they were behind it.

And kneeling before him she asked him for something. Respectful, even worshipful, but with a selfish request.

Say that these two sons of mine are to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your kingdom. The places of highest honour and power beside a king. They took Jesus’ promise of twelve thrones (19:28) and wanted the best two. They still imagined an earthly, political kingdom, coming soon.

The irony. The ones who would be at Jesus’ right and left when he was enthroned as “King of the Jews” were two criminals crucified with him (27:38).

In a sentence. Right after Jesus spoke of his death, James and John, through their mother, asked for the highest places in his kingdom.

On a Tuesday. Are you seeking position, recognition or status, even in Christian service?
verseByVerse.note: In Mark the brothers ask for themselves. Comparing the women at the cross, their mother may be Salome.

parallels.desc: the mother of the sons of Zebedee at the cross

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I am to drink?" They said to him, "We are able." He said to them, "You will drink my cup, but to sit at my right hand and at my left is not mine to grant, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered: you do not know what you are asking. Can you drink the cup that I am going to drink? They said: we can. He said: you will drink my cup, but to sit at my right and left is not mine to grant; it is for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father.

You do not know what you are asking. They did not understand that the way to glory was through suffering.

Are you able to drink the cup that I am to drink? In the Old Testament, a “cup” often pictures God’s judgment poured out on sin: the cup of his wrath (Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15–16). Jesus would drink this cup at the cross, bearing God’s judgment on sin in his people’s place. In Gethsemane he prayed that it might pass from him, if possible (26:39).

They said to him, “We are able.” Confident, and ignorant.

You will drink my cup. They would share his sufferings, though not his atoning work. James was the first apostle martyred, killed by Herod Agrippa about AD 44 (Acts 12:2). John suffered exile on Patmos for the word of God (Revelation 1:9).

But to sit at my right hand and at my left is not mine to grant. Jesus submits to the Father’s plan. Within the Trinity, the Son willingly does the Father’s will (John 5:19, 30).

But it is for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father. The Father has already decided. Rewards in the kingdom are God’s gift, prepared in advance, not won by ambition (25:34).

What it does not mean. Not that the disciples’ sufferings atone for sin. Only Christ drank the cup of God’s wrath; his followers share in suffering for his sake (Colossians 1:24; 1 Peter 4:13). Nor does “not mine to grant” mean that Jesus is less than God. He speaks as the Son who willingly submits to the Father’s plan.

In a sentence. Jesus told the brothers they did not understand the cup of suffering they were asking to share, and that places of honour are the Father’s to give.

On a Tuesday. Following Christ means sharing his cup of suffering. Are you prepared for that, or only for glory?
verseByVerse.note: The “cup” is an Old Testament picture of God’s judgment poured out.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the ten heard it, they were indignant at the two brothers. But Jesus called them to him and said, "You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the other ten heard about it, they were angry with the two brothers. Jesus called them together and said: you know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great men exercise authority over them.

And when the ten heard it, they were indignant at the two brothers. Probably not because they thought the request was wrong, but because they wanted the same places. Their indignation shows the same ambition.

But Jesus called them to him. Gently, all of them, to teach them.

You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them. “Lord it over” (katakyrieuousin) means dominate, rule harshly for one’s own benefit. In the Roman world, power meant domination: the emperor and his officials ruled by force and fear, and expected to be served. The disciples had seen it in Herod and the Roman governors.

And their great ones exercise authority over them. Greatness in the world means having others under you.
