In a sentence. When the ten were angry at the brothers’ ambition, Jesus reminded them how worldly rulers dominate those under them.

On a Tuesday. How do you use whatever authority you have: at work, at home, in church? To dominate, or to serve?

verseByVerse.quote: "It shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant, and whoever would be first among you must be your slave," "even as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many."
verseByVerse.commentary:
It must not be so among you. Whoever wants to be great among you must be your servant, and whoever wants to be first must be your slave, just as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.

It shall not be so among you. The church must be different from the world. Leadership in Christ’s community is not domination.

But whoever would be great among you must be your servant. “Servant” (diakonos) is the word for someone who waits on tables. Greatness in the kingdom is measured by service.

And whoever would be first among you must be your slave. “Slave” (doulos) goes even further: someone with no rights, who belongs to another. The first must be lowest of all.

Even as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve. Jesus himself is the model. The Son of Man of Daniel 7, to whom all peoples should serve (Daniel 7:14), came to serve. At the Last Supper he washed his disciples’ feet (John 13:1–17).

And to give his life as a ransom for many. The heart of the gospel, in Jesus’ own words. A “ransom” (lytron) was the price paid to set a slave or prisoner free. In the Old Testament, it was used for the price that redeemed a life that was forfeit (Exodus 21:30; 30:12). Jesus gives his life as the price to set his people free from sin, death and God’s judgment. “For” (anti) means “in place of”, “instead of”: a substitute. Jesus dies in the place of many. This echoes Isaiah 53:10–12, where the Servant makes his life an offering for guilt and bears the sin of many.

For many. “Many” is a Hebrew way of speaking of a great number, as in Isaiah 53:11–12. It stresses the vast number saved by the one who dies. Reformed theology sees here the definite purpose of the atonement: Christ died for “his people” (1:21), “the many”, and actually secured their redemption. The gospel offer goes to all (28:19); the ransom actually frees those for whom it was paid.

What it does not mean. Not that the ransom was paid to Satan, as some early church writers suggested. Scripture does not say to whom the ransom was paid; it focuses on what it accomplished. But the broader teaching of Scripture shows that Christ satisfied God’s justice by bearing the penalty for sin (Romans 3:25–26; 2 Corinthians 5:21). This is penal substitution: Christ bore the penalty our sin deserved, in our place. Nor does servant leadership mean that leaders have no authority. Jesus had all authority, and used it to serve. Elders are to lead, and to be followed (Hebrews 13:17), but as servants.

Where Christians differ: the atonement. Some see Christ’s death mainly as an example of self-giving love (the moral influence view), or as a victory over evil powers (Christus Victor). These contain truth: the cross does show love (1 John 4:10) and defeat Satan (Colossians 2:15). But Jesus’ word “ransom … in place of many” points to substitution at the centre. Verdict: penal substitution is the heart of the atonement, with example and victory flowing from it.

In a sentence. In Christ’s community, greatness is service, because the Son of Man came to serve and to give his life as a ransom in the place of many.

On a Tuesday. How can you serve someone today in a way that costs you something: your time, your comfort, your preference?

For worship. Thank Jesus that he gave his life as a ransom in your place.
verseByVerse.note: A ransom was the price paid to free a slave or captive.

parallels.desc: he bore the sin of many

verseByVerse.quote: And as they went out of Jericho, a great crowd followed him. And behold, there were two blind men sitting by the roadside, and when they heard that Jesus was passing by, they cried out, "Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David!" The crowd rebuked them, telling them to be silent, but they cried out all the more, "Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they left Jericho, a great crowd followed him. Two blind men sitting by the road heard that Jesus was passing and cried out: Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David! The crowd rebuked them and told them to be quiet, but they shouted all the more.

And as they went out of Jericho. Jericho was about fifteen miles (twenty-four kilometres) northeast of Jerusalem, in the Jordan valley, about 800 feet (250 metres) below sea level. It was the last stop on the pilgrim road to Jerusalem. Mark and Luke place the healing as Jesus entered or left the city: there were two Jerichos, the old ruined city and the new city built by Herod, so both may be true.

A great crowd followed him. Pilgrims heading for Passover.

And behold, there were two blind men sitting by the roadside. Mark names one: Bartimaeus (Mark 10:46). Matthew mentions two, as he often does (see 8:28).

When they heard that Jesus was passing by. This was their only chance. He would not come this way again.

They cried out, “Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David!” They recognise him as the Messiah, the Son of David (see 9:27; 15:22). The blind see what many sighted people do not.

The crowd rebuked them, telling them to be silent. The crowd thought they were a nuisance, unworthy of the teacher’s attention, like the disciples with the children (19:13).

But they cried out all the more. Persistence (15:22–28). Nothing would stop them.

In a sentence. Two blind men cried out to Jesus as the Son of David, and when the crowd tried to silence them, they shouted all the louder.

On a Tuesday. Do not let anyone silence your prayers to Jesus. Cry out all the more.
verseByVerse.note: Jericho lay about 15 miles east of Jerusalem, near the Jordan. Mark names one of the men, Bartimaeus.

verseByVerse.quote: And stopping, Jesus called them and said, "What do you want me to do for you?" They said to him, "Lord, let our eyes be opened."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus stopped, called them and asked: what do you want me to do for you? They said: Lord, let our eyes be opened.

And stopping, Jesus called them. On his way to Jerusalem and the cross, with a great crowd around him, Jesus stopped for two blind beggars. They mattered to him.

What do you want me to do for you? The same question he asked James and John (v. 21). The brothers asked for status; the blind men asked for mercy. Jesus wanted them to express their need and their faith.

They said to him, “Lord, let our eyes be opened.” A simple, specific request.

In a sentence. Jesus stopped for the blind men and asked what they wanted, and they asked for their sight.

On a Tuesday. If Jesus asked you today, “What do you want me to do for you?”, what would you say?

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus in pity touched their eyes, and immediately they recovered their sight and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moved with compassion, Jesus touched their eyes. Immediately they received their sight and followed him.

And Jesus in pity touched their eyes. “Pity” (splanchnistheis) is deep compassion (9:36). His touch shows personal care.

And immediately they recovered their sight. Isaiah’s sign of the messianic age (11:5; Isaiah 35:5).

And followed him. Their first act with their new sight was to follow Jesus, on the road to Jerusalem and the cross. They are a picture of true disciples: they recognised Jesus, cried for mercy, received sight, and followed.

The contrast. The chapter shows two kinds of request: James and John asked for power and were rebuked; the blind men asked for mercy and were healed. The disciples who could see were spiritually blind to the meaning of the cross. The blind men saw who Jesus was.

In a sentence. Jesus had compassion and healed the blind men, who immediately followed him.

On a Tuesday. When God opens your eyes, use your sight to follow Jesus, wherever he leads.

For worship. Thank Jesus for opening your eyes to see him.

20.theology: The atonement as ransom. Matthew 20:28 is Matthew’s clearest statement of substitutionary atonement. The word “ransom” (lytron) carries the weight of a payment that secures release — it is used in the Septuagint for the price paid to redeem a slave or a firstborn. Jesus applies it to his own death: he gives his life as the price that sets the many free from their captivity to sin, death, and judgment. Reformed theology has always insisted that the atonement is primarily objective — it actually accomplishes something in the divine court (the cancellation of debt, the satisfaction of justice) — before it is subjective (inspiring us, moving us, transforming us). The ransom is paid; the captives are free.
20.examples:
Then: James and John wanted the best seats. They had left everything (19:27) and felt entitled to the premium return. Jesus redefines the currency: greatness is measured in service and suffering, not in position and honour. The Twelve would spend the rest of their lives learning this.

Now: The parable of the workers challenges every theology of spiritual merit — the idea that longer service, greater sacrifice, or more faithful obedience earns a greater share of God’s favour. Grace cannot be earned; it can only be received. The workers who grumble are those who have forgotten that any wage at all is mercy. The appropriate response to grace is gratitude, not calculation.

21.title: The King Enters Jerusalem
21.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when they drew near to Jerusalem and came to Bethphage, to the Mount of Olives, then Jesus sent two disciples, <sup>2</sup>saying to them, “Go into the village in front of you, and immediately you will find a donkey tied, and a colt with her. Untie them and bring them to me. <sup>3</sup>If anyone says anything to you, you shall say, ‘The Lord needs them,’ and he will send them at once.” <sup>4</sup>This took place to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet, saying, <sup>5</sup>“Say to the daughter of Zion, ‘Behold, your king is coming to you, humble, and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a beast of burden.’” <sup>6</sup>The disciples went and did as Jesus had directed them. <sup>7</sup>They brought the donkey and the colt and put on them their cloaks, and he sat on them. <sup>8</sup>Most of the crowd spread their cloaks on the road, and others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road. <sup>9</sup>And the crowds that went before him and that followed him were shouting, “Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!” <sup>10</sup>And when he entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred up, saying, “Who is this?” <sup>11</sup>And the crowds said, “This is the prophet Jesus, from Nazareth of Galilee.” <sup>12</sup>And Jesus entered the temple and drove out all who sold and bought in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold pigeons. <sup>13</sup>He said to them, “It is written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer,’ but you make it a den of robbers.” <sup>14</sup>And the blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he healed them. <sup>15</sup>But when the chief priests and the scribes saw the wonderful things that he did, and the children crying out in the temple, “Hosanna to the Son of David!” they were indignant, <sup>16</sup>and they said to him, “Do you hear what these are saying?” And Jesus said to them, “Yes; have you never read, “‘Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise’?” <sup>17</sup>And leaving them, he went out of the city to Bethany and lodged there. <sup>18</sup>In the morning, as he was returning to the city, he became hungry. <sup>19</sup>And seeing a fig tree by the wayside, he went to it and found nothing on it but only leaves. And he said to it, “May no fruit ever come from you again!” And the fig tree withered at once. <sup>20</sup>When the disciples saw it, they marveled, saying, “How did the fig tree wither at once?” <sup>21</sup>And Jesus answered them, “Truly, I say to you, if you have faith and do not doubt, you will not only do what has been done to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, ‘Be taken up and thrown into the sea,’ it will happen. <sup>22</sup>And whatever you ask in prayer, you will receive, if you have faith.” <sup>23</sup>And when he entered the temple, the chief priests and the elders of the people came up to him as he was teaching, and said, “By what authority are you doing these things, and who gave you this authority?” <sup>24</sup>Jesus answered them, “I also will ask you one question, and if you tell me the answer, then I also will tell you by what authority I do these things. <sup>25</sup>The baptism of John, from where did it come? From heaven or from man?” And they discussed it among themselves, saying, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say to us, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’ <sup>26</sup>But if we say, ‘From man,’ we are afraid of the crowd, for they all hold that John was a prophet.” <sup>27</sup>So they answered Jesus, “We do not know.” And he said to them, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things. <sup>28</sup>“What do you think? A man had two sons. And he went to the first and said, ‘Son, go and work in the vineyard today.’ <sup>29</sup>And he answered, ‘I will not,’ but afterward he changed his mind and went. <sup>30</sup>And he went to the other son and said the same. And he answered, ‘I will, sir,’ but did not go. <sup>31</sup>Which of the two did the will of his father?” They said, “The first.” Jesus said to them, “Truly, I say to you, the tax collectors and the prostitutes go into the kingdom of God before you. <sup>32</sup>For John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him, but the tax collectors and the prostitutes believed him. And even when you saw it, you did not afterward change your minds and believe him. <sup>33</sup>“Hear another parable. There was a master of a house who planted a vineyard and put a fence around it and dug a winepress in it and built a tower and leased it to tenants, and went into another country. <sup>34</sup>When the season for fruit drew near, he sent his servants to the tenants to get his fruit. <sup>35</sup>And the tenants took his servants and beat one, killed another, and stoned another. <sup>36</sup>Again he sent other servants, more than the first. And they did the same to them. <sup>37</sup>Finally he sent his son to them, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’ <sup>38</sup>But when the tenants saw the son, they said to themselves, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and have his inheritance.’ <sup>39</sup>And they took him and threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. <sup>40</sup>When therefore the owner of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those tenants?” <sup>41</sup>They said to him, “He will put those wretches to a miserable death and let out the vineyard to other tenants who will give him the fruits in their seasons.” <sup>42</sup>Jesus said to them, “Have you never read in the Scriptures: “‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this was the Lord’s doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes’? <sup>43</sup>Therefore I tell you, the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a people producing its fruits. <sup>44</sup>And the one who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces; and when it falls on anyone, it will crush him.” <sup>45</sup>When the chief priests and the Pharisees heard his parables, they perceived that he was speaking about them. <sup>46</sup>And although they were seeking to arrest him, they feared the crowds, because they held him to be a prophet.
21.overview:
Chapter 21 is the hinge between the Galilean ministry and the Passion Week. Jesus enters Jerusalem not as a military conqueror on a warhorse but as a humble king on a donkey, fulfilling Zechariah 9:9 with deliberate precision. The crowds shout “Hosanna to the Son of David!” — they are celebrating a political liberation that is not coming. Jesus has a different kind of liberation in mind.

The chapter is structured around three confrontational actions: the entry (vv. 1–11), the temple cleansing (vv. 12–17), and the cursing of the fig tree (vv. 18–22), sandwiched around a series of parables and controversies. The fig tree and the temple interpret each other: Israel, like the fig tree, has leaves of religious activity but no fruit. The temple establishment has turned the Father’s house of prayer into a market. Jesus’ authority is challenged (vv. 23–27); he responds with the parable of the two sons (vv. 28–32) and the parable of the tenants (vv. 33–46), both of which declare that the kingdom will be taken from the current tenants and given to a people who produce its fruit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — The Triumphal Entry, Cleansing of the Temple, and the Withered Fig Tree
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus sends for a donkey and her colt, enters Jerusalem to the crowd's Hosannas, cleanses the temple of money-changers and dove-sellers, heals the blind and lame in the temple, and returns to Bethany. The next morning he curses a fig tree that has leaves but no fruit; it withers immediately. He teaches the disciples about faith that moves mountains. In between, children run about the temple courts shouting the same Hosanna, the chief priests object to what they are saying, and Jesus answers them out of Psalm 8 (vv. 15-16).
verseByVerse.theology: The triumphal entry deliberately fulfills Zechariah 9:9: the king who comes humble and mounted on a donkey, not a warhorse. Jesus is not claiming the military kingship Israel wanted; he is claiming the humble-servant kingship Zechariah foresaw. The Hosanna (Hebrew: save now!) from Psalm 118:25-26 is the pilgrims' greeting to the coming king. The crowd who shouts it does not fully understand what they are saying; they are speaking more truly than they know. "Hosanna to the Son of David" is the church's cry from that day to this. Two things the section does that are easily missed. Hosanna is not a cheer but a prayer — hoshia-na, save now — and the crowd prayed it with the wrong emergency in mind, wanting Rome dealt with while he came for something they had not thought to mention. And the psalm they sang is the psalm he quotes back in the temple: the pilgrims shout Psalm 118:26 on the way in (v. 9), and Jesus quotes Psalm 118:22, the rejected stone, to the men who run the place (v. 42). Between two verses of one psalm lies the whole week.
verseByVerse.examples: The cleansing of the temple is an act of prophetic judgment: the court of the Gentiles (the only place where non-Jews could pray) has been turned into a market. The money-changers and dove-sellers served legitimate temple functions, but their location in the court of the Gentiles prevented the very prayer the temple was meant to facilitate. Jesus quotes Isaiah 56:7 — "a house of prayer for all nations" — and Jeremiah 7:11 — "a den of robbers." He restores the temple to its purpose as a place of prayer and healing, then leaves it to be destroyed (ch. 24). The withered fig tree is a living parable of Israel's fruitlessness: outward leaves of religious activity, no fruit of genuine repentance. Three notes on that sign. It belongs to a recognised prophetic genre — Jeremiah smashing a jar, Ezekiel lying beside a brick, Ahijah tearing a cloak — and it is worth observing that in a ministry of raising the dead and healing all who came, the only thing Jesus ever destroyed was a plant, by a roadside, where nobody was hurt. The charge against the tree is precise: not barrenness but advertising, since a fig in full leaf out of season is making a claim that can be checked from the road. So the guard matters for the anxious reader — this condemns pretence, not weakness, and the same Gospel says a bruised reed he will not break (12:20). The children of vv. 15-16, meanwhile, get Psalm 8 quoted in their defence, and the rest of that verse — to still the enemy and the avenger — tells the chief priests which part of the psalm they are standing in.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they drew near to Jerusalem and came to Bethphage, to the Mount of Olives, then Jesus sent two disciples, saying to them, "Go into the village in front of you, and immediately you will find a donkey tied, and a colt with her. Untie them and bring them to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they approached Jerusalem and came to Bethphage on the Mount of Olives, Jesus sent two disciples ahead: go into the village in front of you, and at once you will find a donkey tied, and a colt with her. Untie them and bring them to me.

The setting. This is the beginning of the last week of Jesus’ life, often called Holy Week. Matthew devotes eight chapters (21–28) to it: a third of his Gospel. Jesus arrives on Sunday, five days before he is crucified on Friday. Jerusalem was crowded with pilgrims for Passover; the city’s population of perhaps 50,000 may have swelled several times over.

Now when they drew near to Jerusalem and came to Bethphage, to the Mount of Olives. The Mount of Olives is a ridge east of Jerusalem, across the Kidron Valley, looking down on the city and the temple. Bethphage (“house of unripe figs”) was a small village on its slope, near Bethany. Zechariah 14:4 says the LORD’s feet will stand on the Mount of Olives on the day of the LORD.

Then Jesus sent two disciples. Jesus takes the initiative. He plans his entry deliberately.

Go into the village in front of you, and immediately you will find a donkey tied, and a colt with her. Jesus knows exactly what they will find, either by divine knowledge or by prior arrangement with the owner. Either way, he is in control. Only Matthew mentions the mother donkey as well as the colt. Mark says the colt had never been ridden (Mark 11:2): a sign of an animal set apart for a sacred purpose (Numbers 19:2; 1 Samuel 6:7).

Untie them and bring them to me. Genesis 49:11 speaks of the ruler from Judah tying his donkey’s colt to the vine: a messianic image.

In a sentence. Approaching Jerusalem for the last time, Jesus deliberately arranged to enter on a donkey’s colt.

On a Tuesday. Jesus was in control of every detail of his last week, even as evil closed in. He is in control of yours.
verseByVerse.note: Bethphage was a village on the Mount of Olives, just east of Jerusalem, near Bethany.

verseByVerse.quote: "If anyone says anything to you, you shall say, 'The Lord needs them,' and he will send them at once." This took place to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet, saying,
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone says anything to you, say: the Lord needs them, and he will send them at once. This happened to fulfil what the prophet had said.

If anyone says anything to you, you shall say, “The Lord needs them.” “The Lord” may refer to Jesus himself, as Lord, or to God. Either way, Jesus claims the right to take what he needs. Everything belongs to him.

And he will send them at once. The owner will give them willingly.

This took place to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet. Zechariah 9:9, with the opening words from Isaiah 62:11. Jesus deliberately acts out the prophecy. He is presenting himself publicly, for the first time, as the King.

In a sentence. Jesus claimed the animals as the Lord, deliberately fulfilling the prophecy of the coming King.

On a Tuesday. “The Lord needs it.” What do you have that the Lord might need: your home, car, time, skill? Give it willingly.

verseByVerse.quote: "Say to the daughter of Zion, 'Behold, your king is coming to you, humble, and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a beast of burden.'" The disciples went and did as Jesus had directed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Say to the daughter of Zion: look, your king is coming to you, humble, and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey. The disciples went and did as Jesus had told them.

Say to the daughter of Zion. From Isaiah 62:11. “Daughter of Zion” is a poetic name for Jerusalem and its people.

Behold, your king is coming to you. Zechariah 9:9. In its context, Zechariah promises a king who will come to Jerusalem, bring peace to the nations, and rule from sea to sea (Zechariah 9:10). He is “righteous and having salvation”.

Humble. “Humble” (praus, the same word as “meek” in 5:5 and “gentle” in 11:29). Not a proud conqueror, but a gentle king.

And mounted on a donkey. Kings went to war on horses; a king riding a donkey came in peace. Solomon rode David’s mule to his coronation (1 Kings 1:33–40). Jesus comes not as a military Messiah to overthrow Rome, but as the Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6), who will bring peace through his death.

On a colt, the foal of a beast of burden. Hebrew poetry often repeats an idea in parallel: “on a donkey, on a colt” describes one animal. Matthew mentions two animals (vv. 2, 7), because there were two: the colt, with its mother walking alongside, perhaps to keep the unbroken colt calm. Jesus rode the colt (Mark 11:7).

The disciples went and did as Jesus had directed them. Obedience.

What it does not mean. Not that Matthew misunderstood Hebrew poetry and invented a second animal. He was an eyewitness, and he records that there were two animals, noting how the prophecy’s parallel lines fit.

In a sentence. Jesus came as the King Zechariah promised: humble, gentle, riding on a donkey, bringing peace.

For worship. Worship the King who comes humble and gentle, bringing peace.
verseByVerse.note: A king riding a donkey came in peace, not on a warhorse. Matthew mentions both the donkey and her colt.

parallels.desc: your king comes, humble and mounted on a donkey
say to the daughter of Zion

verseByVerse.quote: They brought the donkey and the colt and put on them their cloaks, and he sat on them. Most of the crowd spread their cloaks on the road, and others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They brought the donkey and the colt and put their cloaks on them, and he sat on them. Most of the crowd spread their cloaks on the road, and others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road.

They brought the donkey and the colt and put on them their cloaks. As a saddle for the King.

And he sat on them. On the cloaks; he rode the colt.

Most of the crowd spread their cloaks on the road. A gesture of homage to a king. When Jehu was proclaimed king, the people spread their garments under him (2 Kings 9:13). It was like laying out a red carpet.

And others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road. John says they were palm branches (John 12:13), which is why the day is called Palm Sunday. Palm branches were a symbol of victory and national hope. When Simon Maccabeus liberated Jerusalem in 141 BC, the people celebrated with palm branches (1 Maccabees 13:51). They also featured in the Feast of Tabernacles (Leviticus 23:40). The crowd was greeting a liberator.

In a sentence. The crowds welcomed Jesus as King, spreading their cloaks and branches on the road.

On a Tuesday. What would it mean for you to “lay your cloak” before Jesus: to honour him with what you have?
verseByVerse.note: Spreading cloaks on the road was a gesture of homage to a king.

verseByVerse.quote: And the crowds that went before him and that followed him were shouting, "Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!" And when he entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred up, saying, "Who is this?" And the crowds said, "This is the prophet Jesus, from Nazareth of Galilee."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowds going ahead and those following shouted: Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest! When he entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred: who is this? The crowds said: this is the prophet Jesus, from Nazareth of Galilee.

And the crowds that went before him and that followed him were shouting. A procession of pilgrims, with Jesus in the middle.

Hosanna to the Son of David! “Hosanna” is Hebrew for “Save, we pray!” or “Save now!”, from Psalm 118:25. By Jesus’ time it had become a shout of praise and welcome. “Son of David”: the Messiah (1:1). The crowd openly hails Jesus as the Messiah-King.

Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Psalm 118:26. Psalm 118 was one of the Hallel psalms (Psalms 113–118), sung by pilgrims at Passover. It was a psalm of a king returning in victory, received at the gates of the temple. “He who comes” was a title for the Messiah (11:3).

Hosanna in the highest! Praise to God in the highest heaven.

And when he entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred up. “Stirred” (eseisthē) means shaken, as by an earthquake (the same root as 27:51; 28:2). The city was shaken, as it had been at his birth when the magi came (2:3).

Saying, “Who is this?” The question of the whole Gospel.

And the crowds said, “This is the prophet Jesus, from Nazareth of Galilee.” A true answer, but incomplete. He is a prophet (Deuteronomy 18:15), but far more. Within five days, many of the same crowds would shout “Let him be crucified!” (27:22). Their enthusiasm was for a political deliverer, not a suffering Saviour.

What it does not mean. Not that the crowd was entirely insincere. Many were genuinely moved. But their understanding was shallow. Popular enthusiasm is not the same as faith.

In a sentence. The crowds hailed Jesus as the Messiah-King with Hosannas from Psalm 118, and the shaken city asked who he was.

On a Tuesday. Who is Jesus to you: a prophet, a great teacher, or the King? Your answer decides how you will stand when the crowd turns.

For worship. Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!
verseByVerse.note: “Hosanna” means “save, we pray,” and had become a shout of praise.

parallels.desc: blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus entered the temple and drove out all who sold and bought in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold pigeons. He said to them, "It is written, 'My house shall be called a house of prayer,' but you make it a den of robbers." And the blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he healed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus entered the temple and drove out all who were selling and buying there. He overturned the money-changers’ tables and the seats of those selling pigeons. He said: it is written, my house shall be called a house of prayer, but you make it a den of robbers. And the blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he healed them.

And Jesus entered the temple. The King comes to his Father’s house. Malachi 3:1 promised that the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple, and asked who could endure the day of his coming.

And drove out all who sold and bought in the temple. The trading took place in the Court of the Gentiles, the large outer courtyard of the temple. Pilgrims needed animals for sacrifice, and buying them in the temple was convenient. But the area meant for Gentiles to pray had become a noisy market.

And he overturned the tables of the money-changers. Every Jewish man had to pay the temple tax (17:24) in a particular silver coin, the Tyrian shekel. Money-changers exchanged foreign coins for a fee, which was often excessive.

And the seats of those who sold pigeons. Pigeons were the sacrifices offered by the poor (Leviticus 5:7; 12:8). Jesus’ own mother offered them at his birth (Luke 2:24). The sellers may have charged exorbitant prices, exploiting the poor.

It is written, “My house shall be called a house of prayer.” From Isaiah 56:7, which continues: for all peoples. God intended the temple to be a place where even foreigners could come and pray. The trading had pushed them out.

But you make it a den of robbers. From Jeremiah 7:11. In Jeremiah’s sermon, the people thought the temple would protect them while they lived wickedly, as robbers hide in a cave between raids. God warned that he would destroy the temple, as he destroyed Shiloh. Jesus’ action is a prophetic sign of judgment: the temple will be destroyed (24:2), as it was in AD 70.

And the blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he healed them. When David captured Jerusalem, a saying arose that the blind and the lame shall not come into the house (2 Samuel 5:8). The Son of David welcomes them in, and heals them. True worship is restored.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus approved of violence as a means of reform. His action was a unique prophetic act by the Lord of the temple, not a model for Christians to use force in church disputes. Nor does it forbid churches from selling anything, ever. The point is the corruption of worship by greed and the exclusion of others from God’s presence.

In a sentence. Jesus drove the traders from the temple, condemning its corruption and announcing its judgment, and healed the blind and lame there.

On a Tuesday. Is there anything in your church, or in your own heart, which God made for prayer, that has become a marketplace?
verseByVerse.note: The trading happened in the outer court, the only place Gentiles could pray. Pigeons were the sacrifice the poor could afford. Money-changers exchanged coins into the currency accepted for the temple tax.

parallels.desc: a house of prayer for all peoples
pigeons for those who cannot afford a lamb

verseByVerse.quote: But when the chief priests and the scribes saw the wonderful things that he did, and the children crying out in the temple, "Hosanna to the Son of David!" they were indignant, and they said to him, "Do you hear what these are saying?" And Jesus said to them, "Yes; have you never read, 'Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the chief priests and scribes saw the wonderful things he did, and the children crying out in the temple, “Hosanna to the Son of David!”, they were indignant. They asked: do you hear what these are saying? Jesus said: yes; have you never read, “Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise”?

But when the chief priests and the scribes saw the wonderful things that he did. The healings (v. 14).

And the children crying out in the temple, “Hosanna to the Son of David!” The children had picked up the crowd’s cry.

They were indignant. The leaders saw the same miracles and heard the same praise, and were angry. They knew what the title meant: the children were calling Jesus the Messiah.

Do you hear what these are saying? They expected Jesus to stop them.

Yes; have you never read, “Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise”? Psalm 8:2, in its Greek form. Psalm 8 is about praise to God; Jesus applies it to praise of himself. The children are praising God by praising Jesus. Once again Jesus claims what belongs to God. The children see what the experts cannot (11:25).

In a sentence. The leaders were indignant at children hailing Jesus as Messiah, but he answered that God has ordained praise from the mouths of children.

On a Tuesday. Children can see Jesus more clearly than experts. Teach them to praise him, and learn from their simple faith.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus quotes the psalm in its Greek form.

parallels.desc: out of the mouth of babies and infants

verseByVerse.quote: And leaving them, he went out of the city to Bethany and lodged there. In the morning, as he was returning to the city, he became hungry.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus left them and went out of the city to Bethany, and spent the night there. In the morning, as he returned to the city, he was hungry.

And leaving them, he went out of the city to Bethany. Bethany was a village about two miles (three kilometres) east of Jerusalem, on the far side of the Mount of Olives. It was the home of Martha, Mary and Lazarus (John 11:1). Jesus stayed there each night of his last week, probably with them (26:6).

And lodged there. The city was overcrowded with pilgrims, and Jesus may have avoided staying inside the city at night for his safety until his hour came.

In the morning, as he was returning to the city, he became hungry. Monday morning. Jesus was truly human, with real hunger.

In a sentence. Jesus spent the night at Bethany and returned to Jerusalem hungry in the morning.

On a Tuesday. Jesus needed rest and food like you. He understands your human needs (Hebrews 4:15).
verseByVerse.note: Bethany was about two miles east of Jerusalem, home of Mary, Martha and Lazarus.

verseByVerse.quote: And seeing a fig tree by the wayside, he went to it and found nothing on it but only leaves. And he said to it, "May no fruit ever come from you again!" And the fig tree withered at once. When the disciples saw it, they marveled, saying, "How did the fig tree wither at once?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seeing a fig tree by the road, Jesus went to it and found nothing on it but leaves. He said to it: may no fruit ever come from you again. And the fig tree withered at once. The disciples were amazed: how did the fig tree wither so quickly?

And seeing a fig tree by the wayside, he went to it and found nothing on it but only leaves. Fig trees in Palestine produced small early fruit, called taqsh, along with their leaves in spring, before the main crop. A tree in full leaf normally promised fruit. Mark adds that it was not the season for figs (Mark 11:13), meaning the main crop. But a tree with leaves and no early fruit at all was barren: it advertised fruit and had none.

And he said to it, “May no fruit ever come from you again!” A prophetic sign, an acted parable. In the Old Testament, the fig tree was a symbol of Israel (Jeremiah 8:13; Hosea 9:10; Micah 7:1). The tree was like the temple and its leaders: impressive, full of leaves (religious activity), but without the fruit God looked for (righteousness, justice, mercy, faith). Jesus had just found the temple the same way (vv. 12–13). The tree’s withering pictures God’s judgment on fruitless religion, which fell on the temple in AD 70.

And the fig tree withered at once. Mark says they noticed it the next morning (Mark 11:20). Matthew compresses the story.

When the disciples saw it, they marveled, saying, “How did the fig tree wither at once?” They were amazed at the power, but did they understand the meaning?

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus was acting in a fit of irritation because he was hungry. This was a deliberate prophetic act, like the prophets’ acted parables (Jeremiah 13:1–11; 19:1–13). It is Jesus’ only miracle of judgment in the Gospels. Nor does it mean that God has rejected the Jewish people for ever. The judgment fell on the temple system and the leaders who rejected the Messiah. Paul shows that God has not finished with Israel (Romans 11).

In a sentence. Jesus cursed a fig tree that had leaves but no fruit, a prophetic sign of judgment on Israel’s fruitless temple religion.

On a Tuesday. Is your Christian life all leaves and no fruit: plenty of activity and appearance, but little real love, obedience and faith?
verseByVerse.note: Mark adds that “it was not the season for figs”; leaves on a fig tree normally promise early fruit. The fig tree was a prophetic picture of Israel.

parallels.desc: no figs on the fig tree

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered them, "Truly, I say to you, if you have faith and do not doubt, you will not only do what has been done to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, 'Be taken up and thrown into the sea,' it will happen. And whatever you ask in prayer, you will receive, if you have faith."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered: truly, if you have faith and do not doubt, you will not only do what was done to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, “Be taken up and thrown into the sea”, it will happen. And whatever you ask in prayer, you will receive, if you have faith.

Truly, I say to you, if you have faith and do not doubt. “Doubt” (diakrithēte) means to be divided, to waver between two opinions (James 1:6–8).

You will not only do what has been done to the fig tree. The disciples could share in Jesus’ power through faith.

But even if you say to this mountain. Probably the Mount of Olives, where they were standing, or the temple mount, visible across the valley.

“Be taken up and thrown into the sea,” it will happen. A vivid picture of doing the impossible (see 17:20). If Jesus pointed to the temple mount, there may be a further meaning: the old temple order would be removed, and God’s people would no longer need it, because they would pray in faith directly to God through Christ.

And whatever you ask in prayer, you will receive, if you have faith. A great promise about prayer, to be read in the light of the rest of Scripture: asking in Jesus’ name, according to God’s will (John 14:13–14; 1 John 5:14–15), and from a heart that forgives (Mark 11:25).

What it does not mean. Not that faith is a technique that guarantees whatever we want, or that unanswered prayers prove a lack of faith. Jesus himself prayed in Gethsemane, “If it be possible, let this cup pass from me”, and it did not pass, because it was not the Father’s will (26:39). Faith trusts God and submits to his will. The promise is that God answers the prayer of faith; he answers as a wise Father, not as a vending machine.

In a sentence. Jesus promised that faith without doubt can do the impossible, and that believing prayer will be answered.

On a Tuesday. Pray today with faith, about a specific need, trusting God to answer in his wisdom.

parallels.desc: ask in faith, with no doubting

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–46 — Authority Questioned: Three Parables of Judgment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chief priests and elders challenge Jesus's authority: by what authority do you do these things? Jesus answers with a counter-question about John's baptism that they refuse to answer, then tells three parables of judgment: the two sons (the one who refused then obeyed vs. the one who agreed but didn't), the wicked tenants who killed the vineyard owner's son, and the implied parable of the rejected cornerstone from Psalm 118. The parables systematically indict the religious leadership of Israel for rejecting God's messengers and the Son himself. The counter-question is not a diversion: John had already answered the authority question in public, so to ask whether John was from heaven is to hand it back in the one form they cannot answer safely. And the verdict between the parables is the sharpest sentence in the chapter — the tax collectors and the prostitutes go into the kingdom ahead of them (vv. 31-32).
verseByVerse.theology: The authority question and Jesus's counter-question about John expose the leaders' bad faith: they do not want to know the source of Jesus's authority; they want to discredit him publicly. Their refusal to answer John's question (whether from heaven or from men) reveals that they are governed by crowd opinion rather than truth-seeking. Jesus therefore refuses to answer them directly — but he answers indirectly and devastatingly through the three parables. The wicked tenants is the most explicit: they will kill the son, and the vineyard will be given to others who will produce its fruits. Two details carry the tenants parable. Jesus quotes Isaiah's Song of the Vineyard almost item for item (Isa 5:1-2) and then changes it: in Isaiah the vine is at fault, here the vine is fine and the tenants are the problem — the indictment is narrowed off the nation and onto its leaders. And the tenants do not kill the son by mistake. This is the heir — recognition is the motive, which is why unbelief in this chapter is never a shortage of information. Note also 2 Chr 36:15-16, which is this parable written four centuries early: God sent persistently by his messengers, and they kept mocking them, until there was no remedy.
verseByVerse.examples: The rejected cornerstone from Psalm 118:22 — the same psalm shouted at the triumphal entry — completes the argument. The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; what the religious establishment rejects, God establishes as the foundation of his kingdom. The chief priests and Pharisees understood that he was speaking about them — and they wanted to arrest him but feared the crowds. The rejection is comprehensive; the judgment is announced; the crowds are the only restraint preventing its immediate human execution. Two applications. Verse 43's taken away from you is about tenancy, not race — the vineyard is re-let, and the people it was first let to were Jews to a man (see the verse-by-verse on vv. 43-44). And verse 45 is the most sobering sentence here for anyone who reads the Bible well: they perceived that he was speaking about them. The parables landed perfectly, were understood completely, and produced not repentance but an arrest plan. Understanding the text is not the goal, and it is possible to be an excellent reader of Scripture and be destroyed by what you have correctly understood.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he entered the temple, the chief priests and the elders of the people came up to him as he was teaching, and said, "By what authority are you doing these things, and who gave you this authority?" Jesus answered them, "I also will ask you one question, and if you tell me the answer, then I also will tell you by what authority I do these things."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus entered the temple and was teaching, the chief priests and the elders of the people came to him and asked: by what authority are you doing these things, and who gave you this authority? Jesus answered: I will also ask you one question. If you answer me, I will tell you by what authority I do these things.

And when he entered the temple, the chief priests and the elders of the people came up to him as he was teaching. Tuesday of Holy Week. The chief priests and elders were members of the Sanhedrin, the ruling council. They controlled the temple. Jesus had just driven out their traders.

By what authority are you doing these things, and who gave you this authority? “These things”: the triumphal entry, the cleansing of the temple, the healings, the teaching. They were the official authorities over the temple; Jesus had no official position. Who did he think he was? It was a trap. If he said “from God”, they could charge him with blasphemy; if he said “my own”, they could dismiss him.

I also will ask you one question. Rabbis often answered a question with a question.

And if you tell me the answer, then I also will tell you by what authority I do these things. Jesus is not evading. His question will reveal the answer to theirs.

In a sentence. The temple authorities challenged Jesus’ authority, and he answered with a question of his own.

On a Tuesday. Are you asking questions about Jesus to find the truth, or to avoid it?

verseByVerse.quote: The baptism of John, from where did it come? From heaven or from man?" And they discussed it among themselves, saying, "If we say, 'From heaven,' he will say to us, 'Why then did you not believe him?' But if we say, 'From man,' we are afraid of the crowd, for they all hold that John was a prophet."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus asked: the baptism of John, where did it come from? From heaven or from man? They discussed it among themselves: if we say from heaven, he will ask us why we did not believe him. But if we say from man, we are afraid of the crowd, for they all hold that John was a prophet.

The baptism of John, from where did it come? From heaven or from man? “Baptism” stands for John’s whole ministry. “From heaven” means from God. If John was sent by God, then his testimony about Jesus was true: he pointed to Jesus as the Coming One (3:11–17). The answer to Jesus’ question is the answer to theirs: Jesus’ authority comes from the same God who sent John.

And they discussed it among themselves. They did not ask what was true, but what was safe.

If we say, “From heaven,” he will say to us, “Why then did you not believe him?” They had rejected John (21:32; Luke 7:30).

But if we say, “From man,” we are afraid of the crowd, for they all hold that John was a prophet. Luke adds that they feared the people would stone them (Luke 20:6). John was popular, and his death at Herod’s hands had made him a martyr.

In a sentence. Jesus asked whether John’s ministry was from God, and the leaders, thinking only of their safety, saw that every answer trapped them.

On a Tuesday. Do you decide what you believe based on what is true, or on what is safe and popular?
verseByVerse.note: “From heaven” means from God.

verseByVerse.quote: So they answered Jesus, "We do not know." And he said to them, "Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things. What do you think? A man had two sons. And he went to the first and said, 'Son, go and work in the vineyard today.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they answered: we do not know. Jesus said: neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things. What do you think? A man had two sons. He went to the first and said: son, go and work in the vineyard today.

So they answered Jesus, “We do not know.” A lie, or a deliberate refusal to commit. The religious leaders, whose job was to judge true and false prophets, claimed not to know. Their refusal to answer showed that they were not seeking truth.

Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things. Jesus will not give further revelation to those who reject what they already have (7:6; 13:12). But his three following parables answer the question indirectly: his authority comes from his Father, who has sent his Son (v. 37).

What do you think? A man had two sons. The first of three parables against the leaders (21:28–22:14). The father pictures God.

And he went to the first and said, “Son, go and work in the vineyard today.” A father has the right to his son’s obedience. The vineyard again pictures God’s kingdom (20:1; Isaiah 5:1–7).

In a sentence. When the leaders refused to answer, Jesus refused to answer them, and began a parable about a father and two sons.

On a Tuesday. Refusing to answer God’s questions does not make them go away.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he answered, 'I will not,' but afterward he changed his mind and went. And he went to the other son and said the same. And he answered, 'I will, sir,' but did not go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first son answered: I will not. But afterward he changed his mind and went. The father went to the other son and said the same. He answered: I go, sir. But he did not go.

And he answered, “I will not,” but afterward he changed his mind and went. A rude refusal, followed by repentance. “Changed his mind” (metamelētheis) means regretted, repented. His first words were wrong, but his actions were right.

And he went to the other son and said the same. The same command.

And he answered, “I go, sir,” but did not go. “Sir” is literally “Lord” (kyrie). A polite, respectful answer, with no obedience. Words without action (7:21).

Textual note. Some manuscripts reverse the order of the two sons, and the leaders’ answer in verse 31 then varies. Verdict: the ESV’s order is best supported; the meaning is the same either way.

In a sentence. One son refused but then obeyed; the other politely agreed but never went.

On a Tuesday. Are you the second son: saying yes to God in church on Sunday, but not doing his will on Monday?

verseByVerse.quote: "Which of the two did the will of his father?" They said, "The first." Jesus said to them, "Truly, I say to you, the tax collectors and the prostitutes go into the kingdom of God before you. For John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him, but the tax collectors and the prostitutes believed him. And even when you saw it, you did not afterward change your minds and believe him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Which of the two did his father’s will? They said: the first. Jesus said: truly, the tax collectors and prostitutes are going into the kingdom of God before you. John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him, but the tax collectors and prostitutes believed him. Even when you saw it, you did not change your minds and believe him.

Which of the two did the will of his father? The answer is obvious.

They said, “The first.” They condemn themselves.

Truly, I say to you, the tax collectors and the prostitutes go into the kingdom of God before you. A shocking statement. Tax collectors (see 9:9) and prostitutes were the most despised sinners in Jewish society. They had said “no” to God by their lives, but repented when John preached. The religious leaders had said “yes” to God by their words and religious practice, but refused to repent. “Before you” may mean “instead of you”: they are entering, and you are not.

For John came to you in the way of righteousness. John preached and lived righteousness: repentance and a changed life (3:1–12).

And you did not believe him, but the tax collectors and the prostitutes believed him. Luke says that tax collectors came to John to be baptised (Luke 3:12; 7:29–30).

And even when you saw it, you did not afterward change your minds and believe him. They saw sinners changed by John’s preaching, and still did not repent. The same word as the first son (v. 29): he changed his mind; they did not.

What it does not mean. Not that being a tax collector or prostitute is a way into the kingdom. It is repentance and faith that bring people in. Nor does it mean that religious people cannot be saved. But they must repent like anyone else, and their religion can make that harder.

In a sentence. Notorious sinners who repented at John’s preaching are entering the kingdom ahead of the religious leaders who said yes to God but refused to repent.

On a Tuesday. Never think you are better than the “obvious sinners”. They may be entering the kingdom ahead of the respectable.

parallels.desc: the tax collectors baptized, the Pharisees refusing

verseByVerse.quote: "Hear another parable. There was a master of a house who planted a vineyard and put a fence around it and dug a winepress in it and built a tower and leased it to tenants, and went into another country. When the season for fruit drew near, he sent his servants to the tenants to get his fruit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus told another parable. A landowner planted a vineyard, put a wall around it, dug a winepress in it and built a watchtower. Then he leased it to tenants and went to another country. When harvest time came, he sent his servants to the tenants to collect his fruit.

Hear another parable. The second of the three parables.

There was a master of a house who planted a vineyard and put a fence around it and dug a winepress in it and built a tower. The details echo Isaiah 5:1–7, the song of the vineyard, which Jesus’ hearers knew well. In Isaiah, God planted a vineyard, cleared it, built a watchtower and dug a wine vat, and looked for good grapes, but it produced wild grapes. Isaiah explains that the vineyard is the house of Israel. The fence protected it from animals; the winepress was a pit cut in rock to crush the grapes; the tower was for watchmen and storage. The owner had provided everything.

And leased it to tenants, and went into another country. Absentee landlords were common in Galilee. Tenant farmers worked the land and paid part of the harvest as rent. The tenants are Israel’s leaders, entrusted with God’s people (v. 45).

When the season for fruit drew near, he sent his servants to the tenants to get his fruit. The owner had a right to his share. God had the right to the fruit of his people: righteousness, justice and faithfulness. The servants are the prophets.

In a sentence. A landowner carefully planted a vineyard, leased it to tenants, and at harvest sent servants to collect his share.

On a Tuesday. Everything you have is God’s vineyard, entrusted to you. What fruit is he looking for from your life?
verseByVerse.note: The setting echoes Isaiah’s song of the vineyard, where the vineyard is Israel. Absentee landlords commonly leased land to tenant farmers.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the tenants took his servants and beat one, killed another, and stoned another. Again he sent other servants, more than the first. And they did the same to them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the tenants seized his servants: they beat one, killed another and stoned another. Again he sent other servants, more than the first, and they did the same to them.

And the tenants took his servants and beat one, killed another, and stoned another. The history of Israel’s treatment of the prophets. Jeremiah was beaten and imprisoned (Jeremiah 20:2; 37:15); Uriah was killed (Jeremiah 26:20–23); Zechariah son of Jehoiada was stoned in the temple court (2 Chronicles 24:20–22). Jesus later says Jerusalem kills the prophets and stones those sent to it (23:37).

Again he sent other servants, more than the first. The owner’s patience is astonishing. A normal landlord would have sent soldiers. God kept sending prophets, century after century (2 Chronicles 36:15–16).

And they did the same to them. Persistent rejection.

In a sentence. The tenants beat, killed and stoned the owner’s servants, and when he patiently sent more, they did the same.

On a Tuesday. God is astonishingly patient. How many times has he sent his word to you through others? Do not test his patience.

verseByVerse.quote: "Finally he sent his son to them, saying, 'They will respect my son.' But when the tenants saw the son, they said to themselves, 'This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and have his inheritance.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Finally he sent his son to them, saying: they will respect my son. But when the tenants saw the son, they said to themselves: this is the heir. Come, let us kill him and have his inheritance.

Finally he sent his son to them. The last messenger, after all the servants. Mark says his beloved son (Mark 12:6). Jesus is distinguishing himself from all the prophets: they were servants; he is the Son. This is the answer to the question about his authority (v. 23): he comes from the Father, as the Son (Hebrews 1:1–2).

Saying, “They will respect my son.” The owner’s hope. It shows the depth of God’s patience and love: he sent his own Son.

But when the tenants saw the son, they said to themselves, “This is the heir.” They recognised who he was. The leaders knew, at some level, that Jesus had a claim on them.

Come, let us kill him and have his inheritance. Under the law of the time, if an owner died without an heir, tenants might be able to claim the land. Their reasoning was absurd: the owner was still alive. But it reveals their motive: they wanted to keep control of the vineyard for themselves. The leaders wanted to keep their power over God’s people, and Jesus threatened it (John 11:48).

In a sentence. Finally the owner sent his son, but the tenants recognised him as heir and plotted to kill him to seize the vineyard.

On a Tuesday. What do you want to keep control of, rather than surrender to Christ, the heir?

parallels.desc: God has spoken by his Son

verseByVerse.quote: "And they took him and threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. When therefore the owner of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those tenants?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They seized him, threw him out of the vineyard, and killed him. When the owner of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those tenants?

And they took him and threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. Jesus predicts his own death in the parable. He was crucified outside the city walls of Jerusalem (Hebrews 13:12–13; John 19:17).

When therefore the owner of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those tenants? Jesus asks his hearers to pronounce the judgment, as Nathan made David pronounce judgment on himself (2 Samuel 12:1–7).

In a sentence. The tenants threw out and killed the son, and Jesus asked what the owner would do to them.

On a Tuesday. Jesus knew exactly how he would die, and told his killers. He went to death with open eyes.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus was crucified outside the city walls.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "He will put those wretches to a miserable death and let out the vineyard to other tenants who will give him the fruits in their seasons." Jesus said to them, "Have you never read in the Scriptures: 'The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this was the Lord's doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They said: he will put those wretches to a miserable death and lease the vineyard to other tenants who will give him the fruit in their seasons. Jesus said: have you never read in the Scriptures, “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this was the Lord’s doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes”?

He will put those wretches to a miserable death and let out the vineyard to other tenants. They condemned themselves. The judgment came in AD 70, when the Romans destroyed Jerusalem and the temple, ending the rule of the priestly leaders.

Who will give him the fruits in their seasons. The new tenants: those who produce fruit (v. 43).

Have you never read in the Scriptures. Jesus quotes Psalm 118:22–23, the same psalm the crowds sang at his entry (v. 9).

The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. The picture changes from a vineyard to a building. The builders (Israel’s leaders) rejected a stone as useless, but God made it the cornerstone (see Ephesians 2:20), the most important stone of the whole building. Jesus, rejected and killed, will be raised and exalted by God to be the foundation of God’s new temple, his people (Acts 4:11; 1 Peter 2:4–8).

This was the Lord’s doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes. The resurrection and exaltation of Jesus is God’s work, astonishing and wonderful.

In a sentence. The leaders condemned the wicked tenants, and Jesus quoted Psalm 118: the rejected stone becomes the cornerstone by God’s doing.

For worship. Praise God for raising the rejected stone to be the cornerstone. It is marvellous in our eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore I tell you, the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a people producing its fruits. And the one who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces; and when it falls on anyone, it will crush him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, I tell you, the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a people producing its fruits. And whoever falls on this stone will be broken to pieces; and when it falls on anyone, it will crush him.

Therefore I tell you, the kingdom of God will be taken away from you. “You” means the leaders and those who follow them in rejecting Jesus. Their privileged position as stewards of God’s people would be taken from them.

And given to a people producing its fruits. “People” (ethnei) is singular: a nation, a people. It is the new people of God, the church, made up of believing Jews (beginning with the apostles) and believing Gentiles: the “holy nation” of 1 Peter 2:9. They produce the fruit God wants: repentance, faith, righteousness.

And the one who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces. Isaiah 8:14–15: a stone of stumbling, over which many will fall and be broken. Those who stumble over Jesus, rejecting him, are broken.

And when it falls on anyone, it will crush him. Daniel 2:34–35, 44–45: the stone cut without hands that strikes and crushes the kingdoms of the world, and becomes a great mountain filling the earth. At the final judgment, the stone falls on those who reject him.

Textual note. Some manuscripts omit verse 44. It may have been added from Luke 20:18. Verdict: the evidence is divided; it is probably original, and Luke confirms that Jesus said it.

What it does not mean. Not that God has rejected the Jewish people as a race and replaced them with Gentiles (a crude form of “replacement theology”). The leaders who rejected Jesus lost their stewardship; the new people includes believing Jews, starting with the Twelve, and Paul hopes for many more (Romans 11:1–2, 11–26). There is one people of God in Christ, the one olive tree, into which Gentiles are grafted and from which unbelieving branches are broken off, and into which Jews who believe will be grafted again (Romans 11:17–24).

In a sentence. The kingdom will be taken from those who reject Jesus and given to a people who bear its fruit, and the stone they reject will break and crush them.

On a Tuesday. Jesus is either the cornerstone you build on, or the stone you stumble over. Which is he for you?
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit verse 44.

parallels.desc: the stone that breaks the kingdoms

verseByVerse.quote: When the chief priests and the Pharisees heard his parables, they perceived that he was speaking about them. And although they were seeking to arrest him, they feared the crowds, because they held him to be a prophet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the chief priests and Pharisees heard his parables, they realised he was speaking about them. They wanted to arrest him, but they were afraid of the crowds, because the people held him to be a prophet.

When the chief priests and the Pharisees heard his parables, they perceived that he was speaking about them. They understood the meaning clearly: they were the second son, and the wicked tenants.

And although they were seeking to arrest him, they feared the crowds. They understood, and instead of repenting, they wanted to do exactly what the parable described: kill the son.

Because they held him to be a prophet. The crowds’ opinion (v. 11) protected Jesus for now. The leaders would wait until they could arrest him away from the crowds (26:4–5).

What it does not mean. Not that understanding God’s word is enough. They understood perfectly and responded with hostility. Knowledge without repentance hardens.

In a sentence. The leaders understood that the parables were about them, and instead of repenting, they plotted to arrest Jesus.

On a Tuesday. When God’s word convicts you, respond with repentance, not resentment.

21.theology: Christ as the true Temple. The temple cleansing in Matthew 21 points to one of the great themes of biblical theology: Jesus as the replacement and fulfilment of the temple. The temple was the place where God dwelt with his people, where sacrifice was made, where prayer ascended. Jesus embodies all three functions: he is Emmanuel — God dwelling with his people; he is the Lamb whose self-offering ends the sacrificial system; he is the mediator through whom prayer reaches the Father (John 14:13–14). John’s Gospel makes this explicit (“the temple he had spoken of was his body”, John 2:21). The destruction of the Jerusalem temple in AD 70 was the confirmation that the type had given way to the antitype.
21.examples:
Then: The crowds welcomed Jesus with genuine excitement and completely wrong expectations. They wanted a Maccabean king who would drive out Rome; they got a crucified Servant who would drive out death. The Palm Sunday crowd’s theology is a warning: it is possible to praise Jesus enthusiastically while fundamentally misunderstanding who he is and what he has come to do.

Now: The fig tree is the perennial warning against fruitless religion — maintaining the form of Christian practice without the substance of faith, repentance, love, and transformed life. The church with its worship services, theological conferences, and evangelical brands may be full of leaves. The question Jesus asks of every institution and every individual is the same: where is the fruit?

22.title: The Great Banquet and the Hard Questions
22.text: <sup>1</sup>And again Jesus spoke to them in parables, saying, <sup>2</sup>“The kingdom of heaven may be compared to a king who gave a wedding feast for his son, <sup>3</sup>and sent his servants to call those who were invited to the wedding feast, but they would not come. <sup>4</sup>Again he sent other servants, saying, ‘Tell those who are invited, “See, I have prepared my dinner, my oxen and my fat calves have been slaughtered, and everything is ready. Come to the wedding feast.”’ <sup>5</sup>But they paid no attention and went off, one to his farm, another to his business, <sup>6</sup>while the rest seized his servants, treated them shamefully, and killed them. <sup>7</sup>The king was angry, and he sent his troops and destroyed those murderers and burned their city. <sup>8</sup>Then he said to his servants, ‘The wedding feast is ready, but those invited were not worthy. <sup>9</sup>Go therefore to the main roads and invite to the wedding feast as many as you find.’ <sup>10</sup>And those servants went out into the roads and gathered all whom they found, both bad and good. So the wedding hall was filled with guests. <sup>11</sup>“But when the king came in to look at the guests, he saw there a man who had no wedding garment. <sup>12</sup>And he said to him, ‘Friend, how did you get in here without a wedding garment?’ And he was speechless. <sup>13</sup>Then the king said to the attendants, ‘Bind him hand and foot and cast him into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.’ <sup>14</sup>For many are called, but few are chosen.” <sup>15</sup>Then the Pharisees went and plotted how to entangle him in his words. <sup>16</sup>And they sent their disciples to him, along with the Herodians, saying, “Teacher, we know that you are true and teach the way of God truthfully, and you do not care about anyone’s opinion, for you are not swayed by appearances. <sup>17</sup>Tell us, then, what you think. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not?” <sup>18</sup>But Jesus, aware of their malice, said, “Why put me to the test, you hypocrites? <sup>19</sup>Show me the coin for the tax.” And they brought him a denarius. <sup>20</sup>And Jesus said to them, “Whose likeness and inscription is this?” <sup>21</sup>They said, “Caesar’s.” Then he said to them, “Therefore render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” <sup>22</sup>When they heard it, they marveled. And they left him and went away. <sup>23</sup>The same day Sadducees came to him, who say that there is no resurrection, and they asked him a question, <sup>24</sup>saying, “Teacher, Moses said, ‘If a man dies having no children, his brother must marry the widow and raise up offspring for his brother.’ <sup>25</sup>Now there were seven brothers among us. The first married and died, and having no offspring left his wife to his brother. <sup>26</sup>So too the second and third, down to the seventh. <sup>27</sup>After them all, the woman died. <sup>28</sup>In the resurrection, therefore, of the seven, whose wife will she be? For they all had her.” <sup>29</sup>But Jesus answered them, “You are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. <sup>30</sup>For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven. <sup>31</sup>And as for the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was said to you by God: <sup>32</sup>‘I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? He is not God of the dead, but of the living.” <sup>33</sup>And when the crowd heard it, they were astonished at his teaching. <sup>34</sup>But when the Pharisees heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, they gathered together. <sup>35</sup>And one of them, a lawyer, asked him a question to test him. <sup>36</sup>“Teacher, which is the great commandment in the Law?” <sup>37</sup>And he said to him, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind. <sup>38</sup>This is the great and first commandment. <sup>39</sup>And a second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. <sup>40</sup>On these two commandments depend all the Law and the Prophets.” <sup>41</sup>Now while the Pharisees were gathered together, Jesus asked them a question, <sup>42</sup>saying, “What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?” They said to him, “The son of David.” <sup>43</sup>He said to them, “How is it then that David, in the Spirit, calls him Lord, saying, <sup>44</sup>“‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet”’? <sup>45</sup>If then David calls him Lord, how is he his son?” <sup>46</sup>And no one was able to answer him a word, nor from that day did anyone dare to ask him any more questions.
22.overview:
Chapter 22 is a day of public controversy in Jerusalem. The religious establishment sends wave after wave of opponents — Pharisees, Herodians, Sadducees — each with a question designed to trap Jesus. He answers all of them and turns the final question back on his attackers, leaving them silenced. Matthew arranges the chapter as a trial in which the judge is the one in the dock: every party that challenges Jesus is exposed by his answers, and the final question — “Whose son is the Christ?” — reveals that the Messiah is not merely David’s descendant but David’s Lord.

The chapter opens with the parable of the wedding banquet, which recapitulates the entire history of Israel’s rejection of God’s invitations and the extension of grace to the Gentile roads and byways. “Many are called, but few are chosen” is not a statement about the inefficacy of the gospel but about the mystery of election: the call goes out wide; the choice of God secures who will respond. The banquet hall will be full — but with those God has chosen, not those who presumed on their invitation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — The Parable of the Wedding Banquet and the Question about Taxes
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus tells the parable of the wedding banquet: a king invites guests to his son's wedding, they refuse and some kill his servants, the city is destroyed, and the hall is filled instead with whoever is found at the road junctions, both bad and good. One guest is discovered without a wedding garment and is cast out. Then the Pharisees and Herodians, in an alliance of convenience, try to trap him on the Roman poll tax; he asks for a coin, and answers that what bears Caesar's image goes to Caesar and what bears God's image goes to God. They marvel, and leave him.
verseByVerse.theology: The invitation is free, finished and urgent. Everything is ready is perfect tense throughout — the oxen are already slaughtered, nothing is pending, and the only thing outstanding is attendance. And the guests who refuse had already accepted, since invitations in that world went out twice; they are the second son of 21:30 again, whose word and whose feet have parted company. Grace then reaches the road junctions and gathers both bad and good with no screening at the door, which is the Gentile mission in parabolic form. But grace is not universalism: the king walks the room, and the man without the garment is speechless because nothing had been withheld from him — he had declined what was offered, not failed to manufacture what was required. On the tax, Jesus neither divinises Caesar nor anarchises the gospel. The coin bears Caesar's image and may be returned to him; the image on the man is God's, and that Caesar may never have.
verseByVerse.examples: Notice what the first guests were doing instead: one went to his farm, another to his business. Not vice, not blasphemy — a field that needed walking and a shop that needed running. The most effective rival to God in most lives has never been wickedness but respectable occupation, and it works because nobody has to defend it. Indifference and violence end in the same place in this parable, which should sober anyone who has assumed that not being hostile is the same as being safe; nobody here is condemned for opposing the king, only for not turning up. The tax scene has its own sting: asked for a coin, they produced one — in the temple, from men professing scruples about Caesar's tribute, a denarius inscribed Tiberius Caesar, son of the divine Augustus and Pontifex Maximus. It is easy to hold a principled objection while living comfortably inside the thing, and be unaware of the gap. The test is not what you would say if asked, but what turns up when somebody says: show me. And verse 22 names the most respectable way of rejecting Christ — they marvelled, and they left him.

verseByVerse.quote: And again Jesus spoke to them in parables, saying, "The kingdom of heaven may be compared to a king who gave a wedding feast for his son,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus told another parable: the kingdom of heaven is like a king who prepared a wedding feast for his son.

And again Jesus spoke to them in parables. The third of three parables against the leaders (21:28–22:14). The first showed their refusal to repent; the second their rejection of the Son; this one their refusal of God’s invitation, and God’s invitation going to others.

The kingdom of heaven may be compared to a king who gave a wedding feast for his son. The king is God; the son is Jesus. A royal wedding was the greatest celebration in the ancient world, and could last a week. In Scripture, the age to come is pictured as a great feast (Isaiah 25:6–9), and the relationship between God and his people as a marriage (Isaiah 54:5; Hosea 2:19–20). Jesus is the bridegroom (9:15; 25:1–13). The final consummation is the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:7–9).

In a sentence. In a third parable, Jesus compared the kingdom to a king’s wedding feast for his son.

On a Tuesday. God’s kingdom is a feast, a celebration of joy. Do you think of following Christ as a burden or as an invitation to a wedding?
verseByVerse.note: A royal wedding feast could last a week.

parallels.desc: the marriage supper of the Lamb

verseByVerse.quote: and sent his servants to call those who were invited to the wedding feast, but they would not come. Again he sent other servants, saying, "Tell those who are invited, See, I have prepared my dinner, my oxen and my fat calves have been slaughtered, and everything is ready. Come to the wedding feast."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king sent his servants to call those who had been invited to the wedding feast, but they would not come. He sent other servants: tell those who are invited, see, I have prepared my dinner, my oxen and fattened calves have been slaughtered, and everything is ready. Come to the wedding feast.

And sent his servants to call those who were invited to the wedding feast. In the ancient world, guests were invited in advance, and then summoned again when the feast was ready (Esther 6:14; Luke 14:17). The first invitation is God’s call to Israel through the Old Testament prophets and John; the guests had been told the feast was coming. Now the servants announce that it has come.

But they would not come. A deliberate refusal. To refuse a king’s invitation was a grave insult.

Again he sent other servants. The king’s patience, as with the tenants (21:36).

See, I have prepared my dinner, my oxen and my fat calves have been slaughtered, and everything is ready. A lavish feast, with the best meat, which was rarely eaten by ordinary people. Everything is ready: the guests need bring nothing, only come. This is grace. The gospel is the announcement that God has prepared everything in Christ.

Come to the wedding feast. A personal, urgent invitation.
