In a sentence. The invited guests refused to come, but the king patiently sent more servants to say that the lavish feast was ready.

On a Tuesday. God’s invitation is still “Come; everything is ready.” Have you accepted it?
verseByVerse.note: Guests were invited ahead of time and then summoned when the meal was ready.

verseByVerse.quote: But they paid no attention and went off, one to his farm, another to his business, while the rest seized his servants, treated them shamefully, and killed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they paid no attention and went off, one to his farm, another to his business. The rest seized his servants, treated them shamefully and killed them.

But they paid no attention. “Paid no attention” means they made light of it, did not care.

And went off, one to his farm, another to his business. Two kinds of rejection. Some were indifferent: they had more important things to do. Their farms and businesses were not wrong in themselves, but they put them before the king’s invitation (13:22; Luke 14:18–20).

While the rest seized his servants, treated them shamefully, and killed them. Others were violent, as the tenants were (21:35). God’s messengers, the prophets, John, and later the apostles, were persecuted and killed (23:34; Acts 7:58–60; 12:2).

In a sentence. Some guests ignored the invitation for their business, and others murdered the king’s servants.

On a Tuesday. Indifference is as deadly as hostility. What “farm or business” keeps you from responding wholeheartedly to God?

parallels.desc: the servants in the vineyard beaten and killed

verseByVerse.quote: The king was angry, and he sent his troops and destroyed those murderers and burned their city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king was angry. He sent his troops, destroyed those murderers and burned their city.

The king was angry. God’s just anger at those who reject his grace and kill his messengers.

And he sent his troops and destroyed those murderers and burned their city. An unusual detail in a story about a wedding: a war in the middle of the preparations. It points to the destruction of Jerusalem by the Roman army in AD 70, which burned the city and the temple. Josephus describes the catastrophe in detail. Jesus is speaking prophetically of judgment on the city that rejected him (23:37–38; 24:2). God can use pagan armies as instruments of his judgment (Isaiah 10:5–6).

What it does not mean. Not that God hates the Jewish people, or that Christians may hate them. The judgment fell on a generation that rejected the Messiah, and Christians have often sinfully misused such passages to justify anti-Semitism. Jesus himself wept over Jerusalem (23:37; Luke 19:41–44).

In a sentence. The angry king destroyed the murderers and burned their city, a picture of the coming judgment on Jerusalem.

On a Tuesday. God’s patience is great, but it has an end. Do not presume on it.
verseByVerse.note: Many see here a pointer to the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to his servants, "The wedding feast is ready, but those invited were not worthy. Go therefore to the main roads and invite to the wedding feast as many as you find."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the king said to his servants: the wedding feast is ready, but those invited were not worthy. Go to the main roads and invite to the feast as many as you find.

The wedding feast is ready, but those invited were not worthy. Not worthy because they refused. Worthiness here means willingness to come, not merit (see 10:11).

Go therefore to the main roads. Literally “the partings of the ways”: where a city street leads out into the country roads, where travellers, beggars and all kinds of people gathered. The invitation goes out beyond the original guests.

And invite to the wedding feast as many as you find. No restrictions. Anyone. This is the gospel going to the Gentiles and to the outcasts of Israel (8:11; 21:31; 28:19). The feast will be full.

In a sentence. Since the invited guests refused, the king sent his servants to invite everyone they could find.

On a Tuesday. You are one of the servants sent out to the roads. Whom could you invite to the feast this week?

parallels.desc: we are turning to the Gentiles

verseByVerse.quote: And those servants went out into the roads and gathered all whom they found, both bad and good. So the wedding hall was filled with guests.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servants went out into the roads and gathered all they found, both bad and good. So the wedding hall was filled with guests.

And those servants went out into the roads and gathered all whom they found. The servants obeyed and invited everyone.

Both bad and good. The invitation is not based on moral merit. Notorious sinners and decent people alike are invited. The gospel net catches all kinds (13:47–48).

So the wedding hall was filled with guests. God’s purpose will not fail. His house will be full (Luke 14:23).

In a sentence. The servants gathered everyone, bad and good, and the wedding hall was full.

For worship. Thank God that his invitation reached you, whatever you were.

parallels.desc: the net gathers fish of every kind

verseByVerse.quote: But when the king came in to look at the guests, he saw there a man who had no wedding garment. And he said to him, "Friend, how did you get in here without a wedding garment?" And he was speechless.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the king came in to look at the guests, he saw a man who was not wearing a wedding garment. He said: friend, how did you get in here without a wedding garment? And the man was speechless.

But when the king came in to look at the guests. The king inspects his guests: a picture of God’s final judgment.

He saw there a man who had no wedding garment. Guests at a wedding wore clean, festive clothing. To come in ordinary, dirty clothes was an insult to the host. Some have suggested that kings provided special garments for their guests, which would make refusing one an act of contempt. There is little firm evidence for this custom. But the point is clear either way: this man came on his own terms, without the clothing the occasion required.

What is the wedding garment? In Scripture, clothing often pictures righteousness and salvation. Isaiah rejoices that God has clothed him with the garments of salvation and covered him with the robe of righteousness (Isaiah 61:10). The bride of the Lamb is clothed in fine linen, which is the righteous deeds of the saints (Revelation 19:8). Zechariah saw the high priest’s filthy garments removed and replaced with clean ones, a picture of forgiveness (Zechariah 3:3–5). The wedding garment is the righteousness that God requires and gives: Christ’s righteousness credited to those who trust him, and the new life of righteousness that follows (5:20; Galatians 3:27; Romans 13:14). The man accepted the invitation but did not repent or put on Christ. He wanted the feast without the change.

Friend, how did you get in here without a wedding garment? “Friend” is a cool, polite address (see 20:13).

And he was speechless. He had no excuse. On the day of judgment, every mouth will be stopped (Romans 3:19).

What it does not mean. Not that we earn our place at the feast by our own good works. The invitation is free to all, bad and good (v. 10). But accepting the invitation means coming on the king’s terms: being clothed with the righteousness he provides. Those who claim to belong to the kingdom but have never repented and trusted Christ will be exposed.

In a sentence. The king found a guest without a wedding garment, a picture of someone who accepts God’s invitation outwardly but has not been clothed with righteousness in Christ.

On a Tuesday. Are you clothed in Christ’s righteousness, or only present at the feast in your own clothes?
verseByVerse.note: The wedding garment stands for the fitting clothing the host requires — the righteousness God gives and the life that matches it.

parallels.desc: clothed with the garments of salvation
fine linen, the righteous deeds of the saints

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king said to the attendants, "Bind him hand and foot and cast him into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth." For many are called, but few are chosen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the king told the attendants: bind him hand and foot and throw him into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. For many are called, but few are chosen.

Then the king said to the attendants, “Bind him hand and foot and cast him into the outer darkness.” Bound so that he cannot return. Thrown out of the brightly lit hall into the darkness outside (see 8:12).

In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. The anguish of final judgment (see 8:12; 13:42).

For many are called, but few are chosen. The key saying. “Called” (klētoi) here means invited: the gospel invitation goes out to many, to everyone (v. 9). “Chosen” (eklektoi) means elect: those whom God has chosen, who respond to the invitation with true faith and are clothed in righteousness. Not everyone who hears the invitation responds truly. The gospel call is universal; God’s election is particular.

The two callings. Reformed theology distinguishes the external call of the gospel, which goes to all who hear it, from the effectual or inward call by which the Spirit brings the elect to faith (Romans 8:30; 1 Corinthians 1:23–24; Westminster Confession 10.1, 10.4). Matthew’s word “called” here is the external call. Paul often uses “called” for the effectual call. Both are biblical.

What it does not mean. Not that God refuses those who want to come. The invitation is genuine, to all. Those who are not chosen are those who refuse the invitation (vv. 3–6) or come without the garment (v. 12); they are responsible for their response. God’s election does not make anyone a victim; it guarantees that some will come. Nor does “few” give us a number; it means fewer than those invited.

Where Christians differ: election. Arminians read “chosen” as those who choose to respond, so that election follows human decision. Reformed theology reads it as God’s prior choice, which produces the response (John 6:44; Ephesians 1:4–5; Acts 13:48). Verdict: unconditional election. But the invitation goes to all, and everyone who comes will be received (11:28; John 6:37).

In a sentence. The man without the garment was thrown out, for the gospel invitation goes to many, but only the chosen respond truly.

On a Tuesday. The invitation to you is real. Respond to it fully: come to Christ, and be clothed with him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Pharisees went and plotted how to entangle him in his words. And they sent their disciples to him, along with the Herodians, saying, "Teacher, we know that you are true and teach the way of God truthfully, and you do not care about anyone's opinion, for you are not swayed by appearances."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the Pharisees went and plotted how to trap Jesus in his words. They sent their disciples to him, along with the Herodians, saying: Teacher, we know that you are true and teach the way of God truthfully, and you do not care about anyone’s opinion, for you are not swayed by appearances.

Then the Pharisees went and plotted how to entangle him in his words. Unable to arrest him openly (21:46), they try to trap him into saying something that would turn the crowds against him, or give them grounds to accuse him to the Romans. This begins a series of three test questions (vv. 15–40).

And they sent their disciples to him. They sent their students, perhaps to make the trap look innocent.

Along with the Herodians. Supporters of Herod Antipas and his family, who cooperated with Rome. The Pharisees resented Roman rule; the Herodians supported it. They were natural enemies, united against Jesus (Mark 3:6). Whatever Jesus said about taxes, one group would accuse him.

Teacher, we know that you are true and teach the way of God truthfully. Flattery, intended to make him answer boldly. Ironically, everything they say is true.

And you do not care about anyone’s opinion, for you are not swayed by appearances. Literally “you do not look at the face of people”: you are impartial, unafraid of anyone, including Caesar.

In a sentence. The Pharisees and Herodians, normally enemies, joined to trap Jesus, opening with flattery.

On a Tuesday. Beware of flattery. It is often a trap.
verseByVerse.note: The Herodians supported Herod’s family and Roman rule; the Pharisees resented Rome. Their alliance was a trap.

verseByVerse.quote: "Tell us, then, what you think. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tell us, then, what you think. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not?

Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not? “Lawful” means according to God’s law. The tax was the poll tax (kēnsos, from the Latin census), a yearly tax of one denarius per person paid directly to the Roman emperor. It was bitterly resented as a symbol of foreign rule. When it was introduced in AD 6, a revolt led by Judas the Galilean broke out, with the slogan that God alone was Israel’s king (Acts 5:37). The Zealot movement grew from it.

The trap. If Jesus said “Yes, pay”, he would lose the support of the crowds, who hated the tax and hoped the Messiah would end Roman rule. If he said “No”, the Herodians could report him to the Romans as a rebel, and he would be arrested for sedition. Either way, he loses.

In a sentence. They asked whether it was right to pay the hated Roman tax, a question designed to trap Jesus either way.

On a Tuesday. Some questions are designed to trap, not to learn. Ask God for wisdom to answer them.
verseByVerse.note: This was the poll tax paid directly to Rome, bitterly resented. “Yes” would anger the people; “no” would be treason.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus, aware of their malice, said, "Why put me to the test, you hypocrites? Show me the coin for the tax." And they brought him a denarius.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus, aware of their malice, said: why are you testing me, you hypocrites? Show me the coin used for the tax. And they brought him a denarius.

But Jesus, aware of their malice. “Malice” (ponērian) means wickedness, evil intent. He sees through the flattery.

Why put me to the test, you hypocrites? They pretended to seek his opinion; they wanted to destroy him.

Show me the coin for the tax. The tax had to be paid in Roman coin.

And they brought him a denarius. A silver coin, a day’s wage (20:2). Notice: Jesus did not have one; they did. By producing a Roman coin in the temple courts, they showed that they were already using Caesar’s money and benefiting from his rule.

In a sentence. Seeing through their trap, Jesus asked for the tax coin, and they produced a denarius.

On a Tuesday. Jesus is never fooled by our pretences. Be honest with him.
verseByVerse.note: The denarius was a silver coin, a day’s wage for a labourer.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to them, "Whose likeness and inscription is this?" They said, "Caesar's." Then he said to them, "Therefore render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus asked them: whose likeness and inscription is this? They said: Caesar’s. He said: then give to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.

Whose likeness and inscription is this? The denarius of that time bore the head of the emperor Tiberius (AD 14–37), with an inscription reading, in Latin abbreviation, “Tiberius Caesar, son of the divine Augustus, Augustus”. On the reverse: “High Priest”. To devout Jews, the image and the claim to divinity were offensive, breaking the second commandment.

They said, “Caesar’s.”

Therefore render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s. “Render” (apodote) means give back, pay what is owed. The coin bears Caesar’s image; it belongs to him. Paying taxes to the government is a legitimate obligation. Governments are established by God and have a right to taxes (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Peter 2:13–17). Even a pagan, oppressive government.

And to God the things that are God’s. The deeper point. The coin bears Caesar’s image; human beings bear God’s image (Genesis 1:26–27). Give Caesar his coin; give God yourself, your whole life. Caesar may claim taxes, but not worship. Caesar’s coin called him divine; Jesus quietly denies it. God alone is God.

What it does not mean. Not that life is divided into two separate areas, religious and secular, with God ruling only the first. Everything belongs to God (Psalm 24:1), including Caesar. Caesar’s authority is under God’s. Nor does it mean that governments must always be obeyed. When the state commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands, we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). The apostles obeyed Caesar in paying taxes and refused him when he demanded worship.

Where Christians differ: church and state. Some Christians want the state to enforce Christian law (theonomy, or Christian nationalism). Others want complete separation of religion from public life. The Reformed tradition has generally held that the state and the church are distinct institutions, each under God, with different roles: the state bears the sword for justice; the church bears the keys of the kingdom (Romans 13; Matthew 16:19; Westminster Confession 23). Verdict: Christians should be good citizens, paying taxes, praying for rulers, and seeking justice, while giving ultimate loyalty only to God.

In a sentence. Give the government what it is owed, since the coin bears Caesar’s image, but give God yourself, since you bear his.

On a Tuesday. Pay your taxes honestly. And ask: have I given God what is his, my whole self?
verseByVerse.note: The coin bore the emperor’s head — probably Tiberius — and an inscription calling him son of the divine Augustus.

parallels.desc: be subject to the governing authorities

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard it, they marveled. And they left him and went away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they heard it, they were amazed, and they left him and went away.

When they heard it, they marveled. Jesus’ answer escaped their trap completely, and went deeper than their question.

And they left him and went away. Defeated, but not converted. They marvelled at his wisdom, but did not submit to it.

In a sentence. Amazed at Jesus’ answer, they left him, defeated but unchanged.

On a Tuesday. It is possible to admire Jesus’ wisdom and still walk away. Do not just marvel; obey.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–46 — Resurrection, the Great Commandment, and David's Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three delegations in succession, and then Jesus asks a question of his own. The Sadducees construct a levirate-marriage absurdity with seven brothers to make resurrection look ridiculous, and are told they know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God — the resurrection proved out of the Torah they accepted, from the present tense of one verb at the burning bush. The crowd is astonished. The Pharisees regroup and send a lawyer to ask which commandment is greatest, and receive the Shema and Leviticus 19:18, on which the whole Law and Prophets hang. Then Jesus asks whose son the Christ is, quotes Psalm 110, and nobody is able to answer him a word or dares question him again.
verseByVerse.theology: Two failures are named in one sentence and almost every serious error in the church lands under one of them: you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. The Sadducees had the Torah by heart, which is what makes the first charge devastating — knowing the Scriptures is not the same as having them. And they believed in God while not believing he could do anything, which is a God cut down to the size of arrangements we already understand. The resurrection argument turns on covenant: God binds himself by name to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and says I am, not I was, six hundred years after Abraham died. He does not attach his name to dust. Then the double love command, where the verb is krematai — the Law and Prophets hang on two pegs, so the 613 commandments are not separate obligations but the outworking of two. And Psalm 110 closes the sequence: the Christ is David's son according to the flesh and David's Lord according to his eternal nature, which is Matthew's own first chapter put as a riddle (1:23).
verseByVerse.examples: Like angels in heaven needs its guard: it does not mean we become angels or lose our bodies. The comparison is made in one respect only, and the sentence names it — angels do not marry. On the tender question every widow and every married reader brings here, see the verse-by-verse on vv. 29-30: what ends is the institution, not the love. Notice also the woman in the Sadducees' story, whom nobody in it notices — she has buried seven husbands and appears purely as a question of ownership, and Jesus's answer incidentally gives her back what their question took away. As yourself in v. 39 is a measure, not a recommendation of self-esteem: you never have to be reminded to take an interest in your own toothache, and that automatic attention is the standard. Test it where it bites — when something goes wrong for you the mind supplies context, and when it goes wrong at somebody else's hands the mind supplies character. And v. 33 is a warning laid inside a victory: astonishment is not allegiance, and within three days a crowd in this city would be shouting for Barabbas.

verseByVerse.quote: The same day Sadducees came to him, who say that there is no resurrection, and they asked him a question, saying, "Teacher, Moses said, 'If a man dies having no children, his brother must marry the widow and raise up offspring for his brother.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same day, Sadducees came to Jesus. They say there is no resurrection. They asked him: Teacher, Moses said that if a man dies having no children, his brother must marry the widow and raise up children for his brother.

The same day Sadducees came to him. The second test question. The Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy, wealthy and politically powerful, who controlled the temple (see 3:7). They accepted only the five books of Moses as fully authoritative.

Who say that there is no resurrection. They denied the resurrection of the body, life after death, angels and spirits (Acts 23:8). They believed that the soul perished with the body. They argued that the resurrection was not taught in the books of Moses.

Teacher, Moses said, “If a man dies having no children, his brother must marry the widow and raise up offspring for his brother.” The law of levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5–6; compare Genesis 38:8). If a man died childless, his brother was to marry the widow, and their first son would carry on the dead man’s name and inherit his property. The purpose was to preserve the family line and land, and to protect the widow.

In a sentence. The Sadducees, who denied the resurrection, came to Jesus with a question based on the law of levirate marriage.

On a Tuesday. Some people use the Bible to argue against what the Bible teaches. Read it whole.
verseByVerse.note: The Sadducees, the priestly party, rejected the Pharisees’ oral traditions and probably held the five books of Moses above the rest of Scripture and denied the resurrection. The law of levirate marriage kept a dead man’s name alive.

parallels.desc: Sadducees say there is no resurrection

verseByVerse.quote: "Now there were seven brothers among us. The first married and died, and having no offspring left his wife to his brother. So too the second and third, down to the seventh."
verseByVerse.commentary:
There were seven brothers among us. The first married and died, and having no children, left his wife to his brother. The second did the same, and the third, down to the seventh.

Now there were seven brothers among us. A hypothetical story, designed to make the resurrection look absurd. Perhaps it echoes the book of Tobit, where a woman had seven husbands who all died.

The first married and died, and having no offspring left his wife to his brother. Following the levirate law.

So too the second and third, down to the seventh. All seven died childless, each having married her in turn.

In a sentence. The Sadducees told of a woman who married seven brothers in turn, all of whom died childless.

On a Tuesday. Clever arguments against God’s truth often rest on false assumptions. Look for them.

verseByVerse.quote: "After them all, the woman died. In the resurrection, therefore, of the seven, whose wife will she be? For they all had her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Last of all, the woman died. In the resurrection, then, whose wife will she be of the seven? For they all had her.

After them all, the woman died.

In the resurrection, therefore, of the seven, whose wife will she be? The trap. If there is a resurrection, she would have seven husbands, which is absurd and against the law. So, they argued, the resurrection must be false. Moses, by giving this law, could not have believed in it.

For they all had her. All seven were married to her.

The assumption. The Sadducees assumed that resurrection life would simply continue this life, with marriage and family arrangements carried on. The Pharisees taught the resurrection, and some may have described it in very earthly terms. Jesus will expose the assumption.

In a sentence. The Sadducees asked whose wife the woman would be in the resurrection, trying to make the resurrection absurd.

On a Tuesday. Do not imagine heaven as simply this life continued. It is far greater.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus answered them, "You are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered: you are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. In the resurrection people neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven.

You are wrong. Literally “you are deceived”, “you have gone astray”. A strong statement to the leading priests.

Because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. Two errors. They did not understand the Scriptures, which teach the resurrection (vv. 31–32; Daniel 12:2; Isaiah 26:19; Job 19:25–27; Psalm 16:10). And they underestimated God’s power: the God who created life can raise the dead and create a new kind of life, not merely restore the old one (1 Corinthians 15:35–44). Every error about God comes from one of these: ignorance of Scripture or a small view of God’s power.

For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage. Men “marry”; women were “given in marriage” by their fathers. Marriage belongs to this age. Its purposes, companionship, the bearing of children, and picturing Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31–32), will be fulfilled. In the resurrection, there is no death, so no need for children to continue the family line, which was the whole purpose of levirate marriage. And the marriage that earthly marriage pictured, between Christ and his people, will be complete (Revelation 19:7–9).

But are like angels in heaven. Like angels in not marrying, and in being immortal (Luke 20:36). The Sadducees did not believe in angels either (Acts 23:8), so Jesus is answering two of their denials at once.

What it does not mean. Not that people become angels in heaven. Believers remain human, with resurrected bodies (1 Corinthians 15:42–44; Philippians 3:21). Nor does it mean that husbands and wives will not know each other or love each other in heaven. Love will be perfected, not erased. But the exclusive bond of marriage will give way to a greater union, in which every relationship is perfected in Christ. Those who grieve a spouse need not fear that heaven will be less than marriage; it will be more.

In a sentence. The Sadducees erred because they did not know Scripture or God’s power: in the resurrection there is no marriage, and people are immortal like the angels.

On a Tuesday. Study the Scriptures, and do not limit what God can do. Most errors come from one of those two mistakes.

verseByVerse.quote: "And as for the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was said to you by God: 'I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob'? He is not God of the dead, but of the living."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what God said to you: I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob? He is not God of the dead, but of the living.

And as for the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was said to you by God. Jesus answers from the books of Moses, the part of Scripture the Sadducees accepted. “Said to you”: Scripture is God speaking to every generation, not merely an old record.

I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. Exodus 3:6, God’s words to Moses at the burning bush, centuries after the patriarchs had died.

He is not God of the dead, but of the living. How does this prove the resurrection? Not from the present tense of the verb, which is not actually in the Hebrew. The argument rests on the covenant. When God says “I am the God of Abraham”, he is naming himself by his covenant relationship with Abraham. That covenant included promises to Abraham himself: a land, a seed, a blessing, and God being his God (Genesis 17:7–8). Abraham died without receiving them (Hebrews 11:13). If death were the end of Abraham, then God would have failed to keep his promises, and his covenant would have been with a corpse. But God does not bind himself in covenant love to people only to abandon them to dust. A God who calls himself “the God of Abraham” must keep Abraham alive to enjoy the promises, and keep him whole, body and soul, since God made him a body-and-soul creature. So the covenant guarantees the resurrection. Abraham, Isaac and Jacob are alive to God (Luke 20:38), and their bodies will be raised.

What it does not mean. Not that the patriarchs are already in their resurrection bodies. Their souls are with God now; their bodies await the resurrection at the last day (1 Thessalonians 4:16; Revelation 6:9–11). Nor is the argument a mere play on grammar. It is about who God is: the faithful God of the covenant, whose love outlasts death.

In a sentence. Because God binds himself in covenant to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and calls himself their God, they must live to receive his promises, and so the resurrection is certain.

On a Tuesday. If you belong to God, he is your God, and death cannot break that bond. Let that comfort you in grief and in the face of death.

For worship. Praise the God of the living, who keeps his promises beyond the grave.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus answers from the books of Moses, the part of Scripture the Sadducees held highest.

parallels.desc: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob

verseByVerse.quote: And when the crowd heard it, they were astonished at his teaching.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the crowd heard it, they were astonished at his teaching.

And when the crowd heard it, they were astonished at his teaching. Jesus had silenced the most powerful religious leaders with the Scriptures they claimed to know. Luke adds that some scribes said, Teacher, you have spoken well (Luke 20:39).

In a sentence. The crowds were astonished at how Jesus answered the Sadducees.

On a Tuesday. Let Jesus’ teaching still astonish you.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the Pharisees heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, they gathered together. And one of them, a lawyer, asked him a question to test him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the Pharisees heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, they gathered together. One of them, an expert in the law, asked him a question to test him.

But when the Pharisees heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, they gathered together. “Silenced” literally means muzzled. The Pharisees may have been pleased that their rivals were defeated, but they were still opposed to Jesus. They gathered, perhaps echoing Psalm 2:2: the rulers take counsel together against the LORD and his Anointed.

And one of them, a lawyer. An expert in the law of Moses, a scribe (Mark 12:28).

Asked him a question to test him. The third test question. Mark presents this scribe more favourably: Jesus told him he was not far from the kingdom of God (Mark 12:34). Perhaps he was more sincere than those who sent him.

In a sentence. After the Sadducees were silenced, the Pharisees gathered, and one of their law experts came to test Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Even a question asked to test can lead someone near the kingdom. Answer questions about your faith with care.
verseByVerse.note: A lawyer was an expert in the law of Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: "Teacher, which is the great commandment in the Law?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Teacher, which is the great commandment in the law?

Teacher, which is the great commandment in the Law? The rabbis debated which commandments were “heavy” and which were “light”, and whether one could sum up the law in a single principle. Later rabbinic tradition counted 613 commandments in the law of Moses (248 positive and 365 negative). Some teachers tried to summarise them all in one. The question may have been a test: would Jesus downplay some commands, or show himself unorthodox?

In a sentence. The law expert asked Jesus which commandment was the greatest.

On a Tuesday. What do you think is the most important thing God asks of you? Compare your answer with Jesus’.
verseByVerse.note: Later rabbis counted 613 commandments in the law; teachers debated which were weightiest.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind. This is the great and first commandment."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said: you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind. This is the great and first commandment.

You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind. From Deuteronomy 6:5, part of the Shema (“Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one”, Deuteronomy 6:4), which devout Jews recited twice daily. The command is love, not merely obedience: wholehearted, personal devotion to God.

Heart, soul, mind. Not three separate parts of a person, but a way of saying “with everything you are”. The heart is the centre of the person (will, desires, thoughts). The soul is the life, the self. The mind is the understanding (Deuteronomy says “might”, meaning strength; Mark includes both mind and strength, Mark 12:30). God wants all of you: your thinking, your desires, your will, your energy. Nothing held back.

This is the great and first commandment. First in importance, and the source of all the others. All other commands flow from love for God. To keep every rule without loving God is to miss the point (15:8).

Why love? Because God first loved us (1 John 4:19; Deuteronomy 7:7–8). Love cannot be commanded into existence by willpower alone; it grows in response to love received. The gospel, showing us God’s love in Christ, is what makes this command possible.

What it does not mean. Not that love for God is only a feeling. In Scripture, love is shown in obedience (John 14:15), trust and worship. Nor does anyone keep this command perfectly except Christ. It shows us our sin and drives us to him, and it is the goal of the new heart he gives (Deuteronomy 30:6).

In a sentence. The greatest commandment is to love God with all your heart, soul and mind: with everything you are.

On a Tuesday. What part of you is not yet given to God in love: your thinking, your desires, your time, your energy?

For worship. Love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul and mind, because he first loved you.

parallels.desc: love the LORD your God with all your heart

verseByVerse.quote: "And a second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments depend all the Law and the Prophets."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A second is like it: you shall love your neighbour as yourself. On these two commandments depend all the Law and the Prophets.

And a second is like it. The questioner asked for one; Jesus gives two, because they belong together. “Like it” means of the same nature and importance. Love for God shows itself in love for others (1 John 4:20–21).

You shall love your neighbor as yourself. Leviticus 19:18. Jesus joins two verses that were not usually linked. “Neighbour” includes everyone, even enemies (5:43–44; Luke 10:29–37). “As yourself” assumes that we naturally care for ourselves: we feed, protect and seek good for ourselves. We are to seek others’ good with the same energy.

On these two commandments depend all the Law and the Prophets. “Depend” literally means “hang”, as a door hangs on its hinges. Every command in the Old Testament is an expression of one or both of these. The first four of the Ten Commandments show how to love God; the last six show how to love our neighbour. Paul says love is the fulfilling of the law (Romans 13:8–10).

What it does not mean. Not that the specific commands of the law can be ignored as long as we have loving feelings. Love does not replace God’s law; it fulfils it. Love tells us why we obey; the law tells us how love behaves. Nor does “as yourself” command self-love as a separate duty, as some modern teaching suggests. It assumes the natural care we already have for ourselves.

In a sentence. The second command is to love your neighbour as yourself, and the whole Old Testament hangs on these two commandments.

On a Tuesday. Who is the neighbour you find hardest to love? How would you treat them today if you loved them as yourself?

verseByVerse.quote: Now while the Pharisees were gathered together, Jesus asked them a question, saying, "What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?" They said to him, "The son of David."
verseByVerse.commentary:
While the Pharisees were gathered together, Jesus asked them a question: what do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he? They said: the son of David.

Now while the Pharisees were gathered together, Jesus asked them a question. Jesus has answered three tests; now he asks one himself.

What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he? The question that matters most.

They said to him, “The son of David.” The standard answer, and a correct one (1:1; 2 Samuel 7:12–16). But was it the whole truth? Most Jews expected the Messiah to be a human descendant of David, a great king who would restore Israel.

In a sentence. Jesus asked whose son the Messiah is, and the Pharisees answered: David’s.

On a Tuesday. Your answer to “What do you think about the Christ?” is the most important answer of your life.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "How is it then that David, in the Spirit, calls him Lord, saying, 'The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said: how is it then that David, speaking by the Spirit, calls him Lord? For he says: the Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet.

How is it then that David, in the Spirit, calls him Lord. “In the Spirit”: inspired by the Holy Spirit. Jesus affirms that David wrote Psalm 110 and that it is God’s word.

The Lord said to my Lord. Psalm 110:1. In Hebrew: “The LORD (Yahweh) said to my Lord (Adonai)”. God speaks to David’s Lord, the Messiah. David, the greatest king of Israel, calls the Messiah his Lord: his superior, his master.

Sit at my right hand. The place of highest honour and authority, beside God himself.

Until I put your enemies under your feet. The Messiah will reign until every enemy is defeated (1 Corinthians 15:25–26). Psalm 110:1 is quoted or alluded to in the New Testament more than any other Old Testament verse (Acts 2:34–35; Hebrews 1:13; 10:12–13). It describes Christ’s ascension and present reign.

In a sentence. Jesus pointed out that in Psalm 110 David, inspired by the Spirit, calls the Messiah his Lord, enthroned at God’s right hand.

For worship. Worship Christ, seated at God’s right hand, reigning until every enemy is under his feet.
verseByVerse.note: Psalm 110:1 is among the Old Testament verses most often quoted in the New.

verseByVerse.quote: "If then David calls him Lord, how is he his son?" And no one was able to answer him a word, nor from that day did anyone dare to ask him any more questions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If David calls him Lord, how can he be his son? No one could answer him a word, and from that day no one dared to ask him any more questions.

If then David calls him Lord, how is he his son? In that culture, a father would never call his son “Lord”; a son honoured his father, not the reverse. How can the Messiah be both David’s son (his descendant) and David’s Lord (his superior)? The only answer: the Messiah is more than a human descendant of David. He is a man, born in David’s line (1:1), and he is God’s Son, the eternal Lord (16:16; Romans 1:3–4). Jesus is hinting at his own identity: fully human and fully divine.

And no one was able to answer him a word. The experts could not answer, because the answer was standing in front of them, and they would not accept it.

Nor from that day did anyone dare to ask him any more questions. The tests are over. Jesus has silenced every group. Now he will speak against them (chapter 23), and then they will act against him (26:3–5).

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus denied being the son of David. He accepted the title (20:30–31; 21:9, 15). His point was that it was not enough. The Messiah is David’s son and David’s Lord.

In a sentence. Jesus showed that the Messiah must be more than David’s son, since David calls him Lord, and no one could answer him.

On a Tuesday. Is Jesus only a great man in history to you, or your Lord? He is both David’s son and David’s Lord, and yours.

22.theology: Election and the free offer of the gospel. The parable of the wedding banquet and the phrase “many are called, but few are chosen” bring together two truths that Reformed theology has always insisted must be held together. The general call of the gospel goes out to all people without exception — “Go therefore to the main roads and invite as many as you find.” This is the free and genuine offer of the gospel, and it must be preached without restriction. At the same time, the effectual call of God draws the chosen to the feast. Both are real; both are necessary. The preacher does not know who the elect are; he simply opens the banquet doors as wide as the gospel goes and trusts God with the result.
22.examples:
Then: The religious leaders tried to trap Jesus with politics (tribute coin), doctrine (resurrection), law (greatest commandment). He answered all three with Scripture, clarity, and a question they could not answer. The one they thought to judge was the judge.

Now: The same four questions are still asked of Christians today — political, doctrinal, ethical, and Christological. The answers Jesus gives are still sufficient. Render to Caesar what is Caesar’s; God claims your whole self made in his image. The resurrection is secured by the living God who keeps covenant. Love God with everything; love your neighbour as yourself. And the Christ is both Son of David and Lord of David — the God-man who saves.

23.title: Woe to You, Scribes and Pharisees
23.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Jesus said to the crowds and to his disciples, <sup>2</sup>“The scribes and the Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat, <sup>3</sup>so do and observe whatever they tell you, but not the works they do. For they preach, but do not practice. <sup>4</sup>They tie up heavy burdens, hard to bear, and lay them on people’s shoulders, but they themselves are not willing to move them with their finger. <sup>5</sup>They do all their deeds to be seen by others. For they make their phylacteries broad and their fringes long, <sup>6</sup>and they love the place of honor at feasts and the best seats in the synagogues <sup>7</sup>and greetings in the marketplaces and being called rabbi by others. <sup>8</sup>But you are not to be called rabbi, for you have one teacher, and you are all brothers. <sup>9</sup>And call no man your father on earth, for you have one Father, who is in heaven. <sup>10</sup>Neither be called instructors, for you have one instructor, the Christ. <sup>11</sup>The greatest among you shall be your servant. <sup>12</sup>Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted. <sup>13</sup>“But woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you shut the kingdom of heaven in people’s faces. For you neither enter yourselves nor allow those who would enter to go in. <sup>15</sup>Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you travel across sea and land to make a single proselyte, and when he becomes a proselyte, you make him twice as much a child of hell as yourselves. <sup>16</sup>“Woe to you, blind guides, who say, ‘If anyone swears by the temple, it is nothing, but if anyone swears by the gold of the temple, he is bound by his oath.’ <sup>17</sup>You blind fools! For which is greater, the gold or the temple that has made the gold sacred? <sup>18</sup>And you say, ‘If anyone swears by the altar, it is nothing, but if anyone swears by the gift that is on the altar, he is bound by his oath.’ <sup>19</sup>You blind men! For which is greater, the gift or the altar that makes the gift sacred? <sup>20</sup>So whoever swears by the altar swears by it and by everything on it. <sup>21</sup>And whoever swears by the temple swears by it and by him who dwells in it. <sup>22</sup>And whoever swears by heaven swears by the throne of God and by him who sits upon it. <sup>23</sup>“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you tithe mint and dill and cumin, and have neglected the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others. <sup>24</sup>You blind guides, straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel! <sup>25</sup>“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you clean the outside of the cup and the plate, but inside they are full of greed and self-indulgence. <sup>26</sup>You blind Pharisee! First clean the inside of the cup and the plate, that the outside also may be clean. <sup>27</sup>“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful, but within are full of dead people’s bones and all uncleanness. <sup>28</sup>So you also outwardly appear righteous to others, but within you are full of hypocrisy and lawlessness. <sup>29</sup>“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you build the tombs of the prophets and decorate the monuments of the righteous, <sup>30</sup>saying, ‘If we had lived in the days of our fathers, we would not have taken part with them in shedding the blood of the prophets.’ <sup>31</sup>Thus you witness against yourselves that you are sons of those who murdered the prophets. <sup>32</sup>Fill up, then, the measure of your fathers. <sup>33</sup>You serpents, you brood of vipers, how are you to escape being sentenced to hell? <sup>34</sup>Therefore I send you prophets and wise men and scribes, some of whom you will kill and crucify, and some you will flog in your synagogues and persecute from town to town, <sup>35</sup>so that on you may come all the righteous blood shed on earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah the son of Barachiah, whom you murdered between the sanctuary and the altar. <sup>36</sup>Truly, I say to you, all these things will come upon this generation. <sup>37</sup>“O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing! <sup>38</sup>See, your house is left to you desolate. <sup>39</sup>For I tell you, you will not see me again, until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.’”
23.overview:
Chapter 23 opens the fifth and final discourse of Matthew — and the most sorrowful. It begins with a warning to the crowds and disciples about the Pharisees (vv. 1–12), then delivers seven woes against the scribes and Pharisees (vv. 13–36), and closes with a lament over Jerusalem (vv. 37–39) that is one of the most heartbreaking passages in all of Scripture. The woes are not vindictive; they are diagnostic. Jesus names the disease precisely so that it can be seen for what it is: a religion of external performance concealing internal corruption, a leadership that burdens rather than shepherds, a tradition that has become a wall keeping people out of the kingdom.

The lament over Jerusalem (“O Jerusalem, Jerusalem”) reveals the heart behind the woes. Jesus does not pronounce judgment with cold severity; he pronounces it with the grief of a hen who would have gathered her chicks but could not because they would not come. The image is maternal, tender, aching. The holy Judge is also the loving Shepherd who weeps over the city he must judge. Both are true: God is not willing that any should perish, and God judges unrepentant hardness of heart. The cross, which is days away, is where both truths converge.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — Seven Woes: The Hypocrisy of Scribes and Pharisees (Part One)
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus turns from silencing his opponents to warning the crowds about them, and this is his last public address in Matthew. He concedes the office before he indicts the men: the scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses' seat, so what they read from it binds Israel even when their lives do not match it. Then the indictment — burdens tied on other people's shoulders and not lifted with a finger, phylacteries widened and fringes lengthened to be seen, titles and seats and greetings craved — followed by the levelling of the disciples under one Teacher and one Father. The first three woes follow: shutting the kingdom in people's faces, making converts twice as much children of hell, and the whole scribal machinery of binding and non-binding oaths.
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter begins with a distinction the church has needed ever since: the authority of a pulpit is borrowed, every word of it. When a man sits on Moses' seat and reads out what God has said, the hearer is bound and the messenger's hypocrisy does not release him; when he steps off that seat, the conscience is free. So do and observe whatever they tell you is not a blank endorsement of Pharisaic teaching, which this same Gospel calls leaven (16:12) and says made void the commandment of God (15:6). On titles, the reason given is Christological rather than merely moral: no disciple is to be called rabbi because the seat is occupied — there is one Teacher, and he names him as the Christ. And the first woe is the head of all seven. The other six describe men damaging themselves; this one describes men standing in a doorway between other people and the kingdom, and it is put first for that reason.
verseByVerse.examples: The burdens are worth making concrete: thirty-nine categories of forbidden Sabbath work, each subdivided, down to whether a chair might be dragged in case dragging scratched a furrow. None of it was invented by wicked men; it was produced by serious people trying to be careful, which is how such systems are always produced. And the same tradition supplied the devices by which those who knew it could live within it — so the men who designed the yoke were the ones least troubled by it. Matthew makes the contrast with the same noun: heavy burdens here (phortia), and my burden is light at 11:30 (phortion). The phylacteries and fringes were both commanded, and Jesus wore the fringes himself (9:20) — the objection is to the width and the length, which is why this woe cannot be legislated against. The test that gets underneath it is not what you do but who is watching: take something genuinely good in your religious life, suppose it were certain nobody would ever know of it, and see what quietly deflates.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus said to the crowds and to his disciples, "The scribes and the Pharisees sit on Moses' seat,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus spoke to the crowds and to his disciples: the scribes and the Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat.

The setting. Chapter 23 is Jesus’ last public teaching in Matthew, given in the temple on the Tuesday before his death. After silencing his opponents (22:46), he now warns the crowds and his disciples against them, and then speaks directly to the scribes and Pharisees in seven “woes”. The chapter ends with his lament over Jerusalem. It is the most severe speech in the Gospels.

Then Jesus said to the crowds and to his disciples. The warning is for ordinary people and for his followers: do not be like them.

The scribes and the Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat. “Moses’ seat” stands for the authority to teach and interpret the law of Moses. Some synagogues had a stone chair at the front for the teacher of the law; one was found at Chorazin. The scribes and Pharisees were the recognised teachers of the law, in Moses’ place. “Sit” may suggest they had taken the seat themselves.

What it does not mean. Not that every scribe and Pharisee was a hypocrite. Nicodemus, Joseph of Arimathea, Gamaliel and Paul came from among them. Jesus speaks of the movement as a whole, and its characteristic sins. Nor is this chapter a licence for Christians to despise Jews. Its warnings apply above all to religious people today, including Christians and church leaders.

In a sentence. Jesus began his warning about the scribes and Pharisees, who held the authority to teach Moses’ law.

On a Tuesday. Read this chapter as a mirror, not a window. The question is not “How bad were the Pharisees?” but “Where am I like them?”
verseByVerse.note: “Moses’ seat” stands for the authority to teach the law; synagogues may have had a stone chair for the teacher.

verseByVerse.quote: "so do and observe whatever they tell you, but not the works they do. For they preach, but do not practice."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So do and observe whatever they tell you, but do not do what they do. For they preach, but do not practise.

So do and observe whatever they tell you. In so far as they teach the law of Moses faithfully, it should be obeyed. The word of God does not lose its authority because the teacher is a hypocrite. Jesus has already criticised their traditions (15:1–20), so “whatever they tell you” means whatever they teach from Moses, not their added rules.

But not the works they do. Do not follow their example.

For they preach, but do not practice. The heart of hypocrisy: saying without doing. Paul makes the same charge (Romans 2:21–23): you who teach others, do you not teach yourself?

What it does not mean. Not that we should follow every teaching of a leader simply because of his position. Jesus has warned against blind guides (15:14) and their leaven (16:12). Every teaching must be tested by Scripture. But truth from God’s word is to be obeyed, whoever speaks it.

In a sentence. Obey God’s law when they teach it, but do not follow their example, because they do not practise what they preach.

On a Tuesday. Do you practise what you preach to your children, your colleagues, your friends? Hypocrisy is not only a sin of leaders.

parallels.desc: you who teach others, do you not teach yourself?

verseByVerse.quote: "They tie up heavy burdens, hard to bear, and lay them on people's shoulders, but they themselves are not willing to move them with their finger."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They tie up heavy burdens, hard to bear, and lay them on people’s shoulders, but they themselves will not lift a finger to move them.

They tie up heavy burdens, hard to bear. The picture is of a load tied up in a bundle and placed on a pack animal or a porter. The burdens were the many rules the Pharisees added to the law: Sabbath regulations, purity rules, tithing details (12:1–14; 15:1–9). They made religion an exhausting load. Peter later called the law, as the Pharisees taught it, a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear (Acts 15:10).

And lay them on people’s shoulders. They demanded that others carry them.

But they themselves are not willing to move them with their finger. Two meanings. Either they did not keep the rules themselves (finding loopholes, as with Corban, 15:5), or they gave no help to those weighed down by them: no compassion, no grace, no assistance. Contrast Jesus: come to me, all who are heavy laden, and I will give you rest; my yoke is easy and my burden is light (11:28–30).

What it does not mean. Not that God’s commands are burdensome in themselves (1 John 5:3). The problem is human rules added to God’s word, and religion without grace.

In a sentence. The Pharisees loaded people with heavy religious rules and would not lift a finger to help them carry them.

On a Tuesday. Are you placing burdens on others that God has not placed: rules, expectations, standards? And are you helping those who are weighed down?

parallels.desc: a yoke our fathers could not bear

verseByVerse.quote: "They do all their deeds to be seen by others. For they make their phylacteries broad and their fringes long, and they love the place of honor at feasts and the best seats in the synagogues"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They do all their deeds to be seen by others. They make their phylacteries wide and their tassels long, and they love the place of honour at feasts and the best seats in the synagogues.

They do all their deeds to be seen by others. Their religion was a performance (6:1–18). They wanted applause.

For they make their phylacteries broad. Phylacteries (tefillin) were small leather boxes containing tiny scrolls of Scripture passages (Exodus 13:1–16; Deuteronomy 6:4–9; 11:13–21), strapped to the forehead and left arm during prayer. They came from a literal reading of God’s command to bind his words as a sign on your hand and frontlets between your eyes (Deuteronomy 6:8). Making them broad showed off one’s devotion.

And their fringes long. The tassels on the corners of the outer garment, commanded by God to remind Israel of his commandments (Numbers 15:38–40). Jesus himself wore them (9:20). Making them long drew attention.

And they love the place of honor at feasts. Seats nearest the host, a sign of status (Luke 14:7–11).

And the best seats in the synagogues. The front seats facing the congregation, where everyone could see them.

What it does not mean. Not that religious symbols or clothing are wrong in themselves. The phylacteries and tassels were based on God’s commands. The problem was using them for display. Nor does it forbid honouring leaders appropriately (1 Timothy 5:17). The sin is loving honour.

In a sentence. The Pharisees did their religious acts to be admired, exaggerating their religious dress and loving the best seats.

On a Tuesday. What do you do to be seen as spiritual: by others, or on social media? Do it for God alone.
verseByVerse.note: Phylacteries were small leather boxes holding verses of Scripture, strapped to the forehead and arm. Fringes were the tassels on a garment’s corners.

parallels.desc: bind them on your hand and between your eyes

verseByVerse.quote: "and greetings in the marketplaces and being called rabbi by others. But you are not to be called rabbi, for you have one teacher, and you are all brothers."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They love greetings in the marketplaces and being called rabbi. But you are not to be called rabbi, for you have one teacher, and you are all brothers.

And greetings in the marketplaces. Respectful public greetings, in which ordinary people would stop and bow to them.

And being called rabbi by others. “Rabbi” means “my great one”, “my master”, a title of respect for a teacher of the law. It was becoming a formal title.

But you are not to be called rabbi. Jesus’ disciples must not seek titles that set them above others.

For you have one teacher. Christ himself (v. 10). Every Christian teacher is a student of the one Teacher, with no independent authority.

And you are all brothers. In Christ’s community, all are equal as brothers and sisters. There is no religious hierarchy of superior and inferior believers.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians may never use any titles at all, or that there are no teachers in the church. The New Testament speaks of teachers, elders and overseers (Ephesians 4:11; 1 Timothy 3:1–2; James 3:1), and honours them (Hebrews 13:17). Calling someone “pastor” or “doctor” is not forbidden. What is forbidden is the love of titles and status, and the spirit that sets leaders above other believers as masters. The test is the heart: do we want the title for the honour, or do we serve as brothers under one Master?

In a sentence. Jesus forbade his disciples to seek titles of honour, because they have one Teacher and are all brothers.

On a Tuesday. Do you care about titles, position or recognition in the church? Remember that you are a brother or sister, under one Teacher.
verseByVerse.note: “Rabbi” means “my great one,” a title of respect for a teacher.

parallels.desc: not many of you should become teachers

verseByVerse.quote: "And call no man your father on earth, for you have one Father, who is in heaven. Neither be called instructors, for you have one instructor, the Christ."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Call no one on earth your father, for you have one Father, who is in heaven. And do not be called instructors, for you have one instructor, the Christ.

And call no man your father on earth. “Father” (abba) was used of revered teachers and leaders, the “fathers” of tradition. Jesus forbids giving any human being the kind of spiritual authority that belongs only to God.

For you have one Father, who is in heaven. God alone is our Father in the ultimate sense (6:9).

Neither be called instructors. “Instructor” (kathēgētēs) means a guide, a tutor, a leader.

For you have one instructor, the Christ. Jesus calls himself the Christ, the one instructor. He claims an authority equal to the Father’s.

What it does not mean. Not that we cannot call our natural fathers “father”. Jesus himself honoured father and mother (15:4). Paul called himself a spiritual father to the Corinthians (1 Corinthians 4:15) and Timothy his son (1 Timothy 1:2). Jesus speaks against titles that give human leaders a status that belongs to God. Protestants have often applied this verse against the Roman Catholic and Orthodox practice of calling priests “Father”. The real issue is not the word but the attitude: no human leader may stand between the believer and God as an authority over conscience.

In a sentence. No human leader may be given the ultimate authority of a spiritual father or instructor, because God is our one Father and Christ our one instructor.

On a Tuesday. Do you treat any Christian leader as if their word were final? Respect your leaders, but your ultimate authority is Christ.

parallels.desc: have we not all one Father?
one God, the Father, and one Lord

verseByVerse.quote: "The greatest among you shall be your servant. Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The greatest among you must be your servant. Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.

The greatest among you shall be your servant. The same teaching as 20:26–28. True greatness is service. The Pharisees sought honour; Jesus’ followers seek to serve.

Whoever exalts himself will be humbled. God brings down the proud (Proverbs 3:34; Luke 1:51–52). Self-exaltation ends in humiliation, if not now, then at the judgment.

And whoever humbles himself will be exalted. God lifts up the humble (James 4:10; 1 Peter 5:6). Jesus himself humbled himself to the cross, and God highly exalted him (Philippians 2:8–9). The passive “will be exalted” means by God.

What it does not mean. Not that we should humble ourselves as a strategy to get exalted. True humility does not seek a reward. But God does honour it.

In a sentence. The greatest must be servants, for God humbles the proud and exalts the humble.

On a Tuesday. How can you serve someone in your church this week in a way that no one will notice?

verseByVerse.quote: "But woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you shut the kingdom of heaven in people's faces. For you neither enter yourselves nor allow those who would enter to go in."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! You shut the kingdom of heaven in people’s faces. You neither enter yourselves nor allow those who would enter to go in.

But woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! The first of seven woes. A “woe” (ouai) is a cry of grief and warning, announcing coming judgment, used by the prophets (Isaiah 5:8–23; Habakkuk 2:6–19). It is the opposite of “blessed” (5:3–12). Jesus speaks not with glee but with sorrow; the chapter ends in tears (v. 37). The seven woes may deliberately contrast with the eight Beatitudes.

For you shut the kingdom of heaven in people’s faces. As teachers of the law, they held the “keys” of knowledge (Luke 11:52). They should have opened the way to God. Instead, by rejecting Jesus and teaching a religion of human merit, they slammed the door shut.

For you neither enter yourselves nor allow those who would enter to go in. They refused Jesus, and they discouraged others from following him (John 9:22; 12:42). False teaching is doubly destructive: it damns the teacher and those he leads.

In a sentence. The first woe: the scribes and Pharisees shut the kingdom in people’s faces, refusing to enter and stopping others.

On a Tuesday. Is anything in your life or church making it harder for people to come to Christ: legalism, coldness, hypocrisy?
verseByVerse.note: A woe is a solemn lament and warning of judgment, used by the prophets.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you travel across sea and land to make a single proselyte, and when he becomes a proselyte, you make him twice as much a child of hell as yourselves."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! You travel across sea and land to make a single convert, and when he becomes one, you make him twice as much a child of hell as yourselves.

Textual note. Some manuscripts add verse 14: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you devour widows’ houses and for a pretence you make long prayers; therefore you will receive the greater condemnation.” It is missing in the earliest manuscripts and was probably copied from Mark 12:40 and Luke 20:47. Verdict: not original in Matthew, though Jesus did say it.

For you travel across sea and land to make a single proselyte. A proselyte was a Gentile who converted fully to Judaism, through circumcision, baptism and sacrifice. Some Pharisees were zealous in seeking converts, though the extent of Jewish missionary activity is debated. They took great effort to win even one.

And when he becomes a proselyte, you make him twice as much a child of hell as yourselves. “Child of hell” (literally “son of Gehenna”) means someone who belongs to hell, destined for it. Converts often become more zealous than their teachers. The Pharisees taught them a religion of rules without grace, and their converts adopted it with double fervour. They became more legalistic, more proud, and further from God.

What it does not mean. Not that evangelism or zeal for converts is wrong. Jesus commands it (28:19). The problem is converting people to the wrong thing: to a system or a party rather than to God; to rules rather than grace. Christians can fall into the same trap, making converts to a denomination, a culture or a set of rules rather than to Christ.

In a sentence. The second woe: they worked hard to win converts, but made them even worse than themselves.

On a Tuesday. When you share your faith, are you bringing people to Christ, or to your church culture and preferences?
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 14, a woe about devouring widows’ houses and long prayers for a pretence. A proselyte was a Gentile convert to Judaism.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to you, blind guides, who say, 'If anyone swears by the temple, it is nothing, but if anyone swears by the gold of the temple, he is bound by his oath.' You blind fools! For which is greater, the gold or the temple that has made the gold sacred?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you, blind guides, who say: if anyone swears by the temple, it means nothing, but if anyone swears by the gold of the temple, he is bound by his oath. You blind fools! Which is greater, the gold or the temple that has made the gold sacred?

Woe to you, blind guides. The third woe (see 15:14). They claimed to guide the blind, but could not see.

Who say, “If anyone swears by the temple, it is nothing.” “Nothing” means it is not binding. They had developed a system of oaths (see 5:33–37). An oath sworn by the temple could be broken; an oath sworn by the temple’s gold, its treasury or golden decorations, was binding.

But if anyone swears by the gold of the temple, he is bound by his oath. These rules allowed a man to choose in advance which of his oaths he would keep. Someone could swear impressively “by the temple” and know he was not bound. It was a system of legalised lying.

You blind fools! “Fools” (mōroi) means morally foolish, people who reject God’s wisdom. Jesus forbade calling a brother “fool” in contempt (5:22), but here he is not insulting a brother in anger; he is making a judgment about their teaching, as God’s word does (Psalm 14:1).

For which is greater, the gold or the temple that has made the gold sacred? The gold was holy only because it belonged to the temple, God’s house. The temple was greater. Their priorities were upside down. They valued the gold more than the God it was dedicated to.

In a sentence. The third woe: their oath rules were absurd and dishonest, valuing the temple’s gold above the temple itself.

On a Tuesday. Do you leave yourself loopholes in your promises? Let your yes be yes (5:37).
verseByVerse.note: These rules let a man decide which of his oaths were binding.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you say, 'If anyone swears by the altar, it is nothing, but if anyone swears by the gift that is on the altar, he is bound by his oath.' You blind men! For which is greater, the gift or the altar that makes the gift sacred?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And you say: if anyone swears by the altar, it means nothing, but if anyone swears by the gift on the altar, he is bound by his oath. You blind men! Which is greater, the gift or the altar that makes the gift sacred?

And you say, “If anyone swears by the altar, it is nothing.” The same evasion. The altar of burnt offering stood in the temple court, where sacrifices were offered.

But if anyone swears by the gift that is on the altar, he is bound by his oath. The gift was the sacrifice placed on the altar.

You blind men! For which is greater, the gift or the altar that makes the gift sacred? The altar made the gift holy (Exodus 29:37). Again, they valued the lesser thing above the greater.

In a sentence. They also taught that oaths by the altar did not bind, but oaths by the gift did, absurdly valuing the gift above the altar that made it holy.

On a Tuesday. Our values can become upside down, valuing the gift above the Giver. What do you value more than God?

parallels.desc: whatever touches the altar shall become holy

verseByVerse.quote: "So whoever swears by the altar swears by it and by everything on it. And whoever swears by the temple swears by it and by him who dwells in it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever swears by the altar swears by it and by everything on it. And whoever swears by the temple swears by it and by the one who dwells in it.

So whoever swears by the altar swears by it and by everything on it. You cannot separate the altar from its gifts.

And whoever swears by the temple swears by it and by him who dwells in it. God himself dwells in the temple (1 Kings 8:13; Psalm 26:8). Every oath by the temple is an oath by God. You cannot escape him by swearing by something else.

In a sentence. Every oath by the altar or the temple is really an oath by God who dwells there, so all such oaths bind.

On a Tuesday. Every promise you make is made before God, whether or not you mention his name.

parallels.desc: a place for you to dwell in forever

verseByVerse.quote: "And whoever swears by heaven swears by the throne of God and by him who sits upon it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And whoever swears by heaven swears by the throne of God and by the one who sits on it.

And whoever swears by heaven swears by the throne of God and by him who sits upon it. Heaven is God’s throne (5:34; Isaiah 66:1). All oaths, however phrased, involve God. Their system of evasions was a lie before the God who sees everything.

In a sentence. An oath by heaven is an oath by God himself, who sits on its throne.

On a Tuesday. Live as one who speaks every word before God’s throne. Be truthful in everything.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–39 — Seven Woes Concluded and the Lament over Jerusalem
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The last four woes drive from the outside inward: tithed garden herbs while justice, mercy and faithfulness are neglected; a cup scoured outside and full of plunder within; whitewashed tombs; and monuments built to murdered prophets by men arranging a murder. Then the language hardens further — serpents, brood of vipers, fill up the measure of your fathers — and the blood of the righteous from Abel to Zechariah is laid on that generation. And then the voice breaks: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem… how often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing. The chapter ends not on desolation but on a single word: until.
verseByVerse.theology: Woe and lament sit in one chapter and must be held together, because each without the other is a distortion. Woe is ouai, the prophets' cry of grief rather than a curse, and it is aimed with precision: not at sinners — no harsh word in this Gospel ever falls on a prostitute, a tax collector or a dying thief — but at men shutting the door on them. Severity toward a shepherd fleecing the flock is mercy toward the flock. Then the remedy, which is the most important clause here for anyone who reads the seven and wants out: first clean the inside of the cup and the plate, that the outside also may be clean. The order is the whole difference between the gospel and moralism, and the promise is that the outside follows. It is also the one thing no one can do for himself, which is why the honest response is David's after his worst year: create in me a clean heart (Ps 51:10). And the measure of v. 32 explains the patience of God — judgment waited four hundred years for the Amorites' cup to fill (Gen 15:16) — without promising that the delay is permanent.
verseByVerse.examples: Two images repay their background. The gnat and the camel is a joke: straining wine through cloth to catch an unclean insect was ordinary practice, the camel was the largest unclean animal in the country, and in Aramaic the words chime — qalma and gamla. And the whitewashed tombs were limed before Passover not for beauty but as a warning, since touching a grave barred a pilgrim from the feast for seven days (Num 19:16); the mark meant to keep people away was what made them gleam. Which makes the charge worse than inconsistency: such men are contagious, and their respectability is the danger. The seventh woe is the one to watch for while reading this chapter — if we had lived in the days of our fathers is the cheapest sentence in the world, because the sins of a previous age are labelled and ours are still disguised as normal life. Everyone is certain he would have hidden Jews in 1942. The certainty costs nothing and is almost always false. The seven translated into their modern forms, and the guard on whether we may speak as Jesus does here, are set out in the verse-by-verse on vv. 33-34.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you tithe mint and dill and cumin, and have neglected the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others. You blind guides, straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! You tithe mint, dill and cumin, and have neglected the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy and faithfulness. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others. You blind guides, straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel!

For you tithe mint and dill and cumin. The fourth woe. A tithe was a tenth of one’s produce, given to God (Leviticus 27:30; Deuteronomy 14:22–23). The law required tithes of grain, wine and oil. The Pharisees extended it to the smallest garden herbs, counting out every tenth leaf of mint.

And have neglected the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness. “Weightier” means more important. Justice means fairness to others, especially the poor and powerless. Mercy means compassion. Faithfulness means loyalty, both to God and to others. The prophets summed up God’s requirements this way: to do justice, to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God (Micah 6:8; Hosea 6:6; Zechariah 7:9–10). The Pharisees were careful about small matters and careless about great ones.

These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others. Jesus does not abolish tithing or condemn attention to detail. They should have done both. But the weightier matters come first.

You blind guides, straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel! A comic, vivid picture. A gnat was the smallest unclean creature; a camel the largest (Leviticus 11:4, 20–23). Strict Jews strained their wine through cloth to avoid swallowing a gnat and becoming unclean. The Pharisees carefully avoided tiny sins, while swallowing enormous ones: injustice, cruelty, unfaithfulness. In Aramaic there may be a wordplay: gnat (qalma) and camel (gamla).

What it does not mean. Not that small matters of obedience do not matter. Jesus says they ought to tithe. Faithfulness in small things matters (25:21). Nor does it mean that Christians are bound to the Old Testament tithe as law. The New Testament calls for generous, cheerful giving (2 Corinthians 8–9), and many Christians rightly use the tithe as a starting point. The point is priority: justice, mercy and faithfulness are the heart of God’s law.

In a sentence. The fourth woe: they carefully tithed tiny herbs while neglecting justice, mercy and faithfulness, straining out gnats and swallowing camels.

On a Tuesday. Are you careful about small religious duties while neglecting justice, mercy and faithfulness toward the people around you?
verseByVerse.note: The law required a tithe of produce; the Pharisees extended it to kitchen herbs. Both gnats and camels were unclean; wine was strained through cloth to remove insects.

parallels.desc: a tithe of the seed of the land
do justice, love kindness, walk humbly
