But the day and hour are known only to the Father, which means the calling of the church today is exactly what it was yesterday: proclaim the gospel to all nations, and be found faithful when he comes.

25.title: Ready, Faithful, and Merciful
25.text: <sup>1</sup>“Then the kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins who took their lamps and went to meet the bridegroom. <sup>2</sup>Five of them were foolish, and five were wise. <sup>3</sup>For when the foolish took their lamps, they took no oil with them, <sup>4</sup>but the wise took flasks of oil with their lamps. <sup>5</sup>As the bridegroom was delayed, they all became drowsy and slept. <sup>6</sup>But at midnight there was a cry, ‘Here is the bridegroom! Come out to meet him.’ <sup>7</sup>Then all those virgins rose and trimmed their lamps. <sup>8</sup>And the foolish said to the wise, ‘Give us some of your oil, for our lamps are going out.’ <sup>9</sup>But the wise answered, saying, ‘Since there will not be enough for us and for you, go rather to the dealers and buy for yourselves.’ <sup>10</sup>And while they were going to buy, the bridegroom came, and those who were ready went in with him to the marriage feast, and the door was shut. <sup>11</sup>Afterward the other virgins came also, saying, ‘Lord, lord, open to us.’ <sup>12</sup>But he answered, ‘Truly, I say to you, I do not know you.’ <sup>13</sup>Watch therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour. <sup>14</sup>“For it will be like a man going on a journey, who called his servants and entrusted to them his property. <sup>15</sup>To one he gave five talents, to another two, to another one, to each according to his ability. Then he went away. <sup>16</sup>He who had received the five talents went at once and traded with them, and he made five talents more. <sup>17</sup>So also he who had the two talents made two talents more. <sup>18</sup>But he who had received the one talent went and dug in the ground and hid his master’s money. <sup>19</sup>Now after a long time the master of those servants came and settled accounts with them. <sup>20</sup>And he who had received the five talents came forward, bringing five talents more, saying, ‘Master, you delivered to me five talents; here, I have made five talents more.’ <sup>21</sup>His master said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a little; I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your master.’ <sup>22</sup>And he also who had the two talents came forward, saying, ‘Master, you delivered to me two talents; here, I have made two talents more.’ <sup>23</sup>His master said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a little; I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your master.’ <sup>24</sup>He also who had received the one talent came forward, saying, ‘Master, I knew you to be a hard man, reaping where you did not sow, and gathering where you scattered no seed, <sup>25</sup>so I was afraid, and I went and hid your talent in the ground. Here, you have what is yours.’ <sup>26</sup>But his master answered him, ‘You wicked and slothful servant! You knew that I reap where I have not sown and gather where I scattered no seed? <sup>27</sup>Then you ought to have invested my money with the bankers, and at my coming I should have received what was my own with interest. <sup>28</sup>So take the talent from him and give it to him who has the ten talents. <sup>29</sup>For to everyone who has will more be given, and he will have an abundance. But from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away. <sup>30</sup>And cast the worthless servant into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.’ <sup>31</sup>“When the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the angels with him, then he will sit on his glorious throne. <sup>32</sup>Before him will be gathered all the nations, and he will separate people one from another as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats. <sup>33</sup>And he will place the sheep on his right, but the goats on the left. <sup>34</sup>Then the King will say to those on his right, ‘Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. <sup>35</sup>For I was hungry and you gave me food, I was thirsty and you gave me drink, I was a stranger and you welcomed me, <sup>36</sup>I was naked and you clothed me, I was sick and you visited me, I was in prison and you came to me.’ <sup>37</sup>Then the righteous will answer him, saying, ‘Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you, or thirsty and give you drink? <sup>38</sup>And when did we see you a stranger and welcome you, or naked and clothe you? <sup>39</sup>And when did we see you sick or in prison and visit you?’ <sup>40</sup>And the King will answer them, ‘Truly, I say to you, as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.’ <sup>41</sup>“Then he will say to those on his left, ‘Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. <sup>42</sup>For I was hungry and you gave me no food, I was thirsty and you gave me no drink, <sup>43</sup>I was a stranger and you did not welcome me, naked and you did not clothe me, sick and in prison and you did not visit me.’ <sup>44</sup>Then they also will answer, saying, ‘Lord, when did we see you hungry or thirsty or a stranger or naked or sick or in prison, and did not minister to you?’ <sup>45</sup>Then he will answer them, saying, ‘Truly, I say to you, as you did not do it to one of the least of these, you did not do it to me.’ <sup>46</sup>And these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.”
25.overview:
Chapter 25 closes the Olivet Discourse with three parables that together answer the question of how to live between the ascension and the return. The ten virgins teach readiness — oil cannot be borrowed at the last moment; what is needed must be present when the bridegroom comes. The talents teach faithfulness — the servant who buries what he has been given is condemned not for wickedness but for fearful inaction. The sheep and goats teach that love for Christ is expressed in love for the vulnerable — the hungry, the stranger, the naked, the sick, the imprisoned.

Together the three parables describe the whole Christian life in the waiting period: ready (sustained by the Spirit’s inward work), faithful (investing rather than hoarding what has been given), and merciful (serving Christ in the face of the suffering neighbour). The final scene — the separation of sheep and goats, the commendation and the condemnation, the declaration of eternal life and eternal punishment — is Matthew’s most solemn eschatological passage. It is not a salvation-by-works text but a fruits-of-faith text: those who truly love the King will inevitably love those he loves.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–30 — The Ten Virgins and the Parable of the Talents
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two parables press the same point from opposite sides. Ten girls go out to escort a bridegroom; five have brought a flask of oil and five have not, and the difference is invisible until a cry at midnight and a door that shuts. Then a man going abroad hands three servants a fortune and leaves; two trade and double it, and the third buries his in the ground because he believes his master is a hard man. The first parable asks what you brought. The second asks what you did.
verseByVerse.theology: Neither failure in these parables is an act of wickedness. The foolish girls lacked something inward that could not be borrowed at midnight or bought in a hurry, and the parable declines to name it beyond telling us four things: it is needed for the long haul, it is untransferable, it cannot be acquired late, and it cannot be seen from outside. The one-talent servant did nothing wrong in any ordinary sense; he stole nothing and lost nothing, and his ruin traces to a doctrine of God stated in his first breath, I knew you to be a hard man. Men do not take risks for someone they believe is waiting to catch them out. Both parables define nominal religion: enough to look ready, and nothing underneath that lasts a delay.
verseByVerse.examples: Watch, in v. 13, cannot mean stay awake, because all ten slept and five were commended. It means be provisioned — a state rather than an activity, built in the un-urgent hours of an ordinary afternoon, which is freeing and considerably more demanding than a fever of expectancy. The talents parable removes the commonest excuse: the acceptable minimum was the bank, requiring no skill and no nerve, and it would have been enough. Note too that no servant in the story tries and fails — that scene is missing, and its absence is the point, because it is the scene most of us are afraid of. The failure judged here is not the failed attempt but the burial. And the cure for the third servant is not to try harder but to know God better: this master hands slaves a fortune unsupervised, is delighted rather than grudging when they succeed, and rewards them not with a bonus but with an invitation to come inside and share his joy.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then the kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins who took their lamps and went to meet the bridegroom. Five of them were foolish, and five were wise."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom. Five of them were foolish, and five were wise.

The connection. Jesus continues his teaching on readiness for his return (24:36–51). Chapter 25 has three parts: the ten virgins (be ready, even if the wait is long), the talents (be faithful with what you have been given), and the sheep and the goats (the final judgment).

Then the kingdom of heaven will be like. “Then”: at the coming of the Son of Man.

Ten virgins who took their lamps and went to meet the bridegroom. “Virgins” means young unmarried women, bridesmaids, friends of the bride. In a Jewish wedding, the bridegroom went with his friends, usually in the evening, to the bride’s home to fetch her, and then led a procession back to his own home for the wedding feast. The bridesmaids waited to join the procession and escort the couple with torches or lamps. “Lamps” here may be torches: rags soaked in oil wrapped around a stick, which needed fresh oil every so often. The bridegroom is Christ (9:15).

Five of them were foolish, and five were wise. “Foolish” and “wise”, as with the two builders (7:24–27). All ten look the same. All are invited, all have lamps, all are waiting. The difference will show only when the bridegroom comes.

In a sentence. In a parable of Christ’s return, ten bridesmaids waited with lamps for the bridegroom: five foolish, five wise.

On a Tuesday. Those who are ready and those who are not may look the same today. What will distinguish you when Christ comes?
verseByVerse.note: At a wedding the bridegroom went at night to fetch his bride, and the party escorted them with lamps — probably torches fuelled with oil.

verseByVerse.quote: "For when the foolish took their lamps, they took no oil with them, but the wise took flasks of oil with their lamps."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the foolish took their lamps, they took no oil with them, but the wise took flasks of oil with their lamps.

For when the foolish took their lamps, they took no oil with them. They had lamps, but no reserve of oil. They expected the bridegroom to come quickly, and did not prepare for a delay.

But the wise took flasks of oil with their lamps. They prepared for a long wait.

What is the oil? Jesus does not say, and we should not press the details too far. The main point is preparedness. But many have seen the oil as the reality of saving faith and the inner life of the Spirit (in Scripture, oil often pictures the Holy Spirit, Zechariah 4:1–6), as opposed to the outward appearance of religion (the lamp). The foolish have the form of godliness without its power (2 Timothy 3:5). The lamp without oil is a profession of faith without genuine faith and new life.

In a sentence. The foolish took lamps but no extra oil; the wise prepared with flasks of oil.

On a Tuesday. Do you have the lamp (outward religion) without the oil (genuine faith and the Spirit’s life)?

verseByVerse.quote: "As the bridegroom was delayed, they all became drowsy and slept. But at midnight there was a cry, 'Here is the bridegroom! Come out to meet him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the bridegroom was delayed, they all became drowsy and fell asleep. But at midnight there was a cry: here is the bridegroom! Come out to meet him.

As the bridegroom was delayed. The theme of delay (24:48). Christ’s return has been delayed beyond what many expected. Readiness must last through a long wait.

They all became drowsy and slept. All ten, wise and foolish. Sleep is not the problem here (unlike 24:42–43); the wise slept too. The difference is preparation made before they slept. You cannot prepare in the moment the bridegroom arrives.

But at midnight there was a cry. At the most unexpected time, in the middle of the night (24:44).

Here is the bridegroom! Come out to meet him. The announcement of his coming (1 Thessalonians 4:16). “To meet” (apantēsin) was the word used for a delegation going out to meet an arriving king and escort him back to the city. Paul uses the same word for believers meeting the Lord in the air (1 Thessalonians 4:17): not to leave with him, but to welcome him back to earth.

In a sentence. When the bridegroom was delayed, all ten fell asleep, until a cry at midnight announced his arrival.

On a Tuesday. Prepare now, while there is time. When the cry comes, it will be too late to get ready.

parallels.desc: lest he come suddenly and find you asleep

verseByVerse.quote: "Then all those virgins rose and trimmed their lamps. And the foolish said to the wise, 'Give us some of your oil, for our lamps are going out.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then all the virgins woke up and trimmed their lamps. The foolish said to the wise: give us some of your oil, for our lamps are going out.

Then all those virgins rose and trimmed their lamps. They trimmed the wicks and added oil to make them burn brightly.

And the foolish said to the wise, “Give us some of your oil, for our lamps are going out.” Their lamps had been burning, but now were sputtering out. They had enough for a short time, but not for a long wait. The appearance of faith can last for a while, then fail (13:20–21).

In a sentence. When the bridegroom came, the foolish found their lamps going out and begged the wise for oil.

On a Tuesday. Is your faith sustained, or running on borrowed fuel from others?

verseByVerse.quote: "But the wise answered, saying, 'Since there will not be enough for us and for you, go rather to the dealers and buy for yourselves.' And while they were going to buy, the bridegroom came, and those who were ready went in with him to the marriage feast, and the door was shut."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wise answered: there will not be enough for both us and you. Go instead to the dealers and buy for yourselves. While they were going to buy, the bridegroom came. Those who were ready went in with him to the wedding feast, and the door was shut.

Since there will not be enough for us and for you. This may sound selfish, but it makes the point: some things cannot be shared. No one can give another person their faith, their relationship with God, or their readiness. Each person must have their own. A godly parent, spouse or friend cannot believe for you.

Go rather to the dealers and buy for yourselves. Perhaps unrealistic at midnight, which is the point: it is too late.

And while they were going to buy, the bridegroom came. The decisive moment arrives when they are not ready.

And those who were ready went in with him to the marriage feast. “Ready” is the key word (24:44). The feast is the joy of the kingdom (22:2; Revelation 19:9).

And the door was shut. Final, irreversible. Like the door of Noah’s ark, which God shut (Genesis 7:16). There comes a time when the opportunity ends.

In a sentence. The wise could not share their oil, and while the foolish were away, the bridegroom came, the ready went in, and the door was shut.

On a Tuesday. No one can be ready for you. Is your own faith in Christ real and alive today?

verseByVerse.quote: "Afterward the other virgins came also, saying, 'Lord, lord, open to us.' But he answered, 'Truly, I say to you, I do not know you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Later the other virgins came and said: Lord, lord, open to us. But he answered: truly, I do not know you.

Afterward the other virgins came also, saying, “Lord, lord, open to us.” “Lord, lord”: the same words as 7:21–22. They address him with respect and urgency. But it is too late.

But he answered, “Truly, I say to you, I do not know you.” The same words as 7:23: I never knew you. They had a lamp, an invitation, a place in the group, but no relationship with the bridegroom. In Scripture, “to know” means a personal relationship (John 10:14; Galatians 4:9).

What it does not mean. Not that true believers can lose their salvation. The foolish virgins were never truly ready; their oil was never sufficient. Nor does the parable teach that we earn entry by having enough “oil” (good works). The oil pictures genuine readiness: true faith, which God gives.

In a sentence. The foolish virgins arrived too late, and the bridegroom said he did not know them.

On a Tuesday. Does Christ know you, personally? Not just: do you know about him?

verseByVerse.quote: "Watch therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Watch therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour.

Watch therefore. “Watch” (grēgoreite), stay awake, be ready (24:42).

For you know neither the day nor the hour. The lesson of the parable. Since no one knows when Christ will come (24:36), be ready at all times. Readiness is not frantic watching of signs, but faithful living.

In a sentence. Be ready, because no one knows when Christ will return.

On a Tuesday. Are you ready for Christ to come today? If not, what needs to change?

verseByVerse.quote: "For it will be like a man going on a journey, who called his servants and entrusted to them his property. To one he gave five talents, to another two, to another one, to each according to his ability. Then he went away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
It will be like a man going on a journey, who called his servants and entrusted his property to them. To one he gave five talents, to another two, to another one, each according to his ability. Then he went away.

For it will be like a man going on a journey. The second parable of readiness. The man is Christ, who will go away (ascend) and return.

Who called his servants and entrusted to them his property. He hands over his wealth to his servants to manage while he is away. Everything they have is his.

To one he gave five talents, to another two, to another one. A talent (talanton) was a unit of weight for silver or gold, worth about 6,000 denarii, about twenty years’ wages for a labourer. Even one talent was a huge sum. Our English word “talent”, meaning a natural ability, comes from this parable. But in the parable, the talents represent everything God entrusts to us: abilities, opportunities, money, time, relationships, the gospel itself.

To each according to his ability. The master knows his servants. He gives each what they can handle. Different amounts, but each is responsible for what he received.

Then he went away.

In a sentence. In a second parable, a master going away entrusted his servants with large sums, each according to his ability.

On a Tuesday. List what God has entrusted to you: gifts, money, time, people. It all belongs to him.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a talent was worth about twenty years’ wages for a labourer — a huge sum even for the one-talent servant.

parallels.desc: a man going on a journey

verseByVerse.quote: "He who had received the five talents went at once and traded with them, and he made five talents more. So also he who had the two talents made two talents more."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who had received five talents went at once, put them to work, and made five more. In the same way, the one with two made two more.

He who had received the five talents went at once and traded with them. “At once”: he did not delay. “Traded” (ērgasato) means worked, did business. He used what he had been given, took risks, and worked hard.

And he made five talents more. He doubled it.

So also he who had the two talents made two talents more. He also doubled it. Same faithfulness, different amount.

In a sentence. The servants with five and two talents put them to work at once and doubled them.

On a Tuesday. Faithfulness is measured by what you do with what you have, not by how much you have.

verseByVerse.quote: "But he who had received the one talent went and dug in the ground and hid his master's money."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the one who had received one talent went and dug in the ground and hid his master’s money.

But he who had received the one talent went and dug in the ground and hid his master’s money. Burying money was considered a safe way to protect it from thieves (13:44). Under Jewish law, someone who buried money entrusted to him was not liable if it was stolen. He did the safe thing. But he did nothing with it. He was not a thief; he simply wasted the opportunity.

In a sentence. The servant with one talent buried it in the ground.

On a Tuesday. What have you “buried”: a gift you are not using, an opportunity you are avoiding, because it feels safer?
verseByVerse.note: Burying money was a common way to keep it safe.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now after a long time the master of those servants came and settled accounts with them. And he who had received the five talents came forward, bringing five talents more, saying, 'Master, you delivered to me five talents; here, I have made five talents more.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
After a long time, the master of those servants returned and settled accounts with them. The one who had received five talents came forward, bringing five more: master, you entrusted me with five talents; here, I have made five more.

Now after a long time the master of those servants came. “A long time”: another hint that Christ’s return would be delayed (24:48; 25:5).

And settled accounts with them. The day of reckoning. Every servant will give account (Romans 14:12; 2 Corinthians 5:10).

Master, you delivered to me five talents; here, I have made five talents more. He reports joyfully. He knows the talents were the master’s.

In a sentence. After a long time, the master returned to settle accounts, and the first servant presented his doubled talents.

On a Tuesday. One day you will give account to Christ. What will you be able to show him?

verseByVerse.quote: "His master said to him, 'Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a little; I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your master.' And he also who had the two talents came forward, saying, 'Master, you delivered to me two talents; here, I have made two talents more.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
His master said: well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a little; I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your master. The one with two talents also came forward: master, you entrusted me with two talents; here, I have made two more.

Well done, good and faithful servant. The words every Christian longs to hear. “Good” and “faithful”: the master praises character and reliability, not just results.

You have been faithful over a little. Five talents was a fortune, yet the master calls it “a little”. Compared to what he is about to give, everything in this life is small.

I will set you over much. The reward for faithfulness is greater responsibility in the kingdom (24:47; Luke 19:17). Heaven is not idleness, but joyful service.

Enter into the joy of your master. The greatest reward: sharing the master’s own joy, at his feast, in his presence (Psalm 16:11; Hebrews 12:2).

And he also who had the two talents came forward. He gives the same report.

In a sentence. The master praised the faithful servant, promised him greater responsibility and invited him into his joy, and the second servant came forward too.

For worship. Thank God that he rewards faithfulness with his own joy.

verseByVerse.quote: "His master said to him, 'Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a little; I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your master.' He also who had received the one talent came forward, saying, 'Master, I knew you to be a hard man, reaping where you did not sow, and gathering where you scattered no seed,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
His master said: well done, good and faithful servant; you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much; enter into the joy of your master. Then the one who had received one talent came forward: master, I knew you to be a hard man, reaping where you did not sow and gathering where you scattered no seed.

Well done, good and faithful servant. Word for word the same praise as the first servant. He received less and made less, but was equally faithful, and received the same commendation and the same joy. God does not compare us with others; he looks for faithfulness with what each received.

Then he also who had received the one talent came forward.

Master, I knew you to be a hard man. “Hard” means harsh, demanding, severe. His view of the master was wrong. The master had generously entrusted him with a fortune. But he saw only demands.

Reaping where you did not sow, and gathering where you scattered no seed. He accuses the master of exploiting others, profiting from others’ work. A false view of God produces fear and paralysis.

In a sentence. The second servant received the same praise as the first, but the third servant came accusing his master of being harsh.

On a Tuesday. How do you see God: as a generous master who delights in your faithfulness, or as a harsh one you fear? Your view of God shapes your service.

verseByVerse.quote: "'so I was afraid, and I went and hid your talent in the ground. Here, you have what is yours.' But his master answered him, 'You wicked and slothful servant! You knew that I reap where I have not sown and gather where I scattered no seed?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I was afraid, and I went and hid your talent in the ground. Here, you have what is yours. But his master answered: you wicked and lazy servant! You knew that I reap where I have not sown and gather where I scattered no seed?

So I was afraid. Fear of failure, fear of the master. Fear paralysed him. Perfect love casts out fear (1 John 4:18).

And I went and hid your talent in the ground. Here, you have what is yours. He returns it unchanged. He thinks this is enough: he has not lost anything. But he has not done what he was meant to.

You wicked and slothful servant! “Slothful” (oknēre) means lazy, hesitant. His sin was not theft but doing nothing. Sins of omission are real sins (James 4:17).

You knew that I reap where I have not sown and gather where I scattered no seed? The master does not agree with his description, but takes him at his word: if you really believed that, you should have acted accordingly.

In a sentence. The third servant returned the unused talent out of fear, and the master called him wicked and lazy.

On a Tuesday. Is fear keeping you from serving God: fear of failure, of what others think, of getting it wrong? Do something with what he has given you.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Then you ought to have invested my money with the bankers, and at my coming I should have received what was my own with interest. So take the talent from him and give it to him who has the ten talents.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then you ought to have invested my money with the bankers, and at my coming I would have received what was mine with interest. So take the talent from him and give it to the one who has ten talents.

Then you ought to have invested my money with the bankers. The minimum: put it in the bank. Even that would have shown some effort.

And at my coming I should have received what was my own with interest. Any return would have been better than nothing.

So take the talent from him and give it to him who has the ten talents. The unused gift is taken away and given to the faithful servant.

In a sentence. The master said the servant should at least have banked the money, and gave his talent to the one with ten.

On a Tuesday. Even a small step of faithfulness is better than doing nothing. What small step could you take with what God has given you?

verseByVerse.quote: "'For to everyone who has will more be given, and he will have an abundance. But from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away. And cast the worthless servant into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
To everyone who has, more will be given, and he will have an abundance. But from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away. Cast the worthless servant into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

For to everyone who has will more be given, and he will have an abundance. The same principle as 13:12. Those who use what God gives receive more.

But from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away. Those who do not use what they have will lose it.

And cast the worthless servant into the outer darkness. “Worthless” (achreion) means useless, unprofitable. He is excluded from the master’s joy.

In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Final judgment (8:12).

What it does not mean. Not that salvation is earned by being productive. The faithful servants were rewarded because their faithfulness showed they truly knew and trusted their master; the wicked servant’s fear and laziness showed he did not. His view of his master was false; he did not love him. Works are the evidence of faith (James 2:17–18), not its basis. Nor does it mean that God is only interested in results. He looks for faithfulness.

Stewardship. This parable is the foundation of the Christian idea of stewardship: everything we have belongs to God, and we are responsible to use it for him. Stewardship is not covetousness: using wealth, gifts and opportunities to increase them, for the Master’s sake, is commended. The difference lies in whose they are and whom they serve.

In a sentence. Those who use what God gives receive more, but the useless servant who buried his talent was thrown out.

On a Tuesday. How are you investing what God has given you: money, abilities, time, relationships? Invest it for his kingdom.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–46 — The Judgment of the Nations
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Olivet Discourse closes with the Son of Man enthroned in his own glory, all the nations gathered, and the flock parted as a shepherd separates sheep from goats at evening. Both groups are judged by the same six items — food, drink, welcome, clothing, a visit in sickness, a visit in prison — and both are astonished, the sheep because they cannot remember doing any of it and the goats because they never noticed the chance. The King's ground in each case is the same: as you did it to one of the least of these, you did it to me. Note that this is no longer a parable; it is a description.
verseByVerse.theology: Who are the least of these my brothers? The narrower reading observes that in Matthew my brothers nearly always means Jesus' disciples, and that the least echoes the little ones and sent messengers of ch. 10, so the nations are judged by their response to the King through his despised people. The broader reading takes it of any suffering person. The first is probably the passage's own point; the principle underneath it is true wherever need is found. Either way the doorway is guarded before a single deed is named: the sheep inherit — nobody earns an inheritance — a kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world, that is, before any of these people existed and before there was anything to reward. The works are produced as evidence, never as the purchase price. Note also the asymmetry at v. 41: the blessing is by my Father and the curse is attributed to nobody, and the fire was prepared for the devil and his angels, not for human beings. And at v. 46 one adjective governs both destinies, which is why the punishment cannot quietly expire unless the life does too.
verseByVerse.examples: Everything on the King's list is a service to somebody who cannot repay it and mostly cannot even report it — which is precisely why it is the list. Prison is the sharpest case: Roman prisons did not feed their inmates, so a man without visitors went hungry, and carrying food through that door announced publicly that you were associated with a criminal. The modern equivalents are the illness where the cards stop after three weeks, the man whose trouble is his own fault, and the visit to someone with dementia who will not remember by teatime that you came. Note what the goats' defence actually admits: we would have, had we recognised you. Their service was available to importance and not to need, and they state it themselves in front of the assembled nations. So the test is whether the trouble you take over a person varies with what that person can do for you. And the sheep could not produce a list of their own good deeds — which is worth weighing by anyone who could.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the angels with him, then he will sit on his glorious throne. Before him will be gathered all the nations, and he will separate people one from another as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the angels with him, he will sit on his glorious throne. All the nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate people from one another as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats.

When the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the angels with him. Christ’s return in glory (16:27; 24:30). The humble carpenter who is about to be crucified describes himself as the Judge of all the earth.

Then he will sit on his glorious throne. As King and Judge (19:28; Daniel 7:9–14).

Before him will be gathered all the nations. All people, of every nation, Jew and Gentile, believer and unbeliever (Romans 14:10; 2 Corinthians 5:10; Revelation 20:11–15). Not only nations as groups, but every individual within them.

And he will separate people one from another as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats. In Palestine, sheep and goats often grazed together during the day in mixed flocks, but were separated at night, because goats needed to be kept warmer. They looked similar from a distance, but a shepherd could tell them apart easily. Ezekiel 34:17 pictures God judging between sheep and sheep, rams and goats. Christ will separate humanity with perfect accuracy.

In a sentence. When Christ returns in glory, he will sit as King and Judge over all nations, and separate them as a shepherd separates sheep from goats.

On a Tuesday. Every person you meet today will stand before Christ’s throne. Let that shape how you see and treat them.
verseByVerse.note: Sheep and goats often grazed together in mixed flocks and had to be separated.

parallels.desc: the Son of Man given dominion
all the holy ones with him
I judge between sheep and sheep, rams and male goats

verseByVerse.quote: "And he will place the sheep on his right, but the goats on the left."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He will put the sheep on his right, but the goats on the left.

And he will place the sheep on his right. The right hand was the place of honour and blessing (Psalm 110:1; Genesis 48:13–20).

But the goats on the left. The place of rejection. Goats are not evil animals; the image simply describes the separation.

In a sentence. Christ will place the sheep on his right, the place of honour, and the goats on his left.

On a Tuesday. On which side will you stand? Ask the Good Shepherd to make you one of his sheep (John 10:27–28).
verseByVerse.note: The right hand was the place of honour.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then the King will say to those on his right, 'Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry and you gave me food, I was thirsty and you gave me drink, I was a stranger and you welcomed me,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the King will say to those on his right: come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry and you gave me food, I was thirsty and you gave me drink, I was a stranger and you welcomed me.

Then the King will say. The Son of Man is the King. Jesus calls himself King only here in Matthew.

Come, you who are blessed by my Father. “Come”: the invitation of 11:28, now completed. “Blessed”: favoured by the Father. Their blessing comes from God’s grace.

Inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. “Inherit”: a gift received as children, not wages earned. “Prepared from the foundation of the world”: God planned their salvation before creation (Ephesians 1:4; 2 Timothy 1:9). This is grace, rooted in God’s eternal choice.

For I was hungry and you gave me food, I was thirsty and you gave me drink. The evidence. Their works show that they belong to the King.

I was a stranger and you welcomed me. “Stranger” means a foreigner, a traveller, someone without a home. Hospitality to strangers was a sacred duty in Scripture (Leviticus 19:34; Hebrews 13:2).

In a sentence. The King will invite the blessed to inherit the kingdom prepared for them from eternity, pointing to their acts of mercy to him.

On a Tuesday. Is there a hungry, thirsty or lonely person near you? Serve them today.

parallels.desc: share your bread with the hungry
chosen before the foundation of the world

verseByVerse.quote: "'I was naked and you clothed me, I was sick and you visited me, I was in prison and you came to me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I was naked and you clothed me, I was sick and you visited me, I was in prison and you came to me.

I was naked and you clothed me. Gave clothing to those who lacked it.

I was sick and you visited me. “Visited” means cared for, looked after.

I was in prison and you came to me. Prisoners in the ancient world depended on friends and family for food and care. Visiting Christians in prison could be dangerous, as it identified you with them (Hebrews 10:34; 13:3; 2 Timothy 1:16–17).

Six acts of mercy. Food, drink, welcome, clothing, care for the sick, visiting prisoners. Ordinary, practical acts, not spectacular ones. Anyone can do them.

In a sentence. The King lists clothing the naked, visiting the sick and coming to prisoners as acts done to him.

On a Tuesday. Who is sick or in prison that you could visit this month?

verseByVerse.quote: "Then the righteous will answer him, saying, 'Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you, or thirsty and give you drink? And when did we see you a stranger and welcome you, or naked and clothe you?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the righteous will answer him: Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you, or thirsty and give you a drink? When did we see you a stranger and welcome you, or naked and clothe you?

Then the righteous will answer him. “The righteous”: those made right with God, whose lives show it.

Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you? They are surprised. They did not serve these people in order to earn a reward, or even consciously as serving Christ. They simply showed love. True righteousness is unselfconscious. Their left hand did not know what their right hand was doing (6:3).

In a sentence. The righteous are surprised, not remembering serving the King himself.

On a Tuesday. The best acts of love are often the ones you forget. Serve without keeping score.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And when did we see you sick or in prison and visit you?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when did we see you sick or in prison and visit you?

And when did we see you sick or in prison and visit you? Their surprise continues. They had not seen Christ in those they served; but Christ was there.

In a sentence. The righteous do not remember visiting the King when he was sick or in prison.

On a Tuesday. Ask God to help you see Christ in the needy believers around you.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the King will answer them, 'Truly, I say to you, as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The King will answer them: truly, as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.

Truly, I say to you, as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me. The heart of the passage. Christ identifies so closely with “the least of these my brothers” that what is done to them is done to him. When Saul persecuted the church, Jesus asked, why are you persecuting me? (Acts 9:4).

Who are “my brothers”? Two main views:

1. The poor and needy in general. Christ identifies with every suffering person, and the passage calls everyone to care for the poor. This is the most common view today.

2. Christ’s disciples. In Matthew, Jesus calls his disciples his brothers (12:48–50; 28:10), and “the least” or “little ones” refers to humble disciples (10:42; 18:6). In 10:40–42, those who receive his messengers, even with a cup of cold water, receive him. So the nations will be judged by how they treated Christ’s people, especially his messengers in need: hungry, homeless, imprisoned for the gospel.

Verdict: in Matthew’s usage, the second is more likely: Christ’s needy disciples. But the rest of Scripture clearly commands care for all who are poor and suffering (5:44–45; Galatians 6:10; Proverbs 19:17; James 1:27). The passage cannot be used to excuse indifference to anyone in need.

What it does not mean. Not that we are saved by doing good works to the poor, or that anyone who does good is secretly a Christian. The kingdom was prepared for them by grace (v. 34). Their works were evidence of their belonging to Christ, not the cause of it. The Reformers put it this way: we are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone; it works through love (Galatians 5:6).

In a sentence. Whatever is done to the least of Christ’s brothers is done to Christ himself.

On a Tuesday. How you treat the least important Christian you know is how you treat Christ. Think of one, and serve them this week.

For worship. Thank Christ that he so identifies with his people that he counts every kindness to them as done to himself.

parallels.desc: not ashamed to call them brothers

verseByVerse.quote: "Then he will say to those on his left, 'Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry and you gave me no food, I was thirsty and you gave me no drink,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he will say to those on his left: depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry and you gave me no food, I was thirsty and you gave me no drink.

Then he will say to those on his left, “Depart from me.” The opposite of “Come” (v. 34). Separation from Christ, the source of every good (7:23; 2 Thessalonians 1:9).

You cursed. The opposite of “blessed”. Notice: not “cursed by my Father”. The blessed are blessed by God’s grace; the cursed are cursed by their own choice.

Into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. Hell was not prepared for human beings, but for the devil and the fallen angels (Revelation 20:10). The kingdom was prepared for the blessed (v. 34); hell was prepared for the devil. Those who go there join him because they refused God (2 Peter 3:9).

For I was hungry and you gave me no food, I was thirsty and you gave me no drink. Their sins were sins of omission: not cruelty, but neglect. They simply did nothing.

In a sentence. Christ will send those on his left into the eternal fire prepared for the devil, because they did nothing for him in his needy brothers.

On a Tuesday. Not doing good is a real sin. What good are you leaving undone?

parallels.desc: the devil thrown into the lake of fire

verseByVerse.quote: "'I was a stranger and you did not welcome me, naked and you did not clothe me, sick and in prison and you did not visit me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I was a stranger and you did not welcome me, naked and you did not clothe me, sick and in prison and you did not visit me.

I was a stranger and you did not welcome me. The same list, with “not”. They passed by the needy, perhaps without noticing, perhaps deliberately.

Naked and you did not clothe me, sick and in prison and you did not visit me. The neglect of every kind of need. It reveals hearts without love, and so without Christ (1 John 3:17).

In a sentence. The King lists the needs they ignored: the stranger, the naked, the sick and the prisoner.

On a Tuesday. Who are you walking past? Notice the needs around you.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then they also will answer, saying, 'Lord, when did we see you hungry or thirsty or a stranger or naked or sick or in prison, and did not minister to you?' Then he will answer them, saying, 'Truly, I say to you, as you did not do it to one of the least of these, you did not do it to me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they too will answer: Lord, when did we see you hungry or thirsty or a stranger or naked or sick or in prison, and did not serve you? He will answer: truly, as you did not do it to one of the least of these, you did not do it to me.

Lord, when did we see you hungry or thirsty or a stranger or naked or sick or in prison, and did not minister to you? They are also surprised. They call him “Lord”, but they never recognised him in his people. They may have thought they would gladly have served Jesus himself, if they had seen him.

Truly, I say to you, as you did not do it to one of the least of these, you did not do it to me. To neglect Christ’s people is to neglect Christ.

In a sentence. Those on the left are surprised, and Christ tells them that by neglecting the least of his brothers they neglected him.

On a Tuesday. You cannot love Christ while ignoring his people (1 John 4:20).

parallels.desc: whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker

verseByVerse.quote: "And these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.

And these will go away into eternal punishment. “Punishment” (kolasin) means penalty, chastisement. “Eternal” (aiōnion) means belonging to the age to come, without end.

But the righteous into eternal life. “Eternal life” is the life of the age to come, with God, for ever (19:16, 29; John 17:3).

The same word. The same word, “eternal”, describes both the punishment and the life, in the same sentence. If the life is everlasting, so is the punishment. This is one of the strongest texts for the traditional view of hell as everlasting, conscious punishment.

What it does not mean. Not that God takes pleasure in punishment (Ezekiel 33:11). Hell is the just consequence of rejecting God, and it is real. Nor does it mean that all who go to hell suffer equally. Jesus speaks of degrees of punishment (10:15; 11:22–24; Luke 12:47–48).

Where Christians differ: hell. Universalists hold that all will eventually be saved. Annihilationists (conditional immortality) hold that the wicked are destroyed and cease to exist, so that the “eternal” punishment is eternal in its result, not its experience. The traditional view, held by the church throughout history and by the Reformed confessions, is that hell is eternal, conscious punishment (Westminster Confession 33.2). Verdict: the traditional view. The parallel between eternal punishment and eternal life in this verse is decisive. It should make us sober, humble and urgent in sharing the gospel.

In a sentence. The wicked will go away into eternal punishment, and the righteous into eternal life.

On a Tuesday. Eternity is real, and every person you know will spend it in one of two places. Let that make you urgent to share Christ.

For worship. Thank God for the gift of eternal life in Christ, and pray for those who do not yet know him.

parallels.desc: some to everlasting life, some to everlasting contempt

25.theology: Faith and works in the final judgment. The parable of the sheep and goats is sometimes misread as teaching salvation by charity. It teaches the opposite: those who are blessed by the Father (elect from the foundation of the world, v. 34) demonstrate their status through the fruit of mercy. Works do not earn salvation; they reveal it. James and Paul are not in contradiction: Paul says we are justified by faith alone (Rom 3:28); James says a faith without works is dead (Jas 2:26). Matthew 25 stands with James: the living faith that justifies is the faith that produces mercy. The absence of mercy is evidence not of an imperfect Christian but of a heart that has never truly encountered the merciful King.
25.examples:
Then: The early church was remarkable for its care of the poor, the sick, the orphan, and the widow — in a culture that largely left the vulnerable to die. Pagans observed and were astonished. The church was not performing charity as a strategy; it was loving Christ in the face of the neighbour. The Roman emperor Julian complained: “The godless Galileans feed not only their own poor but ours also.”

Now: The parable of the talents is a rebuke of every Christian who sits on their gifts out of fear — fear of failure, fear of criticism, fear of the cost. Every person reading these words has been entrusted with something by the master: a relationship, a skill, a platform, a message, an opportunity. The question at the end will not be “how much did you have?” but “what did you do with what you were given?” Faithfulness, not magnitude, is the measure.

26.title: The Last Supper and Gethsemane
26.text: <sup>1</sup>When Jesus had finished all these sayings, he said to his disciples, <sup>2</sup>“You know that after two days the Passover is coming, and the Son of Man will be delivered up to be crucified.” <sup>3</sup>Then the chief priests and the elders of the people gathered in the palace of the high priest, whose name was Caiaphas, <sup>4</sup>and plotted together in order to arrest Jesus by stealth and kill him. <sup>5</sup>But they said, “Not during the feast, lest there be an uproar among the people.” <sup>6</sup>Now when Jesus was at Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, <sup>7</sup>a woman came up to him with an alabaster flask of very expensive ointment, and she poured it on his head as he reclined at table. <sup>8</sup>And when the disciples saw it, they were indignant, saying, “Why this waste? <sup>9</sup>For this could have been sold for a large sum and given to the poor.” <sup>10</sup>But Jesus, aware of this, said to them, “Why do you trouble the woman? For she has done a beautiful thing to me. <sup>11</sup>For you always have the poor with you, but you will not always have me. <sup>12</sup>In pouring this ointment on my body, she has done it to prepare me for burial. <sup>13</sup>Truly, I say to you, wherever this gospel is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her.” <sup>14</sup>Then one of the twelve, whose name was Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests <sup>15</sup>and said, “What will you give me if I deliver him over to you?” And they paid him thirty pieces of silver. <sup>16</sup>And from that moment he sought an opportunity to betray him. <sup>17</sup>Now on the first day of Unleavened Bread the disciples came to Jesus, saying, “Where will you have us prepare for you to eat the Passover?” <sup>18</sup>He said, “Go into the city to a certain man and say to him, ‘The Teacher says, My time is at hand. I will keep the Passover at your house with my disciples.’” <sup>19</sup>And the disciples did as Jesus had directed them, and they prepared the Passover. <sup>20</sup>When it was evening, he reclined at table with the twelve. <sup>21</sup>And as they were eating, he said, “Truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me.” <sup>22</sup>And they were very sorrowful and began to say to him one after another, “Is it I, Lord?” <sup>23</sup>He answered, “He who has dipped his hand in the dish with me will betray me. <sup>24</sup>The Son of Man goes as it is written of him, but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed! It would have been better for that man if he had not been born.” <sup>25</sup>Judas, who would betray him, answered, “Is it I, Rabbi?” He said to him, “You have said so.” <sup>26</sup>Now as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and after blessing it broke it and gave it to the disciples, and said, “Take, eat; this is my body.” <sup>27</sup>And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he gave it to them, saying, “Drink of it, all of you, <sup>28</sup>for this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins. <sup>29</sup>I tell you I will not drink again of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father’s kingdom.” <sup>30</sup>And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives. <sup>31</sup>Then Jesus said to them, “You will all fall away because of me this night. For it is written, ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.’ <sup>32</sup>But after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee.” <sup>33</sup>Peter answered him, “Though they all fall away because of you, I will never fall away.” <sup>34</sup>Jesus said to him, “Truly, I tell you, this very night, before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times.” <sup>35</sup>Peter said to him, “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you!” And all the disciples said the same. <sup>36</sup>Then Jesus went with them to a place called Gethsemane, and he said to his disciples, “Sit here, while I go over there and pray.” <sup>37</sup>And taking with him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, he began to be sorrowful and troubled. <sup>38</sup>Then he said to them, “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death; remain here, and watch with me.” <sup>39</sup>And going a little farther he fell on his face and prayed, saying, “My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.” <sup>40</sup>And he came to the disciples and found them sleeping. And he said to Peter, “So, could you not watch with me one hour? <sup>41</sup>Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” <sup>42</sup>Again, for the second time, he went away and prayed, “My Father, if this cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done.” <sup>43</sup>And again he came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were heavy. <sup>44</sup>So, leaving them again, he went away and prayed for the third time, saying the same words again. <sup>45</sup>Then he came to the disciples and said to them, “Sleep and take your rest later on. See, the hour is at hand, and the Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. <sup>46</sup>Rise, let us be going; see, my betrayer is at hand.” <sup>47</sup>While he was still speaking, Judas came, one of the twelve, and with him a great crowd with swords and clubs, from the chief priests and the elders of the people. <sup>48</sup>Now the betrayer had given them a sign, saying, “The one I will kiss is the man; seize him.” <sup>49</sup>And he came up to Jesus at once and said, “Greetings, Rabbi!” And he kissed him. <sup>50</sup>Jesus said to him, “Friend, do what you came to do.” Then they came up and laid hands on Jesus and seized him. <sup>51</sup>And behold, one of those who were with Jesus stretched out his hand and drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his ear. <sup>52</sup>Then Jesus said to him, “Put your sword back into its place. For all who take the sword will perish by the sword. <sup>53</sup>Do you think that I cannot appeal to my Father, and he will at once send me more than twelve legions of angels? <sup>54</sup>But how then should the Scriptures be fulfilled, that it must be so?” <sup>55</sup>At that hour Jesus said to the crowds, “Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs to capture me? Day after day I sat in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me. <sup>56</sup>But all this has taken place that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled.” Then all the disciples left him and fled. <sup>57</sup>Then those who had seized Jesus led him to Caiaphas the high priest, where the scribes and the elders had gathered. <sup>58</sup>And Peter was following him at a distance, as far as the courtyard of the high priest, and going inside he sat with the guards to see the end. <sup>59</sup>Now the chief priests and the whole council were seeking false testimony against Jesus that they might put him to death, <sup>60</sup>but they found none, though many false witnesses came forward. At last two came forward <sup>61</sup>and said, “This man said, ‘I am able to destroy the temple of God, and to rebuild it in three days.’” <sup>62</sup>And the high priest stood up and said, “Have you no answer to make? What is it that these men testify against you?” <sup>63</sup>But Jesus remained silent. And the high priest said to him, “I adjure you by the living God, tell us if you are the Christ, the Son of God.” <sup>64</sup>Jesus said to him, “You have said so. But I tell you, from now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven.” <sup>65</sup>Then the high priest tore his robes and said, “He has uttered blasphemy. What further witnesses do we need? You have now heard his blasphemy. <sup>66</sup>What is your judgment?” They answered, “He deserves death.” <sup>67</sup>Then they spit in his face and struck him. And some slapped him, <sup>68</sup>saying, “Prophesy to us, you Christ! Who is it that struck you?” <sup>69</sup>Now Peter was sitting outside in the courtyard. And a servant girl came up to him and said, “You also were with Jesus the Galilean.” <sup>70</sup>But he denied it before them all, saying, “I do not know what you mean.” <sup>71</sup>And when he went out to the entrance, another servant girl saw him, and she said to the bystanders, “This man was with Jesus of Nazareth.” <sup>72</sup>And again he denied it with an oath: “I do not know the man.” <sup>73</sup>After a little while the bystanders came up and said to Peter, “Certainly you too are one of them, for your accent betrays you.” <sup>74</sup>Then he began to invoke a curse on himself and to swear, “I do not know the man.” And immediately the rooster crowed. <sup>75</sup>And Peter remembered the saying of Jesus, “Before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times.” And he went out and wept bitterly.
26.overview:
Chapter 26 is the most theologically dense chapter in Matthew. In a single evening Jesus institutes the Lord’s Supper, reveals his betrayer, predicts Peter’s denial, agonises in Gethsemane, is arrested by a crowd with swords, and is condemned by the Sanhedrin. Every scene is simultaneously the action of history and the fulfilment of Scripture: Judas’ betrayal for thirty pieces of silver (Zech 11:12–13), the scattering of the disciples (Zech 13:7), the suffering servant (Isa 53), the enthroned Son of Man (Dan 7:13).

Gethsemane is the chapter’s theological centre. Jesus does not walk to the cross with stoic detachment; he falls on his face and prays that the cup might pass. His agony is real — the weight of the wrath of God against sin, the drinking of the cup of Jeremiah 25 and Isaiah 51, the bearing of the curse. And then: “not as I will, but as you will.” This is the most perfect prayer ever prayed — complete honesty about human desire, complete submission to divine will. The cross is not the defeat of the Son; it is the triumph of obedience.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–46 — The Plot, the Anointing, the Last Supper, and Gethsemane
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus finishes the last of his five discourses and immediately names the day of his own execution. The council meets to arrange it and rules out Passover; a woman in a leper's house breaks a year's wages over his head and is scolded for waste; Judas goes out and lets the priests set a price. In a borrowed upper room Jesus keeps the Passover with the twelve, names his betrayer, and gives them bread and a cup as his body and his blood of the covenant. Then the Hallel, the walk to Gethsemane, the prediction that all of them will fall away, and a night on the ground in an olive grove asking for the cup to pass.
verseByVerse.theology: The section's engine is the difference between what appears to be happening and what is happening. The council schedules the arrest for after the feast and he dies during it; Judas names no price and lets them value the Son of God at the compensation rate for a gored slave (Ex 21:32; Zech 11:12-13); the disciples see waste where Jesus sees a burial anointing. At the table the new covenant is inaugurated in the words of Sinai with one word changed — my blood of the covenant (Ex 24:8) — and Jeremiah's promise of forgiveness is attached to a cup. Gethsemane then shows that the atonement was not endured from behind any protective screen: Matthew's verb for his distress is the strongest available in the Greek of the period, and the cup is the Old Testament cup of wrath (Isa 51:17; Ps 75:8). He asked three times for it to pass, was refused, and got up and went to meet the betrayer.
verseByVerse.examples: Three things in this section are unusually usable. The woman's jar had to be broken to be poured, so the extravagance was decided before a drop touched him — and the test she leaves is whether anything in your Christian life has lately been indefensible on grounds of usefulness. You always have the poor with you is quoted to excuse doing nothing, and it is a quotation of Deuteronomy 15:11, where the permanence of poverty is the stated reason for permanent open-handedness; he quotes the middle of the verse and lets the table supply the end. And Gethsemane is the passage for anyone in real mental anguish: he said out loud how bad it was, asked friends to stay near him, asked three times for it to be lifted, and fell on his face — and what heaven sent was not the removal of the cup but strength to drink it. That is very often the shape of the answer, and it is not a lesser one.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus had finished all these sayings, he said to his disciples, "You know that after two days the Passover is coming, and the Son of Man will be delivered up to be crucified."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus had finished all this teaching, he told his disciples: you know that after two days the Passover is coming, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified.

The passion narrative. Chapters 26–28 tell of Jesus’ suffering (his “passion”, from the Latin for suffering), death and resurrection: the climax of the Gospel, toward which everything has been moving (16:21).

When Jesus had finished all these sayings. The last of the five formulas closing Jesus’ great discourses (7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1). “All”: his teaching ministry is complete. Now comes his saving work.

You know that after two days the Passover is coming. Passover was the great annual festival commemorating Israel’s rescue from Egypt (Exodus 12). On the night of the exodus, each household killed a lamb and put its blood on the doorposts; when the LORD struck Egypt’s firstborn, he passed over the houses marked by blood. Every year at Passover, lambs were sacrificed in the temple on the afternoon of 14 Nisan (in March or April), and eaten that evening in families. Pilgrims crowded Jerusalem. It was probably Tuesday or Wednesday when Jesus said this.

And the Son of Man will be delivered up to be crucified. Jesus links his death to the Passover. He is the true Passover Lamb, whose blood saves his people from God’s judgment (John 1:29; 1 Corinthians 5:7). He knows not only that he will die, but when. His death is not an accident overtaking him; it is the plan he is fulfilling.

In a sentence. Jesus announced that at the coming Passover he would be handed over to be crucified, as the true Passover Lamb.

On a Tuesday. Jesus walked into his death knowing the day. Let his deliberate love for you sink in.
verseByVerse.note: Passover recalled Israel’s rescue from Egypt, when the blood of a lamb protected each household. Jerusalem swelled with pilgrims for the feast.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the chief priests and the elders of the people gathered in the palace of the high priest, whose name was Caiaphas, and plotted together in order to arrest Jesus by stealth and kill him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the chief priests and elders of the people gathered in the palace of the high priest, Caiaphas, and plotted together to arrest Jesus by stealth and kill him.

Then the chief priests and the elders of the people gathered. At the same time as Jesus spoke of his death, his enemies were planning it. Two plans meet: God’s and theirs (Acts 2:23; 4:27–28).

In the palace of the high priest, whose name was Caiaphas. Joseph Caiaphas was high priest from about AD 18 to 36, unusually long, which suggests he cooperated well with Rome. His father-in-law Annas had been high priest before him and still had great influence (John 18:13). In 1990, an ornate ossuary (bone box) inscribed “Joseph son of Caiaphas” was discovered in Jerusalem, probably his. John records that Caiaphas had said it was better that one man should die for the people than that the whole nation perish, an unknowing prophecy (John 11:49–52).

And plotted together in order to arrest Jesus by stealth and kill him. “By stealth” means secretly, by trickery. They could not arrest him publicly because of the crowds.

In a sentence. The religious leaders met at Caiaphas’ palace and plotted to arrest Jesus secretly and kill him.

On a Tuesday. Even the darkest human plots serve God’s purposes. Nothing that is done against you is outside his control.
verseByVerse.note: Caiaphas was high priest from about AD 18 to 36; his father-in-law Annas had held the office before him.

verseByVerse.quote: But they said, "Not during the feast, lest there be an uproar among the people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they said: not during the feast, or there may be a riot among the people.

But they said, “Not during the feast, lest there be an uproar among the people.” The festival crowds were huge, and many supported Jesus. Riots at festivals were common, and the Roman governor came to Jerusalem with extra troops at Passover to keep order. The leaders feared a riot that might bring Roman retaliation (John 11:48).

God’s timing. They planned to wait until after the feast. But God’s plan was that Jesus would die at Passover, as the Passover Lamb. Judas’ offer (v. 15) changed their timetable. Human plans bent to God’s purpose.

In a sentence. The leaders planned to wait until after the festival, but God’s timing would overrule theirs.

On a Tuesday. God’s timing is not ours. Trust him with the timing of the events of your life.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus was at Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, a woman came up to him with an alabaster flask of very expensive ointment, and she poured it on his head as he reclined at table.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While Jesus was at Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, a woman came to him with an alabaster flask of very expensive ointment, and poured it on his head as he reclined at table.

Now when Jesus was at Bethany in the house of Simon the leper. Bethany, about two miles east of Jerusalem (21:17). Simon had probably been healed of leprosy, perhaps by Jesus; otherwise he could not have hosted guests. John places this meal six days before Passover and says Martha served and Lazarus was at the table (John 12:1–8). Matthew places it here, not necessarily in strict time order, to contrast the woman’s love with Judas’ betrayal.

A woman came up to him. John names her: Mary, the sister of Martha and Lazarus (John 12:3). (Luke 7:36–50 records a different anointing, earlier, by a sinful woman in Galilee.)

With an alabaster flask of very expensive ointment. Alabaster was a soft, translucent stone used for perfume flasks, often with a long neck that was broken to pour out the contents. Mark and John say it was pure nard, a costly perfume imported from India, worth over three hundred denarii: a year’s wages (Mark 14:3–5; John 12:3, 5). Perhaps it was her family’s savings, or her dowry.

And she poured it on his head as he reclined at table. Anointing the head was done for honoured guests (Psalm 23:5), and for kings (1 Samuel 10:1; 2 Kings 9:6). John says she anointed his feet and wiped them with her hair (John 12:3); she probably did both. Jesus is the Messiah, the Anointed One, anointed by a woman’s love.

In a sentence. At a meal in Bethany, a woman poured an extremely costly perfume on Jesus’ head.

On a Tuesday. What is your “alabaster flask”: the most precious thing you have? Would you pour it out for Jesus?
verseByVerse.note: John names the woman as Mary, sister of Martha and Lazarus. Alabaster was a soft stone used for perfume flasks; Mark and John say the ointment was pure nard, worth about a year’s wages.

parallels.desc: a different anointing, by a sinful woman in Galilee

verseByVerse.quote: And when the disciples saw it, they were indignant, saying, "Why this waste? For this could have been sold for a large sum and given to the poor."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the disciples saw it, they were indignant: why this waste? This could have been sold for a large sum and given to the poor.

And when the disciples saw it, they were indignant. John says Judas led the complaint, not because he cared for the poor, but because he was a thief who kept the money bag and helped himself from it (John 12:4–6). The others joined in.

Why this waste? “Waste” (apōleia) means loss, destruction. The same word is used of Judas himself, the “son of destruction” (John 17:12). To them, pouring it on Jesus was throwing it away.

For this could have been sold for a large sum and given to the poor. It sounded pious. Giving to the poor was especially expected at Passover (John 13:29). But it missed the moment: Jesus was about to die.

What it does not mean. Not that concern for the poor is wrong. Jesus commands it (19:21; 25:35–40). But there is a time for extravagant devotion to Christ himself. Love for Christ and love for the poor are not rivals.

In a sentence. The disciples, led by Judas, called the woman’s gift a waste that should have gone to the poor.

On a Tuesday. Is anything you give to Christ ever wasted? Beware of criticising other people’s devotion.
verseByVerse.note: John says the complaint came from Judas.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus, aware of this, said to them, "Why do you trouble the woman? For she has done a beautiful thing to me. For you always have the poor with you, but you will not always have me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus, aware of this, said: why do you trouble the woman? She has done a beautiful thing to me. For you always have the poor with you, but you will not always have me.

Why do you trouble the woman? Jesus defends her.

For she has done a beautiful thing to me. “Beautiful” (kalon) means good, noble, fitting. Her act was not wasteful but beautiful: love expressed lavishly and at the right moment.

For you always have the poor with you. Echoing Deuteronomy 15:11: there will never cease to be poor in the land; therefore open your hand to your brother. Jesus is not saying poverty does not matter; he assumes they will always care for the poor.

But you will not always have me. Jesus would be with them physically only a few more days. There was a unique opportunity to honour him in person, which she took.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should be indifferent to poverty, as the verse is sometimes misused to suggest. Deuteronomy 15:11, which Jesus echoes, commands generosity to the poor precisely because they will always be there.

In a sentence. Jesus defended the woman’s beautiful act, since the poor would always be there but he would soon be gone.

On a Tuesday. Some opportunities to show love come only once. Do not miss them.

parallels.desc: there will never cease to be poor in the land

verseByVerse.quote: "In pouring this ointment on my body she has done it to prepare me for burial. Truly, I say to you, wherever this gospel is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In pouring this ointment on my body, she has prepared me for burial. Truly, wherever this gospel is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will be told in memory of her.

In pouring this ointment on my body, she has done it to prepare me for burial. In Jewish custom, bodies were anointed with spices and perfume before burial. Jesus would be buried in haste, before the Sabbath, without the usual anointing (27:57–61; Mark 16:1). Whether she understood it or not, her act anointed him in advance. She perhaps understood his coming death better than the disciples.

Truly, I say to you, wherever this gospel is proclaimed in the whole world. Jesus is certain that the gospel will be preached throughout the world after his death (24:14; 28:19).

What she has done will also be told in memory of her. And it has been: here, in every Bible, in every language. Her act of love has a permanent memorial. Judas’ name is remembered with shame; hers with honour.

In a sentence. Jesus said she had anointed him for burial, and promised that her act would be told wherever the gospel was preached.

On a Tuesday. No act of love for Christ is forgotten by him. What could you do for him today?

For worship. Pour out your love on Jesus in worship today, without counting the cost.
verseByVerse.note: Bodies were anointed with spices for burial; Jesus would be buried in haste.

verseByVerse.quote: Then one of the twelve, whose name was Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests and said, "What will you give me if I deliver him over to you?" And they paid him thirty pieces of silver.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then one of the twelve, Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests and said: what will you give me if I hand him over to you? And they paid him thirty pieces of silver.

Then one of the twelve. “Then”: right after the woman’s extravagant gift. The contrast is stark. She gave everything for Jesus; Judas sold him. “One of the twelve”: the horror is that it was an insider, chosen by Jesus, who had seen everything (10:4).

Whose name was Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests. He went on his own initiative. Luke and John say that Satan entered him (Luke 22:3; John 13:27). Both are true: Judas chose freely, and Satan used him.

What will you give me if I deliver him over to you? His motive was at least partly money (John 12:6). Some suggest disappointment that Jesus was not a political Messiah, or anger at the rebuke at Bethany. Scripture does not fully explain; sin is never fully rational.

And they paid him thirty pieces of silver. Only Matthew names the sum. Thirty shekels was the price the law set as compensation for a slave gored by an ox (Exodus 21:32): the price of a slave. And it fulfils Zechariah 11:12–13, where the shepherd of God’s people is valued at thirty pieces of silver, a lordly price, said with bitter irony, and the money is thrown into the house of the LORD to the potter (fulfilled in 27:3–10).

In a sentence. Judas, one of the Twelve, went to the chief priests and sold Jesus for thirty pieces of silver, the price of a slave.

On a Tuesday. For what price might you betray Christ: money, reputation, comfort? Judas was close to Jesus and still fell. Guard your heart.
verseByVerse.note: Thirty shekels of silver was the price the law set for a slave gored by an ox.

parallels.desc: thirty pieces of silver, the shepherd’s wages

verseByVerse.quote: And from that moment he sought an opportunity to betray him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And from that moment he looked for an opportunity to betray him.

And from that moment he sought an opportunity to betray him. An opportunity away from the crowds (Luke 22:6). Judas knew where Jesus went at night to pray (John 18:2). He would lead them there.

In a sentence. From then on Judas looked for the right moment to betray Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Sin often begins with a decision, then waits for an opportunity. Do not give it one.

verseByVerse.quote: Now on the first day of Unleavened Bread the disciples came to Jesus, saying, "Where will you have us prepare for you to eat the Passover?" He said, "Go into the city to a certain man and say to him, 'The Teacher says, My time is at hand. I will keep the Passover at your house with my disciples.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the first day of Unleavened Bread, the disciples asked Jesus: where do you want us to prepare for you to eat the Passover? He said: go into the city to a certain man and say: the Teacher says, my time is at hand; I will keep the Passover at your house with my disciples.

Now on the first day of Unleavened Bread. The Feast of Unleavened Bread lasted seven days, beginning with the Passover meal (Exodus 12:15–20; Leviticus 23:5–6). All leaven was removed from homes. The Passover lambs were sacrificed in the temple on the afternoon of 14 Nisan, and the meal eaten after sunset, which began 15 Nisan. This was Thursday.

Where will you have us prepare for you to eat the Passover? Preparation involved buying a lamb, having it sacrificed at the temple, roasting it, and preparing unleavened bread, wine, bitter herbs and a sauce. The meal had to be eaten within Jerusalem.

Go into the city to a certain man. Jesus keeps the place secret, perhaps so Judas could not tell the authorities in advance. Mark and Luke say they would meet a man carrying a water jar (Mark 14:13; Luke 22:10), which was unusual, since women normally carried water.

The Teacher says, My time is at hand. “My time” (kairos): the appointed time of his death (John 13:1).

I will keep the Passover at your house with my disciples. A large upper room, already furnished (Mark 14:15). Some think this was the house of Mark’s mother, where the church later met (Acts 12:12).

Was it a Passover meal? Matthew, Mark and Luke present it as the Passover meal. John seems to place Jesus’ death on the day of preparation, when the lambs were being killed (John 18:28; 19:14). Explanations include different calendars used by different groups, or John’s phrases referring to the whole Passover week. Verdict: the Last Supper was a Passover meal, as the first three Gospels say; John’s language fits this when read carefully, and his emphasis is that Jesus died as the Passover Lamb.

In a sentence. Jesus arranged for his disciples to prepare the Passover in a house in the city, because his appointed time had come.

On a Tuesday. Jesus was in control of every detail of his last days. Trust him with the details of yours.
