verseByVerse.note: Unleavened Bread was the week-long feast that began with Passover; lambs were sacrificed at the temple that afternoon.

verseByVerse.quote: And the disciples did as Jesus had directed them, and they prepared the Passover. When it was evening, he reclined at table with the twelve.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples did as Jesus had directed and prepared the Passover. When evening came, he reclined at table with the twelve.

And the disciples did as Jesus had directed them, and they prepared the Passover. Obedience.

When it was evening. The Passover meal began after sunset.

He reclined at table with the twelve. At the first Passover, Israelites ate standing, ready to leave (Exodus 12:11). By Jesus’ time, Jews reclined at the Passover, as free people, not slaves, leaning on the left elbow around a low table.

The Passover meal. The meal had a set order. The head of the household explained its meaning: the lamb (God passed over the houses marked with blood), the unleavened bread (the haste of the exodus), the bitter herbs (the bitterness of slavery). Four cups of wine were drunk at different points. The Hallel psalms (113–118) were sung. Jesus would give new meaning to the bread and one of the cups.

In a sentence. The disciples prepared the Passover, and that evening Jesus reclined at the table with the Twelve.

On a Tuesday. Jesus chose to spend his last evening at table with his friends. Value fellowship with other believers.
verseByVerse.note: The Passover was eaten after sunset, reclining.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were eating, he said, "Truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me." And they were very sorrowful and began to say to him one after another, "Is it I, Lord?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they were eating, Jesus said: truly, one of you will betray me. They were very sorrowful, and began to say to him one after another: surely not I, Lord?

Truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me. A shocking announcement in the middle of the meal, the most intimate fellowship. Psalm 41:9: even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me (John 13:18).

And they were very sorrowful. Distressed, grieved.

And began to say to him one after another, “Is it I, Lord?” The Greek expects “no”: “Surely it is not I, Lord?” Each disciple looked at himself rather than at the others. None was certain of himself. They knew their own hearts were capable of betrayal. This is healthy self-suspicion (1 Corinthians 10:12).

In a sentence. Jesus announced that one of the Twelve would betray him, and each one, grieved, asked, surely not I?

On a Tuesday. When you hear of sin in the church, ask first, “Lord, is it I?”, before you look at others.

verseByVerse.quote: He answered, "He who has dipped his hand in the dish with me will betray me. The Son of Man goes as it is written of him, but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed! It would have been better for that man if he had not been born."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He answered: the one who has dipped his hand in the dish with me will betray me. The Son of Man goes as it is written of him, but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed! It would have been better for that man if he had not been born.

He who has dipped his hand in the dish with me will betray me. At the Passover meal, everyone dipped bread or herbs into a shared bowl of sauce. This does not single out Judas to the others; it means “one who is eating with me, sharing the closest fellowship”. The betrayal is all the worse because it comes from intimacy.

The Son of Man goes as it is written of him. Jesus’ death fulfils Scripture (Psalm 22; Isaiah 53). It is God’s plan.

But woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed! God’s sovereign plan does not excuse Judas. He is fully responsible. Here are both truths, side by side in one sentence: God ordained it, and Judas is guilty (Acts 2:23).

It would have been better for that man if he had not been born. A terrible statement. Judas’ end was so dreadful that non-existence would have been better. It implies that his punishment would be eternal; if he were finally saved, his existence would not have been worse than non-existence.

What it does not mean. Not that Judas was a helpless pawn forced to betray Jesus against his will. He chose freely, for his own reasons, and God used his evil for good (Genesis 50:20). Nor does it mean that Judas could not have repented. His remorse (27:3–5) was real, but it led to despair, not to Christ.

In a sentence. Jesus said his betrayer was one who shared his dish, and that though his death was foretold, it would have been better for the betrayer not to have been born.

On a Tuesday. God’s sovereignty never excuses our sin. Take responsibility for your own choices today.
verseByVerse.note: Dipping bread in a shared dish was a mark of close fellowship.

parallels.desc: my close friend, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me

verseByVerse.quote: Judas, who would betray him, answered, "Is it I, Rabbi?" He said to him, "You have said so."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judas, who would betray him, said: surely not I, Rabbi? Jesus said to him: you have said so.

Judas, who would betray him, answered, “Is it I, Rabbi?” The others called Jesus “Lord” (v. 22). Judas calls him “Rabbi”, teacher, the title used by outsiders in Matthew. He has already sold him (v. 15), and asks the question with breathtaking hypocrisy.

He said to him, “You have said so.” A guarded “yes”: “Your words, not mine”, or “You said it.” Jesus will use the same phrase to the high priest (v. 64) and to Pilate (27:11). It is a quiet, unmistakable answer, probably not heard by the others (John 13:28–29).

In a sentence. Judas hypocritically asked if it was him, and Jesus quietly answered yes.

On a Tuesday. Jesus knows every heart. You cannot hide from him behind religious words.
verseByVerse.note: “You have said so” is a guarded yes.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and after blessing it broke it and gave it to the disciples, and said, "Take, eat; this is my body." And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he gave it to them, saying, "Drink of it, all of you,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they were eating, Jesus took bread, blessed it, broke it and gave it to the disciples, and said: take, eat; this is my body. And he took a cup, gave thanks and gave it to them, saying: drink of it, all of you.

Now as they were eating, Jesus took bread. The unleavened bread of the Passover. At the meal, the head of the household broke the bread and explained: this is the bread of affliction that our fathers ate in Egypt (Deuteronomy 16:3).

And after blessing it broke it and gave it to the disciples. The same actions as at the feedings (14:19; 15:36): took, blessed, broke, gave.

And said, “Take, eat; this is my body.” Jesus gives the bread a new meaning. It represents his body, which will be broken in death for them. Luke and Paul add: which is given for you; do this in remembrance of me (Luke 22:19; 1 Corinthians 11:24). The broken bread pictures his body broken on the cross, and eating it pictures receiving him and his benefits by faith.

And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks. Probably the third cup of the Passover meal, the “cup of blessing” (1 Corinthians 10:16), after the meal. “Given thanks” is eucharistēsas, from which comes “Eucharist”.

He gave it to them, saying, “Drink of it, all of you.” All of them, every disciple. (The medieval church withheld the cup from lay people; the Reformers restored it, on the basis of this verse.)

The Lord’s Supper. Jesus here institutes what the church calls the Lord’s Supper, Communion or the Eucharist, to be repeated until he returns (1 Corinthians 11:23–26).

Where Christians differ: “This is my body.” What does “is” mean? Four main views:

1. Transubstantiation (Roman Catholic). The bread and wine are changed in substance into Christ’s actual body and blood, while keeping their appearance.

2. Real presence (Lutheran). Christ’s body and blood are truly present “in, with and under” the bread and wine, which remain bread and wine.

3. Memorial (Zwinglian). The bread and wine are symbols that remind us of Christ’s death.

4. Spiritual presence (Calvin and the Reformed). The bread and wine remain bread and wine, and Christ’s body is in heaven, but by the Holy Spirit believers truly feed on Christ, spiritually and by faith, receiving his life and benefits. The sign and the thing signified are united in the Spirit’s work.

Verdict: the spiritual presence of Christ, as Calvin taught (Westminster Confession 29.7). Jesus was physically present, holding the bread, when he said “This is my body”; the disciples would not have thought they were eating his literal flesh. He often spoke in pictures (“I am the door”, John 10:9). But the Supper is not a bare symbol. Christ truly meets his people there, and feeds them by faith (1 Corinthians 10:16).

In a sentence. At the Passover, Jesus gave his disciples bread as his body and the cup to all of them, instituting the Lord’s Supper.

On a Tuesday. When you next take the Lord’s Supper, come expecting to meet Christ, and to be fed by faith.
verseByVerse.note: At the Passover meal the head of the household explained the bread and cups; Jesus gives them a new meaning.

verseByVerse.quote: "for this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins. I tell you I will not drink again of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father's kingdom."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins. I tell you, I will not drink again of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father’s kingdom.

For this is my blood of the covenant. At Mount Sinai, Moses sprinkled the blood of sacrifices on the people and said, Behold the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you (Exodus 24:8). Covenants were sealed with blood. Jesus’ blood seals a new covenant between God and his people.

Which is poured out. As the blood of sacrifices was poured out at the altar (Leviticus 4:7, 18). Jesus’ death is a sacrifice.

For many. Echoing Isaiah 53:12: he poured out his soul to death and bore the sin of many (see 20:28).

For the forgiveness of sins. Only Matthew includes these words. The new covenant promised by Jeremiah: I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more (Jeremiah 31:31–34). This is why Jesus came: to save his people from their sins (1:21). His blood is the price of their forgiveness (Hebrews 9:22; Ephesians 1:7).

Textual note. Some manuscripts add “new” before “covenant”, probably from Luke 22:20 and 1 Corinthians 11:25. Verdict: not original in Matthew, but the meaning is the same: this is the new covenant Jeremiah promised.

I tell you I will not drink again of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father’s kingdom. “Fruit of the vine” was the phrase used in the Jewish blessing over wine. Jesus looks beyond his death to the messianic banquet, when he will eat and drink with his people again in the fully come kingdom (8:11; Revelation 19:9). The Lord’s Supper looks back to the cross and forward to the feast (1 Corinthians 11:26).

In a sentence. The cup is Jesus’ blood of the covenant, poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins, and he will drink it again with them in the coming kingdom.

On a Tuesday. Your sins are forgiven because Christ’s blood was poured out. Believe it, and live in its freedom.

For worship. Thank Jesus for his blood, poured out for the forgiveness of your sins.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts insert “new” before “covenant.”

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives. Then Jesus said to them, "You will all fall away because of me this night, for it is written, 'I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives. Then Jesus told them: you will all fall away because of me this night. For it is written: I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.

And when they had sung a hymn. The Passover ended with the second half of the Hallel psalms (Psalms 115–118). Psalm 118 includes the words: the stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this is the day that the LORD has made. Jesus sang these words on the way to his death.

They went out to the Mount of Olives. Across the Kidron Valley, east of the city (21:1).

You will all fall away because of me this night. “Fall away” (skandalisthēsesthe) means stumble, desert. Not one would stand with him.

For it is written, “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.” Zechariah 13:7. In Zechariah, God himself strikes his shepherd. Jesus is the shepherd struck by God, bearing God’s judgment, and the disciples will scatter.

In a sentence. After singing the Passover psalms, Jesus told his disciples they would all desert him that night, as Zechariah foretold.

On a Tuesday. Jesus knew his friends would fail him, and loved them anyway. He knows your failures too.
verseByVerse.note: The hymn was probably from the Hallel psalms (Pss 113–118), sung at Passover.

parallels.desc: you will be scattered, each to his own home
strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered

verseByVerse.quote: "But after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee." Peter answered him, "Though they all fall away because of you, I will never fall away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee. Peter answered: though they all fall away because of you, I will never fall away.

But after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee. Even as he predicts their desertion, Jesus promises restoration. Like a shepherd going ahead of his sheep, he will regather them in Galilee (28:7, 10, 16). The scattering is not the end.

Peter answered him, “Though they all fall away because of you, I will never fall away.” Peter’s confidence: even if everyone else fails, I won’t. He compares himself with others and thinks himself stronger. Pride goes before a fall (Proverbs 16:18).

In a sentence. Jesus promised to meet them in Galilee after his resurrection, and Peter boasted he would never fall away.

On a Tuesday. Beware of thinking you are stronger than others. Rely on Christ’s strength, not your own.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to him, "Truly, I tell you, this very night, before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times." Peter said to him, "Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you!" And all the disciples said the same.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to him: truly, this very night, before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times. Peter said: even if I must die with you, I will not deny you. And all the disciples said the same.

Truly, I tell you, this very night, before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times. Very specific: tonight, before dawn, three times. “Rooster crows” may refer to an actual rooster, or to the Roman military trumpet signal at the end of the third watch (3 a.m.), called “cockcrow”.

Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you! Peter meant it. He did draw a sword and was willing to fight (v. 51; John 18:10). But he did not know his own heart.

And all the disciples said the same. All of them promised loyalty. All of them fled (v. 56).

In a sentence. Jesus foretold that Peter would deny him three times before dawn, but Peter and all the disciples insisted they would die rather than deny him.

On a Tuesday. Sincere promises are not the same as strength. Ask God for grace to keep your commitments.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus went with them to a place called Gethsemane, and he said to his disciples, "Sit here, while I go over there and pray." And taking with him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, he began to be sorrowful and troubled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Jesus went with them to a place called Gethsemane, and told his disciples: sit here while I go over there and pray. He took Peter and the two sons of Zebedee with him, and began to be sorrowful and troubled.

Then Jesus went with them to a place called Gethsemane. “Gethsemane” means “oil press”. It was an olive grove on the lower slope of the Mount of Olives, perhaps with an olive press. John calls it a garden where Jesus often met with his disciples (John 18:1–2). Some ancient olive trees still grow there.

Sit here, while I go over there and pray. In his hour of greatest need, Jesus prays.

And taking with him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee. James and John: the inner circle, who had seen his glory on the mountain (17:1). Now they would see his agony. James and John had said they could drink his cup (20:22); Peter had sworn loyalty.

He began to be sorrowful and troubled. “Troubled” (adēmonein) means deeply distressed, anguished, in turmoil. Jesus experienced real human emotion: dread, grief, horror. He was not a calm philosopher facing death, like Socrates. He faced something far worse than death.

In a sentence. In the olive grove of Gethsemane, Jesus took his three closest disciples aside and began to be overwhelmed with grief and distress.

On a Tuesday. Jesus knew deep distress. When you are overwhelmed, you have a Saviour who understands (Hebrews 4:15).
verseByVerse.note: Gethsemane (the name means “oil press”) was an olive grove on the lower slope of the Mount of Olives, across the Kidron Valley.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to them, "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death; remain here, and watch with me." And going a little farther he fell on his face and prayed, saying, "My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to them: my soul is very sorrowful, even to death. Stay here and watch with me. And going a little farther, he fell on his face and prayed: my Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.

My soul is very sorrowful, even to death. Echoing Psalms 42:5 and 43:5: why are you cast down, O my soul? “Even to death”: grief so heavy it could kill. Luke says his sweat became like great drops of blood (Luke 22:44).

Remain here, and watch with me. “Watch” means stay awake (24:42). Jesus wanted his friends near. He was truly human, longing for companionship in his suffering.

And going a little farther he fell on his face. Prostrate on the ground, a posture of extreme anguish and humility.

My Father. Even in agony, Jesus addresses God as “Father” (Mark: Abba, Mark 14:36).

If it be possible, let this cup pass from me. The “cup” in the Old Testament is the cup of God’s wrath against sin (Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15). What Jesus dreaded was not merely physical pain or death, terrible as crucifixion was. It was bearing the full weight of God’s judgment on the sins of his people: being made sin for us (2 Corinthians 5:21), becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), and being forsaken by his Father (27:46). The holy Son, who had known only the Father’s love, was about to experience God’s wrath. That is why he trembled.

Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will. Perfect submission. Jesus had a true human will, which naturally shrank from such suffering. He submitted it entirely to his Father’s will. Where Adam, in a garden, said “my will”, Jesus, in a garden, said “your will”. This is the obedience that saves us (Romans 5:19; Hebrews 5:7–9).

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus was reluctant to save us, or that he and the Father were in conflict. He came to do the Father’s will (John 6:38), and willingly laid down his life (John 10:18). His prayer shows the real cost of our salvation, and his real humanity. Nor was it weak faith. It was the honest prayer of a human heart, perfectly submitted. Christians may pray honestly about their fears, as long as they also pray “your will be done” (6:10).

In a sentence. In overwhelming grief, Jesus asked the Father to remove the cup of God’s wrath if possible, yet submitted fully to his will.

On a Tuesday. You may tell God honestly what you fear and what you want. Then pray with Jesus: not my will, but yours.

For worship. Thank Jesus for drinking the cup of wrath so that you never will.
verseByVerse.note: The “cup” is the Old Testament picture of God’s judgment poured out.

parallels.desc: why are you cast down, O my soul?

verseByVerse.quote: And he came to the disciples and found them sleeping. And he said to Peter, "So, could you not watch with me one hour? Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He came back to the disciples and found them sleeping. He said to Peter: so, could you not watch with me one hour? Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.

And he came to the disciples and found them sleeping. It was late, after a large meal and wine, and Luke says they were sleeping for sorrow (Luke 22:45). Exhausted by grief.

And he said to Peter, “So, could you not watch with me one hour?” Addressed to Peter, who had promised to die with him (v. 35). “You” is plural: all three.

Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The temptation that was coming: to desert him, to deny him. The only protection was watchfulness and prayer (6:13). Jesus prayed and stood firm; the disciples slept and fell.

The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak. Jesus understands. Their spirit, their sincere intention, was willing; they really wanted to be faithful. But the flesh, human weakness, was not able. Good intentions are not enough without God’s strength, sought in prayer.

What it does not mean. Not that the body is evil and the spirit good. “Flesh” here means human weakness in general.

In a sentence. Finding the disciples asleep, Jesus urged them to watch and pray against temptation, because the willing spirit is held back by weak flesh.

On a Tuesday. Where are you relying on good intentions without praying for strength? Pray today about the temptation you know is coming.

verseByVerse.quote: Again, for the second time, he went away and prayed, "My Father, if this cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done." And again he came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were heavy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A second time he went away and prayed: my Father, if this cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done. And again he came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were heavy.

Again, for the second time, he went away and prayed. Persistent prayer.

My Father, if this cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done. His prayer moves forward. The first time: if possible, let it pass. Now: if it cannot pass unless I drink it. He accepts that there is no other way to save his people. “Your will be done”: the words of the Lord’s Prayer (6:10), prayed in agony.

And again he came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were heavy. Again they failed. Jesus faced the cup alone.

In a sentence. Praying a second time, Jesus accepted that the cup could not pass unless he drank it, and found the disciples asleep again.

On a Tuesday. Prayer can change our hearts even when it does not change our circumstances. Keep praying until you can say “your will be done”.

verseByVerse.quote: So, leaving them again, he went away and prayed for the third time, saying the same words again. Then he came to the disciples and said to them, "Sleep and take your rest later on. See, the hour is at hand, and the Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Leaving them again, he went away and prayed a third time, saying the same words. Then he came to the disciples and said: are you still sleeping and resting? See, the hour is at hand, and the Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners.

So, leaving them again, he went away and prayed for the third time, saying the same words again. Three times, like Paul praying three times about his thorn (2 Corinthians 12:8). Repetition is not empty when it is earnest (6:7).

Sleep and take your rest later on. Or “Are you still sleeping and resting?” (ESV text). Either way, the time for watching is over.

See, the hour is at hand. The hour of his betrayal and death (John 12:23, 27; 17:1).

And the Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. The holy one delivered to the unholy. Jesus has come through his agony and is ready. He goes to meet his betrayer with calm resolve.

In a sentence. After praying the same prayer a third time, Jesus told the sleeping disciples that his hour had come.

On a Tuesday. Prayer prepared Jesus for his hour. Prayer prepares you for yours.

verseByVerse.quote: "Rise, let us be going; see, my betrayer is at hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rise, let us be going. See, my betrayer is at hand.

Rise, let us be going. Jesus does not flee. He goes forward to meet his enemies. He could have escaped over the Mount of Olives into the desert. Instead he walks toward the cross.

See, my betrayer is at hand. Judas and the crowd are approaching, with torches and lanterns visible in the dark (John 18:3).

In a sentence. Jesus rose to meet his betrayer, who was already approaching.

On a Tuesday. Jesus walked toward what he dreaded, for you. Ask for courage to walk toward the hard thing God has called you to.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 47–75 — The Arrest, the Trial before the High Priest, and Peter's Denial
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judas arrives with an armed crowd and identifies Jesus with a kiss; a disciple draws a sword and is told to sheathe it; every one of the eleven runs. Jesus is taken to the high priest's house, where a court that cannot assemble two agreeing witnesses finally convicts him out of his own mouth when Caiaphas puts him on oath. He is condemned, spat at and blindfolded and struck. Outside in the same courtyard, warming himself at the fire, Peter is asked three times whether he knows him, and says no three times, and hears a rooster.
verseByVerse.theology: Two men are on trial in this section and Matthew cuts between them deliberately. Inside, under oath, with his life at stake, Jesus tells the truth about who he is; outside, with nothing at stake but embarrassment, Peter lies about knowing him. The confession that condemns Jesus uses the same two titles as Peter's own confession at Caesarea Philippi (16:16), which is why the pairing is so pointed. And the answer Jesus gives is the most exalted claim ever made in a courtroom: Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13 combined, so that the prisoner tells the court the seating will be reversed at the next hearing, beginning from now on. Caiaphas understood him exactly, which disposes of the notion that the claim to deity was a later invention of the church: the one man in the room with every professional reason to find a smaller meaning heard it instantly and called it blasphemy.
verseByVerse.examples: The phrase to carry away is following at a distance (v. 58). Peter has more courage than the ten who ran — he is the only one who follows at all — and it is the distance, not the flight, that undoes him: far enough in to be recognised, far enough back to want not to be. The ten were never asked, because they were not there. Note too where the ground is actually slippery. Peter had prepared, sincerely, to die; he had not prepared for a servant girl by a fire, and the accuser with no authority to arrest anybody is the one who brings him down. Most denials of Christ happen exactly there — in the staff room, at the family table, where a laugh is available and the cost of being counted in suddenly seems out of proportion to the occasion. And the escalation is the signature of a lie under pressure: evasion, then an oath, then a self-curse, each answer defending the one before it rather than defending anything worth defending.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was still speaking, Judas came, one of the twelve, and with him a great crowd with swords and clubs, from the chief priests and the elders of the people. Now the betrayer had given them a sign, saying, "The one I will kiss is the man; seize him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
While he was still speaking, Judas, one of the twelve, came, and with him a great crowd with swords and clubs, from the chief priests and elders. The betrayer had given them a sign: the one I kiss is the man; seize him.

While he was still speaking, Judas came, one of the twelve. Matthew repeats “one of the twelve” (vv. 14, 47) to stress the horror.

And with him a great crowd with swords and clubs. Temple police armed with clubs, and, according to John, a detachment of Roman soldiers (John 18:3, 12). A large force for one unarmed teacher and eleven frightened men: a sign of how much they feared him.

From the chief priests and the elders of the people. Official authority.

Now the betrayer had given them a sign, saying, “The one I will kiss is the man; seize him.” In the dark, the soldiers might not recognise Jesus or might seize the wrong man. A kiss was the normal greeting of a disciple to his teacher, on the cheek or hand. Judas turned the sign of love and respect into the sign of betrayal.

In a sentence. Judas arrived with an armed crowd sent by the leaders, having arranged to identify Jesus with a kiss.

On a Tuesday. Outward signs of love can hide betrayal. Let your love be genuine (Romans 12:9).
verseByVerse.note: A kiss was the normal greeting of a disciple to his teacher.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came up to Jesus at once and said, "Greetings, Rabbi!" And he kissed him. Jesus said to him, "Friend, do what you came to do." Then they came up and laid hands on Jesus and seized him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judas went straight up to Jesus and said: greetings, Rabbi! And he kissed him. Jesus said: friend, do what you came to do. Then they came up, laid hands on Jesus and seized him.

And he came up to Jesus at once and said, “Greetings, Rabbi!” “Greetings” (chaire), literally “rejoice”, an ordinary greeting. “Rabbi”: as in verse 25, not “Lord”.

And he kissed him. The word suggests an emphatic, lingering kiss, perhaps to make sure the soldiers saw. Proverbs 27:6: faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy. Luke records Jesus’ question: Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss? (Luke 22:48).

Jesus said to him, “Friend, do what you came to do.” “Friend” (hetaire), a cool, distant address (20:13; 22:12). Even now, Jesus does not curse Judas. He is in control. He tells Judas to get on with it.

Then they came up and laid hands on Jesus and seized him. The arrest. Jesus allowed it.

In a sentence. Judas betrayed Jesus with a kiss, and Jesus calmly told him to do what he came for, and was arrested.

On a Tuesday. Jesus was betrayed by a friend. If you have been betrayed, he understands. Bring your hurt to him.

parallels.desc: profuse are the kisses of an enemy

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, one of those who were with Jesus stretched out his hand and drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his ear. Then Jesus said to him, "Put your sword back into its place. For all who take the sword will perish by the sword."
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of those with Jesus drew his sword, struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his ear. Jesus said to him: put your sword back in its place, for all who take the sword will perish by the sword.

And behold, one of those who were with Jesus stretched out his hand and drew his sword. John names him: Simon Peter (John 18:10). Peter carried a sword (Luke 22:38), and he kept his promise to fight (v. 35). It was the wrong kind of loyalty.

And struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his ear. John names the servant: Malchus (John 18:10). Luke, a doctor, adds that Jesus touched his ear and healed him (Luke 22:51): Jesus’ last miracle before the cross was healing an enemy.

Put your sword back into its place. Jesus stops the violence.

For all who take the sword will perish by the sword. Violence leads to more violence. Jesus’ kingdom does not advance by the sword (John 18:36). Those who take up arms against him would perish (the Zealots who fought Rome were destroyed in AD 70).

What it does not mean. Not that all use of force is forbidden in every situation. Governments bear the sword for justice (Romans 13:4). Jesus is speaking of defending him and advancing his kingdom by violence (see 5:38–42). The gospel never spreads by the sword.

In a sentence. When Peter struck the high priest’s servant with a sword, Jesus told him to put it away, for violence breeds violence.

On a Tuesday. Are you tempted to defend Christ or your faith with aggression, anger or force? That is not his way.
verseByVerse.note: John names the swordsman as Peter and the servant as Malchus; Luke adds that Jesus healed the ear.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do you think that I cannot appeal to my Father, and he will at once send me more than twelve legions of angels? But how then should the Scriptures be fulfilled, that it must be so?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you think I cannot appeal to my Father, and he will at once send me more than twelve legions of angels? But how then would the Scriptures be fulfilled, that it must happen in this way?

Do you think that I cannot appeal to my Father. Jesus is not helpless. He chooses not to resist.

And he will at once send me more than twelve legions of angels? A Roman legion had about six thousand soldiers. Twelve legions: perhaps one for each disciple, and one for himself. Some seventy-two thousand angels. One angel killed 185,000 Assyrian soldiers in one night (2 Kings 19:35). Jesus could have been rescued in an instant. He refused, as he refused the devil’s temptation to call on angels (4:6–7).

But how then should the Scriptures be fulfilled, that it must be so? “Must”: God’s plan, revealed in Scripture, required Jesus’ suffering and death (16:21; Luke 24:25–27, 44–46). He submits to God’s word.

In a sentence. Jesus could have called on armies of angels, but chose to suffer so that the Scriptures would be fulfilled.

On a Tuesday. Jesus was not a victim. He chose the cross for you. Let that reshape how you see his love.
verseByVerse.note: A Roman legion numbered several thousand soldiers.

parallels.desc: my servants would have been fighting

verseByVerse.quote: At that hour Jesus said to the crowds, "Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs to capture me? Day after day I sat in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me. But all this has taken place that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled." Then all the disciples left him and fled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At that hour Jesus said to the crowds: have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs to capture me? Day after day I sat in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me. But all this has taken place so that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled. Then all the disciples left him and fled.

Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs to capture me? “Robber” (lēstēs) could mean a bandit or an armed revolutionary. They were treating him like a dangerous criminal.

Day after day I sat in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me. He had taught openly all week. Their secret arrest at night exposed their fear and their bad conscience.

But all this has taken place that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled. Isaiah 53:12: he was numbered with the transgressors. And Zechariah 13:7: strike the shepherd.

Then all the disciples left him and fled. Exactly as he had said (v. 31). All of them, including Peter, who had sworn he would never fall away. Mark records a young man who fled naked (Mark 14:51–52). Jesus was utterly alone.

In a sentence. Jesus exposed the cowardice of his night-time arrest and declared that Scripture was being fulfilled, and all his disciples fled.

On a Tuesday. Jesus was abandoned by all his friends, so that you would never be abandoned by God (Hebrews 13:5).

parallels.desc: the young man who fled naked

verseByVerse.quote: Then those who had seized Jesus led him to Caiaphas the high priest, where the scribes and the elders had gathered. And Peter was following him at a distance, as far as the courtyard of the high priest, and going inside he sat with the guards to see the end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who had seized Jesus led him to Caiaphas the high priest, where the scribes and the elders had gathered. And Peter was following him at a distance, as far as the courtyard of the high priest, and going inside he sat with the guards to see the end.

Then those who had seized Jesus led him to Caiaphas the high priest. John records a preliminary hearing before Annas, Caiaphas’ father-in-law (John 18:13, 19–24). Then Jesus was taken to Caiaphas.

Where the scribes and the elders had gathered. Members of the Sanhedrin, called together in the middle of the night. Jewish law later recorded in the Mishnah required capital trials to be held in daytime, not on a festival or its eve, with a day’s delay before a guilty verdict. The trial broke many of these rules (if they applied then), showing its unjust haste.

And Peter was following him at a distance. Peter had fled, but came back. His love brought him; his fear kept him at a distance. Following Jesus at a distance is dangerous.

As far as the courtyard of the high priest. An open courtyard surrounded by the rooms of the palace.

And going inside he sat with the guards to see the end. He sat among Jesus’ enemies, trying to blend in. He wanted to see what would happen, but not to be identified with Jesus.

In a sentence. Jesus was taken to Caiaphas, where the council had gathered, and Peter followed at a distance into the courtyard.

On a Tuesday. Are you following Jesus at a distance: close enough to watch, far enough to avoid the cost?
verseByVerse.note: John records a first hearing before Annas.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the chief priests and the whole council were seeking false testimony against Jesus that they might put him to death, but they found none, though many false witnesses came forward. At last two came forward
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chief priests and the whole council were looking for false testimony against Jesus so that they could put him to death, but they found none, though many false witnesses came forward. At last two came forward.

Now the chief priests and the whole Council. The Sanhedrin, the supreme Jewish council of seventy-one members: chief priests, elders and scribes, presided over by the high priest. Under Roman rule, it had authority over Jewish religious matters, but not to carry out executions (John 18:31).

Were seeking false testimony against Jesus that they might put him to death. They had already decided the verdict. They were looking for evidence to justify it. Not a trial, but a show.

But they found none, though many false witnesses came forward. Mark says their testimony did not agree (Mark 14:56). Under the law, two or three witnesses had to agree (Deuteronomy 19:15). False witnesses were to suffer the penalty they tried to bring on another (Deuteronomy 19:16–19).

At last two came forward. The minimum required by law.

In a sentence. The council sought false testimony to condemn Jesus, but could find none that agreed, until at last two witnesses came.

On a Tuesday. Jesus was falsely accused. If you are slandered, he understands, and he will vindicate you.
verseByVerse.note: The council is the Sanhedrin, the ruling body of about seventy elders, chief priests and scribes. The law required two agreeing witnesses.

parallels.desc: false witnesses have risen against me

verseByVerse.quote: and said, "This man said, 'I am able to destroy the temple of God, and to rebuild it in three days.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They said: this man said, I am able to destroy the temple of God and to rebuild it in three days.

This man said, “I am able to destroy the temple of God, and to rebuild it in three days.” A distortion of what Jesus had said. Early in his ministry, he said: destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up (John 2:19). John explains that he was speaking about the temple of his body, which they would destroy and he would raise (John 2:21). They twisted it into a threat to destroy the temple himself. Threatening the temple was a serious charge. The irony: in killing Jesus, they would destroy the true temple, and in three days he would rise, fulfilling his words exactly.

In a sentence. The witnesses twisted Jesus’ words about the temple of his body into a threat against the temple.

On a Tuesday. Jesus’ enemies quoted his words and twisted them. Make sure you understand his words in context.

parallels.desc: “Destroy this temple” — the temple of his body

verseByVerse.quote: And the high priest stood up and said, "Have you no answer to make? What is it that these men testify against you?" But Jesus remained silent. And the high priest said to him, "I adjure you by the living God, tell us if you are the Christ, the Son of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The high priest stood up and said: have you no answer to make? What is this these men testify against you? But Jesus remained silent. The high priest said: I put you under oath by the living God, tell us if you are the Christ, the Son of God.

And the high priest stood up and said, “Have you no answer to make?” He wanted Jesus to defend himself, perhaps hoping he would say something incriminating.

But Jesus remained silent. Isaiah 53:7: like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth. Jesus did not defend himself against false charges. He did not need to. His silence was dignified, and fulfilled Scripture (1 Peter 2:23).

I adjure you by the living God. “Adjure” means put under oath. An oath by the living God legally obliged the person to answer truthfully (Leviticus 5:1).

Tell us if you are the Christ, the Son of God. The real question. If Jesus claimed to be the Messiah and the Son of God, they could charge him with blasphemy.

In a sentence. Jesus stayed silent before false accusations, until the high priest put him under oath to say whether he was the Christ, the Son of God.

On a Tuesday. Jesus was silent before false accusers. Sometimes the wisest response to slander is silence.
verseByVerse.note: An oath “by the living God” obliged the one questioned to answer.

parallels.desc: like a sheep that before its shearers is silent

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to him, "You have said so. But I tell you, from now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven." Then the high priest tore his robes and said, "He has uttered blasphemy. What further witnesses do we need? You have now heard his blasphemy."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said: you have said so. But I tell you, from now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven. Then the high priest tore his robes and said: he has uttered blasphemy. What further witnesses do we need? You have now heard his blasphemy.

You have said so. Yes (see v. 25). Mark records: I am (Mark 14:62). Under oath, Jesus openly confesses that he is the Christ, the Son of God.

But I tell you, from now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power. Psalm 110:1 (22:44). “Power” was a reverent way of saying “God”. Jesus claims that he will sit at God’s right hand: not merely be honoured, but share God’s throne.

And coming on the clouds of heaven. Daniel 7:13–14 (see 24:30). The Son of Man comes to the Ancient of Days and receives everlasting dominion. “From now on”: from his death and resurrection onward, they would see the evidence of his enthronement: in his resurrection, the outpouring of the Spirit, the spread of the church, and the fall of Jerusalem. And he will come in glory as Judge. The prisoner on trial declares that he will be their Judge.

Then the high priest tore his robes. Tearing one’s clothes was a sign of grief or horror (2 Kings 18:37). The law forbade the high priest to tear his priestly garments (Leviticus 21:10), but later rabbinic tradition required judges to tear their clothes on hearing blasphemy.

He has uttered blasphemy. For a man to claim to sit at God’s right hand and to come as the divine Son of Man was, if false, the worst blasphemy. And it was true.

What further witnesses do we need? You have now heard his blasphemy. They no longer need false witnesses. Jesus’ own words condemn him, in their eyes.

In a sentence. Under oath, Jesus confessed he was the Christ and declared he would sit at God’s right hand and come on the clouds, and the high priest called it blasphemy.

On a Tuesday. Jesus was condemned for telling the truth about who he is. Do you believe it?

For worship. Worship the Son of Man, seated at the right hand of Power.
verseByVerse.note: Tearing one’s robes was a sign of horror or grief; the high priest does it at what he hears as blasphemy.

verseByVerse.quote: "What is your judgment?" They answered, "He deserves death."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What is your judgment? They answered: he deserves death.

What is your judgment? The high priest asks the council for its verdict.

They answered, “He deserves death.” The penalty for blasphemy under the law was death by stoning (Leviticus 24:16). Mark says they all condemned him (Mark 14:64). (Joseph of Arimathea, a council member, did not agree, Luke 23:51, so perhaps he was absent.) But they could not carry out the sentence themselves; they needed Rome (27:1–2).

The great exchange. “He deserves death.” They were wrong about Jesus: he was innocent. But they spoke a truth about us. We deserve death for our sins (Romans 6:23). Jesus, who did not deserve it, took the death we deserved (1 Peter 3:18).

In a sentence. The council declared that Jesus deserved death.

On a Tuesday. Jesus was condemned so that you would not be (Romans 8:1).

verseByVerse.quote: Then they spit in his face and struck him. And some slapped him, saying, "Prophesy to us, you Christ! Who is it that struck you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they spat in his face and struck him. Some slapped him, saying: prophesy to us, you Christ! Who is it that struck you?

Then they spit in his face and struck him. Spitting in someone’s face was the deepest insult (Numbers 12:14; Deuteronomy 25:9). Isaiah 50:6: I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting. The judges themselves joined in the abuse.

And some slapped him. Mark says they blindfolded him first (Mark 14:65).

Prophesy to us, you Christ! Who is it that struck you? Mocking his claim to be the Messiah and a prophet. A game: guess who hit you. The irony: at that very moment, his prophecy about Peter was being fulfilled in the courtyard below.

In a sentence. The council members spat on Jesus, beat him, and mocked his claim to be the Messiah and a prophet.

On a Tuesday. The Lord of glory endured spitting and mockery in silence, for you. How do you respond when you are mocked for him?

parallels.desc: I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting

verseByVerse.quote: Now Peter was sitting outside in the courtyard. And a servant girl came up to him and said, "You also were with Jesus the Galilean." But he denied it before them all, saying, "I do not know what you mean."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meanwhile Peter was sitting outside in the courtyard. A servant girl came up to him and said: you also were with Jesus the Galilean. But he denied it before them all: I do not know what you mean.

Now Peter was sitting outside in the courtyard. At the same time as Jesus was confessing the truth under oath inside, Peter was denying it outside.

And a servant girl came up to him. Not a soldier, not a priest, but a servant girl, someone with no power at all.

You also were with Jesus the Galilean. She recognised him, perhaps from the temple, or the light of the fire (Luke 22:56).

But he denied it before them all, saying, “I do not know what you mean.” The first denial: pretending not to understand. Evasion. The man who drew a sword against armed soldiers was afraid of a servant girl.

In a sentence. When a servant girl identified Peter as one of Jesus’ companions, he denied it in front of everyone.

On a Tuesday. Denial often begins with evasion: pretending not to know, changing the subject. Where are you evading?

verseByVerse.quote: And when he went out to the entrance, another servant girl saw him, and she said to the bystanders, "This man was with Jesus of Nazareth." And again he denied it with an oath: "I do not know the man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he went out to the entrance, another servant girl saw him and said to the bystanders: this man was with Jesus of Nazareth. And again he denied it with an oath: I do not know the man.

And when he went out to the entrance. Moving away, trying to escape attention.

Another servant girl saw him, and she said to the bystanders, “This man was with Jesus of Nazareth.” Now she tells others.

And again he denied it with an oath: “I do not know the man.” The second denial, stronger. Now he swears, calling God as witness to a lie (5:33–37). And he calls Jesus “the man”, not even using his name.

In a sentence. When another servant girl identified him, Peter denied Jesus with an oath, saying he did not know the man.

On a Tuesday. One compromise leads to another. Stop at the first.

verseByVerse.quote: After a little while the bystanders came up and said to Peter, "Certainly you too are one of them, for your accent betrays you." Then he began to invoke a curse on himself and to swear, "I do not know the man." And immediately the rooster crowed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After a little while the bystanders came up and said to Peter: certainly you are one of them, for your accent betrays you. Then he began to invoke a curse on himself and to swear: I do not know the man. And immediately the rooster crowed.

After a little while. Luke says about an hour (Luke 22:59).

Certainly you too are one of them, for your accent betrays you. Galileans had a distinctive accent, considered rough by Jerusalem people; they could not pronounce certain guttural sounds clearly. Peter’s speech gave him away. John adds that one of them was a relative of Malchus, who had seen Peter in the garden (John 18:26).

Then he began to invoke a curse on himself and to swear. The third denial, the strongest. He called down a curse on himself if he was lying (“May God strike me if I know him”), or perhaps cursed Jesus. And he swore an oath.

I do not know the man. The same words as before.

And immediately the rooster crowed. At the very moment, as Jesus had said (v. 34). Luke adds that the Lord turned and looked at Peter (Luke 22:61).

In a sentence. When bystanders identified him by his accent, Peter cursed and swore that he did not know Jesus, and immediately the rooster crowed.

On a Tuesday. Peter’s fall shows that anyone can fall. But his story does not end here. Neither does yours.
verseByVerse.note: Galileans spoke with a recognisable regional accent.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter remembered the saying of Jesus, "Before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times." And he went out and wept bitterly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter remembered the saying of Jesus: before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times. And he went out and wept bitterly.

And Peter remembered the saying of Jesus. The rooster’s crow brought Jesus’ words back to him.

Before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times. Exactly as Jesus said. Every detail.

And he went out and wept bitterly. Deep, broken grief: true repentance. Compare Judas, who also felt remorse (27:3–5), but went out and hanged himself. Peter’s sorrow led him back to Jesus; Judas’ sorrow led him to despair. Paul describes the difference: godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation, but worldly grief produces death (2 Corinthians 7:10). Jesus had prayed for Peter that his faith would not fail (Luke 22:31–32), and after the resurrection, he restored him three times, matching his three denials (John 21:15–19). Peter went on to preach at Pentecost and to die for Christ.

What it does not mean. Not that Peter lost his salvation when he denied Jesus. His faith faltered, but did not finally fail, because Jesus prayed for him. True believers can fall seriously, but God brings them back to repentance (Psalm 37:24).

In a sentence. Peter remembered Jesus’ words and went out and wept bitterly, in a repentance that would lead to his restoration.

On a Tuesday. If you have failed Christ badly, do not despair like Judas. Weep like Peter, and come back to Jesus. He restores.

For worship. Thank Jesus that he prays for his people and restores those who fall.

26.theology: The cup of wrath and substitutionary atonement. The cup that Jesus prays might pass in Gethsemane and then drinks on the cross is the Old Testament cup of divine wrath — the concentrated judgment of God against human sin. That he drinks it “for many” (26:28) and “for the forgiveness of sins” is Matthew’s clearest statement of penal substitutionary atonement: Christ in the place of sinners, bearing the penalty that was theirs, so that the forgiveness that is his might become theirs. This is the heart of the gospel — not merely that God loves us (though he does) or that Jesus shows us how to live (though he does) but that the holy God, in the person of his Son, absorbed the full penalty for human sin so that justice and mercy could be simultaneously satisfied at the cross.
26.examples:
Then: The disciples slept in Gethsemane while Jesus prayed. They could not watch one hour. Their failure is not recorded to condemn them but to reveal the bankruptcy of human resolve — and to show that the cross was accomplished not by the strength of the disciples but by the obedience of the Son, alone, in the dark, sustained only by the Father.

Now: Every celebration of the Lord’s Supper is a proclamation of Gethsemane and the cross. The bread and cup carry the weight of that night — the betrayal, the agony, the submission, the arrest, the trial. To eat and drink worthily (1 Cor 11:27–29) is to remember not merely a past event but the present ground of our standing before God: his blood, poured out for many, for the forgiveness of sins. That includes every sin we brought to the table today.

27.title: The Crucifixion of the King
27.text: <sup>1</sup>When morning came, all the chief priests and the elders of the people took counsel against Jesus to put him to death. <sup>2</sup>And they bound him and led him away and delivered him over to Pilate the governor. <sup>3</sup>Then when Judas, his betrayer, saw that Jesus was condemned, he changed his mind and brought back the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and the elders, <sup>4</sup>saying, “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood.” They said, “What is that to us? See to it yourself.” <sup>5</sup>And throwing down the pieces of silver into the temple, he departed, and he went and hanged himself. <sup>6</sup>But the chief priests, taking the pieces of silver, said, “It is not lawful to put them into the treasury, since it is blood money.” <sup>7</sup>So they took counsel and bought with them the potter’s field as a burial place for strangers. <sup>8</sup>Therefore that field has been called the Field of Blood to this day. <sup>9</sup>Then was fulfilled what had been spoken by the prophet Jeremiah, saying, “And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him on whom a price had been set by some of the sons of Israel, <sup>10</sup>and they gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord directed me.” <sup>11</sup>Now Jesus stood before the governor, and the governor asked him, “Are you the King of the Jews?” Jesus said, “You have said so.” <sup>12</sup>But when he was accused by the chief priests and elders, he gave no answer. <sup>13</sup>Then Pilate said to him, “Do you not hear how many things they testify against you?” <sup>14</sup>But he gave him no answer, not even to a single charge, so that the governor was greatly amazed. <sup>15</sup>Now at the feast the governor was accustomed to release for the crowd any one prisoner whom they wanted. <sup>16</sup>And they had then a notorious prisoner called Barabbas. <sup>17</sup>So when they had gathered, Pilate said to them, “Whom do you want me to release for you: Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?” <sup>18</sup>For he knew that it was out of envy that they had delivered him up. <sup>19</sup>Besides, while he was sitting on the judgment seat, his wife sent word to him, “Have nothing to do with that righteous man, for I have suffered much because of him today in a dream.” <sup>20</sup>Now the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowd to ask for Barabbas and destroy Jesus. <sup>21</sup>The governor again said to them, “Which of the two do you want me to release for you?” And they said, “Barabbas.” <sup>22</sup>Pilate said to them, “Then what shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ?” They all said, “Let him be crucified!” <sup>23</sup>And he said, “Why? What evil has he done?” But they shouted all the more, “Let him be crucified!” <sup>24</sup>So when Pilate saw that he was gaining nothing, but rather that a riot was beginning, he took water and washed his hands before the crowd, saying, “I am innocent of this man’s blood; see to it yourselves.” <sup>25</sup>And all the people answered, “His blood be on us and on our children!” <sup>26</sup>Then he released for them Barabbas, and having scourged Jesus, delivered him to be crucified. <sup>27</sup>Then the soldiers of the governor took Jesus into the governor’s headquarters, and they gathered the whole battalion before him. <sup>28</sup>And they stripped him and put a scarlet robe on him, <sup>29</sup>and twisting together a crown of thorns, they put it on his head and put a reed in his right hand. And kneeling before him, they mocked him, saying, “Hail, King of the Jews!” <sup>30</sup>And they spit on him and took the reed and struck him on the head. <sup>31</sup>And when they had mocked him, they stripped him of the robe and put his own clothes on him and led him away to crucify him. <sup>32</sup>As they went out, they found a man of Cyrene, Simon by name. They compelled this man to carry his cross. <sup>33</sup>And when they came to a place called Golgotha (which means Place of a Skull), <sup>34</sup>they offered him wine to drink, mixed with gall, but when he tasted it, he would not drink it. <sup>35</sup>And when they had crucified him, they divided his garments among them by casting lots. <sup>36</sup>Then they sat down and kept watch over him there. <sup>37</sup>And over his head they put the charge against him, which read, “This is Jesus, the King of the Jews.” <sup>38</sup>Then two robbers were crucified with him, one on the right and one on the left. <sup>39</sup>And those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads <sup>40</sup>and saying, “You who would destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, save yourself! If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross.” <sup>41</sup>So also the chief priests, with the scribes and elders, mocked him, saying, <sup>42</sup>“He saved others; he cannot save himself. He is the King of Israel; let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in him. <sup>43</sup>He trusts in God; let God deliver him now, if he desires him. For he said, ‘I am the Son of God.’” <sup>44</sup>And the robbers who were crucified with him also reviled him in the same way. <sup>45</sup>Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land until the ninth hour. <sup>46</sup>And about the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying, “Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?” that is, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” <sup>47</sup>And some of the bystanders, hearing it, said, “This man is calling Elijah.” <sup>48</sup>And one of them at once ran and took a sponge, filled it with sour wine, and put it on a reed and gave it to him to drink. <sup>49</sup>But the others said, “Wait, let us see whether Elijah will come to save him.” <sup>50</sup>And Jesus cried out again with a loud voice and yielded up his spirit. <sup>51</sup>And behold, the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom. And the earth shook, and the rocks were split. <sup>52</sup>The tombs also were opened. And many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised, <sup>53</sup>and coming out of the tombs after his resurrection they went into the holy city and appeared to many. <sup>54</sup>When the centurion and those who were with him, keeping watch over Jesus, saw the earthquake and what took place, they were filled with awe and said, “Truly this was the Son of God!” <sup>55</sup>There were also many women there, looking on from a distance, who had followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering to him, <sup>56</sup>among whom were Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of James and Joseph and the mother of the sons of Zebedee. <sup>57</sup>When it was evening, there came a rich man from Arimathea, named Joseph, who also was a disciple of Jesus. <sup>58</sup>He went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. Then Pilate ordered it to be given to him. <sup>59</sup>And Joseph took the body and wrapped it in a clean linen shroud <sup>60</sup>and laid it in his own new tomb, which he had cut in the rock. And he rolled a great stone to the entrance of the tomb and went away. <sup>61</sup>Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were there, sitting opposite the tomb. <sup>62</sup>The next day, that is, after the day of Preparation, the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered before Pilate <sup>63</sup>and said, “Sir, we remember how that impostor said, while he was still alive, ‘After three days I will rise.’ <sup>64</sup>Therefore order the tomb to be made secure until the third day, lest his disciples go and steal him away and tell the people, ‘He has risen from the dead,’ and the last fraud will be worse than the first.” <sup>65</sup>Pilate said to them, “You have a guard of soldiers. Go, make it as secure as you can.” <sup>66</sup>So they went and made the tomb secure by sealing the stone and setting a guard.
27.overview:
Chapter 27 is the centre of the universe. Everything in the Old Testament moves toward it; everything in the New Testament moves from it. The crucifixion of Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews, is the event by which God reconciles a broken world to himself. Matthew narrates it with restraint — he does not linger on the physical agony of crucifixion — but saturates every scene with Old Testament allusion: Psalm 22 (the cry of dereliction, the dividing of garments, the mocking); Zechariah 11 (thirty pieces of silver); Isaiah 53 (numbered with transgressors, interceding for sinners).

The theological climax comes in three simultaneous signs at the moment of death: the tearing of the temple veil, the earthquake and split rocks, and the opening of tombs. The veil torn from top to bottom is God’s own act: the barrier between the holy and the profane is removed. The way into the presence of God is now open to all who come through the crucified King. The centurion’s confession — “Truly this man was the Son of God!” — is the Gentile answer to the question Jesus asked in chapter 16: spoken at the foot of the cross, by a soldier, at the moment of death.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–44 — The Trial before Pilate and the Crucifixion
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The council reconvenes at dawn to give the night's verdict a legal form, then takes Jesus to Pilate, because they may condemn but may not execute. Judas returns the silver, is told to see to it himself, and hangs himself; the money buys a burial field for foreigners. Before Pilate the charge is quietly rewritten from blasphemy to kingship. Pilate tries the Passover custom, is warned by his wife, finds no fault, washes his hands, and condemns him anyway. Barabbas goes free. Jesus is scourged, mocked by the cohort, crowned with thorns, and led out to Golgotha, where he is crucified between two brigands and jeered at by passers-by, priests and the dying.
verseByVerse.theology: Substitution is not imposed on this section by later theology; it is the shape of the narrative. One cross and two candidates: a guilty insurrectionist walks free for exactly one reason, which is that the innocent man took his place, and Matthew records both in a single verse (v. 26). The mockery carries the same doctrine inside out. He saved others; he cannot save himself is true in every word and false in every intention: not a failure of power, but a necessity built into substitution, since a substitute who steps out from under the weight has stopped being one. He could have saved himself or saved them. There was never an afternoon in which he did both.
verseByVerse.examples: Pilate is the study in this section, and he is a modern figure. Nobody in the chapter sees more clearly: he is amazed at the prisoner, warned by his wife, told by his own judgement that the charge is driven by envy, and asks what evil he has done and declares himself innocent of his blood. And nobody does less with what he sees. He never once considers simply doing what a judge is for; he looks instead for a procedure that will produce justice at no personal cost — the crowd, the custom, the basin — and when no such route exists he chooses the cost he can bear and lets the innocent man pay the other. Admiration is not allegiance. Pilate was impressed by Jesus in the early morning and signed his death warrant before it was out.

verseByVerse.quote: When morning came, all the chief priests and the elders of the people took counsel against Jesus to put him to death. And they bound him and led him away and delivered him over to Pilate the governor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When morning came. They reconvene at first light, and the reason is procedural. Everything done in Caiaphas's house during the night was irregular by their own rules, so a second session is held in daylight to give the verdict a form that will stand. It changes nothing; the decision was taken hours ago. This is paperwork.

Then a detail that explains the whole rest of the chapter: they take him to Pilate. Under Roman administration the Sanhedrin retained wide powers but had lost the right of capital punishment — it is not lawful for us to put anyone to death, as they tell Pilate in John's account (Jn 18:31). They can condemn; they cannot execute. Which means that to kill him they must persuade a Gentile governor, and to persuade a Gentile governor the charge must change. Blasphemy is nothing to Rome. Kingship is everything to Rome. Watch how the accusation is quietly reworded between this verse and verse 11.

And notice the verb once more: they delivered him over — paradidomi, for perhaps the tenth time since chapter 26. Judas delivered him to the priests; the priests deliver him to Pilate; Pilate will deliver him to be crucified. Every party in the story is handing him on to somebody else, and each hand-off is a small act of evasion — nobody wants to be the one holding him at the end.

Under all of it Paul puts the sentence that reaches behind every human hand in the chain: he who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Rom 8:32) — and the verb Paul uses is the same one. The passing of the parcel that looks like a series of men avoiding responsibility is, at another level, the Father handing over the Son, on purpose, for us.

One more word: they bound him. He had spent three years loosing people — a bent-over woman loosed from her infirmity, a dead man loosed from his grave clothes, sinners loosed from their debts. The last thing done to him before the Gentiles take him is that his hands are tied.
verseByVerse.note: The Jewish leaders could not carry out a death sentence under Roman rule. Pontius Pilate was the Roman governor of Judea from AD 26 to 36.

parallels.desc: not lawful for us to put anyone to death

verseByVerse.quote: Then when Judas, his betrayer, saw that Jesus was condemned, he changed his mind and brought back the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and the elders, saying, "I have sinned by betraying innocent blood." They said, "What is that to us? See to it yourself."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The trigger is precise: when Judas, his betrayer, saw that Jesus was condemned. Something he had not expected has happened, and the most likely reading is the plainest one — he had not thought it would go this far. Perhaps he assumed the council would humiliate Jesus and release him, or that Jesus would finally act and force the confrontation everyone had been waiting for. The verdict lands and the thing becomes real.

Matthew's verb is metamelomai — he was sorry, he regretted it. It is not the word this Gospel uses for repentance, which is metanoia, a change of mind that turns and goes the other way. Judas felt the full weight of what he had done. What he did not do was turn round.

And his confession is theologically flawless. I have sinned by betraying innocent blood. He names the act, calls it sin, uses the first person, and declares the victim innocent — which is more than Caiaphas said, more than Pilate managed, and more than the crowd would allow. If words could save a man, these words would have done it.

He said them to the wrong people. That is the tragedy of the verse. Fifty yards away was the only man in Jerusalem who could have done anything with that sentence, and Judas took it to a committee of priests, who gave him the answer committees give: What is that to us? See to it yourself. They had used him, paid him, and were finished with him, and they tell him his conscience is his own business.

Was Judas truly sorry? He felt remorse, and he confessed that he had betrayed innocent blood. But he did not turn to Christ. Paul distinguishes godly grief, which produces repentance, from worldly grief, which produces death (2 Cor 7:10). Peter’s tears led him back; Judas’s led him away. Jesus called him the son of destruction (John 17:12) and said it would have been better for him not to have been born (26:24). Judas was lost not because his sin was too great to forgive, but because he would not come to the one who forgives.

Watch that phrase, because Matthew is about to use it again. In twenty verses Pilate will wash his hands in front of the crowd and say see to it yourselves — the same formula, handed on from the priests to the governor and back to the people. Everybody in this chapter is trying to put the blood somewhere else. Judas tries to give the money back; the priests will not take it into the treasury; Pilate calls for a basin; the crowd shouts that they will have it on their own heads. Not one of them can get rid of it, because there is only one place that blood can actually go, and none of them will take it there.

verseByVerse.quote: And throwing down the pieces of silver into the temple, he departed, and he went and hanged himself. But the chief priests, taking the pieces of silver, said, "It is not lawful to put them into the treasury, since it is blood money."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judas throws the silver into the temple — perhaps toward the sanctuary — as a futile act of rejection. Then he hangs himself. His death is recorded without embellishment; Matthew's theological point is already made. The priests' scrupulous concern about the legal status of blood money is devastating irony: they will not defile the treasury with money used to purchase innocent blood, yet they have just condemned innocent blood to death. Their legal fastidiousness is hypocrisy at its most refined — straining out the gnat of treasury regulations while swallowing the camel of judicial murder. It is as clear a case of religion without conscience as the Gospels contain: the rulebook consulted over the accounting of the money, and never once over the murder it paid for.

"He went and hanged himself" is five words, and they collide with the only other account we have. Luke, reporting Peter's words in Acts, says of Judas that "falling headlong he burst open in the middle and all his bowels gushed out" (Acts 1:18) — and adds that Judas acquired a field with the reward of his wickedness, where Matthew says the priests bought it. Two deaths and two buyers, say the critics. In fact both pairs settle without strain.

Take the death first. The two statements are not rivals; they are the beginning and the end of one event. A man hangs himself, and the body stays where it hangs. Then something gives — the rope, the branch, or the hand of whoever finally cut him down — and the body falls. The traditional site is a cliff above the valley of Hinnom, which makes the fall a long one; and a corpse that has hung for a day or more in that climate does exactly what Luke describes when it strikes rock. Matthew tells you what Judas did to himself. Luke tells you what was found, and why the place got the name it did. Neither has to be corrected for the other to be true.

The field is simpler still. The money was legally Judas's — that is precisely the priests' problem, which is why they will not put it in the treasury and why they must spend it on his behalf rather than their own. A purchase made with a dead man's money, in a matter he set in motion, is naturally credited to him; we still speak that way about estates. Acts is not picturing Judas out inspecting land. It is saying what his thirty pieces of silver finally bought.

Is suicide the unforgivable sin? No. Judas’s death is recorded, not approved, and he was lost because he rejected Christ, not because of how he died. Scripture never makes suicide the one sin Christ cannot forgive, and the believer’s security rests on Christ’s grip, not on the state of his mind in his last moments (John 10:28–29; Rom 8:38–39). Anyone tempted to take his own life should speak to someone today, a friend, a pastor or a doctor, and look to the one who restored Peter.

And notice what the two accounts share, which is more striking than what divides them: a field in Jerusalem that everybody could point at, with a name in the local dialect that everybody knew — Akeldama, Field of Blood. Invented stories do not usually come with an address.

parallels.desc: the wages of a dog into the house of the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: So they took counsel and bought with them the potter's field as a burial place for strangers. Therefore that field has been called the Field of Blood to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They will not put the money in the treasury and they cannot give it back, so they spend it — and the committee's solution is a burial ground for foreigners. Jerusalem at festival time was full of pilgrims from across the empire, and some of them died there; a plot for strangers was a genuine civic need, and buying one was a respectable use of awkward funds. They have found a way to be charitable with the price of a man's life.

A potter's field was worked-out ground — clay quarried until the soil was useless, littered with the broken pots that failed on the wheel. Nothing would grow there. It was cheap because it was finished.

So the thirty pieces buy a piece of exhausted earth full of smashed pottery, to bury foreigners with no family to claim them. And within a few years the message the priests were protecting the treasury from would be carried by Jewish believers to exactly those foreigners — to Cyrene and Rome and Ethiopia and Asia — and the men buried in that field as nobodies were the very sort of people the Son of God had just died for.

Then Matthew's aside: therefore that field has been called the Field of Blood to this day. He is writing decades after the event, in a city where the place still had the name, and where anybody reading his account could walk out and look at it. Luke gives the Aramaic — Akeldama (Acts 1:19). The priests bought a plot to keep their books clean, and instead they erected a permanent public monument to what they had done, with a name attached that no one could scrub off.

They were careful men, and it is worth noticing what carefulness achieved here. They protected the treasury and named a graveyard after their own crime.

And the reasoning that got them there is one Matthew has shown us before. Twelve chapters earlier Jesus had exposed the trick by which a man could declare his money dedicated to God and thereby avoid supporting his own parents — so for the sake of your tradition you have made void the word of God (15:5-6). The mechanism is identical here. The silver is treated as the thing that has been defiled, and the men who paid it out are treated as untouched. Money can be unclean; the hand that spends it apparently cannot. It is possible to build an entire moral system that asks scrupulous questions about objects and no questions at all about the man holding them.
verseByVerse.note: A potter’s field was probably land used for digging clay. Acts calls it Akeldama, “Field of Blood.”

verseByVerse.quote: Then was fulfilled what had been spoken by the prophet Jeremiah, saying, "And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him on whom a price had been set by some of the sons of Israel, and they gave them for the potter's field, as the Lord directed me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
An honest reader with a reference Bible will stop here, and should. Matthew says this was spoken by the prophet Jeremiah, and then quotes something that reads much more like Zechariah — the thirty pieces of silver, weighed out as the price of a shepherd and thrown to the potter in the house of the LORD (Zech 11:12-13). Turn to Jeremiah for those words and you will not find them. What is going on?

Four explanations are offered and three of them are serious. A copyist's slip is possible but weakly supported. More likely is that Matthew is doing something Jewish writers did regularly: citing a composite of prophetic texts under the name of the more prominent prophet. And there is a genuine Jeremiah strand in the material — Jeremiah is the prophet of the potter (he is sent to watch a potter work in ch. 18, then buys an earthen flask and smashes it at the Potsherd Gate in ch. 19), and Jeremiah is the prophet who buys a field with weighed-out silver as a sign (ch. 32). The potter, the field, and the weighed silver all come from Jeremiah; the thirty pieces and the throwing into the house of the LORD come from Zechariah. Matthew has fused them and named the collection after the major prophet — and there is evidence that in some Jewish orderings Jeremiah stood first among the prophetic books, which would make his name a natural label for the whole scroll.

Now notice what Jeremiah 19 actually says, because it is more than a source for a word. Jeremiah is told to take the elders and priests out to the valley of Hinnom by the Potsherd Gate, smash a jar in front of them, and announce that because they have filled this place with the blood of innocents, it will be called no longer Topheth but the Valley of Slaughter, and they will bury in it until there is no room (Jer 19:1-6, 11).

A field of broken pottery. Priests and elders standing in it. Innocent blood. A burial ground. A new name for the place.
