They remembered. That is the astonishing sentence in these two verses, and it is at the expense of everybody who loved him. Jesus had predicted his resurrection plainly to the Twelve, three separate times, in the clearest possible terms; each time they had argued, misheard, or been afraid to ask. On this Saturday morning the disciples are behind locked doors with no expectation whatever, and the women are resting until the Sabbath is over, with spices ready to anoint a body that is going to stay where it is. Not one person who followed him is preparing for a resurrection. His enemies are, and they are the only ones who take the prediction seriously enough to act on it.

Their fear is a backhanded testimony and it is the second one in this chapter — Pilate's wife called him righteous, and now the council concedes that his words are dangerous even after his death. They call him that impostor in the same breath as they take precautions against his coming back. Nobody posts a guard on a fraud.

How does after three days fit a Friday death and a Sunday resurrection? In Jewish reckoning any part of a day counted as a day, so after three days and on the third day mean the same span (cf. Esth 4:16 with 5:1). The leaders themselves treat them as the same: they ask for the tomb to be guarded until the third day (v. 64).

There is something in that for a discouraged believer. If your grasp on the promises is poor this week — if you find you have forgotten what he said, or never quite believed it would apply to you — you are in the company of the eleven, not the council. Everything that happened on the third day happened while his own people had given up on it. The resurrection did not wait for anybody's faith to be in good order. Their expectation contributed nothing to it, and neither does ours.
verseByVerse.note: The day of Preparation was Friday, the day before the Sabbath.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore order the tomb to be made secure until the third day, lest his disciples go and steal him away and tell the people, 'He has risen from the dead,' and the last fraud will be worse than the first." Pilate said to them, "You have a guard of soldiers. Go, make it as secure as you can."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their request is precise and their reasoning is sound. Seal the tomb until the third day, in case the disciples steal the body and start a story — and the last fraud will be worse than the first. They are thinking like men who have handled public opinion before, and they are right that a stolen body would be unanswerable.

Pilate's reply is short and reads as though he has had enough of them: you have a guard of soldiers; go, make it as secure as you can. He has given them a crucifixion already; he is not going to argue about a graveyard.

So consider what is now in place around that tomb by Saturday afternoon. A rock chamber with a single entrance. A stone weighing a ton. A Roman seal, which was a cord across the stone fixed at both ends with clay bearing the imperial stamp, so that breaking it was a serious offence against the authority of Rome. And an armed guard, on duty, whose lives depended on nothing happening.

Every one of those measures was taken to prevent a fraudulent resurrection, and every one of them became, three days later, part of the evidence for a real one. The precautions eliminated the alternatives one by one. The disciples could not have moved the stone past a guard. The guard could not have slept through it and also known what happened. The seal could not be broken quietly. The theft theory the council invented on Sunday morning was refuted in advance by the arrangements the council made on Saturday.

It is the pattern of the whole chapter. Pilate wrote a mocking title and published the truth; the priests bought a field and named their own crime; the crowd called down blood on themselves and asked for the only thing that could save them; and now the council builds the strongest possible case for the resurrection while trying to prevent one. Men who set themselves against God do not merely fail. They are made to serve the thing they are resisting, and they hand in the work themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: So they went and made the tomb secure by sealing the stone and setting a guard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter closes with a sealed stone and armed men in front of it, and by every measure available to anyone alive on that Saturday evening, the story is over.

Count what has been settled. The teacher is dead, and a Roman execution detail does not make mistakes about that. The body is in a tomb belonging to a named man at a known address, wrapped and spiced. The disciples are scattered; the one who talked most is somewhere in the city with the memory of a rooster. The betrayer is dead by his own hand. The authorities have won completely and are, for the first time in three years, able to plan a week without him in it.

And there is a Sabbath here that nobody planned. The whole of Saturday passes in silence in all four Gospels — no narrative, no dialogue, nothing. The Son of God keeps the Sabbath in a grave, having said it is finished the evening before, exactly as the Creator rested on the seventh day when the work was done.

It is worth staying in this verse rather than hurrying to the next chapter, because a great deal of Christian life is lived on Saturday. The disaster has happened, the prayers were not answered, the stone is in place, and the promise about the third day — which was made, and made plainly — is remembered by nobody except the opposition. Everybody who loved him spent that day certain it was finished in the other sense.

They were wrong for one more night. Every arrangement made in this verse — the stone, the seal, the guard, the sheer administrative competence of it — was in place by Saturday evening, and by Sunday morning it was all still in place and the tomb was empty anyway. Nothing in the sealed grave was disturbed by human hands, and nothing in it held.

And there is a last irony to leave the chapter with. The soldiers posted here to make sure nothing happened are the only human beings on earth who will be present when it does. They are standing at the stone on Sunday morning when the earth shakes and the angel comes down, and they go into the city and report to the chief priests exactly what they saw (28:11). The men hired to prevent a resurrection story become its first eyewitnesses, and the council has to pay them to keep quiet. Nothing in this chapter that was set against him failed to end up serving him.
verseByVerse.note: A seal (a cord fixed with wax or clay) would show if the stone had been tampered with.

parallels.desc: the stone sealed over the lions’ den

27.theology: The atonement: the cross as the world’s turning point. Matthew 27 narrates the event that is the hinge of history. Reformed theology has always insisted on the objective reality of what happened at the cross: the wrath of God against sin was exhausted in the person of the Son; the legal debt of humanity was paid; the judgment that was ours was borne by him. This is not one theory among many — it is the heart of the apostolic proclamation. “Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures” (1 Cor 15:3). The tearing of the veil demonstrates it architecturally: the barrier is gone. The centurion’s confession demonstrates it personally: the cross reveals the Son of God. Every subsequent generation is invited to stand at the foot of the cross and make the centurion’s confession their own.
27.examples:
Then: The women who watched from a distance (v. 55), who followed him from Galilee, who served him, who would be the first to the tomb on Sunday morning — they stayed when the disciples fled. Love kept them at the cross when fear drove others away. The crucifixion was not the end of their faith; it was its most costly expression.

Now: The cross is the Christian’s only boast (Gal 6:14). Not our moral achievement, not our spiritual progress, not our theological sophistication — the cross of Christ crucified is the one thing on which salvation rests. Charles Spurgeon preached: “I have a great need for Christ; I have a great Christ for my need.” Matthew 27 is the ground of that confidence. The stone rolled over the tomb is the last attempt of human power to contain what cannot be contained.

28.title: He Is Risen — Go and Make Disciples
28.text: <sup>1</sup>Now after the Sabbath, toward the dawn of the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary went to see the tomb. <sup>2</sup>And behold, there was a great earthquake, for an angel of the Lord descended from heaven and came and rolled back the stone and sat on it. <sup>3</sup>His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing white as snow. <sup>4</sup>And for fear of him the guards trembled and became like dead men. <sup>5</sup>But the angel said to the women, “Do not be afraid, for I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified. <sup>6</sup>He is not here, for he has risen, as he said. Come, see the place where he lay. <sup>7</sup>Then go quickly and tell his disciples that he has risen from the dead, and behold, he is going before you to Galilee; there you will see him. See, I have told you.” <sup>8</sup>So they departed quickly from the tomb with fear and great joy, and ran to tell his disciples. <sup>9</sup>And behold, Jesus met them and said, “Greetings!” And they came up and took hold of his feet and worshiped him. <sup>10</sup>Then Jesus said to them, “Do not be afraid; go and tell my brothers to go to Galilee, and there they will see me.” <sup>11</sup>While they were going, behold, some of the guard went into the city and told the chief priests all that had taken place. <sup>12</sup>And when they had assembled with the elders and taken counsel, they gave a sufficient sum of money to the soldiers <sup>13</sup>and said, “Tell people, ‘His disciples came by night and stole him away while we were asleep.’ <sup>14</sup>And if this comes to the governor’s ears, we will satisfy him and keep you out of trouble.” <sup>15</sup>So they took the money and did as they were directed. And this story has been spread among the Jews to this day. <sup>16</sup>Now the eleven disciples went to Galilee, to the mountain to which Jesus had directed them. <sup>17</sup>And when they saw him they worshiped him, but some doubted. <sup>18</sup>And Jesus came and said to them, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. <sup>19</sup>Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, <sup>20</sup>teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age.”
28.overview:
The Gospel of Matthew ends not with a conclusion but with a commission. The resurrection of Jesus is announced by an angel, confirmed by the empty tomb, and experienced in a personal encounter — the women grasp his feet and worship. Then comes the mountain in Galilee: the eleven, some worshipping and some still doubting, gathered around the risen Lord. And from the mountain — the place where Moses received the law, where Jesus gave the Sermon, where Peter heard “listen to him” — the final and greatest declaration is made: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.”

The Great Commission is the Matthew bookend that closes the Emmanuel bracket. In chapter 1, an angel announced “they shall call his name Emmanuel — God with us.” In chapter 28, the risen Lord promises “I am with you always, to the end of the age.” Emmanuel is still with us — not in a manger, not on a cross, but in the risen, enthroned, all-authoritative presence of the Son of God who goes with his people to the ends of the earth. The Gospel does not end; it is sent. The reader is commissioned. Every disciple who has read these twenty-eight chapters is addressed by the last three verses.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — The Resurrection and the Great Commission
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At dawn on the first day the two Marys come to the tomb; there is an earthquake, an angel rolls back the stone and sits on it, and the guards collapse. The women are told he is risen as he said, invited to inspect the empty place, and sent to the disciples — and on the way the risen Jesus meets them himself and calls the men who deserted him his brothers. Meanwhile the guards report everything to the chief priests, who convene, pay them, and put out the story that the body was stolen. In Galilee the eleven meet him on a mountain, worship, and some waver; and he sends them to all nations with all authority and an unbroken promise.
verseByVerse.theology: The resurrection is the hinge of everything: without it the cross is a tragedy, with it the cross is the decisive act of redemption, declared effective and guaranteed. Note that the angel identifies the risen Lord as Jesus who was crucified — a perfect participle, a standing title. The resurrection does not cancel the cross; it vindicates it, and the marks stay. The commission then rests on a royal decree rather than on human enthusiasm: all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me is the ground of therefore go, and it is Daniel 7:14 fulfilled. Baptism is into one name, singular, held by three persons — the clearest Trinitarian sentence in the Synoptics.
verseByVerse.examples: Three things in this chapter are worth carrying away. First, the section Matthew alone records (vv. 11-15): the guards give the chief priests a complete eyewitness account, and the priests neither investigate nor go and look — they buy a story. Nobody pays a large sum to suppress a report he believes is nonsense, and the alibi they purchase destroys itself, since sleeping men cannot testify to what happened while they slept. It closes the thread opened at 12:39 — they demanded a sign, were promised the sign of Jonah, received it on the day he specified, and paid to have it denied. Evidence has never been the problem. Second, the word my brothers (v. 10), spoken over deserters before one of them had apologised. Third, the clause Matthew could have tidied away and did not: some doubted (v. 17). He commissioned waverers, and went with them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now after the Sabbath, toward the dawn of the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary went to see the tomb. And behold, there was a great earthquake, for an angel of the Lord descended from heaven and came and rolled back the stone and sat on it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The women who watched at the cross and sat opposite the burial return at the first possible moment — dawn on the first day. Their devotion is the thread connecting death and resurrection: the same faithful love that would not leave the cross arrives earliest at the tomb. The earthquake echoes the crucifixion's earthquake (27:51) — divine power shaking the earth at both death and resurrection. The angel rolls back the stone not to let Jesus out (he is already risen, v.6) but to let the witnesses in. The stone is moved for the women, not for Jesus. The stone was moved as a declaration to human witnesses, not out of any necessity for the risen Lord, who would that same evening come into a room whose doors were locked (Jn 20:19).

This is the point at which a reader comparing the four Gospels usually stops, because no episode in Scripture is more often produced as proof that they contradict one another. The differences are real and should be stated plainly rather than hurried past. When did the women come? John says "while it was still dark" (Jn 20:1); Mark says "when the sun had risen" (Mk 16:2). How many came? Matthew names two Marys; Mark names three; Luke speaks of the women who had followed from Galilee; John mentions only Mary Magdalene. How many angels? Matthew has one, sitting on the stone; Mark a young man inside the tomb; Luke two men; John two angels.

Take them in order. The hour is the easiest: dawn is not a moment but a process, and a party that sets out in the dark arrives as the sun is coming up. Both sentences describe one walk, and anyone who has made an early start knows it. The number of women is settled by John himself, and rather beautifully — his Mary, apparently alone, runs to Peter and says, "we do not know where they have laid him" (Jn 20:2). We. John knew perfectly well she had company; he simply followed the one he meant to write about. None of the four lists claims to be complete, and a writer who names two has not denied a third. The angels work the same way: where there are two, there is certainly one, and an account that reports the one who spoke has not contradicted an account that counts the company. Matthew and Mark name the speaker; Luke and John count the room.

But there is something better to see here than a set of answers. Differences of exactly this kind are the fingerprint of independent witnesses rather than of collusion. Four statements agreeing word for word would prove the witnesses had conferred; four that vary in the details and converge on the substance are what honest testimony has always looked like, in any court in any century. And converge they do, on every point that matters: the stone was moved, the tomb was empty, heaven announced it, the Lord was alive, and the women were there first.

That last detail is worth pausing on, because no one inventing this story would have written it. In that world a woman's testimony carried little weight in a legal proceeding, and Josephus states the disqualification without embarrassment. A movement fabricating a resurrection would have put its most credible men at the tomb and left them there. Instead all four accounts hand the first news of the empty tomb, and the first sight of the risen Christ, to the very witnesses their own culture was most inclined to dismiss — for the plain reason that this is how it happened. The Gospels report it not because it was persuasive but because it was true; and God, who chose what is low and despised to shame the strong, evidently thought it fitting that the first people on earth to know were the ones who had refused to leave the cross.
verseByVerse.note: The first day of the week is Sunday.

verseByVerse.quote: His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing white as snow. And for fear of him the guards trembled and became like dead men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Matthew describes the angel in two phrases and both are borrowed. His appearance was like lightning — the same image this Gospel used four chapters earlier for the coming of the Son of Man, visible from east to west (24:27). And his clothing white as snow is the wardrobe of Daniel's throne room, where the Ancient of Days takes his seat and his clothing is white as snow (Dan 7:9). The messenger is dressed in the livery of the court he came from.

Then the guards, and Matthew allows himself one flash of irony in an otherwise unornamented account. These are professional soldiers. Sleeping on watch or deserting a post carried the death penalty in the Roman army; men in that trade were not easily frightened, and they had spent the night at a grave without incident. For fear of him the guards trembled and became like dead men.

Read the sentence again and notice what it does. There were dead men at that tomb on Sunday morning, and they were the ones guarding it. The man they had been posted to keep in was up and out and gone; the soldiers were flat on the ground and unable to move. The whole arrangement of that hillside had been reversed while nobody was looking.

And this is only a servant. Whatever knocked those men down was not the glory of Christ but the reflected brightness of a creature sent to open a door — and it emptied the strength out of trained soldiers in a second. Matthew has shown his readers the other thing once, on a mountain, when the face shone like the sun and three men fell on their faces and had to be touched before they could get up (17:2, 6-7).

One honest observation before leaving these verses, because it is easily missed and it matters. Nobody saw the resurrection. There is no account anywhere in Scripture of the moment itself — no description of the body stirring, no witness inside the chamber. The stone is rolled back and the tomb is already empty; the angel does not let him out, he lets the witnesses in. Even the guards, who were closer than anyone, saw only the aftermath. The one event on which everything depends took place in the dark, unobserved, between God and God.

parallels.desc: his face like the appearance of lightning

verseByVerse.quote: But the angel said to the women, "Do not be afraid, for I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified. He is not here, for he has risen, as he said. Come, see the place where he lay."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first thing said on the first Easter morning is do not be afraid, and the striking thing is who it is said to. The soldiers are lying on the ground in a state of collapse and the angel does not address them at all. He turns to the women. The same glory that flattened the guards is accompanied, for these two, by a word telling them they need not be frightened of it.

Then: I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified. The Greek is a perfect participle — the crucified one — a completed action with a standing result. It has become a name. He is risen, glorified, and vindicated, and heaven's own way of identifying him on resurrection morning is still by the worst thing that ever happened to him. The resurrection does not cancel the cross or tidy it away; it vindicates it. When John is given a sight of the throne room he sees a Lamb standing as though it had been slain (Rev 5:6). The marks stay.

He has risen, as he said. Five words carrying an enormous weight, because he had said it, plainly, three separate times — after Peter's confession (16:21), gathering in Galilee (17:22-23), and on the road up to Jerusalem (20:19) — and every time it had gone past them. They argued, or did not understand, or were afraid to ask. The only people in Jerusalem who had taken the prediction seriously enough to act on it were the chief priests, who posted the guard now lying in the grass.

So the angel's small clause is a verdict on everything else he ever said. If this prediction held, they all hold. The kingdom belongs to the poor in spirit; the meek will inherit the earth; his words will not pass away; whoever loses his life for his sake will find it. Every one of those is underwritten by the empty shelf of rock the angel is pointing at.

And then, remarkably: come, see the place where he lay. They are invited to inspect. Not to feel something, not to accept a report, but to walk in and look at the slab and satisfy themselves. Christianity has never asked to be believed on the strength of an atmosphere. It rests on a claim about an event, at an address, on a datable morning, of the kind that could have been destroyed at any time by the production of a body — and the invitation to check was issued by heaven before it was ever issued by the church.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then go quickly and tell his disciples that he has risen from the dead, and behold, he is going before you to Galilee; there you will see him. See, I have told you." So they departed quickly from the tomb with fear and great joy, and ran to tell his disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The message they are given has two halves, and the second one had been spoken before. He is going before you to Galilee. Turn back two chapters and there it is, from his own mouth on the way to Gethsemane: after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee (26:32).

And look at what he said just before, on the same walk: this night you will all fall away. He announced the reunion in the same breath as the desertion. The arrangement to meet them in Galilee was made while they were still promising they would never leave him, and it was not cancelled when they did. He had booked the meeting on the far side of a failure he had already predicted.

Notice also the destination. Not the temple, where he had taught; not the upper room; not the Mount of Olives. Galilee — the northern province, the working country, where they had boats and families and a lake and where every one of them had been called off an ordinary job in the first place. The risen Lord's first appointment with his church is at the place they started from, and he gets there ahead of them.

They departed quickly from the tomb with fear and great joy. Both at once, and nobody who has received overwhelming news will find that strange. Fear on its own would have sent them home; joy on its own would not have been honest, because the ground had just moved under everything they understood about how the world works. Matthew gives us two women running through the half-light carrying the two emotions together, and running is the detail that persuades.

And consider who is doing the running. They are carrying the first Christian message ever delivered, they are carrying it under angelic commission, and they are carrying it to the apostles. Before there was a church, before Pentecost, before a word of the New Testament existed, the resurrection was preached — by two women, to eleven men who did not believe them.

parallels.desc: I will go before you to Galilee

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, Jesus met them and said, "Greetings!" And they came up and took hold of his feet and worshiped him. Then Jesus said to them, "Do not be afraid; go and tell my brothers to go to Galilee, and there they will see me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The risen Jesus meets the women before they reach the disciples — a gracious appearing to those who were faithful first. "Greetings" (chairete) — literally "rejoice" — the first word of the risen Christ is joy. They take hold of his feet: he is physically present, bodily risen, not a ghost or a vision. They worship him — the Greek proskuneo is the word for prostrate homage, and here it is plainly worship. Jesus calls the disciples "my brothers" — restoring the relational bond severed by their betrayal and flight. He does not call them "my disciples" or "the eleven" but brothers, signaling that the failure of Gethsemane and Golgotha has not permanently defined the relationship. Resurrection is the word of forgiveness and restoration.

Do not read past that word "brothers" too quickly, because of everyone this book has followed, the men it names here had earned something other than a brotherly greeting. The last time we saw them they were running. One had sworn, with oaths, that he never knew the man now standing in front of the women (26:74); the rest had promised to die with him and then vanished into the dark (26:56). By any reckoning the risen Christ had grounds to send a different message — a summons, a rebuke, a probation to be worked through before the relationship could be considered repaired. He sends none of that. Before they have apologized, before Peter has wept his way back, before a single word of theirs reaches him, the first thing the risen Lord calls the men who abandoned him is my brothers.

But Jesus told Mary Magdalene, Do not cling to me (John 20:17). He was not forbidding all touch; he let these women hold his feet and invited Thomas to touch his wounds (John 20:27). He was telling Mary not to hold on to him as if the old way of being with him had simply returned, because he was going to the Father. Both accounts make the same point: the risen body was real.

If you are a Christian who has failed him badly — who went quiet when you should have spoken, who denied by your silence what you would not deny with your mouth, who ran when it cost something to stay — this is the sentence to take home. The resurrection did not only defeat death; it reached back and gathered up the men who had let him down, and it named them family before they had done anything to deserve the name. Your failure, real as it is, has not been given the power to define what he calls you. He calls you brother. That is where restoration starts — not with your climb back to him, but with his word over you while you are still ashamed to lift your head.

parallels.desc: not ashamed to call them brothers

verseByVerse.quote: While they were going, behold, some of the guard went into the city and told the chief priests all that had taken place. And when they had assembled with the elders and taken counsel, they gave a sufficient sum of money to the soldiers,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Matthew alone tells us what happened to the guards, and the first detail is the one to catch. They do not report to Pilate. Their commanding authority was Roman, and a soldier who has an incident on watch reports to his own officer — but these men had been seconded to the chief priests, and it is to the chief priests that they go. They know who has an interest in the story and who will pay to shape it.

And Matthew says they told them all that had taken place. Take the force of that. Professional witnesses, with no stake in the outcome and every reason to keep quiet about a post they had failed to hold, gave the religious leadership of Israel a complete eyewitness account of an earthquake, an angel, a rolled-away stone and an empty grave. For a few hours on that Sunday morning the best-informed men in Jerusalem about the resurrection of Jesus Christ were the men who had condemned him.

What they do with it is the last act of the story. They call an emergency session — the chief priests assembling with the elders on the morning after Passover — and they take a decision, and the decision is money. Matthew's phrase is a sufficient sum, which is to say enough to be persuasive. They do not investigate. They do not go and look, though the tomb is a short walk away and they know exactly where it is. They buy a story.

And it is worth stating what their willingness to pay concedes. Nobody spends a large sum suppressing a report he believes to be nonsense. If the priests had thought the guards were lying or drunk or covering an embarrassment, the answer was to say so publicly and let the matter die. The bribe is an admission that the testimony was credible and that they could not answer it.

Which closes a thread this Gospel opened long before. Twice they had come demanding a sign from heaven, and twice he had refused them everything except one — the sign of Jonah, three days and three nights, a man coming up out of the earth (12:39-40; 16:4). They asked for a sign; they were promised exactly this one; it was delivered on the day and hour he specified, attested by their own guards, and reported to them before breakfast. And they took counsel and paid to have it denied. The problem was never the evidence, and this chapter is the proof of it.

verseByVerse.quote: and said, "Tell people, 'His disciples came by night and stole him away while we were asleep.' And if this comes to the governor's ears, we will satisfy him and keep you out of trouble."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The story they buy is the weakest in the history of legal defence, and it fails on its own first clause. His disciples came by night and stole him away while we were asleep. Men who were asleep are the one class of witness who cannot testify to what happened. If they slept, they saw nothing; if they saw it, they were not asleep. The priests have paid good money for an alibi that destroys itself in the telling, which is what happens when a story is written to a required conclusion rather than from the facts.

And consider what the theft theory needs. It needs the eleven — the same men who ran from an arresting party in the dark on Thursday, whose leader had been broken by a servant girl by a fire — to have crossed the city at night, overpowered or crept past an armed Roman guard, broken an imperial seal that carried the death penalty, and moved a stone of a ton or more uphill in its channel without waking anyone. It needs them to do this on the strength of a hope that not one of them held, since none of them was expecting a resurrection.

There is a further detail the theory never accounts for, and John supplies it: the grave clothes were still lying there, and the cloth that had been round his head was folded up in a place by itself (Jn 20:6-7). Body-snatchers working against the clock in enemy territory take the body as it lies. They do not stop to unwrap seventy-five pounds of spiced linen and fold the napkin.

Then the sweetener: if this comes to the governor's ears, we will satisfy him and keep you out of trouble. That is not a courtesy. Sleeping on watch was a capital offence in the Roman army, and the priests are offering to save these men's lives — which tells you both how much they wanted the story and how much the soldiers needed the protection.

And the last irony of Matthew's Gospel belongs to the council. The day before, they had gone to Pilate and called Jesus that impostor, and asked for a guard in case his followers should deceive the people (27:63-64). They are now paying soldiers to lie, arranging to manage the governor, and putting a fabricated story into public circulation. The deception they came to prevent is the one they end up committing, and they commit it knowingly, having heard the truth first.
verseByVerse.note: A Roman soldier who slept on watch could be punished with death.

parallels.desc: the guards executed after Peter’s escape

verseByVerse.quote: So they took the money and did as they were directed. And this story has been spread among the Jews to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This story has been spread among the Jews to this day. Matthew is writing decades after the morning he is describing, and he tells us the counter-story is still in circulation. He is not reporting a rumour that died; he is answering one his readers have heard. A century later Justin Martyr was still complaining that the same explanation was being actively circulated, which means it outlived everyone who was there.

And that hostile persistence has handed the church something no friendly witness could have given it. Look carefully at what the opposition said, because of what they never said. They did not say the women went to the wrong tomb. They did not say he had not really died. They did not say the whole thing was a Galilean fantasy and there was no grave to speak of. They said the disciples took the body.

That is a concession, and it is the earliest one on record. The first anti-Christian explanation in existence begins by granting that the tomb was empty on Sunday morning and then argues about how it got that way. Friend and enemy agreed on the fact and differed only on the cause — which is precisely the position the church has been in ever since.

Consider too what the authorities did not do, having every reason and every resource to do it. The one action that would have ended the Christian movement in a week was to produce the body. They had the manpower, the motive, the jurisdiction, and the address; and when the apostles began preaching the resurrection in that same city seven weeks later, and thousands believed, the leadership arrested them, threatened them, flogged them, and killed one of them — and never once walked the half mile to the tomb and settled the matter. The cheapest refutation in history was available and was never used.

And weigh the two accounts against each other one last time. One asks you to believe that God raised his Son from the dead. The other asks you to believe that a dozen frightened men pulled off a burglary they had no reason to attempt, kept the secret perfectly for the rest of their lives, and then went to prison, exile and execution — each of them in a position to end his own suffering by producing a body he had buried himself, and not one of them ever doing it. People will die for a lie they believe. Nobody dies for a lie he personally manufactured.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the eleven disciples went to Galilee, to the mountain to which Jesus had directed them. And when they saw him, they worshiped him, but some doubted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Galilee appearance brings the disciples full circle — back to the region where they were first called, where the Sermon on the Mount was delivered, where most of the ministry happened. The mountain setting recalls the Transfiguration (17:1–9) and the Beatitudes (5:1). When they see him, they worship — and "some doubted." Matthew does not smooth over the doubt; it is part of the honest record. The word need not mean the doubt of unbelief; it can carry the sense of hesitating, of being in two minds, and some were very likely paralysed by the sheer impossibility of what was standing in front of them. Either way the point stands: the Great Commission is handed to a group that includes waverers. He does not wait for perfect faith before commissioning his church; he meets them in their awestruck, half-persuaded state and sends them anyway.

That short clause — "but some doubted" — is worth more to an honest believer than a hundred triumphant ones, so do not let the harmonizing that follows crowd it out. Here is the risen Christ, visible, standing on the mountain, near enough to touch; and even now, in the best conditions faith has ever been offered, some of the eleven wavered. Matthew could have tidied it away. He left it in, because it is true, and because you needed to see it. Notice what Jesus does with their doubt: he does not quarantine the doubters until they are sure, does not divide the group into the qualified and the disqualified, does not withhold the commission from the ones still wrestling. He gives the whole company — worshippers and waverers together — the same all-authority and the same marching orders, and the same promise to be with them to the end. If you have assumed that your doubt shuts you out of usefulness, that God can only send people whose faith never trembles, look again at who is standing on that mountain. He commissioned doubters. He sent them out to disciple the nations while some of them were still not certain what they were looking at — and he went with them. Faith that worships with a tremor in it is faith he can use, and has used, from that morning to this.

A reader who lines up the four Gospels will ask a fair question here: did the risen Jesus appear in Galilee, as Matthew says, or in and around Jerusalem, as Luke and John describe? Skeptics press it as a flat contradiction. But the accounts do not compete; they select. The appearances stretched across forty days (Acts 1:3), and they moved with the disciples. On the first day the Lord showed himself in and near Jerusalem — to the women, to Mary at the tomb, to the two walking to Emmaus, to the ten behind locked doors. Then, exactly as both the angel and Jesus had commanded (vv. 7, 10), the disciples travelled north to Galilee, where this mountain meeting and the Great Commission took place, along with the lakeside breakfast of John 21 and, most likely, the appearance to more than five hundred at once (1 Cor 15:6). Afterward they returned to Jerusalem, and from the Mount of Olives he ascended (Luke 24:50-51; Acts 1:9-12). Each evangelist tells the part that serves his purpose: Luke, whose whole Gospel drives toward Jerusalem, keeps his lens there; Matthew, who began with "Galilee of the Gentiles" (4:15) and whose last word is a mission to all nations, climbs one more Galilean mountain to send the church out from it. None of them claims to tell everything — John says the world could not hold the books (John 21:25). Different windows onto the same forty days, not different stories.

parallels.desc: more than five hundred at one time

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus came and said to them, "All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"All authority in heaven and on earth" — this is Daniel 7:14 fulfilled: the Son of Man receives dominion, glory, and a kingdom from the Ancient of Days. The authority is comprehensive (heaven and earth), current (given — the resurrection and exaltation have already accomplished this), and the basis for the commission ("therefore go"). The Great Commission flows from the reality of Christ's universal lordship, not from human enthusiasm. Baptism in the Trinitarian name — one name with three distinct persons — is the clearest Trinitarian formula in the Synoptic Gospels. To be baptized into this name is to be brought into the life and covenant of the triune God. It is the richest theological sentence in any commission he ever gave.

One difficulty must be faced here, because a reader who moves on into Acts will meet it within two chapters. Jesus commands baptism "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" — yet every baptism in Acts that names a name is done "in the name of Jesus Christ" or "of the Lord Jesus" (Acts 2:38; 8:16; 10:48; 19:5). Did the apostles disobey their Lord in the very first week? Some have concluded that these words of Jesus were composed later by the church; others, in the opposite direction, hold that only the words "in the name of Jesus" may lawfully be spoken over the water, and rebaptize those who were baptized with the triune name.

Both miss what Luke is doing. He is not recording a liturgy; he is telling you whose baptism it was. That was a live question in a city full of washings — proselyte baths for Gentile converts, the ritual immersions of the devout, and John's baptism of repentance, which was not the same thing. When Paul meets men at Ephesus who had received John's baptism, the issue he settles is precisely that one, and Luke reports the outcome in the same shorthand: they were baptized "in the name of the Lord Jesus" (Acts 19:1-5). The phrase distinguishes Christian baptism from every rival; it is not a set of syllables required at the font. And "in the name of" was ordinary legal and commercial language for transfer into someone's ownership — a sum paid into a man's name became his. To be baptized into the name of Jesus is to be handed over to him and marked as his.

Nor are the two expressions in any competition, once you notice what Jesus actually said. It is "in the name" — singular — "of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit": one name, three persons, which is the whole doctrine of the Trinity compressed into a preposition and a definite article. There is no belonging to the Son that is not also belonging to the Father who sent him and the Spirit who applies his work. To be baptized into Christ is to be baptized into the triune God, which is exactly why Luke's shorthand and Matthew's fuller wording can sit side by side without strain.

Who should be baptized? Christians who baptize infants appeal to the household baptisms in Acts (16:15, 33), to the link Paul draws between baptism and circumcision (Col 2:11–12), and to the covenant sign given to Abraham’s children (Gen 17). The more likely reading is that baptism is for disciples. The command runs in order: make disciples, baptize them, teach them. In Acts, those baptized are those who received the word (Acts 2:41), and no baptism in the New Testament is said to be of an infant.

And is this commission for every Christian? Yes. The promise that follows reaches to the end of the age, so the command does too. The apostles’ foundational role has ended, but the whole church is sent, and every believer has a share, by going, sending, praying and teaching.

As for the suggestion that these words were added later: the manuscripts have been faced candidly wherever they genuinely divide — the close of the Lord's Prayer (6:13), the verse about prayer and fasting (17:21), verse 11 of chapter 18, verse 14 of chapter 23. This is not such a case. Every Greek manuscript of Matthew contains the triune name; not one lacks it. So if you were baptized with these words, or with the name of Jesus, let no one unsettle you. What matters is not which formula was pronounced over you but the God into whose name you were given.
verseByVerse.note: Disciples of every nation are to be baptized into the one name of Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

parallels.desc: to the end of the earth
all peoples, nations and languages should serve him

verseByVerse.quote: "teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The commission ends with the part most often left off it. Teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you — and each of those words is doing work. Not teaching them what he taught, but teaching them to observe; the verb is tereo, to keep, to guard, to put into practice. And not some of it, but all. Disciple-making, on this definition, is not the transfer of information from one head to another. It is finished when somebody is living differently.

Notice that Matthew has spent his whole Gospel supplying the curriculum. Five great blocks of teaching — the Sermon on the Mount, the mission charge, the parables of the kingdom, the discourse on life together, and the Olivet discourse — are built into this book on purpose, each closed with the same formula. The last command is to teach everything he commanded, and the reader has been holding the manual the entire time.

Then the last sentence of the Gospel, and it answers the first chapter. At 1:23 Matthew quoted Isaiah over the child in the womb: they shall call his name Immanuel, which means, God with us. Here at the end, on a hillside in Galilee, the last words out of his mouth are I am with you always, to the end of the age. The book opens with a name that means God with us and closes with the man himself saying it in the first person. Everything in between is the demonstration.

Take the words one at a time, because they are chosen. I am — present tense, not a promise about the future but a statement about now. With you — not watching from a distance, not waiting at the destination. Always is literally all the days: not a vague perpetual arrangement but every individual day, one after another, counted out — including the dull ones, the humiliating ones, the days of ordinary work when nothing spiritual seems to be happening, and the day nobody wants to think about. And to the end of the age is the same phrase the disciples used when they asked him about the end (24:3), so the promise runs precisely as long as the mission does. There is no point at which the church is sent and he is not there.

Consider who is standing on that mountain receiving it. Eleven men, one place short of twelve. Every one of them had run. Their spokesman had denied him with oaths. Matthew has just told us that as they worshipped, some of them were still wavering. And it is to that company — deserters, a denier, and men not yet sure what they were looking at — that all authority in heaven and on earth is handed, with the nations for a parish and a promise of unbroken company.

And Matthew does not write an ascension. Mark's longer ending has him taken up, Luke has him carried into heaven, Acts has the cloud and the two men in white; Matthew ends with Jesus on the mountain, speaking, and simply stops. There is no departure scene because the last thing this Gospel wants in the reader's eye is Christ leaving. He is left standing there, mid-promise, with his people — which is exactly the situation the church has been in ever since, and the reason the book has no proper ending is that the story it tells has not finished. Immanuel. God with us. Still.

parallels.desc: I will not leave you as orphans

28.theology: The resurrection as the foundation of everything. Matthew 28 establishes the resurrection as the ground of mission, authority, and presence. Without the resurrection, the Great Commission has no basis (no authority), no confidence (no living Lord accompanying the missionaries), and no goal (no risen Christ to present to the nations). Reformed theology has always insisted that the resurrection is not a supplement to the cross but its necessary vindication: the cross without the resurrection is a tragedy; the resurrection without the cross is a mystery. Together they are the gospel: he died for our sins and was raised for our justification (Rom 4:25). The risen Christ on the Galilean mountain, commissioning doubting disciples with unlimited authority, is the culmination of the new genesis that began in Matthew 1:1. The biblos geneseos — the book of the new beginning — ends with the world opened to the word of the King.
28.examples:
Then: Eleven ordinary men — fishermen, a tax collector, a zealot — were commissioned to disciple all nations. They had no army, no empire, no money, no social status. They had a risen Lord with all authority and a promise of presence. Within a generation the gospel had reached Rome. Within three centuries the Roman Empire had been transformed. The mustard seed had become the tree.

Now: The Great Commission has not been rescinded or transferred. Every church, every believer, every generation stands in the Galilean company — some worshipping, some doubting, all commissioned. The command is threefold: go, baptize, teach. The ground is unchanging: all authority belongs to the risen Christ. The promise is absolute: I am with you always. This is enough. It has always been enough. Go.
